title: Demographic and Comorbidity Characteristics of U.S. Veterans in a Retrospective Descriptive Matched Cohort Study Addressing Problematic Gambling
abstract: Abstract Introduction Problematic gambling is an increasing public health concern that also affects U.S. Veterans. Problematic gambling in Veterans correlates with several other factors, including socio-economic issues like homelessness and legal problems, and mental health issues like post-traumatic stress disorder, and suicide attempt. Our objective was to analyze differences between U.S. Veterans experiencing problematic gambling compared to similar U.S. Veterans who did not, according to diagnostic codes. Materials and Methods Electronic health records from the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) for health care encounters between 2016-01-01 and 2024-12-31 served as data for this study. We performed a one-to-one match on age, race, ethnicity, gender, and VA station for 775 Veterans diagnosed with problematic gambling by International Classification of Diseases 10 th edition codes, to Veterans not receiving one of the diagnostic codes relevant to gambling. We then compared comorbidity diagnoses, marital status, and VA care encounters, applying chi-squared and t-test analyses. Results There were many statistically significant differences in care use, marital status, and comorbidities. Veterans with problematic gambling were more likely to experience other substance abuse, including opioid use disorder (22.5% vs 8.4%) and alcohol use disorder (56.3% vs 25.9%). Veterans with problematic gambling were also more likely to experience mental illness, including major depressive disorder (64.9% vs 46.7%), post-traumatic stress disorder (50.8% vs 43.1%), and suicide attempt (5.3% vs 3.0%), and socio-economic issues, including economic hardship (28.7% vs 16.3%), homelessness (33.9% vs 14.8%), legal problems (13.4% vs 6.8%) and social/family problems (53.6% vs 46.5%). Veterans experiencing problematic gambling also were less likely to be married and received more VA outpatient care. Conclusions The findings suggest that problematic gambling in Veterans correlates with worse outcomes when comparing similar Veterans receiving care through the same facilities. It is feasible to screen for problematic gambling in primary care encounters, however the extent of screening in VA care is unknown. Screening for problematic gambling in VA primary care may enable providers to assist patients experiencing problematic gambling to find directed care.

title: A Common CD36 Variant and the Genetic Landscape of Dilated Cardiomyopathy in Individuals of African Ancestry.
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is a major cause of heart failure that disproportionately affects individuals of predominantly African ancestry, among whom familial clustering of disease is more pronounced relative to those of predominantly European ancestry. Truncating variants in TTN, which encodes the sarcomeric protein titin, are the most common established monogenic cause of DCM. A common CD36 nonsense variant enriched among individuals of African ancestry has also been shown to account for a substantial burden of DCM.
OBJECTIVE: To compare the contribution of a CD36 nonsense variant to DCM risk with that of truncating variants in TTN and pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in other established genes for DCM.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: Multicohort genetic association study including participants of African and European ancestry with exome or genome sequence data and DCM case status from the following 4 US datasets: All of Us Research Program (recruitment: 2017-present; last follow-up: August 27, 2024), Million Veteran Program (recruitment: 2011-present; last follow-up: September 30, 2024), Penn Medicine Biobank (recruitment: 2013-present; last follow-up: November 14, 2022), and the DCM Precision Medicine Study (recruitment: 2016-2020; last follow-up: March 15, 2020).
EXPOSURE: Carrier status for TTN truncating variants, pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in 11 high-confidence genes for DCM, and the nonsense variant CD36 Y325* (0, 1, or 2 copies).
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Risk of DCM, prevalence of variant carriers among DCM cases, and population attributable fraction of DCM.
RESULTS: Among 82 623 individuals of predominantly African ancestry across 4 cohorts, the mean age was 53.4 years (SD, 13.9 years), 47 124 were male, and 1316 had DCM. Individuals who were homozygous for the CD36 Y325* risk allele had a higher risk of DCM (odds ratio [OR], 4.8; 95% CI, 3.1-7.3) as did those who were heterozygous (OR, 1.4; 95% CI, 1.2-1.7). TTN truncating variants also conferred an elevated risk of DCM in participants of African ancestry (OR, 8.5; 95% CI, 5.5-13.0). Among 1316 individuals of African ancestry classified as DCM cases, 33 (2.5%) were homozygous for CD36, 56 (4.3%) had TTN truncating variants, and 16 (1.2%) had pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in other high-confidence genes for DCM. In population-level analyses incorporating both heterozygous and homozygous CD36 Y325* carriers, the population attributable fraction for CD36 (9.0% [6.2% for heterozygous carriers and 2.8% for homozygous carriers]) surpassed the population attributable fraction for TTN truncating variants (3.7%).
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In 4 US cohorts, an ancestry-specific CD36 variant contributed more to DCM burden among individuals of African ancestry than established genes for DCM, including TTN truncating variants that are typically considered the most common genetic cause. These findings reshape the known genetic architecture of DCM in individuals of African ancestry and highlight the importance of representation in genomic research.

title: Sociobehavioral Comorbidities and Outcomes After Colectomy in a National United States Veteran Cohort.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the independent association between sociobehavioral comorbidities (SBCs) and complications after colectomies in a national Veteran cohort.
BACKGROUND: SBCs are determinants of health outcomes, and Veterans represent a high-vulnerability population. However, the relationship of SBCs with postoperative complications remains understudied, and current surgical risk models underestimate risk among patients with significant SBC burden.
METHODS: We conducted an observational study of Veterans undergoing elective colectomy included in the Veterans Affairs Surgical Quality Improvement Program (VASQIP). Structured data from the Veteran Health Administration Corporate Data Warehouse were used to identify 6 SBC phenotypes (mental health disorder, suicide risk, substance use, social isolation, housing instability, and food insecurity) across 3 preoperative ascertainment windows: ≤90 days, ≤365 days, and lifetime. The outcome was any 30-day VASQIP-defined postoperative complication. Multilevel logistic regression estimated associations between SBCs and complications.
RESULTS: Among 38,188 Veterans undergoing colectomy between 2009 and 2025, the median age was 66 years; 5% were female; 30% were non-white; and 48% had cancer. Mental health disorder, social isolation, or substance use were each associated with an 8%-40% increase in the odds of a complication across all ascertainment windows. Within the most proximal window, risk of complication increased as SBC burden increased: 16% increased odds with 1 SBC (aOR 1.16, 95% CI: 1.09-1.23) and 80% increased odds with 4-6 SBCs (aOR 1.80, 95% CI: 1.32-2.36).
CONCLUSIONS: In a national Veteran cohort, SBCs were associated with postoperative colectomy complications. The strongest associations were observed with SBCs ascertained within the 90-day window, and the odds increased in a dose-response relationship with increasing SBC burden.

title: Longitudinal Pain Profiles and Their Clinical and Genetic Correlates in 624,996 U.S. Veterans
abstract: Importance: Pain varies in its intensity and course, yet much of our understanding of pain is based on cross-sectional assessments or longitudinal studies of selected clinical populations. Routinely collected electronic health record data may enable characterization of longitudinal pain patterns at scale. Objective: To identify longitudinal pain profiles among U.S. Veterans and characterize their clinical and polygenic correlates. Design: Cohort study using electronic health record and genomic data from the Million Veteran Program, with up to 16 years of pain assessments collected between 2000 to 2025. Setting: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs health care system. Participants: Million Veteran Program participants assigned to African-like, Admixed American-like, East Asian-like, European-like, or South Asian-like genetically inferred ancestry groups who have at least three years of outpatient numeric rating scale pain records. Exposures: Outpatient pain ratings and polygenic scores for psychiatric, sleep, and substance use traits. Main Outcomes and Measures: Pain profiles were identified using Gaussian finite mixture modeling of pain intensity, directional change, and within-person variability. Profiles were characterized by pain, psychiatric and substance use diagnoses, opioid exposure, body mass index, and polygenic scores. Results: Among 624,996 participants (Mean [SD] age at first pain rating=53.4 [13.5] years; 568,833 [91.0%] male), 51,731,567 outpatient pain ratings were analyzed. Three profiles were identified: stable no pain, stable mild pain, and mild-to-moderate increasing pain. Compared with the stable no pain profile, the increasing pain profile had higher odds of chronic pain (OR=21.14 [95% CI: 18.96-23.57]), opioid use disorder (OR=9.32 [95% CI: 8.31-10.45]), opioid exposure (OR=8.61 [95% CI: 8.41-8.83]), major depressive disorder (OR=3.77 [95% CI: 3.67-3.87]), and posttraumatic stress disorder (OR=3.72 [95% CI: 3.61-3.84]). Associations were attenuated but remained after adjustment for mean pain severity. Polygenic scores for depression, insomnia, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, and tobacco use disorder were the most consistent predictors of increasing pain across the three largest genetically inferred ancestry groups. Conclusions and Relevance: Longitudinal modeling of routinely collected pain scores identified pain profiles associated with clinical burden and polygenic liability. These profiles captured clinically meaningful information beyond mean pain severity alone, highlighting the value of longitudinal pain phenotyping in electronic health record data. Key Points: Routinely collected pain scores can be used to characterize heterogeneity in the course of pain and factors associated with more burdensome pain patterns.

title: Interpretable deep learning maps spatial morphological phenotypes to HCC and LUAD survival.
abstract: The clinical adoption of deep learning in pathology is largely hindered by the "black box" nature of current models, which often obscure the biological basis of prognosis. Here, we introduce MorphX, an interpretable framework that predicts patient survival by explicitly decoding multi-scale morphological patterns from whole-slide images. Unlike conventional methods relying on latent features, MorphX fuses macro-scale tissue texture with micro-scale nuclear metrics to attribute risk to interpretable biological phenotypes. In a multi-center study spanning 1,067 patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), MorphX achieves concordance indices of 0.775-0.799 in discovery cohorts. Crucially, we derive eight distinct morphology-based biomarkers-driven by texture heterogeneity in necrotic regions, lymphocyte density, and nuclear shape-that demonstrate reproducible survival associations across independent cohorts, offering a granular resolution of tumor aggressiveness that transcends traditional histological grading. By translating opaque computational predictions into validated biological insights, MorphX supports trustworthy, transparent, artificial intelligence (AI)-driven precision oncology.

title: Trans-ancestry genome-wide association meta-analysis of gallstone disease
abstract: Abstract Gallstone disease is a highly prevalent and costly gastrointestinal disease. Yet, genetic variation in gallstone susceptibility and its implication in metabolic pathways remain to be explored. We report a trans-ancestry genome-wide association meta-analysis of gallstone disease including 100,856 cases and 1,596,602 controls in the UK Biobank, FinnGen, Biobank Japan, and Million Veteran Program. We identified 116 (59 novel) risk loci across meta-analysis and found replication in statistically compelling signals in the All of Us Research Program. A polygenic risk score constructed from trans-ancestry lead variants was positively associated with liver chemistry and alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency and negatively associated with total cholesterol and low-density lipoprotein levels among trans-ancestry and European ancestry groups in the Penn Medicine BioBank. Colocalization of risk loci with 44 traits and with expression quantitative trait loci from eight tissues yielded 321 and 110 significant colocalizations, respectively. These findings broaden our understanding of the genetic architecture of gallstone disease.

title: Where Women Veterans Seek Emergency Care: Patterns and Predictors of VA and Community Emergency Department Use.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Women using Veterans Health Administration (VA) facilities have nearly doubled over the past decade. Women Veterans have distinct emergency care needs across their lifespan; examining care setting (VA versus non-VA, hereafter Community Care) can inform service planning. Despite ongoing improvement efforts, there has not been a recent comprehensive, national assessment of emergency care utilization patterns among women Veterans.
OBJECTIVE: We sought to describe women Veterans' emergency department (ED) utilization across VA-provided and VA Community Care settings, identify predictors of setting, and compare patterns to that of men Veterans. DESIGN, PARTICIPANTS, MAIN MEASURES: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of VA enrollees with at least one ED visit (VA-provided or Community Care) from 10/2022 to-9/2023. Patient- and visit-level characteristics were derived from VA administrative data. Descriptive statistics compared characteristics by sex. Among women Veterans, logistic regression with generalized estimating equations identified predictors of receiving VA-provided versus Community Care ED care.
KEY RESULTS: Among 1.6 million Veterans with ED visits, most ED visits by women occurred at VA sites (60%). In adjusted models, women had higher odds of using VA EDs for low acuity (OR 1.62, 95% CI 1.59-1.64) and behavioral health conditions (OR 1.10, 95% CI 1.06-1.14). Racially and ethnically minoritized women had greater odds of using VA EDs than White women. VA ED use was less likely among women experiencing homelessness (OR 0.90, 95% CI 0.86-0.93), with emergency care-sensitive conditions (OR 0.61, 95% CI 0.60-0.63), or living farther from VA EDs.
CONCLUSIONS: While a majority of women Veterans-particularly those with complex medical, mental health, and social needs-continue to rely on VA EDs for care, two-fifths utilize Community Care EDs with geographic distance and visit acuity being drivers. Findings underscore the need to improve care coordination and ensure that both VA and community ED providers are equipped to meet the diverse needs of women Veterans.

title: Abstract 7481: Resistant Hypertension in Male Veterans - Gaps in Secondary Workup and Guideline-Directed Therapy
abstract: Background: Resistant hypertension (RH) is uncontrolled blood pressure (BP) despite ≥ 3 antihypertensive agents including a diuretic, or controlled BP requiring ≥ 4 agents, affecting 8.5-20% of hypertensive U.S. adults. Veterans represent a high-risk population with significant medical and psychosocial comorbidities contributing to treatment resistance. Guideline-directed care emphasizes exclusion of pseudo-resistance [i.e., inaccurate measurements, white coat hypertension (WHTN), medication noncompliance] and evaluation for secondary causes, yet real-world implementation remains inconsistent. Methods: We identified veterans assigned to the resident-clinic with hypertension (HTN) and a most recent BP reading ≥140/90 mmHg on ≥ 4 antihypertensive agents. A retrospective chart review was performed to collect data on demographics, comorbidities, antihypertensive regimens, hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) use, number of medications, BMI, prior RH workup, and psychosocial factors. Results: All veterans were male with a mean age of 73.1 years (range 53-94). The cohort was 64.3% White, 28.6% Black, and 7.1% undetermined, with mean BMI 32.5 kg/m 2 . Blood pressure remained poorly controlled (systolic BP 117-226 mmHg; diastolic BP 62-102 mmHg) despite polypharmacy: 75.0% were on 4 agents and 25.0% on ≥ 5 agents. HCTZ use was low (32.1%), and patients averaged 6.5 primary care visits over two years. Only 35.7% underwent any secondary HTN workup, with just 5 patients receiving testing beyond renin-aldosterone levels. Comorbidities included ischemic heart disease (28.6%), chronic kidney disease, (35.7%) hyperlipidemia (46.4%), interstitial lung disease (35.7%), malignancy (32.1%), autoimmune disease (10.7%), and heart failure (17.9%). Psychosocial burden was substantial as 50% had tobacco use history and 14.3% reported illicit drug use. Additional barriers included homelessness, cancer-related distress, family stressors, and psychiatric comorbidities (post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety, depression, bipolar disorder). Medication-related challenges included calcium-channel blocker-induced edema, hypokalemia and reported WHTN. Conclusions: Significant gaps exist in guideline-directed RH care among male veterans, including underuse of thiazide diuretics and incomplete secondary evaluation. High comorbidities and psychosocial burden likely contribute to persistent uncontrolled HTN. These findings support the need for standardized secondary workup protocols and multidisciplinary approaches addressing social determinants of health. This project represents an initial step in identifying patients who would benefit from systematic re-evaluation. Next steps include implementing a comprehensive secondary HTN workup and optimizing antihypertensive regimens per current guidelines.

title: Motivational interviewing delivered in groups enhances treatment attendance among homeless veterans with substance use disorders.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Veterans experiencing homelessness with substance use disorders (SUD) represent a large and clinically complex population within the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs. Group Motivational Interviewing (GMI) may offer a scalable approach to enhancing treatment attendance and examining substance use outcomes. This randomized controlled trial evaluated GMI compared to a Life Skills Education Group (LSEG) among homeless Veterans with SUD, most of whom had co-occurring psychiatric disorders.
METHODS: A total of 185 dually diagnosed homeless Veterans were randomized to four sessions of GMI or LSEG and followed for 6 months. Treatment attendance and substance use were primary outcomes of interest. Outcomes were analyzed at each follow-up using regression models appropriate to distributional characteristics, including negative binomial, log-normal, and two-part models.
RESULTS: At 6-month follow-up, GMI participants attended significantly more SUD treatment sessions (IRR = 1.84, p < 0.001), general mental health treatment sessions (IRR = 2.89, p < 0.001), and twelve-step meetings (IRR = 1.74, p = 0.001) compared to LSEG. No significant differences were observed between conditions on substance use outcomes, with the exception of higher peak drinking in GMI at 3 months (p = 0.04).
CONCLUSION: GMI significantly enhanced treatment attendance but did not reduce substance use relative to an educational control. These findings suggest that brief GMI may improve treatment engagement, but additional intervention components or longer follow-up may be needed to produce measurable substance use reductions among homeless Veterans with SUD.

title: MDMA-assisted therapy for veterans with comorbid posttraumatic stress disorder and alcohol use disorder: Clinical outcomes from the first open-label pilot trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Co-occurring posttraumatic stress disorder and alcohol use disorder (PTSD-AUD) are highly prevalent among U.S. Veterans and associated with greater symptom severity, functional impairment, and poorer outcomes than either disorder alone. Existing treatments demonstrate modest effectiveness, with persistent challenges in engagement, retention, and sustained improvement.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the feasibility, safety, tolerability, and preliminary clinical outcomes of investigational 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA)-assisted therapy for Veterans with comorbid PTSD-AUD.
METHODS: We conducted the first open-label trial of MDMA-assisted therapy in Veterans (N = 10) with PTSD-AUD. The intervention included 11 therapy sessions (three preparatory, two MDMA assisted therapy sessions, and six integration), followed by a 4-week follow-up. Primary outcomes were PTSD symptom severity and alcohol consumption, measured by the Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale for DSM-5 (CAPS-5) and Timeline Follow-Back (TLFB). Secondary outcomes assessed safety and tolerability. Exploratory outcomes included alcohol craving and substance misuse.
RESULTS: Recruitment and retention were strong with 90% of enrolled participants completing treatment. MDMA-assisted therapy was associated with significant reductions in PTSD symptoms (p = 0.006, d = 1.241). Descriptive reductions were observed in alcohol consumption, including a 31% reduction in drinks per drinking day and a 54% reduction in heavy drinking days, although these changes did not reach clinical significance. No serious adverse events were reported. Treatment-emergent adverse events were non-serious and consistent with expected acute MDMA effects under protocol monitoring. Substance-use measures did not indicate systematic increases in alcohol or other substance use; one participant reported an isolated recurrence of cocaine use.
CONCLUSIONS: Findings support the safety, feasibility, and tolerability of MDMA-assisted therapy and provide preliminary descriptive evidence of improvement in PTSD symptoms and alcohol-related outcomes. Larger randomized controlled trials are needed to evaluate efficacy, durability, and benefit-risk profile in this population.

title: Firearm Injury Prevention Bystander Intervention for Adolescents in Shooting Sports: A Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial.
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Firearm injury is the leading cause of death for adolescents in the US. Few adolescent firearm injury prevention interventions exist that center partnership with firearm-owning communities.
OBJECTIVE: To measure the impact of the Guardians 4 Health shooting sports firearm injury prevention bystander intervention among youth in 4-H Shooting Sports (4HSS).
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This parallel cluster randomized clinical trial enrolled youth in the US at 4HSS clubs with 6 or more adolescents and the ability to use video conferencing technology. Sites were enrolled from June 2022 to July 2024; they were block randomized and stratified by rurality and state-level child access prevention laws. Intervention sites received the shooting sports firearm injury prevention curriculum, and wait-listed control sites continued standard 4-H programming. Outcome data were collected by survey and aggregated across 5 hypothetical scenarios at baseline, 3 months, and 6 months. Analyses followed intention-to-treat principles. Complete-case analyses used linear mixed models adjusting for baseline and randomization variables; multilevel multiple imputations were adjusted for baseline covariates.
INTERVENTION: A 3-session novel adolescent firearm injury prevention bystander intervention curriculum, previously developed in conjunction with 4HSS.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was behavioral intention to use bystander intervention. Secondary outcomes were knowledge, subjective norms, attitudes, and perceived behavioral control.
RESULTS: A total of 61 sites from 28 states were randomized (32 to intervention and 29 to control); 50 sites (intervention, 26 sites of 250 youth; control, 24 sites of 174 youth) completed baseline data collection. Of 424 participants, the median (IQR) age was 14 (13-16) years; 226 were male (53.3%). Among 333 participants with nonmissing family firearm ownership data, 291 reported ownership (87.4%). Linear mixed-model analyses showed a small difference in behavioral intention between groups at 3 months (Β = 0.10; 95% CI, 0.003-0.19) but not at 6 months; multiple imputation results were similar. Significant positive intervention effects on firearm injury risk knowledge were observed at both time points in both analyses and on perceived behavioral control at 3 months.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Results of this nationwide cluster randomized clinical trial of a codeveloped adolescent firearm injury bystander intervention curriculum demonstrated a small short-term positive effect on intention to use bystander interventions and a durable effect on firearm injury risk knowledge. Findings support partnership between shooting sports organizations and public health researchers and the value of the firearm injury prevention bystander intervention within 4HSS. Consideration of boosters and larger-scale evaluation is warranted.

title: Treatment patterns following next-generation sequencing in U.S. Veterans with metastatic cancer across social determinants of health.
abstract: 699 Background: Social determinants of health (SDoH) such as race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status (SES), and rurality affect access to cancer care. This study evaluated whether SDoH impacts systemic treatment patterns following next-generation sequencing (NGS) among Veterans with common cancer within the integrated U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA). Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of U.S. Veterans diagnosed with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), colorectal cancer (CRC), or prostate cancer who received NGS testing between 2019 and 2023. Data were obtained from the VA Corporate Data Warehouse, VA Cancer Registry, and the National Precision Oncology Program (NPOP) database, which records the FoundationOne Tissue and Liquid CDx NGS data. For each cancer type, we assessed use of FDA approved systemic therapies (chemotherapy, immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI), targeted, and hormone) as a first treatment following NGS testing. Associations between treatment utilization and SDoH, including self-reported race, ethnicity, age, gender, rurality, and SES, were examined using multivariable logistic regression to estimate odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Results: Among 4,413 Veterans with metastatic cancer that received NGS testing, 97.3% were male and 67.2% White, with broad variation in rurality, income, and education. Overall, 76.9% received a systemic therapy following NGS testing, with 68.0% initiating treatment within 90 days. Chemotherapy (53.7%) was the most common in Veterans with CRC, followed by targeted therapy (20.4%) and ICI (2.3%). For patients with NSCLC, ICI (51.5%) had the highest use, followed by chemotherapy (8.0%) and targeted therapy (6.9%). The majority of Veterans with prostate cancer received hormone therapy (81.6%), followed by chemotherapy (6.4%), targeted therapy (1.6%), and ICI (0.6%). Patients with CRC had higher targeted therapy use in Veterans ≤65 years (OR 1.94, CI 1.19-3.19) but had no differences between SDoH. For NSCLC patients, ICI utilization was lower in female (OR 0.47, CI 0.27-0.82), multi-racial (OR 0.27, CI 0.09-0.77), and Asian (OR 0.21, CI 0.04-0.91) Veterans and patients residing in highly rural areas (OR 0.21, CI 0.05-0.81). Disparities were not observed in Veterans with prostate cancer receiving targeted therapy, but hormone therapy use was lower in patients ≤65 years (OR 0.51, CI 0.34-0.76) and higher in Hispanic (OR 5.09, CI 1.55-31.4) Veterans. Conclusions: Among NGS-tested Veterans, treatment patterns varied across SDOH with substantial adoption of ICIs in NSCLC, hormone therapy in prostate cancer and targeted therapies in CRC. Access to targeted therapies in prostate cancer appeared to be unaffected by SDOH. Future work will incorporate additional genomic platforms and biomarker specific analysis to identify drivers of treatment variation in the VA.

title: Reframing traumatic brain injury and spinal cord injury as chronic multisystem disorders: toward integrated, long-term care.
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) and spinal cord injury (SCI) affect more than 220 million people worldwide and are associated with cardiometabolic, endocrine, neurological, and psychiatric sequelae for years to decades after an acute injury. However, most health systems still treat neurotrauma (TBI and SCI, collectively) as a time-limited event, leaving long-term surveillance of these patients fragmented or absent, which leads to preventable mortality and avoidable readmissions. TBI and SCI in adults should be reclassified as acute-onset multisystem chronic-risk conditions. Existing cardiovascular, endocrine, and psychiatric services do not capture neurotrauma-specific risks, including trauma-induced hypopituitarism, autonomic dysregulation, accelerated ageing, and cognitive-behavioural impairment, so neurotrauma care is best framed as a missing node in chronic neurological care. We propose a risk-stratified pathway of care navigation, multisystem screening, and telehealth; convergence with adjacent stroke, cardiometabolic, memory, psychiatric, pain, and epilepsy services; and the financing, workforce, and registry reforms needed to deliver measurable reductions in 5-year mortality, avoidable rehospitalisation, and long-term disability.

title: Emerging Patterns of Mental Health Comorbidities Among Those With Blast or Blunt Mechanism TBI: Leveraging Total Brain Diagnostics Data.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is associated with postinjury mental health (MH) sequelae, yet associations between injury-related risk factors (eg, injury mechanism, multiple injuries) and outcomes remain poorly understood. We leveraged a newly harmonized national dataset to evaluate relationships between TBI characteristics and MH outcomes.
DATA SOURCES: We analyzed data from the Total Brain Diagnostics (TBD) dataset, a harmonized data source including 2 large, multisite, longitudinal prospective cohort studies: the Long-term Impact of Military-relevant Brain Injury Consortium's (LIMBIC) and the Translational Research Center for TBI and Stress Disorders (TRACTS).
PARTICIPANTS: Veterans and Service Members (n = 3771).
DESIGN: Pooled cross-sectional analyses of harmonized data.
MAIN MEASURES: TBI Characteristics (Predictors): Number of TBIs, whether the participant had experienced a blast-related TBI, and whether the participant had experienced loss of consciousness secondary to a TBI. Mental Health Conditions/Symptoms (Outcomes): Probable post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), probable depression, probable anxiety, suicidal ideation, suicide attempts, and probable unhealthy alcohol use.
RESULTS: Blast TBI was associated with greater odds of probable PTSD (OR 1.85, P < .001, 95% CI: 1.57-2.17), probable depression (OR 1.66, P < .001, 95% CI: 1.42-1.95), and probable anxiety (OR 1.73, P < .001, 95% CI: 1.45-2.05) compared with blunt TBI. Post-hoc analyses suggested differences in the frequency of co-occurring MH outcomes among those with blast versus blunt TBIs.
CONCLUSIONS: Findings suggest unique MH outcomes driven by blast injury mechanism, highlighting potential differences in underlying etiology.

title: Probable alcohol use disorder in the U.S. Veteran population: Results from the 2025-2026 National Health and Resilience in Veterans study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is a pervasive public health problem in the United States, and military veterans are at elevated risk. A prior wave of the National Health and Resilience in Veterans Study (NHRVS) estimated the prevalence of past-year probable AUD at 10.5 % in 2019-2020. Updated national surveillance data are needed given demographic shifts in the veteran population and evolving drinking patterns in the post-pandemic era.
METHODS: Using data from the 2025-2026 NHRVS (N = 2,620), we estimated the weighted prevalence of probable AUD and compared it to that of the prior NHRVS wave. Multivariable analyses examined sociodemographic, military, trauma and mental health characteristics associated with probable AUD.
RESULTS: The weighted prevalence of probable AUD in 2025-2026 was 12.1 %, compared with 10.5 % in 2019-2020 (difference, 1.6 percentage points; 95 % CI, -0.6 to 3.8), a difference that was not statistically significant. Independent correlates of probable AUD included younger age, unpartnered status, homelessness history, higher household income, and more adverse childhood experiences. When all lifetime psychiatric diagnoses were examined simultaneously, self-reported provider-diagnosed attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) remained significantly associated with probable AUD (OR = 2.40). Veterans with probable AUD also had significantly greater odds of past-year suicidal ideation (OR = 2.02; 31.6 % vs. 11.7 %) and lifetime suicide attempt (OR = 1.67; 11.8 % vs. 4.0 %).
CONCLUSIONS: The prevalence of probable AUD among U.S. veterans remains elevated and is characterized by early adversity, co-occurring psychiatric conditions, and elevated suicide risk. Enhanced screening for social determinants of health and psychiatric concerns, including routine ADHD assessment in AUD treatment settings, alongside targeted outreach and integrated approaches are essential to address this complex and important problem.

title: PTSD is Associated with Advanced Epigenetic Age in 43,155 US Military Veterans.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) has been associated with advanced biological age in DNA methylation data, but results have been inconsistent. This study evaluated PTSD in association with epigenetic age in the largest cohort to date (by ∼20 fold).
METHODS: Participants were 43,155 US Veterans (92.96% male) enrolled in the VA's Million Veteran Program, with VA electronic health record (EHR), self-report PTSD severity (n = 21,999), and DNA methylation and genotype data. PTSD diagnoses predated the blood draw for obtaining DNA by ≥ one year.
RESULTS: PTSD diagnosis and symptom severity were associated with age-adjusted metrics of epigenetic age ("age residuals") per the Horvath, Hannum, PhenoAge, GrimAge, and DunedinPACE algorithms after multiple testing adjustment. PTSD severity showed the most consistent associations with epigenetic age residuals, ranging from up to ∼7 months (Horvath) to ∼2 years (GrimAge) advanced age and up to 16 days faster pace per year (DunedinPACE). The relationships between PTSD severity and GrimAge, PhenoAge, and DunedinPACE residuals were stronger among younger vs. older Veterans. PTSD was associated with all epigenetic age residuals in the European ancestry subgroup (n = 26,630), but fewer significant associations emerged in the African ancestry participants (n = 11,119). Associations were similar across male and female Veterans.
CONCLUSIONS: PTSD was associated with advanced epigenetic aging in the largest study to date to evaluate this question. Effects were generally small in magnitude, though meaningful when considering the personal and healthcare system impact of advanced aging in the large population of VA users with PTSD.

title: Abstract 7443: Housing Instability Unmasks Unrecognized Heart Failure and Disparate Hospitalization Risk: A National Veterans Cohort Analysis
abstract: Introduction: Housing instability is recognized as a social driver of cardiovascular health. Veterans incur both housing instability and heart failure (HF) disproportionately. However, the extent of unrecognized HF and the factors driving HF hospitalization within this population are not well known. Research Question: Among veterans with recent housing instability, we sought (a) to characterize the burden of previously unrecognized heart failure and (b) to identify sociodemographic and clinical factors associated with HF-related hospitalization in the year after an incident housing instability indicator. Methods: Veterans Affairs healthcare data were queried for Veterans with incident housing instability from 2014 to 2018. We then identified Veterans with incident HF (no prior diagnosis) in the year following the housing instability indicator, and HF-related hospitalizations within this group. Descriptively, we classified those without an outpatient HF diagnosis prior to hospitalization as having unrecognized HF. To characterize predictors of HF-related hospitalizations, we considered demographics, comorbidities, and prior healthcare utilization with multivariable logistic regression. Results: Among 572,264 Veterans with incident housing instability, 11,307 (2.9%) had incident HF, and 1,344 (11.9%) had a HF-related hospitalization. Among these 1344, 376 (28.9%) had no prior HF diagnosis. On multivariable analysis, unmarried Veterans had higher odds of HF hospitalization than married Veterans (OR 1.40, p<0.0001), white Veterans had lower odds of admission than Black Veterans (OR 0.82, p=0.003), and female Veterans had lower odds of admission than males (OR 0.69, p=0.026). Veterans with diabetes, obesity or valvular heart disease had increased odds of HF admission (ORs of 1.18, 1.25, 1.49 respectively, p-values <.01). The likelihood of HF-related hospitalization was also associated with VA homeless program engagement (OR 1.15, p=0.025) and with an ED visit (OR 1.36, p<0.0001, a computation that excludes those ED visits producing HF admissions). Conclusions: Among Veterans with housing instability, nearly one in three HF-related hospitalizations lacked a preceding HF diagnosis, representing a critical gap in outpatient recognition warranting investigation. HF-related hospitalizations in this group were associated with race, with male sex, with clinical diagnoses, and with utilization of VA homelessness and acute care services. These findings suggest that proactive HF screening and help for Veterans with housing instability might reduce preventable HF hospitalizations.

title: Adapted Massed Exposure Therapy Enhanced with MDMA for PTSD (aMETEMP): A randomized, double-masked protocol adapted for Veterans Affairs healthcare system.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) remains prevalent and disabling, especially among veterans, with a substantial proportion failing to achieve remission following first-line evidence-based trauma-focused psychotherapies. 3,4-Methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) is hypothesized to enhance psychotherapy outcomes through effects on fear extinction, cognitive flexibility, and emotional engagement, and is being studied as a promising augmentation strategy for PTSD psychotherapy. There is limited research combining MDMA with evidence-based PTSD treatment. MDMA-assisted psychotherapy trials to date have also been limited by lack of an active comparator and functional unmasking. We describe the methodology of an ongoing randomized, double-masked, pilot trial evaluating massed prolonged exposure (PE) therapy enhanced with MDMA for PTSD (aMETEMP), adapted for a U.S. Veterans Affairs outpatient setting. Up to 20 veterans with PTSD in the VA will receive a 6-8hr in-person MDMA dosing session (randomized dose 35 mg - 125 mg) integrated with a 3-week massed exposure protocol. The remaining visits are virtual and include PE sessions and sessions to prepare for and process the MDMA session (28-30hrs total over 11 visits), with the use of telehealth intended to improve access and ease patient burden. After treating the first 4 participants, who were fully informed of the trial design, we switched to using an incomplete disclosure strategy (not disclosing the number of treatment arms or specific possible doses) to further improve masking. Primary outcomes include PTSD severity using the Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale for DSM-5, safety, feasibility, and masking success. Findings are intended to provide preliminary descriptive information regarding feasibility, safety/tolerability, masking integrity, and symptom-change signals for aMETEMP with incomplete disclosure in a large outpatient healthcare system.

title: Smoking Cessation Among Underserved Patients Referred for Lung Cancer Screening: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services requires that health systems offer smoking cessation services to patients undergoing lung cancer screening. However, the most effective methods to achieve smoking cessation among medically underserved patients undergoing lung cancer screening are unknown.
OBJECTIVE: To compare the effectiveness of 4 strategies for promoting smoking cessation among medically underserved persons referred for lung cancer screening.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This randomized clinical trial included currently smoking individuals referred for lung cancer screening at 4 US health systems (5 centers) who identified as Black, Hispanic, living in a rural area, or being of low socioeconomic status. The first participant was enrolled on May 17, 2021, and the date of last follow-up was April 29, 2025.
INTERVENTION: Patients were randomized to 1 of 4 groups. Participants received either an ask-advise-refer strategy to smoking cessation services (usual care); usual care plus free pharmacotherapy (ie, nicotine replacement and reimbursement for varenicline or bupropion); usual care, free pharmacotherapy, and financial incentives up to $600 contingent on biochemically confirmed smoking cessation; or usual care, free pharmacotherapy, and financial incentives plus a mobile health tool motivating patients to think about their future health.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary end point was biochemically confirmed, sustained tobacco abstinence through 6 months, measured with cotinine, anabasine, or carboxyhemoglobin.
RESULTS: Of the 9963 patients assessed for eligibility, 3259 patients were randomized and 3220 were included in the primary analysis. The median (IQR) age was 61.1 (56.6-66.0) years, 1948 (60.3%) were female, 823 (25.5%) were Black, 287 (8.9%) were Hispanic, 1251 (38.8%) lived in rural areas, 1519 (74.9%) had low socioeconomic status, and 1792 (55.5%) reported smoking more than 10 cigarettes per day at enrollment. Sustained tobacco abstinence rates through 6 months were 4.3% with usual care, 5.1% with the addition of pharmacotherapy, 8.8% with the addition of financial incentives, and 7.2% with the addition of mobile health tool. Adding financial incentives increased the adjusted rate of sustained tobacco abstinence compared with usual care (difference, 4.6% [95% CI, 2.1%-7.0%]; P < .001) and usual care plus free pharmacotherapy (difference, 4.1% [95% CI, 1.7%-6.4%]; P < .001). Adding free pharmacotherapy to ask-advise-refer was not superior to ask-advise-refer alone (difference, 0.5% [95% CI, -1.7% to 2.6%]; P = .66).
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Among medically underserved adults who currently smoked cigarettes and were referred for lung cancer screening, rates of sustained tobacco abstinence were higher through 6 months with addition of financial incentives compared with ask-advise-refer alone or with addition of free pharmacotherapy.

title: Impact of a National Stepped-Care Model of Opioid Use Disorder Treatment on Access to Medication Therapies Among Homeless-Experienced Veterans.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To determine whether the Veterans Health Administration's (VHA) Stepped Care for Opioid Use Disorder Train-the-Trainer (SCOUTT) initiative increased medication treatment for opioid use disorder (MOUD) among persons experiencing homelessness (PEH).
STUDY SETTING AND DESIGN: We conducted a national retrospective cohort study of MOUD, including buprenorphine, naltrexone, or methadone, in federal fiscal years (FY) 2016-2020. In late FY2018, VHA regional directors nominated facilities to receive SCOUTT implementation support to expand prescribing of MOUD (primarily buprenorphine) in select primary care, pain, and general mental health settings. We used mixed-effects quasi-Poisson regression models with entropy balancing to estimate the Average Treatment Effect on the Treated in the years after SCOUTT was implemented (FY2019-2020), controlling for pre-implementation levels of MOUD. Secondary analyses applied synthetic difference-in-differences (DiD) to estimate changes associated with SCOUTT.
DATA SOURCES AND ANALYTIC SAMPLE: We used yearly pooled cross-sectional data from VHA electronic health records, FY2016-2020. The sample included annual cohorts of PEH with an opioid use disorder diagnosis and ≥ 1 primary care visit in the pre-implementation (FY2016-2018, n = 31,354) or post-implementation (FY2019-2020, n = 20,746) periods.
PRINCIPAL FINDINGS: From FY2016-2020, MOUD receipt increased more in SCOUTT facilities (n = 30, 45.0% to 61.1%) than in non-SCOUTT facilities (n = 811, 41.9% to 49.7%). In post-implementation years, PEH in SCOUTT facilities, compared to non-SCOUTT facilities, were more likely to receive any MOUD (risk difference [RD] = 6.16, 95% CI = 2.33-9.99), including buprenorphine (RD = 7.16, 95% CI = 4.35-9.97). There were no significant differences in methadone (RD = -0.19, 95% CI = -1.03-0.65) or naltrexone (RD = 0.10, 95% CI = -1.85-2.05). Synthetic DiD offered similar results: any MOUD DiD = 7.85, 95% CI = 2.15-13.55; buprenorphine DiD = 9.31, 95% CI = 3.56-15.06.
CONCLUSIONS: A national initiative to advance a stepped-care model that encourages MOUD initiation outside specialty addiction settings improved access to buprenorphine among PEH. Similar initiatives could help to close treatment gaps in health care settings serving PEH.

title: Sex and gender dynamics in health outcomes of partner dance
abstract: As populations age globally, activities like dance gain prominence for their ability to prevent age-related health declines (Pessoa et al., 2019;World Health Organization, 2020).Partner dance requires two individuals to synchronize their movements and interpret music together. This activity combines physical, cognitive, and social benefits, and in some cases, improves quality of life (Marie-Sophie et al., 2012). Partner dance can be light, moderate, or vigorous in intensity depending on style, tempo, and format (e.g., slow ballroom dances: 3 Metabolic Equivalent of Tasks (METs) vs. faster styles: 5.5 METs) (Ainsworth et al., 2011), as it meets the thresholds for aerobic exercise only in some circumstances, alongside its cognitive and social demands.The health benefits of partner dance are not universally experienced and are profoundly shaped by sex and gender (Editage, 2019). Sex refers to biological attributes-chromosomal composition (typically XX for females and XY for males), hormonal profiles, and anatomical structures-that influence physiological responses to exercise (Mazure, 2021). Gender, by contrast, encompasses sociocultural constructs, including roles, behaviors, identities, and expectations, which evolve and shape participation in activities like dance (Conger, 2017).Despite this distinction, sex and gender terms are frequently used interchangeably in public conversation and research settings, creating confusion about whether role differences arise from biological capacities or culturally reinforced expectations. To address the inconsistency, standardized research frameworks, such as those from the National Institutes of Health's (NIH) Specialized Centers of Research Excellence (SCORE) on Sex Differences, are essential for improving clarification (Office of Research on Women's Health, 2024). With these inconsistencies in mind, this opinion paper explores how sex and gender influence health outcomes in partner dance. Figure 1 synthesizes key considerations across three stages (Foundation, Bridge, and Goal) and, building on these, offers recommendations for future intervention design, with role switching as a central theme. The following sections examine how sex-based biological responses and gendered roles, expectations, and social dynamics may interact to shape health outcomes in partner dance.Evidence from a recent systematic review consisting of 11 randomized controlled trials and 1412 participants suggests that dance may contribute to cognitive reserve and reduce the risks of age-related cognitive decline; however, intensity was reported on only three trials (moderate intensity or 60-80% of maximum heart rate) (Hewston et al., 2021). This review also identified ballroom dance as the most frequently investigated modality (six studies; 54.5%), while highlighting the absence of direct comparisons between partner dance and other dance forms (Hewston et al., 2021). Partner dance involves a unique combination of physical tasks (stepping, turning, and balancing) with cognitive tasks (pattern recognition, memory, and decision-making) (Abraham et al., 2024;Allen et al., 2017;Hackney & Earhart, 2010;Merom et al., 2016), making it an ideal model for examining sex-based differences in health outcomes. These sex differences stem from physiological variations in males and females that influence responses to exercise.Borrowing from the exercise field, females may derive greater cognitive benefits than males from exercise (Barha et al., 2017). A meta-analysis of aerobic and resistance training (moderate-intensity) indicated enhanced executive functions, attention, working memory, and inhibitory control in older females as compared to older males (Barha et al., 2017). Although these findings come from structured, moderate-intensity exercise rather than partner dance, which reach comparable intensity only in some styles and formats, partner dance provides a relevant context for examining such sex differences. A study of partnered dancing (intensity not reported) provoked improvements in mood (i.e., feeling less depressed and happier) in females than males; however, this study was not designed to examine sex-or gender-specific effects (Lakes et al., 2016). Partner dance may offer a useful context for investigating sex differences in cognitive benefits, as dance-based interventions have been associated with improvements in motor-cognitive dual-task performance, global cognition, and executive function in older adults (Hamacher et al., 2015) (Hewston et al., 2021).One mechanism driving these associations may be related to the neuroprotective effects of estrogen (Enns & Tiidus, 2010;Yu et al., 2022). Because many older female participants are post-menopausal, current circulating estrogen and cumulative lifetime estrogen exposure should be considered separately. Current circulating estrogen can be assessed using sensitive serum assays (Hesson, 2012;Lee et al., 2006;Xu et al., 2007), while cumulative exposure can be estimated from reproductive history and exogenous hormone use (Hesson, 2012;Salliot et al., 2022). Estrogen has been associated with increased neuroplasticity and hippocampal volume (Barha & Liu-Ambrose, 2018). Thus, lifetime hormonal exposure may be a useful variable to examine in future studies of cognitive responses to exercise and partner dance, particularly in relation to menopausal status and hormone therapy.In contrast, males may achieve greater cardiorespiratory gains than females from intense exercise due to greater oxygen uptake and substrate utilization (Cobbold, 2018).Additionally, males may experience greater muscle hypertrophy and aerobic adaptations such as a larger increase in VO₂ max, cardiac output, and lactate threshold due to higher testosterone levels, which support lean muscle mass development (Landen et al., 2023;Nuzzo, 2023). These sex-related physiological differences may be relevant to physically demanding partner-dance movements, particularly in styles and formats that reach vigorous intensity, although their implications for dance-specific health outcomes remain unclear. Such differences may also influence performance in strength-and power-demanding elements, including lifts in ballroom dance and rapid turns in tango, warranting further investigation into sex-specific physiological responses to partner dance (Hunter et al., 2023).Partner dance also relies heavily on balance and flexibility. Females generally demonstrate better static balance and greater joint flexibility, enhancing aesthetic movement but increasing susceptibility to hypermobility-related injuries such as hip labral strain (Pappas et al., 2011;Steinberg et al., 2016). While males typically show stronger dynamic balance and greater muscular power, supporting lifts and directional control, these processes may elevate the risk of upper-body overuse injuries (Wanke et al., 2013). Importantly, substantial overlap exists between females and males in these characteristics (i.e., balance, flexibility, and power), and individual fitness, training history, and dance experience may also influence intervention outcomes and injury risk. Nonetheless, both sexes experience similar overall physical health benefits from moderate-intensity activities, and dance interventions have demonstrated physical, inflammatory, mood, and neurocognitive benefits in different populations (Borges et al., 2019;Hackney et al., 2020;Lakes et al., 2016).Sex differences may confer distinct health-related risks and benefits during partner dance, whereas gender norms may indirectly shape health outcomes by influencing the dance environment and opportunities for cognitive and social engagement. These norms may also affect cognitive reserve through unequal lifelong access to cognitively stimulating activities, with implications for health disparities.In many traditional partner dance styles, social conventions-often aligned with binary gender norms-assign women take the follower role, interpreting cues with responsiveness, adaptability, and active styling, while men the leader role, where they initiate movements, select figures, and guide the dance's direction (Hackney et al., 2024). Both roles require active cognitive engagement, although following requires continuous sensory integration and adaptive responses to partner cues, whereas leadership may emphasize planning and spatial awareness (Abraham et al., 2024;Den Kulturella Hjärnan, 2014;Foster Vander Elst et al., 2023).However, rigid role assignments may limit cognitive diversity by reinforcing normative gender expectations. For example, women limited to follower roles may have fewer opportunities to develop planning skills, potentially impacting cognitive reserve (Qi et al., 2024).Conversely, men who consistently lead may have fewer opportunities to practice the rapid sensory integration and adaptive responsiveness required of followers. Accordingly, challenging normative role assignments may be an important consideration for maximizing cognitive engagement and health equity in dance-based interventions.Cultural norms strongly shape gendered role expectations in partner dance, influencing who leads, who follows, and how movement qualities are valued (Risner, 2010). Many dance traditions reinforce heteronormative scripts that associate following with feminine responsiveness, shaping cognitive and motor demands placed on each role and leadership with masculine assertiveness (McMains, 2015;Royce, 2008). Cultural expectations may also affect participation patterns and access to cognitively demanding roles, influencing long-term engagement and health outcomes. Integrating cultural context is therefore essential for understanding how gendered movement practices influence equity in dance-based interventions.Gender roles in dance are rapidly evolving, particularly in inclusive activities like queer tango, where individuals choose roles based on identity or comfort (Lucchi Basili & Sacco, 2025). Allowing participants to choose or alternate roles may increase opportunities to engage with different cognitive, motor, and social demands while reducing reliance on traditional gender expectations. More broadly, frameworks centered on joint action emphasizing interpersonal coordination, reciprocal adaptation, and the co-construction of movement between individuals (Sebanz et al., 2006) offer a complementary lens for conceptualizing these more fluid role dynamics. By challenging heteronormative standards, inclusive partner dance settings promote equity and broaden cognitive engagement, aligning with global calls for gender-sensitive health interventions (World Bank, 2024).Role switching in partner dance might build cognitive reserve by engaging diverse cognitive processes (Hackney et al., 2024), but this is a theoretical pathway that requires direct investigation in partner dance interventions. Switching between follower and leader roles may require dancers to integrate different combinations of planning, sensory processing, spatial awareness, and partner cues; whether this translates into measurable cognitive or psychosocial benefits remains an important research question. Historically, women have faced barriers to education and professional advancement, which limit cognitive reserve. Although the precise reason for women's higher Alzheimer's rates remains unknown (Moutinho, 2025), cognitive reserve has been associated with lifestyle activities and other cognitively stimulating experiences (Qi et al., 2024), suggesting that gendered differences in lifelong opportunities may warrant further investigation. Contemporary shifts, with increased participation of women in higher education and professional spheres, may reduce these disparities, but further research is needed.Despite the growing recognition of partner dance as a multifaceted health intervention, significant gaps in literature hinder its optimization for diverse populations (Fong Yan et al., 2024;Kattenstroth et al., 2013). The evidence base includes relatively few studies designed to examine sex-or gender-specific effects, and many findings are extrapolated from general exercise or broader dance research. Additionally, heterogeneity in dance styles, participant populations, and outcome measures limits comparability across studies, and the overreliance on self-reported or indirect measures weakens causal inferences (Delattre et al., 2024;Noetel et al., 2024). Addressing these limitations requires more rigorous, targeted research to clarify how biological and sociocultural factors shape the health effects of partner dance across diverse populations.Current research often fails to disaggregate data by sex or analyze sex differences, obscuring how biological variability may shape health outcomes (Barha et al., 2017;Nuzzo, 2023). For example, previous work has rarely explored how menstrual cycles or menopausal status affect sex-and gender-based responses to exercise, limiting the development of tailored interventions (Sims & Heather, 2018). The limited research available suggests that hormonal fluctuations across the menstrual cycle can influence exercise performance, vascular endothelial responses, and physiological mechanisms underlying cardiopulmonary and neuromuscular function (Ghniem et al., 2025;Heinrich & Behringer, 2023;Hicks et al., 2023;Wen et al., 2025). Future partner-dance studies should therefore record relevant hormonal or reproductive characteristics when appropriate rather than assuming that age or sex alone captures hormonal status. Similarly, gender analyses are underdeveloped, with minimal research examining how traditional role assignments-such as women following and men leading -impact cognitive reserve or psychosocial benefits across genders (Hackney et al., 2024). Researchers should record role allocation and experience and, where appropriate, compare fixed-role and role-switching protocols to determine whether role flexibility influences cognitive load. It is currently unknown whether learning roles sequentially rather than simultaneously reduces cognitive load for beginners. Finally, research focusing specifically on health outcomes and role preferences of non-binary and transgender dancers remains critically underexplored (Jones et al., 2019).It is important to note that the studies reviewed here operationalize "partner dance" across distinct contexts, including clinical rehabilitation programs for specific populations and unstructured social/ballroom dancing, which may influence participant demographics, adherence, and outcomes. This heterogeneity underscores the need for standardized definitions in future research, which should integrate guidelines (e.g., NIH SCORE) on sex/gender equity, measure sex and gender separately without assuming binary chromosomal categories, and foster interdisciplinary collaboration to maximize the potential of partner dance as an inclusive public health tool for diverse populations. Partner dance offers a unique lens for examining sex (biological) and gender (socially constructed) dynamics in health outcomes, with traditional follower-leader roles often reflecting heteronormative gender expectations. Inclusive practices like same-sex partnerships and roleswitching promote equity and can maximize intervention benefits. Role-switching and inclusive practices may jointly shape physical, cognitive, and psychosocial benefits, typically targeted through separate exercise programs, positioning partner dance as a uniquely engaging intervention with beneficial outcomes across domains.

title: Leukocytes and age-related macular degeneration.
abstract: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a leading cause of vision loss. Leukocyte subtypes have been implicated in the pathogenesis, but causality remains uncertain. We investigated whether leukocyte counts are causally associated with clinically diagnosed AMD using observational and genetic analyses in three prospective cohorts. We included 117,714 individuals from the Copenhagen General Population Study (CGPS), 388,758 from the UK Biobank (UKB), and 285,612 from the Million Veteran Program (MVP), all of European ancestry and without clinically diagnosed AMD at baseline. In total, 27,130 incident AMD cases were identified. Baseline leukocyte counts were log2-transformed and standardized. Observational associations with incident AMD were estimated using Cox regression in CGPS and UKB, and then meta-analysed. Genetic instruments derived from genome-wide association studies were used for one-sample mendelian randomization (MR) and multivariable MR (MVMR) analyses in UKB and MVP, and estimates then meta-analysed. Observationally, a 1-standard deviation (SD) increase in leukocyte (Hazard ratio (HR) [95% confidence interval (CI)], 1.07 [1.05-1.09]), neutrophil (1.07 [1.05-1.09]), monocyte (1.05 [1.03-1.07]), basophil (1.06 [1.04-1.08]), and eosinophil (1.05 [1.03-1.06]) counts was associated with increased risk of clinically diagnosed AMD (all p < 0.0001). In the genetic analyses, a 1-SD increase in genetically determined eosinophil counts was causally associated with increased risk of clinically diagnosed AMD in the MR (OR [95% CI], 1.07 [1.00-1.15]; p = 0.038) and MVMR (OR [95% CI], 1.12 [1.03-1.21]; p = 0.006) analyses. This large-scale study provides observational and genetic evidence that elevated eosinophil counts are causally linked to risk of clinically diagnosed AMD. These findings highlight systemic eosinophil-driven immune pathways as potential contributors to AMD pathogenesis.

title: Predictors of Seizure Occurrence After Mild Cognitive Impairment and Alzheimer’s Disease in Older Adults in the Veterans Affairs Healthcare System: A Retrospective Cohort Study
abstract: INTRODUCTION: This was a retrospective epidemiological study to identify the predictors of incidence seizures among older adults with all-cause mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) receiving care in the Veterans Affairs Healthcare System (VAHS). METHODS: Veterans aged ≥ 50 years with MCI or AD were identified using pre-specified diagnostic code and clinical note algorithms in VAHS electronic health records, with linkage to Medicare claims where available, during 2016-2023. Seizures were identified using ICD-10-CM codes for convulsions and epilepsy (R56.x and G40.x), excluding codes considered unlikely to represent unprovoked seizures (e.g., G40.5). Individuals with any seizure/epilepsy diagnosis prior to the index MCI/AD date (or matched control date) were excluded. Multivariate Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate associations but not causal relationships between baseline comorbidities and subsequent seizure risk. RESULTS: A total of 747,475 individuals with AD or MCI and 747,475 age- and sex-matched non-MCI/AD comparators were identified; after excluding those with pre-index seizures, the analytic cohorts included 482,364 MCI, 223,312 AD, and 736,118 comparator veterans. Compared with non-MCI/AD controls, seizure risk was higher in MCI (HR 2.89, 95% CI 2.80-2.99) and AD (HR 3.19, 95% CI 2.99-3.41). In adjusted analyses, seizure risk was higher among black veterans (HR 1.38, 95% CI 1.31-1.46) than white veterans. Comorbidities with the strongest adjusted associations included traumatic brain injury (HR 1.88, 95% CI 1.68-2.10), central nervous system infection (HR 1.88, 95% CI 1.21-2.92), cerebrovascular disease (HR 1.72, 95% CI 1.63-1.81), and hemorrhagic stroke (HR 1.61, 95% CI 1.39-1.86). Much of the excess risk was associated with cerebrovascular and neurologic comorbidity. CONCLUSION: Our study showed that seizure risk is elevated in MCI and AD, with specific comorbidities associated with risk of seizure occurrence and cognitive decline, suggesting potentially actionable targets for risk stratification and clinical monitoring.

title: Moral injury, perceived burdensomeness, thwarted belongingness, and suicidal ideation in post-9/11 US combat veterans
abstract: Background: Moral injury – the psychological harm resulting from acts of wrongdoing or betrayals – correlates with negative psychosocial outcomes, including increased suicide risk. The Interpersonal Theory of Suicide (IPTS) suggests that perceived burdensomeness (the belief that one is a burden to others), and thwarted belongingness (psychological pain from unmet social connectedness) confer risk of suicidal ideation.Objective: The current study evaluates the degree to which perceived burdensomeness and thwarted belongingness mediates the associations of acts of wrongdoing and betrayal with current suicidal ideation.Method: We used a generative modelling approach with Bayesian latent variable models in a sample of 312 United States combat-deployed veterans.Results: Acts of wrongdoing were (1) directly associated with current suicidal ideation, with small effect (β = 0.15, 95% credible interval (CI): −0.01, 0.30); (2) indirectly associated via perceived burdensomeness, with small effect (β = 0.14, 95% CI: 0.06, 0.24); and (3) indirectly associated with thwarted belongingness, with negligible effect (β = 0.04, 95% CI: 0.00, 0.10). Acts of betrayal had negligible associations with current suicidal ideation.Conclusions: Feelings of burdensomeness warrant further investigation as a potential clinical target for veterans with moral injury exposure. Thwarted belongingness may be less potent, although measurement error complicates its interpretation.

title: Abstract 17025: A Common CD36 Variant and the Genetic Landscape of Dilated Cardiomyopathy in Individuals of African Ancestry
abstract: Introduction: Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is a major cause of heart failure that disproportionately affects individuals of African genetic ancestry. Established monogenic variants in DCM risk genes, primarily identified in European (EUR) populations, offer basis for a smaller fraction of AFR DCM cases. Recently, rs3211938 (Y325*), a common AFR-specific nonsense variant in CD36 , has been shown to confer significant DCM risk. Research Question: What is the DCM risk posed by CD36 Y325* relative to other monogenic drivers of DCM? Methods: This study used data from All of Us, Penn Medicine Biobank, Million Veteran Program, and The DCM Precision Medicine Study. Premature truncations in cardiac exons (PSI90%) of the gene TTN ( TTN tv) were identified using VEP-109 and LOFTEE. CD36 Y325* carrier status was established based on the number of risk-allele individuals carried. Variants in other high-evidence DCM genes were identified using the ClinVar database. Firth’s logistic regression was used to model DCM risk posed by genetic factors in an ancestry specific fashion, and models were adjusted for age, sex, and the first ten principal components of genetic ancestry. Results: Among 82,623 AFR individuals across four studies, the mean age was 53.4 years and 1,625 individuals had DCM. CD36 Y325* heterozygote carriers had 1.4-fold (95% CI: 1.2-1.7) odds of DCM while CD36 Y325* homozygote carriers had 4.8-fold (95% CI: 3.1-7.3) increased odds of DCM. TTN tv confer elevated risk of DCM in AFR participants (OR: 8.46, 95% CI: 5.3-12.3). CD36 Y325* homozygotes comprised 2.5% of AFR DCM cases, second to only TTN tv (4.3%) and exceeding the contribution of all other high-evidence DCM genes (1.5%). Population-level analyses reveal that the population-attributable risk of CD36 Y325* (9.0%) surpasses that of TTN tv (3.6%) in AFR populations. Conclusions: CD36 Y325* contributes more to DCM in AFR ancestry than established monogenic DCM risk genes, including TTN tv. These findings reshape the genetic architecture of DCM in African ancestry and highlight the importance of representation in genomic research.

title: Molecular predictors of minimal residual disease in newly diagnosed multiple myeloma treated with quadruplet therapy
abstract: Quadruplet therapy, combining anti-CD38 antibodies, immunomodulatory drugs, proteasome inhibitors and dexamethasone, is now the standard induction treatment for newly diagnosed multiple myeloma (NDMM). However, treatment response is heterogeneous and molecular predictors are needed to guide early therapeutic decisions. We performed integrated genomic, transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling of 423 tumor samples from patients with NDMM from the MIDAS cohort to characterize molecular heterogeneity and its association with measurable residual disease (MRD) after quadruplet induction with isatuximab, carfilzomib, lenalidomide and dexamethasone (Isa-KRd). Postinduction MRD-negativity rates varied significantly across gene expression subtypes, with HP1/HP3 and MS groups showing superior responses compared to the MF and CD2 subtypes. B cell differentiation was associated with MRD positivity, while proliferation and MYC programs were associated with MRD negativity. These MRD-associated transcriptomic features were independently validated in the CASSIOPEIA cohort. Whole-genome sequencing revealed both known (APOBEC mutagenesis, chromothripsis) and new genomic instability phenotypes validated in the MMRF cohort, including mismatch repair deficiency driven by pathogenic MSH2 mutations and a focal deletion signature linked to BRCA2 inactivation. New driver alterations were identified, including translocations activating IRAK1 and FOXR1 fusions, with independent validation. Genomic instability features and driver genes such as CCND1 and MYC correlated with differential MRD outcomes. DNA methylation profiling identified nine MRD-linked subgroups distinguished by the extent of hypomethylation in quiescent chromatin and cis/trans signatures of driver translocations. A multimodal random forest model integrating genomic, transcriptomic and epigenomic features predicted MRD status after induction, with an area under the curve of 0.77, outperforming clinical and genomic models, while providing comparable discrimination and improved calibration relative to the transcriptomic and epigenomic models. These findings define a multiomic classification of NDMM linked to Isa-KRd response. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04934475 .

title: Caring Letters and Suicide Mortality Among US Veterans Who Contacted the Veterans Crisis Line: A Prespecified Secondary Analysis.
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Caring letters (CL) is one of the only suicide prevention interventions to ever reduce suicide mortality in a randomized clinical trial, but the results have not been replicated. The US Department of Veterans Affairs Veterans Crisis Line (VCL) CL intervention was previously evaluated, but suicide mortality data were not available at that time.
OBJECTIVES: To examine the association of the VCL CL intervention with suicide mortality among US veterans, and to determine whether there are differences in outcomes by signatory.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This prespecified secondary analysis of a randomized clinical trial includes a randomized parallel trial of US veterans, combined with an observational comparison of no CL receipt with any CL receipt. Veterans Health Administration (VHA) patients (aged ≥18 years) who contacted the VCL between June 11, 2020, and June 10, 2021, were randomized to receive CL from either a VA clinician or a peer veteran signatory. Veterans who contacted the VCL between June 11, 2018, and June 10, 2021, and did not receive the intervention were included as an observational historical control group. Suicide mortality analyses were completed between March and September 2025.
INTERVENTION: Veterans received 9 CL messages over a period of 1 year from either a clinician or peer veteran signatory. The signatory was randomly assigned.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The main outcome for these analyses was suicide mortality among veterans in the 12 months following the index VCL contact. Suicide mortality was compared using χ2 tests and time-to-event models.
RESULTS: This study included 227 502 VHA patients (mean [SD] age, 53.6 [16.9] years; 84.4% men) who contacted the VCL. A total of 87 926 veterans received the CL intervention; the remaining 139 576 comprised the historical control group. A total of 625 suicides (0.27%) occurred during the study period. The suicide mortality rate was similar between the CL and historical control groups (0.29% and 0.27%, respectively; P = .31). Within the CL group, outcomes did not differ between peer letter and clinician letter recipients (0.21% and 0.22%; P = .95).
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this analysis, among VHA patients who contacted the VCL, CL receipt was not associated with suicide mortality, and no differences in outcomes were identified by signatory. Future research should explore the potential benefits of increased health care utilization, a finding reported in the parent trial.

title: Human-validated LLM-assisted assessment of a large-scale online precision medicine course in diabetes
abstract: Precision medicine increasingly relies on multimodal data and artificial intelligence, creating a need for scalable education and assessment. We developed an online diabetes precision medicine course and conducted an observational single-group pre–post evaluation of knowledge, confidence, and rubric-scored open-ended responses among 435 learners who completed the course. Because manual scoring of open-ended responses is time-consuming and subject to variability and human judgment, we developed a human-validated, large language model (LLM)-assisted scoring workflow. Knowledge, confidence, and open-ended response scores increased by 30.0 percentage points, 1.32 points, and 0.39 points, respectively (all p < 0.001). Across 4350 responses evaluated by the LLM-assisted workflow, only 12 (0.3%) required human review. In a stratified 300-response validation sample, the final LLM consensus score achieved 75.3% exact agreement, 99.3% adjacent agreement, and 0.7% major disagreements (LLM unanimity, 74.0%; human unanimity, 65.7%) with the final human score. Course completion was associated with improvements in knowledge, confidence, and open-ended response scores, while the findings also support human-validated LLM-assisted assessment as a scalable approach for evaluating open-ended responses.

title: Home-Based Primary Care and Emergency Department Use Among Veterans With Dementia
abstract: BACKGROUND: As the veteran population ages, the Veterans Health Administration (VHA) faces challenges in how to meet the care needs of patients with dementia. Providing high-quality, integrated care models in the home, such as home-based primary care (HBPC), can offer care aligned with veteran goals and present potential cost-savings to the VHA. OBJECTIVE: Examine the effect of VHA HBPC on the probability of emergency department/urgent care (ED) use. RESEARCH DESIGN: Cohort analysis using an instrumental variable approach. SUBJECTS: Veterans aged 65+ with dementia (2021-2023). MEASURES: We define HBPC as beginning the first month veterans have 2+ HBPC claims within 91 days. ED use is the key outcome. RESULTS: Among 133,846 veterans with dementia, 17.36% (n=23,240) received HPBC during the evaluation period. Compared with non-HBPC veterans, veterans in HBPC were older and more likely to be female, reside in a metropolitan area, be Hispanic, be Black/African American, have post-traumatic stress disorder, a traumatic brain injury, have more Elixhauser conditions, and have higher ED use (7.1% vs. 5.9%). When using the instrumental variable of lagged HBPC penetration to address selection into HBPC ( F -stat>100), we find that HBPC enrollees were 3.60 percentage points less likely to have ED use than non-HBPC enrollees ( P <0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Reducing ED visits among people with dementia may signal improved care and offer potential cost-savings to health care systems. Our findings can help inform VHA efforts to invest in the optimal allocation of resources to best support veterans with dementia while containing costs by avoiding potentially avoidable, high-cost care.
