title: Depression burden and differential treatment effects in PTSD and substance use disorder comorbidity: findings from Project Harmony.
abstract: Background: Depression commonly co-occurs with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and substance use disorders (SUDs), yet it remains unclear whether depression meaningfully alters treatment response for individuals with PTSD/SUD. Prior studies have examined depression as an individual predictor with mixed findings but no studies to date have evaluated depression's moderating role across a broad range of PTSD/SUD treatment modalities using harmonised individual patient data (IPD).Objective: To determine whether baseline depression moderates within- and post-treatment changes in PTSD symptom severity, alcohol use, and drug use across trauma-focused, SUD focused, integrated and pharmacologic interventions in a large PTSD/SUD IPD treatment dataset.Method: Data were drawn from Project Harmony, an individual patient data meta-analysis of 36 randomised controlled trials. Latent PTSD, alcohol, and drug use severity outcomes were estimated using moderated nonlinear factor analysis. Treatment effects were evaluated longitudinally using multilevel models with propensity score weighting. Depression was examined as both an individual-level and study-level moderator.Results: Analyses did not detect moderation of individual-level depression across outcomes. In contrast, study-level depression burden significantly moderated selected treatment effects, such that the proportion of participants with depression within each original RCT shaped treatment response. In studies with higher depression burden, trauma-focused psychotherapy produced stronger post-treatment reductions in PTSD symptom severity and alcohol use but smaller in-treatment improvements. Integrated trauma-focused psychotherapy demonstrated comparatively better in-treatment PTSD outcomes. High-depression contexts yielded attenuated PTSD improvements and mixed effects on alcohol use for SUD-focused psychotherapy.Conclusion: Analyses did not detect evidence that baseline depression, as operationalised within this harmonised dataset, moderated treatment response at the individual level. In contrast, study-level depression burden was associated with differential treatment effects across treatment modalities. These findings suggest that characteristics of treatment populations may influence comparative treatment performance and warrant further investigation in implementation and comparative effectiveness research.

title: Role of Plasma Proteins in the Association Between Socioeconomic Status and Cardiovascular Disease Events: Results From Trans-Omics for Precision Medicine Cohorts.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Socioeconomic status (SES) is strongly associated with cardiovascular disease burden and risk. Plasma proteins may elucidate a biological mechanism through which low SES increases the risk of cardiovascular disease.
METHODS: Participants from the following 3 cohorts were included: the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (n=2139), Jackson Heart Study (n=967), and Women's Health Initiative (n=1104). SES was approximated using a cumulative score (range 0-3) across education, income, and employment status. A meta-analysis of Cox proportional hazards ratios was used to assess the association between SES and incident events for coronary heart disease (CHD) and stroke. Linear regression was used within each cohort to determine associations between SES and Olink proteins (n=1270 proteins) and the results were meta-analyzed across cohorts. Regression-based mediation analysis was used to determine whether the identified proteins were statistical mediators of the association of SES and incident events.
RESULTS: Higher SES scores were associated with a lower risk of CHD (hazard ratio [HR], 0.74 [95% CI, 0.63-0.87]) and stroke (HR, 0.81 [95% CI, 0.66-1.00]). After correcting for multiple testing (P<3.937×10-5), 233 proteins were associated with SES in the meta-analysis. Of these 233 proteins, 21 had a significant indirect effect on SES and CHD. Because the SES-stroke association was not statistically significant, proteins were not tested as mediators.
CONCLUSIONS: Our analysis of multiple cohorts identified evidence of different proteomic pathways associated with SES and cardiovascular disease. This work suggests that exogenous social factors (eg, SES) may influence cardiovascular disease via proteomic profiles.

title: Quality of cancer care for telehealth users using QOPI-adapted hospice at end-of-life measures.
abstract: 294 Background: The Veterans Health Administration's National TeleOncology (NTO) was designed to increase access to specialized cancer services for Veterans despite geographic location, and for those facing other limitations due to medical complexity, or social determinants of health. Oncology care is also provided by telehealth (TH) outside of NTO. However, there is limited understanding of how the quality of cancer care delivered differs between Veterans receiving telehealth (TH users), and those who are not (non-users). Timely hospice care near the end of life is a well-established indicator of high-quality cancer care as defined by ASCO's Quality Oncology Practice Initiative (QOPI) program. The goal of this study is to evaluate differences in cancer care quality between TH users and non-users using the Hospice Visits in the Last Days of Life (HVLDL) measure adapted from ASCO's QOPI program, as an indicator of care quality. Methods: This retrospective cohort study included 122,971 veterans (3,537 TH users) diagnosed with breast, colon, lung, prostate, or rectal cancer between 1/1/2017 and 12/1/2024. Marginal structural modeling was used to estimate the causal association of TH engagement with hospice use prior to death, accounting for age, sex, race, ethnicity, rurality, prior hospice use, cancer type, cancer stage, year of diagnosis, cancer history, and Care Assessment Needs scores. Results: The rate of death among TH users was substantially higher than that of non-users: 42.2% vs. 18.9% at 6 years, respectively. The proportion of patients who received a hospice visit within 3 days of death did not differ between TH users and non-users (11.1% vs. 11.3%, respectively; p=.81). However, a greater proportion of TH users received a hospice visit any time between cancer diagnosis and death compared to non-users (45.1% vs. 34.0%, respectively; p<.001). Conclusions: This study adapted well-supported quality indicators to evaluate differences in cancer care quality between telehealth users and non-users, demonstrating that telehealth can provide comparable cancer care quality to in-person care. Telehealth such as NTO may expand Veteran access to specialty cancer care while maintaining cancer care quality comparable to in-person care. NTO may serve as a model for expanding telehealth-delivered care for other serious conditions.

title: The Unbroken Integrative Psycho-Trauma Care Model
abstract: Importance: The ongoing war in Ukraine has generated an unprecedented burden of psychological trauma, frequently compounded by posttraumatic stress disorder, traumatic brain injury, severe physical injury, and the psychiatric consequences of captivity among former prisoners of war. In large military conflicts, civilian hospital systems are essential for delivering trauma-informed mental health care at scale while managing patients with complex, overlapping medical and psychiatric conditions under active conflict, with limited implementation guidance. Observations: This Special Communication describes the implementation and clinical workflow of the Unbroken Integrative Psycho-Trauma Care Model, a multidisciplinary health system approach embedded in the Lviv First Medical Union in Western Ukraine to organize trauma-informed mental health care within a wartime civilian hospital. From February 24, 2022, through December 31, 2025, the Lviv First Medical Union treated more than 15 000 individuals for war-related injuries and cared for more than 400 former prisoners of war. During this period, 7538 unique individuals received psychiatric care through the Unbroken Model, including 4165 who received trauma-focused psychotherapy. The model was implemented through proactive psychiatric rounds across medical and surgical departments, structured triage into 4 clinical pathways, stabilization-first care sequencing, and longitudinal case management integrated with neurological, surgical, and rehabilitation services. This organization of care enabled early identification of trauma-related distress, continuity between medical and psychiatric treatment, and adaptive delivery of trauma-focused psychotherapies within a high-volume conflict setting. Conclusions and Relevance: The Unbroken Model demonstrates how trauma-informed mental health care can be delivered at scale within a civilian hospital during active conflict. Its primary innovation lies in the organization of care delivery, integrating proactive outreach, triage-driven pathways, multidisciplinary coordination, and stabilization-first sequencing into a unified, scalable framework. This approach may be applicable to conflict-affected and postconflict health systems worldwide.

title: Mild depressive symptoms in older U.S. veterans: Prevalence, correlates, and psychiatric and functional burden.
abstract: Mild depressive symptoms are more prevalent than threshold-level depressive symptoms, yet epidemiologic and clinical data on mild depressive symptoms among veterans are limited. We examined the prevalence, correlates, and psychiatric and functional burden of mild depressive symptoms in a nationally representative sample of older U.S. veterans. Cross-sectional data were analyzed from 2979 veterans aged 60 and older who participated in the National Health and Resilience in Veterans Study (NHRVS). Depressive symptoms were assessed using the Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2) and categorized as none, mild, or a positive PHQ-2 screen. Weighted multivariable regression models examined associations with psychiatric disorders, suicidal thoughts and behaviors, and functional measures. Results revealed that mild depressive symptoms (18.2%) were 4-times more prevalent than a positive PHQ-2 screen (4.3%) and associated with higher adjusted prevalence of posttraumatic stress and generalized anxiety disorders, past-year suicidal ideation, and lifetime suicide attempt. Greater depressive symptom severity was associated with progressively higher levels of psychiatric and functional burden. Mild depressive symptoms are prevalent and associated with significant psychiatric and functional burden among older U.S. veterans, underscoring the importance of further assessment, monitoring, and evaluation of whether interventions targeting these symptoms can improve outcomes in this population.

title: Cumulative burden of mild TBI in Veterans: Accelerated age-related regional white matter deterioration along major white matter pathways.
abstract: Veterans experience mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) at significantly higher rates than civilians, alongside high rates of comorbid conditions such as PTSD, mood disorders, and alcohol abuse. These conditions have documented impacts on brain health that compound with age. Prior work has demonstrated reduced white matter (WM) integrity and greater age-related trends in WM deterioration in Veterans with mTBI compared to Veterans without mTBI. These studies provide important insights, yet were limited in their ability to differentiate mTBI effects from those of common comorbid conditions. It remains unclear whether specific WM tracts are more vulnerable to mTBI overall or if effects are limited to specific portions of tracts. This study assessed the impact of cumulative mTBI burden on WM aging in U.S. Veterans [n = 710, ages = 19-80, mean age = 37]. Associations between age, mTBI burden, and WM integrity measured via fractional anisotropy, and mean, axial, and radial diffusivity were analyzed using multivariate regression of whole-tract means and along-tract effect clustering via Freesurfer's TRACULA package. Whole-tract interactions by mTBI on age-related deterioration were found in the ventral cingulate bundle and optic radiation. Along-tract analysis identified interactions clusters along these and five additional tracts. In all cases, higher mTBI burden was associated with steeper cross-sectional relationships between age and microstructural integrity. mTBI differentially impacted specific sections of affected WM tracts. These results suggest greater age-related WM deterioration with higher mTBI burden after acute injury recovery extending into later age.

title: Alzheimer’s disease genetics converges on microglial and neuronal dysregulation
abstract: . Here we analysed data from 109,479 cases, 74,141 proxy cases, 2,131,799 controls and 499,708 proxy controls from diverse ancestries, identifying 118 loci in a multi-ancestry analysis and 9 additional loci in ancestry-specific analyses, 48 of which are new. We identified new AD risk genes, prioritized potential drug targets, and found that genes upregulated in microglia and downregulated in neurons in cases compared with controls were enriched for AD-associated genetic risk. Moreover, we improved polygenic prediction and estimated a SNP heritability of 16%, nearly threefold higher than previous estimates. Together, our findings show that the common-variant contribution to AD has been substantially underestimated, and reveal new molecular and cellular mechanisms as well as specific targets for future drug development research.

title: Supplementing the Interference Preservation Hypothesis With Motivational Interviewing–Based Feedback in a Rural Military Veteran With Moral Injury: Formative Case Study
abstract: Background: Veterans experiencing moral injury (ie, having witnessed or done something during military service that conflicts with one's value system) may encounter challenges that affect engagement and learning in online contexts. Objective: This formative case study examined the feasibility of integrating motivational interviewing (MI)-based delayed feedback, a key tenet of the interference preservation hypothesis, into an online program focused on machine learning instruction for a veteran with self-reported probable moral injury. Methods: One veteran completed a moral injury assessment and 17 training modules with various checkpoint assessments, followed by a machine learning module incorporating a pretest, MI-based delayed feedback, and a posttest. Results: The participant completed all instructional and assessment components. Checkpoint scores ranged from 66.7% to 100%, with 7 of 10 checkpoints exhibiting a perfect score. Machine learning performance increased from 90% at pretest to 100% at posttest following MI-based delayed feedback. Conclusions: These findings demonstrate the feasibility of integrating MI-based delayed feedback within an online data science instruction program and provide formative evidence supporting evaluation in larger samples.

title: Assessing Chiropractic, Complementary and Integrative Health, and Whole Health Services Utilization Among a Cohort of Pregnant and Postpartum Veterans.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Musculoskeletal (MSK) pain is common among women veterans and may be exacerbated during pregnancy and postpartum. However, little is known regarding pregnant veterans' engagement with chiropractic, complementary and integrative health (CIH), and Whole Health (e.g., health and wellness coaching) services in this population.
METHODS: Pregnant and postpartum veterans were identified from a longitudinal, prospective, multisite cohort study. Demographic and clinical characteristics were collected via Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) electronic health record and study survey data. Visits to VA-funded chiropractic, CIH, and Whole Health services during pregnancy, the first 9 postpartum months, and the 5 years preceding pregnancy were identified. We described participants' engagement with these services and assessed factors associated with use of any of these services during pregnancy and/or postpartum using logistic regression.
RESULTS: Of the 1,139 veterans included, 109 (10%) engaged with chiropractic, CIH, and/or Whole Health services during pregnancy and/or postpartum. Chiropractic (53%), acupuncture (20%), and massage therapy (10%) were the most used services. Visits to services were similar between pregnant (54%) and postpartum (46%) timeframes. Engagement with these services in the 5 years preceding pregnancy (odds ratio [OR]: 6.90; 95% confidence interval [CI] [4.24, 11.25]) and presence of a mental health diagnosis (anxiety, depression, and/or posttraumatic stress disorder) (OR: 1.79; 95% CI [1.02, 3.17]) were significantly associated with chiropractic, CIH, and/or Whole Health service use during pregnancy and/or postpartum. All other demographic and clinical variables were nonsignificant.
CONCLUSIONS: Results from this study may inform future implementation and administrative investigations of pregnant and postpartum veterans' use of chiropractic, CIH, and Whole Health services.

title: Rural and Non-Rural U.S. Veterans Receiving Virtual Geriatric Mental Health Services in the Clinical Resource Hubs.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Veterans Health Administration Clinical Resource Hubs are regional telehealth hubs that provide Veterans access needed to geriatric mental health (GMH) services without long drive times to urban centers to find specialists. This analysis characterized the GMH telehealth services to examine differences between rural and non-rural Veterans.
METHODS: Electronic health record data were extracted (October 2021 to September 2023) for encounters delivered by telehealth GMH teams staffed by geriatric psychiatrists, pharmacists, geropsychologists, and neuropsychologists. Variables included Veteran demographics, diagnoses, severity of care needs, services delivered and visit modality. Descriptive statistics, chi-square and t-tests summarized the data and examined rural and non-rural differences.
RESULTS: GMH clinicians completed 9282 encounters with 2013 Veterans (Mean age = 75.8). Most services were video to home (48.2%) followed by video to clinic (25.4%), and phone (22%) with no differences in service delivery modality among rural and non-rural Veterans. Rural Veterans had a higher proportion of psychotherapy and dementia-related services, and lower proportions of medication management and services for depression, anxiety, and serious mental illness compared with non-rural Veterans.
CONCLUSIONS: Older Veterans access virtual GMH care for a wide range of mental health and cognitive disorders. The apparent higher utilization of psychotherapy and dementia services for rural compared with non-rural Veterans may relate to barriers to obtaining these services locally, although it may be partially explained by variations in virtual team compositions and settings served.
RELEVANCE TO CLINICAL PRACTICE: This evaluation suggests high acceptability of video-delivered care for older, rural Veterans with high care needs.

title: Functional seizures: care experiences of U.S. Veterans and their care partners.
abstract: Functional seizures (FS) present substantial diagnostic and treatment challenges, particularly for Veterans with multiple medical and psychiatric comorbidities including post traumatic stress disorder, mood disorders and traumatic brain injury. To more effectively care for Veterans with FS and neuropsychiatric comorbidities, the US Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) neurology program office developed an interdisciplinary Mind Brain Program (MBP) to bridge the gap between neurology and mental health care for Veterans. In the context of expandeding MBP program development targeting Veterans with FS and complex comorbidities, this quality improvement project explored Veterans' lived experiences navigating FS diagnosis and treatment to identify opportunities for enhancing seizure care. Between April and July 2024, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 19 participants: 10 Veterans and 9 care partners. Using rapid qualitative analysis, we coded data into predefined themes to identify opportunities for improving care. Three major themes were identified within the predefined framework, with emergent subthemes. First, diagnostic challenges included clinicians' limited FS knowledge resulting in delayed video-EEG monitoring, and patient stigma, delaying diagnostic clarity. Second, limited access to specialty care was shaped by geographical barriers, lack of local expertise, scheduling difficulties, and reliance on community care referrals. Third, communication gaps within and between VA and community clinicians contributed to fragmented care, duplicated testing, and increased care partner burden. Findings are limited by a small sample from a single health system and by reliance on interview notes. Despite these limitation, findings highlight opportunities to improve FS care through standardized diagnostic pathways, enhanced clinician and patient education, strengthened communication within and between VA and community, and formal inclusion of care partners. These results can inform ongoing efforts to optimize FS care across the VA system.

title: Pharmacologic Treatments for Female Menopausal Vasomotor Symptoms: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis for the American College of Physicians.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Vasomotor symptoms (VMS) are common in perimenopausal and postmenopausal females.
PURPOSE: To evaluate benefits, harms, patient values and preferences, and cost-effectiveness of pharmacologic treatments for VMS.
DATA SOURCES: MEDLINE ALL, Embase, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials from inception to 3 March 2026.
STUDY SELECTION: Randomized trials of at least 8 weeks' duration of eligible medications in females with VMS reporting VMS frequency and severity, menopause-related quality of life (QoL), sleep quality, endometrial hyperplasia or cancer, and/or serious adverse events (SAEs); U.S. Food and Drug Administration and European Medicines Agency labels for additional harms.
DATA EXTRACTION: Data were abstracted by 1 reviewer and verified by a second reviewer. Independent, dual risk-of-bias assessments were performed. Certainty of evidence (COE) was assessed by 1 reviewer and overread by a second reviewer.
DATA SYNTHESIS: Ninety trials were included. COE was low to moderate for most comparisons. Compared with placebo, estrogens with or without progestogens, conjugated estrogen with bazedoxifene (CE/BZA), and oxybutynin reduced VMS frequency and severity. Compared with placebo, neurokinin receptor antagonists (NKRAs), serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs), selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), gabapentin, and progestogens reduced VMS frequency but not severity. Estrogen efficacy varied by dose but not route. Estrogens with and without progestogens, CE/BZA, NKRAs, SNRIs, and SSRIs improved menopause-related QoL; gabapentin, NKRAs, oxybutynin, SNRIs, and SSRIs improved sleep quality. Few SAEs were reported. Evidence was insufficient for patient values and preferences. Estrogens with or without progestogens are of high economic value (high COE). The NKRA fezolinetant has low value (moderate COE).
LIMITATIONS: Most studies were short-term and were not designed to evaluate SAEs or long-term harms. Observational studies that could address long-term harms were not included.
CONCLUSION: Estrogens reduced VMS frequency and severity and improved QoL (with or without progestogens and with BZA). NKRAs, SNRIs, and SSRIs improved VMS frequency, QoL, and sleep. Estrogens with and without progestogens were of high economic value. Harms data were limited. Little comparative information exists.
PRIMARY FUNDING SOURCE: American College of Physicians. (PROSPERO: CRD42024558116).

title: Skeletal muscle vasomotor function, ergonomics, histopathology, and gene expression in Veterans with Gulf War Illness
abstract: Abstract Background Gulf War Illness (GWI) is a constellation of debilitating symptoms including fatigue and muscle weakness reported in one-third of Veterans from coalition countries deployed in the Gulf War (1990-1991). We hypothesized that muscle vasomotor function, physiology, structure, and gene expression were different between 49 cases with GWI and 22 controls Veterans defined by the symptom-based Kansas GWI questionnaire. Methods We assessed profunda artery microvascular vasomotion with intra-arterial infusions of acetylcholine 10 −4 M (endothelium-dependent) and adenosine (endothelium-independent), and aerobic function by a symptom-limited cardiopulmonary exercise test. Biopsies of the vastus lateralis were frozen for later histology, western blot analysis, and unbiased gene expression using bulk RNA sequencing (RNAseq). Results Veteran GWI cases and controls have similar microvascular endothelium-dependent function (difference = −6.6%, 95%CI = −31.5%, 18.4%), endothelium independent function (difference = −10%, 95%CI = −95%, 75%) vasomotor function. The study has adequate power to identify known factors related to impaired microvascular endothelium-dependent function, such as smoking (difference = −42.5%, 95%CI = −79.0%, − 6.0%). Cases and controls have similar aerobic capacity (difference peak V̇O 2 = −1.5, 95%CI = −4.8, 1.9 mL/kg/min), V̇O 2 at anabolic threshold (difference = −1.0, 95%CI = −4.1, 2.1 mL/kg/min). Cases and controls have similar muscle histology, mitochondrial volume and density, and content of glycolytic, anerobic, tricarboxylic acid cycle and mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation enzymes. RNAseq reveals no metabolic pathway gene dysregulation associated with GWI. Conclusions Symptoms of GWI triggered by the physical and psychological trauma of war are unrelated to multiple peripheral vascular and muscle parameters. GWI patients should obtain a similar training effect from physical activity as those without GWI.

title: A CCL21 gene-modified dendritic cell vaccine combined with pembrolizumab in advanced non-small cell lung cancer: a phase I trial.
abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed treatment for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but resistance to these therapies is common. We report here results from a phase I trial combining intratumoral injection of a CCL21-expressing dendritic cell (CCL21-DC) vaccine with pembrolizumab in patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03546361). The primary objectives were to determine the maximum administered dose (MAD) in the dose escalation phase and the objective response rate (ORR) in the dose expansion. Eleven patients were enrolled in the dose escalation cohort, and 12 patients were treated in the dose expansion cohort at the MAD of 3 ×107 cells/injection. The trial did not meet its primary endpoint for ORR as no objective responses were observed, though 36.8% of patients achieved a best response of stable disease. The combination therapy was well tolerated. Post-hoc analyses of longitudinal biopsies revealed that the therapy increased tumor infiltration by CD4+ T cells and novel T cell clones. Disease stability was associated with increased T cell receptor diversity and greater expansion of novel clones following therapy. However, many novel clones failed to persist over time, and immunosuppressive myeloid signaling signatures were identified across time points. Our findings overall demonstrated that CCL21-DC vaccination combined with pembrolizumab can promote T cell infiltration, but this did not translate into meaningful clinical efficacy, potentially due to limited tumor specificity of the T cell response and an inability to fully reprogram the tumor microenvironment.

title: Digital and Coaching Interventions for Uptake of Cancer Genetic Testing: The MiGHT Randomized Clinical Trial.
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Germline genetic testing (GT) for hereditary cancer risk can inform cancer treatment, screening, and prevention, yet testing rates remain low. Alternative strategies are needed to improve facilitation of GT.
OBJECTIVE: To compare 2 patient-level interventions to increase uptake of hereditary cancer GT against usual care.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: The Michigan Genetic Hereditary Testing (MiGHT) randomized clinical trial analyzed self-reported GT outcome data from participants meeting clinical GT criteria between April 21, 2022, and November 21, 2025. Participants were adults (age ≥18 years) who met national criteria for genetic evaluation and had not previously completed germline GT recruited from oncology, primary care, and gastroenterology practices; research registries; and the general public in Michigan. Data were analyzed from April 30, 2025, to May 1, 2026.
INTERVENTIONS: Participants were randomized to either telephone-based health coaching, a self-directed digital intervention, or usual care. Both interventions incorporated genetics education and motivational interviewing concepts.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: GT uptake was assessed at 6- and 12-month time points. The primary outcome was completion of GT by 6 months. The effects of study group on GT uptake were evaluated using logistic regression, adjusting for cancer history, age, gender, and race.
RESULTS: A total of 793 participants (median [IQR] age, 64 [51-71] years; 458 [57.8%] female) were randomized to health coaching (261 participants), the digital intervention (265 participants), or usual care (267 participants). Overall, 31 participants (4.9%) reported completing GT by the 6-month time point, and 76 participants (9.6%) underwent GT across the 12-month study period. Compared with usual care, participants in the digital intervention group had higher odds of completing GT by 6 months (adjusted odds ratio [AOR], 3.88; 97.5% CI, 1.27-14.80), while those in the health coaching group had higher odds of completing GT by 12 months (AOR, 2.25; 97.5% CI, 1.11-4.77). Participants in the digital intervention group were more likely to express intention to test at 6 months (AOR, 2.36; 95% CI, 1.44-3.93), whereas those in the health coaching group had higher intention at both 6 (AOR, 2.99; 95% CI, 1.83-4.95) and 12 (AOR, 2.29; 95% CI 1.29-4.15) months compared with usual care.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this randomized clinical trial of GT interventions, GT uptake was higher among participants who received the digital or health coaching interventions compared with usual care, although overall testing rates were low. These results underscore the importance of content delivery, motivational messaging, and alternative GT care models.

title: CRISPR-Cas9 screen identifies eIF4G2 as a regulator of CD8+ T cell dysfunction.
abstract: CD8+ T cells directly target and kill cancer cells and are required for effective antitumor immunity. However, CD8+ T cells may become dysfunctional when exposed to chronic antigen stimulation during cancer. Dysfunction is characterized by reduced proliferation, increased expression of inhibitory receptors, and impaired effector function, yet the genetic mechanisms controlling dysfunction remain poorly understood. Therefore, we developed a murine ex vivo chronic stimulation model that recapitulates features of CD8+ T cell dysfunction observed within the tumor microenvironment. By coupling this system with genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 loss-of-function screening, we discovered that the progression of murine CD8+ T cells to a dysfunctional state required eIF4G2, a noncanonical mRNA translation factor. Deletion of eIF4G2 restored CD8+ T cell survival and proliferation during chronic stimulation conditions in vitro. Transcriptomic, proteomic, and flow cytometric analyses revealed that eIF4G2 deletion shifts CD8+ T cell phenotype from a dysfunctional state to a proliferative state. eIF4G2 depletion reduced oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation, and accumulation of misfolded protein aggresomes during chronic in vitro stimulation. Finally, eIF4G2-depleted cells mediated enhanced tumor control in a murine model of melanoma. These data suggest that targeting eIF4G2 may promote CD8+ T cell resilience and improve therapeutic antitumor immunity.

title: Patient Travel Experiences for Methadone Dosing Visits.
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Patients often experience travel-related barriers to methadone dosing at opioid treatment programs (OTPs), but the nature of their experiences are not well understood.
OBJECTIVE: To characterize patient experiences with travel to OTPs for regular methadone dosing visits at a large multisite OTP in Washington state.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This qualitative study utilized an embedded mixed-methods design. Our sample included patients currently receiving methadone treatment at 2 OTP sites in Washington state from November 2024 to February 2026 (including mobile units that operated as extension of the sites). Data were analyzed between February and July 2026.
EXPOSURES: Experiences of travel to OTPs for regular, in-person observed methadone dosing.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Results of a survey administered to patients regarding the modality, time, and cost (eg, gas, childcare) of traveling to the OTP. A subsample of surveyed patients were interviewed about their experiences with and perspectives on traveling for dosing visits. Survey data were analyzed descriptively. Interviews were coded using rapid assessment process.
RESULTS: Our sample included 98 survey participants and 16 qualitative interview participants (median [IQR] age, 43.0 [38.8-50.3] years; 8 cisgender women [50.0%]). Among survey respondents, 54 (55.1%) drove themselves to the OTP, 21 (21.4%) were driven by another person, 12 (12.3%) took public transportation, and 6 (6.1%) took insurer-sponsored medical transportation; 18 (18.4%) reported a disabling condition and 16 (16.2%) needed an assistive device for walking. Participants spent a mean (range) 82.5 (10.0-330.0) minutes round trip and $15.80 ($0-$200.00) in travel-related costs for each visit. Qualitative interviews illuminated that, while distance was often a barrier, unpredictable OTP wait times or conflicts with work, medical, or family obligations also mattered considerably. Participants shared that dosing visits directly prohibited their ability to work, but missing visits put participants at risk for return to opioid use and treatment stagnation.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this mixed-methods qualitative study, requiring regular visits for in-person observed methadone dosing presented significant structural barriers that affect patients' treatment experience, adherence, and lives. Increasing the flexibility and accessibility of methadone treatment-through policies and novel care practices that actively seek to minimize burden of travel to the OTP and destigmatize care-is essential to enhance care quality and equity.

title: Effect of home blood pressure monitoring on major adverse cardiovascular events and all-cause mortality – results from the VA HOMESTEAD study
abstract: Abstract Importance Home blood pressure monitoring (HBPM) has been shown to lower blood pressure (BP) in randomized trials, however its real-world effect on clinical outcomes is not known. Objective To determine the association between HBPM and clinical outcomes including cardiovascular events and mortality. Design Target trial emulation employing matched cohorts with index-date follow-up. Setting Veterans Health Administration (VHA) telehealth program. Participants Eligible Veterans had uncontrolled BP (defined as a systolic BP >140 mmHg) at a primary care visit within VHA, with a systolic BP >140 mmHg at the prior primary care visit or average systolic BP >140 mmHg over the year prior. The HBPM (intervention) group included eligible Veterans who were enrolled in a HBPM program for hypertension between January 1, 2013 and December 31, 2019. Individuals in the control group (usual care) were selected from eligible Veterans who were not enrolled in HBPM. Controls were matched with those in the intervention, in part, on demographics, baseline blood pressure and antihypertensive medication use, baseline frailty, mortality risk, and selected comorbidities. Exposure HBPM in the VHA telehealth program Main Outcomes All-cause mortality and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), defined as the first occurrence during follow-up of acute myocardial infarction, stroke, acute heart failure, or unstable angina. Results Among 30,203 Veterans enrolled in HBPM and 30,096 non-enrolled controls, with a median duration of 202 days of HBPM and 6.4 years of follow-up, HBPM was associated with 8.3% lower risk of mortality (hazard ratio 0.92; 95% confidence interval 0.89, 0.95) and a 4.1% higher risk of MACE (HR 1.04; 95% CI 1.01, 1.08). In analyses calibrated for negative control outcomes, there was no longer a statistically significant association between HBPM and MACE. Conclusions and Relevance HBPM as utilized in routine clinical care among a large national cohort of adults with uncontrolled hypertension was associated with reduced risk of mortality. The association between HBPM with increased risk of MACE may have been due to ascertainment differences between those enrolled and not enrolled in HBPM.

title: Genome-Wide Association Study Meta-Analysis of Central Serous Chorioretinopathy
abstract: Importance: The pathophysiology of central serous chorioretinopathy (CSC) remains incompletely understood, and there is ongoing debate regarding the origin of primary dysfunction. Objective: To elucidate the genetic architecture of CSC and map susceptibility loci to specific ocular cell types and molecular pathways. Design, Setting, and Participants: This genetic association study was a genome-wide association study (GWAS) meta-analysis aggregating data from 5 large biobank cohorts and included 2584 patients with CSC and 1 044 455 control participants of European ancestry. Cohort data were from July 1, 2010, to October 31, 2023; data analysis was performed from Febuary 2024 to January 2026. Post-GWAS functional mapping was performed using mendelian randomization, bayesian colocalization, and single-cell disease relevance scoring across human ocular tissue atlases. The relevance of the genetic findings was demonstrated by building a CSC genetic risk score and applying it to the UK Biobank (UKB). Main Outcomes and Measures: Identification of risk loci reaching the genome-wide threshold, prioritized putative causal genes, enrichment of genetic risk within specific ocular tissues and cell types, and performance of a GRS in the independent UKB dataset. Results: The meta-analysis identified 10 risk loci reaching the genome-wide threshold (P < 5 × 10-8), including 3 novel loci (TGFB1, LINC00551, and LOC105375630) and 7 replicated loci (CFH, GATA5, PREX1, CD46, NOTCH4, PTPRB, and TNFRSF10A). Integrative post-GWAS analysis prioritized 10 genes, including TGFB1, TNFRSF10A, and CFH, as likely causal effectors. Single-cell enrichment mapping revealed that CSC genetic risk is concentrated in scleral tissue (P < .001) and vascular endothelial cells (P < .001). Mendelian randomization pointed to circulating TGFB1 and TNFRSF10A levels as associated with CSC risk. A CSC genetic risk score applied in UKB revealed a higher frequency of CSC-relevant abnormalities on macular optical coherence tomography in participants in the top 1% of polygenic risk (18/109 [16.5%] vs 8/134 [6.0%]; difference, 10.5 percentage points; 95% CI, 2.6-19.1; adjusted odds ratio, 4.05; 95% CI, 1.65-10.87; P = .002). Conclusions and Relevance: Convergent genetic evidence supports CSC as a primary disorder of the sclera and choroidal vasculature with retinal pigment epithelium changes likely representing a downstream consequence. Integrative post-GWAS analysis pointed to complement regulation (CFH, CD46), vascular integrity and endothelial cell signaling (PTPRB, TNFRSF10A, NOTCH4, PREX1), and scleral extracellular matrix biology (TGFB1) as important in CSC.

title: Abstract 5545: Genetic Prioritization of Nitric Oxide Signaling as a Therapeutic Target for Resistant Hypertension
abstract: Background: Hypertension affects over 100 million adults in the United States, and blood pressure (BP) control remains difficult to achieve for ~25% of treated individuals. Apparent treatment-resistant hypertension (aTRH), defined as uncontrolled BP despite treatment with three antihypertensive medications or use of four or more medications regardless of control, is a high-risk phenotype associated with elevated cardiovascular, renal, and all-cause morbidity and mortality. Despite this burden, few therapies target the biology underlying treatment resistance, which remains poorly understood. Fewer than 40 loci have been identified for aTRH through genome-wide association studies (GWAS). Methods: We performed a large multi-ancestry GWAS meta-analysis of aTRH (92,242 cases and 119,407 individuals with controlled hypertension, including five multi-national cohorts), enabling improved representation of non-European genetic ancestries. This analysis was integrated with a genetically-informed drug repurposing pipeline to identify existing FDA-approved therapies for other indications that may have potential to treat aTRH. S-PrediXcan analyses identified genes with predicted expression associated with aTRH risk. Gene targets were mapped to drugs using DrugBank, Connectivity Map, Open Targets, and DGIdb. Drug-gene pairs were prioritized based on clinical relevance, safety/feasibility, and consistency with therapeutic direction. Two-sample Mendelian randomization was used to evaluate whether modifying target activity, proxied by predicted gene expression, influenced aTRH risk. Results: The GWAS meta-analysis identified 113 significant independent loci, including 83 novel. Predicted expression of GUCY1A1, PPARG, and HTR4 proxied 13 FDA-approved medications. The strongest protective signal implicated nitric-oxide guanylate cyclase signaling: increased GUCY1A1 expression, aligned with effects of vericiguat and sodium nitroprusside, was associated with lower aTRH risk (odds ratio [CI] = 0.89 [0.84-0.93], p = 3.37x10 -2 ). In contrast, PPARG -targeting drugs for type II diabetes and hypertriglyceridemia and HTR4 -proxied prucalopride were associated with increased risk. No evidence of directional pleiotropy was observed. Discussion: In the largest multi-ancestry genetic study of aTRH to date, soluble guanylate cyclase signaling emerged as a genetically supported therapeutic target. Genetic evidence linking increased GUCY1A1 expression to lower risk highlights nitric oxide signaling as a potential mechanism underlying treatment resistance. Among prioritized candidates, vericiguat emerged as the most clinically promising repurposing candidate. Currently approved to treat heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, vericiguat enhances nitric oxide signaling to promote vasodilation, representing a novel means of treating aTRH.

title: Abstract 9597: Polygenic Risk Scores, Statin Use, and Cardiovascular Outcomes in People with HIV: A Million Veteran Program (MVP) Study
abstract: Background: People with HIV (PWH) have an elevated cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk that is underestimated by current risk calculators. Excess risk reflects traditional risk factors plus HIV-specific mechanisms, including persistent immune activation, chronic inflammation, and antiretroviral therapy (ART)-related metabolic effects. Polygenic risk scores (PRS), largely derived from European ancestry populations, have uncertain performance in PWH and may not generalize across diverse populations. Research Question: Evaluate PRS performance for CVD outcomes and determine whether PRS modifies the association between statin use and incident CVD for PWH. Methods: We analyzed Million Veteran Program participants’ genomic data which is linked to longitudinal Veteran Administration (VA) electronic health records. Two samples were used: (1) the full cohort (n=412,684; 7,951 PWH) to evaluate PRS for coronary artery disease (CAD), peripheral arterial disease (PAD), and LDL cholesterol across European (EUR), African (AFR), and Hispanic (HIS) ancestry groups and (2) a statin-exposed subset (n=99,134; 1,645 PWH) for Cox models of statin use and incident CVD. Outcomes included myocardial infarction (MI), ischemic stroke, PAD, composite CVD, and CVD mortality. Models were adjusted for age, sex, BMI, total cholesterol, systolic blood pressure, HDL cholesterol, ancestry group, smoking, diabetes, PRS LDL , PRS PAD and PRS CAD , and among PWH, ART use, CD4 count, and HIV viral load. Results: PRS performance varied by ancestry. In PWH, PRS CAD was associated with myocardial infarction and composite CVD in EUR (p<0.001, p=0.043 respectively) and AFR (p=0.024, p=0.041, respectively), and only with MI in HIS groups (p=0.023). PRS LDL and PRS PAD were not associated with outcomes across ancestries. In adjusted models, statin use was associated with lower composite CVD risk in PWH (HR, 0.68, 95% CI 0.55-0.84]), where the benefit was largely driven by lower PAD risk (EUR: HR 0.60; AFR: HR 0.69). Statins were beneficial across ancestry groups, and their effect was unmodified by PRS. Conclusion: In PWH, PRS showed limited and ancestry-dependent utility for CVD risk prediction, with reduced performance outside EUR ancestry populations. Statin therapy reduced CVD risk largely through PAD reduction and was effective across ancestry groups independent of PRS. These findings support statin use in PWH regardless of PRS-based risk stratification and highlight the need for inclusive genomic risk models.

title: Facilitators and barriers to lethal means counseling in veterans with substance use disorder: A qualitative analysis of veteran and clinician perspectives.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: U.S. Veterans with substance use disorders are at disproportionately high risk for suicide. Lethal Means Counseling is a collaborative approach where clinicians and Veterans discuss strategies to reduce access to lethal means. While evidence is strong for lethal means counseling reducing suicide risk broadly, the unique needs and experiences of this population are not well understood. This qualitative study sought to elicit perspectives from U.S. Veterans and Veterans Health Administration clinicians about barriers and facilitators to the delivery of and participation in Lethal Means Counseling for Veterans with substance use disorders.
METHODS: In this pragmatic and postpositivist study, semi-structured qualitative interviews were conducted with 15 U.S. Veterans with substance use disorders identified through electronic health record review and recent completion of lethal means counseling and with 10 Veterans Health Administration clinicians who administered lethal means counseling. Interviews explored experiences with lethal means counseling and substance use in relation to suicide risk. Inductive and iterative thematic analyses were used to code transcripts of interviews for barriers and facilitators at the Individual, Inner Setting, Outer Setting, and Innovation levels of the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research.
RESULTS: Six themes were identified for barriers, including substance use as a coping strategy, lack of assessment and access to care, nondisclosure and autonomy, ease of access, military culture, and substances increase risk. Three themes were identified for facilitators, including recognition of use as problematic, sharing resources, and providing a rationale for lethal means counseling.
CONCLUSION: Veterans with substance use disorders experience unique challenges that interfere with efforts to reduce suicide risk. The findings of this study highlight current gaps and opportunities for improving conversations during Lethal Means Counseling and may help enhance implementation among those with Substance Use Disorders. Substance use magnifies suicide risk and it will be important for future research to develop strategies to help mitigate this risk.

title: Evaluating symptom reduction and functional recovery among combat veterans undergoing the Stress Inoculation Training Health Sustainment and Restoration (SIT-HSR) protocol.
abstract: This study reports a multisite program evaluation of Stress Inoculation Training-Health Sustainment and Restoration, a manualized, group-based intervention delivered within routine Veterans Affairs care for veterans with posttraumatic stress, depression, and related comorbidity. The purpose of the evaluation was to examine feasibility across implementation periods and delivery contexts and to describe symptom and functional improvement during participation, rather than to test intervention efficacy. A total of 281 veterans enrolled across three implementation periods and multiple Veterans Affairs sites; measure availability varied by period and outcome. The Posttraumatic Stress Disorder Checklist for Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fifth edition; Beck Depression Inventory-II; Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test; Brief Addiction Monitor; and Situational Adaptation to Stress Scale were used as available at pre- and posttreatment. Linear mixed-effects models were treated as the primary inferential analyses because they accounted for repeated measurement, site-level clustering, and incomplete data, whereas measure-specific Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and site/period comparisons were treated as secondary sensitivity analyses. Participants improved during program participation on posttraumatic stress disorder, depression, alcohol use, and stress adaptation outcomes, with the largest gains observed for stress adaptation and functioning. Mean Posttraumatic Stress Disorder Checklist for Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fifth edition, scores decreased from 50.56 to 42.52, and mean Beck Depression Inventory-II scores decreased from 31.35 to 25.46, while mean Situational Adaptation to Stress Scale scores increased from 20.82 to 31.13. Improvement patterns were observed across implementation periods and in both in-person and telehealth delivery contexts. An overall difference in Posttraumatic Stress Disorder Checklist for Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fifth edition, scores was observed between Periods 2 and 3, but change over time did not differ significantly by period. Overall, these findings support the feasibility of implementing Stress Inoculation Training-Health Sustainment and Restoration across Veterans Affairs settings and suggest that participation in the program was associated with symptom reduction and functional improvement. As the design was observational and lacked a comparison condition, the results should not be interpreted as establishing intervention effectiveness, equivalence across formats, or scalability beyond the contexts studied. title: Understanding and Leveraging Implementation Science Within a Clinical Informatics Framework for Allergy/Immunology.
abstract: The integration of research discoveries into routine clinical care is often slow and resource-intensive, particularly in allergy and immunology, where advances in biologics, immunotherapy, precision diagnostics, and guideline-driven management continue to evolve rapidly. Implementation science provides a structured approach to understand and address the gaps between research discovery and real-world patient care. In asthma, food allergy, atopic dermatitis, drug allergy, and primary immune disorders, variation in clinician knowledge, health system infrastructure, reimbursement models, patient demographics, and staffing patterns contribute to inconsistent uptake of evidence-based interventions. Implementation science offers tools to systematically evaluate these contextual factors and develop strategies that improve adoption, fidelity, sustainability, and equity in allergic and immunologic care. By offering theory-informed frameworks to design, adapt, and evaluate interventions across diverse clinical settings, implementation science advances the study of evidence-to-practice care gaps in allergy and immunology. When applied thoughtfully, these methods enhance implementation of specialty guidelines, practice parameters, and emerging therapies, while addressing multilevel determinants of care delivery. With the rapidly growing application of precision medicine and augmented intelligence to allergy and immunology practice, the study of how to best apply technological and research discovery to clinical practice will be needed to promote equitable uptake of evidence-based care.

title: Implementation of a novel video telehealth program for musculoskeletal disorder self-management in U.S. military veterans during the COVID-19 pandemic combining yoga therapy with education.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) are highly prevalent, costly, and burdensome. Over 40% of United States military veterans are diagnosed with chronic pain related to the spine. Various clinical practice guidelines recommend nonpharmacological treatments for the management of chronic MSDs including spinal pain. During the COVID-19 pandemic, face-to-face healthcare was diverted to telehealth platforms to minimize exposure of communicable disease. To address barriers to in-person treatment, veterans experiencing pain associated with MSDs at one Veterans Health Administration Medical Center were offered a novel evidence-based approach incorporating patient education and experiential movement through a telehealth modality.
METHODS: We describe a novel telehealth clinic for self-management of MSDs offered from February 2021 to September 2021. The clinic consisted of a one-hour class offered weekly for four weeks, and included didactic lecture content and movement therapy. The classes were offered by a chiropractor and a yoga instructor. We retrospectively evaluated implementation of the telehealth clinic, including program attendance. Attendance of three or more of the four sessions (75%) was selected as a pragmatic descriptive indicator of patient participation.
RESULTS: Seventeen veterans participated in three cohorts over six months. The mean age of participants was 54.8 years (SD: 14.6; range 34 to 80), and 12 (70.6%) were male. Seven participants (41.2%) attended at least three of the four sessions, including five (29.4%) who attended all four sessions. Participants represented a geographically diverse population, with varying distances from VA facilities and VA facilities with chiropractic services.
CONCLUSIONS: We describe a clinical demonstration of a telehealth clinic for MSDs offering evidence-based content with experiential movement. This program was delivered through video telehealth and a subset of participants sustained attendance across most of the four-session series. The preliminary information reported could be used for development and expansion of this type of clinic for telehealth chronic MSD management. Future studies are needed to determine the impact of telehealth delivery of MSD care on outcomes, cost, and patient preference. Expanding telehealth delivery of MSD care may be particularly valuable for rural veterans, those lacking access to transportation, or patients who experience barriers to attending in-person appointments.

title: Outcomes from a Pilot Trial of a Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) Tobacco Cessation Intervention for Veterans at Heightened Risk for Suicide
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Tobacco use has consistently been linked to suicide risk, and some data suggest that tobacco cessation may reduce risk. However, higher risk individuals are typically excluded from clinical trials. Dialectical Behavior Therapy is a psychotherapy approach originally designed to reduce suicide risk that may also be beneficial in treating addiction by enhancing emotion regulation and distress tolerance skills. METHODS: The present study was a randomized pilot trial comparing a standard tobacco cessation intervention to a DBT-based integrated intervention for tobacco cessation and suicide prevention. Veterans (n = 68) who were daily users of cigarettes and/or e-cigarettes were randomized to DBT for cessation (DBT-C) or to treatment as usual (TAU). Participants in both conditions attended 12 weekly group psychotherapy sessions and were followed for a total of 24 weeks to evaluate changes in tobacco use, suicidality, emotion regulation and overall satisfaction with the intervention. RESULTS: DBT-C and TAU participants did not differ in terms of abstinence at end-of-treatment or 24-week follow-up. There was a trend toward greater improvement in emotion regulation in DBT-C versus TAU. Participants generally were satisfied with the intervention. CONCLUSIONS: This pilot trial provides preliminary evidence that individuals who use tobacco and are at elevated suicide risk can be effectively engaged in tobacco cessation interventions, and that such interventions may benefit emotional functioning as well as reducing tobacco use. DBT-C appears to be a potentially effective approach but additional, larger-scale research is needed to enable a more thorough assessment.

title: Shared additive- and variance-associated genetic architecture of cardiac structure and function
abstract: Cardiac remodeling underlies cardiomyopathy and heart failure, yet how common genetic effects are organized across the four chambers, and whether they influence phenotypic variability beyond additive genetic effects, remains unclear. We analyzed 22 cardiac magnetic resonance phenotypes in up to 77,271 UK Biobank participants. Additive mapping identified 748 locus-trait associations across 239 regions. Multivariate fine-mapping revealed that 96% of signals showed effects across multiple cardiac chambers, while resolving independent signals with distinct anatomical profiles, including predominantly atrial and ventricular signals at RBM20. Fine-mapped signal sharing formed three robust communities corresponding broadly to atrial function, chamber remodeling and ventricular systolic function. Variance mapping identified 19 associations, 13 without a nearby additive signal. Individual variance loci and polygenic effects generalized to clinical echocardiographic phenotypes and outcomes in the Penn Medicine Biobank. These findings reveal cardiac common-variant architecture as broadly shared yet locally heterogeneous and identify phenotypic variability as a partly distinct genetic dimension.

title: Adipocyte enhancer binding protein 1 (AEBP1) inhibition mediates cardiac reverse remodeling by regulating MRTFB and RUNX2 signaling
abstract: Persistent activation of cardiac fibroblasts drives excessive extracellular matrix deposition, promoting maladaptive myocardial fibrosis, adverse remodeling, and heart failure (HF) progression. Although Adipocyte enhancer binding protein 1 (AEBP1) and Aortic carboxypeptidase-like protein (ACLP, full-length protein coded by AEBP1) have been implicated in pathological fibrosis across multiple organs, including the heart, its functional role in cardiac fibrosis remains unknown. Here, we demonstrate that AEBP1 is a mediator of myocardial fibrosis and adverse cardiac remodeling. Fibroblast-specific knockout or myocardial knockdown of Aebp1 significantly improves cardiac function and prevents pathological remodeling in murine models of myocardial ischemia and pressure-overload induced injury. In human myocardial tissue culture studies, ACLP overexpression induces pathological remodeling in non-failing hearts, whereas AEBP1 knockdown induces structural reverse remodeling in failing myocardium. Mechanistically, ACLP regulates the expression of MRTFB, RUNX2, SM22 and COL1A1, thereby orchestrating fibroblast activation. Collectively, these findings identify AEBP1 as a mediator of myocardial fibrosis and highlights its inhibition as a potential anti-fibrotic therapy following acute injury. Cardiac fibrosis contributes to adverse remodeling and heart failure progression, but its molecular drivers remain poorly understood. Here, the authors show that ACLP/AEBP1 promotes cardiac fibrosis and AEBP1 inhibition following injury, improves cardiac structure and function.

title: Late radiation-induced brain injury is associated with functional cerebrovascular impairment without structural vessel loss in mice
abstract: ABSTRACT Background Radiation-induced brain injury (RIBI) is a major and often irreversible complication of cranial radiotherapy, affecting up to 90% of long-term survivors. Although cerebrovascular damage is a leading mechanistic hypothesis, whether chronic resting hypoperfusion occurs independently of structural vessel loss remains unknown. The aim of this study was to comprehensively characterize cerebrovascular, structural, and behavioral outcomes in a murine model of late RIBI to determine the primary drivers of vascular dysfunction. Methods Adult C57BL/6 mice underwent 12 Gy whole-brain irradiation and were assessed one year later using laser speckle contrast imaging (LSCI), 7T MRI, immunohistochemistry, and behavioral testing. Results Irradiated mice exhibited reduced pial flow velocity and flow area by LSCI, indicative of upstream cerebrovascular dysfunction, while bulk cortical tissue perfusion was preserved. This pial hypoperfusion was accompanied by cerebral atrophy, decreased T2* relaxation time and tissue iron deposition consistent with chronic microhemorrhage across multiple brain regions by MRI, blood-brain barrier disruption reflected by reduced ZO-1 and VE-cadherin expression, and increased anxiety-like behavior. Strikingly, capillary density, pericyte coverage, astrocyte endfeet, and NeuN-positive neuronal nuclei were all preserved. Conclusion These findings demonstrate that functional vascular impairment - not structural vessel or neuronal loss - drives hypoperfusion and blood-brain barrier disruption in late RIBI. This dissociation between vascular dysfunction and rarefaction reframes the pathophysiology of RIBI and identifies endothelial dysfunction as a tractable therapeutic target for intervention.

title: A systematic review with meta-analysis of psychosocial suicide prevention interventions among U.S. military service members and veterans.
abstract: Suicide rates among U.S. military service members and veterans are disproportionately high relative to civilians and increasing over time. Veterans and service members experience unique suicide risk factors, highlighting the need for suicide prevention approaches optimized for this community. A vast number of psychosocial suicide prevention treatments produce variable effects (ranging from small to moderate) on suicidal thoughts and behaviors in the general population, and findings often do not concur with studies conducted in military and veteran samples. The present study systematically reviewed 47 and meta-analyzed 41 controlled trial studies (N = 5,540,004) published in EBSCO, PubMed, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials and other sources between 1996 and 2026 assessing the efficacy of psychosocial suicide prevention interventions among U.S. military veterans and service members. Risk of bias and several participant, intervention, and study design characteristics were assessed for potential moderating effects. Suicide prevention interventions significantly outperformed control conditions in reducing risk of suicide attempts (RR = 0.68, 95% CI [0.56, 0.83], p < .001) and self-harm (RR = 0.79, 95% CI [0.67, 0.93], p = .004), but not suicidal ideation (ps > 0.50). Meta-analysis for suicide death outcomes was inconclusive due to sample limitations. Few participant, intervention, or study design moderators of treatment efficacy emerged, contrary to hypotheses (e.g., no effect of CBT, clinical severity). Findings suggest that psychosocial suicide prevention interventions demonstrate efficacy in reducing risk of suicidal behaviors but do not establish efficacy in reducing suicidal ideation or suicide death risk in the U.S. military and veteran community.

title: Genetic Liability to Opioid Use Disorder and Dementia-Related Biological Pathways: A Mendelian Randomisation Study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Opioid use disorder (OUD) is increasingly recognised as a risk factor for cognitive impairment and dementia, but the biological mechanisms underlying this association remain unclear. We aimed to investigate the involvement of established neurodegenerative, vascular, or inflammatory pathways.
METHODS: We performed a two-sample Mendelian randomisation study using summary-level genetic data from nine genome-wide association studies of individuals predominantly of European ancestry. Genetic instruments for OUD liability were used to estimate associations with neurodegenerative, vascular, and inflammatory phenotypes, including amyloid-β, tau, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, cerebral microinfarcts, and C-reactive protein (CRP). Causal effects were estimated using inverse-variance weighted Mendelian randomisation, with replication and Bayesian colocalisation analyses used to further evaluate the findings.
RESULTS: There was little evidence that genetic liability to OUD was associated with amyloid-β, tau, or vascular phenotypes. A modest positive association was observed with CRP (β = 0.11, 95% CI 0.04-0.18, p = 2 × 10-3). This association was replicated in an independent dataset (β = 0.12, 95% CI 0.05-0.19, p = 1.59 × 10-3). A nominal inverse association was also observed with IL-15 (β = -0.23, 95% CI -0.43 to -0.03, p = 2.2 × 10-2), although colocalisation did not support a shared causal variant at implicated loci.
CONCLUSIONS: Genetic liability to OUD showed little evidence of association with the neurodegenerative or vascular phenotypes examined; however, these findings do not exclude the involvement of Alzheimer's disease or cerebrovascular pathways, particularly given the limited power and the use of only three genetic instruments. The observed inflammatory associations should be considered hypothesis-generating, particularly given the lack of colocalisation support, and require further investigation.

title: Examining the Etiological Specificity of Genetic Risk for Alcohol Use Disorder and Alcohol Consumption through Symptom-Level Mediation Analyses
abstract: Abstract Introduction Polygenic scores (PGSs) for alcohol use disorder (AUD) may capture genetic liability related to alcohol consumption as well as broader transdiagnostic traits, including impulsivity, aggression, and neuroticism. However, the extent to which these traits account for associations between an AUD PGS and the presentation of AUD symptoms remains unclear. Thus, to better understand the genetic influences captured by an AUD PGS, the present study used mediation analyses to examine whether these transdiagnostic traits differentially mediate the relations between PGSs for AUD and individual AUD symptoms while conducting a parallel analysis using a PGS of alcohol consumption to examine differences in the genetic influences underlying AUD and consumption. Method Participants were drawn from the UCSF Family Alcoholism Study. Separate mediation models examined maximum habitual drinks ( N = 1,611) and MMPI-2 Personality Psychopathology Five (PSY-5) scales ( N = 1,464) as mediators of the association between AUD/alcohol consumption PGSs and individual AUD symptoms. Covariates included sex, age, and 10 ancestry principal components. Observations were modeled as clustered within families, and a Bonferroni correction was applied ( p < .0045). Results Relations between the AUD PGS and AUD symptoms were fully mediated by maximum habitual drinks and partially mediated by neuroticism for nearly all symptoms, but not by other PSY-5 scales. Relations between the alcohol consumption PGS and AUD symptoms were fully mediated by maximum habitual drinks alone, with no mediation observed through any personality psychopathology measure. Discussion Current AUD and alcohol consumption PGSs appear to capture genetic liability that operates predominantly through alcohol consumption. However, the AUD PGS may capture genetic influences on broader transdiagnostic factors as well, with neuroticism acting as a partial mediator. Thus, etiological interpretations of the AUD PGS as solely a measure of AUD risk should be made cautiously.

title: Type I IFN promotes ILC2-to-ILC1 plasticity in pre-clinical radiation-induced lung injury.
abstract: Radiation-induced lung injury (RILI) is a common dose-limiting toxicity after radiotherapy for lung cancer, but the immunological mechanisms contributing to RILI pathogenesis remain poorly understood. Here we analyze a RILI mouse model using high-dose, restricted-field irradiation to the left lung. Flow cytometry and cytokine profiling analysis of innate lymphoid cells (ILC) reveals a radiation-induced shift from lung-resident type 2 ILCs (ILC2) toward pro-inflammatory type 1 ILCs (ILC1). Single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis of mouse lung ILC populations after radiation suggests that type I interferon (IFN) promotes radiation-induced ILC2-to-ILC1 plasticity. In vitro, IFN-β stimulation of mouse ILC2s leads to increased expression of the ILC1 markers T-bet and IFN-γ, while IFN-β stimulation of human peripheral blood mononuclear cells increases the ILC1-to-ILC2 ratio. In vivo, inhibition of type I IFN signaling attenuates lung damage after irradiation in our RILI model. Thus, our findings indicate that radiation-induced type I IFN induces ILC2-to-ILC1 plasticity to contribute to RILI pathogenesis, and suggest that targeting type I IFN signaling may be a therapeutic strategy to mitigate radiation-induced lung injury.

title: Feasibility, acceptability, safety, tolerability, and changes in alcohol consumption associated with off-label medications for alcohol use disorder among patients with HIV: protocol for an open-label pilot study
abstract: Abstract Background Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is associated with poorer health outcomes among people with HIV (PWH) including serious interactions with medications. However, we lack treatments that address AUD in the context of HIV and polypharmacy. We describe the protocol for three open-label pilot studies to determine the feasibility, acceptability, safety, tolerability, and potential changes in alcohol consumption associated with the off-label use of medications with potential efficacy for the treatment of AUD – spironolactone, varenicline, and semaglutide – among PWH with AUD and polypharmacy. We hypothesize that off-label use of each of these three medications with a Clinical Pharmacist-delivered behavioral intervention will be feasible, acceptable, safe, tolerable and demonstrate changes in alcohol consumption. Methods Conducted as part of the HIV and Alcohol Research Center focused on Polypharmacy (HARP) activities, we aim to enroll 60 adults (20 participants per pilot study) with AUD, phosphatidylethanol (PEth) levels > 20 mg/nL, and with polypharmacy (> 5 medications) receiving care at the Atlanta Veterans Affairs Infectious Disease Clinic. Participants will be prescribed the study medication for 12 weeks by an Addiction Physician and will meet with a Clinical Pharmacist to receive a motivational interviewing-based counseling session regarding their personal health risks related to alcohol use in the context of polypharmacy. Feasibility will be assessed by study recruitment, enrollment, and retention, as well as visit attendance and study medication adherence, with the primary outcome being the proportion of patients offered participation who completed enrollment. Acceptability will be assessed through a participant satisfaction questionnaire as well as analyses of qualitative data collected from a subset of participants regarding different components of the intervention and their impact on alcohol consumption. Safety and tolerability will be assessed through review of clinical and laboratory data as well as frequency of adverse events. Descriptive data will compare pre- and post-intervention readiness to change metrics, self-reported and laboratory-based measures of alcohol consumption including PEth, levels of polypharmacy, self-reported and laboratory-based measures of tobacco use, bothersome symptoms, and biomarkers of health related to HIV. Discussion Interventions that address AUD in the context of polypharmacy among PWH are needed. Future research will focus on further evaluating the most promising of these pilot studies through randomized controlled trials to evaluate the efficacy of these novel intervention packages. title: Fatty acids in the tumor microenvironment reprogram neutrophils to induce adenosine-mediated immunosuppression in mice
abstract: As solid tumors progress, the tumor microenvironment becomes increasingly immunosuppressive, impairing cytotoxic T-cell activity and limiting the efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade. However, the mechanistic drivers of this immunosuppression remain poorly understood. Here, we identify a tumor-derived lipid–neutrophil–adenosine axis as a critical regulator of immune suppression in advanced colorectal cancer (CRC). We show that fatty acids enriched in tumor interstitial fluid reprogram neutrophils toward an immunosuppressive phenotype through PPARα activation, upregulation of CD39 and CD73, and adenosine generation, ultimately leading to T-cell suppression. AB928, a dual A2aR/A2bR adenosine receptor antagonist currently in clinical trials, restores T-cell proliferation, effector function, and tumor-killing capacity in vitro and in vivo. Importantly, AB928 synergizes with anti-PD-1 therapy to enhance survival in an immunotherapy-resistant autochthonous model of metastatic CRC. Thus, our findings define a metabolic immune evasion mechanism in the microenvironment and provide a rationale for targeting neutrophil-derived adenosine signaling to improve immunotherapy responses in CRC. Lipid accumulation in solid tumors supports tumor progression by promoting immune evasion. Yet the molecular basis of this lipid-mediated immunosuppression remains unclear. Here, using murine models of advanced colorectal cancer, the authors uncover a metabolic-immune axis whereby tumor-derived fatty acids activate neutrophil PPARα, resulting in adenosine generation and T cell suppression. Importantly, treatment with a dual adenosine receptor antagonist restores T cell-mediated antitumor immunity and synergizes with anti-PD-1 therapy to enhance animal survival.

title: A clinical laboratory test-wide association scan of polygenic scores identifies biomarkers of psychiatric disorders
abstract: Background: Psychiatric disorders pose a significant public health burden, and their complex genetic architecture underlies multiple biological pathways, contributing to a lack of diagnostic biomarkers. Laboratory-Wide Association Studies (LabWAS) leverage electronic health record laboratory data as intermediary phenotypes to link genetic risk to physiology. Methods: Polygenic Scores (PGS) for 25 health-related, psychiatric, and substance use phenotypes were generated for individuals of African (AFR; N=10,473) and European (EUR, N=35,131) ancestry from the Penn Medicine Biobank. Laboratory data was prepared using the LabWAS pipeline, encompassing 78 laboratory tests and 6 vital signs. Linear regression models tested the association of each lab value with PGS adjusting for sex, age, and ten within-ancestry genetic principal components. Results: Four PGS were significantly associated with at least one laboratory value in AFR individuals and 22 PGS in EUR individuals. In EUR individuals, psychiatric PGS partitioned into three physiological profiles: anxiety, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, major depressive disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder shared a metabolic/inflammatory signature (higher BMI, glucose, and monocytes; lower high density lipoprotein cholesterol and oxygen saturation); anorexia nervosa, obsessive compulsive disorder, and schizophrenia were characterized by lower BMI; and bipolar disorder demonstrated a more circumscribed profile with lower electrolytes and renal makers. Substance use disorder PGS similarly clustered: tobacco use disorder and externalizing showed metabolic/inflammatory profiles; alcohol-related phenotypes showed lower red blood cell indices; and cannabis use disorder had a more circumscribed profile. Conclusions: LabWAS reveals physiologic signatures associated with genetic risk for psychiatric disorders, offering new biological insights into their pathology.

title: An Imaging Risk Score for Bipolar Disorder: Multimodal Comparison and Integration with Polygenic Risk
abstract: Summary Background Biological risk scores provide objective markers of bipolar disorder (BD) liability. Large-scale genome-wide association studies (GWASs) have led to polygenic risk scores (PRSs) that capture genetic liability to BD at the individual level. We lack a comparable large-scale effort to leverage a brain-wide association study (BWAS) to create an imaging risk score (IRS) that captures brain structural liability to BD at the individual-level. Here, we conduct the largest multivariate BWAS of BD and develop a BD IRS. We compare the BD IRS to the PRS and assess their combined predictive performance in multimodal risk score (MRS) models. Methods Our multivariate BD BWAS used 153 structural neuroimaging features from 3902 cases and 6855 controls (mean age (sd)=35.47 years (13.42), 56.70% female) in a cross-validated machine learning approach. Using the resulting model coefficients, we constructed an IRS. We then evaluated the out-of-sample performance of the IRS, PRS derived from the largest GWAS to date, and combined MRS model using logistic regression in a subset of individuals with imaging and genetic data (n BD =486, n controls =1701, age (sd)=33.10 (12.02), 56.47% female). We also performed stratified analyses for demographic and BD clinical groups. Prediction performance was quantified using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Subsequent analyses examined associations between each risk score and BD relevant symptoms in developing youth. Outcomes In predicting case status, the BD BWAS model achieved a mean AUC BD of 0.62 (sd BD =0.08) and in stratified analyses, had higher prediction than subgroup-specific BWAS models. The BD type II BWAS was the only exception (AUC BDII =0.60, sd BDII =0.07 vs AUC BD =0.58, sd BD =0.09). The BD PRS had an AUC BD of 0.65 (CI 95% =0.63-0.68) and a higher AUC than subtype-specific PRS in stratified analyses. The PRS typically attained a higher AUC than the IRS. Notably, the IRS and PRS were uncorrelated (r=0.03, p=0.11). MRS models outperformed the prediction of individual PRS and IRS with the strongest prediction for BD type I (AUC BD =0.74, CI 95% =0.70-0.78). The IRS had the strongest associations with BD-related symptoms in developing youth including increased energy (OR=1.21, p fdr =0.03) and distress from psychotic-like experiences (OR=1.23, p fdr =0.04). Interpretation Our BD IRS is a novel biological indicator of BD risk. The lack of correlation between the IRS and PRS along with improved MRS prediction suggests the two risk scores capture some orthogonal liability to BD. We show that integrating imaging and genetics is useful for biological characterization of BD and should be considered for the development of clinically relevant prediction models.
