title: LungAI: An AI Biomarker that Refines Lung-RADS v2022 Triage of Screen-Detected Pulmonary Nodules
abstract: Background: The Lung-RADS algorithm standardizes the management of screen-detected pulmonary nodules, but its risk assessment is driven chiefly by nodule size and attenuation. This misallocates a meaningful fraction of patients: a nontrivial share of small malignancies receive 12-month surveillance while large benign nodules proceed to invasive workup. Artificial intelligence (AI) may supply risk information independent of the imaging features Lung-RADS already uses. Methods: We validated LungAI, an investigational deep learning nodule malignancy classifier not yet cleared by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), on the held-out NLST test partition of Ardila et al. (2,747 low-dose CT examinations from 1,244 patients with at least 1 solid or part-solid 4-30 mm nodule; 89 pathologically confirmed cancers, prevalence 3.2%). We compared discrimination against Sybil, mean nodule diameter, and estimated nodule volume. A board-certified radiologist assigned Lung-RADS v2022 categories to a positives-enriched random subset (226 eligible examinations; 78 cancers), projected to the full cohort by contingency weighting. A per-category reclassification algorithm shifted patients along the existing Lung-RADS management ladder using a-priori score cutpoints. We evaluated a separately locked follow-up configuration on examinations with a prior scan. Results: LungAI achieved AUROC 0.92 (95% CI 0.88-0.95) and AUPRC 0.47 (0.35-0.61), outperforming Sybil (delta AUROC 0.07; delta AUPRC 0.18), diameter (delta AUROC 0.14; delta AUPRC 0.34), and volume (delta AUROC 0.14; delta AUPRC 0.38; all P<0.001). Against Lung-RADS v2022 scored ordinally on the weighted annotated subset, LungAI improved AUPRC (delta AUPRC 0.31, P=0.003) but not AUROC (delta AUROC 0.03, P=0.20). LungAI added discriminative information independent of diameter (likelihood-ratio chi squared = 161, P < 10e-36; delta AUROC 0.10) and, on follow-up examinations, independent of delta diameter, volume doubling time, and new-nodule status (chi squared = 79, P < 10e-18). Integrated with Lung-RADS, LungAI reduced cancers on the slowest (12-month rescan) pathway by 46% (3.1 --> 1.6 per 1,000 examinations) and benign biopsy referrals by 20% (32.7 --> 26.2 per 1,000 examinations) at approximately unchanged total biopsy volume (51.0 --> 50.1 per 1,000). Assuming full adherence to recommended follow-up, the combined approach yielded 25 months of net diagnostic lead time, an estimated net cost saving of ~$2,200, and 6.5 fewer benign biopsies per 1,000 examinations; accounting for published adherence rates, it yielded 1.6 additional cancer diagnoses within 1 year per 1,000 examinations. Conclusions: LungAI contributes malignancy-risk information orthogonal to the size- and growth-based features underlying Lung-RADS and improves the allocation of screening patients across the existing management spectrum while potentially decreasing invasive procedures for benign lesions. Multi-site, multi-geography validation is required to demonstrate practical generalizability.

title: Two Tumors, Same Size, Different Prognosis: Lung Capacity Indexing Reclassifies T Category and Identifies Higher-Risk Patients in Early-Stage NSCLC
abstract: Introduction Tumor size is central to non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) staging, yet it remains unclear whether absolute diameter or patient-scaled metrics better predict outcomes. We evaluated whether tumor size indexed to predicted total lung capacity (pTLC) improves prognostic discrimination in early-stage NSCLC. Methods We performed a retrospective cohort study of Veterans undergoing curative-intent resection for clinical stage I NSCLC within the Veterans Affairs (2006–2020). pTLC was estimated using European Respiratory Society reference equations, and tumor size was indexed to a reference lung capacity of 6.91 L. Tumors were categorized in 10-mm increments; "upsizing" was defined as reclassification into a higher category after indexing. Associations of absolute and pTLC-indexed size with overall survival (OS) and cumulative incidence of recurrence (CIR) were assessed using Cox and Fine–Gray regression with multivariable adjustment. Secondary analyses evaluated associations between upsizing and pathologic nodal involvement. Results Among 11,713 Veterans (mean age 68), 12.2% were upsized after indexing. Both absolute and pTLC-indexed size were associated with worse OS and CIR in a stepwise fashion. pTLC-based upsizing was associated with increased risk of death (aHR 1.08, 95% CI 1.02–1.15) and recurrence (sHR 1.13, 95% CI 1.02–1.26), even after adjustment for absolute size. Upsizing was also associated with greater odds of pathologic nodal involvement (aOR 1.23, 95% CI 1.00–1.52). Conclusion Lung capacity indexing reclassifies a subset of patients into a higher tumor size category, and these patients have worse survival, higher recurrence, and more occult nodal disease than absolute diameter alone would suggest.

title: Data from: Pre-Existing Trauma and Breast Cancer: A Systematic Review
abstract: This dataset underlies a systematic review that is currently under review. The review was conducted in accordance with the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions and PRISMA reporting guidelines. The research team developed and followed an a priori protocol registered in PROSPERO (#CRD420250601980). The review was conducted between January 2025 and July 2026. The file SearchStrategies.pdf contains a reproducible search strategy for a search conducted on January 6, 2025 and updated on July 7, 2026, for the databases: Medline (OVID), Embase (Elsevier), APA PsycInfo (EBSCOhost) and Web of Science Core Collection (Clarivate). The file PICOTS.pdf contains the review questions, PICOT statement, and notes about the methodology. The CSV files contain screening data from stages of the review generated by Covidence systematic review software. The search was developed and conducted by a professional medical librarian in consultation with the author team. Search terms included keywords and subject headings related to abuse; adult survivors of child adverse events; breast cancer; breast malignancy; breast neoplasm; post-traumatic stress disorder; sexual violence; and trauma. Searches yielded a total of 4740 citations after removal of duplicates, 47 of which were assessed at the full-text stage for eligibility. Each study was reviewed by two reviewers independently at the title and abstract level. Studies included by at least one reviewer were reviewed at full text also by two independent reviewers. Data from included studies were abstracted into Covidence by one reviewer and over-read by a second reviewer. Disagreements were resolved by consensus or by obtaining a third reviewer’s opinion when consensus was not reached between the first and second reviewers. All screening and data extraction activities were carried out using Covidence software for systematic review management.

title: Cumulative antiresorptive exposure and dentoalveolar procedures increase medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw risk in U.S. veterans treated for fracture prevention.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ) is a rare but serious complication of bisphosphonate (BP) or denosumab therapy. Prior studies evaluating MRONJ risk factors largely involve cancer populations, small samples, claims-based data, or limited covariate assessment. We sought to determine MRONJ risk factors among patients receiving antiresorptives for osteoporosis.
METHODS: A retrospective cohort study of adults ≥50 years in the U.S. Veterans Health Administration with comprehensive dental benefits prescribed ≥1 oral (alendronate, risedronate, ibandronate) or intravenous (zoledronic acid, ibandronate) BP or denosumab between 10/1/1999-12/31/2022 was performed. Individuals with non-osteoporosis indications or dosing regimens, other BP or anabolic osteoporosis medication use, or missing covariates were excluded. Demographics, clinical characteristics, and medications were determined. Invasive dentoalveolar procedures were ascertained using Current Dental Terminology codes. Natural language processing of electronic medical records identified MRONJ events through 12/31/2023. Cox models estimated hazard ratios (HRs). Baseline characteristics were fixed, while comorbidities, medications (including cumulative antiresorptive exposure), and dental procedures were modeled as time-varying, updated at 90-day intervals.
RESULTS: Among 42,378 Veterans contributing 381,437 person-years, 44 developed MRONJ. Cumulative 20-year MRONJ incidence was 0.18% (95% confidence interval (CI): 0.13-0.25%). In multivariable-adjusted analyses, Multiracial versus White race (HR: 5.47; 95% CI: 1.31-22.91), baseline body mass index (HR: 0.89 per 1 kg/m2 increase; 95% CI: 0.84-0.96), cumulative antiresorptive exposure (HR: 1.34 per 1-year increase; 95% CI: 1.15-1.56), and recent invasive dentoalveolar procedure (HR: 4.40; 95% CI: 1.70-11.38) were independently associated with MRONJ.
CONCLUSIONS: MRONJ incidence was very low among patients receiving antiresorptives for osteoporosis, although associations of cumulative antiresorptive exposure and dentoalveolar procedures with MRONJ risk may inform shared decision-making.

title: Treatment of Advanced Biliary Tract Cancer: ASCO Living Guideline, Version 2026.1.0
abstract: PURPOSE This living guideline provides recommendations for liquid biopsy and treatment of patients with advanced biliary tract cancer . METHODS The American Society of Clinical Oncology convened an Expert Panel to conduct a systematic review of relevant studies and develop recommendations for liquid biopsy and systemic therapy for patients with advanced biliary tract cancer. RESULTS Six studies provided estimates of concordance between liquid biopsy and tissue biopsy. Nine RCTs were included in the evidence base for first-line therapy. One phase III RCT and four phase II RCTs were included in the evidence for second-line chemotherapy. Eleven single studies or reviews supported biomarker-specific second-line therapy recommendations. RECOMMENDATIONS Testing with broad-based tissue DNA and RNA NGS testing to determine the presence of targetable biomarkers is recommended at the time of diagnosis at any stage. Liquid biopsy with plasma is generally recommended only when tissue biopsy is unavailable. As first-line therapy for patients with pMMR/MSS advanced BTC, immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) plus chemotherapy is recommended. Options for patients with advanced BTC who are not candidates for ICIs are included in the guideline. Pembrolizumab monotherapy is an option for patients with dMMR/MSI-H advanced BTC. For patients with disease progression on first-line treatment and who have no identified biomarkers, FOLFOX with active symptom control, or active symptom control alone are recommended; options for patients who are ineligible for oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy are included in the guideline. Second-line therapy options are recommended for patients with dMMR/MSI-H, IDH1 mutations, FGFR2 fusions or rearrangements, BRAF V600E mutations, HER2 overexpression, RET, NTRK1/2/3, or NRG1 fusions. Additional information is available at https://ascopubs.org/guidelines/living-guidelines

title: Ascending Aortic Calcium Identifies Patients at Risk Despite Normal Myocardial Flow, Perfusion and Coronary Calcium: A 13-Site Cohort Study
abstract: Abstract Background Patients with normal perfusion, normal myocardial flow reserve (MFR) and no coronary artery calcium (CAC) on myocardial perfusion imaging are considered low risk. Yet, adverse events still occur and no routinely reported imaging marker stratifies residual risk. This study aims to determine whether fully automated ascending aortic calcification (AAC) from the attenuation correction CT stratifies risk in these patients. Methods In the multicenter REFINE-PET registry, AAC was quantified from non-contrast CT using deep learning aortic segmentation and Agatston scoring. Triple-normal was defined as stress total perfusion deficit (TPD) <5%, MFR >2 and CAC 0. The primary endpoint was cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or heart failure admission, with heart failure admission as key secondary endpoint. Cox models were adjusted for clinical confounders. Results Of 21,923 patients, 3,580 (16.3%) were triple-normal, of whom 1,322 (36.9%) had AAC (median Agatston 65, IQR 22-212). Agreement with three blinded readers was good to excellent (Intraclass correlation coefficient 0.87-0.90). Over a median follow-up of 52 months (IQR 26-69), 194 primary events occurred. Per standard deviation, AAC was independently associated with the primary endpoint (adjusted HR 1.24, 95% CI 1.09-1.40; p<0.001), heart failure admission (adjusted HR 1.30, 95% CI 1.10-1.55; p=0.003) and all-cause mortality (adjusted HR 1.17, 95% CI 1.04-1.32; p=0.009). AAC improved model fit beyond clinical factors, MFR and TPD (p≤0.009), with modest gains in discrimination (ΔC 0.007-0.009). Conclusions In patients with normal PET readouts, automated AAC was independently associated with adverse outcomes, most strongly heart failure admission, beyond clinical risk factors, perfusion and flow. Clinical Perspective What Is New? In 3,580 patients with normal perfusion, normal myocardial flow reserve and no coronary artery calcium on PET, more than one in three had ascending aortic calcification on the attenuation correction CT. Ascending aortic calcification was independently associated with cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or heart failure admission (adjusted hazard ratio per SD 1.24, 95% CI 1.09-1.40), most strongly with heart failure admission. A fast, fully automated method scored ascending aortic calcification with agreement to expert readers similar to agreement between readers. What Are the Clinical Implications? A normal perfusion PET with normal flow and no coronary calcium does not mean uniformly low risk when the ascending aorta is calcified. Because ascending aortic calcification is scored automatically from the CT acquired with every perfusion PET, it could be reported routinely without additional scanning, cost or radiation. Patients presumed low risk who have ascending aortic calcification may warrant heart failure-oriented prevention, such as natriuretic peptide screening, pending prospective validation.

title: Divergent Cardiac and Renal Outcomes by Systolic Blood Pressure in HFrEF.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Elevated systolic blood pressure (SBP) is associated with paradoxically lower mortality in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), but whether this reflects underlying pathophysiology or residual confounding remains uncertain. Because higher SBP is also a risk factor for kidney failure, we tested the hypothesis that a higher risk of kidney failure despite lower mortality would support a pathophysiological explanation for this mortality paradox.
METHODS: We assembled a propensity score-matched cohort of 59,834 patients with HFrEF, hypertension, and no baseline kidney failure. The 29,917 pairs with SBP ≥130 versus <130 mmHg were balanced on 77 baseline characteristics. Outcomes were two-year all-cause mortality and incident kidney failure. Cox regression estimated associations of SBP ≥130 mmHg with outcomes, and restricted cubic splines assessed nonlinearity across the SBP continuum.
RESULTS: All-cause mortality occurred in 24.9% of patients with SBP <130 mmHg and 23.0% of patients with SBP ≥130 mmHg (HR associated with SBP ≥130 mmHg, 0.91; 95% CI, 0.88-0.94). Corresponding rates for kidney failure were 1.0% and 1.5% (HR, 1.44; 95% CI, 1.24-1.66). SBP had a nonlinear association with mortality (P<0.001 for nonlinearity), with progressively higher risk at SBP below 130 mmHg but no higher risk above 130 mmHg. The association with kidney failure was linear (P=0.68 for nonlinearity) with progressively higher risk above 130 mmHg.
CONCLUSIONS: In patients with HFrEF, elevated SBP is associated with lower mortality but a higher risk of kidney failure. These opposing cardiac and renal associations support a pathophysiological explanation for the inverse relationship between SBP and mortality in HFrEF.

title: The PSA test for prostate cancer screening: an abridged Cochrane review.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To assess the effects of prostate cancer screening compared to no screening in men with no prior diagnosis of prostate cancer.
METHODS: This systematic review represents an update of a prior Cochrane review from 2013, searching multiple databases up to November 2025. We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) of prostate cancer screening vs no screening. We used standard Cochrane methods, including rating the certainty of the evidence following a Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) approach.
RESULTS: Six RCTs (789 086 participants; follow-up 3.2-23 years) were included: five evaluated prostate-specific antigen (PSA)-alone screening; one evaluated PSA combined with a kallikrein panel and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (ProScreen). Results are based on the certainty of evidence for each outcome and are therefore mainly derived from a sensitivity analysis by risk of bias, using the European Randomised Study of Screening for Prostate Cancer (ERSPC) trial: screening likely results in a reduction in prostate cancer-specific mortality (sensitivity analysis from ERSPC: risk ratio [RR] 0.87, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.80-0.95; one study, 162 236 participants; moderate-certainty evidence; minimal clinically important difference [MCID]: one per 1000 participants). Assuming a baseline risk of 16 prostate-cancer-related deaths per 1000, this corresponds to two fewer (95% CI three fewer to one fewer) per 1000. Based on the analysis that included all eligible trials, screening may reduce overall mortality, although the CI includes the possibility of little to no effect (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.97-1.00; I2 = 22%; four studies, 675 121 participants; low-certainty evidence; MCID: one per 1000 participants). Assuming a baseline risk of 491 deaths from any cause per 1000, this corresponds to five fewer (95% CI 15 fewer to 0 fewer) per 1000. Screening may result in little to no difference in adverse events (RR 1.32, 95% CI 0.48-3.65; low certainty) or quality of life. In the ProScreen trial (60 745 participants, 3.2-year follow-up), combined screening probably has little to no effect on overall detection (RR 1.85, 95% CI 1.56-2.19; moderate certainty), localised detection (RR 1.88, 95% CI 1.55-2.27; moderate certainty), or advanced detection (RR 1.78, 95% CI 1.19-2.66; moderate certainty). Mortality data are not yet mature.
CONCLUSIONS: Screening likely reduces prostate cancer-specific mortality and may reduce overall mortality. It may have little to no effect on adverse events (as measured by intervention-related mortality). Study limitations, inconsistency, and imprecision reduced our confidence in the effect estimates. Interpretation of these findings is highly sensitive to the choice of MCID. Emerging alternatives, such as screening with a kallikrein panel and MRI, may have little to no effect on diagnoses of prostate cancer, but the results on mortality are not yet known.

title: Developing an Intervention to Improve Informed Decision Making in Veterans With Prostate Cancer Considering Germline Testing With Their Oncologist: A Mixed-Methods Study
abstract: Purpose Informed consent is an important part of oncologist-directed germline testing in prostate cancer (PCa), but patients have knowledge gaps in the elements of informed consent. Our objective was to develop an intervention to improve informed decision making about germline testing in Veterans with advanced PCa. Materials and Methods We followed three stages of a design thinking approach: (1) Needs Assessment, (2) Prototype Development, and (3) Iterative Refinement. We applied behavior change and implementation frameworks to data obtained from literature review, stakeholders, patient interviews, and oncologist focus groups at the San Francisco Veterans Affairs (VA) Medical Center. Results Needs Assessment: 41 Veterans, eight caregivers, six oncologists, and two genetics providers contributed to identifying five target behaviors: (1) Patient reviews educational resources, (2) oncologist communicates informed consent elements, (3) patient asks questions during consultation, (4) patient recalls information about germline testing, and (5) patient and oncologist use shared decision making. Prototype Development: we matched behaviors to evidence-based interventions consisting of a patient decision aid, coaching for question listing and consultation audio recording, audit feedback for oncologists, and education/training for oncologists. Iterative Refinement: Eleven Veterans and three oncologists viewed the intervention favorably and endorsed its personalization to Veteran needs. Intervention facilitators included Veterans' trust in oncologists and caregiver support. Barriers included Veteran access to technology and intervention complexity. Feedback led to a simplified intervention with optional coaching and a shorter version of the decision aid. Conclusion We developed a multilevel, tailored intervention intended to improve patient decision making about PCa germline testing that was viewed favorably by patients and oncologists. We also demonstrated the feasibility and utility of combining design thinking and implementation science principles for behavioral intervention development. Next steps include implementing and evaluating the impact of the intervention.

title: Transient symptom increases and clinician-patient dyad response in trauma-focused treatment.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Research has demonstrated that short-term cognitive-behavioral psychotherapies, such as cognitive processing therapy (CPT), lead to substantial and sustained improvements in posttraumatic stress disorder. One barrier to CPT use is clinician perception that treatment can worsen patients' symptoms or distress. This study used session-level data to evaluate (a) if characteristics often hypothesized to be related to transient symptom increase (TSI) were associated with TSI and (b) how clinician-patient dyads work through TSI.
METHOD: Clinicians (n = 57) and patients (n = 95) were drawn from an implementation trial of CPT. Presence or discussion of childhood interpersonal trauma, multiple/repeated traumas, self-harm, suicidal ideation or behavior, substance use, encoding difficulties, and life stress were examined as predictors of TSI. Hierarchical logistic regression was used.
RESULTS: Patient and trauma characteristics were not associated with TSI. Presence of a current life stressor was the only predictor of TSI. When a life stressor was discussed in session, it increased the likelihood that a patient reported a TSI at the next session by approximately 76%.
CONCLUSIONS: The findings suggest that current life stressors can heighten the experience of traumatic stress symptoms; however, patient or trauma characteristics should not deter clinicians from recommending CPT or offering evidence-based posttraumatic stress disorder treatments to the full spectrum of patients who may benefit from them out of concern that it would lead to symptom worsening. title: Reducing Low-Value Care Through the Smarter Care Virginia Initiative.
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Low-value care costs more than $100 billion annually and remains pervasive despite decades of evidence documenting its clinical and financial harms. While several US states have begun discouraging its use, the feasibility of such statewide interventions in partnership with large health systems remains unknown.
OBJECTIVE: To investigate the effectiveness of a clinician-led, multistakeholder, statewide initiative to reduce low-value care in the Commonwealth of Virginia.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This quality improvement study used a difference-in-differences analyses comparing low-value service changes among patients attributed to 6 health systems vs 12 control systems in the Commonwealth of Virginia preintervention (January 1 to December 31, 2019) vs postintervention (January 1 to December 31, 2022). Any patient eligible to receive 1 or more of the 9 measured low-value services in the 18 health systems evaluated were included. Data were analyzed between December 1, 2023, and September 1, 2026.
EXPOSURE: The intervention, Smarter Care Virginia, included health system financial support, clinician education, and quarterly peer-comparison performance scorecards.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was the percentage of patients receiving any of 9 selected low-value services: (1-3) preoperative laboratory, imaging, and cardiac testing; (4-5) electrocardiogram/cardiac screening and cardiac stress testing; (6-7) diagnostic imaging and opioids for acute back pain; (8) advanced diagnostic eye imaging; and (9) peripherally inserted central catheter lines for patients with chronic kidney disease. Secondary outcomes included adverse events (eg, myocardial infarction-related hospitalization) and per-capita spending on the 9 low-value services.
RESULTS: A total of 17 223 clinicians (7222 in the intervention group and 10 001 in the control group) and 4.5 million patients (approximately 68% of Virginia's adult population) were identified. In 2019, 10.5% of patients in the intervention group and 10.7% of patients in the control group received 1 or more low-value services; in 2021 to 2022, rates declined to 8.5% and 9.1%, respectively. The intervention was associated with 10.4% fewer patients receiving 1 or more low-value services (absolute reduction, -1.1 percentage points; 95% CI, -2.1 to -0.1 percentage points; P = .04). There was no statistically significant change in adverse events (0.03%; 95% CI, -0.02% to 0.03%; P = .84) or spending on the 9 low-value services ($0.33; 95% CI, -$3.43 to $4.11).
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this quality improvement study, a statewide, clinician-led initiative was associated with a small but statistically significant reduction in low-value care delivery without evidence of harm. Achieving larger reductions may require combining such health system-driven efforts with additional strategies, such as payment reform and physician and hospital accountability, that discourage the use of low-value care.

title: Targeted Use of Kudzu for Binge Drinking Among Adults With Alcohol Use Disorder: A Phase 2b Randomized Trial.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study was to determine the efficacy and acceptability of targeted use of kudzu, an herbal supplement, in adults with alcohol use disorder (AUD) who binge drink.
METHODS: In a double-blind placebo-controlled trial, 120 adults with AUD who binge drink were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to targeted (as-needed) use of oral kudzu extract (2 grams taken on days when binge drinking was anticipated) or matching placebo, plus weekly counseling for 12 weeks. The primary outcome was number of binge-drinking days in the past week. Prespecified secondary outcomes included number of self-reported binge-drinking weeks, number of drinks, and measurements of changes in alcohol use using biomarkers, including ethyl glucuronide (EtG) and phosphatidylethanol (PEth).
RESULTS: Retention was high: 88% completed the trial, and 86% of weekly follow-up visits were completed. In the primary intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis, assignment to kudzu versus placebo reduced number of binge-drinking days (incidence rate ratio [IRR]=0.73, 95% CI=0.54, 0.99); as-treated (taking medication ≥2.7 days per week) analysis estimated a stronger effect (IRR=0.58, 95% CI=0.38, 0.89). Secondary outcomes showed lower number of binge-drinking weeks in ITT analysis (relative risk [RR]=0.79, 95% CI=0.62, 0.99). In as-treated analyses, reductions in number of binge-drinking weeks (RR=0.68, 95% CI=0.47, 0.98) and PEth positivity (RR=0.82, 95% CI=0.67, 0.99) were also significant. The number of binge-drinking days showed significant sustained reductions at the 3-month posttreatment visit (RR=0.68, 95% CI=0.47, 0.97). The overall frequency of adverse events was similar between groups. No serious adverse events related to kudzu occurred during follow-up.
CONCLUSIONS: Targeted use of kudzu reduced self-reported binge-drinking outcomes among adults with AUD during treatment compared to placebo. Greater reductions in binge drinking and PEth were observed among those who took medication more frequently. Reductions in self-reported binge drinking persisted at the posttreatment visit. Kudzu may be a helpful pharmacologic treatment for binge drinking among people with AUD.

title: Magnetic Resonance Imaging and Mammography Outcomes by Advanced Breast Cancer Risk.
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Few studies have examined advanced breast cancer rates in women undergoing routine mammography and/or breast magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
OBJECTIVE: To compare screening outcomes of breast MRI vs mammography by advanced breast cancer risk and screening round.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This cohort study included women aged 40 to 74 years who had a screening MRI performed with or without a screening film, digital, or digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) mammogram within 12 months (MRI group) or a screening digital or DBT mammogram (mammography-only group) performed at breast imaging facilities participating in the Breast Cancer Surveillance Consortium (BCSC) between January 1, 2005, and December 31, 2021, and breast cancers diagnosed between January 1, 2005, and December 31, 2022. Data analysis was performed from April 2025 to August 2026.
EXPOSURES: MRI and mammography; advanced breast cancer risk score calculated using the BCSC advanced cancer risk model and categorized as low (0% to <0.172%), average (0.172% to <0.3797%), intermediate (0.3797% to <0.6582%), or higher (≥0.6582%).
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Advanced (prognostic stage II or higher) and screen-detected early-stage (prognostic stage I) invasive cancer and false-positive biopsy recommendation rates per 1000 examinations adjusting for registry, examination year, age, race and ethnicity, family history, prior breast biopsy, and breast density.
RESULTS: A total of 172 865 examinations performed in 105 532 women (median [IQR] age, 52 [46-59] years) were studied. After mammography, the intermediate to high vs low to average risk group had significantly higher advanced cancer (0.6 vs 0.3; difference, 0.4; 95% CI, 0.1-0.6), screen-detected early-stage cancer (2.8 vs 1.8; difference, 1.1; 95% CI, 0.5-1.7), and false-positive biopsy recommendation (18.1 vs 14.7; difference, 3.4; 95% CI, 1.7-5.2) rates per 1000 examinations. In the MRI group, rates per 1000 examinations of advanced cancer (0.8 vs 1.1; difference, -0.3; 95% CI, -1.3 to 0.7), screen-detected early-stage disease (10.3 vs 11.4; difference, -1.1; 95% CI, -4.9 to 2.7), and false-positive biopsy recommendation (94.0 vs 93.3; difference, 0.7; 95% CI, -9.9 to 11.3) were not significantly different between intermediate to high and low to average advanced cancer risk groups. Advanced cancer rates were not significantly different for MRI vs mammography between risk groups (difference, 0.6; 95% CI, -0.4 to 1.6). Screen-detected early-stage rates were significantly higher for MRI vs mammography for low to average risk (11.4 vs 1.8; difference, 9.6; 95% CI, 7.3-12.0) and intermediate to high risk (10.3 vs 2.8; difference, 7.5; 95% CI, 4.9-10.1) groups as were false-positive biopsy recommendation rates for low to average risk (93.3 vs 14.7; difference, 78.6; 95% CI, 72.5-84.8) and intermediate to high risk (94.0 vs 18.1; difference, 75.9; 95% CI, 68.3-83.5) groups. Women who underwent subsequent vs first MRIs had significantly lower advanced cancer rates (0.4 vs 2.0; difference, 1.6; 95% CI, 0.3-2.8) and higher advanced cancer risk (median [IQR] BCSC advanced cancer risk score, 0.348 [0.238 to 0.490] vs 0.301 [0.213 to 0.429]; P < .001).
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this cohort study, intermediate to high advanced breast cancer risk was associated with higher advanced cancer rates with screening mammography. MRI screening was associated with higher screen-detected early-stage cancer rates compared with mammography but not lower advanced cancer rates, except among women who underwent repeat MRIs. These results suggest that women with elevated advanced cancer risk should discuss MRI screening with their physician.

title: Abstract 10252: A Personalized Intervention to Improve Self-Care and Prevent Foot Lesions in Veterans with Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy - Primary Outcomes of the PATRIOT Randomized Clinical Trial
abstract: Background: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN), the most common microvascular complication of diabetes, is a potent risk factor for diabetic foot ulcers, which are a major risk factor for amputation and death. Preventing diabetic foot ulcers requires optimizing foot care. We conducted a RCT to evaluate whether a personalized behavioral intervention (PBI) enhances foot self-care, reduces pre-ulcerative and ulcerative foot lesions, and decreases serious events compared to current best practice (CBP). Methods: PATRIOT is a 2-arm, parallel RCT (1:1 allocation; stratified by site and self-care) conducted at the Manhattan and Brooklyn VA Medical Centers (August 2015-June 2021). Veterans with DPN and without a previous diabetic foot ulcer were eligible. The PBI arm received in-person education at study visits and between-visit calls and mailings targeting foot care (self-care, temperature self-monitoring) and general diabetes care (diet, exercise, medications). The CBP arm received VA standard care for DPN, with calls and mailings focused on preventing non-diabetes illnesses to preserve participant blinding. Outcomes were assessed in person at 6 and 12 months by blinded observers. Foot lesions were captured via high-resolution foot photographs. Foot care skills were assessed by the validated VA foot self-care survey, (score range: 1 to 5). Serious events (ER visits, hospitalizations, deaths) were ascertained through medical records or by self-report with verification. At baseline, we assessed balance between PBI and CBP by significance testing. Between-group differences in foot care skills were evaluated using Wilcoxon rank-sum tests; differences in proportions with new foot lesions were tested with Chi-square tests. Differences between arms in all-cause events (ACE) and cardiovascular events (CVE) were assessed using logistic regression. Results: We randomized 406 Veterans with DPN (PBI n=203; CBP n=203). At baseline, there were no differences between groups in demographic, behavioral or clinical characteristics (all p-values >.1). At 6 months, PBI had a higher mean foot care skills score than CBP (4.51 vs. 4.12; p<0.001), indicating better foot self-care skills. At 12 months, foot lesion incidence did not differ between arms (PBI 41.4% vs. CBP 40.1%; p>0.05). For ACEs, the OR (95% CI) comparing PBI to CBP, was 0.45 (0.27-0.72; p=0.001); after accounting for multiple ACEs in the same person by negative binomial regression, the OR was 0.51 (0.29-0.89; p=0.02). The corresponding ORs for CVEs were 0.29 (0.12, 0.64; p=0.003) and 0.29 (0.09, 0.77; p=0.01). Conclusions: PBI led to better foot care skills than CBP at 6 months. There was no difference in foot lesion incidence between groups at 12 months. PBI was associated with fewer ACEs and CVEs than CBP over the duration of the trial, suggesting benefits of the PBI beyond foot outcomes alone. Registration: NCT02356757

title: Abstract 4746: Posttraumatic Stress Disorder and Cardiovascular Disease Risk in Women Veterans
abstract: Introduction/Background: Women Veterans have higher rates of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and elevated cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk compared to civilian women, and higher rates of PTSD compared to male Veterans. Biological, psychosocial, and behavioral mechanisms, including hypertension, hyperlipidemia, obesity, smoking, and physical inactivity, may contribute to this elevated CVD risk. PTSD has been independently linked to many of these same risk factors, yet the mechanisms driving the PTSD-CVD relationship in women Veterans, including health behaviors and sex-specific biological factors, remain poorly understood. Research Questions: We examined whether PTSD is an independent predictor of CVD among women Veterans and identified differences in CVD risk profiles between women Veterans with and without PTSD. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among WVs receiving care at a large VA medical center or affiliated Community-Based Outpatient Clinics. Participants self-reported CVD diagnoses and traditional CVD risk factors, and completed the PC-PTSD-5 and PHQ-8. Analyses included descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, Wilcoxon rank-sum tests, and multivariable logistic regression with multiple imputation for missing data. Covariates included age, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, obesity, smoking, depression severity, race/ethnicity, employment, and relationship status. Results: Among 380 participants, 38% screened positive for probable PTSD. Compared to WVs without PTSD, those with PTSD were younger, had higher rates of obesity (41% vs. 32%) and depressive symptoms (67% vs. 24%), and greater racial/ethnic diversity. PTSD was not a statistically significant independent predictor of CVD (OR = 0.98, 95% CI = 0.82-1.17, p = 0.82). Hyperlipidemia was the only significant predictor (OR = 1.8, 95% CI = 1.02-3.19, p = 0.04). Conclusions: Although PTSD did not independently predict CVD in this sample, the high prevalence of comorbid obesity and depression underscores the importance of integrated preventive strategies for women Veterans. Interventions combining trauma-informed mental health care with lifestyle modification programs may reduce long-term CVD risk. Early intervention in younger women Veterans and routine PTSD screening in primary care may facilitate holistic risk management. Future research should include longitudinal designs, clinical measures of CVD, and exploration of mediating pathways, including health behaviors, comorbidities, and female-specific military factors such as military sexual trauma, to clarify the PTSD-CVD relationship in this population.

title: Abstract 7413: Effect of an Integrative Transitional Care Program on Hospital Readmissions in a Veteran Population: A Comparative Effectiveness Trial
abstract: Background: Veterans are at increased risk for hospital readmission due to advanced age, multimorbidity, and complex healthcare needs. Transitional care interventions may improve post-discharge outcomes and reduce rehospitalizations. Research Question/Hypothesis: Does an innovative telehealth-based transitional care program (TTCP) reduce 30-day hospital readmissions and preserve quality of life among veterans at high risk for rehospitalization compared with standard care? We hypothesized that veterans receiving TTCP would experience fewer 30-day hospital readmissions and better preservation of quality of life than those receiving standard care. Methods: We conducted a prospective, single-center randomized controlled trial at the James J. Peters Veterans Affairs Medical Center (Bronx, NY). High-risk veterans with multimorbidity were identified during an index hospitalization based on LACE score and admission history and randomized to standard care (SC) or transitional care (TC). Standard care included discharge planning, medication reconciliation, and follow-up scheduling. The TC intervention combined a telephone call within 72 hours of discharge with weekly telephone or tablet-based video telehealth visits for approximately 30 days. Interventions were individualized and included care coordination, motivational interviewing, specialty referral assistance, and dietary and lifestyle counseling. Primary outcomes were 30-day hospital readmission and emergency department (ED) utilization. Quality of life was assessed using the SF-36 questionnaire. Results: A total of 259 veterans were randomized (SC n=128, TC n=131). Nine participants were excluded from analysis because of incomplete data collection (SC n=4, TC n=5). Baseline demographic characteristics and readmission risk were similar between groups (mean LACE score 12.48 vs. 12.19; p=0.824). Thirty-day ED utilization did not differ between groups. However, the incidence of 30-day hospital readmission was significantly lower in the TC group compared with the SC group (7.0% vs. 17.1%; p=0.036), representing an absolute risk reduction of 10.1% and a relative risk reduction of 59%. Among patients with the five most common Medicare readmission diagnoses, readmissions occurred in 5.1% of TC patients versus 24.4% of SC patients (p=0.028). SF-36 scores significantly declined in the SC group (ΔQOL=4.09, p<0.0002), whereas no significant change was observed in the TC group (ΔQOL=-0.024, p=0.835). Conclusions: A telehealth-based transitional care program significantly reduced 30-day hospital readmissions among high-risk veterans while maintaining quality of life. These findings suggest telehealth transitional care is an effective, scalable strategy for reducing readmissions in medically complex veterans at high risk for rehospitalization.

title: Meaning of work: Perception of employment among veterans with substance use disorders.
abstract: BackgroundEmployment plays a significant role among veterans including facilitating their transition into the civilian society and is an important indicator of treatment progression for veterans presenting with substance use issues. While the Veterans Health Administration has instituted programs aimed at increasing employment outcomes among veterans, unemployment continues to be a significant problem among veterans presenting with substance use disorders (SUDs) in the United States.ObjectiveThe present study explored the perception and experience of work among veterans with a substance use history with a goal of understanding the complex meanings participants ascribe to employment.MethodsThe study utilized a qualitative research design. 25 veterans with self-identified history of substance use participated in the study.ResultsFour overarching themes were identified through thematic analysis: (a) source of economic support and independence, (b) provides structure, purpose and sense of accomplishment, (c) contribute to society and social connection, and (d) consequences of drug use on employment.ConclusionOverall, our findings indicate that despite the high unemployment rates among veterans with SUD, they are conscious of the benefits associated with being employed, which transcends the conventional role of employment as a mere source of income. Rehabilitation counselors and other professionals involved in the care for veterans with SUD should utilize an integrative treatment approach to care that includes employment as a critical component of recovery.

title: Anxiety and suicide risk: mechanism, timing, and clinical utility
abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Anxiety disorders are associated with suicidal thoughts and behaviors, yet diagnosis and trait measures offer limited clinical utility. We review recent disorder-level and transdiagnostic evidence, focusing on what it adds to explanation, measurement, and prevention. RECENT FINDINGS: Recent studies indicate elevated risk across panic disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, social anxiety disorder, and posttraumatic stress disorder, but estimates differ by disorder and shrink after accounting for depression and other comorbidity. Within-person studies show that anxiety-related affect and rumination covary with suicidal thinking but seldom predict what happens next. Several transdiagnostic anxiety-related processes are modifiable, although durable effects on suicidal outcomes remain unestablished. SUMMARY: Assessment should emphasize processes measured at timescales that match acute risk and interpreted against each person's baseline vulnerability. Mechanism-targeted components should be tested in micro-randomized experiments during periods of acute risk.

title: Who Is Caring for Male Veterans with Breast Cancer? A National Analysis of Surgical Burden Within the Veterans Health Administration.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The epidemiology of breast cancer among men is poorly characterized. As the Veterans Health Administration (VA) serves a disproportionally male population, a larger percentage of breast cancer cases diagnosed and treated in VA are among male patients. However, whether current breast oncology operational infrastructure is prepared to address this need is unclear.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: The VA Breast and Gynecologic Oncology System of Excellence (BGSoE) established a tracking dashboard for all incident breast and gynecologic malignancies in VA in 2021. All breast surgery cases within the VA performed on male Veterans for an indication of cancer in 2023 were reviewed and mapped by the Veterans Integrated Service Network (VISN). Operative cases performed for gynecomastia were excluded. To determine the total affected population, incidence of male breast cancer was calculated using data from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database. Breast surgeries, reported as a fraction of incident cases, were plotted. The number of active surgeons performing breast surgery in 2023 was garnered from the staff surgeon identified in the BGSoE dashboard.
RESULTS: Based upon SEER age-adjusted estimates of breast cancer in men nationally and current Veteran census data, there were estimated to be 188 incident cases of breast cancer among male Veterans in 2023. In comparison, 82 (44%) male Veterans underwent surgery for their breast cancers in VA in 2023. The median age of the cohort was 72 years (interquartile range 58-78). Geographic variability in surgical volume was noted, with the number of surgeries performed in each VISN ranging from 0 to 13 cases. VISNs performed between 0% and 112% of the expected number of cancer operations for male Veterans. All VISNs had at least 1 surgeon performing breast surgery among this population in 2023 (range: 1-15).
CONCLUSIONS: There is wide variation in incident cases of breast cancer among male Veterans treated in VA. Whether these geographic differences are reflective of differential incidence, discrepancies in access, or availability of breast oncology health services is unclear. Although most patients with breast cancer do present with resectable disease, the proportion of incident cases among male Veterans by our estimates with stage IV disease (not amenable to surgery) cannot be ascertained. Future work will be aimed at characterizing availability of multidisciplinary breast cancer care in VA.

title: Developing an Empirically Derived Head Trauma Burden Assessment Score for Intimate Partner Violence–related Neurotrauma
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To develop a statistically derived and clinically informed intimate partner violence-related head trauma (IPV-HT) Burden Assessment Score that accounts for diverse brain injury mechanisms (eg, nonfatal strangulation, blunt force), exposure chronicity, and injury severity. SETTING: Community-based sample. PARTICIPANTS: Females (N = 146; 38.7 ± 10.2 years old, 56.8% White/Non-Hispanic) reporting at least 1 IPV-HT on the Brain Injury Screening Questionnaire IPV module (BISQ-IPV). DESIGN: Cross-sectional analysis. MAIN MEASURES: Candidate variables representing injury mechanism, frequency, severity, and IPV relationship history were extracted from the BISQ-IPV. Multicollinearity screening and multivariable linear regression selected variables predicting Rivermead Postconcussion Symptoms Questionnaire (RPQ) total scores. Leave-one-out elimination identified the most predictive variables determined by change in R2 when removed. Retained variables were standardized and combined to calculate the IPV-HT Burden Assessment Score, normalized to range 1-100 (low-to-high burden). Scores were correlated with Adverse Childhood Experiences questionnaire (ACEs), Headache Impact Test (HIT-6), cognition subscale of the Quality of Life in Neurological Disorders (NeuroQoL), Post-traumatic Stress Disorder Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5), Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD-Q-IV), and Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D). RESULTS: Five variables were retained in the final model, achieving 25% explainability of RPQ total scores (R2 = 0.25; adjusted R2 = 0.22). Count of unique IPV-related brain injury mechanisms explained most RPQ variance (∼19%), followed by number of IPV relationships, and duration of the 3 most severe relationships. The model also retained the proportion of injuries due to nonfatal strangulation meeting brain injury criteria and the average brain injury severity. The final IPV-HT Burden Assessment Score (mean = 31.7 ± 18.24, range = 2-86) positively correlated with ACEs (r = 0.17, P = 0.043), HIT-6 (r = 0.27, P = 0.001), PCL-5 (r = 0.23, P = 0.006), GAD-Q-IV (r = 0.17, P = 0.043), and CES-D (r = 0.29, P < 0.001) and negatively correlated with NeuroQoL T-scores (r = -0.30, P < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: The IPV-HT Burden Assessment Score captures diverse IPV-HT exposures and shows preliminary validity through associations with psychosocial and neurological outcomes.

title: Current perspectives on the pharmacotherapeutic management of insomnia in Veterans.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Insomnia is a highly prevalent sleep disorder among Veterans and frequently co-occurs with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), depression, chronic pain, and substance use disorders.
AREAS COVERED: This review synthesizes the current evidence on pharmacological management of insomnia in Veterans with attention to guideline recommendations, veteran-specific safety considerations, and comorbidity-driven prescribing. We discuss the rationale for reducing long-term reliance on benzodiazepines and benzodiazepine receptor agonists (BZRAs) in favor of agents with more favorable long-term risk profiles. Concurrent prescribing of GABAergic hypnotics with opioids is addressed in the context of existing VA Opioid Safety Initiative policy, FDA labeling, and observational overdose data. Off-label agents such as trazodone and quetiapine continue to be widely used despite limited efficacy evidence for insomnia; their use is best reserved for cases in which better-supported options have failed.
EXPERT OPINION: Contemporary guidance places cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia as first-line treatment, while pharmacotherapy is reserved for patients who do not respond to, cannot access, or decline behavioral treatment. The 2025 VA/DoD guideline suggests several medications when pharmacotherapy is used, including daridorexant, doxepin, eszopiclone, lemborexant, suvorexant, zaleplon, and zolpidem, and recommends against antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, and trazodone for chronic insomnia disorder.

title: Charting Cervical Spinal Cord Morphometry Across the Lifespan.
abstract: Spinal cord morphometry provides essential biomarkers of neurological health, but clinical interpretations are confounded by inter-subject variability and a lack of normative references across the full human lifespan. We address this gap by generating the first comprehensive lifespan charts for cervical spinal cord morphometry. From 78,269 T1-weighted brain MRI sessions, we identified a final cross-sectional cohort of 24,251 healthy or cognitively normal controls from 33 datasets (ages 0-100 years) with cervical cord coverage. To overcome contrast variability, we employed a state-of-the-art contrast-agnostic deep learning segmentation method, extracting cross-sectional area (CSA), anteroposterior (AP) and right-left (RL/transverse), and shape indices (AP/RL ratio, eccentricity, and solidity) from C1 to C7. Normative trajectories were modeled using Generalized Additive Models for Location, Scale, and Shape (GAMLSS). The resulting charts reveal distinct non-linear lifespan changes: rapid growth through childhood and adolescence, peak maturation occurring in early-to-mid adulthood (e.g., mid-30s for CSA), followed by gradual decreases. Significant regional variations along the cervical cord and consistent sex differences (males > females for size metrics) were quantified. Spinal cord trajectories showed strong temporal coupling with brain white matter and brainstem volumes, suggesting integrated CNS development and aging. These lifespan charts provide a robust normative framework, enabling age- and sex-specific centile scoring of individual spinal cord morphometry. This resource offers a critical tool for differentiating typical variation from pathological changes, enhancing the clinical utility of spinal cord MRI in studies of development and neurodegeneration.

title: Characterizing lesbian, gay, and bisexual patients' experiences with elder abuse: A chart review study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Older adults who identify as lesbian, gay, or bisexual (LGB) may be at increased risk of elder abuse (EA) due to unique risk factors; however, research in healthcare settings has been limited by the lack of data on sexual orientation. Since 2022, the Veterans Health Administration (VHA) has collected self-reported sexual orientation for all patients. The objective of this chart review study was to use newly available electronic health record (EHR) data to explore the documented experiences of older LGB adults identified with EA concerns.
METHODS: We randomly sampled 100 of 201 Veterans aged ≥60 years with an outpatient visit between 10/2022-9/2023 who identified as LGB and had a social work visit for possible abuse/neglect. We conducted protocolized chart reviews of clinical notes within ±180 days of the social work visit for 23 LGB patients, with EHR documentation confirming EA, to describe key characteristics and documented EA experiences.
RESULTS: Among 23 EA cases in LGB Veterans, 8 (35%) had cognitive impairment, 8 (35%) reported a history of child maltreatment, and 7 (30%) reported military sexual trauma. Veterans' sexual orientation was sometimes noted to contribute to past abuse experiences; however, the relationship between sexual orientation and EA or EA care processes was rarely documented by clinicians.
DISCUSSION: Findings highlight important considerations for sexual orientation minority patients experiencing EA, including opportunities to examine both contributors to EA risk among older LGB patients and to address LGB-specific care needs for this population in future research.

title: Dynamic change patterns in suicidal ideation differ in Brief Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (BCBT) and Present-Centered Therapy (PCT).
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Although Brief Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (BCBT) is more effective than Present-Centered Therapy (PCT) for preventing suicide attempts, the two treatments have similar efficacy for reducing suicidal ideation severity. Traditional severity scores may obscure meaningful differences in how specific dimensions of suicidal ideation actually change during treatment. This study examined how quickly and consistently different dimensions of suicidal ideation changed during BCBT and PCT.
METHOD: The first five items of the Scale for Suicidal Ideation (wish to live, wish to die, reasons for living versus dying, suicidal desire, and passive desire for death) were administered at every scheduled therapy session during a randomized clinical trial comparing BCBT to PCT among high-risk U.S. military personnel and veterans. We estimated separate continuous-time multivariate change models for each item and applied eigen-decomposition to the matrix of regression coefficients to characterize dominant change patterns.
RESULTS: In both treatments, some dimensions of suicidal ideation changed quickly while others changed slowly, and change was not evenly distributed across all five dimensions. Dimensions of suicidal ideation changed faster and in greater synchrony during BCBT than PCT.
CONCLUSIONS: Suicidal ideation reductions may arise through qualitatively different change processes across treatments even when the overall magnitude of change is similar. BCBT appeared to produce faster, more coordinated change across dimensions of suicidal ideation whereas PCT produced slower change that was less consistent across dimensions. These findings highlight the value of dynamical systems approaches for understanding mechanisms of therapeutic change that go beyond mean-level severity scores.

title: Veterans Health Administration Pain Management Quality Improvement in a Post-Commission on Accreditation for Rehabilitation Facilities Era.
abstract: Tertiary interdisciplinary pain rehabilitation programs (IPRPs) provide integrated, comprehensive pain rehabilitation using an evidence-based biopsychosocial approach delivered by teams offering multi-modal care. A 2009 Veterans Health Administration (VHA) Directive mandated implementation of Commission on Accreditation for Rehabilitation Facilities (CARF) accredited IPRPs in each Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) service network. Commission on Accreditation for Rehabilitation Facilities accreditation included regular program surveys to reinforce continuous quality and improvement standards. IPRPs are integral to the VHA's capacity to provide a stepped-care model including advanced pain diagnostics and functional rehabilitation to best meet the needs of veterans with complex chronic pain. Recently, VHA ended its enterprise-wide contract with CARF International for accreditation across all programs. The absence of a formal external accreditation process created a gap in sustaining quality oversight and may put VA IPRPs at risk for closure or losing their relevance as tertiary pain care centers. As such, the VA national Pain Management, Opioid Safety, and Prescription Drug Monitoring Program (PMOP) is launching an initiative to ensure governance, sustainability, and alignment with VHA and PMOP strategic priorities. PMOP's provision of oversight, support, and strategic direction is critical as the VA continues to sustain the highest quality standard for pain management and rehabilitation in the post-CARF era. This commentary will discuss current PMOP initiatives for VA IPRPs to address gaps left by the absence of the CARF accreditation framework.

title: Acetyltransferase MOF Regulates Macrophage Inflammation in Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAAs) are a life-threatening cardiovascular disease for which there is a lack of therapy preventing aortic rupture. During AAA formation, pathological vascular remodeling is driven by an imbalance of proinflammatory and anti-inflammatory macrophage responses, and mechanisms regulating macrophage-mediated inflammation remain undefined. Recent evidence suggests that males absent on the first (MOF), a histone acetyltransferase, can play a critical role in establishing macrophage phenotype and modulating innate immune response.
METHODS: Single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of human AAAs and control tissues was performed to analyze MOF expression in aortic monocyte/macrophages and the inflammatory immune response. Mice underwent 2 murine AAA models: either Ang II (angiotensin II) or topical porcine pancreatic elastase. To investigate the role of MOF in AAA development, targeted inhibition was performed with MG-149 administration or in mice genetically deficient in macrophage-specific MOF (Moff/fLyz2Cre+). Finally, flow cytometry and chromatin immunoprecipitation were conducted to analyze macrophage phenotype and levels of histone (H) lysine (K) acetylation (H4K16ac) in human and murine AAA macrophages.
RESULTS: Using single-cell RNA sequencing of human AAA tissues and multiple murine AAA models, we identified that MOF is increased in aortic monocyte/macrophages associated with upregulation of inflammatory transcriptional programs. Mechanistically, TNF-α (tumor necrosis factor alpha) signaling promotes the induction of MOF, which in turn induces NF-κB (nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B)-mediated inflammatory gene transcription by increasing the activating H4K16ac mark on gene promoters in infiltrating aortic macrophages. In vivo targeted inhibition of the MOF pathway, with myeloid-specific genetic depletion (Moff/fLyz2Cre+) or pharmacological inhibition in the elastase- and angiotensin II-induced AAA model, preserved macrophage function, decreased elastin fragmentation, attenuated aortic inflammation, and markedly reduced AAA development.
CONCLUSIONS: Our study provides important evidence that MOF regulates macrophage phenotypic function and inflammation during human and murine AAA development. Targeting the MOF pathway affords the opportunity to prevent pathological macrophage infiltration within the aortic wall and potentially limit AAA development.

title: Effectiveness of the mRNA-1345 Vaccine Against Respiratory Syncytial Virus in US Veterans.
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: In clinical trials, the messenger RNA (mRNA)-1345 vaccine provided protection against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) illness. Data on mRNA-1345 effectiveness in broader patient populations are needed.
OBJECTIVE: To estimate the effectiveness of mRNA-1345 vaccination during a single respiratory illness season.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This cohort study used a target trial emulation framework to assess veterans 50 years and older receiving care in the Veterans Health Administration. Eligible vaccine recipients were matched with up to 4 unvaccinated individuals in 4 monthly, nested, sequential trials from October 1, 2025, to January 31, 2026. Outcomes were ascertained through May 31, 2026, or 24 weeks.
EXPOSURE: A single dose of mRNA-1345 RSV vaccine vs no RSV vaccination.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was any positive RSV test result from day 14 after the matched index date. Secondary outcomes included RSV-associated emergency department (ED) or urgent care (UC) encounters and RSV-associated hospitalizations. Vaccine effectiveness was estimated as 100 × (1 - risk ratio). A sensitivity analysis comparing veterans who received same-day mRNA-1345 and influenza vaccination to influenza vaccination alone (active comparator arm) was performed to explore potential bias from differences in health care-seeking behavior and outcome ascertainment between comparator groups.
RESULTS: A total of 74 926 vaccinated veterans were matched to 286 425 unique control individuals, weighted to represent 74 926 individuals, for a total of 149 852 study participants (median [IQR] age, 73.0 [63.3-78.6] years; 136 756 [91.3%] male). During a median (IQR) follow-up of 160 (130-168) days, estimated vaccine effectiveness was 60.3% (95% CI, 49.0%-70.4%) against any documented infection, 60.2% (95% CI, 47.2%-71.5%) against RSV-associated ED or UC encounters, and 81.8% (95% CI, 58.1%-99.9%) against RSV-associated hospitalizations. Estimated effectiveness against documented infections decreased with increasing age, from 82.9% (95% CI, 64.0%-96.7%) in the 50- to 59-year age group to 28.6% (95% CI, -12.0% to 60.4%) in the 80-year or older age group. With an active comparator arm, estimated effectiveness was 67.1% (95% CI, 48.9%-82.6%) against documented RSV infections, 69.5% (95% CI, 49.7%-85.4%) against RSV-associated ED and UC encounters, and 86.9% (95% CI, 56.5%-100.0%) against RSV-associated hospitalizations.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this cohort study using a target trial emulation of mRNA-1345 vaccine effectiveness during 24 weeks, vaccination was associated with protection against RSV illness and associated health care use in adults 50 years and older. Comparative effectiveness studies are needed to determine the relative benefits of available RSV vaccine products.

title: How coaching supports the well-being of physician trainees: A qualitative analysis of the better together coaching program.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Physician coaching improves trainee well-being in randomized trials, but mechanisms remain unclear. Identifying these mechanisms can inform the design of trainee support programs. Self-Determination Theory (SDT) offers a useful conceptual framework to examine how coaching achieves its effect.
METHODS: This study analyzed recorded coaching transcripts between physician coaches, and thirty-one women graduate medical education trainees who volunteered into the Better Together coaching program from September 1, 2022, to January 4, 2023. Sessions were analyzed through a mixed inductive and deductive-SDT lens.
RESULTS: Two themes emerged: 1) psychological safety as the foundation, and 2) coach support of SDT psychological needs. Coaches created psychological safety through validation, normalization, and appreciation. Participants then described experiences of SDT need frustration: lack of autonomy, co-occurring with moral injury, lack of competence with impostor syndrome, and lack of relatedness with low self-compassion. Coaches used reflective questioning and reframing to support need restoration, ultimately helping trainees access intrinsic motivation and shift from passive ("I have to") to active ("I choose") stances. Thought awareness emerged as a cross-cutting mechanism.
CONCLUSION: Coaching appears to foster physician trainee well-being by supporting autonomy, competence, and relatedness within a psychologically safe environment. Coaching interactions did not eliminate external stressors, rather, they facilitated shifts in participants' perceptions and sense of agency, allowing for movement toward psychological need satisfaction. These findings suggest that coaching programs designed to foster psychological safety, support SDT needs, and build metacognitive capacity may offer a replicable model for trainee well-being and highlight coaching practices to incorporate.

title: Region-Specific Microglial Remodeling Following Low-Dose Space Radiation in Female Rats
abstract: As human spaceflight advances toward long-duration missions beyond low Earth orbit, understanding how space radiation (SR) affects the central nervous system (CNS) is increasingly important. Some cognitive processes relevant to decision-making appear susceptible to SR exposure, although reported effects vary according to the task and experimental conditions. The underlying cellular mechanisms remain unclear. Microglia are important regulators of the brain’s response to radiation, yet the extent to which their responses differ between brain regions remains poorly understood. In this study, adult female rats were exposed to 10 cGy He particles or a simplified GCR simulation (SGS). Microglial number and morphology were quantified using unbiased stereology and morphometric analyses in the dorsomedial striatum, subventricular zone (SVZ), dentate gyrus (DG) granule cell layer (GCL), and the dentate hilus. Neither radiation exposure significantly altered Iba1+ microglial numbers in the regions examined, providing no evidence of generalized microgliosis. In contrast, both radiation paradigms induced significant, region-specific morphological remodeling, with robust changes occurring in the SVZ, dorsomedial striatum, and DG GCL, whereas the dentate hilus remained comparatively unaffected. Even neighboring regions exhibited distinct responses to identical radiation exposures. Together, these findings demonstrate that 10 cGy SR induces region-specific microglial remodeling without detectable changes occurring in microglial numbers, suggesting that microglial morphology may reflect the response of local tissue environments to radiation.

title: Integrated B and T cell repertoire analysis reveals organized but heterogeneous adaptive immunity in chronic experimental stroke
abstract: Ischemic stroke drives prolonged accumulation of lymphocytes within the injured brain, and we recently showed that the T-cell compartment of the chronic infarct is not a random infiltrate but a reproducibly organized oligoclonal repertoire. Whether this organization is a broader property of the post-stroke adaptive immune response, extending to B cells and coordinated across lymphocyte lineages, has remained unknown. Here we performed immunoglobulin heavy-chain (IGH) repertoire sequencing of chronic infarct tissue across different mouse cohorts spanning age, sex, experimental stroke models, and independent study centers, and integrated these data with T-cell receptor β (TRB) repertoires from the same lesions. Chronic infarcts exhibited increased B-cell receptor clonality relative to matched splenic repertoires, a pattern reproducible across age, sex, models, and centers, yet heterogeneous among individual lesions owing to variable expansion of dominant clonotypes. Dominant B-cell clonotypes showed recurrent V(D)J gene usage across animals, and a subset of recurrent receptor frameworks contained public CDR3 amino-acid sequences despite substantial overall sequence diversity. Integrated analysis revealed that B- and T-cell repertoire concentration was positively associated within individual infarcts while remaining heterogeneous in its relative organization across lesions, and complementary immunoglobulin light-chain analyses supported the overall pattern of localized B-cell remodeling. Together, these findings show that persistent adaptive immunity after stroke is organized across multiple hierarchical levels, from clonal concentration to recurrent receptor architecture and paired B- and T-cell repertoire organization, yet remains biologically heterogeneous across individuals. This organizational framework, together with the publicly deposited repertoire dataset, provides a foundation for future studies of the antigenic drivers and functional consequences of chronic post-stroke adaptive immunity.

title: Understanding post-9/11 U.S. veterans' perspectives on moral injury: An exploratory study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Research on moral injury (MI) continues to grow despite a lack of consensus definition, and qualitative, exploratory studies can enable further construct clarification. This study sought to understand how post-9/11 veterans perceive MI and how these perceptions impact their responses to existing measures of MI.
METHOD: Twelve veterans completed a cognitive interview utilizing the Moral Injury Questionnaire-Military Version and the Expressions of Moral Injury Scale-Military Version. Using thematic analysis, qualitative data were coded and analyzed for their connection or divergence to existing theoretical frameworks of MI.
RESULTS: Veterans' narratives focused on themes of institutional betrayal, collective betrayal, and discharge as a betrayal-based potentially morally injurious experience. Some veterans did not perceive experiences to be morally injurious if they happened outside of combat. Other veterans perceived the construct as too narrow in scope to account for what they considered morally injurious.
CONCLUSION: Further construct clarification is needed to determine betrayal's role in MI. Definitions and conceptualizations of MI may need to expand to be inclusive of experiences of betrayal that do not come from high-stakes situations or explicitly distinguish MI from other constructs such as institutional betrayal. Veterans' perceptions that MI is primarily based in combat experiences has significant implications for adequately capturing and assessing MI. title: Treatment of status epilepticus: Too low, too slow
abstract: Abstract This review of the treatment of convulsive status epilepticus (SE) in adults examines why, with so many new tools, we have made so little progress. Major advances in basic mechanisms and increased number of available drugs, clinical trials, and publications have not led to a commensurate improvement in clinical outcomes. The central role of N‐methyl‐D‐aspartate (NMDA) receptors in initiation and maintenance of SE is now understood, but its therapeutic implications have not been translated into clinical trials or clinical practice. Failure of inhibition from inactivation of synaptic γ‐aminobutyric acid type A receptors (GABA A Rs) and KCC2 chloride transporters and runaway excitation from increases in NMDA receptors (NMDARs) and α‐amino‐3‐hydroxy‐5‐methyl‐4‐isoxazolepropionic acid receptors (AMPARs) are all under NMDAR control, yet no current guidelines recommend early treatment with NMDAR antagonists. Time plays a critical role in SE‐associated morbidity and mortality, and in the response to benzodiazepines and antiseizure medications, yet most patients are treated after time t2 and are often underdosed. Traditional SE treatment leaves too much time for NMDAR‐dependent pharmacoresistance to develop. There is a gap between the therapeutic strategies suggested by preclinical studies and the design of clinical trials, and between therapeutic recommendations from clinical trials and their real‐life application (too low, too slow). Prehospital treatment should be standardized, home treatment should be encouraged, and underdosing is not acceptable. “Time‐to‐needle” must become an integral part of SE treatment. In untreated SE, if treatment delay (stage “1 plus”) predicts failure of benzodiazepine monotherapy, more vigorous initial treatment should be considered. A recent double‐blind pediatric SE study showed that initial treatment with midazolam plus ketamine was superior to and better tolerated than midazolam alone; we need a similar clinical trial in adults. When benzodiazepines fail, time to the next agent should be minimized, and we need a prehospital trial of ketamine as second agent. We have the tools to improve the outcome of SE; let us use them.

title: Abstract 13852: Time in Normal-High Potassium Range and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Cardio-Kidney-Metabolic Syndrome: A FINE-HEART Analysis
abstract: Background: Serum potassium is a known prognostic marker in patients with heart failure (HF) and chronic kidney disease (CKD), with both hypo- and hyperkalemia associated with adverse outcomes. The POTCAST trial demonstrated that targeting a potassium range of 4.5-5.0 mmol/L may be optimal in patients at high risk for ventricular arrhythmias. Research Questions: We investigated the association between potassium control—defined as time-in-target range (TIR) within 4.5-5.0 mmol/L—and subsequent CV outcomes among broader risk patients with cardio-kidney-metabolic syndrome. Methods: We pooled individual participant data from three randomized clinical trials comparing finerenone with placebo. FIDELIO-DKD and FIGARO-DKD enrolled adults with type 2 diabetes (T2D) and albuminuric CKD, with urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio 30-5,000 mg/g and trial-specific estimated glomerular filtration rate ranging from 25 to ≥90 mL/min/1.73 m 2 . FINEARTS-HF enrolled adults aged ≥40 years with symptomatic HF and LVEF ≥40%, irrespective of T2D status. For each participant, daily serum potassium values during the first year after randomization were estimated by interpolation between scheduled potassium measurements obtained at prespecified study visits (mean # of visits per patient 5.3 ± 1.3 in FINEARTS-HF, 4.8 ± 0.7 in FIDELIO-DKD/FIGARO-DKD). The TIR within 4.5-5.0 mmol/L was then calculated for each participant. The continuous association between individual-level TIR during the first year and subsequent risk of the composite outcome of first HF hospitalization or CV death and its individual components, was assessed using landmark Cox proportional hazards models with linear splines, adjusted for covariates including baseline potassium levels, trial, and randomized treatment arm. Results: Among 18,991 participants (mean age 67±10 years; 35% women), the median TIR during the first year was 32%, corresponding to ≈117 days. Randomization to finerenone increased TIR by 8% (95% CI 7-9) compared with placebo, with a rightward shift in the distribution of potassium TIR (median 38% vs. 23%; Fig 1). Higher TIR was independently associated with a lower subsequent risk of the composite of HF hospitalization or CV death (P=0.006; Fig 2A) which appeared driven by lower risks of CV death (P=0.042; Fig 2B) compared with HF hospitalization (P=0.23; Fig 2C). Doubling in potassium TIR was associated with a 20% lower risk of the composite outcome (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.70-0.92, P=0.001). Conclusions: In nearly 19,000 patients enrolled in the FINE-HEART program, greater sustained control of serum potassium between 4.5-5.0 mmol/L was independently associated with a lower subsequent risk of cardiovascular events, mainly driven by lower CV death. These data support prospective testing of a strategy of targeting high-normal potassium levels across a broader risk population with cardio-kidney-metabolic syndrome.

title: The impact of leukocyte-associated RNA retention on platelet RNA-based cancer detection.
abstract: Platelet RNA profiling is a promising liquid biopsy approach, offering minimally invasive insights into systemic diseases, such as cancer. Yet, the effect of leukocyte-associated RNA retention on platelet transcriptomic signatures remains unclear. This study provides the first comprehensive evaluation of how leukocyte-associated RNA retention influences platelet RNA sequencing and machine learning (ML)-based cancer detection. Using the largest publicly available platelet transcriptomic dataset (2351 human RNA samples) and single-cell/single-platelet RNA sequencing from 29 donors, we quantified leukocyte-associated RNA retention in matched sample groups (low vs. high retention) via a novel 132-gene leukocyte marker panel. Diagnostic implications were assessed using 10 ML algorithms for binary classification (cancer vs. healthy), examining the contribution of leukocyte-derived transcripts. Interestingly, models trained on high-retention samples often showed slightly improved performance, suggesting complementary diagnostic value from leukocyte signals. Importantly, post hoc correction using remove unwanted variation (RUV) and linear modeling effectively mitigated retention effects. However, adding the leukocyte-associated RNA retention score to the full-cohort classifier changed cancer-detection AUC only minimally (0.9247 to 0.9249). Thus, whether this signal should be corrected, recalibrated, or reported should depend on the study question rather than assuming routine removal.
