title: Healthcare resource utilization and costs of US patients with small cell lung cancer treated with second-line therapies: a retrospective real-world database study
abstract: Aims To examine all-cause and myelosuppressive event (MYSPE)-related healthcare resource utilization and costs among patients with small cell lung cancer (SCLC) in the United States treated with second-line therapies.Materials and Methods This retrospective cohort study of the Optum Market Clarity database included adult patients with SCLC who completed platinum-based first-line induction therapy and initiated second-line treatment (1 January 2020 to 31 May 2023); second-line treatment initiation was the index date. Patients were continuously enrolled for at least 1 month after the index date. Total standardized all-cause and MYSPE-related costs were calculated. Adjusted 12‑month costs were estimated using Lin’s weighted regression.Results The final analysis included 1,063 patients across 5 treatment cohorts: lurbinectedin monotherapy (N = 350), platinum-based chemotherapy (with any agent except lurbinectedin) (N = 249), immuno-oncology therapy (without lurbinectedin, topotecan, or platinum) (N = 154), topotecan-based therapy (without lurbinectedin or platinum) (N = 138), and other combinations (N = 172). Lurbinectedin monotherapy was associated with fewer MYSPEs than chemotherapies; mean MYSPE-related per-patient per-month costs were $1,407 with lurbinectedin monotherapy compared to $1,791 with platinum-based therapy and $2,314 with topotecan-based therapy. Mean unadjusted all-cause per-patient per-month costs were $24,274 in the lurbinectedin monotherapy cohort, $24,069 in the immuno-oncology therapy cohort, and $25,074 in the platinum-based therapy cohort. Mean adjusted 12-month all-cause costs of lurbinectedin monotherapy ($168,975) were lower than the costs for platinum-based ($249,914; p < 0.001) or immuno-oncology ($220,258; p = 0.004) therapies and higher than the costs for topotecan-based therapy ($121,865; p < 0.001).Limitations There may be misclassification or under-identification of SCLC cases due to the absence of specific SCLC diagnosis codes and potential underreporting of MYSPEs.Conclusions Lurbinectedin monotherapy was associated with decreased all-cause healthcare costs compared to platinum-based and immuno-oncology therapies, but not topotecan-based therapy, and decreased MYSPEs and MYSPE-related costs compared with chemotherapies.

title: Higher risk of Long COVID among patients with autoimmune rheumatic diseases and immunomodulatory therapy: a retrospective cohort analysis of national US data.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Little is known about the prevalence of and factors associated with Long COVID in patients with autoimmune rheumatic diseases (AIRDs).
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using data from the National Clinical Cohort Collaborative (N3C). We included adults with a first documented SARS-CoV-2 infection between September 2021 and December 2023, with follow-up through December 2024. Long COVID was defined as ICD-10-CM code U09.9 or a Long COVID clinic visit occurring 28 to 365 days after first infection. We compared patients with AIRD with matched non-AIRD controls using 1:1 nearest-neighbor propensity score matching on age with exact matching on sex, race/ethnicity, SARS-CoV-2 variant-dominant period, and data-contributing organization. We estimated hazard ratios using multivariable Cox regression models. Among people with AIRD, we assessed risk by AIRD type and medication exposure before acute COVID-19.
RESULTS: In the matched cohort of 187,106 patients, Long COVID occurred in 2.8% of AIRD patients and 1.5% among non-AIRD patients. In multivariable analyses, AIRD was associated with an increased risk of Long COVID compared with non-AIRD patients (aHR 1.56, 95% CI 1.45-1.67). Among patients with AIRD, higher acute COVID-19 severity, pulmonary disease, obesity, and exposure to rituximab or glucocorticoids were associated with an increased risk of Long COVID. Sjögren's syndrome was associated with a higher risk of Long COVID.
CONCLUSION: The higher risk of developing Long COVID among AIRD patients compared with those without AIRD underscores the need to identify potential risk factors for Long COVID in this population to minimize its long-term effects.

title: Androgen receptor inhibitor double therapies in the management of metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer: a cost-effectiveness analysis
abstract: AIMS: To evaluate the cost-effectiveness of darolutamide plus androgen deprivation therapy (DARO+ADT) versus enzalutamide plus ADT (ENZA+ADT) and apalutamide plus ADT (APA+ADT) as first-line androgen receptor pathway inhibitor (ARPI) double therapies for metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer (mCSPC) from a US healthcare sector perspective. METHODS: network meta-analysis-derived hazard ratios. Costs (drug acquisition, adverse event management, subsequent therapy, end-of-life care) and utilities were derived from trial data, published literature, and US cost sources. Costs and outcomes were discounted at 3% annually. Deterministic, probabilistic, and two-way sensitivity analyses assessed parameter uncertainty at a willingness-to-pay threshold of $150,000/QALY. RESULTS: DARO+ADT generated 4.18 QALYs versus 4.03 (ENZA+ADT) and 3.99 (APA+ADT), driven by longer treatment persistence and lower adverse-event-related disutility. Versus ENZA+ADT, DARO+ADT yielded 0.15 incremental QALYs at $12,564 incremental cost (ICER: $85,108/QALY; net monetary benefit: $9,579). Versus APA+ADT, DARO+ADT was dominant (0.19 additional QALYs, $4,293 lower cost; net monetary benefit: $33,153). Two-way sensitivity analyses varying off-treatment utilities and post-discontinuation therapy costs showed that DARO+ADT remained cost-effective versus ENZA+ADT and dominant versus APA+ADT, respectively, across the parameter ranges tested. Probabilistic sensitivity analysis showed DARO+ADT was cost-effective in 51% and 52% of simulations versus ENZA+ADT and APA+ADT, respectively, which demonstrates uncertainty around the incremental findings. LIMITATIONS: The analysis relies on indirect comparisons and extrapolated modeling, factors that may limit the generalizability of the findings. CONCLUSIONS: DARO+ADT was cost-effective versus ENZA+ADT and dominant versus APA+ADT, driven by improved tolerability and treatment persistence, supporting its value as a first-line mCSPC option.

title: Content validity of overtreatment and undertreatment in older adults with cancer: A multi-stakeholder qualitative study of new definitions.
abstract: 382 Background: Over- and undertreatment (OT/UT) are widely cited in the care of older adults with cancer, yet the terms lack standardized definitions. We previously proposed new definitions that incorporate geriatric assessment and patient preferences alongside cancer-specific factors, and grounded these definitions in core ethical principles (DuMontier et al., BMC Med Ethics, 2025). To ensure that the definitions are comprehensive in reflecting the relevant facets of the patient lived experience and clinical realities, we sought to assess their content validity through interviews with older adults, caregivers, and oncologists. Methods: We conducted semi-structured virtual interviews (May 2025–January 2026) with older adults with cancer (≥70 years), caregivers, and oncologists. Participants were purposively sampled through patient and professional networks to capture diverse perspectives (e.g., oncology subspecialty and cancer type). The research team, including patient advocates (CARG SCOREboard), developed interview guides with a focus on clarity, relevance, value, comprehensiveness, and acceptability. Interviews were conducted by an experienced qualitative researcher and analyzed by framework analysis, with triangulating across group perspectives. Recruitment continued until meaning saturation was achieved (Hennik et al., Qual. Health Res., 2017). Results: Participants (n=18) confirmed the relevance, value, and comprehensiveness of the proposed definitions of OT/UT. Participants endorsed them as improving upon current approaches for older adults with cancer by providing clearer criteria that emphasized treatment decision-making grounded in a holistic understanding of the patient. All groups supported incorporating patient values and formal frailty assessment into treatment decisions, consistent with prior evidence that such assessment informs benefit-harm evaluation; however, participants raised feasibility concerns in clinic and the risks of over-reliance on frailty scores without contextualization. Among oncologists, the definitions offered a beneficial structure to support treatment recommendations that may vary from guideline-recommended regimens, especially amid pressures to prioritize aggressive cancer control when misaligned with frailty or patient preferences. Participants provided minor critiques on grammar and clarity. Conclusions: These findings confirm and enhance the content validity of OT/UT definitions through incorporation of stakeholder perspectives. Participants viewed the definitions as more structured and clinically useful than current practice, offering an ethical reference to support treatment recommendations that differ from guideline- or standard-intensity approaches when clinically and ethically appropriate for the individual patient.

title: Simplified BMI-stratified diagnostic NT-proBNP thresholds in patients with HFpEF
abstract: Abstract Background Obesity is associated with lower natriuretic peptide concentrations, potentially reducing the diagnostic accuracy of N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) for heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). Several body mass index (BMI)–adjusted NT-proBNP thresholds have been proposed, but their performance in large, clinically diagnosed HFpEF populations remains uncertain, particularly according to heart rhythm. Purpose To evaluate the diagnostic performance of guideline-recommended, BMI-adjusted, and recently proposed NT-proBNP thresholds in HFpEF. Methods We analyzed baseline NT-proBNP concentrations in 3,468 participants from the I-Preserve trial, which enrolled patients with a clinical diagnosis of HFpEF defined as a left ventricular ejection fraction ≥45% and NYHA class II-IV functional limitation with hospitalization for HF in the prior 6 months or NYHA class III-IV functional limitation with corroborative evidence (at least one of: chest x-ray evidence of pulmonary congestion; left bundle branch block or left ventricular hypertrophy [LVH] on an electrocardiogram; echocardiographic LVH or left atrial enlargement in the absence of atrial fibrillation [AF]). There were no enrolment restrictions related to BMI or NT-proBNP concentration (investigators were blind to NT-proBNP concentration). We tested guideline-recommended, BMI-adjusted, and recently proposed NT-proBNP thresholds for diagnostic rule-out and rule-in, overall and according to AF status. Results NT-proBNP concentrations declined with increasing BMI. The conventional “rule-out” threshold of 125 pg/mL failed to identify more than one-quarter of patients (130 of 493; 26%) with BMI ≥35 kg/m² who had a clinical diagnosis of HFpEF (Figure 1A). Lower BMI-specific thresholds (50 pg/mL for BMI <35 kg/m² and 35 pg/mL for BMI ≥35 kg/m²) identified over 90% of HFpEF cases in patients in sinus rhythm (Figure 1B). In contrast, in patients with AF, >95% exceeded all rule-out thresholds (Figure 1C). When considering both the recently proposed “rule-in” and “rule-out” thresholds (Figure 1D), values falling between these thresholds were classified as an “indeterminate zone,” in which patients may require exercise testing to confirm or refute a diagnosis of HFpEF. Of the patients in sinus rhythm, 60% and 48% of those with a BMI of <35 kg/m2 and ≥35 kg/m2, respectively, fell into the “indeterminate zone”, whereas the corresponding proportions for those in AF were 12% and 4% (Figure 1D). Conclusions BMI-specific NT-proBNP rule-out thresholds substantially improve diagnostic sensitivity for HFpEF in patients in sinus rhythm. In patients with AF, substantially higher rule-in thresholds are required, although current cut-points may still misclassify a meaningful proportion of patients. These findings support reconsideration of natriuretic peptide–based diagnostic pathways incorporating BMI and heart rhythm-specific thresholds.Figure 1

title: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonism in heart failure with improved ejection fraction; PRAISE-HFiEF
abstract: Abstract Background Heart failure with improved ejection fraction (HFimpEF) is an emerging phenotype defined by prior systolic dysfunction with subsequent EF recovery, yet relapse and residual risk remain substantial.1 Obesity and diabetes are prevalent drivers of ongoing risk. GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA) improve outcomes in HFpEF, but small HFrEF trials suggested possible harm,2 creating uncertainty regarding their safety in HFimpEF – a phenotype in which they have never been studied. Purpose To evaluate the association between GLP-1RA initiation and heart failure hospitalization (HFH) or mortality in obese patients with HFimpEF using a nationwide active-comparator, new-user design. Methods PRAISE-HFiEF is a nationwide multicenter cohort study across 170 U.S. Veterans Affairs hospitals. Using centralised electronic health records (2000-2022), we identified patients with type 2 diabetes, obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m2), and HFimpEF (prior LVEF <50% with subsequent LVEF >50%) using a validated algorithm.3 An active-comparator, new-user design compared GLP-1RA initiators to dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor or sulfonylurea (DPP4i/SU) initiators between 2015-2021. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) based on the propensity score balanced 32 covariates including demographics, comorbidities, HF severity indices, and baseline pharmacotherapy. The primary outcome was time to composite of HFH or all-cause mortality, using IPTW-weighted Cox models. HFH was additionally evaluated using Fine-Grey competing risk models. Results A total of 2,061 patients were included (GLP-1RA: n=1,165; DPP4i/SU: n=896) (Figure 1). Mean age was 68.9±8.1 years; median BMI was 36.8 kg/m2 (IQR 33.3-41.4); 97.6% were male. After IPTW, standardized differences were <10%. Over a median follow-up of 3.6 years, 1,349 patients (65.3%) experienced the primary outcome. Crude incidence rates were 18.6 and 16.7 per 100 person-years for GLP-1RA and DPP4i/SU, respectively. After adjustment, GLP-1RA was not associated with reduced risk of the primary outcome (IPTW HR 1.05, 95% CI 0.91-1.20, p=0.53) (Figure 2A). Competing risk analysis showed no difference in HFH (subdistribution HR 1.10, 95% CI 0.90-1.34, p=0.37). In prespecified subgroup analyses, GLP-1RA was associated with lower risk among those with BMI >40 kg/m2 (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.57-0.97) compared with BMI 30–40 kg/m2 (HR 1.23, 95% CI 1.02-1.47; interaction p=0.002). No significant interactions were observed by age, coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation, beta-blocker use, or SGLT2 inhibitor use (Figure 2B). Conclusion In the first large-scale real-world evaluation GLP-1RA in HFimpEF, initiation was not associated with excess risk of HF hospitalization or mortality, supporting cardiovascular safety in this phenotype. The observed benefit in severe obesity suggests obesity-mediated heterogeneity of treatment effect supports randomized evaluation of higher-dose GLP-1RA in obese HFimpEF.Figure 2

title: Targeting sterylglucosidase 1 attenuates virulence and enables immune protection against Candida albicans.
abstract: Sterylglucosidases are fungus-specific enzymes that regulate ergosterol 3-β-D-glucoside (Erg-SG) homeostasis and represent promising targets for antifungal intervention. Previous studies demonstrated that sterylglucosidases from Cryptococcus neoformans and Aspergillus fumigatus contribute to fungal virulence, and that deletion of these enzymes elicits protective immunity. However, whether sterylglucosidase-mediated pathways similarly influence Candida albicans pathogenicity remains unknown. Here, we identified C. albicans Sgl1 as a bona fide sterylglucosidase that selectively hydrolyzes Erg-SG but not fungal glucosylceramide. Deletion of SGL1 resulted in marked Erg-SG accumulation without altering glucosylceramide levels, confirming its conserved role in sterylglucoside homeostasis. Although the Δsgl1 mutant displayed largely preserved growth, morphogenesis, and stress adaptation, it exhibited impaired biofilm formation. Biochemical characterization, inhibitor profiling, and structural analyses revealed marked species-specific inhibitor susceptibility among fungal sterylglucosidases despite highly conserved overall architecture and catalytic machinery. Structural modeling and docking studies identified differences in ligand positioning and active-site interactions that likely contribute to these divergent pharmacological responses. Functionally, loss of SGL1 significantly attenuated virulence in a murine model of systemic candidiasis. Importantly, vaccination with heat-killed Δsgl1 cells conferred 70% protection against lethal systemic challenge and markedly reduced kidney fungal burden, providing the first evidence that sterylglucosidase-dependent vaccination can induce protective immunity against a non-pulmonary fungal infection. Collectively, these findings establish C. albicans Sgl1 as a conserved regulator of sterylglucoside homeostasis, fungal pathogenicity, and host protection, and identify fungal sterylglucosidases as promising targets for antifungal drug and immunotherapy development.IMPORTANCEFungal infections are associated with substantial morbidity and mortality, yet effective immunotherapies and novel antifungal targets remain limited. Candida albicans is a major cause of invasive and mucosal fungal disease, highlighting the need for new therapeutic strategies. Here, we identify the fungus-specific sterylglucosidase Sgl1 as a conserved regulator of ergosterol 3-β-D-glucoside homeostasis and a critical determinant of C. albicans pathogenicity. We further demonstrate that fungal sterylglucosidases exhibit distinct species-specific pharmacological responses despite conserved structural frameworks, revealing opportunities for rational antifungal drug design. Importantly, deletion of SGL1 attenuated virulence and enabled protective vaccination against lethal systemic candidiasis, providing the first evidence that targeting sterylglucoside metabolism can elicit protective immunity against a non-pulmonary fungal pathogen. Together, these findings identify Candida albicans Sgl1 as a promising target for antifungal drug and immunotherapy development.

title: Cognitive impairment: Delirium and dementia for oncologists.
abstract: Cognitive function is an important consideration in the assessment and management of older adults with cancer. The development of cancer and cognitive impairment share common risk factors associated with the ageing process. Furthermore, older adults with cancer and cognitive problems are more likely to encounter adverse outcomes. This review by the Young International Society of Geriatric Oncology is divided into the following core sections: cognitive screening, approach to the older adult with pre-existing cognitive impairment, and approach to the older adult presenting with declining cognition. It aims to provide oncologists treating older adults with key considerations when it comes to cognition in this cohort of patients, guidance on differentiating between delirium, cancer related cognitive decline and neurocognitive disorder and some important considerations when it comes to decision-making ability in the context of cognitive decline.

title: Combination Therapy with AKT and MEK Inhibitors is Effective in Patient-Derived Models of Adrenocortical Carcinoma.
abstract: Adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) is a rare, aggressive, chemoresistant malignancy with limited effective systemic therapies and few recurrent actionable oncogenic drivers. Although IGF-2 is overexpressed in approximately 80% of ACCs, clinical inhibition of the IGF-1R/InsR axis has not improved outcomes. To identify clinically tractable combination strategies that enhance IGF-1R/InsR inhibition in ACC, we performed a quantitative high-throughput combinatorial screen of 2,803 mechanistically annotated oncology compounds with the IGF 1R/InsR inhibitor linsitinib in an ACC cell line. Downstream effects of IGF-1R/InsR signaling were assessed to identify actionable nodes for combination targeting. Candidate combinations were validated using short-term ACC patient-derived organoids (PDOs) and patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models. The screen identified MAPK pathway inhibitors-particularly MEK inhibition-as the top synergistic partners with IGF-1R/InsR inhibition. Genetic or pharmacologic inhibition of IGF-1R/InsR and MEK signaling suppressed ACC growth in vitro. Downstream profiling of IGF-1R/InsR signaling identified AKT as a major effector, supporting direct AKT targeting as a translatable substitute for IGF-1R/InsR inhibition in ACC. Accordingly, the AKT inhibitor capivasertib synergized with the MEK inhibitor cobimetinib in ACC cell lines and six ACC PDO models. In vivo, combined AKT and MEK inhibition reduced tumor growth more than either agent alone in an ACC xenograft and two ACC chemotherapy-resistant PDX models with acceptable tolerability. These data identify AKT as a critical survival pathway in ACC and support combined AKT and MEK inhibition with FDA-approved agents as a therapeutic approach for chemotherapy-resistant ACC.

title: Toward clinically actionable lupus biomarkers: a roadmap for research, validation and translation.
abstract: Despite advances in lupus biomarker research, clinical translation has remained limited, leading to delayed diagnosis, imprecise disease monitoring and trial-and-error treatment approaches. This roadmap, developed by the Lupus Research Alliance's Biomarker Roadmap Committee with input from patients and experts, identifies key priorities for translating research into clinical benefit. Three major clinical unmet needs are highlighted: improving diagnostic accuracy of SLE and neuropsychiatric SLE, developing sensitive longitudinal markers for disease activity (including LN), and predicting disease progression and treatment response. We review the current state of biomarker development across these domains and highlight barriers that hinder clinical validation, assay development and clinical adoption. We propose focused strategies to overcome these challenges, emphasizing analytically validated assays, diverse longitudinal cohorts, alignment with meaningful clinical outcomes and consortium-based efforts. The roadmap outlines a path to transform lupus diagnosis, monitoring and precision medicine, enabling research advances to improve patient care.

title: Brain network functional connectivity alterations associated with acute posttraumatic headache.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES/BACKGROUND: To investigate disruptions in resting state networks in participants with acute posttraumatic headache (PTH) due to mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI). Neuroimaging studies have demonstrated alterations in functional connectivity (FC) within core resting-state networks in participants with headache versus healthy controls (HCs), which may provide insights into disease mechanisms; however, the extent to which these alterations relate to PTH remains incompletely understood.
METHODS: In this comparative cross-sectional study with an embedded prospective cohort, participants with acute PTH and HCs were enrolled from the Mayo Clinic Arizona and Minnesota, and the Phoenix Veterans Affairs Health Care between 2020 and 2024. Participants with PTH underwent resting-state magnetic resonance imaging within 2 months following mTBI. We investigated differences within and between functional brain networks in participants with PTH compared to HCs. Associations between altered FC with headache frequency, alterations of mood, post-mTBI symptoms, and concussion history were determined and corrected for age and sex. Relationships between PTH outcomes at 3 months and baseline FC were investigated.
RESULTS: Ninety-six participants with acute PTH (35 male, 61 female) and 84 age-balanced HCs were included. Decreased resting state network connectivity in participants with PTH compared to HCs (False Discovery Rate (FDR) corrected <0.05) was observed in two default mode network (DMN) regions encompassing the bilateral frontal and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), as well as the left postcentral gyrus. Within those DMN regions, exploratory analyses revealed that FC was positively associated with headache frequency in the bilateral ACC, right precuneus and frontal gyrus, and with trait anxiety in the right ACC. In contrast, negative associations were observed between FC and number of mTBIs, as well as state anxiety, in the left ACC (uncorrected, p<0.05). No significant associations with clinical headache variables were observed in the DMN comprising the left postcentral gyrus. Baseline group differences in network connectivity between recovered and nonrecovered participants were found in visual, sensorimotor, default mode, executive control and salience networks. Alterations in baseline connectivity between independent components in recovered and nonrecovered participants were not statistically significant after corrections for multiple comparisons.
CONCLUSION: In participants with PTH, the DMN regions showing decreased connectivity also exhibited associations with headache frequency, state and trait anxiety, and number of lifetime mTBIs, suggesting that these changes relate to the severity and persistence of post-mTBI symptoms. The baseline differences in network connectivity between recovered and nonrecovered participants were not statistically significant after corrections for multiple comparisons, indicating that baseline network connections may not play a significant role in the recovery process.

title: Ketamine/Esketamine in Clinical Practice: Areas of Consensus and Nonconsensus from an American Society of Clinical Psychopharmacology (ASCP) Delphi Panel Task Force.
abstract: Objective: Important aspects of ketamine/esketamine treatment for mood disorders in contemporary practice remain inadequately addressed by the current evidence base, necessitating expert guidance in areas where clinical decision needs and implementation have advanced more rapidly than available data. The American Society of Clinical Psychopharmacology convened an expert task force to address unresolved questions about the practical use of these agents in "real-world" settings and potential disparities with evidence-based literature. Participants: An international panel of 21 academic mood disorder psychopharmacologist-psychiatrists with expertise in ketamine/esketamine clinical care and research. Evidence: Consensus was reached on 35/105 items (33%), encompassing domains involving diagnostic conditions, contraindications, maximum dosing, racemic versus enantiomeric preparations, oral or intramuscular delivery formulations, laboratory/safety monitoring, access, and parameters for judging treatment outcome. Consensus Process: Two successive Delphi rounds were completed alongside multiple virtual, email, and in-person meetings. Consensus was defined a priori as ≥75% agreement/disagreement on 5-point Likert survey items. All authors contributed to the interpretation and drafting of recommendations. Conclusions: Consensus agreement appears elusive for many key decision points involving ketamine/esketamine treatment, reflecting substantial disparities between "real-world" clinical practice and the shortcomings of the clinical trials' evidence base. Uncertainties persist regarding the use of novel formulations (eg, oral or intramuscular), high-dose ketamine infusions, ketamine-assisted psychotherapy, and use in conditions other than major depression. These areas of expert consensus and dissent lay the groundwork for future studies urgently needed to bridge the gap between evidence-based findings and treatment implementation in routine clinical settings.

title: Abstract 10828: Longer Reperfusion Results in Improved Heart Function in Donation After Circulatory Death Hearts Treated with Cyclosporine A
abstract: Background: Donation after Circulatory Death (DCD) hearts sustain ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI) which can be modulated with Cyclosporin A (CyA) treatment at reperfusion. We observed significant decrease in infarct size but no functional improvement in DCD hearts treated with CyA on Langendorff setup perfused for 60 minutes. We hypothesize that longer duration of reperfusion will manifest the benefits of CyA treatment of DCD hearts. Methods: Sprague-Dawley rats (n = 8 to 17 per group) were anesthetized with ketamine/xylazine. Respiratory support was established with ventilator via tracheal intubation. Carotid artery cannulated to administer heparin and vecuronium. Release from ventilator marked the start of DCD ischemia time. DCD hearts were procured after 25 minutes of ischemia and were reanimated on Langendorff setup primed with Kreb-Henseleit (KH) buffer perfused at 74mmHg pressure for 60 minutes. A balloon tip catheter inserted into left ventricle transduced to LabChart measured hemodynamics. Hearts were then procured for infarct size measurement. CyA treated hearts received 0.5 μM CyA mixed in KH buffer, for the first 15 minutes of perfusion. Control non-ischemic hearts, continuous heart-beating donation (CBD) were procured before termination of ventilator support. A similar set of rats were assigned to undergo heterotopic heart transplantation following 25 minutes of in-situ ischemia. CyA (0.5 μM) was administered to the DCD hearts via carotid cannula at the time of procurement. Hearts were heterotopically transplanted into the recipient abdomen by attaching aorta to aorta and pulmonary artery to inferior vena cava (Figure). Recipient rats were allowed to recover for 48 hours and were then anesthetized with isoflurane (2-3%). Transplanted heart function was measured with balloon tip catheter transduced to LabChart software, then procured to measure infarct size. Results: In buffer-perfused hearts, cardiac function was impaired in the DCD group compared to the CBD group, as indicated by a decreased rate pressure product (RPP). Infarct size was larger in DCD hearts compared to CBD hearts (Table 1 & 2). While CyA treatment reduced infarct size in buffer-perfused DCD hearts (Table 2), it did not improve cardiac function (Table 1). In transplanted hearts, cardiac function was also impaired in the DCD group compared to the CBD group and the infarct size was larger (Table 1 & 2). However, CyA treated transplanted DCD hearts had reduced infarct size and improved cardiac function (Table 1 & 2). Conclusions: CyA administered to DCD hearts at reperfusion decreases IRI. Functional improvement requires longer duration of reperfusion. Future studies should explore stunned myocardium as the possible mechanism of this observation.

title: Body Mass Index-Specific Central Adiposity and Risk of Incident Type 2 Diabetes Among Aging Women.
abstract:
CONTEXT: Body mass index (BMI) does not capture central adiposity, which may provide additional information for type 2 diabetes (T2D) risk stratification.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate BMI-specific waist circumference (WC) categories in relation to incident T2D and assess their performance across independent cohorts.
METHODS: Prospective analyses included 133,620 Women's Health Initiative (WHI) participants free of T2D at baseline, randomly assigned to training (70%; n=93,463) and test (30%; n=40,157) samples. External validation included the Health and Retirement Study (HRS; n=2,885) and Healthy Aging in Neighborhoods of Diversity across the Life Span (HANDLS; n=1,037). Cox models estimated T2D risk across BMI and BMI-specific WC categories. Discrimination was assessed using Harrell's C-statistic.
RESULTS: In WHI, T2D risk increased progressively across BMI categories (adjusted hazard ratios [HRs], 1.51-3.30) and joint BMI-WC categories (HRs, 1.40-4.43). Within BMI strata, higher WC generally identified greater T2D risk. Associations were directionally consistent in HRS and HANDLS. Age modified associations, with stronger gradients at younger ages, whereas race and ethnicity interactions were not statistically significant. Model discrimination was modest (C-statistics approximately 0.60-0.75).
CONCLUSIONS: BMI-specific WC categories refine adiposity-related T2D risk stratification beyond BMI alone but provide modest individual-level discrimination. WC may complement BMI in identifying women warranting more comprehensive metabolic risk assessment rather than serving as a stand-alone T2D prediction tool.

title: An Assessment of Knowledge and Self-Efficacy Following Question, Persuade, Refer Gatekeeper Training in Alabama.
abstract: Suicide remains a serious public health concern and is on the rise in some populations. The goal of this research was to examine the attitudes, beliefs, and perceived self-efficacy of those who participated in Question, Persuade, Refer (QPR) Gatekeeper Suicide Prevention Training. The study team conducted pre- and post-training surveys for 508 participants who completed QPR Gatekeeper Training between September 2018 and March 2019. A secondary data analysis was then conducted to examine differences in pre- and post-testing related to suicide knowledge, ability to identify warning signs, and reported self-efficacy to intervene during a potential crisis. Based on pre- and post-test mean scores, there was a statistically significant improvement in attitudes, beliefs, and perceived self-efficacy following QPR Gatekeeper training for 10 of the 12 survey statements. Results demonstrated that evidence-based suicide prevention programs, such as QPR Gatekeeper Training, can positively affect attitudes, beliefs, and perceived self-efficacy of trainees. Furthermore, based on the shorter duration of training when compared with half-day trainings such as LivingWorks SafeTalk and multi-day trainings such as Applied Suicide Intervention Skills Training, QPR Gatekeeper Training may be amendable to a greater number of trainees without losing its effectiveness. This study adds to the existing body of literature on the potency of QPR Gatekeeper Training using an innovative, multi-item scale.

title: Identifying Diagnostic Breakdowns in Patient Experience Survey Comments Using Natural Language Processing: An Evaluation Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patient experience surveys may contain signals of diagnostic breakdowns that are difficult to identify through conventional safety surveillance. Natural language processing (NLP) may enable these narratives to be analyzed at scale.
OBJECTIVE: To develop and evaluate three increasingly context-sensitive NLP approaches for identifying patient-perceived diagnostic breakdowns in ambulatory patient experience survey comments and to explore the potential of prompt-engineered large language models (LLMs) for this task.
METHODS: We analyzed 523 free-text comments from a 2023 ambulatory patient experience survey at a Canadian academic community hospital. Comments were manually coded using a structured framework to establish a finalized reference standard. Three sequential approaches were developed: a TF-IDF-based XGBoost classifier (Phase I), a fine-tuned Twitter-RoBERTa model (Phase II), and a locally deployed LLaMA 3.3 70B model refined through iterative expert-guided prompt development (Phase III). Phases I and II were evaluated using 5×5 nested stratified cross-validation. Phase III was refined and evaluated on the full dataset and therefore represents development-set rather than independent held-out performance.
RESULTS: Following expert review, 51 of 523 comments (9.8%) were classified as diagnostic breakdowns. Compared with Phase I, Phase II showed higher recall (0.767 vs 0.626), F1 score (0.620 vs 0.548), AUROC (0.921 vs 0.810), and AUPRC (0.564 vs 0.490). In Phase III, iterative prompt refinement reduced over-classification of general experiential complaints. The final prompt achieved recall of 0.961, precision of 0.803, specificity of 0.975, and an F1 score of 0.875 on the development dataset.
CONCLUSIONS: Patient-authored survey narratives are an underused source of information for diagnostic safety and quality improvement. Context-sensitive NLP approaches may improve detection of subtle diagnostic concerns, and the strong development-set performance of the prompt-engineered LLM supports further study. External validation and prospective evaluation within diagnostic-safety workflows are needed before broader implementation.

title: Prediction of All-Cause Mortality, Cardiovascular Mortality, and Angiographic Coronary Disease From LVEF Reserve: Findings From the Multicenter REFINE PET Registry.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Left ventricular ejection fraction reserve (LVEF-R), defined as stress EF minus rest EF, is a marker for high-risk coronary artery disease in patients undergoing positron emission tomography myocardial perfusion imaging, but its prognostic and diagnostic significance in large real-world populations remains incompletely defined. We aimed to analyze the association of LVEF-R with mortality and high-risk obstructive coronary artery disease in a large multicenter cohort.
METHODS: We analyzed 34 976 patients from 13 sites who underwent gated rest and vasodilator stress positron emission tomography myocardial perfusion imaging from the Registry of Flow and Perfusion Imaging for Artificial Intelligence with PET. Associations between LVEF-R and all-cause mortality and cardiovascular death were assessed using multivariable Cox regression models. In a subset with invasive coronary angiography (n=6843), the relationship between LVEF-R and angiographic disease was evaluated.
RESULTS: A total of 9392 (26.9%) patients had an LVEF-R<0%. Over a median follow-up of 4.1 years, lower LVEF-R demonstrated a graded association with higher mortality. Compared with LVEF-R>5%, adjusted hazard ratios for all-cause mortality were 1.20 for LVEF-R 0% to 5% ([95% CI, 1.13-1.28]; P<0.001), 1.32 for -5% to 0% ([95% CI, 1.23-1.42]; P<0.001), and 1.38 for ≤-5% ([95% CI, 1.24-1.52]; P<0.001). A negative LVEF-R was also associated with high-risk coronary artery disease, including left main and 3-vessel disease.
CONCLUSIONS: LVEF-R is an independent predictor of mortality, with a graded association between impaired reserve and adverse outcomes. A negative LVEF-R identifies patients with a higher likelihood of multivessel or left-main coronary artery disease, supporting its role as a clinically relevant marker of high-risk disease.

title: Contemporary patterns of lower extremity revascularization for chronic limb-threatening ischemia in the United States: 2016-2022.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI) is a major contributor to morbidity and mortality. Although revascularization improves limb outcomes in CLTI, contemporary practice patterns and real-world outcomes remain poorly characterized, particularly amid conflicting evidence from randomized trials regarding optimal revascularization and nonoperative management strategies. Our study utilized the National Inpatient Sample (NIS) coupled with U.S. Census data to characterize contemporary trends of incidence, revascularization approach, and in-hospital outcomes for adults hospitalized for CLTI.
METHODS: We utilized the NIS (2016-2022) to generate survey-weighted national estimates of U.S. adult hospitalizations for CLTI. Age-normalized incidence rates per 100,000 person-years were calculated using population denominators from the U.S. Census Bureau. Admissions with secondary diagnoses of trauma or arterial dissection were excluded. Our outcomes evaluated the incidence of CLTI hospitalizations and rates of in-hospital revascularization type (open, endovascular, or no revascularization), major amputation, and mortality. Outcomes by revascularization strategies (open vs. endovascular) were stratified a priori by sex, frailty (Risk Analysis Index), diabetes status, and clinical presentation subgroups. Mann-Kendal trend tested monotonic temporal trends.
RESULTS: An estimated 46,915 adult CLTI hospitalizations were included (mean age 69.7 years, 40.0% women, 69.5% White). Overall CLTI incidence was 7.28 per 100,000 person-years, initially declining until nadir in 2020 with reversal and steady rise thereafter. A total of 28,763 (61.3%) CLTI hospitalizations included revascularization (n=14,252 [49.5%] open and/or n=16,950 [58.9%] endovascular). The proportion of open revascularization decreased (ptrend=0.016), while endovascular remained stable (ptrend=0.368), and hospitalizations without revascularization increased (ptrend=0.016) over time. Endovascular revascularization rates did rise among females, non-frail patients, and those presenting with rest pain (all ptrend>0.05). Overall, in-hospital amputation (n=6,270 [13.4%]) and mortality (n=1,086 [2.3%]) remained stable (ptrend>0.05). However, the proportion of patients discharged alive and without amputation increased most substantially among hospitalizations without revascularization (ptrend=0.007).
CONCLUSION: We provide contemporary analysis of U.S. hospitalizations for CLTI, demonstrating increasing rates following 2020. Overall, in-hospital rates of open revascularization declined in favor of nonoperative strategies corresponding with the greatest increase in alive discharges without amputations. Relative selection of endovascular strategies varied notably by sex, frailty, and clinical presentation. Our findings underscore the need for further investigation into optimal CLTI patient selection and coordinated integration of non-operative care, such as medical optimization, with revascularization strategies.

title: Colorectal Cancer among U.S. Adults, 2000-2023.
abstract: AbstractUsing data from the National Cancer Institute's Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) Program, we examined colorectal cancer incidence rates in the United States between 2000 and 2023. SEER 21 covers 45.8% of the U.S. population. The age-adjusted incidence rate was 55.2 per 100,000 (95% CI, 54.8 to 55.6) in 2000, 36.7 per 100,000 (95% CI, 36.4 to 37.0) in 2022, and 38.3 per 100,000 (95% CI, 38.0 to 38.6) in 2023. The apparent increase in 2023 was the first since the inception of SEER 21 and warrants additional surveillance and investigation.

title: Epigenetics in Traumatic Brain Injury.
abstract: Following traumatic brain injury (TBI), changes in proteins, metabolites, and gene expression are highly dynamic and are influenced by genetic and environmental factors, circadian rhythms, and injury characteristics, including injury type (focal or diffuse), severity (mild to severe), and stage of recovery (acute, subacute, and chronic). These molecular alterations are accompanied by epigenetic modifications that regulate gene expression and contribute to injury progression and recovery. In this review, we integrate and summarize preclinical and clinical studies examining DNA methylation, histone methylation and acetylation, microRNA (miRNA)-mediated regulation, RNA epigenetic modifications, and mitochondrial epigenetic (mitoepigenetic) changes following TBI. Most studies have focused on DNA methylation, histone modifications, and miRNAs in experimental models, providing important insights into cell type-specific epigenetic responses after injury. We also review studies evaluating therapeutic strategies, including DNA methyltransferase and histone deacetylase inhibitors, that target epigenetic mechanisms to improve TBI outcomes.

title: Modeling the survival impact of the Inflation Reduction Act out-of-pocket cap in multiple myeloma.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Oral immunomodulatory imide drugs (IMiDs) have become standard of care for newly diagnosed multiple myeloma (NDMM), but high out-of-pocket (OOP) costs may hinder treatment adherence. In 2025, the Inflation Reduction Act introduced a $2,000 annual OOP cost cap (IRAOOPcap) for Medicare Part D beneficiaries. In the absence of post-implementation data, we used comparative modeling to predict its survival impact.
METHODS: The survival submodels of two independent Cancer Intervention and Surveillance Modeling Network (CISNET) natural history of multiple myeloma models were used. The models were parameterized using data from Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER)-Medicare, 2012-2021. We simulated survival among Medicare Part D beneficiaries with NDMM aged 66-75 and ≥76 years, under hypothetical scenarios shifting 0% (pre-IRAOOPcap) to 100% (best-case) of patients to IMiD use with high adherence and a realistic scenario using published data. We computed life-years gained (LYG) by comparing life expectancy (LE) under each scenario with that of the pre-IRAOOPcap scenario.
RESULTS: Across models, the realistic/best-case scenario yielded LYG of 0.17-0.18/1.10-1.35 among patients aged 66-75 years, and 0.20-0.26/1.29-1.53 for those aged ≥76 years. These translated into 4,164-5,005/26,893-32,347 LYG at the population level for beneficiaries with NDMM in 2025.
CONCLUSION: The IRAOOPcap may improve survival through increasing IMiD utilization and adherence among Medicare Part D beneficiaries with NDMM. The projected gains represent a meaningful proportion of contemporary survival for patients. Future research should validate these gains when real-world data are available and inform future policy adaptation and extension.

title: Evaluation of a pharmacist-led pharmacogenomic service and provider acceptance at VA Puget Sound
abstract: PURPOSE: Pharmacogenomic (PGx) testing provides genetic information that supports precision medicine use to improve efficacy and safety. A pharmacist-led PGx service was implemented to help providers manage drug-gene interactions. SUMMARY: A pharmacist-led PGx service had PGx pharmacist conducted chart reviews to identify and make management recommendations for the drug-gene interactions, which were shared with relevant providers. A quality improvement project was performed to assess the effectiveness of implementation. PGx chart review notes written by pharmacy from May 2024 to November 2024 were reviewed. Ninety-eight patients were included in this project. After reviewing the PGx pharmacist's recommendations, providers managed 61% of the patients who had drug-gene interactions, where management was defined as a provider documenting their plans for the interactions in their notes. This is a significant improvement compared to pre-intervention data (from November 2023 to April 2024), where only 10% of interactions were managed by a provider. Not all drug-gene interactions (32%, 22/68) were associated with the specialty of the PGx ordering provider. CONCLUSION: The pharmacist-led PGx service led to a six‑fold increase in healthcare provider-managed drug-gene interactions. The PGx pharmacist's recommendations increased providers' awareness of the drug-gene interactions.

title: Mechanical competence of proximal tibia in persons with spinal cord injury: development of a computational framework to quantify torsional and compressive stiffness and strength.
abstract: This study developed a framework to quantify the mechanical competence of the proximal tibia in spinal cord injury (SCI) and able-bodied (AB) participants. We created subject-specific finite element models of 53 proximal tibias (22 SCI, 5 AB) and quantified two torsional (stiffness, Kt and ultimate strength, Tult) and two compressive (stiffness, Kc and ultimate strength, Cult) metrics. We report the distributions of Kt, Tult, Kc, and Cult, and a minimum number of metrics required to quantify the mechanical competence of the proximal tibia. This work provides a foundation for confidence interval-based thresholds to predict fracture risk in persons with SCI.

title: Investigation of the pharmacological and circuit basis for psychedelic drug effects on interval timing in mice.
abstract:
RATIONALE: Classical psychedelic drugs such as the tryptamine psilocybin can alter temporal perception. Previously, the phenylethylamine psychedelic 2,5-dimethoxy-4-iodoamphetamine (DOI), a 5-HT2A receptor agonist, altered timing precision and accuracy in mice performing the discrete-trials temporal discrimination task (TDT), a retrospective timing task where subjects differentially respond depending on whether a light is illuminated for shorter or longer than 6.5 s.
OBJECTIVES: Although DOI alters TDT performance, it is unclear whether timing is altered by tryptamine psychedelics, which are less selective for 5-HT2 subtypes and also activate the 5-HT1A receptor.
METHODS: To address this knowledge gap, we tested psilocin (the active metabolite of psilocybin) in male C57BL/6J mice performing the TDT and assessed the involvement of 5-HT1A and 5-HT2A receptors in its effects. Because the prefrontal cortex (PFC) is involved in psychedelic drug effects and temporal perception, additional experiments tested whether DOI microinfusion into the medial PFC (mPFC) replicates its systemic effects.
RESULTS: Psilocin (0.8 mg/kg SC) altered timing accuracy and precision in mice performing the TDT, similarly to DOI. Psilocin effects were blocked by the 5-HT2A antagonist M100907 but were unaffected by the 5-HT1A antagonist WAY-100,635. Infusion of DOI bilaterally into mPFC mimicked the effect of systemic administration on TDT performance. Administration of the selective 5-HT2A inverse agonists M100907 and MDL 11,939 altered timing accuracy, demonstrating that both increases and reductions in 5-HT2A receptor activation can modulate perceived clock speed.
CONCLUSIONS: The mPFC appears to play a role in TDT performance and may mediate the effects of psychedelic drugs on interval timing.

title: Growth hormone deficiency after traumatic brain injury: Current insights and the need for preclinical modeling.
abstract: Approximately 50 million people worldwide live with disabilities caused by traumatic brain injury (TBI), highlighting its profound global impact on long-term health and quality of life. A growing body of evidence indicates that hypothalamic-pituitary (HP) axis dysregulation is a critical contributor to chronic TBI morbidity, with growth hormone deficiency (GHD) emerging as the most common diagnosis. Clinicians may misattribute the delayed and nonspecific symptoms of GHD to the broader constellation of TBI-related symptoms or prioritize more immediate medical concerns, which can delay diagnosis and treatment. Emerging clinical and preclinical studies support both the occurrence of abnormal GH secretion following TBI and the potential efficacy of GH replacement in reversing many GHD-related impairments; however, several critical knowledge gaps remain. These include unclear or variable pathophysiological mechanisms underlying GHD development, limitations in diagnostic testing protocols, lack of consensus on dosing adjustments as a function of age and sex, and inconsistent clinical responses to GH therapy likely due to incomplete understanding of the underlying processes, timing, patient selection, and outcome measures. Additionally, opportunities to evaluate novel GH-related interventions and their long-term outcomes remain limited. This review summarizes these challenges, synthesizes the current preclinical literature, and proposes strategies to address these gaps through the development of more robust and translatable animal models that can systematically test these variables and ultimately improve outcomes for patients with TBI-induced GHD.

title: Abstract A088: Barriers to hematology/oncology clinical trial enrollment at the Bronx Veterans Affairs Medical Center
abstract: Abstract Objectives: To identify barriers to hematology/oncology clinical trial enrollment in a diverse group of Veterans. Background: Oncology clinical trials are essential for making novel therapies available safely, particularly for patients who have limited additional treatment options. Participation in cancer clinical trials remains low in the United States. Additionally, patients of low socioeconomic status (SES) and racial minorities are frequently underrepresented, limiting generalizability of findings. An important element of the mission of the Veterans Administration (VA) Health Care System is to serve those in greatest need even if they lack other insurance or financial resources. Veterans who obtain their healthcare from the VA are frequently from racial minorities, of lower socioeconomic status and experience higher rates of comorbidities than the general population. In addition, a recent study found significant interest among Veterans in the James J. Peters Bronx VA medical center in clinical trial participation. We therefore sought to characterize barriers to clinical trial enrollment in this population. Methods: Veterans included had been seen in the Bronx VA Hematology/Oncology Clinic and had been screened for clinical trials for which they were ultimately determined to be ineligible. Clinical data were abstracted from the electronic medical record using a standardized, pre-specified protocol. Results: A total of 95 Veterans were enrolled. Median age was 74.3 years. A 57.9% majority identified as Black/African American, 32.6% as White, 1.1% as American Indian/Alaskan Native and 8.8% did not disclose a race. Of the 95 Veterans, 23.2% identified as Hispanic/Latino. Comorbidities were common with 31.6% having diabetes, 31.6% hypertension and 28% hyperlipidemia. After categorizing reasons for ineligibility, 23 Veterans had been deemed ineligible due to use of medications contraindicated by the protocol, 23 due to laboratory results outside of protocol-specified ranges and 19 due to having a comorbidity excluded by the trial protocol. A 70.5% majority had one reason for clinical trial ineligibility, 24.2% had two reasons and 5.2% had three reasons. Conclusions: In a diverse population of Veterans, we identified multiple reasons for clinical trial ineligibility. In many of these Veterans their ineligibility could have been prevented through thoughtful modification of inclusion/exclusion criteria. This study highlights the importance of carefully selecting eligibility criteria and the design/development of inclusive, pragmatic clinical trials to promote enrollment of diverse populations. title: Assessing Suicide Risk Reduction in the Interval Before Death by Suicide Using Natural Language Processing.
abstract: Objective: High-suicide-risk patients who quickly respond to psychotherapy, such that they cease being classified as high-risk, frequently die by suicide soon after risk declassification. It is accordingly difficult to distinguish symptom improvement and changes that may be fleeting or associated with evading treatment. This exploratory study used natural language processing to examine care patterns preceding suicide among Veterans Affairs (VA) patients whose classified-risk status remained elevated and those whose classified risk diminished in the interval before death by suicide. Methods: We identified (n=89) patients classified as high-suicide-risk whose high-risk status was later removed and died by suicide within 6 months, between 2015-2018 (Reduced Clinical Risk Classification [RCRC]). We then selected comparison (n=89) patients who retained high-risk status and died within the same interval (Sustained Clinical Risk Classification [SCRC]). We analyzed electronic health records using statistical models and topic modeling, a natural language processing method that gauges lexical patterns, and monitored risk fluctuations. Results: RCRC patients were younger, with fewer psychiatric diagnoses. Topics included "Psychotherapy," "Medication," "Outpatient," "Follow-up," and "Suicide-Assessment." After risk declassification, RCRC patients demonstrated sharp declines across all topics, whereas SCRC patients maintained or increased engagement. Conclusion: Our preliminary results suggest that RCRC patient records featured more psychotherapy-related terminology, while SCRC patient records featured more structured and medically oriented terminology. This dichotomy may infer distinct care trajectories. Perceived symptom improvement could prompt reduced surveillance, creating unrecognized vulnerability. Our findings are VA specific and should be interpreted cautiously. Future work will compare patients who died and did not die after risk declassification.

title: Neuropsychological performance, past-month active suicidal ideation, and lifetime suicide attempt history in individuals with psychosis: A cross-sectional study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Individuals with psychosis have elevated suicide risk and neuropsychological dysfunction. Prior research on neurocognition and suicidality in psychosis is mixed, with better cognition linked to both greater and lower history of suicide ideation (SI) and suicide attempts (SA). The current study examined associations between neuropsychological performance, demographics, psychiatric symptoms, past month SI, and lifetime SA history in individuals with psychosis.
METHOD: 235 adults with schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, or bipolar disorder with psychotic features completed clinical interviews, neuropsychological assessment, and symptom measures (positive and negative symptoms; depressive symptoms). Participants were grouped by past month active SI (SI+; n = 110) versus passive/no SI (SI-; n = 125) and lifetime actual SA history (SA+; n = 152) versus no SA (SA-; n = 83). Among SA + participants, we examined lifetime aborted attempts, interrupted attempts, preparatory behaviors, and attempt lethality. False Discovery Rate correction was used for multiple comparisons.
STUDY RESULTS: SI + individuals reported more severe depressive and positive symptoms; only depressive symptoms uniquely predicted SI. SA + individuals were significantly older and had worse working memory and processing speed than SA-individuals, but only age uniquely predicted SA history. Those with aborted attempt history demonstrated better premorbid intellectual functioning and working memory; only working memory remained significant in the multivariable model. After FDR correction, there were no significant predictors of interrupted attempts, preparatory behavior, or attempt lethality.
CONCLUSIONS: Current SI may be more closely associated with symptoms, whereas better working memory may be associated with aborting a suicide attempt.

title: Care of the Sexual or Gender Minority Community Living with Cystic Fibrosis: A Survey of United States and Canadian Multidisciplinary Health Care Providers
abstract: PURPOSE: Lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, intersex, asexual, or another sexual or gender minority (LGBTQIA+) people face health inequities and commonly report health care avoidance. We examined how multidisciplinary subspecialist providers care for LGBTQIA+ people with pediatric-onset chronic conditions, using cystic fibrosis (CF) as a model. METHODS: We conducted a survey of United States and Canadian CF providers regarding their LGBTQIA+ health knowledge, attitudes, comfort, and practices from January-September 2024. We analyzed results descriptively and compared responses by key variables using chi-square tests. RESULTS: Among 389 participants, 15% felt that there are only two genders and 6% reported discomfort working with LGBTQIA+ people based on personal beliefs. Nearly all (87%) agreed that asking about gender identity and sexual orientation is important to health care. Thirty percent felt unprepared to discuss concerns related to sexual orientation or gender identity, and 86% felt that they would be a better clinician if they had more training on supporting LGBTQIA+ people. Fifty-one percent reported asking their CF patients about their sexual orientation, 57% about their gender identity, and 73% about their affirmed name/pronouns. Forty-three percent of U.S. and 20% of Canadian respondents reported receiving training on supporting LGBTQIA+ people. CONCLUSION: CF providers valued addressing LGBTQIA+ health but lacked expertise, training, and resources to routinely do so. Future research should explore the experiences and health outcomes of LGBTQIA+ people with CF and develop needed provider education.

title: Plasma Exchange and Daratumumab for Myeloma Cast Nephropathy
abstract: Multiple myeloma light chain cast nephropathy (LCCN) is often treated with plasma exchange (PLEX) or the anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody, daratumumab. However, rigorous studies supporting these therapies for LCCN are limited. Using data from 25 U.S.-based academic cancer centers, we conducted two target trials examining the association between early receipt of PLEX or early receipt of daratumumab and kidney recovery in patients with newly diagnosed LCCN. Kidney recovery was defined as being alive, not on kidney replacement therapy, and with an improvement of at least one stage of AKI severity, all assessed at 90 days. Secondary outcomes included kidney recovery at 60 and 180 days. Logistic regression with propensity score overlap weights was used to adjust for confounders. Of 549 eligible patients for the PLEX target trial, 158 (28.8%) received PLEX. There was no association between PLEX and kidney recovery at 90 days (OR 1.48, 95% CI: 0.96-2.30). However, in subgroup analyses, PLEX was associated with higher odds of kidney recovery at 90 days among patients with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma compared to those with relapsed disease, as well as higher odds of kidney recovery among those with Stage 3 versus Stage 1 or 2 AKI at the time of LCCN diagnosis. Of 474 patients eligible for the daratumumab target trial, 136 (28.7%) received daratumumab. Daratumumab was not associated with kidney recovery at 90 days (OR 1.46, 95% CI: 0.84-2.55). Thus, in this multicenter cohort study, neither PLEX nor daratumumab was associated with kidney recovery at 90 days.

title: Advancing genetic pathogenicity prediction with three-dimensional proteoform-phenotype analysis.
abstract: Ascertaining the pathogenicity and clinical relevance of genetic mutations is a longstanding challenge across human disease. This is particularly relevant for genes with many variants of unknown significance (VUS), such as PRPH2-retinopathy, where complex variable phenotype patterns and limited genotype correlations hinder application of precision-medicine therapies. Recent AI-based pathogenicity tools, while powerful, may be limited by insufficient mechanistic or phenotypic training data. We established a three-dimensional proteoform-phenotype analysis framework by combining AI-generated protein structural models with clinical genomics data, in which expert consensus adjudicates model outputs through a human-in-the-loop AI approach, to evaluate 46 curated pathogenic missense variants against a background VUS pool. The framework was prospectively validated using an independently evaluated clinical patient cohort. This analysis resolved spatial biophysical signatures corresponding to distinct clinical phenotypes (i.e., retinitis pigmentosa, macular dystrophy, and pattern dystrophy) as well as complex blended presentations. Leveraging these confirmed structural signatures, we prioritized high-risk VUS. This mechanism-resolved framework can be extended to other therapeutically actionable genes to identify novel causal variants and improve diagnosis, prognosis, and better select rare, eligible patients for emerging molecular gene therapy trials.

title: Reclassifying Single Lead Sinus Rhythm ECGs for Improved AF Recurrence Detection With Deep Learning
abstract: BACKGROUND: Atrial fibrillation (AF) remains a common outcome after catheter ablation, with recurrence observed in up to 50% of patients within 5 years. Despite extensive research, challenges remain in optimizing observation and prediction windows for AF recurrence assessment. Therefore, we developed and validated a novel deep learning model that reclassifies sinus rhythm based on past and future AF events using single-lead ECG strips from handheld devices. METHODS: Of the 558 participants, 308 with no documented recurrence during study follow-up contributed Benign Sinus strips, while 250 with documented recurrence contributed sinus rhythm strips recorded within ±3 days of an AF event, defined as Severe Sinus strips. Both clinical feature-based models and a deep learning model were used to classify these ECGs according to their proximity to AF recurrence events. Performance was evaluated using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and F1-score. RESULTS: The strip-level pretrained deep learning model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.86, with sensitivity of 0.79, and specificity of 0.76. The complementary participant-level clinical feature-based Random Forest benchmark achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.71, sensitivity of 0.58, and specificity of 0.69. Feature-based analyses identified associations involving heart-rate variability, mean R-R interval, female sex, left atrial volume, and mean P-wave duration. CONCLUSIONS: Our dynamic deep learning model reclassifies 30-second single-lead sinus rhythm ECGs based on AF events within ±3 days, transforming a brief ECG snapshot into a summarized indicator of short-term AF risk.

title: Transcription factor TBX2 is a key regulator of vascular calcification.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Vascular calcification predicts cardiovascular mortality more strongly than traditional risk factors, yet its molecular basis remains poorly understood. The burden is greatest in chronic kidney disease (CKD), where disordered mineral metabolism accelerates arterial mineral deposition.
METHODS: Cross-trait genome-wide and phenome-wide association analyses were combined with single-cell RNA-seq and ATAC-seq from human kidneys and coronary arteries to identify upstream regulators. Chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing and expression profiling were used to assess direct transcriptional control. Functional relevance was evaluated in multiple gene-edited mouse lines and in primary vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) targeting T-box transcription factor 2 (TBX2), Runt-related transcription factor 2 (RUNX2), NLRP3, CASP1, and GSDMD.
RESULTS: GWAS followed by expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) and Bayesian colocalization analysis prioritized TBX2 as a shared genetic locus associated with kidney function and calcification-related cardiometabolic traits. TBX2-deficient mice exhibited increased susceptibility to vascular calcification, hypercalciuria, kidney injury, bone demineralization, and systemic phosphate dysregulation under CKD-like phosphate stress conditions. TBX2 deficiency promoted VSMC calcification and osteochondrogenic differentiation in vitro. Mechanistically, TBX2 acted as a transcriptional repressor by binding the promoter of RUNX2, a key osteogenic transcription factor, and suppressing its expression. Deletion of RUNX2 in TBX2-deficient VSMCs abolished TBX2 loss-induced calcification. TBX2-deficient VSMCs were also more sensitive to activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome by microcrystals generated from osteogenic VSMCs. Genetic deletion of NLRP3, CASP1, or GSDMD in TBX2-deficient mice attenuated vascular calcification and renal injury. In human samples, TBX2 expression inversely correlated with the severity of kidney fibrosis and was reduced in calcified vascular lesions.
CONCLUSIONS: Integrative genetic, cellular, and animal studies identify TBX2 as a central transcriptional repressor linking mineral dysregulation, osteogenic signalling, and sterile inflammation in CKD-associated vascular calcification. Therapeutic strategies that restore TBX2 function or target its RUNX2-NLRP3 axis may reduce cardiovascular risk in patients with CKD.

title: Multiprofessional and interprofessional simulation training for advance care planning: a systematic review
abstract: Abstract Background Recent international guidelines describe advance care planning (ACP) as evolving from isolated communication tasks toward an iterative, collaborative process integrating goals-of-care (GOC) discussions, documentation, clinical and ethical reasoning. Simulation is a promising approach to support this evolution, yet its design and impact on ACP interprofessional collaborative practice remain unclear. This systematic review synthesised and evaluated the literature on multiprofessional and interprofessional simulation (MP-Sim, IP-Sim) for training healthcare students and professionals in ACP. Methods We addressed four questions on trainees, ACP tasks, simulation design, and outcomes. Six databases (CINAHL, EMBASE, ERIC, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Web of Science) were searched from January 2010 to June 2025. Eligible studies used simulation with trainees from at least two professions to address ACP. Findings were synthesised using a Presage–Process–Product framework, and outcomes were classified according to Kirkpatrick’s levels. Study quality was appraised using the Medical Education Research Study Quality Instrument. Results 28 studies (11 MP-Sim, 17 IP-Sim) included 4,081 participants (83% professionals, 17% students), predominantly physicians and nurses. Simulation programs predominantly targeted GOC conversations, with limited integration of documentation and clinical and ethical reasoning. Most simulations were conducted in hospital settings. Despite heterogeneous methods, studies reported positive outcomes on learner satisfaction, attitudes toward communication and teamwork, and, in some studies, GOC documentation. MP-Sim primarily supported rehearsal of profession-specific ACP tasks, whereas IP-Sim more often enabled collaboration in dyads and teams. Conclusion Simulation-based ACP training can be conceptualized through a dual continuum comprising professional integration (from multiprofessional participation to interprofessional collaboration) and task integration (from communication-focused part-task rehearsal to whole-task ACP practice). This dual continuum provides a practical lens for guiding simulation design towards greater interprofessional collaboration and whole-task ACP practice. Designing simulations that integrate GOC communication, documentation, clinical and ethical reasoning with interprofessional collaboration within longitudinal, multi-stakeholder scenarios may better prepare students and professionals for contemporary ACP practice.

title: Deuterium-Oxide Labelling Proteomics Illustrates the Importance of Sample Timing and the Limitations of Serial Biopsies.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Measuring in vivo protein synthesis is important for testing how interventions, disease and ageing remodel the proteome. A limitation of approaches using short-term infusions of labelled amino acids was that long-term changes had to be extrapolated from short-term measurements. Deuterium oxide (D2O) is now widely used because it can measure protein synthesis over periods of days to weeks. We previously showed that the duration of labelling impacts measured protein synthesis, but many still employ repeated tissue sampling during D2O provision. We hypothesized that the timing of tissue sampling alters which proteins contribute to the overall protein fractional synthesis rate (FSR), thereby invalidating comparisons between serial samples collected during continuous labelling.
METHODS: To test this hypothesis, we used a five-timepoint (0d, 4d, 15d, 30d and 45d) D2O labelling time course followed by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry proteomics to calculate individual protein synthesis rates and plateau values in mouse gastrocnemius muscle. Individual proteins were stratified into slow and fast groups, such that each group was responsible for the slowest or fastest 20% of total synthesis over the first 4 days of labelling, respectively.
RESULTS: In a 4-day period representing a baseline period, the synthesis rate of summed proteins was 2.09%/day. When the period was extended to 15, 30 or 45 days, the synthesis rates of summed proteins declined to 1.64%, 1.31% and 1.10%/day, respectively. The contribution of slow and fast proteins to these rates changed as a function of time. The fast and slow proteins accounted for 4.3% and 34.0% of measured proteome abundance, respectively. From Day 0 to Day 4, fast and slow proteins contributed 19.8% and 20.2% of the calculated FSR, respectively. By Day 45, these contributions shifted to 6.5% and 28.8%. Further, we demonstrated that the assumption that the fraction new of proteins linearly increases to 100% new is not true for the majority of proteins. Instead, most proteins plateaued at some point less than 100%, which stops their individual contribution to a summed protein synthesis rate.
CONCLUSIONS: In continuous long-term labelling studies, biopsy timing changes the measured bulk FSR because the relative contributions of individual proteins to that measurement over time. Fast proteins that plateau early decrease their contribution as labelling time increases. These findings indicate that studies with different labelling periods, or multiple biopsies over time during continuous labelling of days to weeks cannot be compared to biopsies taken at other times in the labelling period.

title: Microplastics inhibit macrophage bioenergetics impairing homeostatic function and immune responsiveness
abstract: Abstract Since the 1950s, microplastics (MPs) have become omnipresent, representing a novel environmental hazard which continually deposits in our airways. Pulmonary macrophages (pMacs) orchestrate the balance between inflammation and tolerance required for homeostasis of the lung and are among the first immune cells to encounter inhaled MPs. Yet, how pMacs react to plastic deposition in the lung and implications for disease remain unknown. Here, we exposed mice in vivo, human precision-cut lung slices (hPCLS) ex vivo, and monocyte-derived macrophages and cell lines to polystyrene MPs in vitro. MP deposition in the lung and extrapulmonary tissues was determined over a 1-week period and pMacs from MP-laden lungs isolated for RNA-sequencing. We compared the effects of MPs or diesel exhaust particulate exposures on hPCLS viability and metabolism, monocyte-derived macrophage transcription, and macrophage mitochondrial function, inflammation, and antigen presentation. MPs readily translocated the lung and were observed in all organs examined within 1-day. pMacs from MP-exposed mice expressed transcriptional pathways associated with endocrine system disorders, tissue remodeling, and malignant disease. Macrophage phagocytosis was impaired through decreased mitochondrial function which could be rescued pharmacologically. MPs inhibited the ability of macrophages to effectively present OVA-antigen preventing TCR-specific activation, an effect that could be restored by blocking PD-1/PD-L1. These findings indicate that MPs impair macrophages via unique mechanisms linking phagocytic and bioenergetic dysfunction. Loss of antigen-presenting capabilities in MP-laden macrophages may compromise immunosurveillance. As such, MPs have the potential to increase susceptibility to lung disease independent of the conventional mechanisms of inflammation and oxidative stress.

title: Opioid manufacturer payments to hospitalists and hospitalists' prescribing of opioids on discharge
abstract: Marketing payments from opioid manufacturers to outpatient physicians are associated with opioid prescribing. We examined the association between opioid-related payments to hospitalists and opioid prescribing at discharge from 2015 to 2023. We linked Medicare Part B Physicians & Other Practitioners public use files, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Open Payments data, and Medicare Part D Prescribers Public Use Files to identify hospitalists' opioid-related payments and opioid prescribing. Of 67,408 hospitalists, 360 (0.53%) received payments, which declined from 581 in 2015 to 65 in 2023. Each payment was associated with a 0.94 percentage-point increase (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.60 to 1.28) in the proportion of outpatient prescription claims for opioids, equivalent to 112 additional opioid claims (95% CI, 70.78 to 154.73). Total payment value was not associated with opioid claims. Opioid-related payments to hospitalists are uncommon and declining, but even minimal exposure is associated with greater opioid prescribing.

title: Gut‒liver‒brain axis signature of cirrhosis-related cognitive impairment is consistent across multi-national cohorts.
abstract: Cognitive impairment in cirrhosis is associated with an altered gut‒liver‒brain axis, but geographic variations in diet and clinical practices may limit generalizability. We investigated consistency of microbial signatures for cirrhosis-related cognitive impairment across four countries. We enrolled outpatients with cirrhosis from USA, Denmark, Lithuania, and Mexico who underwent Psychometric Hepatic Encephalopathy Score (PHES) testing for covert hepatic encephalopathy (CHE), and stool shotgun metagenomic sequencing. Taxonomic and functional associations with PHES were evaluated after adjustment for MELD, country, demographics, sex, proton pump inhibitor (PPI), lactulose, and rifaximin use. We enrolled 221 patients (median age 58 y, 57.9% men, median MELD 12). Cognitive performance varied by country despite adjustment for clinical covariates. Lithuania demonstrated greater microbial richness and better cognition despite higher MELD, accompanied by distinct dietary patterns including greater yogurt and tea consumption. In the entire cohort, increasing MELD was associated with reduced microbial richness and depletion of commensals. Worse PHES performance, however, showed a distinct microbiome signature with increased Streptococcus abundance independent of MELD, country, PPI use, and HE therapies. Twenty-two microbial pathways were associated with PHES, mostly related to amino-acid biosynthesis and nitrogen metabolism. Of these, ornithine degradation and heme B biosynthesis II were uniquely enriched with worse PHES and CHE, which mapped onto Enterobacteriaceae. We conclude that across four geographically and culturally disparate countries, cirrhosis-related cognitive impairment was associated with consistent microbial compositional and functional alterations distinct from advancing liver disease. These findings support a consistent gut‒liver‒brain axis signature involving oral-gut translocation and altered nitrogen metabolism.
