title: NSAID initiation and risk for gastrointestinal bleeding in patients receiving GLP-1 receptor agonists: A retrospective cohort study.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) have been purported to increase risk for gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding. Our objective was to determine whether GLP-1 RAs are associated with increased risk for GI adverse events following the initiation of a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID).
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study used national administrative data from the Veterans Health Administration to identify patients with type 2 diabetes who initiated an NSAID while concurrently receiving a GLP-1 RA or a comparator agent: a sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor (SGLT-2i) or a dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor (DPP-4i). The primary outcome measure was the incidence of a GI bleed or ulcer within 12 months of NSAID initiation. Cox proportional hazards regression was used to compare risk for GI bleeding or ulcer between GLP-1 RA recipients and the comparator groups while adjusting for confounders. A sensitivity analysis was conducted using GI bleed as a secondary outcome.
RESULTS: A total of 13,433 patients received a GLP-1 RA, 24,480 received an SGLT-2i, and 30,968 received a DPP-4i. The primary outcome occurred in 0.9% (n = 117) of patients receiving a concurrent GLP-1 RA, 1.0% (n = 243) of those receiving an SGLT-2i, and 1.0% (n = 308) of those receiving a DPP-4i. In adjusted regression analyses, no difference in risk for GI bleeding or ulcer was observed between GLP-1 RAs and either comparator (SGLT-2i: hazard ratio [HR], 0.85; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.68-1.07; DPP-4i: HR, 0.82; 95% CI, 0.66- 1.01). Similar nonsignificant results were observed for the secondary outcome.
CONCLUSION: We did not observe an increased risk for developing a GI bleed or ulcer within the year following NSAID initiation with concurrent GLP-1 RA therapy, relative to comparator agents.

title: Selective PDE4 inhibition enhances bone mass by stimulating bone formation and suppressing bone resorption
abstract: Osteoporosis is a common skeletal disease that increases fracture risk and is a major cause of morbidity, mortality, and diminished quality of life in the elderly. Although bone anabolic therapies are available, inconvenient routes of administration and concerns regarding potential adverse effects substantially limit their use. Consequently, anti-resorptive drugs that slow further bone loss without rebuilding lost bone mass or restoring load-bearing strength remain the dominant therapies. Many patients nevertheless sustain fractures despite treatment, underscoring the weaknesses of this approach and the need for new anabolic strategies. The immune system plays an important role in regulating both bone formation and resorption, raising the possibility that immune pathways can be therapeutically harnessed to promote bone anabolism. Recent studies have further linked the gut microbiota to this osteoimmune network, demonstrating that microbiota-derived metabolites can promote T cell-dependent anabolic signaling in bone. It has previously been shown that broad-spectrum phosphodiesterase (PDE) inhibitors such as pentoxifylline (PTX) stimulate bone formation and promote bone accrual in animal models. We recently demonstrated that a major mechanism of PTX-induced bone anabolism is through an osteoimmunological pathway in which activated CD8 T cells trigger production of Wnt10b, a bone-anabolic Wnt ligand. However, PTX also directly promotes osteoclast bone resorption, limiting bone gain, while its adverse-effect profile further restricts its therapeutic utility. Here, we investigated the bone anabolic properties of apremilast, an FDA-approved PDE4-selective inhibitor targeting a major PDE regulating cAMP signaling in CD8 T cells. Micro-computed tomography demonstrated significant trabecular bone accrual and improved microarchitecture in femurs and vertebrae of apremilast-treated female C57BL/6J mice. Quantitative histomorphometry confirmed increased bone formation and reduced osteoclast indices. In vitro , apremilast did not directly stimulate osteoblast differentiation or mineralization but increased Wnt10b expression by CD8 T cells, supporting an indirect immune-mediated anabolic mechanism. Critically, unlike PTX, apremilast dose-dependently inhibited osteoclast differentiation from primary monocytes. These findings are consistent with an anabolic pathway, together with suppression of osteoclastogenesis, creating a remodeling environment favorable for net bone gain. These findings identify apremilast as an immunomodulatory regulator of bone remodeling and provide a rationale for further evaluation of PDE4 inhibition in preclinical models of osteoporosis.

title: Modulation of riboflavin biosynthesis enzymes in non-typhoidal Salmonella isolates differentially impacts human MAIT cell activation.
abstract: Invasive non-typhoidal Salmonella (iNTS) sequence type 313 (ST313) isolates have emerged in sub-Saharan Africa, with a high incidence of multidrug resistance, enhanced intracellular persistence, increased dissemination and immune evasion. ST313 isolate D23580 was shown to avoid activation of mucosal-associated invariant T (MAIT) cells compared with a genetically similar, non-invasive Salmonella Typhimurium (S.Tm) 4/74 strain, but the mechanism remains unclear. Here, we studied immune responses to infection with typhoidal strains and ST313 isolates using comparative transcriptomic profiling of human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). MAIT cells responded to typhoidal strains but not to D23580. To uncover underlying mechanisms, we engineered an inducible CRISPRi system targeting riboflavin biosynthesis enzymes (rib), which process MAIT ligands, in D23580 and 4/74 strains. Several rib hypomorphs exhibited prolonged lag time in minimal media, which was more pronounced in D23580 than in 4/74. In PBMC infection, knockdown of lumazine synthase (RibH) and riboflavin synthase (RibE) resulted in contrasting MAIT cell activation phenotypes. RibH knockdown restored MAIT cell activation in D23580 but did not affect activation in 4/74. Conversely, RibE knockdown diminished MAIT cell activation by 4/74 but had no impact on MAIT cell activation by D23580. Metabolomic analysis revealed accumulation of the biosynthetic intermediate DMRL in RibE knockdown and a differential impact on riboflavin biosynthesis end products between D23580 and 4/74 RibH knockdown, suggesting altered pathway flux between the strains. Our results indicate RibH and RibE as pivotal nodes for strain-specific MAIT-activation during Salmonella infection of human PBMCs, illustrating teir central role in the complex interplay between bacterial metabolism and host immunity.

title: Subcellular compartment determines signal dominance: Endosomal cAMP overrides concurrent plasma membrane RhoA activation from a single receptor.
abstract: Cells convey information not only via the identity of activated signaling pathways but also through the subcellular location where those signals originate. Whether spatially distinct signals from a single activated receptor compete to determine net cellular output has remained unclear. Here, we demonstrate this principle for a G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR), showing that endosomal and plasma membrane signals from a single activated receptor are not merely distinct but functionally opposed, with endosomal signaling predominating to reverse the net cellular output. Using the adhesion GPCR GPR64/ADGRG2 as a model system, we show that ligand activation engages two spatially distinct G-protein pathways that are not just additive but functionally opposed: plasma membrane G13/RhoA activation and Gs/cAMP production that persists from endosomes following receptor internalization. The endosomal cAMP pool actively overrides concurrent plasma membrane RhoA activation, resulting in net RhoA inactivation, an outcome that is completely reversed by pharmacological blockade of endocytosis or endosomal Gs inactivation. In parathyroid cells, where GPR64 is highly expressed, this endosomal signal dominance suppresses parathyroid hormone secretion independently of extracellular Ca2+ levels. These findings support a model in which the subcellular compartment, rather than pathway identity, determines the dominant signal and the overall cellular response of a single activated receptor, with implications for understanding the complexity of GPCR signaling.

title: High-Sensitivity Troponin Pathway and Emergency Department Length of Stay.
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: High-sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs-cTn) assays are the diagnostic standard for acute coronary syndrome but present significant implementation and workflow complexity.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate whether implementation of a structured, electronic health record (EHR)-integrated hs-cTn pathway was associated with changes in emergency department (ED) length of stay (LOS) and serial troponin testing times.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This retrospective quality improvement study compared preimplementation conventional cTn assay (June 1, 2021, to March 31, 2022) with a postimplementation integrated hs-cTn pathway (June 1, 2022, to March 31, 2023) in 4 urban EDs within a single health system. Participants were adults (aged ≥18 years) presenting with chest pain and at least 1 troponin assay result. Data analysis was performed from April to September 2024.
EXPOSURES: Implementation of an hs-cTn assay within an EHR-integrated clinical pathway.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was ED LOS, defined as time from patient registration to ED departure. Secondary outcomes included time from first clinician evaluation to disposition (discharge or admission) and interval from the first troponin assay order to the second troponin assay result in patients with serial assays.
RESULTS: Of the 16 094 patient encounters analyzed (9151 [56.9%] female; mean [SD] age, 49.5 [17.4] years), 8486 (52.7%) were in the hs-cTn and 7608 (47.3%) were in the conventional cTn cohort. Overall, hs-cTn implementation with workflow integration was associated with decreased mean ED LOS, from 6.18 (95% CI, 6.10-6.26) hours to 5.64 (95% CI, 5.57-5.71) hours. Compared with conventional cTn, implementation of the hs-cTn pathway was associated with shorter mean ED LOS in admitted patients (9.60 [95% CI, 9.35-9.87] hours vs 10.50 [95% CI, 10.22-10.78] hours; P = .003) and discharged patients (5.02 [95% CI, 4.96-5.08] hours vs 5.33 [95% CI, 5.26-5.40] hours; P = .006). Pathway implementation was also associated with shorter time from evaluation to disposition in patients receiving 2 or more troponin measurements (5.06 [95% CI, 4.97-5.15] hours vs 6.68 [95% CI, 6.52-6.85] hours; P < .001) and time from first troponin order to second troponin result in both admitted patients (3.18 [95% CI, 3.11-3.25] hours vs 5.16 [95% CI, 5.01-5.31] hours; P < .001) and discharged patients (2.78 [95% CI, 2.75-2.82] hours vs 4.54 [95% CI, 4.46-4.62] hours; P < .001).
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this quality improvement study, an EHR-integrated hs-cTn pathway was associated with significantly reduced ED LOS and, in patients with serial troponin measurements, reduced time from evaluation to disposition and reduced time to serial assay results. The findings suggest this structured EHR approach may mitigate operational challenges of hs-cTn adoption and could serve as a scalable model to improve ED efficiency for patients with chest pain.

title: Abstract 14363: Hidden in Plain Sight: AI-Derived Coronary Calcium from Non-Gated Chest CT Predicts Long-Term Mortality Across Age, Sex, and Race
abstract: Introduction/Background: Coronary artery calcium (CAC) is a established marker of atherosclerotic cardiovascular risk. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) has enabled automated CAC quantification from non-gated chest computed tomography (CT) scans across diverse clinical settings. Research Questions/Hypothesis: We hypothesize that AI-derived CAC provides prognostic value for long-term all-cause mortality across heterogenous real-world imaging protocols and diverse patient populations. Methods/Approach: We analyzed 31,262 adults undergoing non-contrast, non-gated chest CT scans from 2010 to 2024 which vastly increased the dataset size of chest CTs compared to the original validation study. A previously validated deep learning was applied to quantify CAC. Patients were categorized as CAC 0, 1-100, 101-400, or > 400. A Cox proportional hazards regression was used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) for all-cause mortality across CAC categories. Kaplan-Meier analysis evaluated survival across CAC stratified across age, sex, and race. Results/Data (descriptive and inferential statistics): Among 31,262 patients, we demonstrated a graded rise in all-cause mortality across AI-CAC categories over the long-term. Compared to CAC of 0, a higher CAC burden was associated with increased mortality risk: CAC 1-100 (HR 1.79 [ 95% CI 1.66-1.92]), CAC 101-400 (HR 2.46 [ 2.3-2.64)], and CAC > 400 (HR 3.73 [3.51-3.96] with all p < 0.005. Kaplan-Meier analysis revealed early divergence with persistent separation of survival curves across our CAC strata. At 10 years, survival decreased stepwise from CAC 0 at 70% to 50.5%, 40.3%, and 25.5% in CAC 1-100, 101-400, and > 400 groups, respectively. CAC prevalence increased markedly with age and consistently higher in men than women across age group. CAC refines risk within age groups as higher CAC categories are associated with progressively increased mortality within each age group. Similarly, age-dependent increases in CAC prevalence were observed across European White and African American, with a higher CAC burden in men compared to women. CAC prevalence was generally higher among White patients compared to African American patients at younger and middle ages, but less so with advancing age. Conclusion(s): In conclusion, AI-derived CAC from routine non-gated CT was associated with increased mortality and improved risk stratification across diverse populations. This supports its use in clinical practice to identify high-risk individuals who may benefit from earlier preventive interventions.

title: Abstract 15944: Cardiovascular Outcomes of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists in Individuals with Family History of Ischemic Heart Disease
abstract: Background: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1) have been shown to reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in individuals with type 2 diabetes (T2DM), obesity, and cardiovascular disease. However, individuals with a family history of premature ischemic heart disease (IHD) are a high-risk population in whom the cardiovascular benefits of GLP-1 receptor agonists remain uncertain. This study compares MACE associated with GLP-1 versus non-GLP-1 use among individuals with a family history of premature IHD without T2DM. Methods: The TriNetX U.S. Collaborative Network was used to analyze MACE risk for individuals aged 18 and above with a family history of premature IHD within one year of initiating GLP-1. This was compared to a control of non-GLP-1 users. Individuals with a history of T2DM, prior myocardial infarction (MI)s, or previous coronary revascularization were excluded. Propensity score matching was performed to balance demographics and covariates including body mass index, chronic kidney disease, and heart failure. The primary outcome was a composite of all-cause mortality and incident MI. Secondary outcomes included individual primary outcome components. Statistical analyses were conducted with Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and multivariate Cox proportional hazard modeling. P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results: After matching, 51,026 individuals were included in each cohort. Baseline patient demographics and clinical attributes were well balanced. Average age of individuals at index was 49. At one year, individuals taking GLP-1 demonstrated significantly lower rates of the primary composite outcome compared to individuals not taking GLP-1 (hazard ratio [HR] 0.19; 95% CI, 0.17-0.22, p < 0.0001). Secondary outcomes of all-cause mortality (HR 0.11; 95% CI 0.09-0.13, p < 0.0001) and MI (HR 0.48; 95% CI, 0.39-0.59; p < 0.0001) were significantly lower in those on GLP-1 compared to those not on GLP-1. The primary composite outcome was also significant through Cox multivariate proportional hazards (HR = 0.30; 95% CI = 0.27-0.33; p < 0.0001). Conclusion: GLP-1 use was associated with significantly lower rates of the composite outcome compared to non-GLP-1 use in individuals without T2DM and with a family history of premature IHD. This suggests that GLP-1s may be useful for risk reduction in those with increased genetic predisposition for incident cardiovascular disease.

title: Abstract 13572: Antecedent Chronic Kidney Disease and Cardiovascular Mortality in 300,000 Incident HFpEF Cases in the United States
abstract: Background: HFpEF has been increasingly viewed as a disorder in which kidney dysfunction may play a central role. However, the distribution of incident HFpEF, across the full spectrum of antecedent kidney function remains poorly characterized, particularly among patients with intact renal function. The prognostic significant of antecedent CKD severity for cardiovascular (CV) mortality after incident HFpEF also remains uncertain. Research Question: In a contemporary incident HFpEF cohort, what is the distribution of HFpEF across antecedent KDIGO based CKD stages including those with intact renal function, and is antecedent CKD severity associated with subsequent 5-year CV mortality? Methods: This cohort included U.S. Veterans Affairs patients with incident heart failure (HF) diagnosed between January 1, 2000, and June 30, 2025. HFpEF diagnosis was ascertained using natural language processing-derived LVEF > 50% closest to the incident HF date and a validated HFpEF algorithm incorporating loop diuretic use, elevated natriuretic peptide levels, and HFpEF-ABA score. Antecedent kidney function was classified using KDIGO criteria based on 2 eGFR measurements obtained ≥90 days apart before incident HFpEF. Patients were grouped as normal kidney function (NKF) (eGFR ≥ 90 ml/min/1.73 m 2 and no urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio [UACR] > 30 mg/g), CKD stage II (eGFR 60-89); and CKD stage III or > (eGFR <60). Outcomes were 5-year all-cause and CV mortality. Fine-Gray model treated non-CV death as a competing event. Results: Among 332,497 patients with incident HFpEF, 198,637 had stable antecedent kidney function and were classified as NKF (20.5%), CKD stage II (24.0%) and CKD stage III or > (55.5%). Advanced CKD was associated with older age and higher prevalence of hypertension, diabetes, CAD, whereas obesity, chronic liver and lung diseases were more frequent in the NKF group. 5-year all-cause mortality increased from 44.4% in NKF to 46.4% in CKD stage II and 63.5% in CKD stage III or > with crude mortality rates per 100 person-years of 13.6, 14.5, and 24.3. In adjusted Cox models, hazard ratios (HR) for all-cause mortality were 0.89 for CKD stage II and 1.24 for CKD stage III or > compared to NKF. CV deaths accounted for 28.1%, 36.0% and 37.8% of all deaths in the NKF, CKD stage II and CKD stage III or > groups, respectively, with corresponding adjusted subdistribution HRs for CV mortality of 1.34 and 2.02 versus NKF. Non-CV death predominated across groups. Conclusion: In the largest nationwide contemporary study of >300,000 rigorously phenotyped patients with incident HFpEF, over one fifth had “renal-intact HFpEF” (eGFR > 90ml/min/1.73 m2 & UACR <30 mg/g), suggesting that a substantial proportion of HFpEF developed in the absence of antecedent kidney dysfunction. Furthermore, worsening antecedent kidney function was associated with a marked stepwise increase in CV mortality following HFpEF diagnosis.

title: Abstract 17341: A Distinct Preclinical Cardiomyopathy Signature in Carriers of the CD36 Y325* Variant
abstract: Background: CD36 Y325* (rs3211938, p.Tyr325Ter) is a nonsense variant in CD36 , which encodes a scavenger receptor critical for myocardial fatty acid uptake and cardiac energy metabolism, and is associated with dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM). Found almost exclusively in individuals of African genetic ancestry (~16% of whom are heterozygous and 1% homozygous), CD36 Y325* has recently emerged as one of the most common genetic contributors to DCM in this population. However, defining the preclinical cardiac and metabolic phenotype of CD36 Y325* carriers is an important step toward developing targeted screening and prevention strategies. Aim: To characterize the preclinical cardiac and metabolic profile of CD36 Y325* carriers using imaging and circulating biomarkers across three population-based cohorts. Methods: We studied 459,245 participants without heart failure from the UK Biobank, the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA), and Jackson Heart Study, including 14,508 of African ancestry. CD36 Y325* associations with cardiac imaging and circulating biomarker phenotypes were evaluated among African ancestry participants given the variant’s ancestry-specific distribution. Parallel analyses in carriers of TTN truncating variants (TTNtv) - the most well-established genetic cause of DCM - were performed in a multi-ancestry sample for comparison. Results: Among participants without clinical evidence of heart failure, 980 (0.4% of all-ancestry participants) carried a TTN tv, while 1343 (16.2% of African-ancestry participants) were heterozygous and 84 (1.0%) were homozygous for CD36 Y325*. CD36 Y325* carrier status was associated with subclinical left ventricular dysfunction, including markedly higher odds of subnormal left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF <50%) in a dose-dependent manner among heterozygotes (OR=2.09; p=0.02) and homozygotes (OR=11.03; p=6.4E-05), as well as elevations in ketone bodies and reductions in circulating CD36 protein without increases in NT-proBNP or troponin. TTN tv carrier status was similarly associated with subclinical left ventricular dysfunction but was differentiated by elevated NT-proBNP and no association with ketone bodies. Conclusions: CD36 Y325* carriers exhibit a preclinical cardiomyopathy profile characterized by subclinical left ventricular dysfunction, reduced circulating CD36 protein, and altered energy metabolism without biomarker evidence of myocardial stretch or injury. This profile differs from that of TTN tv carriers and implicates disrupted myocardial energetics as a distinct mechanism underlying DCM risk, with potential relevance for early risk stratification.

title: Abstract 10606: Machine Learning-Derived Cardiometabolic Phenotypes: Insights from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, 2009-2018
abstract: Introduction: The American Heart Association Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic (CKM) framework was developed to characterize the interconnected burden of cardiometabolic, kidney, and cardiovascular disease (CVD). It remains unclear whether these stages fully capture the heterogeneity of cardiometabolic risk in the population. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that unsupervised machine learning (UML) could identify distinct cardiometabolic phenotypes that transcend conventional CKM staging and provide additional insight into chronic kidney disease (CKD) and CVD risk. Methods: An analysis of 30,352 adults aged≥18 was conducted using pooled NHANES data from 2009-2018. UML using K-means clustering was applied to age, BMI, blood pressure, HbA1c, triglycerides, and HDL cholesterol. Five clusters (Cs) emerged, identified without using CKD, CVD, or CKM stage data. The distribution of CKM stages was assessed, and then CKD and CVD outcomes across Cs. Logistic regression, weighted for the NHANES design and adjusted for age, sex, and race/ethnicity, tested associations between Cs and CKD or CVD. Results: Analysis showed a highly significant association was observed between Cs and CKM stage distribution (χ 2 =9055.9, P<0.001). Although CKM Stage 2 represented the dominant category across most Cs, substantial heterogeneity was identified within this stage. Specifically, 82.2% of individuals in C3, 77.3% in C5, and 67.8% in C2 were classified as CKM Stage 2 despite markedly different cardiometabolic profiles. CKD and CVD were subsequently evaluated as outcomes across Cs. CKD prevalence ranged from 5% in C1 to 46.5% in C2, whereas CVD prevalence ranged from 1.7% in C1 to 24.3% in C4. C2 had the highest CKD burden, while C4 had the highest CVD burden and adverse outcomes. Compared with C1, C2 had the highest odds of CKD (OR 6.15, 95% CI 5.18-7.30), followed by C5 (OR 1.81, 95% CI 1.56-2.10), C4 (OR 1.77, 95% CI 1.51-2.07), and C3 (OR 1.60, 95% CI 1.40-1.82). Similar findings were observed for CVD, with the strongest association in C2 (OR 3.96, 95% CI 3.11-5.05), followed by C3 (OR 2.46, 95% CI 2.02-3.00), C4 (OR 2.14, 95% CI 1.72-2.68), and C5 (OR 1.53, 95% CI 1.23-1.91). Results were consistent across the sensitivity analysis when age was excluded from clustering, showing that Cs and outcomes were not driven solely by age. Conclusion: Although these phenotypes showed significant overlap with CKM stages, substantial heterogeneity within individual CKM stages, particularly stage 2, was observed. ML-derived phenotypes identified clinically meaningful subgroups with markedly different CKD and CVD risks despite being classified in the same CKM stage. These findings suggest that data-driven phenotyping approaches may complement existing CKM staging frameworks and improve risk stratification of cardiometabolic disease beyond conventional categorical classification.

title: Abstract 8105: Rural-Urban Differences in Oral Anticoagulation for Cardiac Implantable Electronic Device-Detected Atrial Fibrillation/Flutter ≥ 24 Hours
abstract: Introduction: U.S. adults living in rural areas have worse cardiovascular outcomes than those in urban areas. One contributing factor may be rural-urban differences in arrhythmia care. Atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter (AF/AFL) increase cardioembolic stroke risk and can be diagnosed with cardiac implantable electronic devices (CIED). The 2023 AHA/ACC AF guideline gives a Class 2a recommendation for oral anticoagulation (OAC) in CIED-detected AF/AFL ≥ 24 hours. Research Question: Does OAC prescription differ by rural vs. urban residence? Methods: This retrospective electronic health-record based study identified veteran patients with new CIED-detected AF/AFL ≥ 24 hours based on clinician adjudication from 1/1/2019 to 5/27/2025 in the national Veterans Health Administration (VHA). Exclusion criteria encompassed recent significant bleeding, OAC prescription within past 180 days, cardiac surgery, or CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc < 2. Cumulative probabilities of OAC prescription were plotted using Kaplan-Meier curves with censoring for cessation of CIED remote monitoring or death. A multivariable Cox proportional hazard model was adjusted for demographics, clinical covariates, substance use, and medications, with a frailty term for VA facility. Results: Among 4,020 patients with new CIED-detected AF/AFL ≥ 24 hours across 126 facilities, 1,506 (37.5%) were rural and 2,514 (62.5%) were urban. Mean CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc was 4.55 in rural vs. 4.57 in urban patients. Rural patients were slightly younger (mean age 78.4 vs. 79.1 years) and more likely to have had myocardial infarction, percutaneous coronary intervention, or coronary artery bypass graft surgery than urban patients. Other comorbidities had similar rates between rural and urban patients. Over 1 year, 59.9% of rural vs. 56.2% of urban patients were prescribed OAC ( Figure ) with shorter median time to anticoagulation in rural vs. urban patients (156 vs. 206 days). In the adjusted Cox model, rurality was associated with a higher OAC prescription rate (hazard ratio [HR] 1.10, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.01-1.20). In patients with CIED-detected AF/AFL > 7 days ( n = 850), rural patients had higher OAC prescription rates than urban patients (HR 1.22, 95% CI 1.01-1.47). There was no significant difference in the proportion of rural vs. urban patients prescribed a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) compared with warfarin (96.6% vs. 96.9%, p=0.83). Conclusion: In the national VHA, there were overall low rates of OAC prescription for patients with new CIED-detected AF/AFL ≥ 24 hours, although higher in rural vs. urban patients. Patient, clinic, and health care system factors should be investigated to improve OAC prescription.

title: Abstract 18121: Heterogeneous Safety Reporting After Catheter Ablation for Scar-Related Ventricular Tachycardia
abstract: Background: Catheter ablation for scar-related ventricular tachycardia (VT) carries procedural risks, but safety outcomes are reported inconsistently across studies. Prior reviews have highlighted heterogeneity in VT ablation outcomes reporting, but complication-specific safety rates and safety-reporting completeness have not been systematically quantified. We characterized pooled safety outcomes and safety-domain reporting across scar-related VT ablation studies. Methods: Safety data were extracted from a systematic review of 51 studies published from 2010-2026, including 8501 eligible patients with ischemic or nonischemic cardiomyopathy. Outcomes included major adverse events (MAEs) and the following events reported separately: procedure-related mortality, tamponade, stroke/transient ischemic attack (TIA), vascular complications, and heart failure (HF) exacerbation. Random-effects pooled proportions were estimated for nonfatal complications; procedure-related mortality was reported as a crude rate because events were rare. A six-domain safety-reporting score (0-6) assessed reporting of these safety outcomes. MAE definitions and surveillance periods were categorized. Results: Safety-domain reporting varied substantially: mean score was 3.7/6, and only 11/51 studies (22%) reported all 6 domains separately. MAEs were reported in 40/51 studies (78%), procedure-related mortality in 38 (75%), tamponade in 35 (69%), vascular complications in 31(61%), stroke/TIA in 29 (57%), and HF exacerbation in only 15 (29%), limiting precision. Random-effects pooled estimates were 8.1% for MAEs (95% CI, 6.6%-9.9%; I 2 =71%), 2.7% for vascular complications (95% CI, 2.0%-3.7%), 2.0% for tamponade (95% CI, 1.6%-2.4%), and 1.0% for stroke/TIA (95% CI, 0.7%-1.3%). Procedure-related mortality was low, with a crude rate of 20/5589 (0.36%). MAE definitions were not reported in 11 studies (22%), and MAE surveillance periods were not reported in 12 (24%). Conclusions: In this systematic review of scar-related VT ablation studies, rates of procedure-related mortality and major adverse events were lower overall but reported MAE rates varied substantially. Safety reporting also differed across clinically relevant domains, with HF exacerbation separately reported in fewer than one-third of studies. To support patient counseling and improve comparability across VT ablation studies and technologies, future studies should consider reporting a consistent minimum safety set where clinically relevant, including procedure-related mortality, tamponade, stroke/TIA, vascular complications, HF exacerbation, and other clearly defined MAEs using prespecified surveillance periods, while recognizing the relevance of specific complications to varying ablation technologies.

title: Abstract 13429: Association of Fibrosis-4 Scores as a Time Varying Covariate with Cardiovascular Disease Outcomes: A Retrospective Cohort Study in A National Cohort of Primary Care Patients
abstract: Background: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, a manifestation of the metabolic syndrome affects around 38% of Americans. It is associated with a higher risk for cardiovascular disease (CVD) events-i.e., acute myocardial infarction (AMI), congestive heart failure (CHF), and ischemic stroke. Fibrosis-4 Index (FIB-4) is calculated using aminotransferases [aspartate (AST) and alanine (ALT)], and platelets [FIB-4 =(Age x AST)/(Platelets x √ALT). It assesses advanced fibrosis risk in patients with chronic liver disease. FIB-4 has been shown to have an association with CVD events but is not utilized as a predictor of CVD outcomes in clinical practice. We wanted to understand the additional predictive information of FIB-4 beyond traditional CVD risk indicators and how this association varies over time, while controlling for cardiometabolic therapies like statins, insulin, metformin, glucagon like peptide 1 receptor agonists (GLP-1a). Methods: This is a retrospective cohort study of electronic health record data from a national cohort of Veterans, extracted from the VA Corporate Data Warehouse. Veterans with calculable FIB-4 scores from January 2011 to December 2025 were identified, and excluded if CVD event occurred before 2011. FIB-4 scores were categorized as low (FIB-4 <1.3), indeterminate (1.3 ≤ FIB-4 <2.67), or high-risk (FIB-4 ≥ 2.67) for advanced fibrosis. We used multivariable complementary log-log (cloglog) regression models to evaluate the association between FIB-4 scores and other potential confounders and covariates with time to composite CVD event outcome (AMI, CHF, and stroke). Results: A total of 2,431,410 unique patients were identified. Approximately 45% of patients were 64 years of age or older, male (93.5%), and White (73.9%). Among this cohort, 43% had diabetes mellitus, 24% had chronic kidney disease (CKD), and 24.2% had severe liver disease (SLD). During a mean follow-up of 10.23 years, patients with FIB-4 scores at high- (HR=1.26; 95% CI [1.25 - 1.27]) or indeterminate-risk (HR=1.26; 95% CI [1.09 - 1.1.09 - 1.10]) for advanced fibrosis were more likely to experience a CVD event compared to those with low-risk FIB-4 scores. Other factors associated with an elevated hazard for CVD events included CKD (HR=1.58; 95%CI [1.57 - 1.59]), SLD (HR=1.31; 95%CI [1.30 - 1.33]), prescription for insulin (HR=1.94; 95% CI [1.93 - 1.96]) and statin (HR=2.02; 95% CI [2.01 - 2.03]). Alternatively, a prescription for GLP-1a and metformin had an associated 19% (HR=0.81; 95% CI [1.93 - 1.96]) and 12% (HR=0.88; 95%CI [0.87 - 0.89]) reduction of CVD event hazard, respectively. Conclusions: In a large cohort of Veterans from primary care, FIB-4 scores at high- and indeterminate-risk for advanced fibrosis were associated with an increased risk of incident CVD over time. The utility of adding FIB-4 components to future CVD risk prognostication requires further exploration.

title: Abstract 9695: Predictors of Adverse Outcomes Among Individuals with ASCVD, CKD, and Inflammation
abstract: Background: Patients with comorbid atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) commonly have inflammation, as measured by elevated high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP). Among such individuals, the relative contribution of inflammation versus alternative risk factors to the likelihood of adverse outcomes is unclear. Research Question: What are the strongest predictors of short-term cardiovascular outcomes in Veterans with ASCVD, CKD, and inflammation? Aims: Rank the relative prognostic contribution of hsCRP level and other clinical variables for a 1-year composite major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE) outcome of myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, or death. Methods: Using national Veterans Health Administration data, we identified Veterans with ASCVD, CKD (eGFR stage 3-4 or Stage 2 with albuminuria), and hsCRP > 2 mg/L. We ascertained the MACE outcome of MI, stroke, or death within one year of the hsCRP measurement date. We used 75 potential predictors, including sociodemographics, comorbidities, procedures, vital signs, and laboratory values. We evaluated the magnitude of the unadjusted association between candidate predictors and the outcome via standardized mean differences. We fit a random forest model given the ability to model non-linear effects and high-order interactions without pre-specification. We ranked variable importance in the random forest model based on the mean decrease in accuracy. Using a 25% hold-out validation sample, we assessed overall prediction via the C-statistic. Results: Of 73,287 Veterans with ASCVD, CKD, and hsCRP > 2 mg/L, 9,354 (12.8%) had a MACE outcome within one year. The table displays characteristics of those with and without MACE. Those with MACE at one year were older, more likely to be frail, and had higher Charlson comorbidity indices. hsCRP was higher among those with 1-year MACE (median: 11.2mg/L [Interquartile range: 5.2-36.6])) compared with those without 1-year MACE (median: 6.5mg/L [Interquartile range 3.7-14.2]). In the validation sample, the C-statistic was 0.73 (95% CI 0.72-0.74) for predicting 1-year MACE, indicating moderate discrimination. The figure displays the relative predictor importance of the top 20 predictors. After age, hsCRP elevation was the second strongest predictor of 1-year MACE. Other characteristics in the top 10 of relative importance included total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, BMI, eGFR, diastolic blood pressure, Charlson comorbidity index, hemoglobin A1c, and heart failure diagnosis. Conclusions: Among Veterans with ASCVD, CKD, and elevated hsCRP, the magnitude of hsCRP elevation was the second strongest predictor of 1-year MI, stroke, or death, suggesting the magnitude of hsCRP elevation is an important prognostic biomarker in this population.

title: Is consumer credit a social determinant of health for older adults? An investigation in the advanced cognitive training for independent and vital elderly (ACTIVE) trial
abstract: PURPOSE: Few empirical studies have considered consumer credit as a social determinant of health (SDoH). Consumer credit reflects both the resources available to individuals and the behaviors needed to manage them effectively; therefore, credit scores may relate to economic aspects of SDoH and others, which influence downstream health outcomes. We investigated how consumer credit relates to five SDoH domains and examined its unique contribution to physical, mental, and cognitive health outcomes. We explored associations between SDoH domains and health, mediated by credit. METHODS: We linked baseline data from the Advanced Cognitive Training for Independent and Vital Elderly (ACTIVE) study-a randomized controlled trial of cognitive training in older adults with detailed SDoH and health measures-to consumer credit data provided by TransUnion®. We evaluated convergent validity of credit scores as a measure of SDoH by examining correlations between consumer credit and SDoH domains. Predictive criterion validity was tested by assessing whether adding credit indicators improved the prediction of health outcomes beyond SDoH domains alone. Mediation was tested using Sobel-Goodman methods. RESULTS: Consumer credit was most strongly aligned with Economic Stability; measures indicating higher debt burden correlated with lower Economic Stability. Incorporating credit measures into models with SDoH factors significantly improved the explained variance in physical and mental health outcomes. Credit also partially mediated relationships between certain SDoH domains and both physical health and memory performance. CONCLUSIONS: Consumer credit contributes unique insights into social and financial contexts beyond traditional SDoH measures and may improve understanding of health disparities among older adults.

title: Structural food access inequalities and aging transitions: A geospatial, multistate and longitudinal analysis of UK Biobank.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The food environment may influence neurodegeneration and mortality. This study examined associations of food deserts (FD) with brain health and survival using UK Biobank data.
METHODS: We analyzed 262,847 participants aged ≥50 years at baseline (2006-2010) with linked geospatial (2018-2020), neuroimaging (2014-2023; 2019-2023), dietary, biological, and health data. FD exposure was aggregated at the local authority (LA) level. Outcomes included incident dementia, Parkinson's disease (PD), and all-cause mortality (ACM) from January 1, 2020, to January 1, 2024. Neuroimaging sub-analyses (n = 2429) assessed brain volumes and white matter microstructure (WMM) using diffusion MRI metrics (FAmean, MDmean, ICVFmean, ISOVFmean, ODmean). Cox, multistate survival, and mixed-effects models were used. Spatial clustering examined co-localization between FD and outcomes. Area-level FD was examined as the primary exposure, with FI evaluated mainly as a secondary effect modifier.
RESULTS: Women had lower FD and FI scores and better cardiovascular and social health. FD (per SD increase) was associated with higher ACM risk (HR = 1.06; 95% CI: 1.02-1.09) after adjustment for demographics and deprivation, attenuating after full adjustment. FD also predicted faster WMM decline among women (ODmean β = +0.1124; p = 0.028), though neuroimaging associations did not survive FDR correction. Spatial analyses revealed threefold higher odds of concordance between FD and ACM, and between FD and FAmean decline. FI did not modify FD-ACM associations.
CONCLUSIONS: Living in food deserts was linked to higher mortality and faster white matter decline, particularly among women. Findings highlight the role of area-level food environments in brain health and aging.

title: White matter microstructure and hyperintensity burden in isolated REM sleep behavior disorder
abstract: Abstract Isolated rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder represents a prodromal phase of α-synucleinopathy. Diffusion MRI provides in vivo markers of white matter microstructural properties, while white matter hyperintensities reflect cerebrovascular injury. However, their relative contributions to cognitive and clinical dysfunctions in patients with isolated rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder remain unclear. We analysed 168 polysomnography-confirmed isolated rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder participants from the North American Prodromal Synucleinopathy Consortium. Multi-shell diffusion MRI was used to derive metrics from diffusion tensor imaging (fractional anisotropy and mean diffusivity) and Neurite Orientation Dispersion and Density Imaging (tissue-weighted neurite density index and orientation dispersion index) across 39 white matter regions using a modified Johns Hopkins University white matter atlas. White matter hyperintensity burden was quantified from fluid-attenuated inversion recovery MRI. Using linear regression adjusted for age and sex, we compared white matter microstructure and hyperintensity burden between clinically impaired and unimpaired participants and examined associations with multiple cognitive and clinical domains, including global cognition, working memory, motor severity, manual dexterity, autonomic dysfunction, olfactory function, prodromal disease severity, and daytime sleepiness. False discovery rate correction was applied to account for multiple comparisons. In our sample (n=168), participants with clinical impairment (n=57) demonstrated higher white matter hyperintensity burden than unimpaired participants (n=111) and showed limited microstructural differences, including lower fractional anisotropy in the superior fronto-occipital fasciculus and inferior occipital white matter and higher orientation dispersion index in inferior occipital white matter. After adjusting for white matter hyperintensity burden, only increased occipital orientation dispersion index remained statistically significant. Diffusion metrics showed widespread associations with digit span forward performance and autonomic dysfunction. In contrast, increased white matter hyperintensity burden demonstrated broader associations with poorer Montreal Cognitive Assessment scores, poorer digit span forward performance, lower Purdue Pegboard performance, and higher Prodromal Synucleinopathy Rating Scale scores, indicating greater prodromal disease severity. Our findings highlight cerebrovascular white matter burden as an important correlate of clinical dysfunction in isolated rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder and underscore the need to consider cerebrovascular lesions when interpreting diffusion imaging markers in prodromal synucleinopathy.

title: Decoding personal and population variability in the human multiome
abstract: Abstract Background With recent advances in technology, multiomic data have proliferated rapidly. Biobanks are now developing genomic, proteomic, lipidomic, and metabolomic data sets on the order of hundreds of thousands of people. However, bridging the gap between population-level data and the individual—a major challenge in precision medicine—remains a novel and challenging task. Methods We analyzed the landscape of contemporary multiomics data and the drivers of population and personal molecular variability using a longitudinal cohort uniquely suited to precision health applications. Using healthy routine visit data (94 participants, median five visits per participant), we profiled the human multiome across eight molecular omic types and 1.2 million measurements, with replication in a sister multiomic cohort (322 participants). Results Molecular data tended to cluster by omes, with the metabolome and proteome showing less intraomic correlation than other data types. While most blood-based molecular measurements followed log-normal distributions, between 2.0% and 8.1% of molecules showed evidence of bimodality, with cases driven by genetic polymorphisms or dietary differences (e.g., SERPINA5 [P = 1.4e-6], 2-piperidinone [P = 5.7e-5]). Molecular variation across the population was generally higher than that within an individual over time (e.g., xenobiotic metabolites, progestin steroids). Analyzing personal molecular variation identified several participants with notable temporal shifts (intraindividual CV > 4 SDs higher than population CV) in free fatty acids (FFA 20:1 and FFA 20:2) or cytokines (IL-17F and IFN-beta), which were unlikely to be detected cross-sectionally. Body mass index (BMI) had a much larger multiomic footprint (23.6% of molecules associated) than demographic factors like sex or age (5.7% and 1.9%, respectively), although machine-learning predictive models of sex (top ROC AUC of 0.98) were more successful than those for BMI (top R 2 of 0.59 by cytokines) or age (top R 2 of 0.34 by metabolites). Purely multiomic predictive models explained modest to high proportions of variation (R 2 = 0.22 to 0.94) in 20 common clinical tests, highlighting the potential clinical utility of these data even within a modestly sized cohort. Conclusion Analysis of the molecular distributions, variation, and covariation of longitudinal multiomics data revealed clinically relevant differences at both the population and personal levels. Based on these findings, we conclude with six key considerations for the next generation of population omics as the field advances toward the goals of precision medicine. Multiomic data have proliferated rapidly in biomedical research, but many aspects of molecular variability remain poorly understood. We investigated in detail the drivers of personal and population variability in a longitudinal, multiomic cohort uniquely suited to precision health applications (94 participants, eight omic types, 1.2 million molecular measurements), with replication in a sister multiomic cohort (322 participants). While most molecules followed log-normal distributions, between 2.0% and 8.1% of molecules were bimodal, with cases driven by genetic polymorphisms or dietary differences (e.g., SERPINA5 [P = 1.4e-6], 2-piperidinone [P = 5.7e-5]). The metabolome and proteome showing less intraomic correlation than the lipidome or cytokines, and molecular variation across the population was generally higher than that within an individual over time with. Analyzing personal molecular variation identified several participants with notable temporal shifts (intraindividual CV > 4 SDs higher than population CV) in free fatty acids (FFA 20:1 and FFA 20:2) or cytokines (IL-17F and IFN-beta), which were unlikely to be detected cross-sectionally. Body mass index (BMI) was more broadly associated with molecular levels (23.6% of molecules associated) than were demographic factors like sex or age (5.7% and 1.9%, respectively), although machine-learning predictive models of sex (top ROC AUC of 0.98) were more successful than those for BMI (top R 2 of 0.59 by cytokines) or age (top R 2 of 0.34 by metabolites). Purely multiomic predictive models were modest to highly predictive (R 2 = 0.22 to 0.94) of 20 common clinical tests, highlighting the potential clinical utility of these data even within a modestly sized cohort. Our findings reveal six key considerations (missing variability, temporality, feasible clinicomics, complex modeling, aging complexity, and molecular matching) for precision medicine.

title: Norepinephrine neurons in the nucleus of the solitary tract mediate allodynia related to systemic inflammation in mice.
abstract: In response to peripheral inflammation, such as the intraperitoneal administration of lipopolysaccharide (LPS), inflammatory cytokines recruit afferent neurons that communicate the inflammation to the brain and, in addition, cytokines are released to the bloodstream and reach circumventricular organs in the brain, such as the area postrema (AP). The nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS) perceives peripheral inflammatory stimuli both directly from afferent peripheral nerves and indirectly through its bidirectional connection to the AP. Norepinephrine (NE) neurons within the NTS are known to mediate behavioral and physiological responses to stress, especially stress related to inflammatory challenges in the periphery. However, the restrictions of traditional pain assays limit the understanding of the influence of NTS NE neurons on pain. Here, we used the Blackbox, a machine-learning assisted behavioral analysis apparatus that was developed specifically for the study of pain in rodents. First, we determined the Blackbox variables that correlate to allodynia in mice submitted to intraperitoneal injection of LPS. IP injection of LPS caused several changes to behavior and posture. Most notably, the distance travelled, hind paw toe spread and hind paw distance significantly decreased in response to LPS and strongly correlated with decreased von Frey mechanosensitivity threshold. Selective chemogenetic activation of NTS NE neurons caused similar pain-related behaviors, while inhibition of NTS NE neurons partially reversed the impact of LPS on pain-related behaviors. Taken together, these data show that the NE neurons within the NTS mediate allodynia in response to peripheral inflammation, contributing to the nociception aspect of sickness behaviors.

title: Trajectories of romantic partners' social functioning across the military deployment cycle.
abstract: Research has documented adverse psychiatric effects of wartime deployment on military spouses/partners, yet studies examining partners' quality of life beyond symptomatology are lacking. This study identified trajectories of social functioning among partners of military personnel across an 18-month deployment cycle. National Guard soldiers and their spouses/partners (N = 1,028 dyads) completed assessments 2-5 months predeployment to Kuwait/Iraq or Afghanistan (Time 1), at 4 months (Time 2) and 8 months (Time 3) during deployment, and 2-3 months postdeployment (Time 4). Latent class growth modeling revealed four distinct trajectories among partners: (a) stable high (72.1%), characterized by consistently high social functioning throughout; (b) recovery (13.3%), experiencing deployment-related decline in social functioning followed by postdeployment improvement; (c) stable moderate (12.9%), demonstrating consistently moderate functioning; and (d) declining (1.7%), showing marked decreases in functioning across the cycle. Trajectories were then compared on partner and soldier predeployment characteristics. Compared to the stable high group, stable moderate partners-and their soldiers-reported higher negative emotionality/neuroticism and lower deployment readiness, relationship satisfaction, and social support. Recovery partners differed only in their own higher neuroticism. In contrast, declining partners differed primarily on external factors, reporting more potentially traumatic events, less social support, and being partnered to soldiers with higher neuroticism. Thus, partners of National Guard soldiers follow diverse social adjustment pathways, challenging monolithic assumptions about military family resilience. These findings advance the field's understanding of the variable ways that partners respond to deployment and may be used to optimize delivery of programs targeting different dimensions of military family well-being. title: Diet at disease onset determines tissue inflammatory memory.
abstract: Obesity, which is often associated with prolonged exposure to an obesogenic diet, substantially alters immunity1-7, but whether brief dietary changes shape acute inflammatory responses and long-term tissue memory remains unclear. Here we show that transient high-fat diet (HFD) exposure at the onset of acute type 17 skin inflammation exacerbates disease in lean mice to levels comparable to those associated with chronic obesity. This effect is restricted to a discrete 4-day peri-initiation window; HFD outside this window has no impact, whereas switching obese mice to a low-fat diet (LFD) during a similar window fully blunts disease amplification. Mechanistically, HFD rapidly recruits neutrophils into the skin, and neutrophils in challenged skin express high levels of Nlrp3 (ref. 8) and Il1b. Neutrophil depletion, genetic Nlrp3 deficiency and pharmacological NLRP3 inhibition each blunt the HFD-induced inflammatory amplification. These findings nominate a neutrophil-NLRP3-IL-1β axis that licences pathogenic IL-1R1+CD4+ T helper type 17 (TH17) cells9,10. After recovery, a chromatin-poised tissue-resident memory T cell population persists. Consequently, mice exposed to HFD at disease onset develop exaggerated inflammation upon recurrence, despite recovery and maintenance on LFD. Transient HFD similarly amplifies lung TH17 inflammation through neutrophil- and IL-1R1-dependent mechanisms. Together, these findings show that dietary state during a narrow temporal window can durably reprogram disease trajectory, suggesting that short-lived physiological states may become embedded in local immune memory11 when they coincide with tissue inflammation.

title: Systematic Review of the Literature on Associations Between Symptoms, Stress, Resilience, and Epigenetic Aging in Patients With Cancer.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cancer and its treatments can have long-term adverse effects that may accelerate aging and worsen symptom burden. The cognitive and behavioral strategies that patients utilize to adapt to their environment and respond to stress may influence inter-individual variability in aging and symptom burden. This systematic review summarizes the relationships between symptoms, stress, resilience, and epigenetic aging in oncology patients and identifies knowledge gaps.
METHODS: A search of relevant databases was done from January 2000 to May 2026. Studies were included that examined DNA methylation patterns to predict biological age using algorithms known as epigenetic clocks in adults with cancer. A qualitative synthesis of the quantitative studies is reported.
RESULTS: Of the 10 studies included in this review, a total of nine different methods were used to predict epigenetic age. The most common methods were the Levine, Horvath, and Hannum clocks. Nine studies reported on associations between symptoms and epigenetic age acceleration; one study reported on an association between stress and epigenetic age acceleration; and one study reported on an association between resilience and epigenetic age acceleration.
CONCLUSION: More longitudinal studies are needed to validate these findings and investigate variations by epigenetic age estimate, timing of assessment, cancer type, and stage of disease. Studies are needed to evaluate the role of stress and resilience in mediating/moderating the relationships between epigenetic age acceleration and symptoms in patients with cancer.
IMPLICATIONS FOR NURSING PRACTICE: A subset of patients with cancer who develop more severe fatigue, pain, sleep disturbance, peripheral motor neuropathy, cognitive, depressive, and/or anxiety symptoms may experience epigenetic age acceleration.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: This systematic review was registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD42024545895).

title: Global Burden of Anorexia Nervosa and Bulimia Nervosa, 1990 to 2023, With Forecasts to 2050: A Global Burden of Disease Study 2023 Analysis.
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Eating disorders are a major cause of nonfatal mental health burden, yet global evidence on their long-term trends, geographic distribution, and future trajectories remains limited.
OBJECTIVE: To estimate the global, regional, and national prevalence and disability burden of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa-and mortality attributable to anorexia nervosa-from 1990 to 2023, and to forecast prevalence to 2050.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: Using Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2023 methods, data were synthesized from systematic literature reviews, population surveys, and vital registration systems. Estimates were produced for 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2023, with forecasts through 2050. These data were analyzed from October 2025 to August 2026.
EXPOSURE: Anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa diagnosis.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Counts and age-standardized rates with 95% uncertainty intervals (UIs) for anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa prevalence, years lived with disability (YLDs), and disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs), and anorexia nervosa mortality, reported by age, sex, and location.
RESULTS: In 2023, an estimated 18.1 million people (95% UI, 13.9-24.0) globally were living with anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa, of whom 12.6 million (69.4%) were female, 5.5 million were male (30.6%), and 41.2% were aged 10 to 24 years. These cases accounted for 3.83 million DALYs (95% UI, 2.23-5.69). Since 1990, the global number of prevalent cases increased by 71.0%, while age-standardized prevalence and DALY rates rose by about 21%. Females experienced substantially higher prevalence and DALY rates than males. The highest age-standardized prevalence rates were observed in high-income regions, particularly Australasia and Western Europe, whereas the largest relative increases in age-standardized prevalence occurred in East Asia, South Asia, and Southeast Asia. Forecasts indicate continued increases in prevalent cases through 2050.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: This GBD 2023 analysis found that anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa contribute substantially to global nonfatal health loss. These findings support the integration of eating disorders into mental health surveillance, prevention, and service planning worldwide.

title: HARP: HARmonizing In-Vivo Single-Shell Diffusion MRI Using Phantom-Only Training.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Combining multi-site diffusion MRI (dMRI) data is hindered by inter-scanner variability, which confounds subsequent analysis. Previous harmonization methods require large, matched or traveling human subjects from multiple sites, which are impractical to acquire in many situations. This study aims to develop a deep learning-based dMRI harmonization framework that eliminates the reliance on multi-site in-vivo traveling human data for training.
METHODS: HARP employs a voxel-wise 1D neural network trained on an easily transportable diffusion phantom. The model learns relationships between spherical harmonics coefficients of different sites without memorizing spatial structures.
RESULTS: HARP reduced inter-scanner variability levels significantly in various measures. Quantitatively, it decreased inter-scanner variability as measured by standard error in FA (12%), MD (10%), and GFA (30%) with scan-rescan standard error as the baseline, while preserving fiber orientations and tractography after harmonization.
CONCLUSION: We believe that HARP represents an important first step toward dMRI harmonization using only phantom data, thereby obviating the need for complex, matched in vivo multi-site cohorts. This phantom-only strategy substantially enhances the feasibility and scalability of quantitative dMRI for large-scale clinical studies.

title: Gut epithelial aryl hydrocarbon receptor deficiency aggravates fungal dysbiosis-mediated neutrophilic allergic airway disease in mice
abstract: Fungal and bacterial dysbiosis are linked to asthma disease severity, yet how overgrowth of the commensal fungus Candida albicans contributes to disease progression is not fully understood. Here, we show that intestinal aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) deficiency exacerbates house dust mite (HDM)-induced allergic airway disease (AAD) during oral Candida albicans colonization through enhanced IL-17 responsiveness and lung structural cell fucosylation. Intestinal AhR deficiency promotes exaggerated IL-17 responses that promotes neutrophil migration and accumulation in the lung and reshapes the gut microbiota, particularly reducing the abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila. Concurrently, increased fucosylation of lung structural cells enhances L-selectin glycan ligand biosynthesis, thereby promoting neutrophil adhesion and retention within inflamed lung tissue. These adherent neutrophils lead to mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and tissue injury in epithelial and endothelial compartments. Administration of A. muciniphila or its derived outer membrane vesicles (OMVs), as well as genetic deletion of Fut2, reduces lung fucosylation, suppresses neutrophil adhesion and NET formation, and attenuates Candida albicans–exacerbated AAD. Together, these findings show that intestinal AhR signaling remotely regulates an IL-17- gut microbiota-fucosylation axis that promotes neutrophil adhesion, mitochondrial dysfunction of lung structure cell, and neutrophilic airway inflammation during Candida albicans–associated asthma. Fungal and bacterial dysbiosis are linked to asthma severity. Here the authors use mice deficient in intestinal epithelial cell AhR to show that in the absence of AhR, house dust mite-induced allergic airway disease is heightened in the presence of Candida albicans and fucosylation of lung structural cells affects neutrophil adhesion and retention in inflamed lung tissue involving inhibition of the mucus-utilising bacterium Akkermansia muciniphila.

title: An Exploration of the Cultural Relevance of Narrative Coherence Criteria with Banyamulenge Congolese Refugee Women
abstract: Due to the extensive violence occurring in the Democratic Republic of the Congo over the past three decades, Congolese refugees account for the largest number of refugees from one country resettled in the United States over the past decade, accounting for 20% of refugee admissions in 2024. Congolese refugees report high levels of trauma, anxiety, depression, and trauma/PTSD and more tools are needed to assess refugees’ mental health. In this qualitative content analysis (QCA) study, we critically examined nine interviews with Banyamulenge Congolese refugee women (ages 25–48) to explore the cultural relevance and applicability of Baerger and McAdams’ measure of narrative coherence. Narrative coherence theory posits the ability to share one’s story in a way that makes sense to the listener indicates the person has integrated and come to terms with their life experiences, which is subsequently related to health and well-being. Participants were also asked to describe their current number and forms of social support, which is documented as a measure of well-being; in this study, it was explored as a potential source of validation for narrative coherence. Responses were placed in two main categories: (a) coherent responses (44% of total responses) and (b) incoherent responses (46% of total responses), indicating that only one of the nine participants demonstrated fully coherent responses to all interview questions. A post-hoc analysis was conducted in an effort to provide a more complete picture of the quality of the narrative coherence among the participants. Hence, a third main category was created, coherent responses without criterion I8, showing a greater number of coherent ratings. These findings provide initial support for the use of a narrative coherence framework as a means of understanding refugee experiences. Clinical and research implications are discussed.

title: Reimagining Cirrhosis Care for Older Adults: A 5Ms Approach.
abstract: Background: Cirrhosis is increasingly prevalent among older adults, driven in part by the rising burden of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, which disproportionately affects this population. These patients are particularly vulnerable to premature geriatric syndromes, including frailty, disability, and cognitive impairment, reflecting the combined-if not synergistic-effects of aging and end-stage liver disease. As a result, they experience high symptom burden and health care utilization. Despite this complexity, cirrhosis care remains largely organized around disease-specific management and liver transplant evaluation, often failing to address geriatric and patient-centered needs. Approach: The Age-Friendly Health Systems initiative, developed by the John A. Hartford Foundation and the Institute for Healthcare Improvement, provides a standardized framework for high-quality care of older adults through the 4Ms: What Matters, Medication, Mentation, and Mobility. Although widely implemented across health systems, its application to hepatology remains limited. We propose an adaptation of the 4Ms framework for hepatology practice, supplemented by a fifth domain-Multicomplexity-to capture the intersecting challenges of symptom burden, multimorbidity, psychosocial vulnerability, and fragmented care. We describe how each domain can be operationalized within routine hepatology care and aligned with existing liver-specific tools and workflows. "What Matters" addresses prognostic uncertainty in cirrhosis and emphasizes structured advance care planning and goals-of-care conversations, particularly in the context of evolving transplant eligibility. "Medication" focuses on reducing polypharmacy and medication-related harm through careful prescribing in the setting of hepatic dysfunction and aging. "Mentation" targets identification and management of cognitive impairment, including minimal hepatic encephalopathy, alongside psychiatric comorbidities. "Mobility" emphasizes assessment and treatment of sarcopenia and frailty using liver-specific tools such as the Liver Frailty Index. "Multicomplexity" captures broader biopsychosocial and system-level challenges, including symptom burden, multimorbidity, social determinants of health, and care fragmentation. We further highlight palliative care as a complementary strategy for operationalizing the 5Ms in hepatology, supported by the PAL-LIVER trial, a multisite cluster randomized study demonstrating that trained hepatologist-delivered palliative care is noninferior to specialist-delivered care in improving quality of life and enhanced emotional well-being and patient satisfaction. Conclusions: An Age-Friendly, 5Ms-based approach adapted for hepatology has the potential to improve quality of life, reduce unnecessary health care utilization, and better align care with what matters most to older adults with cirrhosis. Integrating this framework into routine hepatology practice, supported by palliative care training principles and liver-specific tools, represents a scalable strategy for improving care delivery. Pragmatic implementation studies are needed to evaluate effectiveness, scalability, and sustainability across diverse health system settings.

title: Global, regional and national burden of pertussis in 1990–2023: a Global Burden of Disease study
abstract: Despite long-standing immunization programs, pertussis remains a major cause of vaccine-preventable mortality, particularly among infants. Here we present a primary assessment of global pertussis incidence, mortality and disability-adjusted life years across 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2023. We show that despite short-term pandemic-period fluctuations, the dominant global pattern from 1990 to 2023 was long-term decline: age-standardized mortality decreased by 61.2% and age-standardized incidence by 41.6%. Relative to the anomalously low pandemic-period estimates, incidence and mortality rebounded by 102.6% (95% uncertainty interval, 77.0–128.2%) and 66.1% (95% uncertainty interval, 2.4–174.5%), respectively, between 2020 and 2023. In 2023 alone, we estimated 18.9 million cases and 115,000 deaths attributable to pertussis. This burden remains profoundly inequitable and inversely correlated with the sociodemographic index; sub-Saharan Africa now accounts for roughly 65% of global deaths, with the highest population-adjusted risk concentrated among infants younger than 6 months. Our findings highlight a modeled geographic concentration of pertussis mortality and support strengthening timely infant vaccination, maternal immunization where recommended and feasible and robust surveillance in highly susceptible regions. Updates to the Global Burden of Disease study showed that while global trends in pertussis (whooping cough) declined from 1990 to 2023, the rebound in incidence and mortality since 2020, particularly in high-income regions, reflects stalled vaccination progress worldwide.

title: A Community-Based Intervention to Increase HIV Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis Use among Individuals Receiving Re-Entry Services: Results from a Formative Evaluation
abstract: Abstract Introduction Criminal-legal populations have a disproportionately higher risk of acquiring HIV. Clinical partnerships with community-based organizations have been shown to be effective in overcoming multiple challenges to awareness and linkage to pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). Aims Report findings from a formative evaluation and describe how these data refined our approach to a health coaching intervention designed to enhance linkage to PrEP and embedded in a community-based organization that provides re-entry services. Methods We conducted a formative evaluation using interviews with criminal-legal individuals (clients) and staff of a community-based organization serving greater Dallas County, Texas. Interviews explored knowledge and beliefs about HIV and PrEP, perceived risk, barriers to care, and need for support. Two analysts conducted rapid and thematic content analysis; the research team selected and interpreted representative quotes. Results We completed interviews with ten clients and six staff. Analysis revealed that clients: (1) need social support and mental health care but minimize these needs, often not seeking related services unless their concerns impede daily life activities; (2) have low perceived risk of acquiring HIV and associate HIV with ‘being gay,’ but are open to discussing PrEP; (3) face competing needs that can impede focus on one’s health, limited proficiency with technology, and mistrust and misinformation barriers; and (4) recommend using humor, plain and respectful language, and dispelling myths in HIV prevention education. Conclusion HIV prevention with criminal-legal populations must address preventive health, social support, erroneous beliefs about HIV risk and transmission, and stigmas. Encouragingly, we found an openness to discussing and using PrEP as an HIV prevention strategy, even among those who perceive their personal HIV risk to be low. Any such prevention effort will benefit from taking steps to address common misperceptions about HIV and barriers to prevention, and employing culturally competent messaging in non-judgmental, destigmatizing ways.

title: Co-design process evaluation for the dissemination of evidence-based research findings with mental health providers and patients in the veterans health administration
abstract: Abstract Background Co-design is increasingly used for partner engagement in research but rarely employed at the dissemination stage of research and seldom evaluated. In the US Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), co-design was used to collaborate with end-users to help disseminate research findings related to the evidence-based collaborative chronic care model (CCM) in mental health settings. This work objective is to describe and evaluate the co-design process used to translate and package CCM research findings for active dissemination with end-users. Methods The mixed-method project is aligned with the second phase of the Designing for Dissemination and Sustainability model. Across 4 VA sites, 2 groups of end-users (staff and providers, patients) engaged in 3 site-specific 60-minute co-design sessions and took an anonymous feedback survey developed specifically for this project where they rated co-design principles on a Likert scale from 1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree. They created products that translate CCM research findings in end-users’ preferred language and formats for dissemination with peers. Results Thirteen VA mental health administrative and clinical staff and 9 patients participated in 18 co-design sessions across 4 sites. Participants agreed that all 4 key principles of co-design (joint ownership, participant agency, respect and value for all perspectives, mutual benefit) were upheld with means ≥ 4.20 (range 1–5). Meta-inferences provided interpretation and decision for each co-design session activity to create products for increased use of CCM evidence. Staff and providers were satisfied with their co-designed products called the BHIP-CCM Dissemination Resource (mean 4.82; SD 0.39; range 4–5), the marketing messaging (mean 4.55; SD 0.78; range 3–5), and site-specific dissemination plans (mean 4.64; SD 0.77; range 3–5). Patients were very satisfied with their co-designed products: two infographics for TV/monitor display in virtual and in-person waiting rooms (mean 5.00; SD 0.00), and their marketing messaging (mean 4.67; SD 0.47; range 4–5). Conclusions Co-design was useful and rewarding for engaged participants. Co-design can be instrumental in dissemination to increase use of CCM evidence, improve CCM care delivery in mental health, and build community support for CCM implementation and sustainability. These results speak to the capacity of co-design to support other dissemination efforts.

title: Timeliness of Emergency Care for Intracerebral Hemorrhage Compared With Acute Ischemic Stroke
abstract: Importance: Clinical data comparing time to presentation and stroke quality metrics for intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) and acute ischemic stroke (AIS) are limited. Understanding these differences is essential to provide timely care to all stroke subtypes. Objective: To compare prehospital and emergency department (ED) process quality metrics between patients with ICH and AIS. Design, Setting, and Participants: Cohort study included patients with AIS and ICH admitted to Get With The Guidelines (GWTG)-Stroke participating hospitals from January 1, 2015, to June 30, 2024, who arrived by emergency medical services (EMS). Data were analyzed from 195 hospitals across the US. Main Outcomes and Measures: Prehospital-based and ED-based process metrics (eg, EMS prenotification, door to ED physician assessment time, door to initial brain imaging order) were assessed. Logistic and linear regression models were sequentially adjusted for patient demographics, medical history and presenting factors, and hospital characteristics. Temporal trends of prehospital care metrics were examined. Results: A total of 195 659 patients (median [IQR] age, 74.0 [63.0-83.0] years; 97 978 [50.1%] female; 31 464 with ICH and 164 195 with AIS) from 195 hospitals were included. The median (IQR) National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score was 14 (6-23) for ICH vs 6 (2-13) for AIS (absolute standardized difference, 0.694). ICH (vs AIS) was associated with higher odds of door-to-ED physician assessment of 10 or fewer minutes after adjusting for patient demographics (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.08; 95% CI, 1.02-1.14). This association reversed after adding adjustment for medical history and presenting factors (including NIHSS) and hospital characteristics (aOR, 0.94; 95% CI, 0.89-0.99). This pattern was observed for door to initial brain imaging order of 20 or fewer minutes (demographic-adjusted: aOR, 1.09; 95% CI, 1.02-1.16; fully adjusted with medical history and hospital characteristics: aOR, 0.91; 95% CI, 0.85-0.97). Median last known well to arrival time increased by 32.5% for AIS (151 to 200 minutes; P < .001) and 34.3% for ICH (108 to 145 minutes; P < .001), while rates of EMS prenotification largely remained stable for both ICH and AIS. Conclusions and Relevance: In this cohort study of patients with acute stroke, patients with ICH arrived at the ED faster but were less likely to achieve care targets. In the context of emerging hyperacute ICH therapies and bundled care models, addressing these differences is essential to optimizing acute stroke outcomes.

title: A cell-based multivariate blood test (iCAP) for early detection of Alzheimer’s disease capturing non-amyloid-β biology
abstract: Abstract The indicator cell assay platform (iCAP) is a blood-based diagnostic approach that uses standardized cells as biosensors to transduce complex circulating signals into cell-based gene-expression profiles for multivariate disease classification. We developed an iCAP for early detection of Alzheimer’s disease (AD-iCAP) by incubating plasma from patients with early-stage AD (mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia) and non-affected controls with standardized neurons and training classifiers on transcriptomic responses. Modeling features were restricted to a predefined 84-gene panel derived independently by analyzing 5xFAD mouse plasma in the AD-iCAP. In this exploratory study, a model was trained and tested using 191 retrospectively collected human plasma samples across three cohorts. The classifier achieved AUC = 0.64 (95% CI 0.51–0.78) in an external validation set during model development (n = 82) and AUC = 0.77 (95% CI 0.57–0.96) in a blind test set (n = 23). The multivariate model incorporated 5 genes including AKT3 , GPR50 , PALLD , RGMA , and PCDH10 , implicated in AD, neuronal signaling and/or cytoskeletal dynamics. The cell-based approach is orthogonal to direct detection of circulating amyloid and tau, and these exploratory findings support further evaluation of AD-iCAP in prospective studies for combinatorial diagnostics and patient stratification for clinical trials.
