title: Boldine Attenuates Mechanical Allodynia and Mitigates Transcriptomic Changes in a Mouse Model of Chronic Constriction Injury.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Neuropathic pain is a complex chronic disorder affecting roughly 7-10% of the population. Current neuropathic pain treatments fail to provide adequate relief in at least ~40% of patients and are usually accompanied by side effects that are sometimes severe. In this study, we investigated the effect of boldine, a natural occurring alkaloid, in attenuating peripheral nerve injury-induced neuropathic pain symptoms and transcriptomic changes. Methods: Male C57BL6 mice underwent chronic constriction injury (CCI) to the sciatic nerve. Customized diet containing boldine or control diet was administered immediately after surgery. Mechanical pain responses were measured by Von Frey filament test. Spontaneous pain-like weight bearing behavior was assessed using the dynamic weight bearing system. L3-L5 spinal cords were collected 15 days after injury and subjected to quantitative PCR and bulk RNA sequencing. Results: CCI led to ipsilateral hypersensitivity of mechanical pain responses and weight-bearing deficits including reduced rearing duration, ipsilateral/contralateral weight support ratio, and ipsilateral hind paw posed duration. Boldine treatment substantially attenuated CCI-induced mechanical allodynia but not the weight bearing deficits. Gene expression analysis showed that boldine inhibited CCI-induced upregulation of inflammatory mediators in the spinal cord. RNA sequencing analysis revealed several pain-related canonical pathways and upstream factors after CCI, and boldine treatment markedly reversed these CCI-induced transcriptomic changes. Conclusions: Early oral administration of boldine attenuated CCI-induced mechanical allodynia and was associated with reduced inflammatory gene expression and reversal of multiple injury-related transcriptomic changes in the spinal cord. These preliminary preclinical findings support further investigation of boldine and do not establish therapeutic efficacy in established neuropathic pain.

title: Infection-associated acute kidney injury in resource-limited settings.
abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a frequent and life-threatening complication of infection, and a major contributor to preventable morbidity and mortality in resource-limited settings. In these contexts, AKI is commonly driven by a broad range of infections, including enteric, zoonotic and vector-borne diseases, that occur outside the hospital and in populations with limited access to diagnostics and supportive care. Infection-associated AKI results from diverse and overlapping mechanisms, including hypovolaemia, inflammation, endothelial and microcirculatory dysfunction, haemolysis and direct kidney involvement, and is increasingly shaped by environmental stressors such as heat exposure and climate-related disruptions that amplify dehydration, infection risk and kidney injury. Susceptibility to AKI is further influenced by reduced kidney reserve, which reflects nephron endowment and prior kidney injury, and can be silently depleted by severe or recurrent insults. Repeated infectious exposures and incomplete recovery from AKI might affect long-term kidney health and survival, but these trajectories remain poorly characterized. Challenges in timely recognition of both AKI and infections contribute to delayed treatment and worse outcomes, particularly among vulnerable populations. Strengthening infection prevention, improving context-appropriate diagnostics for AKI and infection, minimizing iatrogenic kidney injury, addressing environmental drivers and developing affordable scalable kidney replacement therapies are essential to reducing inequities and improving long-term kidney health globally.

title: A Daily Clinical Parameters and Outcomes Adjudication Dataset for Critically Ill Patients with Suspected Pneumonia
abstract: Many analyses of critically ill patients focus on admission features and discharge outcomes, overlooking daily events and intercurrent complications. Pneumonia is a syndromic entity that is difficult to adjudicate outcomes without clinical expertise. Here, we examine clinical features on a day-by-day basis, mirroring the practice of daily multidisciplinary rounds, with annotated pneumonia episodes and outcomes. The Successful Clinical Response in Pneumonia Therapy (SCRIPT) CarpeDiem Dataset includes 21,931 patient-hospital-days from 704 patients enrolled in the SCRIPT study between June 2018 and May 2023. These patients were all receiving mechanical ventilation and underwent bronchoalveolar lavage to diagnose and establish the etiology of their pneumonia or an alternative diagnosis. The dataset captures patient demographics, daily clinical parameters, including vital signs, laboratory results, and mechanical support data, detailed pneumonia episode results adjudicated by critical care physicians, and outcomes. All data are de-identified per HIPAA Safe Harbor guidelines. This dataset offers a unique resource for analyzing the clinical trajectories of patients with severe pneumonia.

title: Impact of sedation on the reliability of magnetoencephalographic language mapping in pediatric epilepsy
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Magnetoencephalography (MEG) language mapping in pediatric epilepsy frequently requires sedation, which may alter cortical physiology and compromise the reliability of language lateralization. We hypothesized that sedation disrupts coupling between early auditory processing and higher order language networks, reducing the interpretability of laterality metrics. METHODS: Sixty-nine pediatric patients undergoing presurgical MEG evaluation were analyzed, including 32 nonsedated and 37 sedated participants. Auditory evoked field responses were quantified using the M200/M100 amplitude ratio and interhemispheric asymmetry. Language laterality indices (LIs) were derived from a continuous recognition memory paradigm, and source localization was performed using Fast-VESTAL. RESULTS: Sedation preferentially suppressed late auditory responses, reflected by a significant reduction in the M200/M100 ratio (p < .001) and increased interindividual variability. Despite preserved early sensory responses, auditory-language coupling was numerically attenuated under sedation. Notably, low M200/M100 ratios were frequently associated with highly lateralized LI values, suggesting reduced physiological reliability and the potential for "false certainty" in language lateralization. Source imaging demonstrated preserved primary auditory cortical activity with reduced recruitment of higher order association networks in sedated participants. SIGNIFICANCE: Sedation compromises the physiological reliability of MEG language lateralization by disrupting late auditory and association-level processing. The M200/M100 ratio provides a practical physiological marker for identifying cases in which laterality results should be interpreted with caution. These findings support a physiology-informed framework for improving the clinical interpretation of MEG language mapping in sedated pediatric patients, with direct implications for presurgical planning in pediatric epilepsy.

title: A 4D Bio-Kirigami Strategy for Engineering Complex Tissue Curvatures.
abstract: Native tissues exhibit intricate curvatures essential for their function yet recapitulating structural complexity and dynamic morphogenesis remains challenging. Here, we present a cytocompatible bio-Kirigami system that enables programmable transformation of cell-laden hydrogels into complex three-dimensional tissue constructs. The system consists of (1) a photocrosslinked hydrogel with tunable degradation and swelling behavior to drive shape transformation and (2) a rigid hydrogel frame to provide structural support. Spatial patterning encodes localized swelling differentials via sequential photolithography, enabling controlled deformation and diverse morphing behaviors. Stem cell-laden bio-Kirigami constructs underwent programmed shape transformation and developed into tissue-like structures with complex curvatures under tissue-specific culture conditions. Importantly, the engineered tissue constructs retained their structural integrity and shape after removal of the supporting frame. This bio-Kirigami strategy provides a versatile approach for engineering dynamically transformable tissue constructs that recapitulate the complex geometries of native tissues.

title: Quinolinic acid contributes to maladaptive kidney injury and acute kidney injury–to–chronic kidney disease transition
abstract: The transition from acute kidney injury (AKI) to chronic kidney disease (CKD) remains a major clinical problem with unclear underlying mechanisms. Emerging evidence suggests that alterations in tryptophan metabolism, particularly in the production of downstream metabolites such as quinolinic acid (QA), play a role in renal pathophysiology. QA, an intermediate in de novo nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide biosynthesis, is metabolized by quinolinate phosphoribosyltransferase (QPRT). We investigated whether QA contributes to kidney injury using models of folic acid–induced AKI-to-CKD transition and cisplatin-induced AKI, genetic and exogenous approaches to alter QA, and clinical observations. Untargeted kidney metabolomics identified QA as one of the most elevated metabolites after folic acid injury. After folic acid injury, Qprt haploinsufficiency exacerbated kidney injury and fibrosis-related gene expression; aged Qprt -haploinsufficient mice exhibited increased fibrosis-associated gene expression without overt renal dysfunction. Exogenous QA administration increased serum creatinine in uninjured mice and worsened renal dysfunction and fibrosis-related gene expression in the folic acid AKI-to-CKD model. Conversely, mice deficient in either 3-hydroxyanthranilate 3,4-dioxygenase (HAAO) or kynurenine 3-monooxygenase (KMO), which reduce flux toward QA, showed improved renal outcomes after folic acid injury and cisplatin-induced AKI. Multimodal spatial metabolomics analysis of kidney biopsies from patients with AKI revealed QA accumulation in regions of inflammatory infiltration. Last, children with CKD exhibited higher urinary QA compared with healthy individuals. These findings underscore QA as a potential mediator of kidney injury and a therapeutic target for preventing the progression from AKI to CKD.

title: Mitochondrial psychobiology.
abstract: A field that uses mitochondria to unify biological and psychological sciences and to better understand the basis of health has emerged-Mitochondrial Psychobiology. Mitochondria are the body's cellular hubs for energy transformation and signaling. Mitochondria regulate functions as diverse as metabolism, gene expression, and stress adaptation; consequently, their dysregulation is linked to most chronic illnesses and aging. Here, we propose that mitochondria provide a mechanistic bridge between body and the measurable functions of the mind, including perception, cognition, emotion, and behavior. From this perspective, mitochondria provide a scientifically tractable interface through which bioenergetic processes relate to subjective experiences and behaviors. We outline foundational principles for Mitochondrial Psychobiology, discuss the key gaps that the field needs to address to advance our understanding of mind-mitochondria relationships across the lifecourse, and review emerging approaches to probe the mind-mitochondria connection across levels. This stimulating scientific challenge is a unique opportunity to train the next generation of interdisciplinary scientists, resolve conceptual and technical challenges spanning temporal and spatial scales, and develop a more accurate, holistic model of health. Rooted in general energetic principles, Mitochondrial Psychobiology is poised to productively steer biomedicine over the coming decades.

title: Automated compartment-based quantification reveals distinct patterns of cutaneous innervation with aging and microbial colonization
abstract: Cutaneous innervation is commonly quantified using measures such as intraepidermal nerve fiber density, but these approaches capture only selected anatomical regions or features of nerve structure. We developed an automated image-analysis pipeline to quantify nerve area and nerve-skeleton length across defined epidermal and dermal compartments in whole, stitched mouse plantar skin sections. Automated epidermis-dermis boundary detection showed agreement with manual tracing within the range of inter-observer variation and produced similar downstream measurements. We then applied the pipeline to skin from mice across age and distinct microbial environmental exposures. Conventionalized mice exposed to microbes had greater nerve area and length than germ-free mice in both the epidermis and dermis. In the aging cohort, aged mice had greater dermal nerve area and length than young mice, while epidermal measurements did not differ significantly. We also analyzed the epidermis and dermis together to assess whole-skin innervation. Whole-skin nerve area and length were higher in conventionalized mice than in germ-free mice but did not differ significantly between young and aged mice. These findings show that analyzing the epidermis and dermis separately helps identify where nerve measurements differ, including differences that may not be detected when both skin layers are analyzed together. Compartment-resolved quantification therefore provides a complementary approach for studying changes in cutaneous innervation across biological conditions and behavioral outcomes.

title: SGLT1/2 inhibitor sotagliflozin, but not SGLT2-selective inhibitor empagliflozin, attenuates platelet activation and thrombosis
abstract: As rates of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) have risen, comorbidities of T2DM and cardiovascular disease (CVD) have similarly increased. The adoption of sodium-glucose cotransporter (SGLT) 2 inhibitors as a treatment for T2DM has provided an effective means of decreasing renal glucose reabsorption. In recent clinical trials, sotagliflozin, the first FDA-approved inhibitor of both isoforms of SGLT (SGLT1 and SGLT2), demonstrated a reduction in myocardial infarction and stroke in patients with T2DM at high cardiovascular risk. The cardiovascular protective effect of sotagliflozin compared to the SGLT2-selective inhibitor, empagliflozin, was investigated by evaluating effects on platelet activation and thrombus formation. Employing ex vivo models using blood from healthy donors or T2DM patients, and in vivo mouse models, we demonstrate an inhibitory effect on platelet activity and thrombus formation with sotagliflozin, while empagliflozin has minor to no effects. Further, no impact on hemostasis was observed with sotagliflozin. Finally, a platelet-specific deletion of SGLT1 via Slc5a1fl/fl Gp1ba-Cre⁺ mice resulted in reduced platelet integrin activation and thrombus formation. This study provides insight into a potential explanation for the cardiovascular protection conferred by sotagliflozin observed in patients with T2DM at risk of an ischemic event and reveals an added benefit to SGLT2-selective inhibitors.

title: Progression to castration-resistance and metastatic disease following androgen deprivation therapy for biochemical recurrence after prostate cancer surgery.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Biochemical recurrence after radical prostatectomy for localized prostate cancer impacts nearly one in four patients. While androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) is used in this setting, its impact on metastatic disease outcomes remains unclear in contemporary population-based cohorts.
METHODS: We performed a retrospective cohort study using national Veterans Administration electronic health record and Central Cancer Registry data. Men undergoing radical prostatectomy between 2005-2015 were followed through 2019. We defined biochemical recurrence as prostate-specific antigen (PSA) ≥0.20 nanograms/milliliter. We examined biochemically recurrent prostate cancer management and disease progression to castration-resistance and metastatic disease.
RESULTS: Of 28,452 men with prostate cancer treated surgically, 7,912 (28%) developed biochemical recurrence with 10.5% developing metastatic disease (median follow up 110 months). Salvage ADT with or without radiation therapy was administered to 24% of patients. In adjusted models, salvage ADT use was associated with worse metastasis-free survival (adjusted hazard ratio (aHR) 1.96, 95% CI 1.71-2.25) and increased castration resistant therapy (aHR 20.51, 95% CI 14.48-29.04). Higher pathologic T stage, Gleason grade group, PSA, nodal involvement, and faster PSA doubling times were predictive of metastasis.
CONCLUSIONS: In this large national cohort of men with biochemical recurrence after surgery, most did not develop metastatic disease during nearly 10 years of follow up and one in four patients were treated with ADT. The association between ADT and adjusted outcomes likely reflects more aggressive disease among men selected for hormonal therapy.
IMPACT: These findings underscore the importance of continued risk stratification refinement and management optimization for recurrent prostate cancer.

title: Adaptive landscape of the metallo-β-lactamase NDM-1 to emerging β-lactam-based therapies.
abstract: The New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase (NDM) is a major determinant of carbapenem resistance. This has prompted the development of novel therapeutic strategies to treat NDM producers. Since these therapies impose new selective pressures, their clinical deployment may favor NDM variants carrying escape mutations. To anticipate these events and inform therapeutic decisions, we explored the evolutionary landscape of NDM-1 under different selective constraints. To this end, we generated a diverse library of blaNDM variants and challenged it with zinc starvation, antibiotics, or β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations that represent novel and emerging therapies. Selection under zinc limitation and cefotaxime identified mutational trajectories that recapitulate clinical NDM evolution, validating the diversity of the library and its predictive nature. Drug-specific selections revealed sharply different evolutionary pathways. Mecillinam selected a narrow evolutionary pathway centered on residues N220 and M67, which enhance productive active-site interactions with this penicillin. Cefepime/taniborbactam selected multiple escape routes, dominated by substitutions at E152 and, secondarily, K211, that impair productive interaction with taniborbactam. In contrast, cefiderocol/xeruborbactam under iron-depleted conditions and aztreonam/avibactam did not select NDM variants conferring an improved resistance phenotype in the tested Escherichia coli background. These results show that NDM evolution is constrained by the chemistry of each therapeutic challenge. Substrate adaptation is possible for mecillinam, inhibitor escape is readily accessible for taniborbactam, whereas no NDM-centered escape was detected for the aztreonam- and xeruborbactam-based conditions tested. Mapping drug-specific NDM-centered landscapes can identify therapies that readily select enzyme-level escape and those for which resistance is more likely to require mechanisms beyond blaNDM sequence variation.IMPORTANCECarbapenem-resistant infections by Enterobacterales are increasingly difficult to treat because bacteria can destroy some of the most powerful antibiotics used in the clinic. This study focuses on Escherichia coli carrying variants of the New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase (NDM), an enzyme that enables bacteria to resist carbapenem antibiotics. New therapies are being developed to overcome this problem, but bacteria may evolve again when exposed to these treatments. Here, we tested how New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase can adapt under the evolutionary pressure of last-resort therapies. The results show that not all treatments carry the same evolutionary risk. Some drugs allow the enzyme to adapt through specific mutations, whereas other combinations did not yield improved NDM variants in the tested bacterial background. This work identifies which treatments readily select changes within NDM and which may require resistance mechanisms elsewhere in the bacterial cell. These findings should be integrated with host species, permeability, drug targets, metal uptake, and co-produced enzymes when considering clinical resistance.

title: Depressive and PTSD symptoms are associated with regional differences in light-evoked brain responses in chronic ocular pain.
abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Chronic ocular pain (COP) often co-occurs with depression or post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), but whether these comorbidities confer a distinct biological signature is unknown. Thus, we compared light-evoked blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) responses in individuals with COP, stratified by the presence or absence of clinically relevant depressive and/or PTSD symptoms.
SUBJECTS/METHODS: 43 individuals with COP (pain intensity ≥ 1/10 for ≥ 3 months) underwent event-related functional magnetic resonance imaging using bright-light. Thirty participants were classified as COP with mental health comorbidity (COP + MHC+) based on a Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) score ≥ 5 and/or a PTSD Checklist-Military Version (PCL-M) ≥ 33; 13 were classified as COP without MHC (COP + MHC-). BOLD responses exceeding an exploratory voxelwise threshold of Z > 2.3 were compared within predefined bilateral regions of interest (ROIs) comprising the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), anterior mid-cingulate cortex (aMCC), anterior insula, and amygdala. Regional parameter estimates were correlated with clinical symptoms.
RESULT: Demographics were similar between groups. Participants with COP + MHC+ reported greater dry-eye symptom burden and non-ocular pain, whereas measured ocular surface signs and in-scanner eye-pain and unpleasantness ratings did not differ significantly between groups. In exploratory ROI analyses, COP + MHC+ participants demonstrated greater light-evoked BOLD responses in the right ACC and caudal right aMCC, whereas COP + MHC- participants demonstrated greater responses in the rostral right aMCC and right anterior insula.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that depressive and PTSD symptoms may contribute to heterogeneity in central pain processing among individuals with COP. If confirmed, such differences could help refine COP phenotyping and inform more targeted, mechanism-based treatment strategies.

title: The landscape of polygenic score prediction accuracy and transportability across the phenome in ancestrally diverse populations
abstract: Polygenic scores (PGS) are increasingly common in human genetics research, yet their performance and portability vary substantially across traits and populations. We systematically evaluate prediction accuracy and cross-ancestry portability for 3,994 published PGSs across the phenome in the ancestrally diverse CCPM biobank. We identify widespread trait-specific and cross-trait associations, demonstrating both the utility and breadth of existing polygenic predictors. However, predictive effects frequently differ across ancestry groups, highlighting persistent challenges for portability that threaten equity in downstream applications. We further find that accuracy and portability depend strongly on whether the PGS is continuous or thresholded. Finally, through hierarchical mixed modeling, we identify score-development, genome features, and cohort characteristics associated with improved PGS accuracy and portability. These results highlight key factors supporting future development of robust and portable scores for research and clinical translation.

title: Glucocorticoid dynamics predict susceptibility and resilience to traumatic stress in male and female rats.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The mammalian stress response relies on tightly regulated HPA axis signaling, and disruptions in glucocorticoid feedback are implicated in stress-related disorders such as PTSD. Although many individuals experience trauma, only some develop pathology, suggesting that individual differences in glucocorticoid responsivity may help predict susceptibility or resilience. Here, we examined whether corticosterone (CORT) responses to a mild stressor predict behavioral outcomes following single-prolonged stress (SPS) in male and female rats.
METHODS: Mild stress reactivity was quantified using area-under-the-curve (AUC) CORT responses to light-dark box exposure, after which animals underwent SPS, behavioral assays, and post-reinstatement cFos immunohistochemical analysis.
RESULTS: Females exhibited SPS-induced reductions in basal AM CORT and displayed a robust traumatic stress-related phenotype in which high CORT responders displayed increased anxiety-like behavior, impaired fear extinction, and enhanced reinstatement. Correlational and permutation analyses revealed a consistent pattern in SPS-exposed females in which lower pre-stress basal AM CORT and higher mild stress-induced CORT (AUC) predicted increased fear expression, indicating a dissociation between resting and stress-evoked glucocorticoid signals. In males, mild stress reactivity did not predict SPS-related outcomes; however, reduced pre-stress basal AM CORT in control males predicted increased fear expression, suggesting sex-specific differences in the potential predictive value of CORT dynamics. SPS and CORT responder status also differentially modulated cFos expression across stress-related brain regions, including the PVN, infralimbic cortex, and amygdala in both males and females.
CONCLUSION: These findings demonstrate that mild stress reactivity and basal glucocorticoid dynamics can predict trauma-related phenotypes in a sex-specific manner, identifying them as a potential biomarker of PTSD susceptibility in females.

title: Standardizing Cell Ontology terms for cross-study integration in the female reproductive tract.
abstract: The female reproductive tract is essential for fertility, pregnancy, and overall health, yet many of its cellular components remain poorly defined. Recent advances in single-cell and spatial transcriptomics have begun to reveal this complexity, but inconsistent naming of cell types and states has limited the ability to compare findings across studies. To address this challenge, an international group of reproductive biologists and ontology experts collaborated to harmonize annotations within Cell Ontology, focusing on the ovary, fallopian tube, and uterus. Standardized terms are proposed for major epithelial, stromal, and germ cell populations, supported by marker gene sets and anatomical linkages. This framework provides a shared reference that can be used to harmonize existing datasets and guide annotation of future studies, enabling consistent classification of oocytes, granulosa, theca, luteal, epithelial, stromal, and immune cells across tissues. By establishing a unified taxonomy, this work lays the foundation for integrating datasets, supporting cross-tissue comparisons, and advancing the understanding of reproductive biology, health, and disease.

title: OpenMSK: A modular open-source framework for comprehensive analysis of imaging biomarkers in knee osteoarthritis
abstract: Objective To develop and validate a fully automated, extendable, open-source AI-driven pipeline capable of knee magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) segmentation and quantitative extraction of MRI and positron emission tomography (PET) imaging biomarkers. Design For model training, open-source knee MRI data from 347 knees acquired across 7 scanners using multiple gradient-echo sequences were used. An independent test set of 20 knees from 3T PET-MRI examinations were used for evaluation in this prospective reliability and agreement study. The pipeline segmented femoral, tibial, and patellar bones and cartilage, and medial and lateral menisci using three different deep learning models. Quantitative outputs included cartilage thickness and T 2 relaxation times, meniscus volume and T 2 ∗ relaxation times, bone shape scores, and static and kinetic subchondral bone PET measures. Manual segmentations from two annotators served as reference standards. Segmentation performance was assessed using Dice similarity coefficients (DSC), average symmetric surface distances, and volume differences. Quantitative outcome agreement was evaluated using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), Pearson correlations, and root mean square error. Results Automated segmentations demonstrated high spatial agreement with manual annotations, with DSCs ranging from 0.84 to 0.98 across all tissues. Quantitative PET-MRI biomarkers generally demonstrated high agreement, although confidence intervals were wide for several biomarkers. Conclusion OpenMSK enables multi-tissue knee segmentation and generation of quantitative MRI and PET biomarkers, with performance assessed against two independent annotators and across different U-Net-based segmentation architectures. As a freely available, modular platform, OpenMSK lowers technical barriers to whole-joint quantitative imaging and provides a standardized foundation for OA research and clinical translation.

title: REM sleep infraslow rhythms correlate with neuropsychiatric symptom severity.
abstract:
STUDY OBJECTIVES: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep is commonly divided into phasic and tonic substates based on higher and lower oculomotor activity, respectively. Our previous study described an alternative framework in which REM temporal structure forms a continuum of infraslow rhythms (~0.01 Hz) across brain and body physiology. We now ask whether these infraslow rhythms vary with neuropsychiatric symptoms, given the long-standing but still inconsistent links between REM and mood- or trauma-related disorders.
METHODS: Using a cross-sectional polysomnographic dataset from male veterans, we examined 59 participants for correlations between REM infraslow rhythms and neuropsychiatric symptom scores, excluding participants with moderate/severe apnea.
RESULTS: Oscillations in REM respiratory rate, but not cardiac rate or electroencephalogram beta power, showed higher infraslow frequencies in participants with multiple symptoms, including posttraumatic stress, pain, anxiety, depression, and cognitive difficulties. No significant correlations were found between these symptoms and conventional REM metrics (e.g., REM density, latency and duration). To further examine REM beyond phasic/tonic binarization, we analyzed the timing between oculomotor activity and infraslow oscillations. Eye movements occurred preferentially during periods of high respiratory rate, low beta power and intermediate cardiac rate, with no changes in these temporal relationships across symptom severity.
CONCLUSIONS: Neuropsychiatric associations with REM infraslow rhythms spanned multiple symptom domains but were physiologically specific, with respiratory rate oscillations representing the strongest readout of symptom burden. Furthermore, REM infraslow cycles across brain and body were differentially aligned with eye movements: a temporal pattern that may serve as a physiological target for neuropsychiatric and mechanistic research.

title: Incidence of opioid use disorder among patients prescribed long-term opioid therapy: An observational study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: There are no estimates of incident opioid use disorder (OUD), using current diagnostic criteria, among patients prescribed long-term opioid therapy (LtOT). The U.S. Food and Drug Administration issued a postmarketing requirement to estimate the 12-month incidence of OUD among patients receiving LtOT.
METHODS: Study 3033-1 was a prospective, observational cohort study conducted in 10 health systems with one year of follow up. Data were collected August 2017 to October 2021, analyses were completed December 2025. The primary outcome was pain-adjusted, moderate to severe DSM-5 OUD involving prescription opioids measured using the Psychiatric Research Interview for Substance and Mental Disorders, adapted for assessing OUD among patients treated with opioids (PRISM-5-OP). Secondary outcomes included moderate to severe DSM-5 OUD without pain adjustment and any OUD involving prescription opioids with and without pain adjustment. Overall and stratified incidence were calculated.
RESULTS: 1952 participants were included; 76% were aged 50 + ; 58% were female, 80% were White. The 12-month incidence of the primary outcome was 1.54%, the outcome without pain adjustment resulted in an incidence of 4.46%. Incidence of any DSM-5 OUD involving prescription opioids was 6.92% with pain adjustment and 18.14% without pain adjustment. Incidence estimates were similar across age, sex, and Medicaid status. Some estimates were higher among those with past-year or prior to past-year substance use or major depressive disorders.
CONCLUSIONS: At one year, the incidence of at least moderate OUD ranged from 1.54% to 4.46%. These findings can inform clinician and patient shared decision-making and evaluations of OUD prevention efforts.

title: Claudin-2 protects from enteropathogenic E. coli-infection and colitis by promoting crypt fetalization via β1-integrin/FAK/YAP signaling.
abstract: Citrobacter rodentium (Cra) infection, a murine model of enteropathogenic Escherichia coli (EPEC) infection, induces crypt proliferation that potentially promotes mucosal healing and pathogen clearance, yet the underlying molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. Cra infection upregulates claudin-2 (CLDN2), which has been proposed to facilitate pathogen clearance by enhancing Na⁺ flux and diarrhea. However, CLDN2 is dispensable for intestinal Na⁺ homeostasis. Here, we investigate whether Cra-induced CLDN2 protects against Cra-infection and colitis by regulating crypt proliferation. Using mice with intestinal epithelial-specific CLDN2 overexpression or deletion (Cldn2KO), we evaluate the role of CLDN2 in Cra colonization, inflammation, and epithelial regeneration. Organoid cultures assess epithelial-intrinsic mechanisms, while co-immunoprecipitation identifies CLDN2-associated signaling complexes. CLDN2 overexpression protects against Cra colonization and colitis, whereas Cldn2KO mice exhibit increased bacterial burden, exacerbated inflammation, and impaired crypt proliferation. Mechanistically, CLDN2 promotes crypt fetal-like reprogramming (fetalization), which is suppressed in Cldn2KO mice. Inhibiting EGFR-activation abolishes CLDN2 induction and phenocopies Cldn2KO phenotype. Furthermore, CLDN2 promotes FAK and YAP activation by stabilizing the β1-integrin-FAK complex, thereby driving crypt fetalization. Collectively, these findings identify CLDN2 as a critical regulator of mucosal defense and epithelial regeneration through activation of the β1-integrin-FAK-YAP signaling axis, beyond its classical role in paracellular ion permeability.

title: Voxelwise Lesion Symptom Mapping in Pediatric TBI: An ENIGMA Mega-Analysis.
abstract: Focal lesions are common after complicated mild-to-severe traumatic brain injury (cmsTBI) in children, yet it is unclear whether the location of focal damage relates to cognitive outcome beyond overall lesion burden. Combining 13 international cohorts through the ENIGMA Pediatric cmsTBI working group, we conducted voxelwise lesion-symptom mapping (VLSM) to test whether focal lesion location relates to cognitive outcome, and how this compares with overall lesion volume. From 357 patients with imaging that passed guality assurance, 67 had a focal lesion visible on T1-weighted MRI along with at least one performance-based cognitive outcome (D-KEFS Trail Making conditions and WISC/WAIS Coding). We tested whether lesion location related to cognitive outcome using VLSM, adjusting for age, sex, and time since injury, and separately tested total lesion volume as a predictor of each outcome. Lesions in the right middle frontal gyrus were associated with poorer performance on number sequencing (D-KEFS Trail Making condition 2), a timed visuomotor sequencing task (false discovery rate corrected). In separate regression analyses, greater lesion volume was associated with poorer number-letter switching and motor speed. The switching association remained significant after adjusting for injury severity, whereas the motor-speed association did not. In the largest lesion sample assembled in pediatric cmsTBI to date, focal lesion location and injury burden index separable contributions to cognitive outcome, with number sequencing linked to focal prefrontal damage and switching and motor speed to overall lesion volume, underscoring the value of precise lesion characterization for large-scale multi-site neuroimaging.

title: Neutrophil Percentage-to-Albumin Ratio and Heart Failure Mortality: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Inflammation and malnutrition are important contributors to adverse outcomes in heart failure (HF). The neutrophil percentage-to-albumin ratio (NPAR), derived from routinely available laboratory parameters, integrates inflammatory burden and nutritional status and may provide prognostic value. We conducted a systematic review in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines to evaluate the association between baseline or admission NPAR and all-cause mortality in adults with HF. Two independent reviewers performed study selection and data extraction, and methodological quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Because of heterogeneity in study populations, NPAR cutoff values, and outcome definitions, meta-analysis was not performed and findings were synthesized narratively. Five observational cohort studies comprising more than 4900 patients were included. Across all studies, elevated NPAR was consistently associated with increased short-term (30-90 days) and long-term (1-5 years) all-cause mortality in diverse HF populations, with reported hazard ratios ranging from 1.52 to 2.18. Several studies also demonstrated superior prognostic performance of NPAR compared with neutrophil percentage or serum albumin alone. However, reported NPAR cutoff values varied and remain unstandardized. Elevated NPAR is consistently associated with increased all-cause mortality in patients with HF and may serve as a simple, cost-effective tool for clinical risk stratification. Prospective studies are needed to establish standardized thresholds and validate its prognostic utility across HF phenotypes and clinical settings.

title: Prehistoric global migration of vanishing gut microbes with humans.
abstract: The gut microbiome is crucial for health and is affected strongly by lifestyle1. Many microorganisms commonly found in non-industrialized populations are disappearing or have become extinct in industrialized populations2-6. Studying which microorganisms have been long-term residents of the human gut and may have co-evolved with humans2,7,8 could provide insights into how microbial biodiversity loss affects human health. However, the genetic complexities of microbial evolution and the plasticity of gut microbiome composition have made it challenging to resolve the evolutionary history of these long-term associations. Here we performed deep metagenomic sequencing of the Tsimane horticulturalists of Bolivia and compared their gut microbiomes with those of the Hadza hunter-gatherers of Tanzania3. These two populations, whose ancestors have been separated for tens of thousands of years, share 1,231 microbial species, most of which are rare in or absent from industrialized populations. Population genetic analyses of 636 of the shared species revealed patterns of microbial divergence and gene flow consistent with prehistoric human co-migration, with estimated split times that approximately align with human migration out of Africa and into the Americas. Our findings indicate that a diverse gut microbiome co-migrated with humans worldwide and has persisted over millennia. However, many of these species are now vanishing from industrialized populations and the consequences for human health remain uncertain.

title: A Multicenter 13-Week Evaluation of the twiist Automated Insulin Delivery in Insulin-Treated Type 2 Diabetes: The twiist-T2D Pivotal Trial.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the efficacy, safety, and user satisfaction of the twiist automated insulin delivery (AID) system in adults with type 2 diabetes.
RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS: In a single-arm, multicenter trial, 307 adults with insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, 19-85 years old, initiated use of the twiist AID system for 13 weeks after collection of baseline continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) data. The primary outcome was change in HbA1c from baseline to 13 weeks.
RESULTS: Mean HbA1c decreased by 0.7% (95% CI -0.9 to -0.6) from 8.1% ± 1.5% at baseline to 7.4% ± 0.9% after using twiist for 13 weeks (P < 0.001 for both noninferiority and superiority). The treatment effect was greatest in participants with baseline HbA1c ≥9.0%. A substantial HbA1c reduction was observed when AID was added to prestudy use of a glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonist or sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor drug, which was continued during the trial. Mean CGM-measured time-in-range 70-180 mg/dL increased from 57% ± 26% to 73% ± 17% (mean change 16% [95% CI 14-18]; P < 0.001). All other multiplicity-controlled CGM outcomes reflective of hyperglycemia showed significant improvement from baseline. The frequency of CGM-measured hypoglycemia was low at baseline and remained low during follow-up. Diabetic ketoacidosis occurred in one participant; no severe hypoglycemia events occurred. Using twiist, participant satisfaction was higher than with their prestudy insulin delivery method (P < 0.001) and sleep quality improved (P < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: In this single-arm, 13-week trial in adults with insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, AID with the twiist system was safe and associated with substantially improved glycemia.

title: In vitro activity of cefiderocol against Burkholderia cepacia complex and Burkholderia gladioli clinical isolates from cystic fibrosis patients in the United States.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Burkholderia cepacia complex (Bcc) and Burkholderia gladioli are intrinsically multidrug-resistant pathogens that cause chronic pulmonary infections in individuals with cystic fibrosis (CF) and severe infections in other vulnerable populations. Therapeutic options remain limited as resistance to commonly used agents continues to emerge.
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the in vitro activity of cefiderocol against a collection of Bcc and B. gladioli isolates from individuals with CF in the USA and to compare these findings with historical susceptibility data for 16 other antimicrobial agents.
METHODS: A total of 150 clinical isolates representing multiple Bcc species and B. gladioli were tested. Cefiderocol MICs were determined using iron-depleted broth microdilution (ID-BMD) and iron-depleted agar dilution (ID-AD). Species-specific MIC distributions were assessed, and cefiderocol activity was compared with historical MIC data for 16 other antimicrobial agents previously tested against the same isolate panel. Mechanistic studies evaluated blaPenA expression and hydrolysis of cefiderocol by purified PenA1.
RESULTS: Cefiderocol MIC50 and MIC90 values were 0.06 and 8 mg/L, and 0.03 and 8 mg/L, respectively, by both ID-BMD and ID-AD. Low MIC90 values were observed for Burkholderia cenocepacia, B. cepacia, B. gladioli, and most 'other Bcc' species, whereas elevated MIC90 values were detected for Burkholderia multivorans and Burkholderia vietnamiensis. Cefiderocol demonstrated the lowest MIC50 values when compared with historical data for 16 other agents; did not induce blaPen expression; and was not hydrolysed by purified PenA1.
CONCLUSIONS: Cefiderocol demonstrated broad in vitro activity against Bcc and B. gladioli isolates from individuals with CF and showed stability against key β-lactamase-mediated resistance mechanisms.

title: Diabetes Polygenic Scores Predict Glycemic Indices and Insulin Use in Individuals with Atypical Diabetes
abstract: Aims/Hypothesis: Atypical forms of diabetes often provide diagnostic challenges and are suboptimally treated. We sought to determine whether type 1 and 2 diabetes polygenic scores (PS) would help improve classification of islet autoantibody-negative (IAb-) atypical diabetes cases. Methods: We implemented type 1 diabetes PS (T1D PS) and type 2 diabetes PS (T2D PS) in 309 IAb-individuals' genome sequencing from the Rare and Atypical Diabetes Network (RADIANT), the largest and most comprehensively phenotyped collection of unsolved and atypical diabetes cases. We performed regression analyses to assess associations between PS, clinical characteristics, and glycemic measures. Results: Both T1D and T2D PS were significantly higher in RADIANT than in ancestry-matched controls from UK Biobank. Both PS were associated with C-peptide measures throughout participant oral glucose tolerance tests (OGTT), although in opposite directions; T1D PS was associated with lower C-peptide measures, while T2D PS was associated with higher measures. Participants with T1D PS above a previously established optimal PS value for differentiating cases and controls (T1D PS GRS2>12.88) had 13-fold higher odds of both insulin deficiency on OGTT and use of both basal and bolus insulin therapy. Conclusions/Interpretation: Individuals in RADIANT with ambiguous diabetes subtypes displayed genetic enrichment for both type 1 and type 2 diabetes, despite ascertainment to remove standard type 1 and type 2 diabetes. T1D PS identified individuals with an unrecognized "type 1 diabetes- like " phenotype with insulin deficiency and need for intensive insulin in the absence of islet autoantibodies. PS may help identify individuals with atypical diabetes who will ultimately benefit from insulin therapy.

title: Fear learning-induced brain dynamics predict individual extinction memory expression following transcranial magnetic stimulation.
abstract: Fear learning and extinction unfold as time-dependent processes. Herein, we examined whether fear learning dynamically reorganizes brain activity and whether such reorganization predicts subsequent extinction-memory expression under transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS)-modulated extinction. Eighty-seven healthy adults completed a three-day Pavlovian threat-learning protocol with resting-state fMRI, TMS-modulated extinction, and extinction-memory fMRI. Using coactivation pattern analysis with a hidden Markov model, we identified a fear-learning-induced brain state characterized by increased engagement and transition uncertainty after conditioning. Functional connectivity reorganization within this state predicted individual differences in extinction recall- and renewal-related brain activation under TMS-modulated extinction (cross-validated; recall r = 0.47, p = 0.001; renewal r = 0.37, p = 0.01; permutation-tested), but not natural extinction. In separate brain-behavior correlation analyses, the neural variates identified in the TMS-modulated extinction were associated with behavioral expression. These findings demonstrate that fear learning reshapes brain-state dynamics and identifies a candidate biomarker of neuromodulation-linked extinction-memory expression.

title: Variable task difficulty with augmented sensory feedback for motor training in virtual reality.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: This study examined how motor task difficulty and augmented sensory feedback (ASF) modality influence task performance, physiological responses, and perceptual experience during virtual reality (VR)-based upper-limb motor training. Building on related brace- and VR-based ASF platforms previously examined in neurotypical and spinal cord injury cohorts, the long-term goal is to support neurorehabilitation-oriented adaptive VR training; however, the present study used neurotypical participants as an initial validation step.
METHODS: Fourteen right-handed neurotypical participants used a supportive upper-limb brace and surface electromyography (EMG) for myoelectric control of a virtual robotic arm in a two-dimensional tracking task. A 2 × 2 within-subject design crossed ASF modality (visual feedback versus visual + haptic feedback) with task difficulty (straight-line versus sinusoidal trajectory). Outcomes included normalized path length, task completion time, movement jerk, alpha- and beta-band electroencephalogram (EEG) power over motor cortex, heart rate, EMG amplitude, EMG-displacement-based virtual work, and perceptual ratings of agency, motivation, and utility. Short-term pre-to-post percentage changes were computed for each measure.
RESULTS: VHF straight-line training produced the largest reductions in normalized path length (-4.69%) and completion time (-6.12%), whereas VHF sinusoid training produced the largest reductions in movement jerk (-5.67%) and virtual work (-13.33%). ASF modality affected path length, completion time, jerk, EMG amplitude, and virtual work, whereas task difficulty modulated beta-band EEG power and the physiological index. Changes in path length were positively associated with changes in completion time and EMG amplitude.
DISCUSSION: These findings suggest that ASF modality and task difficulty can differentially shape short-term behavioral, physiological, and perceptual responses in healthy participants. The exploratory distribution of participant-specific best-case conditions motivates future studies using independent trial subsets to evaluate whether behavioral and physiological measures can support individualized VR training.

title: A Long-Acting Farnesoid X Receptor (FXR) Agonist Prevents Fibrosis.
abstract: Despite effective vaccines and antiviral therapies, patients with chronic hepatitis B (CHB) remain at risk of developing progressive liver fibrosis and cirrhosis. Vonafexor (VON), a second-generation synthetic non-steroidal, non-bile acid farnesoid X receptor agonist, has been shown to prevent liver fibrosis and target the HBV cccDNA reservoir. However, adherence to daily oral therapy is an established barrier to successful treatment of chronic infections. To overcome this barrier, VON was transformed into a long-acting (LA) prodrug nanosuspension. The LA prodrug formulation suppressed αSMA, TGFβ, and Col1A1 gene expression in the LX2 hepatic stellate cell line. The formulation was well tolerated and prevented liver and lung damage in a carbon tetrachloride-induced chronic liver injury model. The promising preclinical data support further development of LA VON prodrugs as potential treatments for liver and lung fibrosis.

title: Covariation among higher-order psychopathology dimensions is driven by nomorbidity and not comorbidity.
abstract: Emerging classification frameworks claim that covariation among psychopathology dimensions reflects comorbidity. We scrutinized this claim by applying Bayesian change point models to four waves of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study data (N = 11,868 youths; 48% female) and examined associations among higher-order psychopathology dimensions. Covariation between psychopathology dimensions was driven by nomorbidity, not comorbidity: we observed strong positive associations among psychopathology dimensions at relatively extreme low (asymptomatic) levels (for example, when three to five symptoms were endorsed) and weak positive associations at higher levels. For instance, at wave 1, a 1-point increase in internalizing was associated with a 32% increase in externalizing at nearly asymptomatic levels (B = 0.28), compared with only a 7% increase at higher levels (B = 0.07). These findings challenge existing assumptions about comorbidity in nonclinical samples, suggesting that covariation is more accurately explained by the absence of symptomatology rather than shared psychiatric conditions.

title: Symptom Misrepresentation to Obtain Antibiotics.
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Misrepresentation of symptoms, whether through exaggeration, omission, or fabrication, can represent an important barrier to effective patient-clinician communication and shared decision-making, including in the context of antibiotic treatment.
OBJECTIVE: To examine the prevalence, reasons for, and characteristics associated with self-reported misrepresentation of symptoms to obtain antibiotics.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This survey study recruited a national, nonprobability sample of US adults to participate in an online survey from January 8 to February 13, 2026. Data were analyzed from February to March 18, 2026.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Outcomes of interest were 2 types of symptom misrepresentation (exaggeration and fabrication) to obtain antibiotics and the reasons underlying these behaviors. Additional questions measured antibiotic-related beliefs, experiences, and behaviors and demographics.
RESULTS: Of 1371 eligible participants, the final sample included 959 individuals (mean [SD] age of 50.7 [17.6] years; 478 [49.8%] female). Overall, 268 respondents (27.9%) reported ever misrepresenting their symptoms to a clinician to get antibiotics. This included 108 respondents (40.3%) who exaggerated existing symptoms (eg, told their clinician they had a cough for 2 weeks when they only had it for 1 week), 19 respondents (7.1%) who fabricated symptoms (eg, told their clinician they had a fever when they did not), and 141 (52.6%) who did both. Cold-like symptoms (eg, cough, sore throat) were the most frequently misrepresented (176 respondents [65.7%]). The most commonly endorsed reasons for misrepresenting symptoms were illness severity, perceived antibiotic efficacy, returning to responsibilities, and desire for autonomy in their treatment decisions. Younger age (age 18-33 vs ≥65 years: odds ratio [OR], 3.20 [95% CI, 1.58-6.63]; age 34-55 vs ≥65 years: OR, 3.05 [95% CI, 1.55-6.17]), often feeling that clinicians do not take their symptoms seriously (OR, 2.19 [95% CI, 1.49-3.22]), believing that antibiotic resistance is a hoax (OR, 1.98 [95% CI, 1.34-2.93]), reporting more comorbidities (OR, 1.16 [95% CI, 1.05-1.28]), having higher lying-acceptability scores (OR, 1.49 [95% CI, 1.23-1.80]), and needing help reading health materials (OR, 2.40 [95% CI, 1.62-3.54]) were associated with higher odds of reporting symptom misrepresentation to obtain antibiotics. In contrast, dislike of taking antibiotics (OR, 0.89 [95% CI, 0.81-0.99]) and higher antibiotic knowledge (OR, 0.73 [95% CI, 0.58-0.91]) were associated with lower odds of misrepresentation.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this survey study of US adults, nearly 30% of respondents reported misrepresenting symptoms to get antibiotics from a clinician, most commonly cold-like symptoms. Findings highlight the need for strategies to promote antibiotic knowledge and improve patient-clinician communication to address factors contributing to symptom misrepresentation.

title: Real-World Overall Survival With Abiraterone Acetate and Enzalutamide in Patients With Chemotherapy-Naïve Metastatic Castration-Resistant Prostate Cancer From the Flatiron Electronic Health Records Database.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patients with chemotherapy- and androgen receptor pathway inhibitor (ARPI)-naïve metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) have generally shown worse overall survival (OS) with abiraterone versus enzalutamide in claims database studies. Given limitations of claims data, analysis using detailed electronic health records (EHRs) is needed to confirm this finding.
METHODS: This EHR-based analysis (2014-2023) of the Flatiron Health database included patients with chemotherapy- and ARPI-naïve mCRPC who initiated first-line ARPI (abiraterone or enzalutamide). OS, treatment duration, and time to subsequent therapy were assessed. A subgroup analysis evaluated patients who received first-line ARPI only with no subsequent treatments. Kaplan-Meier method and Cox proportional hazards models evaluated time-to-event outcomes. Stabilized inverse probability treatment weighting (sIPTW) adjusted for baseline differences.
RESULTS: Among 2731 patients, 1316 received first-line abiraterone and 1415 enzalutamide (median follow-up: 21.8 and 23.2 months, respectively). sIPTW-adjusted median OS (24.6 vs. 25.8 months; hazard ratio [HR] 1.13; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.03-1.23), treatment duration (7.9 vs. 9.5 months; HR 1.21; 95% CI, 1.11-1.31), and time to subsequent therapy (14.7 vs. 17.9 months; HR 1.20; 95% CI, 1.08-1.32) were shorter with abiraterone versus enzalutamide. Among the 40% with no subsequent treatment (n = 1102), sIPTW-adjusted median OS (14.0 vs. 17.7 months; HR 1.32; 95% CI, 1.14-1.53), and treatment duration (7.5 vs. 10.6 months; HR 1.30; 95% CI, 1.12-1.50) were also shorter with abiraterone versus enzalutamide.
CONCLUSIONS: Using more detailed data abstraction, these results confirm prior claims-based analyses showing that despite early use of subsequent therapy, first-line abiraterone is associated with shorter OS versus enzalutamide in ARPI- and chemotherapy-naïve mCRPC.

title: Cross-source proteogenomic profiling of human microglia reveals a conserved core membrane protein and HERV signature.
abstract: Microglia are essential immune cells of the brain parenchyma which are responsible for maintaining homeostasis and responding to brain injury. When activated, they induce immune signaling and become phagocytic. In the context of neurodegenerative diseases, they exhibit both pro- and anti-inflammatory properties. Human endogenous retroviruses (HERVs) are the remnants of ancient retroviral germline infections that integrated into the human genome, and their expression has been directly linked to microglial-mediated neurodegenerative diseases. Despite this, HERV expression is not consistently included in analyses characterizing microglia. Investigating the function of microglia across different diseases is critical for elucidating mechanisms of disease progression and for the development of effective therapeutic interventions. Approaches to studying microglia include isolation from post-mortem brain tissues, differentiation from peripheral blood monocytes or differentiation of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC). Ex vivo brain derived microglia (BdMG) are considered most physiologically relevant, but constraints including the unpredictable timing of availability, labor-intensive protocols, and low yields reduce their practicality. Existing alternatives are iPSC-derived microglia (iMG) and monocyte-derived microglia (MDMi) models that circumvent sample accessibility and scalability issues. Here, we explored the transcriptome and proteome of these three microglia sources and identified a common microglia surface marker expression profile, establishing that MDMi and iMG exhibit similar phenotypes relative to BdMG. We also identified a common HERV expression profile across BdMG, iMG and MDMi, indicating deeper similarities across different sources. Altogether, our findings indicate that given the phenotypic similarities of the 2 models, MDMi represent a practical and reliable model for investigating microglial function with iMG models serving for more molecular based approaches, such as CRISPRa/i.

title: Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infection Prevention Practices in US Hospitals.
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) remains a common and morbid health care-associated infection. Although evidence-based prevention strategies are well established, the degree to which hospitals adopt and sustain these practices over time and whether trajectories differ between Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) and nonfederal systems are not well described.
OBJECTIVE: To examine 20-year trends in reported CAUTI prevention practices in US hospitals and compare practice use between VA and nonfederal hospitals.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This survey study used repeated cross-sectional national surveys conducted every 4 years from 2005 to 2025. Surveys were sent to the lead infection preventionist at all VA hospitals, as well as a random sample of nonfederal, general medical, and surgical US hospitals with intensive care units. Data were analyzed from January to August 2026.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The outcome of interest was regular use of specific CAUTI prevention practices, including urinary catheter reminders or stop orders, nurse-initiated discontinuation, bladder ultrasonography, intermittent catheterization, external catheters, aseptic insertion, surveillance systems, and leadership prioritization of CAUTI prevention.
RESULTS: Over the 20 year period, 1461 unique hospitals participated in at least 1 study survey, with mean (SD) response rates for the 6 survey waves of 63.4% (8.4%) for VA hospitals and 56.5% (9.2%) for nonfederal hospitals. Both VA and nonfederal hospitals demonstrated substantial long-term increases in surveillance infrastructure, routine monitoring of catheter duration, and leadership prioritization of CAUTI prevention. In nonfederal hospitals, regular use of urinary catheter reminders or stop orders increased from 34 of 372 hospitals (9.1%) in 2005 to 149 of 306 hospitals (48.7%) in 2025, and nurse-initiated discontinuation increased from 43 of 379 hospitals (11.3%) in 2009 to 179 of 307 hospitals (58.3%) in 2025. VA hospitals also showed significant increases in these practices over time, although use in 2025 was lower than nonfederal hospitals (urinary catheter reminders or stop orders: 10 of 90 hospitals [11.1%] in 2005 and 23 of 73 hospitals [31.5%] in 2025; nurse-initiated discontinuation: 10 of 69 hospitals (14.5%) in 2009 and 28 of 74 hospitals [37.8%] in 2025). Use of silver alloy Foley catheters declined markedly in nonfederal hospitals (from 126 of 389 hospitals [32.4%] in 2005 to 41 of 294 hospitals [14.0%] in 2025) but remained stable in VA facilities. External catheter use increased substantially, particularly in women, with 194 of 310 nonfederal hospitals (62.6%) and 30 of 73 VA hospitals (41.1%) reporting regular use by 2025. Nearly universal use of CAUTI surveillance systems was observed in both settings (309 of 315 nonfederal hospitals [98.1%] and 73 of 74 VA hospitals [98.7%]).
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: This survey study of infection-prevention practice use found that US hospitals substantially expanded use of many CAUTI prevention practices, particularly surveillance and monitoring systems, over the past 20 years. However, variability in use of high-yield practices, such as reminders and nurse-driven discontinuation, persisted, underscoring the need for sustained, system-level strategies to optimize urinary catheter safety across health care settings.

title: Multi-parametric quantitative ultrasound imaging evaluation of rat sciatic nerve regeneration
abstract: Abstract Peripheral nerve injury is a prevalent condition that significantly impairs patients' sensorimotor function. Noninvasive monitoring of peripheral nerve regeneration could serve as a valuable clinical tool for improving the timing and effectiveness of surgical interventions. We present a multiparametric high-frequency quantitative ultrasound evaluation to noninvasively track temporal and spatial peripheral nerve regeneration following early (n = 16) and delayed (n = 15) graft-based repair of rat sciatic nerve gaps, compared with a sham control group (n = 8). Multiple ultrasound parameters—including backscatter coefficient (BSC) spectra-based measurements (integrated BSC and midband fitted slope), homodyned K envelope statistics (μ and $$\kappa $$ ), gray-level co-occurrence matrix (GLCM) texture features, and B-mode morphological measurements were acquired using a Vevo MD UHF 48 transducer at proximal, intra-graft, and distal nerve locations at 1, 2, and 3 months post-repair. Four sciatic nerve samples were extracted after each time point from each experimental group. A histological grading scheme was applied to classify nerve sections into mild, moderate, and severe pathological grades. Principal component analysis (PCA) combined with support vector machine (SVM) classification was employed to establish decision boundaries among pathological groups. Four parameters (μ, cross-sectional area, normalized integrated BSC, midband fitted slope) significantly differentiated groups with varying pathological severity. PCA-SVM analysis achieved excellent classification performance with an area under the ROC curve of 0.93 and accuracy of 0.85 for distinguishing minimal versus severe pathological injured nerves. These findings demonstrate that multiparametric quantitative ultrasound (qUS) effectively characterizes nerve pathologies by integrating complementary information about microstructural changes across different structural scales, potentially offering a comprehensive, noninvasive assessment of the regenerative microenvironment.

title: AI-Driven Multimodal Risk Assessment Combining CT Imaging Biomarkers and Frailty Scores for Enhanced Mortality Prediction in Surgery Patients
abstract: BACKGROUND: Automated frailty assessment predicts postoperative mortality, but routinely acquired CT imaging may provide complementary physiologic information. We evaluated whether AI-derived CT biomarkers improve one-year mortality prediction beyond an ICD-based Risk Analysis Index (RAI-ICD). STUDY DESIGN: This retrospective cohort linked abdominopelvic CT scans obtained from 2013-2018 at a tertiary academic center to non-emergent surgery within 6 months. RAI-ICD was integrated with automated CT-derived muscle, adiposity, bone, and aortic calcification biomarkers using an XGBoost binary classification model, which we deemed the Unified Multimodal Model (UMM). The primary outcome was one-year all-cause mortality; discrimination, calibration, and decision-curve net benefit were evaluated. RESULTS: Among 7,672 patients, one-year mortality was 12.3%; 7,638 patients were included in primary mortality models. RAI-ICD alone achieved an AUROC of 0.75 and outperformed every individual imaging biomarker. Adding all imaging biomarkers increased AUROC to 0.79 (ΔAUROC +0.04; P<0.001). UMM calibration (slope 1.00; intercept 0.01; ICI 0.01) exceeded RAI-ICD calibration (slope 0.72; intercept 0.04; ICI 0.03), particularly at higher predicted risk. At the Youden-optimal threshold, UMM PPV was 0.24, NPV 0.96, and number needed to screen was 4.1. UMM provided significantly greater net benefit overall and among Robust, Frail, and Very Frail strata. CONCLUSIONS: Integrating automated CT biomarkers with RAI-ICD improved one-year postoperative mortality prediction, high-risk calibration, and clinical net benefit compared with frailty assessment alone. External validation is required before clinical implementation.

title: Adaptation and Evaluation of a Multi‐Component School‐Based Sexual Reproductive Health Intervention Safer Choices Programme in Rural KwaZulu‐Natal, South Africa – A Process Evaluation
abstract: INTRODUCTION: We co-adapted and evaluated a multi-component whole-school health-promotion Safer Choices programme to improve sexual and reproductive health (SRH) and uptake of HIV-prevention among learners in rural uMkhanyakude district, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. METHODS: From January 2023 to June 2025, we used the Framework for Reporting Adaptations and Modifications-Enhanced (FRAME) to guide and document Safer Choices adaptations. We used participatory qualitative approaches and a process evaluation to assess intervention acceptability and feasibility. Co-adapting involved a 3-day workshop with 16 learners aged 15-19 (Grade 9-10), four discussions with school leadership and two focus group discussions (FGDs) with parents/guardians, to understand the context and social validity of the programme. Intervention acceptability was assessed through five in-depth interviews with teachers/school leadership and three with peer leaders, two workshops with intervention and clinical delivery teams, two FGDs with community members and five with learners. Interactions were audio-recorded, transcribed and analysed using thematic analysis. RESULTS: Schools were described as learning spaces providing opportunities for health promotion through health and well-being lessons. Teachers and parents/guardians noted a need for Safer Choices to provide SRH/HIV services in schools, as most learners were already sexually active. Provision of mobile SRH/HIV services in schools was perceived to be feasible if negotiated with the school and HIV-status neutral services were provided to minimize stigma. Adaptations to Safer Choices were focused on optimizing intervention delivery or emphasizing social validity of the programme. During implementation of Safer Choices, myths and misconceptions around HIV and pregnancy were addressed. Challenges such as no electricity and large classes made it difficult to deliver Safer Choices. Peer navigators (lay youth-workers) were engaged to help deliver the intervention. CONCLUSIONS: In a context of high sexual risk and vulnerability, it was feasible to co-adapt and deliver the Safer Choices programme, which provided accurate and accessible SRH information and services to address adolescent SRH needs of learners in our rural schools. Adaptation challenges included balancing fidelity to intervention with both the "real-world" context and the practicality of peer navigators supporting intervention delivery. These results suggest that optimizing the impact necessitates appropriately resourcing school-based interventions to address the challenges of programming in rural settings.

title: Association of imipenem/cilastatin with development of acute kidney injury in critically ill patients requiring carbapenem treatment
abstract: Abstract Cilastatin is an inhibitor of drug metabolism in the kidney which is only available for human use in combination with imipenem, a carbapenem antibiotic, as imipenem/cilastatin (I/C). Animal studies demonstrate cilastatin protects against acute kidney injury (AKI) and clinical studies suggest I/C may reduce the risk of AKI. However, the effective dose of cilastatin in animal studies is higher than that approved with imipenem, and rigorous assessment of the effect of I/C on AKI in patients with high risk of AKI, such as those in the intensive care unit (ICU), is indicated. To address this issue, we conducted a retrospective cohort study using 3 large ICU databases, including Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care III (MIMIC-III), MIMIC-IV, and the Amsterdam University Medical Center database (AUMC). Total 3932 patients were included and patients treated with I/C or non-cilastatin carbapenems (NCC) were compared using propensity score-based overlap weighting analysis. AKI development or progression was less commonly observed in I/C-treated patients than in NCC-treated patients in MIMIC-III (odds ratio [OR] and 95% confidence interval of I/C group: 0.52 [0.31–0.86]) while the outcome was similar between the groups in MIMIC-IV (OR: 1.22 [0.81–1.86]) and in AUMC (OR: 1.06 [0.76–1.47]). The outcome development was also similar between the groups with the overall analysis across all datasets by random effect model meta-analysis (OR: 0.90 [0.55–1.47]). In conclusion, I/C and other carbapenems do not differentially associate with AKI risks in ICU, and its putative effects may depend on patient characteristics and clinical settings.

title: Evaluating Transitional Care Investments Across Diverse Hospitals.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Leaders investing in transitional care must consider whether potential economic benefits outweigh costs. We sought to identify drivers of costs/benefits of the nurse-delivered, telephone-based Coordinated Transitional Care (CTraC) program and examine how economic returns varied across facilities.
METHODS: A cohort of patients ≥ 65-years-old, discharged from hospitals to home after a medical or neurological admission (October 2022-September 2023) was used to identify VA facility: patient volume, 30-day unplanned readmission rates, and readmission lengths of stay. We obtained VA bed-day-of-care costs, non-VA charges, and nursing salaries. We estimated facilities' annual net costs/savings from changes in readmissions (2023-dollars), net per patient costs/savings, and number of VA bed-days freed from investing in one nurse, given varying program effectiveness (10%-30% relative readmission reduction). Estimates were also calculated for a hypothetical base-case derived from median facility characteristics.
RESULTS: Among 99,778 patients discharged from 120 VA hospitals: median facility patient volume was 786; 30-day unplanned readmission rate was 14.1%. Given one nurse serving 307 patients/year and a 20% readmission reduction among CTraC patients, CTraC was estimated (base-case) to reduce non-VA hospital readmission charges by $22,369 and free 55.5 VA bed-days-of-care annually. Savings varied across facilities and were associated with readmission rates and volume. Estimates based on median facility characteristics overstated potential benefits for some hospitals and understated it for others.
CONCLUSIONS: Investments in transitional care may reduce readmissions and generate economic benefit, but the magnitude of returns varied across VA hospitals. Facility-specific data were essential for accurate assessment of value and informed policy-making.

title: Management of shift work disorder: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine systematic review, meta-analysis, and GRADE assessment.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The purpose of this systematic review is to provide supporting evidence for a clinical practice guideline on the treatment of adults with shift work disorder (SWD).
METHODS: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine commissioned a task force of six experts in sleep and circadian medicine. A systematic review was conducted to identify randomized controlled trials, observational studies, and treatment trials in which treatments for the symptoms of excessive sleepiness and/or sleep disturbance/insomnia in adults with SWD, and for circadian adaptation to shift work schedules was tested. Evidence from controlled laboratory trials of simulated shift work and of field-based trials of shift workers with and without a diagnosis of SWD was included. Statistical analyses were performed to determine the significance of critical and important outcomes and clinically meaningful thresholds were set to determine the clinical relevance of treatments on the outcomes examined, where possible. Finally, the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) process was used to assess the evidence for making recommendations.
RESULTS: The literature search resulted in 3,045 articles; 118 studies provided data suitable for statistical analyses. The task force provided a detailed summary of the evidence along with the quality of evidence, the balance of benefits and harms, patient values and preferences, and resource use considerations.

title: Depressive Symptoms and Incident Peripheral Arterial Disease Among Adults With CKD: Findings From the Chronic Renal Insufficiency Cohort (CRIC) Study.
abstract:
RATIONALE & OBJECTIVE: Depression is associated with cardiovascular disease among adults with CKD, but its relationship with peripheral arterial disease (PAD) has not been thoroughly examined despite both conditions being common in this population. We evaluated the risk for incident PAD and death associated with elevated depressive symptoms among adults with CKD.
STUDY DESIGN: Observational prospective cohort study.
SETTING & PARTICIPANTS: Adults with mild to moderate CKD in the Chronic Renal Insufficiency Cohort Study (CRIC) Study.
EXPOSURES: Elevated depressive symptoms as defined by a Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) score ≥ 11.
OUTCOMES: Incident PAD, defined as an Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI) < 0.9 or confirmed clinical PAD event (amputation or angioplasty). Composite outcome of incident PAD or death.
ANALYTICAL APPROACH: The association between baseline elevated depressive symptoms and incident PAD, as well as a composite of incident PAD or death, was examined with Cox proportional hazard models. Mediation analysis explored the pathways between elevated depressive symptoms and these outcomes.
RESULTS: Among 2,757 individuals, 25% had elevated depressive symptoms (BDI ≥11) at baseline. During a median follow-up of 10 years, 24% of participants developed incident PAD. The rate of incident PAD was higher in those with elevated depressive symptoms (3.6 events per 100 person-years) compared with those without (2.2 events per 100 person-years). After accounting for other factors, baseline elevated depressive symptoms were associated with a higher risk of incident PAD (HR 1.23; 95% CI: 1.02-1.47). Smoking and physical inactivity mediated 20% and 10%, respectively, of this association. Similar associations were found between baseline elevated depressive symptoms and a composite of incident PAD or death. Findings were not different when elevated depressive symptoms were defined by BDI >14 and BDI ≥16.
LIMITATIONS: Residual bias and confounding. Absence of depression diagnosis.
CONCLUSIONS: Elevated depressive symptoms were associated with a significantly increased risk of incident PAD in adults with CKD, which is partly mediated by smoking and physical inactivity.
INDEX WORDS: Renal failure, depression, peripheral vascular disease, mortality, health behaviors.

title: Best Practices for Optimizing Recovery from Sepsis; Results of an Expert Panel.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Over one million patients survive sepsis annually in the USA. After sepsis, patients often experience new morbidity, with high rates of readmission and post-acute mortality. However, there are limited data to inform best practices to support recovery from sepsis.
METHODS: We convened an expert panel to rate the validity, importance, and resource intensity of 18 care practices aimed to support recovery from sepsis using the RAND/UCLA appropriateness method (a modified Delphi approach). The multidisciplinary panel consisted of 15 experts in sepsis, critical care, hospital medicine, primary care, geriatrics, nursing, and quality improvement, as well as Veteran patient representatives. In addition to the panel members' scores of care practices, panel deliberations were used to understand members' selections.
RESULTS: Among the 18 care practices considered, all received agreement in final grading, 10 (56%) were rated as valid, and eight (44%) were rated as uncertain validity. Among 10 valid practices, five were rated as high importance and only moderately resource-intensive-suggesting they should be prioritized for implementation. The high-importance, moderate resource-intensity practices were as follows: scheduling recommended follow-up prior to discharge; screening for limitations in basic and instrumental activities of daily living (I/ADLs) and need for durable medical equipment (DME); educating patients on signs and symptoms of sepsis; educating patients on common symptoms after sepsis (e.g., fatigue, shortness of breath, brain fog); and counseling patients and/or caregivers on discharge medications and their indications. Study limitations include the panel composition (majority VHA clinicians, no social work representation), which may have impacted ratings.
CONCLUSIONS: The expert panel used a validated method to prioritize care practices for supporting recovery from sepsis. These ratings can be used to improve management, inform quality improvement efforts, and guide resource allocation.
