title: Sex differences in delivery of guideline-recommended COPD care: A national U.S. cohort.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sex-based differences in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) outcomes are well documented, but sex disparities in the delivery of evidence-based, guideline-recommended care remain insufficiently understood. We aimed to compare the receipt of guideline-recommended COPD care between females and males in a national U.S.
METHODS: We performed a retrospective cohort study using national Veterans Health Administration data among individuals with ≥2 encounters with ICD-9 or ICD10 for COPD between 2012 and 2020. We compared receipt of guideline-recommended COPD care among females vs. males. Outcomes included diagnostic confirmation via spirometry, maintenance inhaler prescription and tobacco cessation interventions. Females and males were age-matched at a 1:4 ratio. We used multivariable logistic regression to assess the associations between odds of receiving guideline-recommended COPD care for females vs males, adjusting for age, race/ethnicity, Charlson Comorbidity Index, and Social Vulnerability Index.
RESULTS: Among 882,292 individuals with COPD, 34,645 (3.9%) were females. After 1:4 age matching, the final analytic cohort included 173,225 individuals (34,645 females and 138,580 males). In adjusted analyses, females had higher odds of receiving confirmatory spirometry (aOR 1.24 [95%CI: 1.21-1.27]) and tobacco cessation intervention (aOR 1.23 [95%CI: 1.20-1.27]) compared to males; females had lower odds of receiving maintenance inhaler prescriptions (aOR 0.86 [95%CI: 0.84-0.89).
CONCLUSION: Both female and male patients experience suboptimal receipt of guideline-recommended COPD care in this national cohort. However, females more frequently received spirometry and tobacco cessation but less maintenance inhaler therapy than males, underscoring the need for targeted strategies to address these gaps and ensure equitable, guideline-based care for all.

title: Three Cerebellar Imaging Subtypes in Schizophrenia with Distinct Spatiotemporal Trajectories and Biological Characteristics
abstract: The potential role of the cerebellum in the pathophysiology of schizophrenia has received relatively insufficient attention. Prior studies characterized cerebellar abnormalities mainly at the group level, without fully considering the heterogeneity of the disease. Here, we applied a machine learning approach (Subtype and Stage Inference, SuStaIn) to cross-sectional 3D volumetric MRIs of the cerebellum, including a total of 3,550 individuals with schizophrenia (1423 females; mean age: 32.3 +/- 12.0 years) and 5,771 healthy controls (HC) (2,861 females; mean age: 32.5 +/- 12.9 years), from 34 sites worldwide. SuStaIn identified three distinct spatiotemporal trajectories in cerebellar gray matter volume reduction, respectively originating in lobule X (subtype 1), lobule III (subtype 2) and lobule VIIb (subtype 3), with subtypes 1 and 3 corresponding to the posterior lobe and subtype 2 to the anterior lobe. These trajectories were cross-sectionally inferred in 1,588 individuals with schizophrenia and replicated in another independent samples of 1,334 and 628 patients, respectively. Multimodal analyses using neuroimaging, transcriptomic and behavioral data revealed subtype-specific biological characteristics in brain morphological patterns, cerebellar-cortical connectivity, gene expression and clinical symptoms. Specifically, subtype-related genes were enriched in metabolism-related processes and immunity-related processes, respectively, in subtype 1 and subtype 2; subtype 3 showed more severe brain abnormalities and worse cognitive symptoms. Treatment data from 381 patients, with up to 12 months of follow-up, revealed poorer response to antipsychotic medications in subtype 2 and subtype 3, but better response to transcranial magnetic stimulation in subtype 1, which also had worse emotion-related symptoms. Together, our findings offer a comprehensive characterization of the heterogeneity of cerebellar pathophysiological progresses in schizophrenia, which may help in developing future clinical stratification and targeted intervention strategies.

title: Pooling individual off-pump and on-pump coronary artery bypass patient records from three contemporary multicenter, randomized, controlled trials: an individual participant data meta-analysis protocol
abstract: Abstract Background For over three decades, the comparative effectiveness of off-pump versus on-pump coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) has been debated. Although randomized controlled trials (RCTs) generally report modest long-term advantages for on-pump CABG, potential off-pump benefits remain uncertain particularly among high-risk patients. To address this knowledge gap, this CABG individual participant data meta-analysis (CABG-IPD-MA) will analyze de-identified patient records from the only three multicenter RCTs reporting 5-year follow-up (ROOBY, GOPCABE, and CORONARY) and test five protocol-driven hypotheses. Methods Across short-term, intermediate, and longer-term periods, this PRISMA-IPD-compliant study will use a one-stage IPD meta-analysis framework to compare off-pump versus on-pump CABG for two co-primary endpoints [i.e., all-cause mortality and a composite metric comprised all-cause death, nonfatal acute myocardial infarction, and repeat revascularization (i.e., repeat CABG or percutaneous coronary intervention)] at 1 and 5 years; at 30 days/in-hospital, perioperative stroke will also be included in the composite. Secondary endpoints include individual sub-components of the composite endpoint and resource-utilization; resource-utilization analyses will be exploratory-only. Eligible studies included all post-2001 multicenter RCTs reporting off-pump versus on-pump post-CABG 5-year outcomes. Re-verified June 2025, the original 2019 PRISMA-IPD-guided systematic review identified only three eligible RCTs; prior publications reported these RCTs as having low Cochrane risk-of-bias. All three RCTs’ participants ( n = 9494) will be included. This CABG-IPD-MA study’s hierarchical hypotheses will evaluate: (1) overall unadjusted treatment effects; (2) overall risk-adjusted treatment effects; (3) prespecified high-risk subgroups’ risk-adjusted treatment effects; (4) the impact of complete revascularization; and (5) the concordance between this CABG-IPD-MA study’s findings with an aggregate-data meta-analysis findings. All primary CABG-IPD-MA analyses will utilize an intention-to-treat framework. Prespecified sensitivity analyses will evaluate findings under alternative treatment-conversion and high-risk restrictions. Discussion By pooling and harmonizing individual patient-level records from the only three contemporary multicenter RCTs reporting long-term follow-up, this study was designed to provide precise, clinically relevant assessments of off-pump versus on-pump benefits. These CABG-IPD-MA analyses will evaluate short-, intermediate-, and long-term outcomes exploring whether specific patient subgroups may derive any differential treatment benefits. Findings are expected to generate high-quality, clinically actionable evidence to support future patient-centered decision-making, clinical guideline refinements, and health policy decision-making.

title: Increasing the Availability of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation in the Veterans Health Administration: Implementation, Growth, and Lessons Learned
abstract: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is one of the most important developments in psychiatric treatments in the past few decades. There is now considerable evidence for the effectiveness of TMS for treatment-resistant depression. This population is particularly important for the Veterans Healthcare Administration (VHA). Having recognized the unique opportunity to improve the mental health of our nation's Veterans with this new treatment, the VHA has embarked on an ambitious, nationwide program for TMS. This program's aim is to provide training to VA clinicians by experts in TMS in order for them to deliver evidence-based TMS to as many Veterans as possible. By fostering the establishment of new clinics in VHA medical centers across the nation, growing from six programs to almost 70, this program leverages the unique scale of the VHA and establishes a platform from which to advance clinical implementation. The program provides standardized training for administering TMS and generates harmonized data for well-powered measurement-based evaluation of the clinical utility of TMS in a complex population. Providers who have completed the training program have reported high levels of satisfaction. The VA Palo Alto Health Care System was tasked with leading these efforts. We outline our experiences to date, inclusive of the context for the program as well as its structure and function. The paper focuses on how the program was implemented by describing training provided to VA clinicians as well as limitations and considerations for future programmatic efforts.

title: The Gut-Liver-Brain-Lung Axis in Alcohol Use Disorder: Mechanisms and Therapeutic Implications.
abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is a multi-organ disease associated with an increased risk of severe pneumonia and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). While alcohol-related lung disease has often been attributed to ethanol-mediated injury to the alveolar epithelium, new evidence suggests a more broad and integrated model in which pulmonary vulnerability arises as a consequence of dysregulation in the gut-liver-brain axis. This review proposes a framework to explain how chronic alcohol consumption induces dysregulation in the gut-liver-brain axis and subsequently primes the lung for failure when a secondary hit, such as sepsis or infection, occur. Drawing on human observations and mechanistic studies in experimental preclinical models, we outline four candidate pathways that may link alcohol-related gut, hepatic, and neuroimmune changes to pulmonary vulnerability: 1) alcohol induces gut barrier disruption and dysbiosis, leading to the escape of lipopolysaccharides (LPS) into circulation; 2) the liver transitions to an amplifier of inflammation, releasing inflammatory signals into systemic circulation; 3) simultaneously, neuroimmune circuits such as the vagal cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway and the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis are disrupted by chronic alcohol exposure, resulting in delays in resolving inflammatory responses; and 4) the lungs receive these inputs on a background of glutathione depletion and innate immune dysfunction, resulting in an environment that may appear normal at baseline but is primed to fail. Recognizing alcohol-related lung disease as a potential consequence of altered gut-liver-brain signaling in the context of chronic alcohol use could provide a foundation for developing targeted therapeutic strategies for ARDS in individuals with AUD.

title: Ontogenically distinct macrophages occupy discrete kidney niches and contribute to monocyte recruitment in experimental crescentic glomerulonephritis.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Crescentic glomerulonephritis (cGN) is characterized by aggressive immune-mediated glomerular injury with prominent macrophage accumulation that correlates with disease severity. However, the distinct contributions of kidney-resident macrophages (KRMs) of different ontogenies remain poorly defined.
METHODS: To explore this, we used single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), reporter-based bone marrow chimeras, timed clodronate liposome treatment, and chemokine blockade to define the spatiotemporal dynamics and functional roles of macrophage populations in nephrotoxic serum nephritis (NTSN), a model of cGN.
RESULTS: ScRNA-seq of total kidney and CD45+ immune cells revealed that proliferating macrophages and infiltrating monocytes expanded sharply by day five and declined by day ten, indicating that local proliferation, in addition to monocyte recruitment, contributes substantially to early macrophage accumulation in NTSN. Two major KRM subpopulations were distinguished by high Ccr2 or Mrc1 expression, consistent with bone marrow and embryonically seeded, self-renewing KRM population, respectively. In Cx3cr1-GFP recipient mice reconstituted with Ccr2-RFP+ donor bone marrow, embryonic-derived GFP+ KRMs were enriched in the outer medulla and corticomedullary region, whereas donor-derived RFP+ monocytes/macrophages preferentially accumulated in the cortex, including within and around the inflamed glomeruli. A timed clodronate liposome regimen that preferentially reduced recipient-retained GFP+ KRMs decreased the cortical accumulation of RFP+ cells, albuminuria, and histologic kidney injury in NTSN mice. Cell-cell communication analysis identified macrophage-associated CCL12 expression, a murine ortholog of human CCL2, as a candidate mediator of cortical CCR2+ monocyte recruitment. CCL12 neutralization reduced cortical monocyte accumulation and ameliorated kidney damage in NTSN mice.
CONCLUSION: These findings indicate that ontogenically distinct and spatially segregated macrophage populations cooperate during early cGN and support further investigation of the CCR2 axis as a therapeutic target for macrophage-mediated kidney injury in cGN.

title: Rac1 restrains actomyosin to enable ciliogenesis and mechanosensing in the postnatal kidney.
abstract: Multicystic dysplastic kidney (MCDK) is a severe congenital malformation of unknown cause that is fatal when it affects both kidneys. Rare familial variants associated with congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract (CAKUT) that alter Rho GTPase signaling were recently identified in children with MCDK. Here, we show that mice lacking the Rho GTPase Rac1 in the developing nephron die within weeks of birth from MCDK. This phenotype occurs because Rac1 supports postnatal proximal tubule maturation by coordinating actomyosin regulation, primary cilia formation, and fluid shear stress sensing. Rac1 controls ciliogenesis by restricting GEF-H1-dependent actomyosin contractility, and this pathway promotes apical clearing of the actin cytoskeleton to facilitate ciliogenesis. Pharmacological myosin inhibition restores ciliogenesis and flow-induced differentiation in cells and attenuates cystic-dysplastic remodeling in Rac1 mutant mice. We conclude that Rac1 links postnatal mechanical signals from urine flow to cellular differentiation in the growing kidney, a pathway amenable to therapeutic cytoskeletal targeting.

title: Scaling a multimodal mind-body movement intervention for Veterans with dementia in VA nursing homes: A formative evaluation of the Preventing Loss of Independence through Exercise (PLIÉ) program.
abstract: BackgroundPeople living with Alzheimer's disease and related dementias constitute a substantial proportion of residents in U.S. Veterans Health Administration nursing homes (Community Living Centers, CLCs). Non-pharmacologic interventions have demonstrated positive effects for people living with dementia (PLWD) but face implementation barriers in nursing homes. The Preventing Loss of Independence through Exercise (PLIÉ) program is an evidence-based multimodal mind-body movement program that supports quality of life and function for PLWD.ObjectiveTo identify potential facilitators and barriers that may impact implementation of PLIÉ in CLCs (PLIÉ-CLC) and inform the development of a remote staff training program.MethodsWe conducted a developmental formative evaluation using qualitative methods, guided by the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR). Semi-structured interviews with 30 CLC staff, directors, and VA health system leaders, explored perspectives on implementing PLIÉ-CLC. Data were analyzed using a template analysis approach.ResultsKey facilitators included PLIÉ's evidence base, adaptability, and alignment with person-centered care. Barriers included staffing constraints, workload demands, and limited accessible space. Participants emphasized the need for both synchronous and asynchronous training components to fit staff schedules and enhance feasibility.ConclusionsThis study highlighted the importance of adaptability and evidence-based support in implementing PLIÉ in VA nursing homes. The findings suggest that a flexible, remote training program incorporating both didactic and experiential learning may facilitate the scalability of PLIÉ. Understanding barriers and facilitators can inform strategies to improve the implementation of non-pharmacologic interventions for residents with dementia, ultimately enhancing care quality and outcomes in nursing homes.

title: Observing Skepticism Toward a Breast Cancer Screening Decision Aid Over Time
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Prior research reported that some women are skeptical toward messages about mammography screening evidence, particularly information about overdiagnosis and false positives. The proposed cause of skepticism is that the evidence is surprising and different from other screening messages, a finding which suggests that skepticism might decline as the information becomes more familiar. The present research tested the hypothesis that skepticism declines over time with repeated exposure, and sought to replicate prior evidence for the antecedents of observed skepticism. METHODS: This longitudinal study recruited women ages 39-49 from two health systems. Women received a decision aid (DA) communicating mammography screening evidence prior to an annual well visit. Skepticism toward the DA information was measured immediately after the DA, after the clinic visit, and 3 months later. Hypothesis-relevant predictors of skepticism were assessed. RESULTS: Skepticism was greater toward information about overdiagnosis and false positives compared to benefits, and skepticism was greater among participants who felt the evidence conflicted with past screening messages. We also observed that higher breast cancer anxiety was associated skepticism toward screening harms. Moreover, contrary to predictions, two facets of skepticism-reactance and disbelief-increased over time. Exploratory post hoc analyses suggested that increases in skepticism were associated with participants' perceptions that the DA conflicted with their doctors' screening message. CONCLUSIONS: Some people express skepticism toward mammography evidence, and these feelings are associated with perceived conflicting messages and cancer anxiety. Skepticism may not decline over time if messages from other sources conflict with the DA information. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov registration NCT05838417.

title: No objective evidence of neuropsychological deficits in people with subjective cognitive changes following COVID-19 infection.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Persistent cognitive complaints following COVID-19 infection are common, but whether these complaints reflect measurable cognitive impairment, depressive and anxiety symptoms, or other biological factors is unclear.
METHODS: We compared adults who reported worsening of memory or concentration following COVID-19 (Cases, n = 32) to those who did not (Controls, n = 34), for more than 12 weeks post-infection. Both groups had blood-based APOE-ε4 genotyping and inflammatory marker quantification (sCD14) and completed self-reported measures of mood symptoms using the Beck Depression and Anxiety Inventories (BDI and BAI, respectively). Most participants (Cases, n = 29; Controls, n = 33) underwent neuropsychological testing (MCCB, CVLT-III), from which we derived one objective factor of Cognition using Principal Components Analysis.
RESULTS: Cases and Controls did not significantly differ on univariate tests of Cognition (p = .32) but did diverge on BDI and BAI (p < .001), inflammation (p = .02), and dementia risk (p < .001). Objective cognition, psychiatric symptoms, and blood-based markers were entered sequentially in two logistic regression analyses, one for BDI and one for BAI. Only BDI and BAI remained significant independent predictors of Group. While APOE-ε4 and sCD14 significantly improved model fit, only APOE-ε4 was significant in the multivariate model.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that while biological markers distinguish individuals with post-COVID cognitive complaints from those without, BDI and BAI each account for shared variance across these markers and emerges as the only independent correlates of subjective cognitive complaints and are reasonable treatment targets.

title: Movement Pattern Biofeedback Training Improves Short- and Long-Term Limb Loading Mechanics During Step Descent After Total Knee Arthroplasty: Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Controlled Trial
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the effects of a 10-week movement pattern biofeedback training intervention (MOVE) on limb-loading mechanics during step descent following primary unilateral TKA, compared to a control group. DESIGN: Exploratory secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial. METHODS: One hundred thirty-eight participants were assessed preoperatively, 10 weeks, 6 months, and 2 years after TKA. Three-dimensional motion data were collected during performance of a step-down task. Repeated measures analyses of covariance were used to determine between-group differences in lead limb loading rate and trailing limb peak knee extension moment of both the surgical and non-surgical limbs, controlling for baseline function and sex. Multivariate linear regression models were developed to explore factors associated with loading rate of the leading, non-surgical limb at each follow-up timepoint, controlling for sex and intervention group. RESULTS: The MOVE group displayed smaller surgical and non-surgical limb loading rate 10-weeks and 6-months post-TKA respectively, compared to control (p<.05). No between-group differences in peak knee extension moment were observed at any timepoint. Greater 10-week non-surgical limb loading rate was associated with greater preoperative non-surgical limb loading rate and lower surgical trailing limb peak knee extension moment (p<.05). Greater 6-month non-surgical limb loading rate was associated with greater preoperative non-surgical limb loading rate (p<.05). Greater 2-year non-surgical limb loading rate was associated with greater preoperative non-surgical limb loading rate and lower surgical trailing limb peak knee extension moment (p<.05). CONCLUSION: A novel movement pattern biofeedback training intervention reduced contralateral limb loading rates during step descent after TKA. Variability in loading mechanics at long-term follow up was consistently explained by preoperative movement patterns.

title: Analysis of N-Glycans Released from Glycosylated RNAs.
abstract: Glycosylated RNAs (glycoRNAs) are involved in immune response, cellular function, gene regulation, and disease development. We report a liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) method to analyze glycans released from glycoRNAs. The developed method includes extracting RNA from mouse liver using TRIzol, digesting proteins with proteinase K under denaturing conditions, re-extracting RNA using TRIzol, releasing N-glycans by enzymatic digestion, enriching glycans by solid-phase extraction, and analyzing glycans by LC-MS. The method was optimized to detect low-abundance N-glycans from a purchased mixture of N-glycan standards, and 65 glycans were identified. We then applied the method to analyze the glycans released from the glycoRNAs in mouse liver and identified 244 N-glycans from triplicate analyses. We also detected 40 significantly changed N-glycans in the livers of 32-week-old female and male KvB2 mice. This study establishes a simple and efficient technique for characterizing N-glycans in glycoRNAs and paves the way for future studies to understand the function of glycoRNAs.

title: Mixed pain phenotypes in musculoskeletal disorders: mechanisms and management.
abstract: Pain is categorized into three pain phenotypes: nociceptive, neuropathic and nociplastic, with overlapping pain referring to the coexistence of more than one pain phenotype. Overlapping pain occurs in more than one-third of individuals with musculoskeletal conditions, including inflammatory arthritis, osteoarthritis, spinal disorders and soft-tissue conditions. Whereas nociceptive pain is associated with identifiable tissue pathology and often responds to anatomically focused treatments, the presence of an additional pain phenotype, most commonly nociplastic pain, contributes to clinical complexity, poorer responses to conventional analgesics and procedures, and a greater burden of disease. Clinical identification of overlapping pain relies primarily on history-taking and physical examination, as no validated biomarker or widely accessible diagnostic test is currently available. Quantitative sensory testing and patient-reported questionnaires provide evidence of musculoskeletal overlapping pain but remain underutilized in routine practice. Once the underlying condition has been optimally managed, treatment should adopt a biopsychosocial approach that addresses comorbidities such as psychological distress, promotes self-efficacy and healthy lifestyle behaviours, and incorporates cautious use of pharmacological therapies. Effective clinical care requires recognition of overlapping pain as an important contributor to chronic musculoskeletal pain, with implications for treatment selection, including surgical and interventional decision-making, and for optimizing risk-benefit and cost-effectiveness outcomes.

title: Randomized Trial Comparing Minocycline-EDTA-Ethanol Lock to Standard-of-Care Antibiotic Lock for Management of Central Line–Associated Bloodstream Infection
abstract: BACKGROUND: Central line-associated bloodstream infections (CLABSI) cause substantial morbidity and mortality. Management often requires removing the infected central venous catheter (CVC) and inserting a new one. Effective catheter-salvage strategies are needed. METHODS: An international, multicenter, prospective, randomized superiority trial at 34 centers in the United States, Puerto Rico, and India enrolled patients aged ≥12 years with a long-term central venous catheter (CVC) in place for ≥5 days and CLABSI. Participants were randomized 1:1 to receive systemic antibiotics plus minocycline-EDTA-ethanol lock therapy (MLT) or standard-of-care antibiotic lock therapy (SOC-ALT) for 7 to 14 days. The primary endpoint was median time to catheter failure, defined as clinical failure (death, infection-related catheter removal, worsening symptoms) or microbial failure (persistent/recurrent infection or new deep-seated infection attributable to the index CLABSI). RESULTS: From 2018-2024, 241 patients were randomized; 228 received lock therapy. Catheter retention was higher with MLT than SOC-ALT (57% vs 38%; P = 0.0025). Median time to catheter failure was longer with MLT in both intention-to-treat (not estimable vs 33 days, HR 0.53, P = 0.0006) and modified intention-to-treat populations (not estimable vs 35 days, HR 0.50, P = 0.0005). Clinical catheter failure (13% vs 28%; P = 0.006) and microbiological failure (5% vs 15%; P = 0.012) were lower with MLT. Adverse events, serious adverse events, and mortality were similar between groups, with no drug-related serious adverse events. CONCLUSIONS: MLT was superior to SOC-ALT in salvaging long-term CVCs in CLABSI and was well tolerated, addressing an unmet need in CLABSI management.

title: Pathophysiology of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy: a devasting convergence of dysfunction in brain, respiratory systems, and heart
abstract: Sudden Unexpected Death in Epilepsy, or SUDEP, is the leading cause of death in persons with epilepsy. Although extensively studied, the events that result in SUDEP remain poorly understood, with no reliable biomarkers to predict SUDEP risk in an individual. This review synthesizes the literature across many domains, discussing clinical and preclinical studies in brain, cardio-respiratory centers in the brainstem, and intrinsic alterations in cardiac excitability leading to arrhythmia, to provide a comprehensive picture of our current understanding of SUDEP mechanisms. What we do know is that SUDEP involves complex, multi-system dysfunction in persons with epilepsy at baseline, during seizures, and in post-ictal periods. This situation is further complicated by cases of SUDEP Plus, in which pre-existing conditions in addition to epilepsy, e.g. Brugada syndrome or Long-QT syndrome, may contribute to death during a seizure. Finally, it is likely that multiple etiologies lead to SUDEP outcomes. Here, we highlight gaps in the field requiring additional research.

title: Cranial Electrotherapy Stimulation for Fibromyalgia in Veterans: A Randomized Sham-Controlled Feasibility Study of Resting-State Functional Connectivity Magnetic Resonance Imaging to Evaluate Pain and Treatment Response.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Fibromyalgia is a chronic pain disorder frequently co-occurring with depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and insomnia, particularly in veterans, and safer nonpharmacological therapies are needed. Cranial electrotherapy stimulation, also referred to as cranial electrotherapy stimulation (CES), may help with anxiety and sleep, but its effect on pain is unclear. This feasibility study evaluated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to identify neural correlates of pain and treatment response for CES effects on fibromyalgia pain in veterans.
METHODS: In a randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial at a single US government hospital, veterans aged 20 to 60 with fibromyalgia were assigned to active or sham in-home CES, stratified by sex. Participants self-administered CES for 60 minutes daily over 12 weeks. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) was acquired at baseline, 6 weeks, and 12 weeks with clinical outcomes, including the Defense and Veterans Pain Rating Scale (DVPRS), National Institutes of Health (NIH) Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) measures, and tests of physical function.
RESULTS: Forty-eight participants were randomized (25 active, 23 sham) and 47 were analyzed. Both groups showed significant improvements in DVPRS pain (-1.88 ± 2.2) and pain interference with sleep (-2.25 ± 2.8), mood (-1.88 ± 2.6), activity (-1.83 ± 2.4) and stress (-1.77 ± 3.0) at 12 weeks versus baseline (P < .01), with significant between-group differences only in sleep (P = .04). Neuroimaging revealed significant increases in connectivity between the cerebellar 7b seed and the left occipital fusiform gyrus (0.079 ± 0.1) left lingual gyrus (0.063 ± 0.08), and right lingual gyrus (0.058 ± 0.08) for the CES group and decreases in the sham group (-0.088 ± 0.1; -0.121 ± 0.08; and -0.135 ± 0.1), respectively. No adverse events occurred.
CONCLUSIONS: Both groups improved similarly in pain and function, though new analgesic usage was more prevalent in the sham group. Neuroimaging revealed differential changes in cerebellar-sensory-visual networks and baseline patterns distinguishing responders from nonresponders, supporting feasibility and design of larger, adequately powered CES trials in fibromyalgia.

title: Pharmacologic Treatments for Females With Menopausal Vasomotor Symptoms: A Clinical Guideline From the American College of Physicians
abstract: Description:The American College of Physicians (ACP) developed this clinical guideline on pharmacologic treatments for internal medicine physicians and other clinicians caring in outpatient settings for females with menopausal vasomotor symptoms. Methods:The ACP Clinical Guidelines Committee developed this guideline based on systematic reviews on effectiveness, comparative effectiveness, harms, public and patient values and preferences, and economic evidence of pharmacologic treatments for females with menopausal vasomotor symptoms using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation) approach. ACP recommends that clinicians initiate one of the following (strong recommendation): estrogen in combination with progestogen in females with a uterus (high-certainty evidence) or estrogen monotherapy in females without a uterus (high-certainty evidence). ACP suggests that clinicians use one of the following in females who have contraindications to or do not tolerate first-line treatment (conditional recommendation): serotonin–norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, either desvenlafaxine or venlafaxine (moderate-certainty evidence). ACP suggests that clinicians use one of the following in females who have contraindications to or do not tolerate first-line or second-line treatment (conditional recommendation): selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, either escitalopram or paroxetine (low-certainty evidence); the gabapentinoid gabapentin (low-certainty evidence); or neurokinin receptor antagonists, either elinzanetant or fezolinetant (moderate-certainty evidence). When selecting a treatment of vasomotor symptoms, clinicians should use an informed decision-making approach and discuss benefits, harms, contraindications, comorbid conditions, values and preferences, financial burden, and access to and availability of treatments.

title: Treat-to-Target in Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Promise, Perils, and the Path Forward.
abstract: Treat-to-target has become the organizing framework for contemporary inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) management, yet its evidence base is less robust than its widespread endorsement might suggest. The approach rests on 2 equally essential pillars: defining the right therapeutic target and adjusting treatment iteratively until that target is achieved. Over the past decade, the first pillar has advanced substantially: targets have deepened from symptomatic remission through endoscopic and histologic healing toward transmural and emerging molecular end points, supported largely by association data linking deeper remission to better long-term outcomes. The second pillar has received considerably less scrutiny. Completed randomized trials of iterative treatment adjustment have yielded mixed results in unselected populations, real-world monitoring remains inconsistent, and the most clinically pressing question, whether asymptomatic patients with residual inflammation benefit from optimizing or switching advanced therapies, remains unanswered. In this review, we critically examine both pillars: the evolution and evidence base for treatment targets in IBD, the ability of current therapies to achieve them, the lessons from pivotal treat-to-target trials, and the barriers to real-world implementation. We propose a framework for individualizing treat-to-target decisions based on disease history, inflammatory trajectory, therapeutic options, and patient preferences. Ongoing trials including QUOTIENT, VERDICT, and VECTORS may define whether the second pillar can be placed on as firm a footing as the first.

title: Comprehensive genetic screening of the South African Parkinson's disease study collection using the NeuroBooster array.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Although there have been significant advances in the genetic etiology of Parkinson's disease (PD), most of this research has been conducted in European populations. This study aimed to characterize the genetic landscape of PD in South Africa, whose populations are renowned for their extensive genetic diversity and admixture.
METHODS: We recruited 689 PD probands across South Africa. These participants were genotyped using the NeuroBooster array in collaboration with the Global Parkinson's Genetics Program (GP2). An in-house computational workflow was used to identify pathogenic missense variants, which were validated using Sanger sequencing. The CNV-Finder pipeline was used to screen for copy number variations (CNVs), which were validated using Multiplex Ligation-dependent Probe Amplification (MLPA). Previously identified pathogenic variants were used as positive controls in our analysis.
RESULTS: We identified 16 unique missense variants in 47 individuals, 15 of which were independently confirmed by Sanger sequencing. However, these variants are not considered likely to be associated with PD status. We also identified new homozygous PRKN CNVs in three individuals and a whole-gene SNCA duplication in one individual, all of which were validated by MLPA. In addition, one individual had a CNV in the 5' untranslated region of SNCA, although its pathogenicity remains unclear. When these findings were combined with our previous results, 3.5% of probands (24 individuals) were found to have a genetic basis for their disease.
CONCLUSIONS: We conducted the largest pathogenic variant screening to date in this unique and underrepresented population, and our findings highlight the rare contribution of known pathogenic variants. This study underscores the importance of expanding genetic research in African cohorts to improve global understanding of PD etiology.

title: Sex-specific brain reserve and progression from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease dementia.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Sex differences exist in Alzheimer's disease (AD) treatment response, but the role of sex in disease development and progression remains unclear.
METHODS: We performed multimodal analyses of AD biomarker-positive individuals with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and AD from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI; MCI n = 593, AD n = 270) and National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center (MCI n = 436, AD n = 174). Baseline gray matter volume (GMV) was compared by sex. In ADNI, tau positron emission tomography burden and cerebrospinal fluid growth-associated protein 43 (GAP-43) were assessed. Longitudinal analyses examined atrophy and conversion from MCI to dementia.
RESULTS: Females with MCI exhibited greater baseline GMV than males primarily in the thalamus, caudate, cerebellum, postcentral gyrus, and middle cingulate gyrus, with no differences at the AD stage. Despite this, females exhibited higher baseline GAP-43, greater tau burden in temporal and parietal regions, and more rapid annual hippocampal atrophy. Conversion rates were similar.
DISCUSSION: Findings suggest that females may tolerate greater pathology at early stages but experience faster neurodegeneration later, supporting sex-specific disease trajectories and highlighting the need for sex-informed biomarkers.

title: Changes in age composition and epidemiology of candidaemia, Iceland, 2012 to 2023.
abstract: BACKGROUNDCandidaemia places a substantial burden on healthcare systems. Long-term, population-based studies of candidaemia rates with appropriate adjustments for changes in age composition are lacking.AIMWe aimed to determine trends in candidaemia incidence rates, species distribution, antifungal susceptibility, and concurrent antifungal use in Iceland between 2012 and 2023, as well as long-term (2000-2023) trends in age-standardised incidence rates (ASRs).METHODSWe analysed patient data with blood cultures positive for Candida species, or yeasts previously assigned to the genus Candida. We calculated ASRs, standardised to the 2023 Icelandic population, and performed susceptibility testing on all available isolates.RESULTSOverall, we identified 207 candidaemia episodes in 193 patients. The average ASR was 5.2 cases per 100,000 population. The ASR increased significantly from 2012 to 2023 (incidence rate ratio (IRR) = 1.07; p = 0.001), mainly driven by increased rates among males (IRR = 1.10; p = 0.001). From 2000 to 2023, the ASR remained stable (average 5.8/100,000; IRR = 1.00). The ASR was higher among males, both during 2012-2023 (p = 0.014) and long-term (2000-2023, p = 0.001). Age-specific incidence rate was highest among > 80-year-old males (44.0/100,000). Candida albicans was the most frequent species (41.0%), followed by Nakaseomyces glabratus (27.2%) and Candida tropicalis (11.1%). Fluconazole susceptibility remained high (C. albicans 99%, C. tropicalis 75%, Candida parapsilosis 100%), and echinocandin resistance was rare (1.9%).CONCLUSIONDespite an apparent increase from 2012 to 2023, candidaemia incidence in Iceland has remained stable in a long-term (24-year) perspective, when appropriate adjustments are made for the ageing population. Concurrently, the epidemiology has shifted towards non-albicans Candida infections.

title: Indirect effects of PTSD, depression, and anxiety symptoms on the association between COVID-19 cases/symptoms and intimate partner violence perpetration in the United States.
abstract: Although rates of intimate partner violence (IPV) tend to rise following natural disasters, partly via trauma-related symptoms, the trauma-specific mechanisms underlying IPV perpetration during epidemics and pandemics such as COVID-19 remain unclear. Therefore, the aim of this study was to examine the association between COVID-19 (its incidence or symptoms) and IPV and the contribution of trauma-related symptoms to such association during the first wave of the pandemic (March-April 2020). This study applied generalized linear modeling and structural equation modeling to analyze data from a demographically diverse U.S. online panel survey (N = 1,183). The variables included self-reported data of IPV perpetration, posttraumatic stress disorder, depression, anxiety, and COVID-19 symptoms ("likely COVID-19"). Additionally, we examined COVID-19 state-level data for tested and confirmed cases as reported by the Johns Hopkins University Center during March 2020 ("tested COVID-19"). Groups in states with higher incidence of COVID-19 had significantly higher rates of IPV perpetration than groups in states with lower incidence of COVID-19. Furthermore, the findings indicated that posttraumatic stress disorder and depression symptoms were indirectly associated with likely COVID-19 symptoms and psychological and physical IPV perpetration. These results suggested a connection between COVID-19 and IPV perpetration and indicated how trauma-related symptoms affected this association. The results underscore that trauma-related symptoms during public health crises such as pandemics are a risk factor for IPV perpetration. Trauma-informed screening and intervention can be useful in identifying and reducing IPV during the early stages of such crises. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

title: Phase I Trial of Liquid Nitrogen Spray Cryotherapy concurrent with neoadjuvant chemoradiation for Locally Advanced Esophageal Cancer: Dose Escalation and Long-Term Overall Survival.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Spray cryotherapy (LNSC) is hypothesized to increase effectiveness of neoadjuvant chemoradiation (CRT). We aimed to determine safety of multiple cryotherapy sessions prior to and concurrent with CRT in locally advanced esophageal cancer.
METHODS: "3+3" phase 1 dose frequency escalation trial. Primary outcome was safety; secondary outcomes were Quality of Life (QoL) complete clinical response (cCR), survival, and immunogenic cell death (change in serum HMGB1).
RESULTS: There was no treatment related grade 2 or 3 adverse events when LNSC was administered before or concurrent with CRT (n =13). Maximum Tolerated Dose was 3 sessions (2 prior to CRT, 1 during CRT). Mean QoL score improved from 37 at baseline to 31, 29, and 34 after the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd sessions (p-value 0.002, 0.004, and 0.4 respectively). CR with LNSC + CRT occurred in 70%. Over median follow-up of 36 months, overall survival was 40%. 38% showed >25% decrease in HMGB1 within 30 days.
DISCUSSION: No patient experienced dose limiting toxicity. LNSC was safely administered during CRT, improved QoL and high cCR rates were observed. These results support proceeding with a phase 2 trial.

title: Virtual screening and molecular dynamics identify sulfonamide indole analogs as candidate CBP bromodomain binders
abstract: Bromodomain-mediated recognition of acetylated lysine couples histone acetylation to oncogenic transcription, and the CREB-binding protein (CBP) bromodomain has become a target of interest in prostate cancer and acute myeloid leukaemia. Inhibitors such as CCS1477 have reached clinical trials, but selectivity over the BET family remains difficult to achieve, in part because several reported chemotypes engage both families. Here we take the CBP bromodomain co-crystal structure with the sulfonamide-indole ligand YF2-23 (PDB 7JUO) as a starting point and ask whether substitution on this scaffold can be biased toward CBP. A two-dimensional structural similarity search of the PubChem Compound database returned 392 analogs, which were docked against the acetyl-lysine recognition site. Three compounds, CID135236185, CID66966190 and CID135236309, were the only members of the set to score at or below − 10.0 kcal/mol and were carried forward to duplicate 1 µs all-atom molecular dynamics simulations. CID135236309 formed the most stable complex, with the lowest backbone RMSD (0.233 nm) and RMSF (0.140 nm) and hydrogen bond occupancy comparable to the reference, whereas CID66966190, which lacks a sulfonamide N-H donor, maintained no persistent hydrogen bond to the protein across either replicate. MM-GBSA rescoring over the final 10 ns of each replicate ranked all three analogs below YF2-23, at -34.98, -32.97 and − 25.60 kcal/mol against − 37.26 kcal/mol. Because the configurational entropy term is omitted these values are comparative rankings rather than affinity predictions, and no compound is proposed as more potent than the reference. The study is computational and its predictions are untested experimentally; all structures, poses and simulation inputs are deposited to enable experimental follow-up.

title: Estrogen-related receptor gamma coordinates glutamine dependence and mitochondrial metabolic flexibility in retinoblastoma
abstract: Cancer cells undergo extensive metabolic reprogramming and can become dependent on glutamine to replenish the tricarboxylic acid cycle when glucose-derived carbon is diverted to lactate production, yet the transcriptional programs coordinating this response remain incompletely defined. We previously identified estrogen-related receptor gamma (ESRRG) as a driver of hypoxic adaptation in retinoblastoma (Rb), and here we show that ESRRG also regulates glutamine-responsive metabolism. ESRRG knockdown reduced transcriptional programs associated with glycolysis and glutamine utilization, while pharmacological inhibition with GSK5182 attenuated glutamine-dependent viability and survival. Conversely, ESRRG overexpression increased sensitivity to glutamine withdrawal in mesenchymal stem cells. Functionally, glutamine enhanced basal and maximal respiration, spare respiratory capacity, and ATP-linked respiration in Rb cells, whereas these responses were attenuated by GSK5182. Targeted LC-MS/MS profiling further showed reduced glutamine-responsive accumulation of intracellular glutamine, glutamate, α-ketoglutarate, and downstream TCA-associated metabolites following ESRRG inhibition. These findings identify ESRRG as a regulator of glutamine dependence and mitochondrial metabolic flexibility in Rb and nominates ESRRG-associated glutamine dependence as a potential metabolic vulnerability.

title: Low use of guideline-recommended treatment among Medicare Advantage and traditional Medicare beneficiaries with advanced lung cancer.
abstract: Medicare Advantage (MA) plans have grown in popularity and currently cover over half of all beneficiaries [1]. Although MA plans offer supplemental benefits and out-of-pocket maximums [2], they also employ numerous strategies to control health care spending. Specifically, MA plans often restrict care to in-network providers and require utilization management (e.g., prior authorization, step therapy) for nearly all self- and clinician-administered anticancer therapies [1]. Evidence suggests that MA enrollment is associated with a low likelihood of starting any or high-cost systemic therapies among beneficiaries with advanced lung cancer [1,3], raising concerns that cost-containment strategies could limit access to guideline-recommended care.

title: STING signaling opposes AXL to regulate interferon responses in dedifferentiated human melanoma
abstract: Introduction Cancer cells can evade interferon (IFN) signaling pressures by suppressing intrinsic innate immune signaling pathways or dedifferentiating, giving rise to immunotherapy-resistant cell states. Therapeutic strategies specifically tailored to account for and eliminate such states remain limited. Methods Here, we genetically reintroduced stimulator of interferon genes (STING) in dedifferentiated STING-deficient melanoma cells, used AXL receptor tyrosine kinase (AXL) small-molecule inhibition, and analyzed publicly available single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) datasets to examine connections between dedifferentiation and interferon responses in human melanoma. Results We found that STING reintroduction induced type I IFN signaling, increased expression of antigen-presentation genes, and enhanced sensitivity to exogenous type II IFN. STING signaling silenced expression of AXL, a key marker of melanoma dedifferentiation. AXL small-molecule inhibition partially phenocopied STING reintroduction, potentiating antigen-presentation gene expression and enhancing type II IFN sensitivity in dedifferentiated human melanoma cells. Consistently, analysis of publicly available human melanoma scRNA-Seq data revealed tumor cells with concomitant STING loss and AXL gain are positively enriched for melanocyte stem-cell-like signatures, while negatively enriched for interferon and immune activation signatures. Discussion Together, through manipulation of human melanoma cell lines and analysis of single-cell states, our results support opposing roles for STING and AXL in the regulation of antigen-presenting genes and interferon sensitivity and more broadly implicate changes to interferon sensitivity in the dedifferentiation process.

title: Expert Recommendations for Use of Combined Oral Contraceptives in Preadolescent and Young Adolescent Patients With Acne Vulgaris.
abstract: Acne vulgaris commonly presents in early adolescence with the onset of adrenarche. Treatments for acne in this age group typically mirror those in older adolescents. However, while combined oral contraceptives are an effective hormonal treatment for acne vulgaris in young women, the safety of using a systemic hormonal therapy in younger patients for the management of acne has not been established. Concerns include effects on pubertal development and weight, bone health, cancer risks, and psychiatric effects. This Pediatric Dermatology Research Alliance (PeDRA) consensus project convened a multidisciplinary work group to address these issues and, utilizing a modified Delphi process, to establish best practices regarding the use of combined oral contraceptives in patients under 16 years of age based on available evidence and expert opinion.

title: The Patient Experience Across the Care Continuum: Inpatient Rehabilitation, Discharge Preparedness, and Community Reintegration after Spinal Cord Injuries/Disorders
abstract: The objective was to describe patient experiences, barriers, and facilitators of inpatient rehabilitation, discharge preparedness, and community reintegration after spinal cord injury and disorders (SCI/D) from the perspectives of Veterans with SCI/D. Methods included a descriptive qualitative design using a virtual focus group analyzed via reflexive thematic analysis. Focus group participants (n = 7) were mostly male, white, injured for 1-10 years, with mean age of 52 years. Two domains were identified. The first domain, Barriers and ways rehabilitation could have improved patient experience, included five themes: (1) insufficient preparation for psychological impacts; (2) inadequate preparation for relationship changes; (3) lack of focus on public outings and `real-world' functioning; (4) rehabilitation service delivery gaps, e.g., unsuitable length of stay and not enough therapy; and (5) lack of a caregiving plan before discharge. The second domain, Facilitators and complements to rehabilitation and discharge transition to community living, identified five themes: (1) specialty care by a cohesive multidisciplinary team; (2) suitable length of stay and helpful therapies; (3) preparedness for discharge; (4) care partner readiness efforts; and (5) involvement of peer/advocacy groups. Our findings can be used to optimize patient rehabilitation approaches during the early period after SCI/D to capitalize on factors that facilitate patient experiences during the rehabilitation periods as well as successful community reintegration. Recommendations include having a specialty care focus, care partner readiness, and peer and advocacy group engagement while addressing patient-identified barriers, e.g., lack of attention to emotional recovery, limited preparation for relationship changes, and limited real-world practice.

title: Nutrition and Frailty in the Older Adult: A Case-Based Approach to Assessment, Diagnosis, Intervention, Monitoring, and Evaluation in Preoperative Care
abstract: Background/Objectives: Frailty is a multidimensional syndrome characterized by reduced physiologic reserve and increased vulnerability to adverse outcomes, including postoperative complications, functional decline, and mortality. Malnutrition frequently coexists with frailty and contributes to muscle loss, impaired function, and decreased resilience. This narrative review explores the relationship between frailty and malnutrition and highlights practical approaches to assessment and management in older adults undergoing surgery. Methods: A narrative review of the current literature on frailty, malnutrition, comprehensive geriatric assessment, and prehabilitation was conducted. A fictional case study of Mrs. Jones, a 71-year-old woman undergoing evaluation for colon cancer surgery, was used to illustrate evidence-based assessment and management strategies. Results: Frailty and malnutrition interact in a reciprocal cycle that increases surgical risk and worsens health outcomes. Early screening can identify modifiable deficits, including weight loss, inadequate nutritional intake, impaired physical performance, functional limitations, and social barriers. Comprehensive geriatric assessment facilitates evaluation of medical, nutritional, functional, cognitive, and psychosocial factors. Evidence supports multimodal prehabilitation that combines individualized nutrition interventions, adequate protein and energy intake, exercise, medication optimization, oral-health management, and social support to improve surgical readiness and recovery. Conclusions: Routine screening for frailty and malnutrition, followed by comprehensive geriatric assessment and interdisciplinary management, can help identify reversible risk factors and guide individualized care. Integrating nutrition-focused interventions within prehabilitation programs may improve perioperative outcomes while supporting the preservation of strength, function, independence, and quality of life in older adults.

title: ROCK inhibitor Ripasudil reduces Alzheimer’s pathological proteins and enhances cellular bioenergetics
abstract: ABSTRACT Rho-associated kinase (ROCK) inhibitors have been explored as an Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) therapeutic agent. In this study, we aim to determine the efficacy of a potent ROCK inhibitor, ripasudil, in impacting AD pathological protein tau in mice. The time-course study showed that ripasudil rapidly penetrated mouse brains, reaching maximal concentration half an hour post-injection. To determine the efficacy of ripasudil, we injected App NL-G-F knock-in mice with ripasudil at 30 mg/kg and sacrificed them after three hours. We used Tandem Mass Tag labels and compared the proteomic profiles of mouse brains exposed to ripasudil to those exposed to saline. We also treated AD-patient-derived Neural Stem Cells (NSCs) with ripasudil and performed a Seahorse Mito Stress Test to evaluate their impact on mitochondrial activity. Bioinformatics analysis of the proteomic profiles revealed differentially enriched components of chromosome. The Mito Stress Test of NSCs revealed significant increases in basal oxygen consumption, ATP-linked respiration, maximal respiration, and reserve capacity oxygen consumption compared to untreated NSCs. Importantly, we found a significant reduction of Tau and pTau 396 in brains of mice treated with ripasudil. Overall, our findings highlight the feasibility and promise of ROCK inhibitor ripasudil as an AD therapeutic agent.

title: CD40 ligand and IFN-γ induce proinflammatory activity and microglia-mediated neurodegeneration in human stem cell models
abstract: ABSTRACT The cluster of differentiation 40 (CD40)/CD40 ligand (CD40L) co-stimulatory pathway plays a critical role in the activation and regulation of immune networks involving both adaptive and innate immune cells. Dysregulation of this pathway has been implicated in multiple autoimmune diseases, including multiple sclerosis (MS). MS is characterized by progressive neurodegeneration driven by compartmentalized neuroinflammation within the central nervous system (CNS), sustained low-grade T cell infiltration at the blood-brain barrier, and T cell reactivation at CNS border tissues. CD40L-expressing T cells can activate CD40-expressing microglia, which are a critical effector cell that contribute to neurodegeneration in MS. However, the consequence of this functional interaction in the brain remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that the combination of CD40L and interferon-gamma (IFN-γ), a cytokine produced by activated T cells, induces a robust inflammatory response and cell death in human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSC)-derived microglia. Stimulation with CD40L elicited microglial clustering, morphological transformation, and robust release of proinflammatory cytokines including interleukin-12 (IL-12), tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), and IL-6. Anti-CD40L antibody treatment reversed both cell death and inflammatory response and partially normalized the associated transcriptional changes. Furthermore, using an hiPSC-derived tri-culture system comprising neurons, astrocytes, and microglia, we demonstrated that CD40L and IFN-γ trigger microglia-dependent neuronal dysregulation and death. Anti-CD40L treatment substantially attenuated neuronal injury. Finally, transcriptomic enrichment analysis identified CD40L-mediated microglial gene expression signatures that correlated with CD40 expression in primary progressive MS brain tissue but not in the normal-appearing white matter of healthy controls. Collectively, these findings support a role for the microglial CD40/T cell CD40L axis in MS pathology and suggest CD40L blockade as a potential therapeutic strategy warranting further investigation.

title: KLF15 missense variants and hepatocellular carcinoma susceptibility: a preliminary case–control study in a Pakistani population
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is one of the most lethal malignancies worldwide and develops through a multifactorial process involving genetic, epigenetic and environmental factors. The role of Kruppel-like factor 15 (KLF15) in hepatic metabolism and cell differentiation is established, and KLF15 has recently been implicated in cancer pathways. This study aimed to investigate the association between selected KLF15 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and the risk of HCC development. Various in silico tools were used to filter high-risk KLF15 genetic variants. Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (HWE) was tested to assess genetic stability of control prior to genotypic analysis. In silico findings were validated experimentally using mutation-specific Tetra ARMS PCR to genotype 200 participants for selected KLF15 missense SNPs. The Fisher exact test was used to assess genetic associations with HCC risk and clinicopathological features under six genetic inheritance models. All three KLF15 variants conformed to HWE. In 100 HCC cases and 100 controls, each variant was significantly associated with HCC susceptibility across multiple genetic models. rs755719419 C > G showed the strongest disease association with HCC risk under all six genetic models tested. rs999426548 A > G was significantly associated with increased risk of HCC in codominant, dominant, recessive, allelic and additive model. rs768676875 G > A correlated with significantly increased risk of HCC under codominant, dominant, recessive, allelic and additive models. rs768676875 G > A was also associated with fatty liver, whereas rs755719419 and rs999426548 did not show any association with clinicopathological features. This first genetic association study of KLF15 missense variants in HCC identifies rs755719419 C > G, rs999426548 A > G and rs768676875 G > A as susceptibility variants in a Pakistani population, with rs768676875 also linked to hepatic steatosis.

title: Beyond Training: Expanding Primary Care Capacity for Hepatitis C Treatment in an Integrated Health System Serving Southwest Virginia
abstract: Abstract Background Chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection remains a major challenge in rural US communities, where limited specialist availability restricts access to effective direct-acting antivirals (DAAs). Primary care-based HCV treatment models are clinically effective, yet uptake remains low. We implemented a training and care coordination program within our southwest Virginia health system to address this gap. Methods We conducted a retrospective pre-post evaluation of an HCV program initiated in June 2023, comprising educational modules, webinar series, specialist consultation, and a dedicated HCV Coordinator. Adults with a qualifying HCV RNA result who initiated DAA therapy between January 1, 2022, and February 28, 2025, were included; prescribing providers were grouped by specialty (Family Medicine, Internal Medicine, or Specialist). The primary outcome was expansion of FM treatment capacity. Secondary outcomes included travel distance and time to treatment. Results Of 828 candidate patients, 587 met eligibility criteria. FM providers initiating DAA therapy increased from 12 to 31, and clinic sites from 6 to 17. FM treatment volume increased from 13 to 40 patients (+208%), a significantly greater increase than other specialties combined (OR=2.90, p<0.001). Most newly involved FM prescribers engaged with the program, via the HCV Coordinator. Compared with specialist care, patients treated in FM had shorter travel distances (5.9 vs 18.9 miles; p<0.001) and a non-significantly shorter time to initiation (44 vs 71 days; p=0.15). Conclusions A multifaceted implementation program combining provider education with centralized care coordination was associated with targeted expansion of FM treatment capacity and improved geographic access to HCV care.

title: Abstract 9394: DECIDE-ICM: Defibrillator Efficacy in Cardiac Resynchronization for Ischemic Cardiomyopathy
abstract: Background: Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) is guideline-recommended for HFrEF and electrical dyssynchrony and may be delivered as pacemaker alone (CRT-P), or with an added defibrillator component (CRT-D). Although CRT-D is widely used, no randomized trial has directly compared CRT-D versus CRT-P. Moreover, contemporary medical therapy has reduced sudden cardiac death rates in HFrEF, creating uncertainty of the benefits of defibrillator component, especially in patients receiving CRT. While the ongoing PROFID-EHRA trial is re-evaluating the role of ICD in patients with ischemic cardiomyopathy (ICM), its findings may not directly address the CRT eligible population. We therefore investigated the incremental value of the defibrillator component among CRT eligible patients with ICM. Research Question: Does CRT-D confer superior survival vs. CRT-P in patients with ICM and LVEF <40% in the era of contemporary medical therapy? Methods: Using the Nationwide Veterans Affairs electronic health records from 170 US centers, we identified patients with ICM and LVEF <40% who underwent primary prevention CRT implantation (2006-2020) ( Figure 1 ). Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) based on the propensity score balanced 26 covariates including demographics, comorbidities, pharmacotherapy, LVEF, and implantation year. A doubly robust IPTW-Cox model estimated hazard ratios (HR) for all-cause mortality (primary outcome). Secondary outcomes included rates of generator replacement; device-related infections assessed by Fine-Grey models accounting for death as a competing risk; and CV death, with non-CV death treated as a competing risk. Results: Of 16,609 CRT recipients, 5,601 patients with ICM met primary-prevention criteria (CRT-D = 4,980, CRT-P = 621). Mean age was 70.6 ± 9.0 years and mean LVEF was 25.7 ± 7.8%. The prevalence of both cardiovascular and non-cardiovascular comorbidities was higher in the CRT-P group ( Figure 2 ). CRT-P utilization increased from 3.0% in 2006 to 15.6% in 2020, corresponding to an absolute annual increase of 1.18% (95% CI: 0.98-1.39%). Over a median follow-up of 3.7 years, 3,524 (62.9%) patients died: 63.3% in CRT-D and 59.9% in CRT-P, with no significant difference between groups (adjusted HR: 0.87, 95% CI: 0.70-1.07, p=0.19) ( Figure 3A ). CRT-D was associated with significantly higher rates of generator replacement (n=817; subdistribution HR 1.37, 95% CI: 1.03-1.81, p=0.03). Device infection rates and CV death rates were comparable between groups. There was no heterogeneity across subgroups ( Figure 3B ). Conclusions: In this nationwide observational study of ICM patients with LVEF <40%, CRT-D was not associated with superior survival over CRT-P. Given the progressive decline in sudden cardiac death with modern pharmacotherapy in HFrEF, a randomized trial is needed to test the incremental value of CRT-D over CRT-P in ICM.

title: AAPM Medical Physics Practice Guideline 18.a: Superficial radiation therapy using low-energy kilovoltage x-rays.
abstract: Superficial radiation therapy (SRT), utilizing low-energy kilovoltage (kV) x-rays typically in the 50-100 kVp range, is a well-established modality in dermatology and radiation oncology clinics for the management of non-melanoma skin cancer and various benign dermatological conditions. The comprehensive medical physics practice guidelines presented in this report are designed to facilitate adherence to minimum standards for SRT delivery. A technical overview of commercially available SRT systems in the United States is provided. Detailed guidelines for commissioning and routine quality assurance are presented, specifying daily, monthly, and annual tests, alongside established action limits. The SRT clinical workflow is delineated, encompassing patient simulation, treatment time or monitor unit calculations, data entry, independent treatment plan review, and radiation delivery. A summary of typical state regulatory requirements for x-ray machines is included. Adherence to relevant state regulations is emphasized and radiation safety considerations, comprising structural shielding, radiation surveys, personnel monitoring, signage, periodic spot checks, and machine operation, are discussed to ensure a safe and effective clinical environment. References to relevant societal practice guidance are provided to support standardized clinical implementation.

title: Similar Long-Term Incidence of Hepatocellular Carcinoma in Chronic Hepatitis B Initiating Entecavir Versus Tenofovir Alafenamide: A REAL-B Study.
abstract: Data on potential differences in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) incidence between entecavir (ETV) and tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) in chronic hepatitis B (CHB) patients are limited. This retrospective multinational study included treatment-naïve adults with CHB without a history of HCC who initiated ETV or TAF therapy since 2016 at 23 centres in 4 countries. Baseline characteristics were balanced using inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) and propensity score matching (PSM). HCC incidence and the association between antiviral regimen and HCC were analysed using competing-risk analysis. A total of 1437 patients (710 ETV, 727 TAF) were included, with similar mean follow-up durations (55.5 ± 29.8 vs. 58.0 ± 25.5 months; p = 0.077). ETV-treated patients were older, more frequently male, and more likely to have cirrhosis. After IPTW, both groups had balanced characteristics (all standardised differences < 0.1). After IPTW adjustment, during follow-up, 23 patients on ETV and 20 on TAF developed HCC, with incidence rates of 0.67 and 0.65 per 100 person-years, respectively (p = 0.853). There was no statistically significant difference in HCC risk between the groups (SHR: 1.09; 95% CI: 0.44-2.65; p = 0.851), with consistent findings across subgroups by age, sex, cirrhosis, hepatic steatosis, HBeAg, baseline liver enzymes, HBV DNA levels, diabetes mellitus and in sensitivity analysis using PSM. In this real-world multinational study of treatment-naïve CHB patients, HCC incidence did not significantly differ between ETV and TAF groups, suggesting therapeutic selection should consider cost and patient-specific factors.

title: The altered T cell landscape in systemic sclerosis patients is characterized by dysfunctional type 1 immunity
abstract: T cells in patients with chronic autoimmunity show features of dysfunction. However, the functionally defined T cell subsets that are affected by these changes remain poorly characterized. Here, we sought to reveal aberrations in the composition, phenotype, and function of canonical T cell subsets in the blood of systemic sclerosis (SSc) patients compared with healthy subjects and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) patients. Therefore, we developed a novel multidimensional flow-cytometry panel to simultaneously detect lineage-defining transcription factors, co-inhibitory receptors and other functional markers to characterize T cell subsets without in vitro restimulation. We compared T cell landscapes in SSc and SLE patients, and healthy subjects, using opt-SNE (optimized t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding) and PhenoGraph algorithms. The data show altered distribution and aberrant functional states of transcription factor-defined T cell subsets in patients with autoimmunity, with shared and unique features between diseases and their subtypes. Strikingly, SSc and SLE patients showed deficiencies in subsets of CD8+ and CD4-CD8- T cells that expressed T-bet, which is critical for IFN-γ-dependent type 1 immunity. Moreover, TIGIT+Foxp3+ regulatory T cells, which suppress T helper 1 responses, were increased in diffuse cutaneous SSc and SLE patients. Functionally, T cells from SSc patients produced less IFN-γ, a cytokine that suppresses profibrotic gene expression in fibroblasts, as we demonstrate by transcriptomic analysis. Our study supports a model in which IFN-γ opposes canonical fibrotic gene programs in fibroblasts, and deficiencies in the IFN-γ-producing T cell compartment in SSc patients therefore may contribute to chronic fibrosis development. Aberrant T cell subsets in SSc and SLE represent targets for corrective immunotherapy.

title: 1000 Impact of complement on immune-related toxicity in cancer patients treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors
abstract: Background Immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapies have revolutionized cancer care in the last 15 years. Immune-related adverse events (IRAE) associated with these therapies vary widely between patients, with severity ranging from mild to fatal. The mechanism of development of these toxicities remains poorly defined. This work evaluates the potential impact of complement in IRAE development in a prospectively enrolled cohort of patients with metastatic cancers.Methods Patients with metastatic solid tumors starting a new line of treatment with ICI, and a control group starting a new line of cytotoxic chemotherapy, were enrolled. Patients were ineligible if they received prior ICI, had autoimmune disease, received chronic immune suppressive therapy, or had ongoing infection. ICI combination therapies were allowed, though combinations with chemotherapy were excluded. Complement levels C3a, C4d, and Terminal Complement Complex (TCC) were drawn prior to and after cycle 1 day 1 treatment, and again at 12 and 24 weeks in both groups.Results Forty-nine patients were enrolled in this study across two sites; 37 patients received ICI and 12 were treated with cytotoxic chemotherapy as a control. Twelve total IRAE were documented in 8 of 37 patients in the ICI group, with 3 patients experiencing >1 IRAE. Skin rash occurred in 4 patients (33%), and hypothyroidism in 2 (17%). Most events were Grade 1-2 in severity, though one event of Grade 3 myocarditis was documented. Mean baseline levels of C3a were numerically higher in the subset of patients treated with ICI with IRAE as compared to those without IRAE and the control group, though this was not statistically significant (p = 0.19 and 0.25). There were no significant differences in baseline values of C4d or TCC across groups. When comparing day 1 pre- to post-treatment C3a values, a mean of differences of 16.7 approached significance in the ICI without IRAE group (p = 0.06), whereas that in other groups did not. Mean of differences for C4d and TCC were not statistically significant across groups. A striking increase in C3a post-treatment on day 1 was documented in the patient who experienced the IRAE of grade 3 myocarditis.Conclusions In this prospective cohort of patients, there were trends toward higher baseline levels of C3a in patients who went on to develop IRAE, and a significant increase in C3a levels post-treatment in the one patient who developed a grade 3 IRAE. Ongoing work is warranted to better understand the role of complement in IRAE development.Ethics Approval This study was approved by the Colorado Multi-Institutional Review Board, approval number 17-1940.Consent Written informed consent was obtained from all participants.

title: Physiological Arousal During Alcohol Cue Exposure in Adult Drinkers: Sex Differences in Neural and Clinical Correlates
abstract: ABSTRACT Cue exposure contributes to craving and reinforces alcohol misuse, potentially by altering interoceptive processing and physiological arousal. However, few studies have reported changes in physiological arousal or their neural underpinnings in response to alcohol cues. Here, we addressed these questions in 94 adult drinkers (39 females; age mean ± SD: 59.1 ± 19.1 years and range: 19–85 years) who underwent functional magnetic resonance imaging and skin conductance recording during alcohol and neutral cue exposures and completed clinical assessments including the Alcohol Use Disorder Identification Test (AUDIT; mean ± SD: 4.4 ± 5.5). Imaging data were processed with published routines and evaluated at a corrected threshold. The results showed significantly higher skin conductance response in ‘alcohol>neutral’ blocks (SCR Al‐Ne ) in females than in males. However, SCR Al‐Ne was positively correlated with participants' AUDIT scores in males but not in females. SCR Al‐Ne was also positively correlated with global positive alcohol expectancy and novelty seeking scores in males but not in females. A voxel‐wise two sample test of the contrast ‘alcohol>neutral’ did not show any clusters with significant sex differences in cue reactivity. Whole‐brain regression of the same contrast on AUDIT scores identified a large cluster in the perigenual anterior cingulate cortex (pgACC), with the beta estimates showing a significant positive correlation with the SCR Al‐Ne , again in males only. These sex differences were all confirmed by slope tests. Thus, males with more drinking problems showed higher arousal as well as the pgACC response to alcohol cues in association with alcohol expectancy and novelty seeking. In chain mediation modelling, the pgACC response and alcohol expectancy interlinked SCR Al‐Ne and AUDIT scores in males. In contrast, we failed to observe any significant neural or psychological correlates of physiological arousal, despite higher SCR Al‐Ne , in females. With the caveat of a smaller sample size for females, these findings highlight sex and individual differences in physiological responses to alcohol cues and the neural and psychological underpinnings in male adult drinkers. Whether or how physiological arousal may play a role in the pathophysiology of alcohol misuse remains to be investigated for females.

title: Leveraging immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry and neuropathology to identify the clinical value of different blood tau species in Alzheimer’s disease
abstract: Advances in plasma-based assays have allowed for the study of several tau and p-tau epitopes. P-tau217 has emerged as one of the most robust markers of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) pathology. Despite their strong diagnostic performance, plasma tau biomarkers require further validation to clarify their clinical utility. To investigate the associations between a panel of phosphorylated and non-phosphorylated tau species measured in antemortem plasma and clinical features of autopsy-confirmed AD. Cross-sectional data from 123 participants from the BU ADRC who had antemortem blood draws and brain donation following death. Participants completed neuropsychological testing during life as part of their National Alzheimer’s Coordinating Center-Uniform Data Set (NACC UDS) evaluation. AD neuropathology was diagnosed using NIA-Reagan criteria. Time interval between testing at last visit and autopsy ranged from 0 to 12 years, mean = 5.54 years. Raw neuropsychological test scores were used for analysis. Sample size ranged from 65 to 91 across the tests. Plasma samples were analyzed using immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry (IP-MS) for phosphorylated tau species (p-tau-181, 199, 202, 205, 217, 231) and non-phosphorylated tau (195–209, 212–221) peptides. Two ratios were analyzed, p-tau217/tau212-221 and p-tau205/tau195-209. 123 participants took part in this study, 55 (44.7%) female, and 6 (4.9%) Black/African American. The mean (SD) age at blood draw was 78.17 (8.55). The strongest association between plasma biomarkers with neuropsychological test outcomes was observed with the ratio p-tau217/tau212-221 ( b = − 0.564–0.404, p low-high = 0.00–0.18), followed by p-tau217 ( b = − 0.478–0.377, p low-high = 0.00–0.28), both significantly correlating with six of the eight neuropsychological measures (p < 0.05). Followed by the ratio p-tau205/tau195-209 ( b = − 0.513–0.356, p low-high = 0.00–0.55), p-tau205 ( b = − 0.365–0.226, p low-high = 0.00–0.44), then p-tau231 ( b = − 0.319–0.237, p low-high = 0.02–0.62). Fewer significant relationships and weaker effect sizes were observed among the other biomarkers. The effect sizes of the ratio p-tau217/tau212-221, followed closely by p-tau217 on neuropsychological test outcomes, were observed to be the most similar to the effect sizes of autopsy-confirmed AD ( b = − 0.564–0.393). Plasma p-tau217 and p-tau ratios were comparable to autopsy-confirmed AD in predicting clinical outcomes of AD. This study highlights the promise and potential utility of plasma biomarkers for symptom monitoring.
