title: Individualized machine-learning predictions of pain intensity in chronic low back pain
abstract: Chronic low back pain (cLBP) imposes a major public health burden and its presentation is further complicated by high comorbidity with depression. Processes that maintain cLBP are likely highly individualized and span biological, psychological, and social domains, posing significant challenges for optimal treatment. This proof-of-concept study applied a systematic individualized machine learning (ML) pipeline to predict individual pain intensity from intervenable biopsychosocial variables obtained from ecological momentary assessment and smartwatch wearables. Participants were six adults with cLBP and major depressive disorder (Mage=43.0, SD=15.14; 67% female). In total, 29 candidate predictor variables were measured daily for 30 days, including metrics of physical activity, sleep, heartrate, negative and positive mood, diet quality, and social connection. We fit ML models per participant and determined each participant's top-ranked variables predicting pain intensity. Results revealed models with an average error of 28.4% +/- 12.3% across participants. The top predictors of pain intensity were largely unique to each participant. For example, whereas depressed and anxious mood were within the top five predictors of pain intensity for the majority of participants, predictive strengths varied considerably across participants. We also found notable differences in predictive strengths for positive mood, physical activity, diet quality, and social factors. This study provides proof-of-concept of our systematic individualized ML pipeline for identifying individual, intervenable predictors of pain intensity in adults with cLBP and depression. Future research is required for additional development and validation of the ML pipeline and for its utility for guiding personalized treatment strategies. PERSPECTIVE: Chronic low back pain is highly prevalent and varies across individuals. Our findings demonstrate proof-of-concept of applying a systematic individualized machine learning pipeline to predict individual pain intensity from intervenable biopsychosocial variables. This approach may provide a foundation for future research examining personalized approaches to pain assessment and management.

title: Melanoma of the Scalp Harboring a Novel AGFG1::ERBB4 Fusion: A Case Report With Clinicopathologic and Genomic Characterization.
abstract: ERBB4 (HER4) gain-of-function missense mutations have been implicated in cutaneous melanoma. In contrast, structural rearrangements involving ERBB4 are exceedingly rare. We describe a 59-year-old man with a rapidly enlarging 4.2-cm melanoma of the scalp with high-risk pathologic features, including epithelioid to plasmacytoid cytomorphology, ulceration, brisk mitotic activity, and microscopic satellitosis. RNA sequencing identified a novel in-frame AGFG1::ERBB4 fusion joining AGFG1 exon 2 to ERBB4 exon 2. The ERBB4 portion retains the downstream coding sequence, including the tyrosine kinase domain. Concurrent molecular alterations included a pathogenic NF1 loss-of-function alteration, a TERT promoter mutation, CDK4 and STAT6 copy-number gains, and TP53 copy-number loss in a BRAF/NRAS/KIT-wild-type background.

title: Behavioral economic analysis of the reinforcing effects of fentanyl, cocaine, and mixtures of fentanyl and cocaine in rats
abstract: BACKGROUND: The co-use of opioids, primarily fentanyl, and stimulants has resulted in substantial increases in fatal multi-drug overdoses, yet few studies have systematically investigated the reinforcing effects of fentanyl + stimulant mixtures. Behavioral economic demand curve analyses can quantify the relative value of drug reinforcers across different classes (e.g., opioids and stimulants), making it a valuable method to determine factors that promote polysubstance use. METHODS: The current study used a multiple-component drug self-administration procedure to assess economic demand for fentanyl (0.00032-0.01mg/kg/inf), cocaine (0.032-1.0mg/kg/inf), and mixtures of fentanyl:cocaine at fixed-ratios of 10:1, 3:1, 1:1, 1:3, 1:10 (relative to the dose ranges used for each drug alone) in male and female Sprague-Dawley rats. Available unit doses of drug increased within-session across four components and response requirement (fixed-ratio; FR) increased across sessions. Demand curves for fentanyl, cocaine, and fentanyl:cocaine mixtures were generated, and elasticity coefficients (ɑ) estimated from demand curve analyses were used to assess the reinforcing value of the drugs alone and mixtures. RESULTS: Demand for cocaine was more inelastic than demand for fentanyl (i.e., cocaine was a more valuable reinforcer); demand elasticity for the mixtures became more elastic as the proportion of fentanyl to cocaine increased, and more inelastic as the proportion of cocaine to fentanyl increased. CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that interactions between the reinforcing effects of fentanyl and cocaine are additive in nature, however, it is unclear whether similar interactions would be observed under clinically relevant states, such as physical dependence on opioids or opioid withdrawal.

title: Trial-by-Trial Connectivity Reveals Selective Safety-Learning Alterations in Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
abstract: : Background Prediction errors (PEs) drive fear learning by signaling discrepancies between expected and actual threat. The amygdala-hippocampus and amygdala-vmPFC circuits are preferentially implicated in threat acquisition and safety learning, but whether PE-related connectivity dynamics are disrupted in PTSD remains unknown. Methods We analyzed fMRI data from 65 participants (21 combat veterans with PTSD, 25 trauma-exposed controls, 19 healthy controls) during a reversal threat conditioning task. Trial-by-trial functional coupling was linked to skin conductance-derived PEs using Bayesian multilevel modeling with group-level interaction terms. Results Amygdala–hippocampus coupling tracked positive PEs in all groups (β = 0.08–0.13, all pd > 99%), with no difference between trauma-exposed groups (Δβ = 0.01, pd = 54.9%, 89% HPDi [-0.07, 0.09]). Amygdala–vmPFC coupling diverged by group: both control groups showed negative coupling–PE associations consistent with safety signaling (combat-exposed: β = −0.08, pd = 99.7%; healthy: β = −0.04, pd = 90.9%), whereas veterans with PTSD showed a reversed association (β = 0.03, pd = 88.9%). The direct contrast between trauma-exposed groups confirmed a robust difference (Δβ = −0.12, pd = 99.6%, 89% HPDi [−0.18, −0.05]). Conclusions PTSD was characterized by altered PE-related amygdala–vmPFC connectivity despite preserved amygdala–hippocampal PE signaling, suggesting a selective disruption of circuitry supporting safety-related updating rather than a generalized deficit in threat learning. The contrasting pattern in trauma-exposed individuals without PTSD may reflect a neural signature of resilience.

title: Role of circulating tumour DNA in gastric cancer: a review
abstract: Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) represents an emerging liquid biopsy tool with significant clinical utility in gastric cancer detection, monitoring and prognostication. Multicancer early detection blood tests achieve 66.7% sensitivity for advanced disease and up to 81% for early-stage detection using methylation-based assays. ctDNA predicts treatment response approximately 8 weeks earlier than radiographic imaging, with patients achieving ctDNA negativity after therapy demonstrating substantially improved overall survival (73% vs 34%). For minimal residual disease detection, tumour-informed ctDNA assays identify recurrence 4–6 months before imaging with 95.5% specificity and 85.7% sensitivity, enabling early intervention in high-risk patients. Notably, ctDNA captures tumour heterogeneity and clonal evolution more comprehensively than tissue biopsy alone, identifying resistance-associated mutations and targetable alterations that guide sequential treatment decisions. Integration of ctDNA with tissue biopsy improves molecular concordance from 45% to 87.5%, providing a more complete tumour landscape assessment. These findings support ctDNA as a transformative tool for precision-guided oncologic management and adaptive therapeutic decision-making throughout the gastric cancer patient journey.

title: EP9.4 Imaging Adjustment for Pelvic Coronal Plane Kinematics During Gait: A Reliability Study of Femoral Head Coverage
abstract: Abstract Purpose Gait-related coronal pelvic motion may alter femoral head coverage but is not reflected in conventional static radiographs. Wearable inertial measurement units (IMUs) enable quantification of pelvic kinematics during walking, which can be used for standard imaging adjustment. It was hypothesized that femoral head coverage measurements obtained from adjusted standing pelvic radiographs would demonstrate high inter- and intra-rater reliability. Methods A prospective single-institutional hip preservation registry with 129 cases was screened for unilateral femoro-acetabular impingement syndrome (FAIS) cases, of which 10 patients (20 hips) were selected. The registry includes supine and standing radiographs and motion capture using IMUs. The coronal pelvic kinematics used during walking included contralateral peak pelvic drop and compensatory, ipsilateral femoral adduction. Both dynamic parameters were incorporated into standard standing pelvic radiographs through image adjustment. Two raters independently measured the lateral center-edge angle (LCEA), acetabular index (AI), femoro-epiphyseal acetabular roof index (FEAR), and extrusion index (EI) to determine inter- and intra-correlation coefficients (ICCs). Results The mean peak pelvic drop on the asymptomatic hip was 5.2° ± 1.6° (2.2° to 7.1°), with compensatory femoral adduction of -2.8° ± 5.1° (-13.8° to 4.2°) on the affected side. Inter-rater reliability had ICCs of 0.71 to 0.97 in the first round and 0.86 to 0.96 in the second round for femoral head coverage parameters on the adjusted radiographs, while intra-rater agreement showed ICCs ranging from 0.77 to 0.94 for rater 1 and 0.73 to 0.97 for rater 2. Discussion This study demonstrated high inter- and intra-rater reliability for adjusted radiographs that incorporated dynamic motion data to assess femoral head coverage during gait. Further research is needed to identify factors affecting coronal pelvic kinematics and to examine its possible surgical implications and effect on outcomes.

title: Donor-Derived Metastatic Urothelial Carcinoma
abstract: Renal transplantation continues to be the best therapeutic option for patients with end stage renal disease (ESRD), reaping the benefits of improved mortality and quality of life, despite the risks involved with chronic immunosuppression. Post-transplant management typically includes monitoring of malignancies, as they carry significant morbidity and mortality. Most post- transplant malignancies that develop are de novo in origin, originating from the recipient. In contrast, donor-derived malignancies are exceedingly rare. We describe a unique case of donor derived metastatic urothelial carcinoma who underwent complete cancer remission following transplant nephrectomy and withholding immunosuppression, in the absence of any chemotherapy.

title: 177Lu-Prostate-specific Membrane Antigen Prior to Stereotactic Ablative Radiotherapy in Oligorecurrent Prostate Cancer: Secondary and Exploratory End Point Results from the Randomized Phase 2 LUNAR Trial
abstract: The phase 2 randomized LUNAR trial previously demonstrated that neoadjuvant 177 Lu-PNT2002 before stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) significantly improved progression-free survival (PFS) in patients with oligorecurrent hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (orHSPC). We report updated efficacy and safety outcomes with extended follow-up. Patients with prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT)–detected orHSPC and one to five metastatic lesions amenable to SBRT were randomized 1:1 to SBRT alone or two cycles of neoadjuvant 177 Lu-PNT2002 followed by SBRT. The primary end point was PFS, defined as new lesions on PSMA PET/CT, initiation of salvage hormonal therapy, or death. Secondary end points included hormonal therapy–free survival (HT-FS) and 24-mo progression-free status. Exploratory end points included polymetastatic PFS (poly-PFS), castration-resistant disease-free survival (CRFS), and conventional imaging progression-free survival (CT-PFS). Between September 2022 and November 2023, 92 patients were randomized to SBRT alone ( n = 47) or 177 Lu-PNT2002 plus SBRT ( n = 45). At a median follow-up of 31.9 mo, 177 Lu-PNT2002 significantly improved PFS (median 17.6 vs 7.4 mo; hazard ratio [HR] 0.38, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.23–0.61; p < 0.001) and HT-FS (HR 0.57, 95% CI = 0.34–0.95; p = 0.03). Exploratory analyses demonstrated improved poly-PFS (HR 0.28, 95% CI = 0.08–1.03; p = 0.04), CRFS (HR 0.13, 95% CI = 0.02–1.10; p = 0.03), and CT-PFS (HR 0.46, 95% CI = 0.19–1.09; p = 0.07). No new safety signals were observed. With extended follow-up, neoadjuvant 177 Lu-PNT2002 before SBRT produced durable improvements in PFS and HT-FS. While poly-PFS, CRFS, and CT-PFS were exploratory end points, their improvement provides hypothesis-generating evidence that the addition of radioligand therapy to SBRT may alter disease trajectory beyond delaying PSMA PET/CT–detected recurrence.

title: Implementation of an electronic frailty index for prospective frailty detection and management in an oncology clinic.
abstract: 677 Background: Frailty-guided care is recommended for older adults with cancer, yet its implementation remains limited in busy oncology settings. Electronic frailty indices (eFIs) derived from EHR data enable retrospective analyses incorporating frailty, but their prospective clinical use in oncology remains understudied. We evaluated a clinical decision-support tool incorporating a validated eFI (Veterans Affairs Frailty Index [VA-FI]) for real-time frailty identification and management in an oncology clinic. Methods: We conducted a convergent mixed-methods pilot implementation study Oct-Dec, 2025 of VA GeriOnc AppLication (VA GOAL), a clinical decision-support tool that automatically calculates the VA-FI and provides patient-specific deficits and management recommendations. The study enrolled clinicians in an outpatient multiple myeloma clinic at the VA Boston Healthcare System, including an oncology attending, oncology fellow, and nurse practitioner, representing key stakeholder perspectives. We evaluated the following implementation outcomes. Uptake was defined as (1) VA GOAL access frequency and (2) proportion of eligible patients (age ≥65 years, VA-FI ≥0.2) for whom clinicians viewed individual patient-level frailty assessment and management recommendations. Feasibility was defined as integration into clinical workflows and delivery of prospective information, supported by use across clinic weeks, patient encounters, and usability (System Usability Scale [SUS]). Acceptability and appropriateness were assessed qualitatively using periodic reflections and semi-structured interviews; appropriateness focused on perceived utility for clinical decision-making. Results: VA GOAL was accessed 538 times, with use across all clinic weeks and among 67/68 (99%) eligible patients. Usability was high (mean SUS 99.4). Qualitative findings supported feasibility, acceptability, and appropriateness across clinician roles. Clinicians reported that VA GOAL facilitated interpretation of frailty and informed cancer treatment and supportive care decision-making, including medication management and multidisciplinary referrals. Concerns regarding potential frailty misclassification were mitigated by integrating VA GOAL outputs with clinical judgment. Conclusions: In this pilot study, VA GOAL demonstrated high uptake and usability, with strong feasibility, acceptability, and appropriateness in routine oncology care. Clinicians reported that the tool supported interpretation of frailty and informed treatment and supportive care decisions within existing workflows. These findings suggest that eFI-based tools can facilitate frailty-guided care by enabling integration of frailty into clinical decision-making. Further study is needed to evaluate fidelity of use, effects on decisions, and downstream patient outcomes.

title: Comparative time toxicity of second-line regimens in relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma.
abstract: 391 Background: Time toxicity is an important patient-centered outcome. For relapsed/refractory follicular lymphoma (R/R FL), treatment options range from rituximab monotherapy to regimens combining lenalidomide plus rituximab (R²) with tafasitamab (Tafa-R²) or epcoritamab (Epcor-R²). While these regimens demonstrate progressive efficacy gains, their time burden, particularly regarding immune complications, has not been systematically evaluated. Methods: We applied an established time toxicity framework to estimate acute time burden over a standardized 12-cycle induction period for rituximab monotherapy, R², Tafa-R², and Epcor-R² using published dosing schedules and safety data. Time toxicity was calculated as days with physical health care system contact, including infusions and clinic visits plus unplanned time from serious adverse events. Hypogammaglobulinemia requiring intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) was modeled as a contributor to time burden, assuming monthly infusions for affected patients. Results: Total acute time toxicity was estimated at 13.8 days for rituximab monotherapy, 14.6 days for R², 37.9 days for Tafa-R², and 29.4 days for Epcor-R². R² demonstrated a highly favorable time-efficacy trade-off, with minimal incremental burden (0.8 days) yet median progression-free survival (PFS) improvement from 14.1 to 39.4 months. Triplet regimens achieved further efficacy gains but with distinct time burden profiles. Tafa-R² had the highest time toxicity, driven by 30 scheduled tafasitamab infusions. Epcor-R² demonstrated lower overall burden but with greater contribution from unplanned toxicities and hypogammaglobulinemia (34% use of IVIG, contributing 3.2 days). Conclusions: Incorporating hypogammaglobulinemia meaningfully alters the comparative time burden of contemporary R/R FL regimens. Among triplet strategies, Epcor-R² offers superior efficacy with lower overall time toxicity than Tafa-R², though with a less predictable burden profile. These findings provide a framework for shared decision-making that balances disease control with patient time and aligns treatment selection with individual values and preferences. title: Prospective optimization of potentially inappropriate medications in older adults with cancer guided by an NCCN-adapted scale (GO-PIMs).
abstract: 537 Background: Potentially inappropriate medications (PIMs) are common among older adults with cancer and contribute to toxicity and adverse outcomes. We developed and validated the Geriatric Oncology Potentially Inappropriate Medications (GO-PIMs) scale—adapted from NCCN Older Adult Guidelines—which is associated with frailty and adverse outcomes independent of cancer characteristics and comorbidity (La et al., JNCCN, 2025). Building on this work, we implemented a prospective medication optimization initiative in an outpatient oncology clinic as part of the national VA Center for Medication Safety in Aging Deprescribing Collaborative. We aimed to operationalize GO-PIMs in real time to identify and optimize high-risk medications in older patients with cancer. Methods: We conducted a single-center, prospective quality improvement initiative enrolling Veterans aged ≥65 years with cancer evaluated in a geriatric oncology clinic between March 2025 and March 2026. An interdisciplinary team—including a geriatrician, pharmacy resident, oncology pharmacists, and a palliative care nurse practitioner—participated in structured medication review at the point of care. All chronic and supportive oncology medications were reconciled, and GO-PIMs were identified with the aid of an EHR-based application that automated detection. Additional PIMs not captured by GO-PIMs were identified through clinician adjudication based on individualized risk–benefit assessment. Medication optimization strategies included deprescribing, dose reduction, substitution with lower-risk alternatives, or continued use with close monitoring. Frailty assessment (clinical geriatric assessment and EHR-based frailty index) contextualized medication risk and informed decision-making. Results: Among 81 Veterans, 1,162 medications were reviewed (mean 14.3, SD 6). A total of 423 (36.4%) were PIMs, including 123 GO-PIMs (10.6% of all medications; 29.1% of PIMs). Supportive oncology medications comprised a minority of prescriptions but accounted for 27.9% of all PIMs (p < 0.001). Chronic medications comprised the remaining 72.1%. For each PIM, recommendations included: 167 (39.5%) deprescribed (115 discontinued + 52 dose-adjustments); 25 (5.9%) substituted with safer alternatives, and 231 (54.6%) continued with monitoring. Some recommendations changed over time with evolving frailty and patient preferences. Conclusions: An interdisciplinary process guided by GO-PIMs successfully identified and optimized PIMs in older patients with cancer. Because historical polypharmacy definitions (≥5 medications) saturate in this population, EHR-based tools applying cancer-specific PIM criteria (e.g., GO-PIMs) may help clinicians identify high-risk medications within dense medication lists to reduce medication burden and improve safety.

title: Association of a standardized community health worker enrollment with cancer outcomes and clinical trial enrollment: A secondary case-control analysis.
abstract: 255 Background: The Individualized Management for Patient Centered Targets (IMPaCT) program is a standardized CHW model with proven effectiveness in chronic disease management. However, there are limited studies of CHW effects on cancer treatment and clinical trial enrollment. We evaluated the association between prior IMPaCT enrollment and cancer stage at diagnosis, oncology appointment adherence, and therapeutic cancer clinical trial enrollment. Methods: This was a secondary case-control analysis of patients previously enrolled in IMPaCT. Cases (n=220) were patients within the University of Pennsylvania Healthcare System who completed IMPaCT (2013-2023) and were later diagnosed with cancer; controls (n=440) were cancer patients without prior CHW enrollment. Controls were selected by first creating a base cohort within the Abramson Cancer Center registry meeting low-income zip code and insurance eligibility for IMPaCT enrollment. Then each case with IMPaCT was randomly matched to 2 controls by primary cancer site. Primary outcomes of stage at diagnosis and 24-month oncology no-show rate following cancer diagnosis were analyzed by cumulative and binomial logistic regression respectively. Therapeutic clinical trial enrollment rate was exploratory and modeled using logistic regression. Models were adjusted for age and sex. Race was omitted given homogeneity of the sample. Results: The analysis included 660 patients (median age 62 years; 91.4% Black; 67.1% female). Cases were diagnosed with cancer a median of 2 years following CHW enrollment. The median duration of the CHW enrollment was 6 months. In the adjusted models prior CHW enrollment was significantly associated with higher odds of early-stage presentation (Table 1). There was no significant difference in cancer appointment no-show rates - 17.5% in cases, 20% in controls. Therapeutic clinical trial enrollment trend was higher among CHW-exposed patients (6.4% vs 4.3%) but not statistically significant. Conclusions: Prior enrollment in a standardized CHW program built for chronic disease management was independently associated with earlier cancer stage at diagnosis in a predominantly Black and low-income population. There was a trend towards increased clinical trial enrollment in patients with prior CHW enrollment. Upstream CHW programs may confer sustained downstream benefits for early cancer detection and may hold promise for clinical trial equity. Future trials to evaluate concurrent CHW support during active cancer treatment are warranted. Adjusted odds ratios for prior CHW enrollment (cases vs control) by outcome. title: Promoting gynecologic cancer patients to achieve functional recovery (PROOF) cohort study: Interim analysis of longitudinal outcomes.
abstract: 370 Background: Most data measuring frailty and physical function in older adults with cancer are limited to retrospective analyses relying on proxies such as claims-based diagnoses, performance status, and comorbidities. Moreover, few studies assess patients’ quality of life (QOL) and functional independence longitudinally, outcomes older adults report are as important to them as survival. Methods: The PROOF cohort study is a prospective multi-center study enrolling patients >=50 years old with newly diagnosed, high-grade and/or metastatic ovarian or uterine cancers. Physical frailty testing, QOL assessments, and patient-reported outcomes are obtained at baseline, 3-, 6-, and 9-months along with treatment outcomes. Here we present a planned interim analysis of longitudinal data examining associations between participants’ functional decline and QOL at 9 months. We defined functional decline using validated minimal clinically important differences by a decrease in an objective [Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB) score >=1] or patient-reported measure [NIH PROMIS Physical Function 10b T-score >=5] from baseline to 9 months. Results: To date, 289 participants have enrolled and 114 have completed 9-month follow-up (11/2023-6/2026). The median age is 67.6 years (SD 8.8), 61.2% have ovarian cancer, 70.8% advanced disease, and 34.7% were pre-frail/frail by SPPB score at baseline. Clinically significant deterioration in QOL and functional independence (activities of daily living (ADL)/instrumental ADL scores) was common from baseline to 9 months post-treatment (Table 1). Rates of functional decline at 3-, 6-, and 9-months were 53.5%, 55.4%, and 51.2%, respectively. After adjustment for key baseline covariates identified a priori (frailty, mental health score, cognitive status, and stage) functional decline was significantly associated with lower QOL at 9 months by both global physical (44.9 vs 49.2, p=0.03) and mental (44.7 vs 49.7, p<0.05) health scores, and associated with a loss of independence by lower iADL (aOR 20.9, 95% CI 3.7-118.5), but not ADL scores. Conclusions: In this prospective study of older adults with gynecologic cancer, a majority experienced functional decline early, which persisted at 9-months post-baseline. Functional decline was associated with worse quality of life and loss of independence. Tailoring treatments and identifying interventions that promote functional recovery may improve overall QOL in older adults. title: Epigenetic Aging in Individuals with Substance Use Disorders:Sex, Ancestry, and Age Group Differences
abstract: Background Substance use disorders (SUDs) are associated with premature mortality and age-related diseases, suggesting accelerated biological aging. Yet, the epigenetic mechanisms underlying this relationship remain poorly understood. We investigated the impact of SUDs on biological aging using three DNA methylation (DNAm)-based epigenetic clocks — GrimAge, SkinBloodClock, and DNAmTL — examining sex- and ancestry-specific effects, and the cumulative impact of co-occurring SUDs. Methods Epigenetic clocks were profiled in 989 individuals. Tobacco (TUD), alcohol (AUD), opioid (OUD), cocaine (CoUD), and cannabis (CaUD) use disorders were analyzed in multivariable regression models fit separately for each clock, adjusting for sex, chronological age, ancestry principal components, and cell-type proportions, with Bonferroni correction applied. Models were stratified by sex, ancestry, and age group. Results TUD showed the strongest and most consistent associations, with GrimAge acceleration (β = 3.80 years, p-adj = 2.25E-29), DNAmTL (β = -0.069, p-adj = 7.67E-7). OUD, CoUD, and AUD were also significantly associated with GrimAge acceleration. SkinBloodClock showed no significant associations with any SUD. Females showed greater GrimAge acceleration than males across TUD, OUD, and CoUD. TUD effects were significant in both European and African Americans, while OUD and CoUD effects were only found in European Americans. No effects were observed in Latin Americans. Each additional SUD diagnosis was associated with 1.48 additional years of GrimAge acceleration demonstrating cumulative biological aging burden. Conclusions SUDs are robustly associated with epigenetic age acceleration, with sex- and ancestry-specific patterns and effects that scale with SUD burden, underscoring the utility of epigenetic clocks as molecular markers of biological aging in high-risk populations.

title: A Case of Renal Cell Carcinoma in a Kidney Allograft Presenting as Acute Cyst Rupture
abstract: Renal cell carcinoma in a kidney allograft is a rare event and is often conservatively managed. This case describes a 53-year-old woman with a failed kidney allograft who presented with acute abdominal pain and leukocytosis. She was found to have spontaneous hemorrhagic cyst rupture and infection of her allograft requiring urgent nephrectomy. Pathology demonstrated renal cell carcinoma in the allograft and, later, in her native kidney, which delayed and eventually precluded retransplantation. This case highlights a gap in guidelines for malignancy surveillance in patients with graft failure awaiting second-chance transplantation.

title: Study to evaluate the effect of balcinrenone/dapagliflozin in patients with heart failure and impaired kidney function (BalanceD-HF): background and design
abstract: Abstract Background Despite available guideline-recommended medical therapies for HF there is an unmet need to reduce residual morbidity and mortality in patients with HF and kidney disease. Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs) reduce mortality and morbidity in patients with HF, but they increase the risk of hyperkalaemia resulting in MRA underutilisation in patients with HF and impaired kidney function. Balcinrenone is a novel non-steroidal (ns)MRA (also known as modulator) with cardio-renal protection comparable to approved MRAs in animal models, but with a predicted reduced risk of hyperkalaemia. Dapagliflozin is indicated to reduce the risk of cardiovascular death (CV) or worsening HF in adults with HF across the left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) spectrum. A Phase 2 trial of the combination of balcinrenone and dapagliflozin in patients with CKD demonstrated a reduction in urinary albumin creatinine ratio and another Phase 2 trial in patients with HF identified a dose range with beneficial effects on surrogate cardio-renal biomarkers compared to dapagliflozin alone without increasing the risk of hyperkalaemia. Methods BalanceD-HF is an ongoing Phase 3, randomized, double-blind, parallel group, active controlled, event-driven trial in ambulatory or hospitalised patients with HF and impaired kidney function who had a recent HF event, to evaluate the efficacy and safety of combined balcinrenone/dapagliflozin vs dapagliflozin, in addition to standard of care. An estimated 4800 patients with symptomatic HF (NYHA class II to IV) across the LVEF range, elevated NT-proBNP (>300 pg/mL), eGFR >20 - <60 ml/min/1.73m2, potassium <5.0 mmol/L, a HF event in last 6 months and not taking an MRA will be randomized 1:1:1 to balcinrenone/dapagliflozin 15 mg/10 mg, 40 mg/10 mg or dapagliflozin 10 mg. The primary composite endpoint is the time to first occurrence of CV death, hospitalisation for HF or urgent HF visit (requiring intravenous therapies). Suspected endpoint events are adjudicated by a blinded Clinical Endpoint Committee. An independent Data Monitoring Committee is monitoring safety data. The study started in April 2024 and is targeting 1050 primary endpoint events. BalanceD-HF is underway across 700 sites in 39 countries. Results Not applicable; On-going study. Conclusions BalanceD-HF is a unique trial evaluating the efficacy and safety of the novel nsMRA balcinrenone combined with dapagliflozin in patients with HF and impaired kidney function across the LVEF spectrum and HF care continuum.BalanceD-HF figure

title: Secondary Lower Extremity Lymphedema Disease Specific and Generic Health-Related Quality of Life, Limb Girth, and Compliance over 1 year
abstract: BACKGROUND Secondary lower extremity lymphedema ( S LEL) is associated with major patient and socioeconomic impact. Chronic Venous Insufficiency (CVI) was the most common etiology. Patient Reported Outcomes in S LEL were assessed in patients with CVI and Non-Venous S LEL (NonV) in a prospective longitudinal study employing adjunctive treatment with an Advanced Pneumatic Compression Device (APCD) provided with instruction for each patient. METHODS Four VA centers enrolled 128 secondary S LEL patients from 2016-22 who were followed for 52-wks with interval assessments. Primary LEL patients were excluded. Primary outcome measures of Health-Related Quality of Life (HR-QoL) were obtained during four in-person visits at baseline, 12, 24, and 52 wks using generic SF-36v2™ and disease-specific LYMQOL-leg. Secondary outcome measures were limb circumference, cellulitis events, and compliance with compression therapies. As bilateral S LEL was common, the worst limb was designated the study limb. Analyses were limited to within group comparisons except for demographic data. Parallel descriptions were provided in lieu of direct comparison. RESULTS Mean baseline characteristics were age 67±11 years and BMI 33±7; 90.6% were male. CVI or phlebolymphedema was the etiology of S LEL in 88 (69%) patients. NonV S LEL was attributed to trauma, surgery, and cancer treatment in 40 (31%) patients. Limbs were classified as International Society for Lymphology (ISL) stage I (70.3%), II (25.7%) and III (4%) respectively. Primary outcome CVI patients improved over baseline in all four LYMQOL domains of Function, Appearance, Symptoms (p<0.001), & Emotion (p=0.017) after 52 wks. CVI improved in all 4 domains at 12 and 24 wks; Overall Score for CVI improved at 24 and 52 wks. NonV patients improved over baseline at 52 wks in three of four domains of Function (p=0.042), Appearance (p<.001) and Symptoms (p=0.002). CVI patients improved in five of eight domains of the SF-36v2™ at 52 wks in Physical Functioning (p=0.038), Bodily Pain (p<.001), Vitality (p =0.021), Social Functioning (p =0.006), Role-Physical (p =0.002); and for Physical Component (p<.001). NonV patients registered no improvement in generic SF-36 scores compared to baseline at any time point. A substantial reduction in HR-QoL for all S LEL patients in comparison to US norms was indicated by the findings that at baseline all SF-36v2™ scores were <50; 3 of 8 domains (Physical Function, Pain) and Physical Summary were <40. Secondary Outcomes Reductions in mean limb girth for both groups ranged from 0-1.1cm. Mean limb girth decreased compared to baseline in both groups at 12 wks; CVI differed from baseline at 52 wks (p=0.017). Full compliance (use 5-7 day/wk) with compression therapy improved from 68% to 84% (p<0.001) in the CVI group. Full compliance with APCD declined from a fourth week 89% in CVI and 100% in NonV to 71% and 81% respectively . CONCLUSION Improved generic and disease specific HR-QoL through 52 weeks was noted in a longitudinal study of VA patients with secondary S LEL with adjunctive use of an APCD. CVI patients experienced a robust improvement in HR-QoL out of proportion to the magnitude of reduction in limb girth while maintaining excellent compliance with compression modalities.

title: AI Timeouts: A Structured Approach to Deliberate AI Use in Clinician Education
abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in clinical medicine has outpaced structured education and guidance on how to safely use this new tool. This gap is particularly consequential in medical education where lack of deliberate use of this tool can lead to poor development of clinical reasoning. We propose a set of AI Timeouts for clinician educators, a pair of structured cognitive pauses adapted from the pre-procedural timeout and cognitive forcing strategies used to mitigate diagnostic error. The Intent Timeout precedes AI use and prompts clinicians to consider whether AI is the appropriate tool for the task, address privacy and data stewardship concerns, and weigh the potential impact on their own clinical reasoning. The Appraisal Timeout follows AI use and guides clinicians to evaluate the fit, rationale, and actionable priority of an AI-generated output before acting on it. Because the framework is grounded in a checklist practice already familiar to all clinicians, it requires no specialized AI literacy and can be adopted immediately by an individual clinician, a supervising attending, or an institution.

title: Normal alanine aminotransferase levels underestimate the burden of steatotic liver disease and fibrosis in US adults.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Despite wide use of serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) in screening and evaluating liver disease, the definition of a normal ALT is controversial. Here, we aimed to determine the prevalence of steatotic liver disease, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), metabolic dysfunction and alcohol-associated liver disease (MetALD), and hepatic fibrosis across normal ALT ranges.
METHODS: We performed a cross-sectional study using the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey. Adults were stratified based on ALT levels of ≤ 10, 11-20, 21-30, 31-40, 41-80, and > 80 U/L. Vibration-controlled transient elastography was used to assess hepatic steatosis (controlled attenuation parameter of ≥ 285 dB/m), and clinically significant and advanced fibrosis (> 8.6 kPa and 13.1 kPa, respectively). Outcomes included the prevalence of steatotic liver disease, MASLD, MetALD, and hepatic fibrosis across ALT strata. Multivariable logistic regression examined the association between normal ALT strata and each outcome.
RESULTS: In 5,245 adults, steatotic liver disease prevalence increased stepwise from 17% at ALT ≤ 10 U/L to 26% at ALT 11-20 U/L, 44% at 21-30 U/L, and 52% at 31-40 U/L (p < 0.001). MASLD and MetALD followed similar graded patterns (both P < 0.001). Relative to a reference ALT 11-20 U/L, ALT 21-30 U/L was independently associated with significantly greater odds of steatotic liver disease (aOR, 1.80 [95% CI, 1.26-2.58]), MASLD (aOR, 1.57 [1.18-2.09]), MetALD (aOR, 1.82 [1.41-2.34]), clinically significant fibrosis (aOR, 1.64 [1.12-2.40]), and advanced fibrosis (aOR, 1.94 [1.30-2.89]).
CONCLUSION: A significant burden of steatotic liver disease, MASLD, MetALD, and hepatic fibrosis exists at ALT values commonly considered normal, suggesting current reference ranges may be too high to reliably exclude liver disease.

title: TNF inhibitor therapy is associated with an increase in absolute lymphocyte count that is, in turn, associated with lower mortality across the spectrum of immune-mediated inflammatory diseases
abstract: Introduction We previously observed lower absolute lymphocyte count (ALC) associates with greater subsequent mortality in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and psoriatic arthritis (PsA), and TNF-inhibitor (TNFi) therapy initiation associates with an increase in the ALC that, in turn, associates with lower mortality. We investigated the pathway and disease specificity of these findings over a range of immune-mediated inflammatory diseases (IMID) and biologic and targeted synthetic (b and ts) disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD) therapies. Methods Using the VA Corporate Data Warehouse, we identified patients that initiated TNF, JAK, IL12/23, IL23, IL17, IL6, or costimulation (abatacept) inhibitor therapy 2017–2022 with ALC before and 3–24 months after therapy initiation. We evaluated change in ALC and overall mortality among patients with documented diagnoses of RA, psoriasis (PsO), inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), or ankylosing spondylitis (AS) at drug initiation. Results Among 31,416 patients with a bDMARD or tsDMARD drug initiation, ALC increased by a mean of 0.23 × 10 3 cells/µL (95% CI = 0.22–0.24) in the 22,471 patients with TNFi initiation. Comparing ALC values post-drug initiation and adjusting for baseline ALC, demographics, comorbidities, conventional DMARD use, chronic steroid use, and IMID diagnosis, we found that patients with TNFi had significantly higher ALCs than those initiating any other drug classes (paired ALC differences of 0.18–0.29 × 10 3 cells/µL, p < 0.001 for six comparisons). In survival models predicting all-cause mortality and adjusting for age, race, sex, ethnicity, Charlson comorbidity index, concordant cDMARD, and chronic steroid medication, we found TNFi use, greater baseline ALC, and increased ALC at follow-up to be associated with greater survival. Conclusion TNFi therapy associated with an increase in the ALC across a range of IMID, and this associates with lower subsequent mortality after adjustment for age, sex, and Charlson comorbidity index. Whether the TNFi-induced increase in ALC is mechanistically responsible for improved longevity or is a prognostic biomarker remains to be determined.

title: Integrating uncertainty and practice variability for epilepsy prognostication after intracranial EEG : A meta‐analysis
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) practices and diagnostic testing vary among institutions, limiting standardization and optimization of surgical outcomes. This study estimates resection rates and surgical outcome effect sizes after iEEG and develops individual patient-level data (IPD) models using the missing-indicator method to approximate real-world clinical uncertainties and practice variability in iEEG and surgical decision-making. METHODS: Databases were queried for studies reporting ≥12-month outcomes after epilepsy surgery in patients with drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) who underwent iEEG. Random-effects meta-analysis estimated pooled outcome proportions. IPD analysis was performed using multivariable generalized linear regression and logistic regression models with cross-validation and calibration assessment. Missing values for key predictors were retained as a "not specified" category to evaluate the impact of incorporating uncertainty in common clinical data on outcome prediction. RESULTS: Primary outcomes were seizure freedom (Engel class IA or International League Against Epilepsy [ILAE] 1) and favorable seizure outcomes (Engel I or ILAE 1-2). Of 4975 studies identified, 115 met the inclusion criteria. The pooled frequency of patients undergoing resection after iEEG was 67% (95% confidence interval [CI] 60%-74%), 52% achieved seizure freedom (95% CI 48%-56%), and 58% achieved a favorable outcome (95% CI 54%-62%). IPD analysis included 1305 patients from 29 studies and identified a lesional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI; odds ratio [OR] 1.94, CI 1.48-2.55, p < .0001) and a cortical malformation (OR 1.47, CI 1.08-2.00, p = .01) as independent predictors of a favorable outcome, whereas iEEG implantation strategy (bilateral implantation OR .61, 95% CI .42-.89, p = .01) was an independent predictor of a less favorable outcome. SIGNIFICANCE: About two-thirds of patients undergoing iEEG proceeded to resection, and about half achieved seizure freedom. Multivariable models incorporating clinical uncertainty and practice variability were well calibrated. However, modest discrimination suggests that routinely available clinical variables alone have limited ability to predict individual surgical outcomes. More standardized and granular clinical and practice-related data may improve individualized prognostication after iEEG.

title: Vagus nerve stimulation in obesity: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Background Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) has been investigated as a potential therapy for obesity because of the vagus nerve’s role in satiety, gastrointestinal signaling, autonomic regulation, and metabolic homeostasis. However, studies vary substantially in stimulation site, interface, parameters, species, diet condition, and reported outcomes. Methods PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from inception through May 6, 2026. Eligible studies evaluated chronic electrical stimulation of the vagus nerve or a defined vagal branch, included a comparator, and reported quantitative body weight data. Random-effects meta-analyses using Hedges’ g evaluated final body weight and weekly body weight change, while food intake, adiposity, metabolic outcomes, and safety were summarized narratively. Results Of 629 records identified, 23 publications met the inclusion criteria, yielding 25 experimental comparisons. Across 22 comparisons, VNS was associated with lower final body weight than control conditions (Hedges’ g = −1.07, 95% CI −1.43 to −0.72; I 2 = 55.5%; P < 0.001). Across 14 comparisons, VNS was associated with lower weekly body weight gain or greater weekly body weight reduction (Hedges’ g = −2.82, 95% CI −4.23 to −1.41; I 2 = 93.3%; P < 0.001). In animal studies, modality-specific final body weight estimates favored conventional implanted electrical VNS ( g = −0.84), transcutaneous auricular VNS ( g = −1.54), and self-powered triboelectric VNS ( g = −8.36), although the triboelectric subgroup comprised two comparisons from one publication. Excluding the triboelectric comparisons, VNS remained associated with lower final body weight ( g = −0.93, 95% CI −1.23 to −0.63, I 2 = 39.4%). Food intake was commonly reduced after VNS, and adiposity outcomes generally favored stimulation, whereas metabolic and safety outcomes were reported inconsistently. Conclusion Chronic, anatomically specific VNS was associated with lower body weight across predominantly preclinical studies. The final body weight estimate showed moderate heterogeneity, whereas the weekly body weight change estimate was highly heterogeneous and should be interpreted as supportive rather than as a precise estimate of effect magnitude. Translation to obesity treatment remains limited by sparse human evidence, potential small-study effects, and inconsistent reporting of metabolic and safety outcomes.

title: Lower recorded prevalence of Alzheimer’s disease in natalizumab-exposed older adults with multiple sclerosis: A hypothesis-generating observation
abstract: Adaptive immune mechanisms, including CD8 T cell-mediated neuroinflammation, are increasingly implicated in Alzheimer's disease. We examined whether exposure to natalizumab, an α4-integrin antagonist that restricts leukocyte trafficking into the central nervous system, was associated with Alzheimer's disease prevalence among older adults with multiple sclerosis. Using Epic Cosmos electronic health record data, we identified 875,226 individuals with MS, of whom 9095 had an Alzheimer's disease diagnosis after age 65 years. Alzheimer's disease prevalence differed significantly across disease-modifying therapies, with natalizumab-treated patients demonstrating the lowest prevalence (0.13%; 95% confidence interval: 0.10-0.17%). These findings demonstrate a lower recorded prevalence of late-life Alzheimer's disease among natalizumab-exposed patients; however, given the aggregated nature of the data, this observation should be considered descriptive and hypothesis-generating.

title: Spirometry Utilization and Costs of Expanding Respiratory Monitoring Among People with Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis in the Veterans Health Administration
abstract: Background Respiratory muscle weakness leading to respiratory failure is the principal cause of morbidity and mortality among people living with Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (pALS). ALS-specific guidance recommends serial respiratory assessment at intervals ranging from approximately 2-3 months to at least every 6 months, with frequency individualized according to disease progression and respiratory symptoms, to monitor respiratory decline and guide initiation of non-invasive ventilation (NIV) and supportive therapies. However, adherence to recommendations remains poorly characterized. Research Question What is the frequency of spirometry among pALS receiving care in the Veterans Health Administration (VHA), and what are the projected costs of implementing quarterly spirometry monitoring using clinic-based and remote spirometry? Study Design and Methods We conducted a retrospective cohort study of people living with ALS receiving care in the VHA using administrative data, chart review, patient and caregiver surveys, and economic modeling, to estimate spirometry frequency and model the costs of implementing quarterly pulmonary function testing. Results Among 4,509 pALS receiving VA care, patients underwent an estimated 1.5 spirometry tests per year. Only 3.5% had ≥4 CPT-documented tests in a 12-month period. Implementing a quarterly monitoring strategy would require 11,147 additional spirometry tests annually. Remote spirometry could reduce patient and caregiver time and travel burdens while shifting costs toward the health system. Interpretation Spirometry among pALS occurs substantially less frequently than contemporary clinical guidance recommends. Our quarterly monitoring scenario illustrates the resources required to increase testing to the frequency specified by the current AAN Quality Measurement Set and supported by NICE guidelines. The gap between current and quarterly testing potentially limits opportunities for assessment of respiratory decline and timely initiation of NIV. Remote spirometry offers a strategy to expand longitudinal monitoring while minimizing patient and caregiver burden. Alongside multidisciplinary ALS care, remote spirometry may facilitate earlier recognition of clinically meaningful respiratory decline. Clinical Trial Registration N/A

title: Risk Factors for Retinal Pigment Epithelium Tears in Patients with Neovascular Age-Related Macular Degeneration: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract:
TOPIC: To identify and synthesize clinical, imaging, and treatment-related risk factors associated with retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) tears in neovascular age-related macular degeneration (nAMD).
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: RPE tears are a vision-threatening complication of nAMD, occurring most often in eyes with pigment epithelial detachments (PEDs) and frequently temporally associated with initiation of anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapy. Improved recognition of high-risk PED features may enhance counseling and risk stratification.
METHODS: This systematic review and meta-analysis followed PRISMA guidelines and was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251075278). MEDLINE, Embase, and CENTRAL were searched from inception to December 15, 2025. Randomized and non-randomized studies of adults (≥50 years) with nAMD evaluating candidate predictors of RPE tear were included. Two reviewers independently screened, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias (RoB 2, ROBINS-I). Random-effects meta-analyses were performed for baseline PED height and area, with per-study weighting, standardized mean difference (SMD), and leave-one-out sensitivity analyses. Certainty was assessed using GRADE.
RESULTS: Sixteen studies comprising 4,043 eyes were included. Five studies (55 tear eyes; 370 controls; 425 eyes) showed greater baseline PED height in eyes developing tears (mean difference [MD], 212.39 µm; 95% confidence interval [CI], 133.87-290.91; I² = 24.6%; SMD, 1.09). Four studies (48 tear eyes; 1,312 controls; 1,360 eyes) showed larger baseline PED area (MD, 5.80 mm²; 95% CI, 3.48-8.12; I² = 2.7%; SMD, 0.88). Both persisted across all leave-one-out iterations; omitting the study contributing 43.5% of the area weight increased the effect (MD, 7.11 mm²). Fibrovascular PED, greater basal diameter and volume, subretinal fluid, sub-RPE clefts, radial hyperreflective lines, and occult or hemorrhagic macular neovascularization were also associated with tears. Anti-VEGF agent selection was not consistently associated. Most studies were at moderate to serious risk of bias; certainty was very low.
CONCLUSION: Baseline PED morphology, particularly increased height, is the most consistently reported association with RPE tear in nAMD. Because the evidence is predominantly retrospective, largely unadjusted, and of very low certainty, these are associations rather than validated predictive markers. Prospective studies using standardized imaging protocols are needed.

title: Surgical stress and physiological reserve interact to drive postoperative outcomes after arthroplasty: a data-driven framework for risk stratification
abstract: Abstract Background Postoperative outcomes following total joint arthroplasty (TJA) vary widely, even amongst similar patients. Existing models often fail to integrate two key factors: surgical stress (procedural burden) and physiologic reserve (the patient’s inherent capacity to withstand stress). This study introduces a framework to quantify both using registry data and evaluates their combined effect on short-term arthroplasty outcomes. Methods We analyzed 187,849 TJA cases from ACS-NSQIP (2021–2023). Using principal component analysis, we derived two indices: a Hemodynamic Stress Index (HSI: operative time, RVUs, transfusions, bleeding, BMI, urgency) and a Physiologic Reserve Score (PRS: age, albumin, creatinine, dialysis, function, comorbidities). Patients were stratified into four quadrants: High Stress/Low Reserve (HS/LR), High Stress/High Reserve (HS/HR), Low Stress/Low Reserve (LS/LR), and Low Stress/High Reserve (LS/HR). Multivariable regression assessed complications (HS/HR as reference). Results Among 187,849 patients, 47,074 were classified as LS/HR, 46,851 as LS/LR, 46,850 as HS/HR, and 47,074 as HS/LR. The 30-day composite complication rate increased across cohorts from 2.89% in LS/HR patients to 5.14% in LS/LR, 5.60% in HS/HR, and 11.28% in HS/LR patients. Using LS/HR as the reference, adjusted odds of complications were higher in LS/LR (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.98; 95% CI 1.85–2.12), HS/HR (aOR, 1.79; 95% CI 1.67–1.91), and HS/LR patients (aOR, 3.70; 95% CI 3.48–3.94; all p < 0.001). The HS/LR cohort also demonstrated increased risk across multiple individual complication domains. Bootstrap validation demonstrated stable PCA loadings and an optimism-corrected area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.636, while temporal validation yielded similar discrimination in the development and validation cohorts (0.637 vs 0.635). Conclusion This quadrant-based framework provides an interpretable approach to perioperative risk stratification by jointly considering procedural stress and physiologic reserve. The observed risk gradients and internal validation support further investigation of this framework; prospective and external validation are required before clinical implementation.

title: Physical activity and blood pressure as predictors of cognitive function in the all of us research program
abstract: Abstract Physical activity (PA) is positively associated with cognition, whereas elevated blood pressure shows a negative association. However, most studies relied on subjective, self-reported measures of PA. In this study, we examined associations of PA (daily step count from Fitbit wearable devices), systolic (SBP) and diastolic (DBP) blood pressure spanning 14 years, with end-of-study cognitive performance in 3,093 participants in the All of Us Research Program (AoU). Cognition was assessed by the Gradual Onset Continuous Performance Task (Grad-CPT), Delay Discounting Task (DD-Task), Multiracial Emotional Recognition Task (Emorecog-Task) and Flanker-Task. Baseline PA metrics were positively associated with Grad-CPT (β = 0.31, 95% CI: 0.18 to 0.44), DD-Task (β = 0.05, 95% CI: 0.04 to 0.07), and Flanker-Task (β = 0.26, 95% CI: 0.17 to 0.35). Baseline SBP was negatively associated with DD-Task (β = -0.01, 95% CI: -0.02 to -0.004). Longitudinal k-means clustering identified 3 clusters of individuals—A, B and C— with mean daily steps of 5108, 8875 and 14,161 respectively. Individuals in clusters B and C had higher scores than those in cluster A on the DD-Task, Grad-CPT and Flanker-Task. These findings underscore the potential role of PA promotion and optimal blood pressure management in supporting cognitive health.

title: Establishment of In Vivo Mouse Models to Study Salmonella-Induced Chronic Infection and Gastrointestinal Cancer.
abstract: Salmonella infection increases the risk of chronic diseases, e.g., inflammatory bowel diseases, colon cancer, and gallbladder cancer. However, the mechanisms leading to the development of these conditions are still not completely understood. Here, we describe the methods to establish in vivo mouse models to study Salmonella-induced chronic infection and colon cancer. These models will allow us to investigate the initiation and progression of diseases.

title: Vagus Nerve Stimulation as a Potential Therapeutic Strategy for Alcohol Use Disorder.
abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) contributes to approximately 3 million deaths worldwide each year and leads to substantial emotional, financial, and social implications for individuals and their families. AUD leads to multi-system damage, including the immune system, gut microbiome, neuroendocrine pathways, and the brain. Current treatments for AUD, focused primarily on behavioral and pharmaceutical interventions, insufficiently address alcohol's extensive impact on multiple body systems. Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) has shown therapeutic benefits across a spectrum of neurological conditions, including epilepsy, depression, and addictive disorders. More recently, VNS is being investigated as a potential promising adjunctive treatment for AUD, which may complement currently used treatments by targeting many of the body systems dysregulated in AUD. Preclinical and clinical models have evaluated different VNS paradigms, including invasive, noninvasive, and minimally invasive approaches targeting motor and cognitive rehabilitation, withdrawal symptoms, and relapse during abstinence. However, while VNS has many promising potential benefits for improving AUD outcomes, direct evidence that VNS reduces alcohol consumption, alcohol seeking, or craving in AUD remains limited, and there are several logistical and ethical considerations that researchers, clinicians, and policymakers should evaluate before VNS is considered standard of care. Additionally, optimization of VNS parameters, modality (implanted versus noninvasive or minimally invasive), and development of responder biomarkers could better inform patient selection for VNS. Although significant work remains before transitioning VNS into clinical practice, VNS offers an exciting opportunity for adjunctive treatment in AUD that could potentially target multi-system AUD dysfunction.

title: Private Equity Acquisition of U.S. Hospitals Providing Neonatal and Pediatric Care from 2000-2021.
abstract: Private equity (PE) ownership of U.S. adult hospitals is increasing, but the temporal trends and hospital characteristics of PE-owned hospitals providing neonatal or pediatric care remain unknown. We created a retrospective cohort of neonatal- and pediatric-serving U.S. acute care hospitals with 2000-2021 American Hospital Association and Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) data. We determined the exposure, PE hospital ownership, annually with 3 databases: Pitchbook, the PE Stakeholder Project Hospital Tracker, and the CMS change of hospital ownership file. PE ownership of neonatal- and pediatric-serving hospitals has increased, from 11 (0.3%) to 100 (3.5%) hospitals over 2000-2021 while all neonatal- and pediatric-serving hospitals have decreased from 3,618 to 2,737. PE facilities in 2021 were smaller; located in the rural Southeast; had higher operating margins; and provided less neonatal and pediatric intensive care unit care. Overall, there was higher growth in PE-owned neonatal and/or pediatric acute care hospitals in the face of declining numbers of these hospital overall, with unequal geographic distribution.

title: Sex differences in ADHD Diagnosis and Care Patterns Among Children Enrolled in North Carolina Medicaid.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Delayed diagnosis and treatment for ADHD is associated with significant impairment. Limited research has explored sex differences in diagnostic and treatment patterns before and after ADHD diagnosis and how patterns vary by sociodemographic characteristics. We hypothesized female children, compared to males, would be older at ADHD diagnosis with more prior behavioral health (BH) diagnoses, diagnosed more often by BH clinicians, and less likely to receive empirically-based treatment.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of pediatric Medicaid enrollees ages 5-17 in North Carolina between 2019-2023 with a 2022 ADHD index date (N=12,398). Using claims data, we examined sex differences in characteristics before, during, and after ADHD diagnosis using t-tests, χ2 tests, relative risk, and odds ratios. Race/ethnicity and rurality were examined as moderators.
RESULTS: Females were older at ADHD diagnosis (9.0 vs. 8.0 years), had received over twice as many prior BH diagnoses-including 34% having previous internalizing diagnoses-and were more likely to be diagnosed by BH than primary care providers. Post-diagnosis, females were less likely to receive ADHD medication and more likely to receive psychotherapy. Hispanic females were most likely to be diagnosed > age 12.
CONCLUSIONS: Findings represent the first known study examining sex differences in ADHD care patterns via comprehensive look-back and follow-up periods in a diverse, U.S.-based sample. Results indicate internalizing concerns in females may signal the need for ADHD screening. Findings highlight importance of culturally-informed clinical resources, particularly for Hispanic families. Future research should clarify underlying reasons for sex differences in care patterns.

title: Comparative cardiovascular outcomes of IL-6 inhibitors versus rituximab in rheumatoid arthritis: a claims-based observational study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Interleukin-6 receptor inhibitors (IL-6i), tocilizumab and sarilumab, are FDA-approved therapies for rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Beyond their efficacy in controlling systemic inflammation, growing evidence suggests that IL-6 inhibition may confer cardioprotective effects. This study investigates the long-term cardiovascular outcomes associated with IL-6i in RA patients, comparing IL-6 inhibitors with rituximab and evaluating differences between individual IL-6 inhibitor agents.
METHODS: We conducted an observational cohort study using the TriNetX Linked Network (2010-2025) including adults with RA initiating an IL-6 inhibitor or rituximab and ≥ 2 prescriptions for a drug of interest ≥ 6 months apart. Comparisons were as follows: (1) IL-6 inhibitors (sarilumab, tocilizumab) versus rituximab, and (2) tocilizumab versus sarilumab. Patients receiving both IL-6 inhibitors simultaneously or a non-FDA-approved IL-6 blocker (e.g., siltuximab) were excluded. Outcomes included all-cause mortality, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, heart failure (HF), and venous thromboembolism (VTE) over 5 years. We calculated propensity scores using demographics, cardiovascular risk factors, inflammatory markers, prior TNFi exposure, systemic glucocorticoid use, and conventional DMARDs, and used scores to match exposed individuals 1:1 with comparators. Cox models estimated hazard ratios (HRs) for mortality and cardiovascular outcomes individually. All analyses were conducted using the TriNetX platform.
RESULTS: After matching, 4288 RA patients per group were included for IL-6i versus rituximab and 605 per group for sarilumab versus tocilizumab. Compared to rituximab, IL-6i was associated with lower hazards of mortality (HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.55-0.82), MACE (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.64-0.85), and HF risk (HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.69-0.94), with no significant difference in MI, stroke, or VTE. Amongst IL-6 inhibitors, sarilumab was associated with lower hazards of all-cause mortality compared to tocilizumab (HR 0.52, 95% CI 0.29-0.94), but no significant differences were identified for other cardiovascular outcomes.
CONCLUSIONS: Among adults with RA, IL-6i use was associated with lower rates of all-cause mortality, MACE, and heart failure compared to rituximab, while risks of stroke, MI, and VTE were similar. A lower risk of all-cause mortality was observed with sarilumab compared to tocilizumab. These findings support a potential survival and cardiovascular benefit of IL-6i and highlight the need for larger studies to further distinguish the cardiovascular outcomes with IL-6i agents. Such evidence could inform personalized treatment decisions based on cardiovascular risk factors. Key Points • This study provides long-term real-world evidence that IL-6 inhibitors may offer superior cardiovascular outcomes compared with rituximab in RA patients previously managed with TNFi, an important evidence gap in biologic choice after TNFi failure. • This study directly compares cardiovascular outcomes between sarilumab and tocilizumab, identifying a potential lower myocardial infarction risk with sarilumab.

title: The development and validation of artificial intelligence model to assess the degree of mucosal cleanliness of the upper gastrointestinal tract.
abstract: Mucosal cleanliness of the upper gastrointestinal (UGI) tract is one of the important quality indicators of esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD). The aim of the current study was to create and validate an artificial intelligence (AI)-based system to assess cleanliness during EGD. A total of 520 EGD video samples of the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum were collected between August 2021 and February 2025 at five endoscopic centers and annotated by two endoscopists using the previously validated PEACE scale (from 0-completely obscured, to 3-perfect cleanliness). The dataset was divided into training (332 videos), validation (84 videos), and test (104 videos) datasets. The RegNetY-3.2GF deep learning model architecture was used. The accuracy of videos testing for 12 classes ranges between 90.38% and 100%. The macro recall, precision, F1 score, and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) were 0.669, 0.697, 0.668, and 0.684 respectively. The precision, recall, and F1 score ranged between 0.341 and 0.880, 0.303 and 0.885, and 0.321 and 0.883, respectively. For distinguishing between inadequate (scores 0-1) and adequate (scores 2-3) cleanliness, the algorithm achieved a recall of 0.927, precision of 0.864, and a F1 score of 0.895, with a MCC of 0.77. All reported metrics were computed exclusively on the held-out test set. The current AI model demonstrated a high accuracy for both frames and video assessment of mucosal cleanliness along with appropriate identification of the UGI segments. This model allows for real-time use studies to assess this important EGD quality measure.

title: Performance of the PREVENT-HF Equations Across Heart Failure Subtypes in Community-Based and Ambulatory Healthcare Samples.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The PREVENT-HF equations estimate 10-year risk of overall heart failure (HF), inclusive of both HF with preserved and reduced ejection fraction (HFpEF; HFrEF). Given differential risk factor profiles, pathophysiology, and therapeutic strategies for each HF subtype, we sought to examine the performance of PREVENT-HF for subtype-specific risk assessment.
METHODS: We included data from five pooled longitudinal cohort studies (baseline exam 1989 to 2013) and two longitudinal primary-care electronic health record-based samples (Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center [BIDMC], baseline 2004 to 2014; Mass General Brigham [MGB], baseline 2001 to 2018). We assessed the performance of the PREVENT-HF equations in predicting 10-year incident HFrEF and HFpEF, including model discrimination (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC]; average precision [AP]/event rate) and calibration (integrated calibration index [ICI]), in adults aged 30-79 years without prevalent cardiovascular disease or HF.
RESULTS: The pooled cohort studies included 23,652 (55% women, age 60 ± 13 years), of whom 1,232 developed HF (432 [35%] HFpEF, 522 [42%] HFrEF). The BIDMC sample included 29,815 (55% women, 50 ± 13 years), of whom 259 (1%) developed HF (133 [51%] HFpEF, 101 [39%] HFrEF). MGB included 138,999 (62% women, 52 ± 13 years), of whom 1050 developed HF (586 [56%] HFpEF, 381 [36%] HFrEF). PREVENT-HF demonstrated better discrimination for HFpEF than HFrEF across all samples: in the pooled cohorts, the AUROC for HFpEF was 0.824 (95% CI 0.807, 0.839) versus 0.789 (95% CI 0.770, 0.807) for HFrEF; in BIDMC, the AUROC for HFpEF was 0.897 (95% CI 0.874, 0.918) versus 0.833 (95% CI 0.791, 0.869) for HFrEF; in MGB, the AUROC for HFpEF was 0.864 (95% CI 0.848, 0.880) versus 0.797 (95% CI 0.771, 0.820) for HFrEF. Similar results were reflected in the AP/event rate ratios: 2.92 (95% CI 2.47, 3.54) for HFpEF compared to 2.66 (95% CI 2.33, 3.14) for HFrEF in the pooled cohorts; 8.08 (95% CI 6.12, 12.30) for HFpEF compared to 5.12 (95% CI 3.84, 8.17) for HFrEF in BIDMC; and 6.84 (95% CI 5.66, 8.28) for HFpEF compared to 4.12 (95% CI 3.37, 5.16) for HFrEF in MGB. Calibration was similar for HFpEF and HFrEF across samples. For example, in the pooled cohorts, the ICI for HFpEF was 0.041 (95% CI 0.039, 0.043) and for HFrEF was 0.038 (95% CI 0.036, 0.040).
CONCLUSIONS: PREVENT-HF demonstrated excellent discrimination for both HF subtypes across community-based cohorts and real-world samples, with consistently better discrimination for HFpEF as compared to HFrEF. Given PREVENT-HF was developed to estimate overall HF risk rather than subtype-specific risk, future studies are needed to establish subtype-specific risk thresholds.

title: Toward Artificial Intelligence–Supported Development of Image-Based Tasks in Aphasia
abstract: PURPOSE: Images play a central role in language assessment and therapy for people with aphasia, yet the development of psychometrically robust image stimuli is often time consuming, costly, and difficult to tailor to specific research questions or individual patient needs. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly text-to-image generation models, offer new opportunities to rapidly produce high-quality, customizable visual stimuli. Despite this potential, methodological guidance for integrating AI-generated images into aphasia research and clinical practice remains limited. This tutorial aimed to provide practical recommendations for the use of AI text-to-image tools in developing image-based tasks for people with aphasia. METHOD: Using a case study framework, we demonstrate the development of a semantic judgment task with images generated with the help of the DALL-E 3 model. We outline key decision points that went into this process and provide recommendations across the major stages of task development: task conceptualization, stimulus design, image ideation, prompt engineering, and image quality evaluation by AI models. RESULTS: We demonstrate that structured prompt engineering combined with systematic validation can yield high-quality, interpretable image stimuli suitable for aphasia tasks. The approach allows for flexible control over stimulus characteristics while maintaining consistency across experimental conditions. CONCLUSIONS: AI text-to-image generation offers a promising, scalable approach to developing customized image stimuli for aphasia research and clinical practice. We discuss methodological considerations, limitations, and future directions for the responsible integration of generative AI technologies into aphasia-related research and clinical applications.

title: Abstract 14178: Sex Differences in Cardiovascular Outcomes Among Obese Patients Following Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 (GLP-1) Use
abstract: Introduction: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) have been shown to improve cardiovascular outcomes among overweight and obese patients by reducing all-cause mortality and the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). Whether sex differences exist for these outcomes is not well studied. We evaluated cardiovascular outcomes and all-cause death between sexes by GLP-1 RA use. Hypothesis Among adults with BMI ≥25 kg/m 2 , GLP-1 RA use is associated with reduced mortality and cardiovascular events, with similar benefit for men and women. Methods: We conducted a healthcare-system wide, retrospective cohort study including adults with BMI ≥25 kg/m 2 with and without diabetes. Patients were stratified by sex and categorized by exposure to GLP-1 RA (beginning 2017). Propensity score matching was performed to improve comparability of GLP-1 RA users and non-users. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards modeling was used to estimate hazard ratios. The primary outcome was a composite of all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction (MI), heart failure (HF), ischemic stroke, and major adverse limb events (MALE). Results: At a median of 7.5 years follow-up, the matched cohort included 145,008 women (n= 72,071 GLP-RA1 users) and 88,010 men (n=44,438 GLP-1 RA users). Among the total cohort, the mean age was 50 years for women and 55 for men, 7-10% identified as Black with a mean BMI in both groups of ~36 kg/m 2 . Women had lower rates of CV risk factors and disease including diabetes, hypertension, and coronary artery disease ( Table 1 ). For the primary composite outcome, GLP-RA1 use was associated with a significant reduction in both women vs. men (HR W 0.41, 95% CI 0.39-0.42 vs. HR M 0.48, 95% CI 0.46-0.50, p<0.001, respectively). ( Figure 1 ) Numerically, there was a nominally greater reduction among women compared to men in all-cause mortality [HR W : 0.40 (0.38-0.42) vs HR M : 0.47 (0.45-0.50) , p= <0.001)] and HF (HR M 0.45 (0.42-0.47 vs HR M 0.50 (0.47-0.53), respectively. The subsequent number needed to treat with GLP-1 RA use over a median follow-up of 8 years was similar by sex; 9 in women and 10 in men. Conclusion: GLP-1 RA use in women and men was associated with an estimated 59% and 52% reduction in cardiovascular events/all-cause mortality, respectively, with a NNT of 9-10 over a median of 7.5 years follow-up. Women with GLP-1 RA use had lower rates of CV risk factors and disease.

title: Abstract 16149: Non-Invasive CVP Measurement Predicts Length of Stay and Readmission in Hospitalized Heart Failure Patients: Results of the ezCVP-HF2 Study
abstract: Introduction/background: Central venous pressure (CVP) estimation is essential in managing patients with heart failure (HF) exacerbation. Bedside estimation remains operator-dependent and poorly reproducible. A non-invasive method yielding intuitive hemodynamic parameters for HF care represents a critical unmet need. We previously reported on a non-invasive device which uses a standard blood pressure cuff with a sphygmomanometer pump and oscillometric method to obtain enclosed-zone CVP (ezCVP TM , Nihon Kohden Corp), demonstrating close correlation of non-invasive (CVP NI ) and invasive CVP measurements. In a pilot study involving 22 patients, we showed that CVP NI correlated with clinical course in hospitalized HF patients and was predictive of hospital length of stay (LOS). Research questions/hypothesis: Here, we investigate how CVP NI , tracked throughout admission in patients hospitalized with HF, correlates with LOS and readmission rate. We hypothesized that higher CVP NI at admission would correlate with longer LOS and higher CVP NI at discharge would correlate with increased HF readmission rate. Methods/approach: We enrolled 49 patients admitted with HF exacerbation across two institutions (Stanford Hospital, Palo Alto VA Hospital). CVP NI was measured on admission and daily until discharge. Treatment teams were blinded to CVP NI . Clinical data including weight and renal function as well as patient reported symptoms via dyspnea index and KCCQ score were tracked throughout admission and compared with CVP NI values (paired t-test). CVP NI at admission, grouped into high (≧10mmHg) vs low (<10mmHg) was compared with LOS (independent samples t-test). All patients were followed post discharge for rate of 30-day readmission. We then compared CVP NI (high vs low) at both admission and discharge with incidence of readmission (Pearsons chi-square test). Results/data: 86% of the overall study population was male, with NYHA III (49%) being the most common HF class. Mean CVP NI was 10.6 (SD 7.7) at admission and 6.6 (SD 6.8) at discharge (p=0.003). Mean BUN and Cr at admission increased by time of discharge (32 to 41, 1.5 to 1.6 respectively, p<0.001) and mean weight decreased (101kg to 94kg, p<0.001). High vs low CVP NI at admit correlated with longer LOS (p=0.006), and there was a trend toward higher HF readmission rate (62% vs 35%, OR 3.0, p = .063). There was no significant difference between CVP NI at discharge and readmission rate. Conclusions: Measurement of CVP NI in hospitalized HF patients is technically feasible and correlates with LOS as well as HF readmission rate. CVP NI tracks with other clinical markers of congestion as well as patient reported symptoms. The ability to non-invasively measure CVP as a dynamic marker of congestion in patients being treated for HF has potential to expand capability of treating physicians in reliably tracking CVP both in-person and remotely.
