title: Abstract 14255: Hypothyroidism-Associated High Degree Atrioventricular Block and Stress Cardiomyopathy
abstract: Introduction: Stress cardiomyopathy (SCM) is triggered by a multitude of conditions including thyroid dysfunction. While more frequently associated with hyperthyroidism, SCM has been rarely reported with hypothyroidism. Patient Information: An 84-year-old man with chronic hypothyroidism, hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Clinical Findings and Timeline: The patient reported progressive weakness, lightheadedness, peripheral edema, and exertional fatigue over the past year. He attributed symptoms to hypothyroidism as they were akin to those previously experienced, and he acknowledged nonadherence to levothyroxine. Symptoms acutely worsened, including near syncope that prompted hospital evaluation days later. He denied angina, syncope, palpitations and symptoms of heart failure. He was afebrile, saturating normally on room air, and had heart rate 37 bpm and blood pressure 146/67 mmHg. Examination revealed jugular venous distension and 2+ bilateral lower extremity edema. Diagnostic Assessment and Reasoning: ECG showed sinus bradycardia with second-degree atrioventricular block (AVB) with 2:1 conduction and bifascicular block (Fig 1A). Alternating third degree AVB was noted on telemetry. Labs revealed TSH 11.9 μU/mL (normal 0.46-4.68), free T4 <0.54 ng/dL (normal 0.8-2.2), NT-proBNP 927 pg/mL (normal <124) and undetectable troponin. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) demonstrated severe LV systolic dysfunction with ejection fraction 25-30%, mid-to-apical akinesis with apical dyskinesia (Fig 1B), and low-normal RV systolic function with anterior and apicolateral akinesis. Coronary angiography showed nonobstructive disease (Fig 1C). A diagnosis of symptomatic, hypothyroidism-associated high-degree AVB and SCM was established. Therapeutic Intervention: Guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure was initiated, and an uncomplicated dual-chamber pacemaker was implanted. Hypothyroidism was managed with guidance from Endocrinology. Follow-up and Outcomes: Symptoms improved significantly and the patient was discharged on hospital day 6. TTE repeated 3 weeks later confirmed resolution of all prior abnormalities (Fig 1D). Repeat TSH was normal at 2.89 μU/mL. Ventricular pacing burden decreased without changes in programming, from 99% to <10% at 8 months and <0.2% at 11 months. The patient remains clinically stable at 15 months of follow-up. Discussion and Synthesis: This case illustrates three notable findings: 1) the rare association of hypothyroidism with both symptomatic high-degree AVB and SCM; 2) the potential for favorable outcomes with early detection and management, including reversal of conduction disturbances and recovery of ventricular function; and 3) the importance of a multidisciplinary approach in managing cardiac complications from hypothyroidism.

title: Abstract 13975: Proteomic Scores for Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Imaging Phenotypes and Heart Failure Risk
abstract: Background: Early detection of patients at risk of developing heart failure (HF) is critical. While detection of subclinical cardiac remodeling, a precursor of clinical HF, is possible by cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) derived measures of ventricular and atrial structure and function, it is difficult to implement at the population level. Circulating proteomics may offer a molecular readout of these remodeling processes. We developed proteomic scores as molecular proxies for CMR-derived cardiac phenotypes and examined their associations with incident HF. Methods: Using CMR and plasma proteomics data from 1,101 UK Biobank participants, we examined 17 left ventricular (LV), left atrial (LA), and right-heart structure/function phenotypes. LASSO models were trained in 70% of participants and evaluated in the remaining 30%, with predictive performance assessed using test-set r derived from Pearson correlation. Protein-predicted CMR phenotypes were calculated as weighted sum using the LASSO-derived coefficients and standardized as z-scores using baseline proteomics from 51,441 non-overlapping participants, including 2,394 incident HF cases. Fine-Gray model was used to assess the association between the protein-predicted CMR phenotypes and incident HF, adjusting for risk factors in PREVENT. Results: We created protein-predicted scores for 15 of the 17 CMR phenotypes based on LASSO-selected proteins. Test-set predictive performance was highest for LV myocardial mass ( r = 0.59), RV end-diastolic volume ( r = 0.45), and RV end-systolic volume ( r = 0.40). 11 protein-predicted CMR phenotype scores were strongly associated with incident HF. Higher protein-predicted LA minimum and maximum volume were associated with increased incident HF (HRs of 1.69 and 1.63, respectively), while higher protein-predicted LA ejection fraction was inversely associated with incident HF (HR 0.55). LV remodeling phenotypes were also consistently associated with HF. Protein-predicted LV end-diastolic volume and LV stroke volume were associated with incident HF, with HRs of 1.42 and 1.44, respectively. Three RA CMR phenotypes were associated with incident HF. Adding protein-predicted CMR phenotypes to fully adjusted models improved HF risk discrimination by up to 2.6%. Conclusions: Circulating proteomic signatures of CMR phenotypes were associated with incident HF and improved HF risk prediction, supporting plasma proteomics as a scalable proxy for imaging-defined cardiac remodeling.

title: Abstract 11205: A Rare Destination, a Rarer Presentation: Epicardial Carcinoid Metastasis Adjacent to Left Anterior Descending Coronary Artery
abstract: Introduction: Cardiac metastasis from a neuroendocrine tumor (NET) is rare, occurring in fewer than 5% of metastatic cases, typically involving the right heart via hematogenous spread. Epicardial metastasis in the territory of the left anterior descending artery (LAD) is exceedingly rare with only single-digit cases globally. We present a DOTATATE-confirmed epicardial NET deposit in the LAD territory, presenting as chest pain with coronary vasospasm involving LAD. Clinical Findings and Timeline: An 81-year-old man with metastatic small bowel NET on lanreotide, coronary artery disease with previous percutaneous intervention, deep vein thrombosis, COPD, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm presented with chest pain and hypotension. Electrocardiography was unremarkable and troponin elevated with a downtrending pattern, interpreted as type 2 NSTEMI in the setting of recent gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Echocardiography showed preserved ejection fraction, no wall motion abnormality, and severe aortic stenosis. On day three, crushing substernal chest pain with anterior ST elevation (Fig 1) and troponin rise developed, resolving within minutes. Coronary angiography revealed non-obstructive disease and also incidental aortocaval fistula. Patient subsequently died due to pulseless electrical activity. Diagnostic Assessment: Autopsy confirmed epicardial NET metastasis adjacent to the LAD (Fig 2). Chart review revealed a prior computed tomography identified an indeterminate anterior cardiac mass. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed a 2.1 x 2.1 x 1.1 cm oval mass at the anterior cardiac margin adjacent to the interventricular groove in the LAD distribution, extrinsic to the heart.(Fig 3). DOTATATE positron emission tomography confirmed focal epicardial uptake and an avid mesenteric mass, establishing metastatic small bowel NET with epicardial involvement. Patient was not considered to be a surgical candidate, he was started on lanreotide; serial DOTATATE imaging confirmed stability including even two months prior to this admission. Discussion: This case highlights a rare epicardial NET metastasis adjacent to LAD . The nature of spread is unclear as hematogenous spread involving venous system would be mechanistically not possible and through arterial spread is difficult to postulate. We propose transient anterior ST elevation resulted from serotonin-mediated LAD vasospasm from the adjacent deposit — a mechanism not previously described. Cardiac NET involvement should remain an active consideration in such cases; acute coronary presentations may represent carcinoid manifestations rather than just conventional ischemic events.

title: Abstract 10037: Ziltivekimab in Acute Myocardial Infarction: Rationale, Design and Baseline Clinical Characteristics of the ARTEMIS Study
abstract: Introduction: Cardiovascular (CV) inflammation is associated with major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). Inhibition of interleukin-6 (IL-6), which is upstream to C-reactive protein (CRP), is a promising target for attenuating CV inflammation and may reduce MACE in patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI). Methods: The ARTEMIS study (Effects of ziltivekimab versus placebo on CV outcomes in patients with AMI) is evaluating the impact of ziltivekimab, a human monoclonal antibody targeting the IL-6 ligand, versus placebo in patients with an AMI enrolled across 24 countries (Figure). This double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 CV outcomes study randomized patients within 36 hours of ST-elevation MI (STEMI) or within 72 hours of non-STEMI (NSTEMI) 1:1 to ziltivekimab or placebo, with an initial loading dose of 30 mg subcutaneously and then 15 mg subcutaneously once monthly, on top of standard of care. Participants were required to have angiographic evidence of a type 1 AMI. The primary endpoint of MACE is defined as a composite of CV death, non-fatal MI, non-fatal stroke, and ischemia-driven coronary revascularization. The study was designed using an unstratified Cox model and a power of 90% to confirm superiority using a type I error rate of 2.5% (one-sided) for the primary endpoint, assuming a hazard ratio of 0.77, requiring a total of 616 primary endpoint events. Results: A total of 8584 participants with AMI were screened, and 8346 participants were randomized to ziltivekimab or placebo, administered on top of standard of care. The median age was 62 years (interquartile range [IQR] 54-70), and 20.7% were female. Major comorbidities included hypertension (63.5%), type 2 diabetes (36.0%), heart failure (12.3%), chronic kidney disease (6.3%), prior AMI (15.1%), and prior coronary revascularization (12.5%). A total of 50.4% of participants presented with NSTEMI, and 76.0% had multivessel coronary artery disease during the index AMI. The median time from first hospital contact to study randomization and administration of ziltivekimab or placebo was 28.2 hours (STEMI, 23.9; NSTEMI, 40.4). The baseline median serum high-sensitivity CRP concentration was 10.3 mg/L, serum IL-6 concentration was 17.2 pg/ml, and serum low-density lipoprotein cholesterol concentration was 105 mg/dL. At index AMI discharge, 90.1% were on aspirin, 94.4% on a P2Y12 inhibitor, and 94.0% on a statin. The table describes participant demographics, comorbidities, medications at index AMI discharge, and inflammatory markers, both overall and stratified by NSTEMI versus STEMI presentation. Conclusions: The ARTEMIS study, the largest study of an IL-6 inhibitor in AMI, will determine the safety and efficacy of a novel IL-6 inhibitor, ziltivekimab, in patients with AMI. Participants enrolled in the ARTEMIS study are representative of real-world, high-risk patients with AMI.

title: Abstract 19119: Right Ventricular Dysfunction is Associated with Grossly Altered Oxidative Phosphorylation and Mitochondrial Proteostasis Pathways in Pulmonary Hypertension Rats and Explanted Human Hearts
abstract: Introduction: Right ventricular (RV) dysfunction is a major determinant of mortality in pulmonary hypertension (PH), as well as patients with left heart failure and group II PH. In response to increased afterload, the RV exhibits depressed respiration, mitochondrial remodeling, and pronounced bioenergetic deficits resulting in RV dysfunction and failure. We performed DIA-MS proteomic profiling of RV tissue from rat PH models with varying severity of RV dysfunction and humans with mild and severe RV dysfunction. Methods: Human explanted hearts with left heart failure were stratified using right heart catheterization RAP/PCWP ratio into mild RV dysfunction (RVD–, n=11) and severe RV dysfunction (RVD+, n=11) and compared with unused donor hearts (n=14) RV and LV tissue underwent DIA-MS. In parallel, RV proteomes and cardiac function were compared among mild RV dysfunction Sprague Dawley sugen/hypoxia models (4wk and 7wk SD-SUH, n=6), severe Fisher sugen/hypoxia (4wk CDF-SUH, n=6), and pressure overload pulmonary artery banding (7wk SD-PAB, n=6) models and controls. Ingenuity Pathway Analysis was used for enrichment. Results: The highest enriched decreased signaling cascades across rat models included oxidative phosphorylation, respiratory electron transport, complex I biogenesis, and reduced mitochondrial protein translation, degradation, import, and cristae remodeling. Changes were generally greatest in the more severe 4wk CDF-SUH and 7wk SD-SUH groups. The highest enriched increased cascades included mitochondrial dysfunction and numerous inflammatory pathways. In humans, the most enriched decreased cascades closely mirrored rat PH models, including oxidative phosphorylation, complex I biogenesis, mitochondrial translation/import/degradation, FAO, and cristae formation. Increased cascades similarly included mitochondrial dysfunction and inflammatory signaling. Notably, in human RVD+ and RVD– groups with left heart failure, the RV exhibited substantially greater derangement in mitochondrial respiratory cascades than the LV versus unused donors. Conclusions: Together, these findings identify depressed mitochondrial bioenergetics, proteostasis, and oxidative phosphorylation as central, conserved features of RV dysfunction in humans and preclinical PH models, highlighting heightened mitochondrial vulnerability of the RV as a major contributor to RV failure.

title: Abstract 9377: A Favorable Response to Semaglutide in Advanced Hepatic Fibrosis Secondary to Familial Hypobetalipoproteinemia
abstract: Introduction: Familial hypobetalipoproteinemia (FHBL) is an autosomal semi-dominant disorder caused by truncating APOB variants that impair hepatic secretion of apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins resulting in low LDL-C. While low LDL-C is generally cardioprotective, FHBL predisposes to hepatic steatosis and fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies. Heterozygous FHBL has an estimated prevalence of 1 in 1,000 to 3,000 but remains an uncommon clinical diagnosis. Patient Information: A 45-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with unexplained hypocholesterolemia. He had a family history of low cholesterol in his brother, father, and grandfather. He was previously recommended to adhere to a high-fat diet. Clinical Findings & Timeline: Over a decade of follow-up his LDL-C remained below 30 mg/dL with chronic idiopathic elevated liver enzymes. Diagnostic Assessment & Reasoning: At age 54, viral and autoimmune etiologies were excluded as a cause of elevated liver enzymes. Liver biopsy showed 70% macrovesicular steatosis, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, and stage 3 fibrosis. Further evaluation revealed deficiencies in fat-soluble vitamins despite adequate intake. His bone densitometry progressed from osteopenia to osteoporosis. At age 59 he was referred to clinical genetics where FHBL was diagnosed with a pathogenic monoallelic APOB frameshift variant (c.10848del; p.Gly3617Alafs*6). Therapeutic Intervention(s): Semaglutide 1 mg weekly was initiated in addition to fat-soluble vitamin supplementation and alendronate. Follow-up, Outcomes & Adverse Events: Over 18 months the patient achieved 30-pound weight loss, improved diabetes control (A1c 8.0% to 6.6%) and near-normalization of liver enzymes. Repeat elastography showed stable stage 3 fibrosis. Treatment was well tolerated without new side effects. Discussion & Synthesis: This case presents a decade-long delay in the diagnosis of FHBL. Persistently unexplained hypocholesterolemia with concurrent hepatic steatosis should prompt genetic evaluation. Additionally, a high-fat diet may paradoxically worsen steatosis by increasing the lipid burden on a liver unable to export apoB-containing lipoproteins. The favorable response to semaglutide suggests glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists may benefit FHBL-associated liver disease. However, their potential to further reduce intestinal fat absorption warrants caution given the risk of worsening fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption. Early genetic testing, hepatic and bone density surveillance, and vitamin supplementation are pillars of management. Disease-specific trials of GLP-1 receptor agonists in FHBL may provide further insight.

title: Abstract 9338: Automated Left Atrial Scar Segmentation with Deep Learning Accurately Segments Post-Ablation Lesions
abstract: Introduction: Left atrial (LA) scar segmentation from late gadolinium enhanced (LGE) MRI is an important task for noninvasive assessment of post-ablation cardiac lesions. However, basic thresholding algorithms for scar segmentation show poor agreement with human-annotated scars. Previous studies have applied fully automated convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for scar segmentation but have achieved only moderate performance (Dice scores of ~0.64). Key challenges have been dataset quality and network performance necessary to achieve accurate and repeatable left atrial scar segmentation that aligns with human-guided observations. Hypothesis: We hypothesize that a CNN trained on a multi-observer, ablation-site-guided ground truth dataset will achieve performance at or above the level of inter-observer variability. Methods: Forty-nine post-ablation LGE MRI scans (scan resolution 0.625x0.625x1.25 mm) from patients following first-time ablation for atrial fibrillation were collected from the University of Utah hospital database. Four independent observers selected scar thresholds based on ablation site location (39 PVI, 10 PVI+), and corresponding LA scar segmentations were generated. The segmentations were combined into a single ground-truth LA scar estimate using the STAPLE algorithm (Figure 1A). The dataset was broken into train (N=39) and test (N=10) sets for use with 3 separate CNN setups of the nn-Unet framework, shown in Figure 1B. Of the three networks, one required manual input (LA endocardium and wall), while the other 2 predicted the LA endocardium, wall, and scar from the LGE MRI alone. A held-out validation set was used during training to implement early stopping and avoid overfitting. Fivefold cross-validation was used to ensure each scan in the training set appeared in a validation set. Results: The CNN setup requiring manual input achieved the highest average Dice score of 0.86 and the lowest distance between the prediction and ground truth (average surface distance, ASD) of 0.13 mm on the test set. The multitask and cascaded setups achieved average Dice scores of 0.77 and ASDs of 0.38 and 0.36 mm. Figure 2 shows performance metrics for each setup on the test set. Example outputs, along with their Dice scores and ASD, are shown in Figure 3. Conclusions: We trained three separate models capable of accurately segmenting LA scar. The manual setup surpassed the inter-observer Dice score (0.70-0.81) and likely represents the upper bound of attainable performance on this dataset, given that the ground truth is an observer-bias estimate of the LA scar. The end-to-end methods had lower Dice scores and higher ASDs than the manual setup, but still achieved sub-voxel average error distances in 9 of 10 scans and exceeded previously published Dice scores on similar datasets. Thus, our end-to-end setups offer fully automated, repeatable, and accurate networks for LA scar segmentation.

title: Abstract 8129: Association of Myocardial Texture with Cardiometabolic Risk and Heart Failure
abstract: Background: Heart failure (HF) often develops after prolonged exposure to cardiometabolic risk factors. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) radiomics may provide insight into myocardial tissue texture patterns that are not captured by conventional measures of left ventricular (LV) structure and function. Research Question: We aimed to determine whether cardiometabolic risk factors and HF are associated with radiomic myocardial tissue characteristics in adults in the community. Methods: In 1,008 Framingham Heart Study 2 nd Generation participants who underwent non-contrast 1.5T CMR (Philips Achieva), LV myocardial texture analysis by radiomics were extracted from end-diastolic short-axis cine images (PyRadiomics, Python) and normalized for comparison across radiomics families. Using published reproducible cine CMR features, we eliminated those with high correlation (r≥0.8) and collinearity (VIF≥10) and selected eight top-ranking features from each feature family correlated with coronary heart disease. We examined the association of this parsimonious group of radiomics features with contemporaneously measured (Exam 8) markers of cardiometabolic risk including body mass index (BMI), systolic blood pressure (SBP), fasting glucose, total cholesterol-HDL ratio, and prevalent HF. We conducted multivariable regression models adjusted for age and sex, medication treatment for hypertension, diabetes, and hyperlipidemia, LV mass index, end diastolic volume index, and ejection fraction, and prevalent cardiovascular disease. Results: Adverse cardiometabolic risk factors, including higher BMI, higher total cholesterol-to-HDL ratio, elevated fasting glucose, and higher SBP, were associated with radiomic features reflecting greater myocardial texture heterogeneity and complexity, including higher first-order energy and gray-level co-occurrence matrix features, and lower neighborhood gray-tone difference matrix features ( Table/Figure ). Obesity, elevated SBP, dyslipidemia, and HF were also associated with higher gray-level size-zone matrix non-uniformity, suggesting greater heterogeneity in zones of similar myocardial signal intensity. Higher SBP showed additional associations with gray-level dependence and run-length matrix features, reflecting greater variability in adjacent-pixel texture and linear gray-level patterns. Conclusion: Non-contrast CMR radiomics is able to identify unfavorable patterns of myocardial architecture, independently of clinical measures of LV geometry and function, associated with key markers of cardiometabolic risk and heart failure in a general adult community population. These findings may provide complementary insight into myocardial tissue remodeling related to adverse cardiovascular risk.

title: Abstract 8217: First US Case of Low-Grade Endometrial Stromal Sarcoma with Metastatic Extension to the Inferior Vena Cava and Right Atrium Presenting as an Intracardiac Mass: A Diagnostic and Surgical Challenge
abstract: Introduction: Low-grade endometrial stromal sarcoma (LG-ESS) is a rare uterine mesenchymal malignancy (incidence 0.30/100,000 women/year) with late recurrence in 37-60% of cases. Intracardiac metastasis is exceptionally rare and life-threatening, causing venous obstruction and sudden cardiac death. We report the first documented US case of LG-ESS with metastatic extension to the inferior vena cava (IVC) and right atrium with associated bland thrombus. Case Presentation: A 65-year-old woman with known stage IIb LG-ESS presented with progressive dyspnea. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a large, mobile echogenic right atrial mass. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis demonstrated heterogeneous opacification of the right atrium and IVC. Cardiac MRI characterized a 2.2x2.7 cm right atrial lesion with linear IVC extension, showing mixed viable tumor and bland thrombus on late gadolinium enhancement. Retrospective PET/CT review (September 2025) identified filling defects at the cavoatrial junction, a finding missed due to limited familiarity with intracardiac LG-ESS, illustrating anchoring bias and preventable diagnostic delay. Transesophageal echocardiography confirmed a pedunculated mass from the IVC extending into the right atrium. Intervention and Outcomes: Following multidisciplinary discussion among cardiology, cardiothoracic surgery, and gynecologic oncology, the patient underwent surgical excision via median sternotomy with cardiopulmonary bypass. Intraoperative IVC obstruction by tumor burden required a third venous cannula to maintain hemodynamic stability. The pedunculated mass was successfully excised. Pathology confirmed metastatic LG-ESS with bland thrombus; immunohistochemistry showed positivity for CD10, ER, PR, and SMA. Fulvestrant was initiated based on hormone receptor positivity. Teaching Points: (1) LG-ESS can cause late-life-threatening intracardiac complications for which long-term surveillance is essential. (2) Cardiac MRI is crucial for tumor-thrombus differentiation and multidisciplinary discussion for surgical planning. (3) Awareness of rare extrapelvic LG-ESS presentations prevents diagnostic delays and anchoring bias. (4) Intravascular spread via gonadal and iliac veins into IVC is likely the mechanism of metastasis, consistent with intraoperative finding of IVC stalk. Conclusion: LGESS with metastasis to the IVC and right atrium with attached thrombus is an uncommon, significant, and life-threatening late recurrent feature of this malignancy. Our case highlights the importance of vigilance and a higher index of suspicion in the selected population, especially in those with indolent-to-stable disease. Complete surgical resection is the preferred strategy with multidisciplinary discussion with adjuvant hormonal therapy. Long-term surveillance is important given the high rate of late recurrence in LGESS.

title: Abstract 8151: Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Syndrome Assessment Practices: Baseline Implementation Trends Across 97 Clinical Sites in a National Quality Improvement Initiative
abstract: BACKGROUND: To enhance prevention and management of cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome, a 2023 American Heart Association Presidential Advisory recommended assessment of CKM risk factors across the life course, including screening and integration of social drivers of health (SDOH) into the clinical care model. While evidence supports that standardized CKM assessments facilitate effective risk reduction strategies, adoption of recommended assessment practices remains poorly characterized. HYPOTHESIS: We hypothesized that participating sites would report low baseline uptake of comprehensive CKM assessment activities, particularly for newer approaches such as CKM syndrome staging and CVD risk assessment with the PREVENT equations. METHODS: The American Heart Association invited 150 clinical sites to participate in an initiative focused on adoption of a CKM coordinated care model, including activation of comprehensive CKM-related assessments. Participating sites were selected based on representative factors such as CKM syndrome burden, structural SDOH influences, rurality, and health organization type. During onboarding (August 2025 - June 2026), sites complete a standardized questionnaire to document baseline implementation status. Current results represent data from respondents from August 2025 - April 2026 (n=97 sites). Researchers used additional data from Definitive Healthcare to provide descriptive characteristics regarding participating clinical sites. RESULTS: Most sites identified as outpatient (92%, n=89), with highest representation in primary care (39%, n=38). Sites represented academic (16%, n=16), non-academic (39%, n=38), and safety-net (44%, n=43) organization types (Table 1). Respondents reported which CKM-related assessment activities their sites currently conduct (Table 2). SDOH screening (75%, n=73), screening for clinical CKM co-morbidities (75%, n=73), and actively screening patient populations for CKM risk factors (73%, n=71) were most commonly performed, with frequency of joint UACR and eGFR assessments lower at 58% (n=56). Only 22% (n=21) reported measuring patient waist circumference as standard practice. Activations informed by CKM-related assessments were infrequently demonstrated. Only 28% of sites reported CVD risk estimation via the PREVENT equations (n=27), while 22% reported use of CKM staging (n=21). CONCLUSION: Findings reveal opportunities for augmenting comprehensive CKM assessment uptake across participating clinical sites. While some standard screening practices are commonly performed, assessment-informed clinical actions, including CKM staging and PREVENT-based CVD risk estimation, remain infrequently implemented. As onboarding continues, targeted implementation support to bridge these gaps will be essential for broader adoption of a comprehensive CKM model of care.

title: Current Challenges and Future Directions in US Maintenance Dialysis Care: A Policy-Innovation Perspective.
abstract: Dialysis care for patients with End-Stage Kidney Disease (ESKD) has seen minimal improvement in outcomes over the past decade, despite substantial advancements in other chronic disease fields. This article explores enduring challenges and future opportunities in outpatient dialysis care from a policy-innovation perspective. The current landscape is defined by clinical limitations and a profound economic strain on the healthcare system. However, a period of cautious optimism may be emerging. This is driven by promising innovations, including the development of wearable and implantable artificial kidneys, advanced hemodiafiltration techniques, biologically inspired therapies like bioartificial kidneys, and the integration of artificial intelligence for personalized care. Realizing the full potential of these advancements requires a multi-pronged approach involving a greater emphasis on the patient's voice, payment reforms that incentivize value over volume throughout a person's journey with kidney disease, and supportive policy changes. Yet, hurdles remain, including supply chain vulnerabilities, a growing nephrology workforce crisis, and the need to ensure equitable access to new technologies to avoid amplifying existing health disparities. A collaborative effort is essential to move toward a future where dialysis is less burdensome and facilitates a better quality of life for all people with kidney diseases.

title: Updates in cardiovascular CT imaging in 2025: A year in review.
abstract: The year 2025 brought long-term outcome data supporting coronary CT angiography (CCTA)-guided management of stable chest pain, a proposed reframing of coronary artery disease around atherosclerosis rather than ischemia, and the first large-scale real-world evaluation of a national artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled CT-derived fractional flow reserve (FFR-CT) program. This review summarizes selected advances in cardiovascular computed tomography (CCT) published in print or online during 2025. The studies span coronary artery disease outcomes and prevention, quantitative plaque analysis, photon-counting detector CT, coronary artery calcium scoring, pericoronary inflammation imaging, AI and machine learning, structural and congenital heart disease, and consensus and training documents. For each study we summarize the design, principal findings, limitations, and likely clinical implications, and we close with the barriers, including technical standardization, vendor-specific thresholds, equitable access, and the need for randomized outcome trials, that must be addressed before many of these advances can be implemented broadly.

title: Psychological resilience is associated with increased heterogeneity in the clinical aging phenotypes of patients with cancer.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Cancer and its treatments are associated with accelerated aging. Emerging evidence suggests that patients' self-reports of symptoms, functional status, and resilience can identify clinical aging phenotypes. The purpose was to identify distinct clinical aging phenotypes using: six (evening fatigue, sleep disturbance, depression, state anxiety, cognitive function, physical function); seven (addition of pain); and eight (addition of resilience) clinical indicators and evaluate for differences in patient characteristics and quality of life (QOL) outcomes among the phenotypes.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Outpatients (n = 1340) completed questionnaires prior to their second or third cycle of chemotherapy. Three separate latent variable models using six, seven, and eight clinical indicators were created. Differences among phenotypes in demographic and clinical characteristics and QOL outcomes were evaluated using parametric and non-parametric tests. Determination of clinically meaningful differences in QOL scores was done using Cohen's d.
RESULTS: For the six and seven indicator models, two and three distinct phenotypes were identified, respectively. For the eight indicator model, five distinct phenotypes were identified: Very Low (32.6%), Low (32.2%), Moderate (16.4%), High (13.2%), and Very High (5.6%) clinical age. Being female, younger, having a higher comorbidity burden, and lower functional status were associated with the worst clinical aging profiles. QOL scores decreased in a stepwise fashion and differences were clinically meaningful.
DISCUSSION: Inclusion of a measure of psychological resilience in the model allows for better discrimination of inter-individual variability in clinical aging phenotypes of oncology outpatients. This approach may assist with identification of patients at increased risk for accelerated aging.

title: Using implementation mapping to select implementation strategies for Skills TO Manage Pain (STOMP), a pain self-management intervention tailored to people with HIV
abstract: BACKGROUND: Individuals living with HIV often experience chronic pain, which contributes to diminished physical and mental health. Skills TO Manage Pain (STOMP), a pain self-management intervention tailored for individuals with HIV, has demonstrated immediate and sustained efficacy at reducing pain and strengthening pain self-efficacy. Evaluating STOMP's effectiveness in real-world settings remains a critical next step in advancing its implementation. METHODS: This article describes how we used implementation mapping to develop strategies aimed at strengthening the delivery and long-term sustainability of STOMP in HIV care settings. RESULTS: Through semi-structured interviews with 17 key informants, we identified several barriers to and facilitators of STOMP implementation. Examples included patients potentially feeling their pain is being invalidated because they are being offered a behavioral rather than biomedical intervention; however, STOMP was also an adaptable, evidence-based CBT intervention that people may perceive as a better option than opioids for pain management. We also held a community engagement studio in which key informants provided insights on how to promote equitable implementation of STOMP in HIV clinics. CONCLUSION: Using a rigorous theory-based approach, we selected ten strategies to reduce barriers and strengthen facilitators for STOMP implementation in HIV care settings. This process involved qualitative interviews and a focus group with key informants, including people with lived experience. Implementation mapping appears to be a promising approach to bolster uptake of evidence-based interventions like STOMP. In our future research, we will evaluate both our implementation strategies and the effectiveness of STOMP for improving health in people with HIV and chronic pain.

title: Neoadjuvant Therapy in Mohs Surgery: A Scoping Review of the Literature
abstract: BACKGROUND: Neoadjuvant therapies are increasingly used before Mohs micrographic surgery (MMS) to shrink tumors and reduce defect size, tumor and surgical invasiveness, and reconstruction complexity. Data on neoadjuvant agents used before MMS, their efficacy, and tolerability are limited. OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study was to analyze the literature regarding neoadjuvant therapies in MMS, protocols, outcomes, and tolerability. METHODS: A scoping review of PubMed, Embase, and Scopus was conducted on July 8th, 2025. Articles related to systemic or local chemotherapeutic and immunotherapeutic agents used neoadjuvantly in MMS were included. RESULTS: Thirty-three studies, including 303 patients, met inclusion criteria. Reports of neoadjuvant vismodegib, sonidegib, and imiquimod in basal cell carcinoma support reduction of the final defect and organ preservation. Reports of neoadjuvant imatinib for dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans show reduction in tumor size. Case reports demonstrated benefits from neoadjuvant talimogene laherparepvec in squamous cell carcinoma and pembrolizumab for desmoplastic melanoma and sebaceous carcinoma. CONCLUSIONS: Neoadjuvant therapy can be used before MMS to shrink tumors, decrease surgical defects, and improve cosmetic, functional, and disease outcomes. It should be considered for locally advanced tumors or when preservation of tissue and anatomic function is critical. Larger studies are needed to confirm whether neoadjuvant therapies improve surgical and cosmetic outcomes and reduce recurrence and metastasis.

title: A 2026 update on the epidemiology of obesity, related cardio-kidney-liver metabolic complications and beyond; a call to action.
abstract: Obesity has become a major global public health challenge and is associated with an increasing burden of metabolic and non-metabolic comorbidities. We aimed to provide an updated assessment of the global prevalence of overweight and obesity and to examine temporal trends in selected associated with excess adiposity. Data from the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) Study were analyzed to estimate the prevalence of overweight and obesity among adults aged ≥20 years in 2023, stratified by sex and age group. We additionally examined age-standardized global prevalence trends for obesity and selected diseases associated with excess adiposity, including type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), chronic kidney disease (CKD), cardiovascular disease (CVD), along with other chronic diseases associated with excess adiposity, such as dementias and obesity-related cancers, over 2000-2023.In 2023, the prevalence of overweight was generally higher in men, whereas obesity was more prevalent among women, particularly during middle age. Both overweight and obesity increased from early adulthood, peaked during middle age, and subsequently declined at older ages. Globally, obesity prevalence increased by approximately 95% between 2000 and 2023, reaching 19.5% in 2023. During the same period, the age-standardized prevalence of MASLD, T2DM, CKD, dementias, and obesity-related cancers increased. In contrast, age-standardized CVD prevalence decreased slightly and the divergent trends between obesity and age-standardized CVD prevalence highlight the multifactorial nature of cardiovascular risk and the potential impact of improvements in other cardiovascular risk factors. These findings underscore the urgent need for integrated, population-level strategies to prevent and effectively manage obesity and its complications.

title: An Evaluation of Buprenorphine Transition Strategies in a Pharmacist Led Chronic Pain Clinic.
abstract: Buprenorphine offers comparable analgesia with a superior safety profile compared to full mu opioid agonists, particularly for high-risk populations. However, optimal transition strategies remain unclear, and limited data exists evaluating patient-specific factors which may influence success. This retrospective chart review evaluated 117 patients treated at a Veterans Affairs, pharmacist-led chronic pain management clinic who attempted to transition from long-term opioid therapy (LTOT) to buprenorphine. Two transition methods were assessed: stop/start and cross-titration. Overall, 55.56% of patients successfully transitioned from LTOT to buprenorphine. The stop/start method was associated with greater odds of successful transition compared with cross-titration (OR 4.63, p < 0.001). Adverse drug reactions were more common in the cross-titration group and independently associated with treatment failure (p = 0.006). Concomitant use of non-opioid analgesics was associated with improved outcomes (p = 0.031). These findings suggest that the stop/start method, used alongside non-opioid analgesics, may be associated with more successful transition outcomes and could help inform individualized care plans for patients transitioning from full mu agonists to buprenorphine for chronic pain.

title: A Pilot Study of PMHNP Students' Knowledge, Confidence, and Attitudes to Inform Telemental Health Curriculum Enhancement.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Telemental health (TMH) has been shown to improve access to mental health services. However, a lack of formal telehealth education may be a significant barrier to the widespread effective use of this technology.
AIMS: This pilot study explored psychiatric mental health nurse practitioner (PMHNP) students' knowledge, confidence, and attitudes about delivering telemental healthcare following a telemental health curriculum enhancement.
METHODS: A multi-faceted evidence-based TMH curriculum was integrated into the PMHNP graduate program. To inform future curriculum enhancement, a mixed-methods descriptive study was conducted using a 22-item tele-OSCE (objective structured clinical exam) questionnaire to assess students' knowledge, confidence, and attitudes toward telehealth competencies. Narrative questions were included to gain greater insight into the curriculum's impact. Descriptive statistics and content analysis were used to evaluate the results.
RESULTS: A sample of 11 students showed high knowledge scores except in the areas of understanding laws and regulations for the discipline and policies for their organization. Confidence scores were high in many areas, with a few aspects showing lower scores, such as building rapport and communicating using TMH. Attitude scores were primarily strong. Narrative data indicated some students were able to develop more knowledge of laws and regulations than others. Finally, simulation and clinical aspects of the curriculum enhanced learning.
CONCLUSIONS: Formal TMH education can enhance PMHNP students' knowledge, confidence, and attitudes toward this healthcare delivery modality. The development and integration of standardized telehealth education in nurse practitioner (NP) programs is critical in promoting widespread telehealth use and improving patient outcomes.

title: Adolescent alcohol exposure leads to persistent mechanical allodynia and enhanced inflammatory pain responses in adult female rats.
abstract: Alcohol use during adolescence produces neurobiological adaptations that persist into adulthood and is a major risk factor for alcohol use disorder (AUD). Although acute alcohol use can produce analgesia, chronic use and withdrawal are associated with hyperalgesia, which may promote continued alcohol consumption through negative reinforcement mechanisms. We previously reported that adolescent intermittent ethanol exposure (AIE) produces lasting mechanical allodynia, thermal hyperalgesia, and heightened pain-like responses to acute inflammatory pain stimuli in adult male, but not female, Wistar rats. The present study tested whether increasing the timing and overall burden of AIE would reveal persistent pain-related phenotypes in female rats not previously observed. Female rats were exposed to a modified AIE paradigm from postnatal day (PND) 24-58, whereas males were exposed to the previously established AIE paradigm from PND30-58. Additionally, females exposed to the modified paradigm achieved significantly higher blood alcohol levels (BALs) than males. AIE produced persistent mechanical allodynia in both sexes, with female rats displaying prolonged reductions in mechanical withdrawal thresholds after alcohol exposure. Thermal hyperalgesia was not observed in females despite increased alcohol exposure, whereas males exhibited reduced thermal withdrawal latencies after alcohol exposure. Finally, AIE enhanced formalin-evoked nociceptive responding in both sexes. These findings demonstrate that changes in the timing (earlier) and dosing (higher) of adolescent alcohol exposure in females lead to persistent hyperalgesia in adulthood, suggesting that developmental timing and alcohol exposure burden influence modality-specific and sex-specific long-term consequences of adolescent alcohol exposure.

title: Diagnostic yield and clinical utilitY of strategies for identifying Lynch syndrome in those with colorectal neoplasia.
abstract: Lynch syndrome is the most common hereditary cancer predisposition syndrome, yet remains substantially underdiagnosed despite effective risk reduction strategies. Identification of affected individuals is critical to enable cancer prevention, early detection, and cascade testing of at-risk relatives. Multiple complementary approaches to Lynch syndrome detection exist, each with distinct strengths and limitations across clinical settings.In this review, we summarize established and emerging strategies for Lynch syndrome identification in those with a personal and family history of colorectal neoplasia. Tumor-based mismatch repair deficiency testing remains an effective and cost-efficient screening strategy but is limited by incomplete implementation and imperfect sensitivity. Direct germline testing can overcome some of these limitations and identify additional hereditary cancer syndromes, though considerations regarding yield, cost, and interpretation remain. Family history-based approaches and risk prediction models offer additional tools but are constrained by challenges in data collection and clinical uptake.Optimizing Lynch syndrome identification will require integration of these strategies alongside system-level interventions to improve access, uptake, and equity in genetic evaluation.

title: Pixel classifier-based image analysis of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis in mice.
abstract: Image analysis in histologic assessments has increasingly gained traction in comparative pathology and biomedical research. However, application has been limited by a knowledge gap, particularly for veterinary pathologists without a strong background in coding-intensive image analysis. This study describes a quantitative image analysis pipeline for liver pathology in a special diet-induced metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) mouse model, using the existing open-source, graphic user interface-based program QuPath. A machine learning-based pixel classifier was trained on annotations made in 7 digitized hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained slides to detect normal hepatocytes, macrosteatosis, microsteatosis, vessels, and inflammation. Macrosteatosis annotations were then segmented via pixel thresholding to quantify lipid droplets. Post-processing pixel thresholding was applied to quantify fibrosis in picrosirius red-stained slides and lipid droplets in H&E-stained slides. Results were benchmarked against traditional manual grading by the nonalcoholic steatohepatitis activity score (NAS). Our results revealed a significantly larger macrosteatosis area percentage in MASH diet mice than in regular diet controls. The percentage areas for steatosis, inflammation, and fibrosis strongly correlated with increasing histopathologic scores. Unlike traditional ordinal severity scoring like NAS, this approach generates continuous, quantitative data suitable for parametric statistical analysis. This method is scalable and accessible, requires no coding expertise or commercial software, and offers a blueprint for generating truly quantitative histopathology data to veterinary pathologists and others engaged in MASH research.

title: Effect of Microvascular Disease on Re-amputation Risk after Unilateral Amputation due to Diabetes or Peripheral Arterial Disease: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study was to evaluate the association between manifestations of microvascular disease (MVD) and other factors on re-amputation risk within 12 months following incident unilateral lower extremity amputation.
METHODS: This was a retrospective cohort study of 8 924 patients with first unilateral transmetatarsal, transtibial, or transfemoral amputation secondary to diabetes and or peripheral arterial disease, identified through a Veterans Affairs database. Re-amputation was defined as any subsequent ipsilateral soft tissue or bony revision or amputation to a higher level. The presence of MVD was determined using a composite variable that required the involvement of each subcomponent (neuropathy, nephropathy, and retinopathy), and also by evaluating each of the subcomponent MVD variables separately. Twenty-nine additional risk factors were evaluated in relation to the primary outcome of re-amputation. A competing risk analysis estimated the cumulative incidence of re-amputation. The effect of risk factors on re-amputation risk was estimated by computing subdistribution hazard ratios (sub-HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).
RESULTS: The twelve month re-amputation risk was 38.0% (transmetatarsal), 27.2% (transtibial), and 14.1% (transfemoral). The combined MVD variable was not significantly associated with re-amputation risk. However, re-amputation after transmetatarsal amputation was significantly elevated in patients with retinopathy, leukocytosis, or those who were on kidney dialysis, with the highest risk in those with all three (sub-HR 2.2, 95% CI 1.8 - 2.6). Similarly, for transtibial patients, the risk was higher in the presence of retinopathy, leukocytosis, and kidney dialysis, and in those with a prior ipsilateral revascularisation and those on warfarin. The highest risk was observed in those with all factors present (sub-HR 2.1, 95% CI 1.6 - 2.7).
CONCLUSION: This study identified an important association between the pre-amputation diagnosis of retinopathy and risk for subsequent failure of primary healing and need for re-amputation. Presence of retinopathy should be considered when evaluating potential failure of healing during amputation level decisions.

title: Evaluation of Pirfenidone for Recurrent Acute Pancreatitis: Protocol for a Randomized Trial.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Recurrent acute pancreatitis (RAP) is defined as a syndrome of two or more episodes of acute pancreatitis (AP), with a period of resolution in between. Management of RAP is largely supportive, with no available drug therapy to prevent recurrence or progression to chronic pancreatitis (CP). Our preclinical data suggest that pirfenidone can improve parameters of RAP and decrease progression to CP. Therefore, we decided to conduct a pilot trial to evaluate pirfenidone in patients with RAP.
METHODS: We have designed a double-blinded, multicenter, randomized, pilot clinical trial involving 60 patients. Patients with at least two diagnosed episodes of AP, separated by at least 3 mo, will be included in the trial. Patients with ongoing or recent AP (<30 d) or evidence of CP on cross-sectional imaging or endoscopic ultrasound will be excluded. Patients will be randomized to receive either placebo or pirfenidone in a 1:1 ratio. Treatment will be continued for 6 mo, with a follow-up period of up to 18 mo. The primary end points include completion of the treatment protocol and development of any grade III/IV adverse events. Exploratory secondary end points include number and severity of AP episodes, quality of life assessments, patient-reported outcome score, and progression to CP assessed via secretin MRCP, fecal elastase, and HbA1C testing.
CONCLUSIONS: There is an urgent need to identify novel therapies for RAP. Results of this pilot clinical trial may serve as the basis for a larger study evaluating the efficacy of pirfenidone in patients with RAP.

title: Prevalence and clinical correlates of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease in heart failure.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The nomenclature change from non-alcoholic fatty liver disease to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) better encapsulates the associated metabolic milieu. While MASLD is associated with increased heart failure (HF) risk, characteristics and outcomes of MASLD in patients with HF remain unclear. This paper aims to examine the prevalence and clinical correlates of MASLD in patients with HF from the Asian Sudden Cardiac Death in Heart Failure (ASIAN-HF) Registry.
METHODS: MASLD was defined as evidence of hepatic steatosis, with at least one of five metabolic criteria (among body mass index, glucose, blood pressure, triglycerides and high-density lipoprotein thresholds). Findings were externally validated in Clinical Data Analysis and Reporting System (CDARS), a Hong Kong HF cohort and BIOlogy Study to TAilored Treatment in Chronic Heart Failure (BIOSTAT-CHF), a HF cohort across 11 European countries.
RESULTS: Of 2698 patients with HF in ASIAN-HF, 927 (34.4%) had MASLD. They were younger, more often women and more likely to have HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) compared with those without MASLD. All-cause mortality was lower in MASLD versus non-MASLD (7.1% vs 11.7%, p=0.001), even after multivariable adjustment (adjusted HR (aHR) 0.58, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.86, p=0.007). All-cause mortality was also lower in MASLD versus non-MASLD in CDARS and BIOSTAT-CHF; however, after multivariable adjustment, the association remained significant only in CDARS (aHR 0.82, 95% CI 0.80 to 0.84, p<0.001) and was attenuated in BIOSTAT-CHF (aHR 1.08, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.73, p=0.750). Using waist-to-height ratio instead of body mass index in the MASLD definition reclassified <3% of patients.
CONCLUSIONS: In patients with HF, MASLD is highly prevalent, especially in younger women with HFpEF and is associated with better 1-year survival than in those without MASLD.

title: Impact of proton LET and ultrahigh dose-rate on the structural integrity of DNA in solution.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Ultra-high dose-rate (UHDR) irradiation reduces normal tissue toxicity while maintaining tumor control under isodose conditions with respect to conventional dose-rate (CONV) irradiation (the FLASH effect). But its underlying physicochemical mechanism remains highly debated. This study evaluates whether radical-radical recombination can explain this sparing without invoking bulk oxygen depletion by decoupling the roles of track structure (linear energy transfer, LET) and particle fluence and velocity on free-radical kinetics and DNA damage.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Highly purified pUC19 plasmid DNA in aqueous oxygenated buffer was irradiated with 142.4 MeV protons at CONV (∼1.0 Gy/s) or UHDR (>455 Gy/s). Samples were positioned in a water phantom and received doses ranging from 0 to 160 Gy at LETd (dose-averaged LET) values of 1.7, 4.4, and 6.5 keV/µm. Strand breaks and formamidopyrimidine-DNA glycosylase (Fpg) and endonuclease III (Nth) -sensitive base lesions were quantified by gel electrophoresis. At low LET, fluence was estimated from Φ = ρD/LET and mean nearest-track distance from dNN = 1/(2√Φ), using the dose delivered during one OH• lifetime (approximately 0.91 µs).
RESULTS: At LETd = 1.7 keV/µm, the estimated mean nearest-track distance during one OH• lifetime was ∼275 µm at 1.0 Gy/s and ∼13 µm at 455 Gy/s. Even the UHDR value was ∼100 times larger than the ∼0.1-0.13 µm OH• diffusion distance. Above ∼40 Gy cumulative dose, UHDR produced lower strand-break and enzyme-sensitive lesion values than CONV, and the CONV-UHDR difference decreased as LETd increased.
CONCLUSIONS: Proton dose-rate alone is insufficient to predict the FLASH effect-mediated tissue sparing. Our results demonstrate that sparing is a track-structure-dependent kinetic phenomenon. LET, fluence, spill structure, solution chemistry, and oxygen history must be considered together. The data constrain candidate FLASH mechanisms but do not identify a unique chemical pathway.
DEFINITIONS: Spur: a localized cluster of closely spaced ionizations and excitations.Branch: a lateral secondary-electron trajectory containing one or more additional spurs.Intra-track recombination: reactions among species generated within the same primary-particle track and its branches.Inter-track recombination: reactions between species generated by different primary-particle tracks. Track coincidence requires two tracks to be created close enough in both space and time for their reactive species to meet.Mean nearest-track distance: for randomly and independently positioned, approximately parallel tracks, the average center-to-center distance from one track to its closest neighboring track.

title: Optimizing Clinic Efficiency and Patient Flow in an Outpatient General Surgery Clinic.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Clinic workflow efficiency influences patient and employee satisfaction, impacting effective delivery of care. Utilizing lean methodology, we aim to increase the percentage of patients seen within 15 minutes of scheduled appointment to 75% and reduce nonvalue-added time (NVT) per visit by half within 6 months.
METHODS: Frontline stakeholders observed workflow inefficiencies in an outpatient general surgery clinic, leading to long wait times and generalized dissatisfaction. From August to September 2023, patient and staff flow was captured and appointment component time intervals observed. Only 35.8% of patients were seen within 15 minutes of appointment, with median appointment-to-seen time (AST) 19.00 minutes and NVT 74%. Interventions were implemented through progressive plan-do-study-act (PDSA) cycles, including changes to workflow, rooming, and scheduling template. Appointment time interval data were collected and analyzed using run charts.
RESULTS: PDSA 1 yielded median AST of 15.68 minutes, with 51.7% of patients seen within 15 minutes of appointment. PDSA 2 resulted in a median AST of 8.00 minutes, with 66.4% of patients seen within 15 minutes of appointment and reduced median NVT from 74% to 55.9%. Late in PDSA 2 in December, when the clinic was short-staffed, both median AST and NVT increased. PDSA 3 resulted in reduced median AST of 5.00 minutes, with 82.9% of patients seen within 15 minutes of appointment and reduced median NVT to 51.5%, with improved performance stability particularly with respect to AST.
CONCLUSIONS: Utilization of lean methodology with multiple targeted workflow and scheduling interventions resulted in improved efficiency in an outpatient general surgery clinic.

title: Palliative Care in Surgery: Updated Research Priorities from the Surgical Palliative Care Research Expert Consensus Conference.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Surgical palliative care (SPC) research has advanced since the 2017 research agenda, but persistent gaps in patient selection, intervention delivery, and outcome measurement limit implementation across evolving surgical care settings.
STUDY DESIGN: In November 2025, a national consensus conference convened 28 SPC experts and researchers. Through iterative discussion and consensus-building during the meeting and subsequent months, participants updated research priorities across the surgical continuum and health system context. Full methodology and participant attributes were described in Supplemental Materials https://links.lww.com/JACS/A821.
RESULTS: The updated agenda identified 11 research gaps across 3 priority areas: patient selection; interventions, care processes, and competencies; and outcome measurement. Priorities were mapped at 2 levels: surgical episodes, encompassing patient-, family-, and provider-level factors, and health systems, encompassing organizational and structural factors affecting SPC delivery. The agenda prioritizes identifying which patients benefit from SPC and when; broadening SPC beyond traditional populations; defining primary SPC competencies and the role of specialty consultation; improving communication of surgical intent, trade-offs, and preference-sensitive decisions; integrating and sustaining SPC across heterogeneous systems and care transitions; transforming clinical cultures; and developing patient-centered, context-specific surgical and systems-level outcomes. Emerging electronic health record, natural language processing, and large language model approaches may support scalable patient identification, intervention delivery, and outcome measurement, while requiring attention to bias and task-dependent performance.
CONCLUSIONS: SPC research should move beyond narrow proof-of-concept settings toward pragmatic, scalable approaches that define who should receive SPC, what should be delivered, and how success should be measured across diverse surgical environments.

title: Twenty-five years of the NIDA clinical trials network and the future of addiction research.
abstract: The National Institute on Drug Abuse Clinical Trials Network (CTN) was established in 1999 to bridge the persistent divide between addiction research and clinical practice through partnerships between researchers and community treatment providers. This editorial examines the evolution of the CTN over its first 25 years and considers priorities for its future. Drawing on the historical development of the Network and articles in this 25-year special collection, we examine changes in the populations and settings represented in CTN research, the incorporation of implementation science, the evolution of community partnerships, the scientific value of accumulated CTN data and experience, and emerging clinical and methodological priorities. Over 25 years, the CTN has developed from a network focused principally on clinically relevant effectiveness trials into a broader national infrastructure for clinical trials and translational addiction research. Its research has expanded beyond specialty addiction treatment programs into primary care, emergency departments, hospitals, community health centers, pharmacies, and other settings in which people with substance use disorders receive care. The Network has also increasingly addressed populations historically underrepresented in addiction research, incorporated implementation questions into clinical research, strengthened community engagement, and used accumulated trial data and emerging analytic methods to generate new scientific knowledge. These developments demonstrate that the value of a clinical research network extends beyond individual trial outcomes. Clinical trials should remain at the core of the CTN's scientific mission. However, trial designs and complementary research methods should be determined by the scientific questions being addressed. The CTN's future impact will depend on its ability to conduct rigorous multisite trials while incorporating implementation, representation, community partnership, and accumulated data and responding rapidly to changes in the drug supply and addiction care environment. These capabilities can help the Network generate evidence that is rigorous, relevant, timely, and more likely to improve addiction care.

title: Norfentanyl detection after negative confirmatory testing following heavy illicit fentanyl exposure: A two‐patient case series
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Prolonged fentanyl detection may complicate urine drug testing (UDT). We describe norfentanyl detection after negative confirmatory testing. METHODS: Two patients (N = 2) entering residential treatment after heavy illicitly manufactured fentanyl exposure underwent clinically indicated serial UDT with confirmatory LC-MS/MS. RESULTS: Both had negative confirmatory results followed by subsequent low-level urinary norfentanyl detection. Recurrent exposure could not be excluded. DISCUSSION: These findings demonstrate diagnostic uncertainty rather than a defined pharmacokinetic mechanism. CONCLUSIONS AND SCIENTIFIC SIGNIFICANCE: Low-level norfentanyl after negative confirmatory testing should prompt longitudinal assessment rather than automatic attribution to recurrent use or prolonged detection.

title: Abstract A123: DARC/ACKR1 genotype modifies associations between psychosocial stress and circulating immune-oncology proteins in breast cancer
abstract: Abstract Background: The Duffy Antigen Receptor for Chemokines (DARC/ACKR1) regulates inflammatory chemokine bioavailability and leukocyte trafficking. Highly prevalent among individuals of African ancestry, the Duffy-null (rs2814778 CC) genotype eliminates DARC expression on erythrocytes, altering chemokine homeostasis. Because psychosocial stress can drive immune dysregulation in cancer, we investigated whether DARC genotype modifies the relationship between perceived stress and circulating immune-oncology proteins in breast cancer patients. Materials and Methods: We evaluated a subset of 118 breast cancer patients enrolled in the NCI University of Maryland Breast Stress Study. Participants completed questionnaires assessing demographic, behavioral, and clinical factors, including perceived chronic stress via the 10-item Cohen Perceived Stress Scale. Serum collected at diagnosis underwent proteomic profiling for 92 immuno-oncology markers(Olink Target 96). Germline DNA extracted from blood was genotyped for the rs2814778 polymorphism(qPCR). Multivariable linear regression evaluated associations between perceived stress and immune-oncology protein expression stratified by DARC genotype, as well as stress x DARC interaction effects(P < 0.10). Models were adjusted a priori for age, BMI, tumor stage, and molecular subtype. Subtype-specific analyses were conducted in Luminal-like and triple-negative breast cancer subgroups. Results: Perceived stress was associated with distinct circulating immune profiles according to DARC genotype. Among Duffy-null participants, higher stress was associated with lower levels of proteins involved in immune recognition and inflammatory signaling, including MICA/B, IL-18, IL-13, CCL4, and CX3CL1, and with higher levels of chemotactic and vascular-associated proteins, including CCL20, CCL19, CXCL11, CXCL1, NOS3, TRAIL, and TIE2 (P < 0.1). Several associations were also observed in luminal-like and TNBC analyses, although effect magnitudes varied by subtype. Models evaluating multiplicative interactions between stress and DARC genotype (P < 0.1) identified genotype-dependent immune responses. Significant negative interactions occurred with MICA/B (βinteraction=−0.11, P=0.07), CCL4 (βinteraction=−0.05, P=0.02), and CAIX (βinteraction=−0.04, P=0.08), indicating greater stress-associated reductions in Duffy-null individuals; positive interactions emerged for IL-4 (βinteraction=0.05, P=0.03) and NOS3 (βinteraction=0.03, P=0.09).These findings implicated chemokine signaling, immune regulation, hypoxia, and vascular biology as potential components of genotype-dependent stress responses. Conclusions: DARC genotype substantially modified systemic immune responses to psychosocial stress in breast cancer. High stress preferentially suppressed anti-tumor and angiogenic signaling and amplified Th2 immunosuppression and endothelial nitric oxide signaling in Duffy-null individuals. Future directions will aim to identify underlying molecular networks to provide systems-level insight into DARC-mediated stress biology. Citation Format: Jamirah Y. title: Abstract B059: Patient-reported barriers to clinical trial enrollment: A site-level analysis of DCP-001 non-enrollees at an academic medical center
abstract: Abstract Background: Understanding why eligible patients with cancer decline clinical trial participation is critical to developing targeted accrual interventions. DCP-001 is a National Cancer Institute (NCI) Division of Cancer Prevention protocol within the NCI Community Oncology Research Program (NCORP). The protocol systematically captures patient-reported reasons for non-enrollment at the point of trial decision-making, which provides information rarely available through administrative databases or chart review. At present, there remains a paucity of site-level analyses, which can reveal locally actionable patterns obscured in aggregate data. Methods: This secondary analysis included adults ≥18 years enrolled on DCP-001 from 2017–2024 at the Columbia University Herbert Irving Comprehensive Cancer Center (NCORP) and affiliated sites. Patients eligible for a therapeutic or supportive care study who declined participation were included in the present analysis. Sociodemographic data were collected via the DCP-001 tool and included age, sex/gender, race/ethnicity, country of origin, primary language, education, employment, income, insurance, and marital status. Reasons for non-enrollment were classified into six domains and grouped as personal (autonomy, toxicity concerns, lack of interest) or logistical (access, time, provider timing/communication). Associations between barrier type and sociodemographic factors were assessed using chi-square tests (two-sided P<0.05). Results: Of 498 eligible patients, 324 (65%) enrolled on DCP-001; of these, 219 (68%) enrolled on an NCORP trial (170 [53%] supportive care; 49 [15%] treatment). Enrollment was not associated with race/ethnicity, education, income, or insurance. Non-enrollees had a median age of 57 years, 67% were female, and the group was diverse (40% non-Hispanic White, 35% Hispanic, 18% non-Hispanic Black, 5% Asian). The most common reasons for non-enrollment were autonomy concerns (26%), toxicity concerns (19%), and lack of interest (19%), followed by time constraints (17%), provider timing/communication (16%), and access (12%). Overall, 54% cited personal reasons and 37% logistical reasons. Personal reasons were similar by nativity (61% vs. 62%), but U.S.-born patients reported fewer logistical barriers (24% vs. 38%; P = 0.002). Similarly, English-speaking patients more often cited personal reasons (65% vs. 40%) and less often logistical barriers (23% vs. 60%; P = 0.001). Barrier type was not associated with race/ethnicity, age, education, income, or insurance. Conclusions: Among a diverse cohort of trial-eligible patients who declined participation, personal concerns, particularly about autonomy and toxicity, predominated over logistical barriers, but profiles varied by nativity and language. Site-level DCP-001 data offer a unique window into the decision-making of patients who decline clinical trials and can inform distinct, locally tailored interventions. title: Abstract C116: Tumor-educated platelets function as active regulators of prostate cancer in African Americans rather than passive bystanders in the circulatory microenvironment
abstract: Abstract Prostate cancer (PCa) is the second most diagnosed cancer and the second leading cause of cancer-related death among American men. African Americans (AAs) experience approximately a two-fold higher incidence and mortality rate compared with European Americans (EAs). Cancer-associated thrombosis is also more frequent in AA PCa patients. To investigate mechanisms underlying these disparities, the Lee laboratory has focused on the circulatory microenvironment. As tumor cells enter the bloodstream, they encounter circulating cell types including platelets. Through interactions with tumor cells and exposure to cytokines, platelets become “educated,” generating tumor-educated platelets (TEPs) whose transcriptomes and functional states are altered by tumor-derived signals. Using immunohistochemistry, we demonstrate platelets within the primary tumor microenvironment and physical interactions between AA PCa cells and platelets derived from AA PCa patients, suggesting that platelets act as active regulators of tumor progression rather than passive bystanders. Strikingly, TEPs isolated from AA PCa patients selectively enhanced invasiveness of AA PCa cell lines, a phenomenon not observed with EA-derived TEPs, revealing a previously unrecognized platelet–tumor signaling axis associated with PCa disparities. AA TEPs also induced docetaxel resistance and a quiescent stem cell–like phenotype, evidenced by decreased caspase activity, reduced proliferation, and increased expression of stem cell markers. Reciprocally, AA PCa cells stimulated tumor cell–induced platelet aggregation (TCIPA) of AA TEPs. RNA-seq analysis of AA and EA TEPs and PCa specimens identified platelet–tumor ligand–receptor signaling axes. EGF and NRG2 were overexpressed in AA TEPs, while TGFA, EGFR, and HER2 were elevated in AA PCa samples, with TGFA expression correlating with worse outcomes. Consistent with this signaling axis, the FDA-approved breast cancer therapeutics lapatinib and trastuzumab inhibited TEP-stimulated PCa cell invasiveness, suggesting a potential drug-repurposing strategy for aggressive PCa. RNA-seq also revealed enrichment of pathways associated with a hyper-aggregable platelet phenotype in AA TEPs. Consistent with this, partial inhibition of TCIPA was achieved using neutralizing antibodies targeting ADGRE5 and its ligand CD55, indicating additional pathways contribute to platelet activation. Platelets are also a source of TGFB which has been implicated in cancer stem-cell phenotypes. Supporting this model, TGFB1/2 were elevated in AA TEPs, while TGFBR1 is overexpressed in AA PCa samples. Collectively, these findings support a model in which aberrant platelet–tumor signaling through the EGF/TGFA–EGFR/HER2, CD55–ADGRE5, and TGFB–TGFBR axes promotes enhanced malignancy and drug resistance in PCa. These pathways may represent therapeutic targets and circulating biomarkers for aggressive disease, particularly in populations disproportionately affected by PCa. title: Predictors of Surveillance Imaging Non-compliance Among Patients with TEVAR for Blunt Thoracic Aortic Injury
abstract: Objectives Blunt Thoracic Aortic Injury (BTAI) is the second leading cause of death for patients with blunt trauma. Thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) has become the standard of care for high-grade BTAI, reducing morbidity and mortality while requiring long-term surveillance imaging to ensure graft integrity and prevent future complications. However, adherence to this protocol is poor. Previous studies evaluating the factors associated with post-operative imaging non-compliance have yielded conflicting results. This study aimed to evaluate predictors of post-TEVAR non-compliance inpatients presenting with BTAI. Methods A retrospective study on 23 patients was conducted using a single institution Aortic Center Database (2015-2025). Inclusion criteria included patients who were age >18 years and underwent TEVAR for BTAI. Demographic, comorbidity, hospital course, and follow-up data were collected. The Distressed Communities Index (DCI) score was derived from patient’s home address ZIP code. Time-to-event analysis defined loss to follow up (LTFU) for vascular imaging as the failure event. Patients were censored at death or if compliant through 1 year following the index TEVAR. Statistical analysis included chi-square, t-tests, and Kaplan-Meier survival. Results Based on this single-center review on TEVAR follow-up for BTAI, sex, race, and hospital length of stay did not impact compliance. Medical comorbidities were also non-significant. Patients who presented with a lower injury severity score ( P = 0.02) and lived more than 20 miles from their follow-up appointment ( P = 0.02) were more likely to be LTFU. While the type of facility was not impactful, all patients who were discharged to a non-home location were LTFU. Interestingly, DCI and insurance status had no impact on follow-up non-compliance. Conclusions This study supports the development of targeted, patient-centered surveillance strategies, especially amongst rural populations and those discharged to a non-home location. To fully understand this complex problem, further investigation using a larger database may be indicated.

title: Progressive Cranial Polyneuropathy and Myelopathy as the Initial Manifestation of Leucine Zipper 4-Positive Paraneoplastic Syndrome in Previously Undiagnosed Metastatic Testicular Seminoma.
abstract: A 50-year-old man without a significant medical history developed progressive double vision from a partial right third nerve palsy, as well as right-sided hyperreflexia and decreased temperature sensation in his right hand. Initial contrast MRI of the brain revealed enhancement of the right oculomotor nerve. Cerebrospinal fluid and serologic studies were negative or normal. Over the next 6 weeks, he developed a left sixth nerve palsy and right-sided facial sensory changes, followed by a partial left third nerve palsy and right foot drop. The patient later disclosed a 2-year history of painful right hemiscrotum swelling. Abdominal imaging and testicular biopsy revealed a Stage IIA testicular seminoma and was treated with radical orchiectomy, steroids, intravenous immunoglobulin, and chemotherapy. He continued to deteriorate, with evidence of myelitis on thoracic MRI. Initial paraneoplastic studies were negative, and research-based antibody testing revealed leucine zipper 4 autoantibody positivity, indicating a paraneoplastic syndrome.

title: Burden of hospitalizations in four adolescent and young adult (AYA) cancer survivor populations in the United States, 2006-2020.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: We describe hospitalization rates in adolescent and young adult (AYA) cancer survivors 2-5 years (Y2-Y5) from diagnosis.
METHODS: Observational study of AYA cancer survivors diagnosed 2006-2020 was conducted in two healthcare systems [Kaiser Permanente Southern California (n=7889) and Northern California (n=7338)] and two states [California (47,302) and Utah (n=7935)]. Hospitalizations were ascertained from electronic health records and statewide administrative records and stratified by whether pregnancy-related. Hospitalization rates were calculated by cohort. We estimated patient factors associated with hospitalizations using a Poisson model.
RESULTS: Most AYA survivors were women (~64% of all cohorts), mean age ~31 years at diagnosis, and non-Hispanic white (range 35.1-81.2%) or Hispanic (range 14.3-40.6%). Overall, 21-24% of AYA survivors experienced >1 hospitalization. Unadjusted hospitalization rates declined from Y2 [range 155.1-243.4 per 1000 person-years (PY)] to Y5 (range 105.8-132.0 PY) (p-trend<0.0001 in all cohorts). Factors associated with increased non-pregnancy related hospitalizations were [range of relative risks (RR)]: non-Hispanic Black race/ethnicity (RR 1.46-1.66 vs non-Hispanic white); public insurance (RR 1.57-1.93 vs commercial/military); receipt of chemotherapy (RR 1.51-1.81), and cancer type-breast (RR 1.69-1.97), cervical (RR 2.30-3.31), colorectal (2.76-3.66), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (RR 2.89-5.19), acute myeloid leukemia (2.11-5.05), and sarcoma (RR 2.70-4.96) (vs thyroid).
CONCLUSIONS: While hospitalizations decline as time from diagnosis elapses across health system settings and states, nearly 1 in 5 AYA cancer survivors experience hospitalization in early survivorship.
, IMPACT: Hospitalization rates remain elevated in some AYA patient subgroups in early survivorship, highlighting the need to identify AYAs at risk to mitigate unanticipated hospitalizations and costs.
