title: The diminishing returns of distance: Computational analysis of approach-avoidance behavior under threat of predation.
abstract: Foraging under threat of predation is a paradigmatic scenario involving the interplay between approach and avoidance motivation across species. Previous foraging paradigms in humans have revealed aspects of approach-avoidance behavior and its neural underpinnings, but have generally involved simple choices such as a binary decision to stay or flee. Here, we present results from 40 adult participants who completed the Weighing Opportunity and Loss in Foraging (WOLF) task, a novel two-dimensional foraging context with threat of predation in which participants choose from five possible actions at each turn. We fit computational models in which choices depend on the subjective utility of each option, which itself depends on approach motivation (resource richness) and avoidance motivation (predator distance). Model comparison revealed that an inverse power law model, in which the marginal subjective utility of additional distance from the wolf diminished with wolf distance, outperformed a linear model. Model parameters explained more than 75% of the variance in task performance, mediated by the average resource richness of choices (for the approach-related parameter) and the number of deaths on the task (for the avoidance-related parameters). An exploratory analysis found that self-reported anxious arousal was associated with a more linear relationship between wolf distance and avoidance motivation. The results demonstrate that a behaviorally rich foraging paradigm in which participants select from multiple options at each turn can enable explicit modeling of subjective utilities in the interplay between approach and avoidance motivation. Future work can examine neural underpinnings of complex approach-avoidance behavior and their alteration in mental health disorders.

title: MUC5B Overproduction Disrupts Club Cell Mediated Alveolar Repair in COPD
abstract: RATIONALE: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is characterized by small airway disease (SAD) and emphysema, but mechanisms linking these pathologies remain unclear. SAD arises early and is the primary site of airflow limitation, marked by epithelial injury, mucus obstruction, and bronchiole loss. Excessive production of the mucin MUC5B by bronchiolar club cells is a key feature of SAD and is associated with impaired mucociliary clearance and inflammation. Club cells also function as progenitors for alveolar type II (ATII) cells, yet how their regenerative capacity is altered in COPD is unknown. OBJECTIVES: To determine whether MUC5B overproduction in small airway club cells alters their capacity to regenerate ATII cells and contributes to emphysema progression. METHODS: We assessed MUC5B expression in human emphysematous lungs and a porcine pancreatic elastase (PPE)-induced mouse model of emphysema. Genetic approaches were used to overexpress or conditionally delete Muc5b in club cells to evaluate effects on club-to-ATII differentiation, alveolar structure, and lung function in health and emphysema. RESULTS: MUC5B is overexpressed in small airway club cells in human emphysematous lungs and animal models. Muc5b overexpression impairs differentiation of club cells into ATII cells and worsened lung function decline in emphysema. Importantly, conditional deletion of Muc5b during early disease stages restored club cell-derived alveolar regeneration. CONCLUSIONS: MUC5B overproduction links SAD to defective alveolar repair by limiting club cell progenitor function. Targeting MUC5B may restore epithelial regeneration and slow early COPD progression.

title: Bridging the research–practice gap in infant neuromotor development by harnessing principles from implementation science
abstract: The well-documented research–practice gap in healthcare typically results in an average delay of 17 years between evidence discovery and clinical care integration. This perspective article describes the application of implementation science methods to operationalize new clinical-research concepts into a scalable early physical therapy intervention supporting infant neuromotor development. Through flexible dosage delivery, adaptation of existing resources, structured stakeholder review, standardized training protocols, and systematic fidelity monitoring, we created this intervention for efficient dissemination and uptake. Using a case example, we also demonstrate effective implementation of our clinical-research concepts and suggest that the use of these specific processes of embedding implementation science tenets within trial design may help narrow the research–practice gap across disciplines.

title: Evaluating ChatGPT’s Responses to Chiropractic Patient Questions: A Comparative Study
abstract: Abstract Background Large language models (LLMs) are used at an increased frequency by patients to answer health related questions. Prior studies have evaluated LLMs and their performance with musculoskeletal (MSK) and spine domains, but have not been used to evaluate chiropractic-relevant content. Objective To evaluate ChatGPT responses to commonly asked chiropractic patient questions for concordance with chiropractic clinical practice guidelines. Methods Thirty questions addressing low back pain, neck pain, and chronic musculoskeletal pain were developed based on current U.S. chiropractic clinical practice guidelines (CPGs). ChatGPT (GPT-5.2) generated responses in isolated sessions. Responses were assessed for readability using established indices, then five licensed chiropractors independently rated each response using a 5-point Likert scale across four domains: relevance, clarity, completeness, and accuracy. Inter-rater reliability was evaluated using Krippendorff’s alpha (ordinal). Results Readability measures demonstrated that ChatGPT responses were written at approximately a college-level reading grade. Expert ratings across all domain means (standard deviation) were predominately clustered at the upper end of rating scale (1-5): Relevance 4.72 ± 0.56; Clarity 4.76 ± 0.50; Completeness 4.23 ± 0.81; Accuracy 4.00 ± 1.02. The Krippendorff’s alpha (ordinal) ranged from -0.023-0.214 across the domains, all reflective of poor inter-rater reliability. Conclusion ChatGPT responses were broadly consistent with chiropractic CPGs, though readability levels exceeded recommended patient education standards. While the expert panel frequently assigned similar scores, minor scoring differences and restricted score distributions produced low chance-corrected reliability. These findings suggest that ChatGPT can produce guideline concordant responses but readability and interpretive variability should be considered when integrating LLM generated information into patient education.

title: Iron-Based Contrast for the Heart: Clinical Promise of Ferumoxytol-Enhanced CMR.
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Ferumoxytol is an ultrasmall superparamagnetic iron oxide (USPIO) nanoparticle that was originally approved by the U.S. FDA for treating iron deficiency anemia in patients with chronic kidney disease. It has since emerged as an off-label, versatile intravascular contrast agent for cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging, and in 2025, received FDA approval for brain imaging. This review provides an overview of ferumoxytol-enhanced CMR applications primarily focused on the heart, outlines its key imaging and pharmacokinetic properties, and summarizes its diagnostic safety profile.
RECENT FINDINGS: Unlike gadolinium-based contrast agents (GBCAs), which rapidly wash out from the circulation, ferumoxytol has high r1 and r2 relaxivities and remains confined to the intravascular compartment for prolonged periods. Once metabolized by the reticuloendothelial system, its iron core is incorporated into the body's hematopoietic pathways. These unique properties enable steady-state and delayed-phase imaging, simplify complex imaging workflows, and facilitate accelerated multidimensional cardiac imaging methods. Emerging applications for ferumoxytol-enhanced CMR include myocardial perfusion assessment, multidimensional imaging, vascular and hemodynamic evaluation, and comprehensive structural heart disease imaging.
SUMMARY: Ferumoxytol expands the clinical applications of CMR by enabling imaging techniques that are not feasible with conventional GBCAs and broadening imaging options for patients in whom GBCA administration may be less desirable based on individualized clinical risk-benefit assessment, including selected patients with renal insufficiency, very young children, and pregnant women.

title: Metabolic Burden, Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease, and Cognitive Performance Among Older Adults: Analysis of 1,387 Participants from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is prevalent in older adults, yet its independent contribution to cognitive decline beyond cardiometabolic risk factors remains uncertain.
METHODS: We performed a cross-sectional analysis of 1,387 NHANES 2011-2014 participants aged ≥60 years. MASLD was defined using hepatic steatosis index ≥36 plus ≥1 cardiometabolic risk factor, excluding excessive alcohol use. Cognitive performance across memory, verbal fluency, and processing speed was summarized as a global z-score composite. Advanced fibrosis likelihood was assessed using validated non-invasive scores. Weighted multivariable linear regression adjusted for demographic, lifestyle, and cardiometabolic covariates.
FINDINGS: MASLD was not associated with global cognition (β = 0.027; p=0.526) or individual domains after full adjustment. Advanced fibrosis risk was unrelated to cognition except for lower CERAD memory with high FIB-4 (β = -0.319; p=0.016). Greater metabolic risk factor burden showed graded associations with poorer cognition: ≥2 risk factors linked to lower global cognition (β = -0.23; p=0.036) and memory (β = -0.33; p=0.003); ≥3 showed borderline memory impairment (β = -0.24; p=0.049). In MASLD participants, ≥2 risk factors were associated with lower global cognition (β = -0.19; p=0.021) and ≥3 with reduced verbal fluency (β = -0.27; p=0.045). Processing speed declined only at highest metabolic burden in fibrosis-stratified models (e.g., DSST β = -0.51; p=0.015).
CONCLUSION: MASLD and related fibrosis risk were not independently linked to cognitive impairment. Metabolic risk factor burden primarily drove poorer cognition, especially memory, in both the overall sample and those with MASLD, with processing speed affected only at the highest burden.

title: Diastolic Dysfunction Predicts Cardiorespiratory Fitness and Clinical Outcomes in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
abstract: Abstract Background Echocardiographic indices of diastolic dysfunction are routinely obtained in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), but their relationships with cardiorespiratory fitness and long-term clinical outcomes remain poorly defined. Objectives This study therefore sought to determine the extent to which E/e’, left atrial volume index (LAVi), and peak tricuspid regurgitation velocity (TRV max ) relate to peak oxygen uptake, ventilatory efficiency, their longitudinal trajectories, and clinical outcomes in HCM. Methods We retrospectively studied patients with HCM who completed cardiopulmonary exercise testing within 7 days of resting echocardiography. Each diastolic index was related to percent-predicted peak oxygen uptake (V̇O 2 ), ventilatory efficiency (V̇E/V̇CO 2 slope), their serial trajectories, and a composite of heart failure hospitalization, transplantation, or death. Results Among 441 patients with HCM (mean age 49 ± 16 years; 66% men), each SD higher E/e’, LAVi, and TRV max was independently associated with lower peak V̇O 2 (−6.0, −3.6, and −6.3 percentage points of predicted) and higher V̇E/V̇CO 2 slope (+0.9, +1.0, and +2.5; all P ≤ 0.045), nonlinearly for E/e’ with peak V̇O 2 and LAVi with V̇E/V̇CO 2 slope. On serial testing, only LAVi predicted progressively worsening V̇E/V̇CO 2 slope (+0.4/yr/SD; 95% CI: 0.13-0.68; P = 0.005). Over a median of 4.8 years, 118 of 436 patients (27.1%) reached the composite endpoint, for which LAVi was the strongest echocardiographic predictor (adjusted HR: 1.68/SD; 95% CI: 1.40-2.03). Conclusions In HCM, resting diastolic indices were associated with cardiorespiratory fitness, and higher LAVi was independently associated with a steeper rise in V̇E/V̇CO 2 slope and heart failure events. Resting diastolic phenotyping may complement exercise testing.

title: Implications of the 2026 Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Syndrome Guideline for GLP-1 Receptor Agonist and SGLT2 Inhibitor Eligibility Among US Adults
abstract: ABSTRACT Background The 2026 cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome guideline broadens recommendations for glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA) and sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i), but the increment over pre-2026 standards is unknown. We estimated the number and clinical profile of US adults newly eligible under this guideline. Methods Cross-sectional analysis of adults aged 30-79 years in the 2011-2018 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey. Adults were newly eligible if they met 2026 CKM guideline indications but not pre-2026 American Diabetes Association, American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association heart failure, Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes, or obesity guideline indications. Sensitivity analyses used 2 US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) label standards. Results Among 175.17 million US adults, 111.84 million (63.8%) were already eligible for either class. The CKM guideline added 7.48 million (95% CI: 6.48 to 8.47), a 6.7% increase, all for GLP-1RA and none for SGLT2i: 6.49 million with overweight (body mass index 27.0-29.9 kg/m2, ethnicity adjusted) and no other cardiometabolic disease, and 0.99 million with type 2 diabetes and 10-year PREVENT cardiovascular risk ≥7.5%. Newly eligible adults (86.8% CKM stage 1) were younger (46.2 vs 52.9 years), leaner (27.8 vs 33.0 kg/m2), and at lower 10- and 30-year PREVENT risk (3.6% vs 8.1%; 11.3% vs 19.6%; all P < 0.001). Against FDA labeling, 14.15-25.17 million were newly eligible (7.66-18.20 million for SGLT2i). Assuming a 20% relative risk reduction, the projected number needed to treat per cardiovascular event prevented was 243 over 10 years and 56 over 30 years (ages 30-59) in adults with overweight, versus 61 and 26 in already eligible adults. Conclusions Relative to pre-2026 society guidelines, the 2026 CKM guideline newly confers a GLP-1RA indication on 7.48 million US adults, predominantly at lower cardiovascular risk. Whether treating these adults improves outcomes in a cost-efficient manner remains to be established. What Is Known The 2026 AHA/ACC/ADA/ASN cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome guideline recommends GLP-1 receptor agonists and SGLT2 inhibitors according to CKM stage, comorbidity, and PREVENT-predicted risk, including a GLP-1 receptor agonist for adults with overweight at CKM stage 1. National estimates of eligibility for these agents predate the guideline and have largely used FDA labeling, rather than professional society guidance, as the reference standard. What the Study Adds Relative to pre-2026 society guidance, the guideline newly identifies 7.48 million US adults aged 30 to 79 years as treatment candidates, all for a GLP-1 receptor agonist and none for an SGLT2 inhibitor; most have overweight without other cardiometabolic disease. Newly eligible adults are younger and at lower predicted cardiovascular risk than those already eligible; the projected number needed to treat is 243 over 10 years and 56 over 30 years, so expected benefit rests on a lifetime horizon that outcome trials and cost-effectiveness analyses have not yet tested.

title: USFDA Oncology Drug Approvals from 2014- 2025: Comparing non-immunotherapy and immunotherapy approvals, their endpoints, and their efficacy
abstract: ABSTRACT In the United States the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), and in Europe, the European Medicines Agency (EMA) are responsible for regulatory approvals of anti-cancer therapeutics. We examined regulatory approvals by both agencies in the period between 2014 and 2025 and compared immunotherapy and non-immunotherapy approvals for the treatment of cancer. We asked whether the approvals were similar in terms of trial size, endpoints, and development time. We present the data based on the FDA approvals given that the US agency has approved some therapies either rejected by or yet to be approved by the EMA. Beginning with the approval of pembrolizumab for melanoma in 2014 through early 2025 we identified 143 immunotherapy and 211 non-immunotherapy approvals. In the first few years the time to approvals of immunotherapies was markedly less but over time the duration has approached that of non-immunotherapies – with durations of 2079 and 2357 days in 2024/2025 due largely to a median trial size of 461 and 698 participants. Surrogate endpoints have overwhelmed overall survival as the primary endpoint for approval, and we find that with non-immunotherapies only a median of 60% of the benefit predicted from progression/disease/recurrence/event-free survivals translates to overall survival, significantly less than the 99% of the surrogate benefit translated to overall survival for immunotherapies. While the FDA and EMA approval portfolios are very similar, the EMA is on the whole more skeptical/conservative in its approvals. The last decade has seen substantial advances, but much remains to be accomplished against a formidable foe. The size and duration of trials need to be addressed and meaningfully reduced and the validity of surrogates defended.

title: The blunt truth: The role of marijuana in PTSD after intentional traumatic injury.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Survivors of interpersonal violence experience high rates of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and rates of marijuana use are rising among young adults. There is however, limited understanding of marijuana use patterns among survivors of interpersonal violence with PTSD. We evaluated relationships between PTSD and marijuana use following injury and hypothesized that PTSD-positive patients would report elevated follow-up marijuana use.
METHODS: Between 10/2019 and 7/1/2024, we prospectively collected data on patient demographics, PTSD, substance use (including marijuana), and PROMIS-29 quality of life domains for adult trauma patients admitted to an urban, academic, level-1 trauma center. Participants were screened at baseline and at 6- or 12-month follow-up. Injury characteristics were collected from the institutional trauma registry. Among the intentionally injured, we compared patients by follow-up PTSD screening results. We excluded patients who screened positive for PTSD at baseline. Using multivariable logistic regression we assessed relationships between follow-up PTSD and marijuana use, including demographic and injury characteristics as covariates. Our primary outcome was dichotomized follow-up marijuana use.
RESULTS: Of 105 participants injured by intentional trauma with complete follow-up data, 69 screened negative for PTSD at baseline and therefore were included in this analysis. Patients who screened positive for PTSD at follow-up had greater marijuana use at baseline (29% vs 3%, p = 0.002) and follow-up (42% vs 13%, p = 0.007), and worse PROMIS-29 scores in all domains (p ≤ 0.01), compared to PTSD-negative patients. In multivariable analysis, screening positive for PTSD was associated with 7.1 times greater odds of marijuana use at follow-up (p = 0.007, CI:1.7, 29.5).
CONCLUSIONS: PTSD and marijuana use were closely associated in survivors of interpersonal violence. Screening efforts should account for marijuana use specifically. Routine screening for marijuana use could improve recognition of psychological challenges after trauma and could help identify patients at risk for development of PTSD.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, prognostic/epidemiological.

title: Cefepime-Zidebactam for Infections Caused by Carbapenem-Resistant Gram-Negative Bacteria, Including Metallo-β-Lactamase Producers: A Phase 2, Open-Label, Single-Arm, Multicenter Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Infections caused by carbapenem-resistant (CR) Gram-negative bacteria, particularly metallo-β-lactamase (MBL)-producers, have limited treatment options. Cefepime-zidebactam retains activity against these pathogens, but clinical data are limited.
METHODS: This prospective, open-label, single-arm, multicenter phase 2 trial enrolled adults with CR Gram-negative infections. Participants received intravenous cefepime-zidebactam for 7-21 days with renal dose adjustment. The Micro-ITT population included participants with a confirmed qualifying CR Gram-negative pathogen, and the CME population included those meeting prespecified evaluability criteria. The primary endpoint was investigator-assessed clinical cure at TOC in the CME population. Outcomes were also reviewed by an external adjudication committee.
RESULTS: Seventy-two participants received treatment; 68 were included in the Micro-ITT population and 60 in the CME population. Among 68 qualifying isolates, 56 (82.4%) were MBL producers, predominantly NDM-β-lactamase producers. Investigator-assessed clinical cure at test-of-cure in the CME population was 91.7% (95% confidence interval, 81.6%-97.2%), and favorable microbiological outcome at TOC was 90.0%. Among participants in the CME population with MBL-producing pathogens, clinical cure was 93.9% and favorable microbiological outcome was 91.8%. External adjudication in the CME population yielded clinical cure of 86.7% and favorable microbiological outcome of 85.0%. Twenty-eight-day mortality was 2.8%. Treatment-related adverse events occurred in 15.3%, and serious treatment-related adverse events occurred in 2.8%.
CONCLUSIONS: In 60 evaluable adults with carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative infections, predominantly MBL-producing (81.7%) and cUTI/AP (58.3%), investigator-assessed TOC clinical cure was 91.7%; post hoc adjudicated cure was 86.7%. Day 28 all-cause mortality was 2.8%, and cefepime zidebactam was well tolerated.

title: Mechanistic insights into RAN translation within the huntingtin coding sequence.
abstract: Nucleotide repeat expansions support production of toxic peptides from putatively non-coding regions of the human genome without use of an AUG initiation codon. This process, known as repeat-associated non-AUG (RAN) translation, was originally described at CAG repeats with products generated in all three possible reading frames. Recently, cryptic mis-splicing of messenger RNAs in which the CAG repeat acts as a splice acceptor was proposed as an alternative mechanism for RAN protein production. To investigate this, we generated DNA- and RNA-based reporters to assess RAN translation in the context of a CAG repeat expansion in exon 1 of the Huntingtin gene (HTT), associated with Huntington disease. HTT CAG repeats support RAN translation in both the alanine (GCA) and glutamine (CAG) frames, with or without upstream AUG start codons or near-AUG cognate codons, and at levels comparable to RAN translation from CGG and GGGGCC repeats. CAG RAN translation products were readily detectable from in vitro transcribed RNAs transfected into human cells and rodent neurons-suggesting that plasmid-based aberrant splicing into CAG repeats cannot fully explain the observed phenomena. These findings indicate that RAN translation from HTT CAG repeats shares key mechanistic parameters with other disease-associated repeat expansions.

title: Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) training programs offer hospitalists expertise in research and quality improvement.
abstract: Evidence-based, personalized, safe, and efficient interprofessional care are cornerstones of hospital medicine. Hospitalists are uniquely positioned to conduct the research and improvement needed to identify opportunities for better care. However, this requires expertise that is gained through focused training. The Department of Veterans Affairs has long been a leader in clinician training and has several programs that provide training in research and improvement. These programs allow hospitalists to gain skills and expertise for career development and advancement. Encouraging early career hospitalists to pursue such training is essential to strengthening the field and making hospital care safer, more effective, and efficient.

title: Novel Mechanometabolic Signaling Cascade Linking Efferocytosis to Inflammation Resolution.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Apoptotic cell clearance by macrophages, termed efferocytosis, resolves inflammation and promotes tissue repair, whereas defective efferocytosis contributes to chronic inflammatory diseases such as atherosclerosis. Putrescine biosynthesis, driven by the rate-limiting enzyme ODC1 (ornithine decarboxylase 1), has emerged as a key efferocytosis-induced metabolic pathway that promotes inflammation resolution. However, the mechanisms regulating ODC1 during atherosclerosis remain undefined. Here, we investigated the mechanisms controlling ODC1 and putrescine biosynthesis and identified a novel integrin αv-FAK (focal adhesion kinase)-Rac1 (Rac family small GTPase 1)-STAT3 (signal transducer and activator of transcription 3)-MYC (MYC proto-oncogene) signaling axis that becomes progressively impaired during atherosclerosis.
METHODS: We performed metabolomic and cytokine profiling of human atherosclerotic plaques and assessed ODC1 expression in lesional macrophages from humans and mice. Mechanistic studies used apoptotic cell- or polystyrene bead-exposed macrophages, Ldlr-/- mice with hematopoietic integrin αv deficiency fed a Western-type diet, single-nuclei RNA sequencing, and bulk RNA sequencing.
RESULTS: Putrescine levels negatively correlated with inflammatory mediators, and ODC1 expression in lesional macrophages declined with disease progression in humans and mice. Engulfment of apoptotic cells or polystyrene beads increased ODC1 expression through an integrin αv- and actin polymerization-dependent mechanism. Hematopoietic integrin αv deficiency exacerbated lesion size and necrosis, reduced efferocytosis, and decreased fibrous cap thickness. Single-nuclei RNA sequencing showed no changes in lesional cell composition but revealed activation of inflammatory pathways specifically in integrin αv-deficient macrophages. Mechanistically, phagocytosis-induced ODC1 expression relied on integrin αv-mediated STAT3 activation and MYC-dependent Odc1 transcription. Bulk RNA sequencing showed that apoptotic cell-exposed human macrophages lacking integrin αv upregulated atherogenic mediators and inflammatory pathways, an effect reversed by restoring putrescine levels.
CONCLUSIONS: Together, these findings uncover a previously unrecognized mechanistic link between phagocytosis and macrophage metabolism, which we identify as a case of mechanometabolism, and demonstrate how its dysregulation compromises inflammation resolution and promotes atherosclerosis.

title: 2-Hydroxybenzylamine acetate (2-HOBA) in rheumatoid arthritis: a randomized phase 2 clinical trial
abstract: Patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) have increased oxidative stress, which may contribute to inflammation and elevated blood pressure. 2-hydroxybenzylamine acetate (2-HOBA) scavenges reactive downstream oxidative stress products, including isolevuglandins (IsoLGs), which covalently bind proteins and alter their structure. This pilot study evaluated the safety and tolerability of 2-HOBA, its effect on IsoLG-protein adducts, and potential effects on disease activity and blood pressure in RA. We conducted a single-center, randomized, double-blind, parallel-group, phase 2 clinical trial. Patients with RA ( n = 32) were randomized to receive 2-HOBA 750 mg or matching placebo orally three times daily for 4 weeks. Primary outcomes were safety, tolerability, and change in cells with IsoLG-protein adducts. Exploratory outcomes included changes in disease activity and blood pressure. Linear mixed-effects models assessed treatment effects of 2-HOBA versus placebo. The modified intention-to-treat population included 30 participants (2-HOBA n = 16, placebo n = 14). 2-HOBA was safe and well tolerated, with similar adverse event rates between groups. Compared with placebo, 2-HOBA did not significantly alter cells with IsoLG-protein adducts (treatment effect 3.4%; 95% CI, -4.0 to 10.9; p = 0.35) or plasma IsoLG-lysine adducts (− 2.14 pg/mg protein; 95% CI, -5.01 to 0.73; p = 0.14). No significant effects were observed on DAS28-CRP or blood pressure ( p > 0.05); however, swollen and tender joint counts and systolic blood pressure showed small, non-significant improvements with 2-HOBA. 2-HOBA was safe and well tolerated in patients with RA. Over the 4-week treatment period, no statistically significant changes in cellular or plasma IsoLG-protein adducts or exploratory clinical outcomes were observed. ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05274243. Registered March 1, 2022. https//clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT05274243.

title: Timing of Addiction Consultation and Alcohol Withdrawal Management in Hospitalized Adults
abstract: ABSTRACT Objective To evaluate the association of early addiction consultation with withdrawal pharmacotherapy and complications in hospitalized patients with alcohol withdrawal. Methods Retrospective single-center cohort of adult hospitalizations with alcohol withdrawal (diagnosis code or CIWA-Ar ≥10 within 24 hours) from July 2020 to January 2026. Exposure was an addiction consult service order within 24 hours of arrival, compared with no or later consultation. Primary outcomes were intensive care unit (ICU) transfer after the first 24 hours and delirium tremens or withdrawal seizure not present on admission. Process outcomes included phenobarbital and thiamine administration within 24 hours and benzodiazepine dose in the first 48 hours. Secondary outcomes included length of stay and 30-day death or return to hospital. Results Of 4,663 hospitalizations, 1,379 (29.6%) received early consultation. After adjustment, early consultation was associated with lower odds of ICU transfer (odds ratio [OR] 0.73; 95% CI 0.54–0.99) and fewer episodes of delirium tremens (risk difference −1.09 per 100; −1.45 to −0.73), with no significant difference in withdrawal seizure. Early consultation was associated with phenobarbital (OR 1.57; 1.32–1.86) and thiamine (OR 1.23; 1.07–1.41) within 24 hours, higher 48-hour lorazepam-equivalent dose (ratio of geometric means 1.44; 1.32–1.57), shorter stays (ratio 0.92; 0.88–0.97), and lower odds of 30-day death or return to hospital (OR 0.78; 0.66–0.91). Conclusions Early addiction consultation was associated with earlier, more intensive withdrawal pharmacotherapy, lower odds of ICU transfer, and fewer episodes of delirium tremens, although the complication associations were sensitive to cohort definition.

title: The endoplasmic reticulum resident molecular chaperone, GRP170, is required to maintain podocyte homeostasis and function
abstract: The glomerulus, a unique capillary network in the nephron, filters an entire blood volume approximately 300 times a day. Specialized epithelial cells known as podocytes form a critical component of the glomerular filtration barrier, and diseases linked to podocyte injury include minimal change disease, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, and diabetic kidney disease. Because podocytes are terminally differentiated, their ability to respond to external stress is critical. One class of proteins, molecular chaperones, protects against cell stress by preventing protein misfolding, assisting in protein refolding, maintaining protein solubility, and modulating protein translation. We previously found that depletion of one such molecular chaperone, GRP170, in the renal tubule induces the unfolded stress response (UPR), a stress-responsive pathway originating in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), and causes apoptosis and acute kidney injury in mice. Here we report on a new constitutive podocyte-specific GRP170 knockout mouse (GRP170 Pd-/- ). Surprisingly, GRP170 Pd-/- mice were born healthy. Within a month, however, these mice exhibited profound glomerular injury manifesting as proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, hyperlipidemia, and kidney injury. Concomitant with glomerular injury, we observed increased expression of the pro-apoptotic UPR target, CHOP, and altered ER morphology in podocytes. Our new model not only defines a protective role for GRP170 against glomerular injury but provides a new avenue to test the therapeutic potential of small molecule UPR modulators to treat glomerular diseases.

title: Differential resting-state functional connectivity of anterior and posterior cerebellar divisions with canonical networks in PTSD.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a complex psychiatric condition that may develop following exposure to a singular or series of traumatic events producing disruptions in cognitive and affective processes. Although the cerebellum is traditionally linked to voluntary movement coordination and balance, recent work highlights posterior cerebellar regions are involved in affective and cognitive functions. Our goal was to investigate functional connectivity between the cerebellum and canonical cortical resting-state networks in PTSD, with a particular focus on the posterior cerebellum based on previously reported structural changes associated with PTSD on the posterior cerebellum.
METHODS: A total of 313 participants ( M age = 35, 218 females) were comprised of two groups; 119 PTSD patients and 194 healthy controls from eight study sites within the ENIGMA-PTSD working group. The cerebellum was segmented using ACAPULCO into posterior and anterior divisions. Resting-state fMRI preprocessed with HALFpipe was used to assess the functional connectivity of the anterior and posterior divisions of the cerebellum with major canonical cortical networks.
RESULTS: Compared to the non-PTSD control group, the PTSD group had greater connectivity of the posterior cerebellum with somatomotor (t = 4.32, p = 0.040) and default mode (t = 4.41, p = 0.040) networks. Correspondingly, PTSD symptom severity was linked to greater connectivity differentially affecting the posterior relative to the anterior cerebellum with major cortical networks. PTSD symptom severity was positively associated with greater posterior cerebellum connectivity with the default mode (t = 4.32, pfdr=0.020), somatomotor (t = 3.57, pfdr=0.040), limbic (t = 3.74, pfdr=0.036), salience (t = 3.61, pfdr=0.040) and central executive network (t = 3.59, pfdr=0.040).
CONCLUSION: PTSD symptom severity is associated with altered connectivity of the posterior cerebellum with default mode, salience and central executive networks. Cortical connections with the posterior cerebellum, an important socioemotional hub, are involved in PTSD pathology.

title: Targeting poorly differentiated thyroid cancer with bispecific antibodies and CAR T cells from the human anti-TSHR autoantibody repertoire
abstract: Abstract Background Poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma (PDTC) has no effective systemic treatment option once radioactive iodine and tyrosine kinase inhibitors fail. The thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor (TSHR) is highly tissue-restricted and the anti-TSHR autoantibody repertoire of thyroid autoimmunity offers sequence-defined, fully human binders. We asked whether this repertoire can be converted into an off-the-shelf T cell-redirecting therapy for PDTC. Methods TSHR expression was profiled on a 151-case thyroid cancer tissue microarray (TMA), 50 healthy controls and on fresh tumor material. Eight anti-TSHR clones, four of human autoimmune origin (M22, K1-18, K1-70, 5C9) and four murine (IRI-SAb2, IRI-SAb3, 9D33, 1H7), were reformatted as CD3-engaging bispecific antibodies (bsAbs; anti-TSHR Fab × anti-CD3 scFv) and, for leading clones, as chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells. Activity was compared in vitro , across graded and mixed antigen densities and in a CAL-62-Luc-TSHR xenograft model, using healthy-donor (HD) or thyroid cancer-patient T cells. Results TSHR was retained on a substantial fraction of PDTC, including metastatic lesions. Both formats mediated potent, antigen-selective killing and the leading bsAbs suppressed xenograft growth in vivo . For CAR T cells, scFv heavy/light-chain orientation was decisive. Anti-TSHR bsAbs cleared mixed cultures far beyond the antigen-positive fraction matching mosunetuzumab and indicating a modality-intrinsic bystander effect. Patient-derived T cells obtained on or after oncological treatment retained full effector function. Conclusions The anti-TSHR autoantibody repertoire provides a promising source of binders for off-the-shelf bispecific antibodies targeting TSHR-positive thyroid cancer, while CAR T cells offer an autologous alternative.

title: Association of continuous glucose monitoring metrics with cardiovascular and kidney outcomes in type 2 diabetes: Data from the GRADE-CGM substudy.
abstract:
AIMS: We compared associations of CGM-derived time in range (TIR) and glucose management indicator (GMI) vs. HbA1c with CVD and eGFR decline in type 2 diabetes.
METHODS: We studied 1363 participants with ≥10-day blinded CGM in the GRADE-CGM Substudy. Exposures were TIR and GMI, with HbA1c as comparator. Cox models estimated hazard ratios (HR) for the composite of any CVD or all-cause death. Linear mixed-effects models estimated eGFR slope. Models were adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, treatment group, diabetes duration, and baseline eGFR, then mutually adjusted each CGM metric with HbA1c.
RESULTS: Over median 2.3 years, 74 CVD or death occurred, eGFR slope was -2.37 mL/min/1.73m2/year. GMI, HbA1c, and TIR were each significantly associated with CVD/death (adjusted HR 1.44 [1.21-1.71] per 1% GMI; 1.37 [1.16-1.61] per 1% HbA1c; 0.73 [0.61-0.87] per 20% TIR). Higher GMI and HbA1c were associated with faster eGFR decline (-0.35 [-0.63, -0.07] and - 0.38 [-0.65, -0.11] mL/min/1.73m2/year); TIR was not significantly associated with eGFR slope. After mutual adjustment, most associations of CGM metrics and HbA1c with outcomes were attenuated.
CONCLUSIONS: In type 2 diabetes, GMI and HbA1c were comparably associated with cardiovascular and kidney outcomes, whereas TIR was associated with cardiovascular outcomes only.

title: Evaluating the Interplay and Impact of Quality and Technical Variations on Performance of AI Models in Multi-Institutional Prostate MRI Datasets
abstract: Abstract Purpose To evaluate whether visually assessed high-quality prostate MRI, as defined by the Prostate Imaging Quality (PI-QUAL) scoring system, is sufficient to ensure consistent AI model performance, or whether hidden acquisition-related technical effects introduce variability that cannot be detected through visual inspection. Methods This retrospective study included 568 bpMRI scans from seven institutions, classified using PI-QUAL v2 into high-quality (scores 2-3) and low-quality (score 1) groups. Quantitative image quality features were extracted using MRQy from T2w and ADC sequences. Three experiments were conducted on high-quality scans: (1) unsupervised clustering to identify hidden technical batch effects; (2) V-Net models (M₁) for prostate capsule segmentation on T2w using single-cluster and balanced multi-cluster training strategies; and (3) VoxelMorph-based deformable registration (M₂) to align ADC maps to T2w images. Performance metrics included DSC, precision, recall, volume ratio, HD95, ASSD, and TRE. Kruskal-Wallis tests assessed cross-cluster variability, Two One-Sided Tests (TOST) evaluated performance equivalence, and bootstrap resampling quantified training efficiency. Results Clustering identified four clusters among 277 high-quality bpMRI scans. Single-cluster models showed variable performance (DSC=0.41-0.85) with significant batch effects (p<0.001), even with 140 training samples. The balanced multi-cluster model (n=60) eliminated batch effects (p=0.075), achieved equivalent performance (p<0.001), and demonstrated 2.23-fold greater training efficiency despite using 2.3-fold fewer samples. Registration performance also varied significantly across clusters (TRE=0.86-5.47 mm, p<0.001). Conclusion Acquisition-related batch effects significantly impact AI generalizability in prostate MRI, even among high-quality scans. Quantitative clustering enables detection of technical variations and supports diversity-aware training strategies that achieve equivalent performance with 2.3-fold fewer samples while eliminating batch effects. Summary Acquisition-related batch effects significantly impair AI generalizability in prostate MRI, even among scans meeting PI-QUAL quality standards. Clustering-based diversity-aware training strategies successfully eliminated these batch effects and achieved 2.23-fold greater training efficiency compared to single-site approaches, demonstrating that strategic technical diversity outweighs dataset size for developing robust, clinically deployable AI models. Key Points Acquisition-related batch effects significantly impair AI performance on prostate MRI, exceeding the impact of visual image quality as assessed by PI-QUAL scoring. Even the model trained on the largest single cluster exhibited significant batch effects (p<0.001). In contrast, a balanced multi-cluster model eliminated cross-cluster variability (p=0.075) while maintaining equivalent performance and requiring a smaller sample size. Diversity-aware training achieved 2.23-fold greater training efficiency (95% CI: 2.18-2.29) with 2.3-fold fewer samples, demonstrating that technical diversity outweighs data quantity for robust AI generalization. Clinical relevance Addressing batch effects is essential for developing reliable, generalizable AI tools for prostate MRI interpretation.

title: Physics-informed neural network for predicting myocardial mechanics from in vivo physiological measurements
abstract: Structural heart diseases (SHDs) are characterized by progressive myocardial remodeling, yet the tissue-level mechanical properties underlying this process cannot be measured directly in vivo. This limitation restricts the ability of conventional physiological measurements to fully characterize myocardial remodeling and disease progression. Here, we present a physics-informed neural network (PINN) framework that integrates constitutive biomechanics with organ-level physiological measurements to simultaneously infer myocardial biomechanical descriptors and predict physically consistent stress responses. By embedding a hyperelastic constitutive model within the learning process, the framework links physiological measurements with tissue-level mechanics while preserving biomechanical consistency. Using right ventricular remodeling in pulmonary hypertension (PH) as a representative model of SHDs, the proposed framework accurately reproduced nonlinear stress-stretch behavior and outperformed conventional data-driven machine learning approaches for stress prediction. Furthermore, incorporation of PINN-derived tissue-level descriptors with organ-level physiological measurements improved disease stratification and enhanced separation between control, mild, and severe PH remodeling states. These findings support physics-informed constitutive learning as an interpretable framework for integrating organ-level physiology with tissue-level biomechanics and establish a foundation for future biomechanics-informed characterization of myocardial remodeling across SHDs.

title: Intestinal epithelial- or hepatocyte-specific deletion of polymeric immunoglobulin receptor does not alter ethanol-induced liver disease in mice.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Secretory immunoglobulin A (IgA) is the dominant mucosal antibody and is transported across epithelial cells by the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor (Pigr). Although chronic alcohol consumption disrupts intestinal barrier function and alters mucosal immunity, the contribution of Pigr-mediated IgA transport to alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD) remains unclear.
METHODS: Intestinal epithelial cell-specific (PigrΔIEC) and hepatocyte-specific (PigrΔHep) Pigr-deficient mice and littermate controls were subjected to the oral chronic-plus-binge Lieber-DeCarli ethanol feeding model (NIAAA model). PigrΔHep mice were additionally evaluated in an oral chronic Lieber-DeCarli ethanol feeding model for 8 weeks. Fecal immunoglobulin concentrations, liver injury, steatosis, inflammatory gene expression, bacterial translocation, and ethanol metabolism-associated genes were assessed.
RESULTS: Intestinal deletion of Pigr numerically reduced fecal IgA concentrations following ethanol feeding, although this difference did not reach statistical significance, whereas fecal IgM concentrations remained unchanged. Ethanol-induced liver injury, steatosis and inflammation were comparable between PigrΔIEC and Pigrfl/fl littermate mice. In addition, markers of bacterial translocation, including systemic lipopolysaccharide levels and hepatic bacterial DNA, were similar in both genotypes following ethanol administration. Hepatocyte-specific Pigr deletion similarly did not affect ethanol-induced liver injury, steatosis, inflammatory responses, or bacterial translocation in two ethanol feeding models.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings demonstrate that deletion of Pigr in either intestinal epithelial cells or hepatocytes alone is insufficient to alter ethanol-induced liver disease, indicating that loss of Pigr in either compartment alone is insufficient to disrupt mucosal immune homeostasis during chronic ethanol exposure.

title: Wnt10b is required for the increase in cancellous bone caused by oxidized phospholipids blockade.
abstract: Oxidized phospholipids containing phosphatidylcholine (PC-OxPLs), present on oxidized low-density lipoproteins (OxLDL) and apoptotic cells, are pathogenic in osteoporosis. PC-OxPLs are bound by the IgM E06 antibody, which blocks their deleterious effects. Overexpression of the antigen-binding domain of E06 (E06-scFv) increases bone mass in 6-month-old mice and attenuates high fat diet- and age-induced bone loss by increasing osteoblast number and function. The mechanisms mediating the anabolic effect of oxidized phospholipids blockade are unclear. In previous work, we showed that E06-scFv upregulates the expression of Wnt10b and Wnt signaling in vivo. We report herein that the bulk of Wnt10b in the bone microenvironment originates from osteoblast lineage cells. OxLDL decreases the expression of Wnt10b and Wnt target genes in osteoblastic cells, and single cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) of mesenchymal cells reveals an increase in Wnt10b and Wnt target genes in pre-osteoblasts and osteoblasts of E06-scFv transgenic mice compared to WT. Loss of Wnt10b prevents the increases in BMD by DXA and in vertebral and femoral cancellous bone in 6-month-old E06-scFv transgenic male mice, and attenuates these increases in female mice. Collectively, these findings indicate that oxidized phospholipids decrease bone mass, at least in part, by suppressing Wnt10b.

title: Race-ethnic minoritized veterans diagnosed with sleep apnea, insomnia, and COMISA at the Veterans Health Administration have lower all-cause mortality than Non-Hispanic White veterans.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Few data exist exploring the relationship between sleep apnea (SA), insomnia, comorbid insomnia and sleep apnea (COMISA) and mortality among race-ethnic minoritized (REM) US veterans. This study compares all-cause mortality among Veterans Health Administration (VHA) patients diagnosed with these sleep disorders by race-ethnicity.
METHODS: The study included veterans with confirmed diagnoses and prescribed treatment for insomnia and/or SA, within the VHA, from 1999 to 2023. Using self-reported data, eight race-ethnicity groups were generated (i.e., Non-Hispanic White [NH-W], Non-Hispanic Black [NH-B], Hispanic White [H-W], Hispanic Black [H-B], Non-Hispanic Asian [NH-A], Non-Hispanic American Indian/Alaska Native [NH-AIAN], Non-Hispanic Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander [NH-NHPI]). Sleep diagnoses required International Classification of Diseases documentation. Additionally, insomnia was defined in those prescribed sleep medication or CBT-I while SA was defined in those prescribed positive airway pressure (PAP). All-cause mortality was extracted from national databases. For each sleep disorder, multivariable logistic regression determined the association between race-ethnicity and all-cause mortality, using NH-W as reference. Models were adjusted for demographics, comorbidities, medications, exposure time, and neighborhood socioeconomics.
RESULTS: This cohort consisted of 1,544,541 veterans (70% NH-W, 20% NH-B, 6.0% H-W, 1.2% NH-A, and 0.9% NH-AIAN). In adjusted analyses, compared to NH-Ws, REM veterans had lower mortality in SA (NH-A OR 0.30 [95% CI 0.27-0.33]; NH-NHPI OR 0.79 [95% CI 0.74-0.85], insomnia (NH-A OR 0.34 [95% CI 0.31-0.37]; NH-NHPI OR 0.84 [95% CI 0.74-0.86], and COMISA (NH-A OR 0.28 [95% CI 0.23-0.35]; NH-AIAN OR 0.71 [95% CI 0.61-0.83].
CONCLUSION: These data suggest that REM veterans using VHA sleep care have lower sleep disorder-related all-cause mortality than NH-White veterans, suggesting attenuated racial-ethnic mortality disparities within this equal-access healthcare setting.

title: Innate immune signaling relays environmental cues to mitophagy for metabolic adaptation to obesity.
abstract: The mechanisms by which pancreatic β cells sense and communicate environmental cues to mitochondria to maintain insulin secretion remain poorly understood. We identified that β cells transduce metabolic stress, such as during obesity or glucolipotoxicity, through the innate immune signaling adaptor TRAF6 to regulate mitochondrial quality control. TRAF6 was dispensable for β-cell function at baseline yet was essential for glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in mouse or human β cells following nutrient excess. TRAF6 was required for the recruitment of components of both ubiquitin- and receptor-mediated mitophagy pathways to clear dysfunctional mitochondria following metabolic stress. Interestingly, concomitant loss of the ubiquitin-mediated mitophagy effector Parkin restored glucose homeostasis and mitophagy flux in TRAF6-deficient β cells by relieving impediments in receptor-mediated mitophagy. Together, we found that TRAF6 forms a molecular relay linking environmental signals to multiple mitophagy pathways to equip β cells with the means to adapt to metabolic demand and prevent diabetes.Abbreviations: ADP: adenosine diphosphate; ATP: adenosine triphosphate; BNIP3: BCL2 interacting protein 3; GSIS: glucose-stimulated insulin secretion; HFD: high-fat diet; MFN2: mitofusin 2; PRKN: parkin RBR E3 ubiquitin protein ligase; RNF41/NRDP1: ring finger protein 41; SQSTM1/p62: sequestosome 1; T2D: type 2 diabetes; TAX1BP1: Tax1 binding protein 1; TLR: Toll-like receptor; TRAF6: TNF receptor associated factor 6.

title: Dementia and PDE5 inhibitors: A retrospective cohort study of veterans
abstract: Abstract Background Dementia is an escalating global public health crisis with profound consequences. Repurposing established medications, such as phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5) inhibitors, offers a promising avenue for mitigating dementia risk and progression. Methods This retrospective cohort study utilized national data from the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs to examine whether PDE5 inhibitor use was associated with reduced dementia incidence and delayed dementia diagnosis among 878,240 male Veterans with erectile dysfunction (ED). Propensity score matching generated well-balanced exposed (PDE5 inhibitor users) and unexposed control groups. Baseline dementia prevalence was similarly low in both groups. Results During longitudinal follow-up, new diagnoses of Alzheimer, frontotemporal, and vascular dementia were significantly lower among PDE5 inhibitor users than among controls, with odds ratios (ORs) of 0.91 for Alzheimer dementia (95% CI, 0.85–0.96), 0.83 for frontotemporal (95% CI, 0.69–1.00), and 0.84 for vascular dementia (95%, CI 0.79–0.89). Time-to-diagnosis analyses and Kaplan–Meier curves further demonstrated that PDE5 inhibitor exposure was associated with substantial delays in dementia onset, ranging from two to three years across several subtypes. Associations persisted across sensitivity analyses. Conclusions The observed protective effect may be explained by vascular and neuroprotective mechanisms unique to PDE5 inhibitors. Limitations include reliance on administrative codes, lack of adherence data, and restriction to a male Veteran population with ED, which may limit generalizability. Nonetheless, these findings highlight the potential of PDE5 inhibitors to reduce dementia incidence and delay its onset, warranting further prospective research and possible clinical trials to explore this novel therapeutic strategy.

title: Med1 deletion reprograms dental epithelium into a hair-forming epidermal architecture associated with Trp63 induction.
abstract: Ectodermal fate decisions between tooth enamel and skin hair are governed by transcriptional regulation and tissue architecture. Deletion of the Mediator subunit Med1, which links enhancer activity to transcriptional output, induces a striking lineage conversion characterized by ectopic hair formation in mouse incisors. Here, we investigated the cellular and transcriptional mechanisms underlying this process. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic analyses revealed extensive remodeling of the incisor epithelium following Med1 deletion, whereby dental cells are converted into hair germ-like populations while retaining dental identity. Epidermal fate is associated with induction of the master regulator Trp63. Mechanistically, Med1 deletion leads to chromatin opening where TRP63 enriches at alternative MED12 containing enhancers that associate with the transcription of epidermal genes. Together, these findings suggest that Med1 loss promotes hair formation through unusual reprogramming of the dental lineage to an epidermal state rather than direct trans-differentiation to skin epithelium, providing new insights in ectodermal plasticity.

title: Catastrophic Bone Cement Implantation Syndrome Identified Real Time with Transesophageal Echocardiography.
abstract: Characterized by unexpected hypoxia, hypotension, or hemodynamic collapse, bone cement implantation syndrome (BCIS) is a rare complication of orthopedic surgeries. During the process of utilizing cement to aid in prosthetic implantation, increased intramedullary pressure can lead to embolization of mixed contents (cement, fat, air,) into the heart. By mechanical obstruction and inflammatory response, BCIS can lead to catastrophic cardiovascular collapse. Herein, we present an 81-year-old man with grade three BCIS with pulseless electrical activity during a left hip arthroplasty with the aid of transesophageal echocardiography.

title: β3‑adrenergic receptor agonist improves recovery after volumetric muscle loss and is associated with increased intramuscular brown/beige adipogenic activity in mice
abstract: Abstract Background Volumetric muscle loss (VML) often results in chronic muscle weakness, limb dysfunction, and even permanent disability. Current research primarily focuses on cell and extracellular matrix transplantation, but there is a lack of studies on the physiologically supportive intervention to enhance endogenous muscle recovery after VML. Recent studies have shown that β3-adrenergic receptor (β3AR) agonists can increase intramuscular UCP-1 expression and the proportion of PDGFRα-GFP/UCP-1 double-positive cells, a process associated with muscle recovery. This study aims to elucidate the role of the β3AR agonist Amibegron in promoting intramuscular brown/beige-like adipogenic activity to improve muscle atrophy, fibrosis and limb function after VML injury in mice. Methods Three-month-old PDGFRα-GFP reporter mice and C57BL/6J mice were used in this study. A VML injury model was created in the tibialis anterior (TA) muscle using a biopsy punch. To induce fibro/adipogenic progenitors (FAPs) to differentiate into beige-like adipocytes, the β3AR agonist Amibegron was administered via intraperitoneal injection. Limb function was assessed by gait analysis at 2 and 6 weeks post-VML, and muscle histomorphological examination and RT-qPCR for muscle gene expression analysis were performed at the corresponding time points. Results Compared with the vehicle control group, histology and gait analysis showed that Amibegron administration for 2 and 6 weeks increased intramuscular brown/beige adipogenic activity and modestly improved VML-injured muscle mass, fibrosis, and limb function. Moreover, at 6 weeks of Amibegron administration, limb function showed a significant positive association with uncoupling protein-1 (UCP-1) expression. Conclusions β3AR agonist Amibegron attenuates VML-induced muscle atrophy and fibrosis and improves limb motor function. These improvements are associated with increased brown/beige activity, but the causal role of FAP-derived BAT is not yet established. Given systemic administration, benefits likely involve both local and systemic β3AR effects. This study provides a potential therapeutic strategy for VML.

title: Sleep trajectories in pregnancy: associations with trauma exposure, PTSD, and postpartum depression
abstract: Sleep during the perinatal period is often highly disrupted due to maternal biopsychosocial changes that accompany pregnancy. Poor sleep quality is a symptom of PTSD, while insomnia often emerges after a traumatic event and commonly co-occurs with PTSD. Trauma exposure as well as insomnia have been linked to increased risk for postpartum depression (PPD). The current study examined sleep trajectories across pregnancy and into the postpartum period, the impact of trauma exposure and PTSD on these sleep trajectories, and associations between these sleep trajectories and PPD. Participants completed psychiatric diagnostic evaluations for PTSD and other mental health conditions, as well as validated self-ratings of insomnia and depressive symptoms at four time points across pregnancy and at 6 weeks postpartum. Participants were categorized into one of four groups: (a) trauma exposure with PTSD, (b) trauma exposure with another mental health condition, (c) trauma exposure with no mental health conditions, or (d) no reported trauma exposure or current mental health conditions. Longitudinal growth mixture modeling revealed two distinct sleep trajectories across pregnancy: poor sleep (28.5%) and normative sleep (71.5%). Trauma-exposed participants with PTSD or other mental health conditions were more likely to have poor sleep profiles. Participants with poor sleep profiles had significantly higher depressive symptoms. These findings support the need for targeted interventions addressing insomnia in trauma-exposed pregnant women with psychiatric sequelae to improve outcomes during and after pregnancy.

title: Orexin deficiency and cardiometabolic risk in narcolepsy: mechanistic pathways and therapeutic implications.
abstract: Narcolepsy type 1 (NT1) results from autoimmune destruction of orexin-producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus. While traditionally viewed as a sleep disorder, accumulating evidence indicates that orexin deficiency produces widespread cardiometabolic consequences-including obesity, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, metabolic-associated steatotic liver disease, and major adverse cardiovascular events-that cannot be fully explained by weight gain or medication effects alone. This review examines four overlapping mechanisms through which orexin deficiency drives cardiometabolic risk. First, loss of orexin disrupts the coupling of hunger drive with arousal and energy expenditure. Orexin neurons interact with neuropeptide Y (NPY)/agouti-related peptide (AgRP) and pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) circuits and project to reward and cognitive control pathways; their absence impairs satiety signaling, blunts hedonic reward processing, and uncouples food intake from physical activity. Second, orexin has direct peripheral metabolic effects-enhancing beta-cell function, promoting adipocyte insulin sensitivity, and suppressing hepatic gluconeogenesis. Loss of these actions promotes insulin resistance, atherogenic dyslipidemia, and hepatic steatosis. Third, disrupted sleep architecture and autonomic dysfunction compound metabolic risk. Orexin loss produces state-dependent dysautonomia-reduced resting sympathetic drive with inadequate parasympathetic compensation during sleep-contributing to nondipping blood pressure and elevated cardiovascular risk. Disease-specific barriers, including cataplexy avoidance, further limit physical activity. Fourth, the autoimmune inflammatory process may contribute to systemic metabolic inflammation, though the extent of ongoing inflammation after neuronal loss remains uncertain. These mechanisms are interdependent and mutually reinforcing. Selective orexin receptor 2 agonists such as oveporexton offer the first opportunity to restore lost orexin signaling. Whether this translates into cardiometabolic improvements warrants systematic evaluation in future trials.

title: Depression severity and sleep efficiency's associations with amyloid burden are additive but dependent on underlying genetic risk in late life depression.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Evidence linking late-life depression (LLD) to amyloid beta (Aβ) burden remains mixed, possibly in part due to limited examinations of the confounding role of comorbid sleep disturbance and the moderating role of the apolipoprotein E (APOE) ɛ4 gene.
METHODS: We analyzed 110 older adults (ages 65-88, 66% female) with LLD to jointly model depression severity and sleep disturbance's relationship with Aβ, and to examine the moderating role of APOE ɛ4 genotype.
RESULTS: Depression severity, sleep efficiency, and sleep duration did not demonstrate a direct relationship with Aβ; however, a significant APOE ɛ4 moderation effect occurred for depression severity and sleep efficiency. In APOE ɛ4 carriers only, higher depression severity and lower sleep efficiency were associated with greater total Aβ burden and indicated greater likelihood of reaching clinical cutoffs for amyloid positivity. The effects of depressive symptoms and sleep efficiency were statistically unique and additive. Exploratory analyses demonstrated APOE ɛ4 also moderated the effect of lifetime duration of untreated depression on increased Aβ.
DISCUSSION: Depression severity and sleep efficiency's relationship with Aβ may be dependent on the presence of the APOE ɛ4 allele. This, among other individual differences, may partially explain mixed findings examining LLD as a risk factor for Alzheimer's disease. Furthermore, these findings do not suggest that the relationship between depression severity and amyloid is explained by the confounding role of sleep duration or sleep efficiency.

title: Cannabis for sleep in older adults: use has outpaced the science
abstract: Cannabis use among older adults, defined here as those over 50 years of age, has increased rapidly, and sleep disturbance is among the most common reasons for use. Yet, despite growing use of cannabis and individual cannabinoids to facilitate sleep, evidence supporting their efficacy, tolerability and safety in older adults remains limited. Most experimental studies of cannabinoids and sleep have been conducted in younger adults, often using products and formulations that differ substantially from those currently available. The subjective perception of improved sleep, which may drive increased use is often not supported by objective polysomnography or actigraphy data. Aging is accompanied by changes in sleep physiology, pharmacokinetics, body composition, the endocannabinoid system, multimorbidity, and polypharmacy that may alter cannabinoid effects. As a result, findings derived from younger populations may not generalize to older adults. Furthermore, regular and repeated use of tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and cannabis leads to the development of tolerance and withdrawal-related sleep disruption complicates interpretation of longer-term effects. The evidence for cannabidiol (CBD) and cannabinol (CBN) in sleep remains sparse. Rigorous studies specifically enrolling older adults are virtually nonexistent. Given the rapid growth of cannabis use for sleep in this population, randomized controlled trials incorporating both subjective and objective sleep measures, age-specific pharmacokinetics, drug interactions, and longer-term outcomes are urgently needed to guide clinical care.

title: Multimodal Immune Profile Score (IPS) as a Pan-Cancer Biomarker for Stratifying Outcomes of Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Benefit in Microsatellite Stable Colorectal Cancer and Rare Solid Tumors
abstract: Abstract Background Immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapies have revolutionized oncology, but identifying patients who benefit remains a challenge, particularly in populations where ICIs are not the standard of care, including microsatellite stable colorectal cancer (MSS CRC) and rare solid cancers. We evaluated real-world performance of the Immune Profile Score (IPS), a validated DNA- and RNA-based molecular signature, in these cohorts. Methods In an exploratory analysis, we analyzed two real-world cohorts: 1) MSS CRC; and 2) MSS, tumor mutational burden-low rare solid cancers treated with off-label ICI. IPS-High and IPS-Low were calculated using a previously validated threshold. Cox proportional hazards models were fit to demonstrate prognostic utility for real-world overall survival (rwOS). In MSS CRC, time-to-next-treatment (TTNT) on prior non-ICI therapy was compared to rwOS on subsequent ICI therapy. Results In MSS CRC (n=46), IPS-High patients (13%) demonstrated clinically meaningful improvement in rwOS versus IPS-Low (Median OS: not reached vs 7.3 months; HR = 0.22, 90% CI 0.04-1.16). While IPS was not associated with TTNT on the preceding non-ICI line (HR = 1.07, 90% CI 0.60-1.91), it was associated with OS in patients receiving later line ICI (HR 0.21, 90% CI 0.04-1.22). In the rare cancers cohort (n=90; 26 unique malignancies), IPS-High (17.8%) was associated with longer OS to ICI therapy (HR = 0.26, 90% CI 0.11-0.61), even when restricted to histologies represented in both IPS groups (HR = 0.18, 90%, CI 0.05-0.62). Conclusions Preliminary evidence suggests that IPS may serve as a generalizable, pan-cancer biomarker capable of stratifying outcomes for ICI treatment in populations traditionally excluded from immunotherapy benefit.

title: Neural Repair Therapies After Stroke: II. Principles for Clinical Trials.
abstract: Stroke remains a leading cause of human disability worldwide. Additional approaches beyond acute stroke therapies are needed to improve patient outcomes. Neural repair therapies focus on promoting neural plasticity in surviving tissue rather than modifying the acute injury; examples include behavioral training, drugs, biological therapies, and neural stimulation. This review discusses principles related to patient selection, control group design, intervention timing, choice of outcome measures, experience-dependent plasticity, use of biomarkers, and statistical considerations, each of which emerges from a review of key stroke recovery trials. Patient selection strategies may benefit from incorporating neuroimaging and neurophysiology biomarkers to ensure viability of treatment targets. Modality-specific outcome measures offer advantages over global disability scales for repair-based trials. The timing of intervention is critical given evolving poststroke biology and the existence of critical periods for plasticity. Repair-based therapies benefit from pairing with concomitant experience of sufficient intensity and appropriate type to shape and reinforce brain circuits. Consideration of these key principles is expected to improve the design of trials that aim to promote neural repair and improve function after stroke. Researchers and clinicians should attend to these factors when designing and interpreting clinical trials to maximize the likelihood that neural repair therapies will improve disability after stroke.

title: Neural Repair Therapies After Stroke: I. Therapeutic Advances.
abstract: Stroke is a leading cause of disability worldwide. Neural repair therapies, distinct from acute stroke therapies, target surviving neural elements to promote plasticity after the acute injury has occurred. Repair therapies encompass a broad and rapidly evolving therapeutic landscape, ranging from behavioral training, drugs, and biological agents to neural stimulation. In this review, we highlight major advances across these therapeutic categories, focusing on the evidence base and readiness for clinical adoption. Intensive behavioral interventions, including constraint-induced movement therapy and telerehabilitation, result in meaningful gains even in chronic stroke. Biological therapies-growth factors, monoclonal antibodies, and stem cell approaches-show promise but face translational challenges. Pharmacological strategies targeting serotonergic and dopaminergic systems have yielded mixed results. Neural stimulation approaches span a spectrum of invasiveness, with vagus nerve stimulation now Food and Drug Administration-approved and emerging candidates including cerebellar deep brain stimulation and spinal cord epidural stimulation showing early promise. These studies have provided important lessons for neural repair trial design. Synthesizing evidence across modalities, we highlight how therapeutic advances are reshaping the landscape of poststroke recovery and identify the most promising opportunities for clinical translation. Emerging neural repair strategies stand to substantially improve function after stroke.

title: Spatial Neurophysiological Gradients at High Resolution Differentiate Tumor Types in the Human Cortex at the Tumor-Brain Interface.
abstract: Brain tumors interact bidirectionally with neural circuits, but direct electrophysiological evidence in the human brain across tumor types remains limited. We analyzed intraoperative clinical, mesoscale, and high-density surface electroencephalography recordings from 100 participants undergoing tumor resection, epilepsy surgery, or deep brain stimulation. Population-averaged measures poorly separated diagnoses, whereas spatially resolved aperiodic exponent and high-gamma activity varied with both tumor distance and nearby tumor volume fraction across scales. Gradients differed among IDH-mutant glioma, IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, and metastases. Connectivity further distinguished infiltrative gliomas: beta coherence across tumor-brain connections was reduced in IDH-mutant tumors (p=0.0006; Kruskal-Wallis; mean coherence: tumor-brain 0.26, tumor-tumor 0.44, brain-brain 0.34), unlike IDH-wildtype tumors or metastases. Physiological abnormalities extended into radiographically normal-appearing brain, indicating tumor-type-dependent physiological signatures that may dynamically map the tumor-brain interface complementing structural imaging, with future possibilities as a spatial biomarker of tumor infiltration and network organization in humans.

title: The paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus differentiates threat and safety cues during delayed recall in humans.
abstract: The neural mechanisms supporting delayed threat memory recall in humans remain poorly understood. Animal studies indicate that the paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus (PVT) contributes to threat-memory retrieval after longer retention intervals, but whether the human PVT shows cue-related discriminability during delayed recall remains unclear. Human neuroimaging studies of threat learning have largely focused on memory assessed within 24-48 h, limiting insight into neural responses when previously threatening cues are re-encountered after longer delays. Here, adult participants completed threat acquisition on Day 1 and returned 7-10 days later (n = 28) for a delayed threat-memory recall task while undergoing fMRI. We examined activity in the dorsal midline thalamus centered on a histology-informed PVT region of interest. During Day 1 acquisition, the PVT did not discriminate between CS+ and CS-, despite differential electrodermal activity (EDA) and unconditioned stimulus expectancy ratings. In contrast, during early Day 7 recall, the PVT showed greater activation to previously reinforced CS+ than CS-. In an independent sample (n = 56), PVT activity similarly did not discriminate between CS+ and CS- during acquisition or immediate extinction, but overall PVT activation was greater during acquisition than extinction, regardless of CS type. These findings provide preliminary evidence that a human PVT-centered dorsal midline thalamic region is sensitive to prior threat reinforcement during delayed recall, while also showing engagement during acute threat-learning contexts. More broadly, they support future investigation of PVT-centered thalamic circuitry in the persistence, retrieval, and updating of threat memories, as well as in salience-related processes.

title: Macrophage Plasma Membrane Coating Enhances Nerve Delivery of Stably Labeled Polymeric Nanoparticles
abstract: Abstract Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP) is the leading cause of acute autoimmune flaccid paralysis and the most common subtype of Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS). A key pathogenic event in AIDP is localized inflammation of the blood–nerve barrier (BNB), which enables transendothelial migration of circulating autoreactive leukocytes into peripheral nerves. Experimental autoimmune neuritis (EAN), a well-established rat model of GBS, has provided critical insights into AIDP pathophysiology; however, therapeutic options remain limited, in part due to the restrictive BNB. Nanomedicine offers a unique approach to deliver a therapeutic payload across the BNB and to nerves while minimizing off-target effects and systemic toxicity. We previously found that EAN-associated BNB permeability promotes passive accumulation of long-circulating nanoparticles (NPs) in inflamed nerves at advanced disease stages. While promising, we hypothesize that surface modification with ligands that target the underlying pathology can enhance site-specific targeting and improve NP delivery to EAN nerves. Here, we developed a NP-based drug delivery system using rat macrophage-derived plasma membrane vesicles (mNPs) to target affected peripheral nerves in EAN, leveraging the inflammation-driven pathology of the disease. We demonstrate that mNPs exhibit enhanced specificity and accumulation within inflamed nerves at both early and advanced stages of EAN. Interaction with the BNB is intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1)-dependent and leads to association with endoneurial cellular targets, including myelin-associated glia. These findings highlight the potential of macrophage-mimetic NPs as a platform for targeted therapeutic delivery and support their use as a vector for repurposing promising therapeutics for immune-mediated neuropathies.

title: Association Between Trust in Healthcare Providers and Readiness to Deprescribe in Older Adults: A Cross‐Sectional Comparative Study in the United States and Japan
abstract: ABSTRACT Background Understanding how patient trust in healthcare providers is related to readiness to deprescribe is essential for optimizing deprescribing. This study examined this association among older adults with polypharmacy in the U.S. and Japan. Methods We conducted cross‐sectional surveys involving Japanese older adults receiving care from a community hospital and primary care clinic (Kawasaki City, n = 185) and American older adults recruited to a research registry within a university hospital system (Pittsburgh, n = 107). Cohorts were recruited using similar inclusion criteria (5+ prescriptions, community‐resident, stable regimens, recent physician care, no dementia). Participants completed the 11‐item Patient Perceptions of Deprescribing short form to assess readiness to deprescribe (range 6–30) and trust in healthcare providers (range 5–25). Results Greater trust in providers was associated with lower readiness to deprescribe across both samples, with no significant interaction by location. A higher number of medications was associated with greater readiness. Although U.S. participants had higher readiness (16.7 vs. 15.4, p < 0.05) and trust (21.9 vs. 19.8, p < 0.001), the greater readiness observed among U.S. participants remained after adjustment for demographics and clinical characteristics (+2.45 points, p < 0.01). Conclusions Greater trust in healthcare providers was consistently associated with lower readiness to deprescribe across both samples. Although U.S. older adults demonstrated greater readiness to deprescribe compared to Japanese counterparts, the association between trust and motivation was similar across settings. This finding suggests that how trust functions in patient–provider relationships may be important for designing shared decision‐making interventions for deprescribing.
