title: Kilohertz Transcranial Magnetic Perturbation (kTMP) for Upper Extremity Motor Recovery After Stroke: A Nonrandomized Pilot Trial
abstract: Structured Abstract Importance Upper extremity impairment is a leading cause of post-stroke disability, yet clinically approved neuromodulation therapies are currently limited by the risks and costs of surgical implantation. There is an unmet need for non-invasive brain stimulation. Objective To evaluate the feasibility, safety, and preliminary clinical efficacy of a novel form of non-invasive brain stimulation, kilohertz transcranial magnetic perturbation (kTMP), for upper limb motor recovery after stroke. Design A single-center, open-label trial was conducted between September 2025 and April 2026 and comprised a 4-week standard-of-care baseline period, 4 weeks of active treatment with kTMP combined with motor training, and a 4-week follow-up. Setting Academic research center. Participants Seven individuals with chronic stroke and upper extremity motor deficits. Intervention: Four weeks of kTMP (3 sessions/week), a brain stimulation approach using magnetic induction to generate subthreshold electric fields, paired with motor tasks. Main Outcomes Change in Fugl-Meyer Assessment for Upper Extremity (FMA-UE) scores across study periods (standard-of-care baseline, active treatment, follow up). Secondary outcomes included measures of movement smoothness (Spectral Arc Length, SPARC) and fragmentation (mean velocity peak count), and intervention tolerability ratings. Results Across 7 participants (mean [SD] age, 57.4 [8.7] years; 4 males; mean [SD] time poststroke, 3.5 [2.1] years). No device-related adverse events occurred, and the intervention was well-tolerated (participants rated sensation intensity at an average of less than 0.5 on a 0-10 scale). FMA-UE scores remained stable during the baseline period (mean change, +0.14 points; 95% CI, –1.21 to 1.50; adjusted P =.98), increased significantly following the kTMP-intervention (mean change, +7.00 points; 95% CI, 5.31 to 8.69; adjusted P =.047), and were sustained at the 4-week follow-up (mean change, –1.33 points; 95% CI, –2.42 to –0.25; adjusted P =.13). Movement smoothness improved significantly within 1 week of kTMP onset (mean change, 1.48 points; 95% CI, 0.49–2.47; adjusted P =.03); movement fragmentation showed a similar but nonsignificant trend. Conclusions and Relevance This pilot trial provides preliminary evidence that kTMP combined with motor tasks is safe, feasible, and may support upper extremity recovery. These pilot data warrant large, randomized controlled trials to evaluate efficacy in support of poststroke motor recovery. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier NCT06317194 Key Points Question Is kilohertz transcranial magnetic perturbation (kTMP) a safe, feasible, and effective non-invasive intervention for improving upper extremity motor recovery in chronic stroke? Findings In this single-center, open-label pilot trial of 7 participants with chronic stroke, upper extremity motor impairment (FMA-UE) remained stable during a 4-week baseline period and significantly improved (mean change, +7.0 points) following 4 weeks of active kTMP treatment combined with motor tasks, with gains sustained at 4-week follow-up. No device-related adverse events occurred. Meaning These preliminary findings suggest that kTMP is safe and feasible and may support upper extremity motor recovery after stroke, warranting further evaluation.

title: Applying the Implementation Research Logic Model (IRLM) as a research planning tool in a multi-project, rural health initiative to improve cardiovascular health service delivery outcomes and quality.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Increasingly, domestic and global initiatives are being designed to build synergistic networks of leading researchers to tackle major health challenges. In this case study, we applied the Implementation Research Logic Model (IRLM) to individual projects to enhance collaboration, learning and knowledge generation across a large research network.
METHODS: The ReciPROcal Innovations to Improve Cardiovascular Care in Rural America (Rural PRO-CARE) network, is a five-project initiative funded by the American Heart Association. The network used the IRLM to facilitate implementation planning and learning across projects testing a variety of implementation strategies to improve cardiovascular health outcomes in rural America. A collaborative case study approach identified determinants, implementation strategies, mechanisms and outcomes for each project using the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR), the Expert Recommendations for Implementing Change (ERIC), and Implementation Outcomes Framework (IOF) respectively. Projects developed causal pathway diagrams to define mechanisms of action for their specified implementation strategies. Semi-structured group interviews using an After-Action Review (AAR) approach, elucidated each teams' understanding of how the IRLM worked, what was successful and how the process could improve.
RESULTS: Within the first year of the initiative, each project developed an IRLM which provided a visual and theoretical structure for planning, implementation and evaluation. This process identified similarities and differences across projects' determinants, strategies and outcomes. The most frequently identified barriers to effective implementation of cardiovascular health strategies in rural America were high care and insurance costs, complex cardiovascular intervention workforce limitations, limited scope of practice, misaligned external policies, conflicting patient beliefs/knowledge, and lack of readiness for change. The most frequently identified implementation outcomes across projects were reach, followed by acceptability and sustainability/maintenance. From the AAR, all project teams noted greater ease and use of common implementation language and reported linking facilitators and barriers to strategies, mechanisms, and intended outcomes deepened team members' alignment on project goals. New strategies to overcome barriers were highlighted through the IRLM process and specific measures were selected to assess implementation.
CONCLUSION: The IRLM strengthened cross-site learning by making common determinants and synergies visible across projects enabling the network to target shared challenges more strategically and improve coordination across the initiative.

title: Tissue-specific inflammatory responses to systemic LPS in mice with LysM-lineage Hmgb1 deletion.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Systemic lipopolysaccharide (LPS) exposure induces peripheral inflammation that can engage neuroimmune pathways. High-mobility group box 1 (HMGB1) may contribute to peripheral-central communication, but the role of lysozyme M (LysM)-expressing cells in circulating HMGB1 and compartment-specific inflammatory responses remains unclear.
METHODS: Male 7-8-week-old HMGB1 fl/fl LysM-Cre + mice and HMGB1 fl/fl LysM-Cre - littermate controls received LPS (5 mg/kg, i.p.) or saline. Plasma HMGB1, midbrain inflammatory gene expression, cervical lymph node (CLN) transcriptional responses, and choroid plexus CD45 immunoreactivity were assessed at 3 h and 7 days. Spleen, liver, and bone marrow transcriptional responses and Y-maze performance were assessed at 7 days.
RESULTS: LPS increased plasma HMGB1 at 3 h and 7 days without significant genotype differences. Despite comparable circulating HMGB1, LysM-lineage Hmgb1 deletion was associated with altered expression of selected midbrain inflammatory transcripts at both time points and with distinct acute and temporal CLN transcriptional responses. At 7 days, splenic responses largely overlapped between genotypes, whereas liver and bone marrow gene-level responses were limited. LPS increased choroid plexus CD45 immunoreactivity at both time points without genotype effects. Y-maze outcomes showed no significant genotype, treatment, or interaction effects.
CONCLUSIONS: LysM-lineage Hmgb1 deletion is associated with compartment- and time-dependent inflammatory responses following sublethal LPS-induced endotoxemia. The dissociation between plasma HMGB1 and genotype-associated midbrain and CLN responses indicates that total circulating HMGB1 did not fully reflect compartment-specific responses in this model, highlighting the importance of anatomical context in peripheral-central immune signaling.

title: Electronic Health Record-Embedded Structural Interventions to Improve Sepsis Bundle Quality Measure Performance: A Quality Improvement Initiative at a Veterans Affairs Medical Center.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Though emphasized as a quality metric, sepsis quality measure (SEP-1) compliance remains low nationwide. Electronic health record (EHR)-based interventions show promise, but few have examined EHR laboratory reference value misconfiguration as a distinct driver of noncompliance.
LOCAL PROBLEM: The San Francisco Veterans Affairs, a 110-bed tertiary care center, recorded 3 consecutive quarters of SEP-1 composite performance in the lowest national quintile, nadiring at 31.5%.
METHODS: A multidisciplinary team applied LEAN-A3 methodology to identify root causes of low SEP-1 performance and design targeted countermeasures. The primary outcome was the percentage of suspected sepsis patients with a serum lactate >2.0 mmol/L who received a repeat lactate within 6 hours. Balancing measures included unnecessary repeat lactates and sepsis mortality.
INTERVENTIONS: Three EHR-based interventions were implemented between August and November 2025: (1) an Emergency Department Sepsis order-set embedding dual time-spaced lactate orders; (2) a structured Sepsis Evaluation Note template; and (3) a clinical decision support alert for patients with serum lactate >2.0 mmol/L, implemented to address a laboratory reference range misconfiguration.
RESULTS: Postintervention lactate reassessment compliance rose 14 percentage points (54%-68%), meeting Institute for Healthcare Improvement criteria for special cause variation. Facility 12-month rolling performance rose from 31.5% (lowest quintile) to 64.7% (middle quintile), reaching a quarterly high of 74.3%. No increase in unnecessary repeat lactates or sepsis mortality was detected.
CONCLUSIONS: EHR-embedded structural interventions produced sustained SEP-1 improvement without impacting laboratory utilization or mortality, offering a reproducible model for improvement through systems redesign rather than education alone.

title: Physical and lifestyle predictors of vascular function in postmenopausal East Asian women: the women’s vascular health project
abstract: The cardiovascular disease (CVD) burden is especially pronounced in women after menopause accounting for more deaths worldwide than any other disease. The current research examined physical and lifestyle contributors to vascular health in postmenopausal East Asian women. Approximately 118 apparently healthy postmenopausal East Asian women (mean age, 61.18 ± 5.98 years) were evaluated for selected vascular health markers: carotid–femoral pulse wave velocity (cfPWV), central augmentation index, and mean arterial pressure. Physical measurements encompassed body mass index, waist circumference, skeletal muscle mass (SMM), percent body fat and visceral adipose tissue (VAT). Lifestyle assessments incorporated the 6-minute walk test (6-MWT), the International Physical Activity Questionnaire, and dietary recall. Independent associations with cfPWV, cAIx, and MAP were estimated using multivariate linear regression. After age adjustment, VAT showed a trend toward predicting combined vascular outcomes ( p = 0.058) while VAT and SMM positively predicted cfPWV ( p = 0.007 and p = 0.037, respectively). Higher 6-MWT scores were associated with lower cfPWV values ( p = 0.029). Our findings highlight the importance of VAT, and the 6-MWT in the evaluation of vascular health among postmenopausal East Asian women. Results support promotion of targeted interventions designed to reduce central obesity and increase physical activities that reduce cardiac risk in this population.

title: Irisin fails to rescue bone loss in a rat model of chronic kidney disease - mineral bone disorder (CKD-MBD) but interacts with parathyroid hormone (PTH) in vivo and in vitro in IDG-SW3 osteocytes.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Chronic kidney disease progression leads to bone loss and increased fracture and mortality risk. The myokine irisin, produced by muscle during exercise, has been shown to exert protective effects on bone in healthy animals and exhibits a potential interaction with PTH in vitro. The aims of this study were to determine the effect of irisin on bone in CKD-MBD and determine if an interaction exists with PTH in vitro and in vivo.
METHODS: Early and mature IDG-SW3 osteocytes were treated with recombinant irisin, PTH, or both. Mineralization and osteocyte cell markers were assessed. In a similar 2 × 2 design, male Cy/+IU (CKD-MBD) rats were treated with or without irisin under high and low PTH conditions. Dynamic histomorphometry, bone structure, mechanical properties, and musculoskeletal gene markers were assessed.
RESULTS: In vitro, irisin alone downregulated Dkk1 and Sost, inhibitors of bone formation, and PTH receptor mRNA expression, primarily in early osteocytes. However, in the presence of PTH, no effects of irisin were observed. In vivo, the administration of irisin to animals with progressive CKD also downregulated PTH receptor 1 expression but did not affect bone turnover or structure or mechanical properties.
CONCLUSIONS: Irisin did not meaningfully ameliorate bone loss in an animal model of CKD-MBD but did interact with PTH by downregulating its receptor in vitro in osteocytes and in vivo in bone.

title: A Framework to Monitor Editing of Artificial Intelligence-Generated Medical Documentation
abstract: Objective: To develop and evaluate a framework for characterizing clinician editing of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-generated documentation and assess its feasibility for health system-level monitoring of AI scribes. Materials and Methods: We analyzed outpatient encounters in which an AI scribe was used at a single academic health system, examining the History of Present Illness (HPI) and Assessment and Plan (A&P) sections of notes. We characterized edits on three dimensions: lexical edit intensity based on Levenshtein distance, embedding edit intensity BERTScore, and clinical edit intensity based on removed and added UMLS concepts. We analyzed the Positive Predictive Value (PPV) of clinical edit intensity as a measure of clinically meaningful editing using clinicians as the gold standard, examined correlations among dimensions, and designed exponentially weighted moving-average control charts to monitor longitudinal changes in clinician editing behavior. Results: 268,379 encounters were included (267,654 HPI, 267,594 A&P). Clinical edit intensity ≥1 had an 88.9% PPV for clinically meaningful editing. Lexical and embedding edit intensity were highly correlated (Spearman ρ 0.95), while clinical edit intensity was less strongly correlated with both (ρ 0.77-0.81). Longitudinal monitoring detected changes coinciding with system-wide rollout. Discussion: Clinicians edited A&Ps more heavily than HPIs, potentially reflecting greater attention to content involving clinical decision-making. Over one-third of sections involved clinical concept changes, and clinical edit intensity identified clinically meaningful edits while providing information complementary to lexical editing measures. Conclusion: Clinician editing can be characterized at scale using complementary editing dimensions, providing a scalable signal for post-deployment surveillance of the human-AI documentation process.

title: Longitudinal linear-epitope profiling of SLE identifies novel antigens associated with disease and disease activity
abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is characterized by diverse autoantibodies, yet established biomarkers capture only a fraction of autoreactivity. We profiled 1,268 plasma samples from 695 patients with SLE and 301 healthy controls using phage immunoprecipitation sequencing (PhIP-seq). Machine learning identified a reproducible autoreactivity signature that discriminated SLE from controls across two validation cohorts. SLE autoreactivities were enriched for RNA-binding proteins, while targets containing Basic Acidic Dipeptide repeat domains were associated with high disease activity. A YTHDF2-derived peptide was the most prevalent shared autoreactivity, occurring in ∼25% of patients and exhibiting sequence similarity to Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) lytic switch protein BZLF1. Competition assays demonstrated higher-affinity binding to the viral peptide, consistent with EBV-associated molecular mimicry. Orthogonal validation using a 10-peptide Luminex panel strongly discriminated SLE from healthy controls. These findings expand the SLE autoantibody landscape, identify disease activity associated autoreactivities and insight linking EBV-driven immunity to epitope-specific autoimmunity in lupus.

title: Telehealth as a strategy to build outpatient care resilience during extreme weather
abstract: Abstract Extreme weather events are becoming more frequent and severe, disrupting outpatient care and endangering the health of patients with chronic illness and social vulnerability. Telehealth has the potential to help health systems build resilience during extreme weather, but evidence linking telehealth strategies to specific vulnerabilities and impacts remains fragmented. We conducted a scoping review of 14 studies describing telehealth use during extreme weather events. We mapped telehealth strategies to the system- and patient-level vulnerabilities and impacts they addressed, including chronic disease management, medication access, acute needs triage, and reaching displaced or homebound patients. In every study, telehealth was repurposed from existing infrastructure rather than built for disaster response, functioning as adaptive infrastructure. This mapping identifies actionable pathways for health systems to build resilience in outpatient care to mitigate health risks posed by extreme weather and highlights purpose-built disaster telehealth, integrated into formal preparedness planning, as a significant unmet need.

title: Mental Stress-Induced Myocardial Ischemia and Cardiovascular Events in Women after a Premature Myocardial Infarction: A Prospective Cohort Study
abstract: Background: Women with premature myocardial infarction (MI) have worse outcomes than similarly aged men despite less severe disease, and stress-related factors have been implicated. We examined sex differences in the association of mental stress-induced myocardial ischemia (MSIMI) with cardiovascular outcomes after premature MI and explored vascular and inflammatory mechanisms. Methods: We studied 602 individuals (mean age 51 years; 46% women) within 8 months of MI who underwent 99mTc-sestamibi myocardial perfusion imaging at rest and after mental stress. MSIMI was defined as a summed difference score ≥3. We measured reactive hyperemia index (RHI) as peripheral microvascular reactivity to stress and interleukin-6 (IL-6) as inflammatory response to stress. The primary endpoint was cardiovascular death or nonfatal MI; the secondary endpoint added heart failure hospitalization. Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for sociodemographic factors, clinical, and psychiatric history. Results: MSIMI was more common in women than men (19.2% vs. 13.2%, p=0.04). Over a median follow-up of 34.2 months, 51 primary and 91 secondary endpoint events occurred. The hazard ratio (HR) of MSIMI for the primary endpoint was 3.2 (95% CI, 1.3, 7.6) in women and 1.9 (95% CI, 0.8, 4.5) in men (p for interaction=0.41), which remained similar after multivariable adjustment. The adjusted population attributable fraction was 27.6% (99% CI, 3.9%, 36.9%) in women and 11.1% (95% CI, -5.8%, 18.4%) in men. In exploratory analyses, all MSIMI-related primary endpoint events among women occurred in Black women (HR, 4.3; 95% CI, 1.7-11.1). Associations with the secondary endpoint were weaker and attenuated after adjustment. IL-6 and RHI responses did not attenuate associations. Conclusions: Among women, MSIMI was associated with about threefold increased risk and over one quarter attributable fraction for cardiovascular death or nonfatal MI. Black women were at especially high risk. While larger studies are warranted to confirm sex differences and explore mechanisms, these data underscore the impact of emotional factors on morbidity and mortality in post-MI women.

title: Preferential phosphodiesterase inhibition as a novel strategy to modulate key pathways in systemic sclerosis.
abstract: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a complex autoimmune disease marked by vasculopathy, immune dysregulation, and progressive fibrosis of the skin and internal organs. The high disease burden and impact on quality of life highlight the need for therapies that target underlying pathogenic mechanisms rather than merely treating organ-specific symptoms. Phosphodiesterases, including phosphodiesterase 4B (PDE4B), are key regulators of cellular function and inflammatory responses of several cell types central to SSc pathogenesis. Given PDE4B's broad effects, targeting it may provide benefits beyond organ-specific manifestations and improve current care. Selective PDE4B inhibition represents a novel therapeutic approach for SSc, with improved subtype selectivity compared with earlier pan-PDE4 inhibitors. Nerandomilast preferentially inhibits PDE4B (ninefold over PDE4D), potentially improving tolerability versus oral pan-PDE4 inhibitors by avoiding adverse events such as gastrointestinal intolerance. Preclinical findings in SSc-relevant mouse and cell models show that PDE4B inhibition modulates inflammatory cytokine secretion, smooth muscle cell tension, endothelial and epithelial barrier integrity, and extracellular matrix synthesis under oxidative stress; this suggests nerandomilast could attenuate immune dysregulation, fibrosis, and potentially impact vasculopathy. Two pivotal Phase III trials evaluated nerandomilast in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (FIBRONEER™-IPF; NCT05321069) and progressive pulmonary fibrosis (FIBRONEER™-ILD; NCT05321082), the latter of which included patients with SSc-associated interstitial lung disease (SSc-ILD). The ongoing CONQUEST trial (NCT06195072) is investigating the efficacy and safety of various drugs, including nerandomilast, in patients with early active SSc-ILD. This perspective highlights the rationale for targeting PDE4B in SSc therapy and explores preclinical findings in SSc and clinical findings in SSc-ILD to date.

title: Comparative immunogenicity and relative vaccine efficacy of recombinant and cell culture-based influenza vaccines: Results from a randomized trial of adults in the United States, 2024-2025.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Recombinant (RIV) and cell culture-based inactivated (ccIIV) influenza vaccines could improve seasonal influenza prevention; however, evidence is limited in how protection may differ among non-egg-based vaccines.
METHODS: We conducted a randomized trial of RIV versus ccIIV to compare vaccine immunogenicity in adults aged 18 to 64 years during the 2024-25 influenza season (ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06518577). Active surveillance for influenza-like illness was conducted for six months post-vaccination and cumulative incidence of influenza by vaccine type was compared to estimate relative vaccine efficacy. Participants were tested for influenza by reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction or rapid antigen tests. Immunogenicity was evaluated by hemagglutination inhibition (HAI), virus microneutralization (MN), and neuraminidase inhibition (NAI) assays in a subset of blood specimens collected pre-vaccination and one-month post-vaccination.
RESULTS: Among the 591 participants, 25 cases of influenza A were detected; 2.4% cumulative incidence among RIV recipients versus 6.1% among ccIIV recipients. The probability of influenza was 61% lower with RIV than ccIIV (95% confidence interval: 7 to 84). Among 151 participants, post-vaccination HAI and MN titers vaccine components were higher among RIV recipients while NAI titers were higher among ccIIV recipients.
CONCLUSIONS: RIV provided better protection than ccIIV against influenza A illness in adults during the U.S. 2024-2025 season.

title: GROMTools: scalable individual-level GReX imputation for mega-biobank-scale cohorts.
abstract:
MOTIVATION: The computational burden of individual-level genetically regulated gene expression (GReX) imputation has risen sharply with the growth of human mega-biobanks and the rapid expansion of transcriptomic imputation models across tissues and single-cell hierarchies. Existing tools were not designed for this setting and require complex, memory-intensive workflows that are poorly matched to shared and cloud-based compute environments, where runtime, memory, and I/O directly determine cost and throughput. GROMTools is an open-source C++ engine with an R interface that exploits sparse prediction weights, streams PLINK2 genotypes, and writes compact binary outputs for scalable individual-level GReX imputation.
RESULTS: In UK Biobank (UKB), benchmarks on chromosome 1 across 50,000-450,000 individuals, 388,017 variants, and 11,724 gene-model pairs from 32 single-nucleus transcriptome imputation models, GROMTools produced near-identical predictions to PrediXcan and PLINK2, with minimum Pearson correlation >0.999 and maximum RMSE <0.001 across all of the imputed genes, while reducing CPU time by about 100-fold and peak memory by about 33-fold. These gains make routine biobank-scale individual-level GReX imputation practical and cost-efficient on standard CPU infrastructure.
AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: GROMTools is freely available at https://github.com/voloudakislab/gromtools under the GPL v3 license. Documentation is available at https://voloudakislab.github.io/gromtools/. All scripts used for data quality control and benchmarking, together with log files and a snapshot of the GROMTools code version used for all of our analyses, are archived at DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21926165.

title: Reclassifying Ablation Energy Risk Profiles in Atrial Fibrillation A Narrative-Adjudicated Comparative Analysis of the MAUDE Database
abstract: ABSTRACT Background Pulsed field ablation (PFA) has been rapidly adopted for atrial fibrillation (AF) on the premise of greater safety than thermal ablation. Real-world signals of hemolysis, coronary spasm, and neurologic events have since emerged, and prior Manufacturer and User Facility Device Experience (MAUDE) analyses relied on term matching without prospective signal detection. Methods We queried MAUDE for AF ablation catheter reports received January 2016 through June 2026 and assigned each to PFA, radiofrequency ablation (RFA), or cryoballoon ablation. We adjudicated injury and death narratives into predefined complication families and severity tiers with a large language model, checked against a larger model and by physician review. We calculated reporting odds ratios (ROR) and Bayesian shrinkage estimators compared against an empirical null, applied interrupted time series and prospective sequential detection, and repeated estimates on a 2026 hold-out. Results Among 44,623 reports, 30.1% were PFA, 50.9% RFA, and 19.0% cryoballoon, with 91.8% model agreement on event occurrence ( κ = 0.83). PFA carried an ROR of 527 (95% CI, 33, 8,509) for hemolysis, 2.83 (2.55, 3.16) for arrhythmia, 2.83 (2.30, 3.48) for coronary, and 2.39 (2.10, 2.73) for cerebrovascular events, against 0.024 (0.008, 0.075) for esophageal and 0.34 (0.32, 0.37) for pericardial events. The cerebrovascular excess was largest for VARIPULSE, but without it the class proportional reporting ratio was 1.36 (1.13, 1.65), concordant with the 1.56 measured in EMBOL-AF . In the hold-out, the cerebrovascular, arrhythmia and hemolysis signals replicated, and coronary events kept their direction without meeting the signal rule. Prospective detection flagged cerebrovascular events 13 months before AVANT GUARD published its neurologic events. Conclusions PFA showed disproportionate reporting of hemolysis, cerebrovascular, coronary, and arrhythmic events across sequential testing. Machine learning methods allowed for flagging these signals months before confirmatory trials, demonstrating a scalable tool for early detection of procedural risk. CLINICAL PERSPECTIVE What is Known Pulsed field ablation has been adopted rapidly for atrial fibrillation on the premise of fewer collateral injuries than thermal ablation. Hemolysis, coronary spasm, and neurologic events have since emerged in case series, registries, and a paused trial, while prior analyses of Food and Drug Administration device reports relied largely on term matching without narrative adjudication at scale. What the Study Adds In injury and death reports adjudicated at the narrative level, pulsed field ablation was reported more often than thermal ablation for hemolysis, arrhythmia, coronary, and cerebrovascular events and less often for esophageal and pericardial injury. The cerebrovascular reporting excess was largest for the VARIPULSE catheter but persisted with that platform removed and concentrated in minor stroke and systemic embolism, suggesting an embolic signal not confined to one platform. Sequential detection run on reports adjudicated by a large language model would have flagged the cerebrovascular signal 13 months before AVANT GUARD published its neurologic events, suggesting a role for automated surveillance of new ablation technologies.

title: Real-life Psychological Experiences and Subsequent Cardiovascular Events among Survivors of a Myocardial Infarction in Midlife: Prospective Cohort Study
abstract: Background: Information is lacking about everyday psychological states of individuals with a recent myocardial infarction (MI) and whether they influence outcomes. We investigated real world psychological experiences and their association with subsequent cardiovascular events in survivors of an MI. Methods: We studied 287 individuals ≤ 60 years of age within 8 months from an MI. At the baseline visit, we assessed sociodemographic and clinical factors, and administered a battery of psychological scales of depression, anxiety, anger, perceived stress and social support. Participants underwent a 7-day home monitoring of mood and stress using ecological momentary assessments, and a momentary negative affect (MNA) score, integrating daily mean ratings of sadness, anxiety, anger, distress and loneliness, was calculated. Participants were followed for a median time of 28 months. The study endpoint was a composite index of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), including cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, stroke or hospitalizations for heart failure. Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for sociodemographic and clinical factors. Results: The mean age of the sample was 51 years, and 43% of participants were women. Each standard deviation increase in MNA was significantly associated with a 60% increased risk of MACE (95% confidence interval (CI), 20% to 100%), irrespective of adjustment for sociodemographic factors and clinical characteristics. The association was similar in women and men. Momentary positive mood and momentary perceived stress were not associated with MACE. The MNA score showed a larger independent contribution to MACE compared to the combined battery of baseline psychological assessments and the association was independent of baseline history of depression. Conclusion: Among individuals after MI, moment-to-moment negative affect during one week of monitoring in daily life is a powerful predictor of subsequent cardiovascular events. A prospective evaluation of negative mood during everyday living could represent a novel strategy to uncover residual risk after MI.

title: Elevated Intraocular Pressure Facilitates T-Cell-Mediated Retinal Ganglion Cell Loss.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Our previous work indicated that adoptive transfer of CD3⁺ T cells from glaucomatous mice into healthy recipients results in progressive retinal ganglion cell (RGC) loss, providing evidence that adaptive immune responses contribute to glaucoma pathogenesis. This study tested whether elevated intraocular pressure (EIOP) promotes T-cell-mediated RGC degeneration using an adoptive transfer model of autoreactive T cells primed against RGC antigens.
METHODS: Splenocytes from donor mice that express a green fluorescent protein (GFP)-specific T-cell receptor were transferred into recipient mice expressing GFP in a subset of RGCs. Experimental mice underwent mild IOP elevation; controls remained normotensive or received lipopolysaccharide (LPS). GFP⁺ RGC survival was assessed by fundoscopy and retinal flat mounts. Retinal expression of vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 (Vcam1) was analyzed by immunofluorescence and quantitative PCR.
RESULTS: Fundoscopy 8 weeks posttransfer revealed minimal loss of GFP+ RGCs in naive mice (-4.46%), normotensive controls (-2.83%, P = 0.9899), and LPS-treated animals (-4.5%, P > 0.9999). In contrast, EIOP animals lost 18.43% of GFP⁺ RGCs (P = 0.0034) in the central retina. Similar findings were also observed in retinal flat mounts. EIOP retinas also exhibited increased Vcam1 expression associated with retinal capillaries compared with naive controls.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings indicate that mild EIOP promotes T-cell-mediated degeneration of RGCs, particularly in the central retina. LPS-mediated disruption of the blood-retina barrier alone did not induce RGC loss, indicating that IOP-dependent processes may be required to breach the immune-protective environment of the retina. The increase in Vcam1 expression in EIOP retinas may represent a mechanism facilitating T-cell-mediated retinal neurodegeneration.

title: USP10 Silencing Prevents Scarring and Inflammation in a Modified Rabbit Model of Glaucoma Filtration Surgery.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Trabeculectomy remains the gold standard for lowering intraocular pressure (IOP) in glaucoma, but postoperative scarring and inflammation can cause bleb failure. Because USP10 knockdown is anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic in the cornea, we tested whether USP10 silencing reduces bleb scarring and inflammation in a rabbit glaucoma filtration surgery model.
METHODS: Primary rabbit Tenon's fibroblasts (RTFs) were transfected with fully modified in vivo self-delivering siRNA targeting USP10 (sdRNA, US09) or non-targeting control sdRNA (NTC) to assess myofibroblast conversion and fibronectin expression. Female New Zealand White rabbits underwent modified glaucoma filtering surgery with tube insertion and subconjunctival US09, NTC, or mitomycin C (MMC). Bleb health and vascularity were scored using a modified Moorfields system, IOP was measured with TonoVet Plus, and excised blebs were analyzed for tissue width, apoptosis (TUNEL), α-SMA, and CD45+ cell infiltration. Inflammatory cytokines were profiled from aqueous humor by ELISA.
RESULTS: US09 transfection in RTFs reduced USP10 expression and suppressed myofibroblast activation, lowering α-SMA and fibronectin expression and disrupting fibrillar organization. In vivo, a single US09 dose reduced postoperative apoptosis versus NTC and MMC. Although both US09 and MMC inhibited myofibroblast differentiation and early immune infiltration, only US09 preserved bleb architecture, sustained immune suppression, and avoided MMC-associated ischemic vascularity. US09 treatment was also associated with lower mean levels of several aqueous humor cytokines.
CONCLUSIONS: Perioperative USP10-targeting sdRNA reduced myofibroblast development and sustained an anti-inflammatory, tissue-preserving phenotype after rabbit glaucoma filtration surgery, with advantages over MMC in tissue-preservation and inflammatory endpoints. USP10 silencing may represent a promising anti-scarring strategy to improve long-term trabeculectomy outcomes.

title: AAV Gene Augmentation Therapy Rescues the Phenotype in the RDH5-/- Cat Model of Fundus Albipunctatus.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Retinol dehydrogenase 5 (RDH5) catalyzes the final oxidation for visual pigment regeneration of 11-cis-retinal as part of the visual cycle in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). In humans, RDH5 mutations cause fundus albipunctatus characterized by night blindness, accumulation of white-yellowish fundus spots, and, in a subset of patients, macular degeneration. Currently, there is an unmet need for therapies for patients with RDH5 mutations. Using a large-animal cat model of RDH5-associated disease (RDH5-/-), this study aimed to meet these needs through development of a gene augmentation therapy able to rescue RDH5-associated retinopathies.
METHODS: An adeno-associated virus serotype 2 with triple capsid mutations vector packaged with feline RDH5 cDNA (AAV-VMD2-fRDH5) was subretinally injected into 12 RDH5-/- cats. To assess expression and the impact of treatment on retinal function and structure, immunohistochemistry, high-performance liquid chromatography, rod and cone electroretinograms, spectral-domain optical coherence tomography, and semi-thin resin-embedded sectioning were performed.
RESULTS: The expression of the RDH5 transgene improved rod and cone photoreceptor functional recovery following light exposure and shows promise in slowing/halting area centralis (analogous to the human macula) degeneration.
CONCLUSIONS: This gene augmentation therapy is a promising approach for the treatment of RDH5-associated retinopathies.

title: Titanium Dioxide Exacerbates Calcium Phosphate and Urate-Induced Oxidative Stress, Injury and Inflammatory Response in Human Kidney-2 Cells.
abstract: The widespread use of titanium dioxide (TiO2) nanoparticles (TNPs) in everyday products (ex; cosmetics, food additives) has growing concerns about their harmful effects on humans due to unavoidable exposure. We recently found that TNPs could stabilize both calcium phosphate (CaP) and uric acid (UA) crystals, implicating kidney stone formation. However, the impact of TNPs on the kidney, specifically on kidney tubular cells is unknown. Therefore, we investigated the effect of TiO2 alone or in combination with UA/CaP microcrystals on Ca2+ dynamics by measuring Ca2+ transients, reactive oxygen species (ROS) production by H2DCFDA staining and H2O2 release, oxidative stress and inflammatory response by gene expression analysis, cell death by DAPI and Annexin V/propidium iodide (PI) staining and cytotoxicity by lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release in human kidney (HK-2) tubular cell line. The internalization of CaP/UA crystals with TiO2 in HK-2 cells resulted in an enhanced store-operated Ca2+ entry (SOCE), which was blocked by Pyr6 (SOCE inhibitor). Indeed, the combination of CaP/UA crystals with TiO2 -internalized HK-2 cells showed a pronounced increase in ROS production and LDH release compared to CaP and/or UA crystals groups, which were reduced by SOCE inhibition. Analyses of nuclear morphology via DAPI staining indicated a greater cell injury/death response in the presence of TiO2 with CaP/UA crystals. Annexin V/PI staining revealed a greater percentage of apoptosis/necrosis after internalization of CaP/UA with TiO2, which was decreased upon preapplication of Pyr6. Gene expression analyses show that internalization of CaP/UA+TiO2 crystals evoked upregulation of oxidative stress (NOX4), inflammatory (MCP-1, TNF-α), fibrotic (FN-1) and apoptotic (BCL2) genes. Taken together, TNPs, when combined with CaP/UA, became the activator of SOCE to promote oxidative stress, inflammation, tubular injury and cytotoxicity, underscoring their implications in crystal-induced nephropathy and stone formation.

title: Executive Summary of the Clinical Practice Guideline on Tinnitus Update.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Tinnitus is the perception of sound without an external source. More than 50 million people in the United States have reported experiencing tinnitus, resulting in an estimated prevalence of 10% to 15% in adults. The focus of this guideline is on tinnitus that is both bothersome and persistent (lasting 6 months or longer), which often negatively affects the patient's quality of life. The target audience for the guideline is any clinician, including allied health professionals, involved in managing patients with tinnitus. The target patient population is limited to adults (18 years and older) with tinnitus that is persistent and bothersome.
PURPOSE: The purpose of this guideline is to provide and update evidence-based recommendations for clinicians managing patients with tinnitus. The target audience for this guideline is any clinician involved in managing patients with tinnitus. People with tinnitus may be evaluated by a variety of health care providers, including primary care clinicians, specialty clinicians, and allied health professionals including audiologists and clinical psychologists. The target patient population is limited to adults (18 years and older) with tinnitus that is persistent and bothersome. Most people with tinnitus have associated hearing loss, such as sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) secondary to aging (presbycusis), noise exposure (noise-induced hearing loss), or acoustic trauma. Tinnitus can also be a symptom of numerous auditory and non-auditory system disorders, ranging from middle ear diseases, such as otosclerosis and eustachian tube dysfunction, to inner ear and auditory nerve pathologies such as Ménière's disease and vestibular schwannoma. Nonauditory system disorders that can cause tinnitus include vascular anomalies, myoclonus, and intracranial hypertension. The Guideline Update Group (GUG) placed emphasis on the need for thorough clinical evaluation to identify these potentially treatable and sometimes serious disorders. However, patients with identifiable causative diagnoses other than sensorineural hearing loss are excluded from this guideline as they are excluded from nearly all randomized controlled trials of tinnitus management, making it impossible to generalize trial results to these patients. Nevertheless, clinicians should decide whether to apply the recommendations of this guideline to patients with these conditions on an individualized basis. The guideline also underscores the need to distinguish between subjective, objective, and pulsatile tinnitus to further direct patient evaluation and management. Comprehensive management of objective tinnitus and pulsatile tinnitus is not within the scope of this guideline. Pulsatile tinnitus is the perception of a rhythmic sound in the absence of an external source that may be pulse-synchronous, which is often but not always related to vascular causes, or pulse-asynchronous, which is typically associated with mechanical causes such as palatal or middle ear myoclonus.1 Further, the guideline does not apply to transient ear noise, which is the sudden perception of a tonal or ringing sound in 1 ear, lasting fewer than 5 minutes, that may be accompanied by a sense of hearing loss or aural fullness, as it does not typically require clinical management.2 The guideline also excludes patients with tinnitus related to complex auditory hallucinations or hallucinations related to psychotic or seizure disorders. This is an update to an evidence-based clinical guideline developed for the evaluation and management of tinnitus. This updated guideline provides clinicians with a logical framework to improve patient care and mitigate the personal and social effects of persistent, bothersome tinnitus. The first part of the guideline is focused on the clinical evaluation of patients with tinnitus, including the history, physical exam, and selection and timing of diagnostic testing and specialty referral to identify potential underlying treatable pathology and reduce the risk of self-harm. The remainder of the guideline is focused on the evaluation and treatment of patients with persistent, bothersome tinnitus, with recommendations to evaluate and measure its effects as well as to determine the most appropriate interventions to improve symptoms and quality of life.
ACTION STATEMENTS: The Guideline Update Group made strong recommendations for the following Key Action Statements (KAS): Clinicians should distinguish patients with bothersome tinnitus from patients with nonbothersome tinnitus (KAS 2). Clinicians should inquire about risks for self-harm in a patient with bothersome tinnitus (KAS 3). Clinicians should not obtain neuroradiologic imaging in patients with tinnitus specifically to evaluate the tinnitus unless specific concerning features are present (KAS 6). The Guideline Update Group made recommendations for the following KASs: Clinicians should perform a targeted history and physical examination at the initial evaluation of a patient with tinnitus (KAS 1). Clinicians should obtain a comprehensive audiological evaluation in patients with tinnitus (KAS 5). Clinicians should educate patients with tinnitus about the natural history and effects of, and management strategies for tinnitus (KAS 7). Clinicians should recommend a hearing aid evaluation for patients with hearing difficulties and persistent, bothersome tinnitus (KAS 8). Clinicians should refer patients with persistent, bothersome tinnitus for cochlear implant evaluation when they meet audiologic criteria for referral (KAS 9). Clinicians should recommend Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) to patients with persistent, bothersome tinnitus (KAS 11). Clinicians or their designee should assess and document outcomes of interventions in patients with persistent, bothersome tinnitus (KAS 15). The Guideline Update Group made recommendations against for the following KASs: Clinicians should not routinely recommend antidepressants, anticonvulsants, anxiolytics, or intratympanic medications for a primary indication of treating persistent, bothersome tinnitus (KAS 12). Clinicians should not recommend dietary supplements for the primary indication of persistent, bothersome tinnitus (KAS 13). Clinicians should not recommend repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) for the treatment of patients with persistent, bothersome tinnitus (KAS 14A). The Guideline Update Group offered options for the following KASs: Clinicians may inquire about somatosensory features in patients with persistent, bothersome tinnitus (KAS 4). Clinicians may recommend sound enrichment to patients with persistent, bothersome tinnitus (KAS 10). Clinicians may offer bimodal neuromodulation to patients with persistent, bothersome tinnitus (KAS 14B).

title: Single-cell and population-level neuromodulation dynamics in dual-electrode intracortical microstimulation
abstract: Intracortical microstimulation (ICMS) is widely used to activate cortical networks and evoke sensory percepts. Despite its successful clinical outcomes, how individual neurons respond to adjacent multi-electrode ICMS remains unclear. In this study, we combined two-photon calcium imaging with dual-electrode in mouse visual cortex, allowing us to directly observe how neurons behave converging electrical stimulation inputs. This specific setting revealed that at low stimulation levels (5–7 µA), neural activity changed only modestly during dual-electrode stimulation input compared to single-electrode stimulation. As stimulation increased to intermediate levels (10–15 µA), neurons exhibited diverse nonlinear interactions—yet the overall population response shifted toward enhancement. At stronger stimulation (15–18 µA), the proportion of modulated neurons increased in both enhancement and attenuation directions, however, the net effect at the population level was neutral. Neurons that responded strongly to single-electrode ICMS tended to be attenuated during dual-electrode stimulation, whereas weaker responders were often enhanced. The most pronounced modulatory effects occur at intermediate distances between the two electrodes. Together, our results indicate nonlinear neuromodulatory effects from dual-electrode, reflecting complex circuit-level interactions. This data provides better understanding of single-cell modulation demonstrating how cortical networks integrate multiple ICMS inputs, informing necessary strategies to optimize neuroprosthetic performance.

title: Likelihood of Achieving Physiological Mobility After Cervical Disc Arthroplasty—Assessing Physiological Motion Restoration vs Physiological Motion Preservation
abstract: Background A previous study investigated the likelihood of cervical artificial discs achieving post-cervical disc arthroplasty (CDA) range of motion (ROM) in the physiological range, defined as 5° to 16°. Here, we delve deeper into the capability of a disc prosthesis to restore physiological motion when the patient is preoperatively hypomobile (ROM < 5°) or hypermobile (ROM > 16°), and capability to preserve physiological mobility when the preoperative ROM falls in the 5° to 16° range. Methods This is a secondary analysis of prospectively collected radiographic data from 131 patients who participated in a 1-level clinical trial of the M6-C (Orthofix) artificial disc. We chose this prosthesis for demonstration purposes due to the availability of pre- and postoperative flexion-extension ROM data on each individual patient. This allowed calculation of the number of implanted levels with preoperative and postoperative flexion-extension ROM in the following motion ranges: hypomobile (ROM < 5°), physiological mobility (ROM: 5°–16°), and hypermobile (ROM > 16°), resulting in a preoperative vs postoperative 3 × 3 mobility matrix. Results Preoperatively, 35 of the 131 implanted levels were hypomobile (ROM: 2.2° ± 1.5°). Of these, physiological ROM was restored to 26 implanted segments by 2 years after CDA (ROM: 7.6° ± 2.0°). A total of 89 of 131 levels had physiological mobility preoperatively (ROM: 9.1° ± 3.3°). Of these, 73 segments preserved their physiological range 2 years after CDA (ROM: 10.2° ± 3.1°). Seven of 131 segments were hypermobile preoperatively (ROM: 18.5° ± 0.9°). Of these, physiological motion was restored to 4 segments by 2 years after CDA (10.9° ± 1.4°). Since the group of patients with preoperative hypermobility was small (n = 7), we combined preoperatively hypo- and hypermobile groups in calculating the restoration rate, resulting in a 2 × 2 mobility matrix. The calculated physiological motion restoration rate was 71% (30/[35 + 7] = 0.71), and preservation rate was 82% (73/89 = 0.82). The combined result was that the prosthesis had a 79% likelihood of yielding physiological mobility at 2 years post-CDA follow-up ([73 + 30]/131). Conclusions The ability to restore and preserve physiological motion are 2 distinct mechanisms that combine to yield physiological motion after CDA. The cervical disc prosthesis analyzed in this study restored physiological motion to 71% of segments with preoperatively nonphysiological (hypomobile plus hypermobile) ROM, while preserving physiological mobility in 82% of segments with preoperative ROM in the physiological range. Clinical Relevance Knowing the likelihood of achieving an ideal postoperative motion outcome for a range of preoperative mobilities can help in guiding patient expectations about CDA and give clinicians additional information to use during implant selection. Level of Evidence 2.

title: Perspectives on implementing nerve and tendon transfer surgery in spinal cord injury rehabilitation in the USA and Canada: a qualitative study
abstract: Objectives This study aimed to understand perspectives on implementing nerve and tendon transfer surgeries for individuals with cervical spinal cord injury, with particular attention to communication, knowledge, care coordination and the use of a patient decision aid to support decision-making regarding these options. Specifically, we sought to identify multilevel barriers influencing uptake of these interventions in routine clinical care. Methods We conducted four focus groups with 36 clinicians and health service professionals across the USA and Canada. Participants reviewed an existing patient decision aid and discussed challenges of caring for people with spinal cord injury, uptake of novel surgical approaches, care navigation and referral and team coordination. The Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research was used to inform both the development of the interview guide and the analysis. All focus groups were conducted virtually, recorded, transcribed and coded using inductive and deductive coding. Results Themes emerged at the individual (patient and clinician) and system levels. Clinicians described their approach to communication with patients, including how they consider providing hope along with balanced, accurate and realistic information. Participants highlighted a need for greater awareness and education, improved team collaboration and care coordination and standardised processes to aid in patient evaluation and referral. Training materials and targeted educational resources were viewed as essential to facilitating clinicians’ ability to appropriately support patients considering nerve and tendon transfer surgery. Conclusion Improving uptake of nerve and tendon transfer surgeries requires more than a patient-facing decision aid; it depends on addressing upstream gaps in clinician knowledge, referral pathways and team communication. Integrating these findings into routine care can improve awareness of and access to evidence-based surgical options and support informed patient-centred decision-making.

title: Psychometric Properties of the 3-Item Clinician Administered Dissociative States Scale (CADSS)
abstract: Objective The 23-item Clinician Administered Dissociative States Scale (CADSS) has been widely used as a repeated measure of dissociative symptoms. A shortened version of the CADSS would be useful as a time-saving measure, especially for neurobiological studies of dissociation at multiple time points before and after an intervention. The purpose of this study was to assess the psychometric properties of two versions of a short form of the CADSS in a sample with and without posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Methods Participants with (N=200) and without (N=315) the diagnosis of PTSD were assessed with the 23-item CADSS and/or the 3-item CADSS, the 6-item CADSS, and other psychometric and neuropsychological assessments. Analyses were performed to examine internal consistency, validity as measured by correlation with measures of PTSD and trauma, and sensitivity to change following exposure to personalized scripts of traumatic memories. Results Both the 3-item CADSS (Cronbach’s alpha 0.82) and the 6-item CADSS (Cronbach’s alpha 0.81) showed good internal consistency. Validity for all versions was demonstrated based on correlations with other psychiatric symptom measures and ability to differentiate PTSD and non-PTSD participants. The 3-item CADSS demonstrated sensitivity to change based on a significant increase in scores after exposure to personalized traumatic scripts. Conclusion Both short form versions of the CADSS have acceptable psychometric properties.

title: Alcohol Consumption and Associations With Short‐ and Long‐Term Outcomes in Low Back Pain: A Longitudinal Case‐Crossover Study
abstract: BACKGROUND: The study objectives were to examine associations between participant-reported alcohol consumption and (1) flares of low back pain (LBP) and (2) pain intensity at 1-year follow-up. METHODS: This longitudinal case-crossover study nested in a cohort included 474 participants with LBP who completed up to 36 scheduled assessments and additional patient-initiated assessments (triggered by the onset of new flares) over a 1-year period. Each assessment asked participants to report whether a LBP flare was present using a validated definition. Conditional logistic regression was used to estimate associations between alcohol consumption and subsequent flares. Linear regression was used to estimate associations between baseline alcohol consumption and LBP intensity at 1-year follow-up. RESULTS: In analyses of 10,251 assessments over 1 year, each additional drink in the past 24 h was associated with a slightly lower odds of subsequent LBP flares (odds ratio [OR] per drink 0.95, 95% CI: 0.90, 0.997). Each additional average number of drinks in the past 24 h at baseline was significantly associated with slightly lower LBP intensity 1 year later (-0.19 Numerical Rating Scale (NRS) points [95% CI: -0.38, -0.004]). However, this association was diminished and nonsignificant after adjusting for the number of drinks in the past 24 h at the 1-year follow-up assessment. CONCLUSIONS: This study suggests a small, transient protective association of alcohol with LBP flares in the immediate-term, but no clinically meaningful beneficial associations with pain in the long-term. The findings do not support alcohol use as a pain management strategy. SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT: This epidemiologic study did not find meaningful associations between alcohol consumption and low back pain intensity in the long-term, although a small-magnitude, transient association with lower risk of subsequent flares of low back pain was observed. These findings bridge gaps in the evidence between laboratory studies of acute analgesic effects of alcohol on pain perception and cohort studies examining long-term low back pain outcomes.

title: Adherence to statins with risk of cardiovascular and limb events in peripheral artery disease
abstract: Abstract Background Given the markedly elevated risk of cardiovascular and limb events in peripheral artery disease (PAD), guidelines recommend high-intensity statins in PAD patients to lower this risk. However, adherence to statin medications remains suboptimal, especially in PAD patients, compared with other atherosclerotic cardiovascular diseases. Purpose To investigate the association between statin adherence and cardiovascular events, limb events, and mortality in PAD. Methods The Peripheral Artery Disease: Long-term Survival (PEARLS) is a longitudinal registry of patients with new-onset PAD during 2015-2020 in the U.S. Veterans Affairs Health System. Patients with PAD are identified based on abnormal ankle brachial and toe-brachial index extracted using a validated natural language processing system. Data on key clinical variables including prescription filled are available. Within the registry, we identified patients with persistent statin use in the year following their PAD diagnosis. Statin adherence was assessed during the year after PAD diagnosis by calculating proportion of days covered (PDC) and categorized PDC as >0.90, 0.80 to <0.9, 0.60 to < 0.8, and <0.6. In dichotomous analyses, adherence was defined as PDC ≥ 0.80. Study outcomes included cardiovascular events (hospitalization for myocardial infarction or stroke), limb events (chronic limb threatening ischemia and major amputation), and overall mortality. Last follow up was 31/12/2024. We conducted multivariable hierarchical logistic regression modelling to identify variables associated with adherence. To evaluate associations between statin adherence and cardiovascular events, limb events, and mortality, we developed multivariable Cox proportional hazards models. Results We identified 56,034 PAD patients with persistent statin use. The majority (53%) had PDC > 0.90 (IQR: 0.76-0.98), and 54% were on a high-intensity statin at baseline. Several patient variables were associated with statin adherence, especially Black race and Hispanic ethnicity which were associated with 43% and 25% lower odds of adherence (Table 1). In multivariable Cox regression models, we found a graded association between poor adherence and clinical events (Figure 1). Compared to reference group (PDC >0.90), patients with lowest adherence (PDC<0.6) had 32% higher hazard of cardiovascular events (HR 1.32; 95% CI: 1.25-1.39) and 28% higher hazard of limb events (HR 1.28; 95% CI: 1.18-1.38). Poor adherence to statins was also associated with higher mortality (HR 1.08; 95% CI: 1.04–1.13). Conclusion Although overall adherence to statins was high among persistent users, Black race and Hispanic ethnicity were associated with lower adherence. Low statin adherence was associated with higher risk of cardiovascular events, limb events, and mortality suggesting that overcoming barriers to adherence can mitigate the risk of cardiovascular and limb events, especially in those at the highest risk.For image description, please refer to the figure legend and surrounding text.For image description, please refer to the figure legend and surrounding text.

title: Associations of Cognitive Functions with EEG-based Event-related Potentials and Oscillations in Individuals at Clinical High-Risk for Psychosis: A Canonical Correlation Analysis of NAPLS2 Data
abstract: Background Research examining whether electroencephalography (EEG)-based event-related potential (ERP) and oscillation (ERO) abnormalities reflect pathophysiological mechanisms underlying cognitive deficits in schizophrenia has typically focused on a few measures. Less is known about these relationships in clinical high-risk for psychosis (CHR-P). We ran canonical correlation analysis (CCA) between ERP/ERO and cognitive measures from the multi-site North American Psychosis-Risk Longitudinal Study (NAPLS2) to elucidate the pattern of multivariate relationships between these two domains when multiple measures are considered simultaneously and quantify the extent of cross-domain overlap. Methods CHR-P ( N =454) completed baseline EEG and cognitive testing. 56 converted to psychosis (CHR-C) and 190 were followed for 24 months and did not convert (CHR-NC). ERP/ERO measures included: 1) mismatch negativity (MMN): deviant MMN amplitude; deviant and standard theta inter-trial coherence (ITC) and total power; 2) auditory/visual oddball: P300 amplitudes for targets (P3b) and novels (P3a); 3) 40-Hz auditory steady state response: 40-Hz ITC and total power. CCA was conducted between 11 ERP/ERO and 10 cognitive measures (MATRICS Consensus Cognitive Battery, auditory continuous performance tests). Results The first canonical variate ( r average =.341, p =.016) was significant, with deficits in MMN amplitude and theta ITC for deviants, 40-Hz ITC and total power, visual novel P3a, and auditory target P3b associated with worse cognition (processing speed, working memory, attention/vigilance). Theta ITC and total power for standards were negatively associated with cognition. Associations did not differ between CHR-C/CHR-NC ( ps >.521) or antipsychotic medication status ( ps >.642) groups. Conclusions CCA identified multivariate relationships (modest effect size) between ERP/ERO and cognition domains in CHR-P.

title: Conserved Molecular Markers for Tectorecipient Subdivisions of the Visual Thalamus in Mice and Tree Shrews
abstract: Sensory systems share common circuit organization motifs across mammalian species; however, anatomical subdivisions show varying degrees of complexity depending on ecological niche and species-specific sensory requirements. While neuroanatomical connections seem preserved within the visual system, it remains unknown if molecularly defined cell-types share a similar degree of conservation, regarding not only their functional properties but also connectivity. Here we analyze the organization, molecular marker expression, and connections between two prominent visual centers, the superior colliculus (SC) and the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus (dLGN), in the mouse and the tree shrew, a highly visual, diurnal species closely related to primates. Previous attempts to link molecular markers to subdivisions and connectivity of the dLGN have shown lack of conservation across species, thus preventing the systematic investigation of brain-wide interactions involved in vision. Leveraging recent single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing studies, our results unravel a conserved molecular marker that shows spatial restriction in the dLGN and correlates with the location of connections from the SC in both the mouse and the tree shrew of either sex. We extend our findings by confirming the presence of this molecular marker in the human dLGN. These results provide a molecular definition and genetic access point for subdivisions of the dLGN in the mouse and tree shrew, enabling cell-type specific studies of the parallel processing of visual information.

title: Impact of computed tomography-derived fractional flow reserve on long-term outcomes in patients with stable coronary artery disease: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: In patients with coronary artery disease (CAD), both functional and anatomical assessment are required to guide revascularization. Computed tomography-derived fractional flow reserve (FFR-CT) has emerged as a tool to implement both anatomical and non-invasive functional assessment of coronary stenoses in a single setting, but the association with long-term outcomes is still controversial. We aimed to assess the correlation between FFR-CT with long-term outcomes in patients with CAD.
METHODS: Reconstructed individual patient data were provided by the authors of a previous report published in a previous issue of the Journal. The primary outcome was study-defined major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), while secondary outcomes included the single components of the primary outcome. One-stage and two-stage meta-analyses with mixed-effect and random-effect models were conducted, stratifying patients according to FFR-CT thresholds of 0.8. Heterogeneity sources were explored through sensitivity analyses.
RESULTS: Fifteen studies were pooled from the reconstructed data, encompassing a total of 14,437 patients, with 6335 (43.9%) having a FFR-CT<0.8. After a median follow-up of 16.8 (7.2-35.8) months, FFR-CT<0.8 was associated with higher rates of MACE (hazard ratio: 4.93; 95% CI 4.16-5.84; p < 0.001), myocardial infarction (incidence rate ratio [IRR] 4.38; 95% CI 1.16-16.54; p = 0.029), ischemia driven revascularization (IRR 2.90; 95% CI 1.31-6.44; p = 0.009), and any revascularization (IRR 9.62; 95% CI 3.02-30.61; p < 0.001). Results were consistent across sensitivity analyses.
CONCLUSIONS: In patients with CAD, an FFR-CT <0.80 is associated with a three-to four-fold increase in MACE, being primarily driven by significant increase in myocardial infarction, ischemia-driven revascularization and any revascularization.

title: Age, sex, and hormone therapy are associated with open-angle glaucoma
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Open-angle glaucoma (OAG) is a leading cause of blindness, yet the understanding of sex and age on disease diagnosis remains incomplete. In females, the role of age and hormone therapy (HT) in modulating OAG diagnosis is also uncertain. This study evaluated potential sex- and age-related differences in OAG diagnosis. DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study, using the nationwide Veterans Affairs database, of longitudinally followed U.S. veterans with OAG. PARTICIPANTS: Males and females with a previous negative OAG screening and a current OAG diagnosis were included. METHODS: Propensity-score matching was performed for age, body mass index, diabetes, and hypertension between females not taking HT and males (n = 5102 pairs). Patients were stratified by baseline age cohorts (<45, 45-55, >55 years). OAG diagnoses were estimated using Kaplan-Meier analyses, and Cox proportional hazards regression evaluated covariates including age, sex, body mass index, hypertension, diabetes, myopia, diabetic retinopathy, and cataracts. Then, matched females not taking HT to females taking HT (n = 2655 pairs) were analysed. Outcome measures were median time to OAG diagnosis and significance of covariates influencing age of diagnosis across sex and age groups. RESULTS: Females developed OAG earlier than males in younger cohorts (<45, 45-55 years), whereas sex differences diminished after 55 years of age. HT use was associated with delayed diagnosis in females, with the greatest effect in those <45 years. Diabetes, hypertension, myopia, and cataracts were linked to earlier OAG diagnosis similarly in both sexes. CONCLUSIONS: Females experience earlier OAG diagnosis than males, but this difference narrows with age. HT was associated with later diagnosis, particularly in younger women, highlighting potential sex-specific influences in OAG.

title: Cotransplantation With Human AAT-MSCs Enhances Human Islet Graft Survival in Humanized Mice by Modulating B- and T-Cell Responses.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Immune-mediated rejection remains a major barrier to long-term success of islet/stem cell-derived islet transplantation for type 1 diabetes. We evaluated whether cotransplantation of human islets with human α-1 antitrypsin-overexpressing mesenchymal stromal/stem cells (AAT-MSCs) improves islet graft survival by modulating human immune responses in a humanized diabetic mouse model. Humanized NOD/SCID/IL2Rγ-/- (NSG) mice were generated by irradiation and transfer of human CD34+ hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells, resulting in stable T- and B-cell reconstitution. Diabetes was induced by multiple doses of low-dose streptozotocin (STZ), after which mice received intrahepatic transplants of human islets alone or together with AAT-MSCs and were monitored for 100 days. Cotransplantation with AAT-MSCs markedly improved glycemic control, prolonged graft survival, and reduced the risk of rejection. These beneficial effects were associated with lower serum IgM levels, which inversely correlated with graft rejection, and with expansion of regulatory B cells (Bregs), followed by durable suppression of T helper 1, T helper 17, and cytotoxic T cell responses. Cotransplant grafts showed improved insulin preservation and enrichment of interleukin (IL) 10+ cells within islets. In vitro, AAT-MSCs promoted Breg differentiation, shifted cytokine production toward IL-10 over IL-6, and attenuated activated B cell-mediated cytotoxicity against human islets. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that AAT-MSC cotransplantation promotes immune tolerance and human islet graft function, supporting its translational potential to reduce reliance on systemic immunosuppression in the clinic.
ARTICLE HIGHLIGHTS: Immune-mediated rejection limits the long-term success of islet and stem cell-derived islet transplantation in type 1 diabetes, and strategies that protect the graft without systemic immunosuppression are needed. We asked whether cotransplanting human islets with α-1 antitrypsin-overexpressing mesenchymal stromal/stem cells (AAT-MSCs) improves graft outcomes in humanized mice, and how human immune responses are affected. AAT-MSC cotransplantation improved glycemic control, prolonged graft survival, and shifted immune responses toward a more regulatory, less inflammatory profile. These findings support further development of AAT-MSCs as an adjunct to reduce reliance on systemic immunosuppression in islet transplantation.

title: Evaluating a Health Equity Adaptation to Evidence-based Quality Improvement.
abstract: Patient groups with known vulnerabilities to poor health outcomes may be less likely to receive or benefit from evidence-based practices (EBPs). Implementation science-the study of methods and strategies to promote EBP adoption into routine clinical practice-can both mitigate and exacerbate health inequities. Despite increasing recognition of health equity's importance to implementation science, implementation strategies do not typically integrate health equity. We aimed to pilot and evaluate a health equity adaptation to Evidence-Based Quality Improvement (EBQI), a multi-faceted implementation strategy bundle. The health equity adaptation provided specific steps to incorporate health equity into practice facilitation and quality improvement (QI) training, including a health equity didactic session provided to frontline primary care clinical champions. Our mixed methods evaluation included a clinical champion survey to assess acceptability of the health equity training and clinical champion and practice facilitator interviews to assess feasibility and acceptability of embedding health equity within the implementation strategy. We calculated survey response means and used rapid qualitative analysis to analyze interviews. Survey responses indicated neutral to high acceptability of the health equity didactics. In interviews, clinicians and facilitators reported that equity-infused practice facilitation was valuable and effective in supporting equity considerations in implementation. Facilitators felt comfortable incorporating the adaptation into future EBQI facilitation. Champions noted the equity adaptation influenced how they provided care to their patients. Our evaluation also revealed areas for improvement, and challenges inherent in implementation and health equity work. Future work can refine the health equity adaptation for other implementation projects that use EBQI.

title: Peripheral T- and B-cell immune signatures associated with response to vedolizumab in ulcerative colitis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Vedolizumab (VDZ) blocks integrin α4β7-MAdCAM-1 interactions, limiting leukocyte entry into the gut, yet peripheral-blood immune correlates of clinical response in ulcerative colitis (UC) remain unidentified.
METHODS: Peripheral blood mononuclear cells from healthy controls (HCs) and patients with UC, stratified by VDZ exposure and clinical response, were analyzed using mass cytometry (cytometry by time-of-flight). A 38-marker panel enriched for integrins, chemokine receptors, and activation markers was applied. Major immune populations were interrogated using lineage-specific opt-SNE and FlowSOM clustering.
RESULTS: The dataset included 26 HCs, 30 VDZ-naive UC (Nancy index ≥ 2), 8 VDZ-treated non-responders (Nancy index ≥ 2), and 8 VDZ-treated responders (Nancy index <2). No significant differences were detected in myeloid, NK-cell, or TCRγδ+ T-cell compartments. Integrin α4β7+ cells were detected across multiple immune lineages and were enriched in the B-cell compartment. Between-group differences were observed in the CD4+ T-cell and B-cell compartments. VDZ responders showed enrichment of an α4β7+ effector memory CD4+ T-cell subset compared with VDZ-naive UC. In parallel, responders exhibited reduced frequencies of class-switched plasmablast and activated B-cell populations relative to VDZ-naive UC. Integrin-pairing analysis demonstrated that these B-cell populations contained both α4β7+ and α4β1+ cells. In contrast, VDZ non-responders showed enrichment of an α4β7+ atypical-like IgA+ memory B-cell subset relative to responders, VDZ-naive UC, and HCs.
CONCLUSIONS: Clinical response and non-response to VDZ in UC are associated with distinct circulating T- and B-cell immune phenotypes. Peripheral-blood immunophenotyping may identify correlates of response and non-response. Prospective studies are needed to determine whether these signatures are predictive before VDZ initiation or reflect pharmacodynamic changes after treatment.

title: Potentially psychologically traumatic event exposures among Royal Canadian Mounted Police during the first year of service.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Potentially psychologically traumatic events (PPTEs) exposures are an inherent part of police work and a risk factor for posttraumatic stress injuries that may impact the mental health of police officers during their first year of service. The present study examines PPTE exposures experienced by Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) during their first year of service and examines associations with anxiety-, depressive-, and trauma-related mental health disorders.
METHOD: RCMP (n = 181; 72.8% male) participating in the RCMP Longitudinal Posttraumatic Stress Disorder Study self-reported mental health disorder symptoms and PPTE exposures experienced during their first year of service. Analyses included binomial tests, t tests, one-way analyses of variance, and multivariate logistic regression models.
RESULTS: After 1 year of service, participants reported an average of ∼39 PPTE exposures across ∼ 6 PPTE types. Participants reported higher prevalence for almost all PPTE types than previously reported by the Canadian general population (all ps < .001) but lower prevalences for all PPTE types than previously reported by longer serving RCMP (all ps < .001). Participants most commonly reported physical assault (76.2%), serious transport accident (68.0%), and sudden accidental death (62.4%), with most exposures (90%-100%) reported as "part of my public safety job." The total number of different PPTE types and the total number of PPTE exposures reported after 1 year of service were associated with increased odds of screening positive for posttraumatic stress disorder and major depressive disorder (all ps < .05).
CONCLUSIONS: The present study highlights the substantial number of PPTEs experienced by RCMP during 1 year of service that may increase the risk for mental health disorders, underscoring the need for continuous evidence-based supports to mitigate the impact of PPTEs.
