title: Long-Term Structural Stability and Maturation of Centimeter-Scale Stretch-Grown Sensory Axons Following Collagen Encapsulation.
abstract: Peripheral nerve injury (PNI) remains a significant clinical challenge due to limited biologically active regeneration strategies. Tissue engineered nerve grafts (TENGs) comprising long-projecting, stretch-grown axon tracts have emerged as a promising strategy to guide regeneration by creating a living bridge guiding and aiding native regeneration processes. However, their long-term structural stability remains incompletely understood. In this study, we evaluated the effects of dorsal root ganglia (DRG) plating density on the structural stability and morphology of mechanically stretch-grown TENGs over 5-7 weeks after three-dimensional collagen-encapsulation and removal from the mechanobioreactor. TENGs generated from 20, 40, or 80 DRG maintained neuronal-axonal phenotype and exhibited robust longitudinal axonal alignment across all conditions. While higher-density TENGs demonstrated a modest but significant reduction in length over time, overall contraction remained limited, and contraction rates were not significantly different among the groups. Stretch-grown axons maintained over 90% of their immediate post-stretch length out to 5-7 weeks post-encapsulation. Higher density TENGs also exhibited increased integration and fusion of DRG, forming continuous neuronal somatic fields and the ends of the TENGs and running perpendicular to the stretch-grown axons. Moreover, quantitative analyses revealed density- and time-dependent remodeling of axonal fascicular architecture, characterized by increased fascicle diameter without substantial changes in fascicle number, consistent with progressive axonal thickening, bundling and network consolidation. Despite this maturation-associated remodeling, TENGs preserved overall structural integrity and alignment through 7 weeks in culture. Collectively, these findings establish TENGs as mechanically stable, dynamically remodeling tissues and support their potential use as nerve repair strategies requiring graft stability over clinically relevant timeframes. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: Tissue-engineered nerve grafts (TENGs) use living, stretch-grown axons to guide repair after peripheral nerve injury, but their long-term structural stability has remained unclear. In this study, we show that collagen-encapsulated TENGs generated with different dorsal root ganglia densities remain intact for up to seven weeks, preserve longitudinal axon alignment, and retain more than 90% of their original length. At the same time, their internal architecture continues to mature through axon bundling and fascicle thickening, particularly at higher cell densities. These findings establish that TENGs can undergo biological remodeling without losing overall shape or dimensions. This "dynamic stability" is important for reproducible manufacturing, storage, surgical handling, and future translation of living nerve grafts for peripheral nerve repair.

title: Buzzkill: Surface Acoustic Wave Disruption of Extracellular Vesicles
abstract: Abstract Extracellular vesicles (EVs) have emerged as information-rich specimens for potential biomarker analysis. However, their small size, compositional heterogeneity, and limited sample availability present significant analytical challenges. In particular, lipidomic characterization of EVs is complicated by membrane robustness, aggregation behavior, and incompatibility with conventional preparation workflows. Herein, we investigate surface acoustic wave (SAW) manipulation as a mechanical, reagent-free strategy for controlled EV handling across labeling and lipid release regimes. By varying SAW device conditions such as applied powers and frequency, we employed fluorescence studies, nanoparticle tracking analysis, and electron microscopy to demonstrate that low-power, low frequency conditions can minimally disrupt EVs, while promoting dye-vesicle co-localization. We also report that at higher powers and frequencies, SAWs can be further adapted to induce vesicle disruption for direct mass spectrometric analysis, yielding reproducible detection of cholesterol as a representative lipid marker at a threshold of 60 MHz. In this work, we demonstrate the use of SAWs as a versatile tool for addressing key setbacks in EV analyses, offering tunable mechanical features to manipulate EVs, with potential as a sample-preparation approach for future EV lipid analysis.

title: Abstract 9207: Long-Term Outcomes of Endoscopic or Open Vein Harvesting for Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting - A 10 Year Follow Up of the REGROUP Randomized Clinical Trial
abstract: Background: The saphenous vein is the most common conduit for coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) and can be harvested via open (OVH) or endoscopic (EVH) techniques. Although EVH is used in >80% of North American CABG procedures, its long-term impact remains uncertain. The REGROUP RCT previously showed no difference in all-cause mortality or major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) between OVH and EVH at 3 and 5 years. An observational analysis of the EXCEL trial, however, reported higher ischemia-driven revascularization with EVH at 5 years, though other MACE outcomes were similar. Because saphenous vein graft failure commonly occurs beyond 5 years, extended follow-up is needed. We report 10-year follow up of REGROUP RCT to evaluate long-term outcomes associated with OVH and EVH. Methods: Patients undergoing CABG at 16 VA medical centers (2014-2017) were randomized 1:1 to EVH or OVH. Primary outcomes were all-cause mortality and MACE. Unadjusted event rates were compared using Kaplan-Meier analysis with log-rank testing. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models (HR, 95% CI) assessed the association between harvesting technique and outcomes. All tests were 2-sided; P<0.05 was significant. Results: A total of 1149 participants (mean [SD] age, 66.4 [6.9] years; 99.5% men) were randomized-574 (50%) to OVH and 575 (50%) to EVH. Baseline demographics and comorbidities were well balanced. Median follow-up was 10.1 (IQR, 8.1-11.1) years. All-cause mortality occurred in 222 EVH patients (38.6%) and 212 OVH patients (36.9%) (HR, 1.05; 95% CI, 0.87-1.27; P=0.62). Subgroup analyses stratified by smoking status, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, age (<65 vs ≥65 years), and number of venous grafts (1 vs ≥2) showed no significant difference in mortality between groups. Conclusions: In REGROUP, vein harvesting technique (EVH vs OVH) was not associated with all-cause mortality over 10-year follow-up after CABG. Given the widespread adoption of EVH and our prior findings of fewer wound complications, these results are reassuring. Analyses of 10-year MACE outcomes in REGROUP RCT will be presented.

title: Abstract 5192: Guideline-Directed Medical Therapy and Long-Term Outcomes in ISCHEMIA-EXTEND
abstract: Introduction: Guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) with multiple risk factor goals is recommended for patients with chronic coronary disease (CCD). The relative importance of individual targets for reducing long-term mortality remains unclear. Objectives: To evaluate the association between attaining specific GDMT goals and long-term mortality in CCD. Methods: This observational study includes all ISCHEMIA (International Study of Comparative Health Effectiveness with Medical and Invasive Approaches) participants with extended vital status follow-up regardless of randomization assignment. The outcome was all-cause mortality (hereafter, mortality). GDMT goals included systolic blood pressure (SBP) <130 mmHg, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) <70 mg/dL, not smoking, and antiplatelet therapy (including aspirin), each assessed at baseline and during the median 3.2 year active intervention phase of the randomized trial. A secondary GDMT goal was 150 minutes/week of moderate intensity physical activity (PA). Bayesian joint longitudinal-survival models quantified the association of goal status at baseline and during the active intervention phase with mortality over 11 years (median 9). Results: Among the 5179 ISCHEMIA participants, 4,914 had complete data for all four GDMT goals at baseline and were included. Of these, 386 (9%), 2,073 (42%), 1,843 (38%), and 612 (12%) met a total of 0-1, 2, 3, or 4 goals, respectively, at baseline and throughout the active intervention phase. The 9-year cumulative event rate of mortality was highest among those who did not maintain achievement of any GDMT goal throughout the active intervention phase (42.6%, 95% credible interval (CrI): 29.5, 59.1%) and lowest among those meeting all goals at baseline and throughout the active intervention phase (13.1%, 95% CrI: 11.1, 15.3%). The largest absolute differences in mortality were associated with taking antiplatelet agents (-14.0%, 95% CrI: -31.4, 1.4%) and not smoking (-14.5%, 95% CrI: -22.6, -7.4%), followed by achieving SBP <130 mmHg (-8.0%, 95% CrI: -12.6 -2.7%), and LDL-C <70 mg/dL (-2.6%, 95% CrI: -7.1, 2.1%). In secondary analyses, each 10-mmHg lower SBP and each 1.5-hour/week increase in physical activity during the active trial phase were independently associated with 11% and 8% relative reductions in mortality, respectively (SBP: RR=0.89, 95% CrI: 0.83, 0.94; physical activity: RR=0.92, 95% CrI: 0.89, 0.96). Conclusions: Among participants with CCD, attainment and maintenance of GDMT goals during the active intervention trial phase were associated with lower long-term mortality, particularly antiplatelet therapy and not smoking. Compared with achieving none of the GDMT goals, meeting all four GDMT goals at baseline and throughout the active intervention phase was associated with 29.5% lower absolute mortality rate over 9-year follow-up.

title: Top Ten Tips All Palliative Care Clinicians Should Know About Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder.
abstract: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a trauma- and stressor-related disorder that may substantially affect patients with serious illness. Patients may encounter palliative care (PC) with preexisting PTSD, develop trauma-related symptoms during the course of serious illness, or experience reactivation of prior traumatic stress through medical care and associated loss of control. PTSD can complicate symptom assessment, communication, decision-making, engagement with care, and quality of life. Management in serious illness also requires clinicians to adapt standard psychiatric approaches to prognosis, medical comorbidity, treatment burden, and goals of care. In this article, a multidisciplinary team provides 10 practical tips to help PC clinicians recognize PTSD, respond to trauma-related distress, use trauma-informed care, select appropriate treatments, and address trauma-related suffering near the end of life.

title: Recommendations for enhancing COVID-19 test and treat programmes in four African countries: insights and strategies from a qualitative study.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Sub-Saharan Africa had a significant burden of infections and deaths from COVID-19. However, throughout the pandemic, the region experienced delays and more limited access to diagnostics and treatment than high-income countries. From late 2022 to 2023, nirmatrelvir/ritonavir was introduced in four sub-Saharan African countries (Ghana, Malawi, Rwanda and Zambia) in a test and treat (T&T) model. This manuscript aims to understand the perspectives of key stakeholders, Ministry of Health, public sector personnel and healthcare workers on the recommendations for improvement and strengthening of national COVID-19 T&T programmes deployed in the four study countries.
METHODS: We conducted in-depth, semi-structured interviews with individuals from two key stakeholder groups: Ministry of Health or public sector personnel involved in developing and/or implementing COVID-19 T&T policy (purposive sampling) and healthcare workers involved in administering COVID-19 testing and/or treatment at study sites (convenience sampling). Sample size was driven by information power; our target sample size was 10-12 interviews per stakeholder group per country. We conducted a descriptive qualitative study to explore recommendations for improvement and strengthening of national COVID-19 T&T programmes using the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research to guide qualitative data collection and analysis.
RESULTS: Four key themes were identified by key stakeholders as critical to scaling up COVID-19 T&T programmes across all study countries: increasing community education, engagement and awareness of COVID-19 and the T&T programme; adjusting the T&T programme to ensure programme integration, decentralisation and sustainability; expansion of SARS-CoV-2 testing and ensuring availability of testing kits and oral antivirals through reliable national supply chains; and ensuring ongoing training and support for healthcare workers on the COVID-19 T&T programme.
CONCLUSION: Our findings, that recommendations were largely common across countries, suggest that a unifying framework for introducing new drugs through T&T programmes during future pandemics in sub-Saharan countries may be possible, particularly when implementation strategies can be customised to fit local contexts.

title: Connexin and Pannexin Channels in Traumatic Spinal Cord Injury: Mechanisms of Secondary Injury and Therapeutic Opportunities
abstract: Traumatic spinal cord injury (tSCI) causes immediate mechanical damage followed by a secondary cascade of excitotoxic, oxidative, metabolic, and inflammatory events that expands tissue loss. Connexin (Cx) and pannexin (Panx) channels are increasingly recognized as potential amplifiers of this secondary injury. This focused review summarizes the structural and biophysical properties of these channels that are relevant to the injured spinal cord, their cellular localization, and the experimental evidence linking Cx43 and Panx1 activity to ATP release, calcium dysregulation, neuroinflammation, tissue loss, neuropathic pain, and functional recovery after tSCI. We also review genetic and pharmacologic studies of channel inhibition and discuss the limited but emerging evidence for Cx-mediated signaling in paralyzed skeletal muscle. Evidence is strongest for astrocytic Cx43 hemichannels, whereas the contribution of Panx1 after tSCI remains promising but less completely defined. Throughout, we distinguish findings demonstrated directly after tSCI from mechanisms inferred from other tissues or disease models and identify priorities for translational research.

title: Physical activity levels two years after total knee arthroplasty and preoperative patient characteristics: a secondary analysis of the MOVE randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: At one year after total knee arthroplasty (TKA), patients are less physically active than age-matched peers, but physical activity (PA) trajectories two years after TKA are unclear. This study examined PA levels from baseline to two years post-TKA, quantified return to baseline PA levels over time, and evaluated associations between baseline participant characteristics and post-TKA PA levels.
METHODS: This was an exploratory secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial. Participants (n = 135) aged 50 to 85 years undergoing primary unilateral TKA wore accelerometers preoperatively and 10 weeks, six months, and two years post-TKA to characterize light PA, moderate-vigorous PA (MVPA), and steps/day. Descriptive statistics were used to characterize PA levels. Repeated measures models estimated PA levels over time. The percentage of participants who returned to or exceeded baseline PA levels over time was quantified. Multivariate logistic regressions modeled return to baseline PA levels over time to evaluate associations with baseline participant characteristics. All models controlled for age, sex, and treatment group.
RESULTS: There was an increase of 8% steps/day and 0.75% MVPA from baseline to two years post-TKA. At two years post-TKA, 54.2, 53.1, and 55.6% of participants returned to baseline light PA, MVPA, and steps/day levels. Higher baseline PA levels were associated with lower odds of returning to baseline levels at all timepoints for MVPA (10 weeks odds ratio (95% confidence interval): 0.62 (0.46 to 0.84); six months: 0.55 (0.40 to 0.76); two years: 0.52 (0.36 to 0.75)), as well as light PA and steps/day (all P-values < 0.05). Baseline body mass index, Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Arthritis Index scores, and Functional Comorbidity Index were associated inconsistently with PA levels.
CONCLUSION: While on average, PA levels increased from baseline to two years post-TKA, participants who have higher baseline PA levels had reduced odds of returning to the same level. These findings suggest TKA and current rehabilitation may not fully address PA, and additional support (e.g., behavioral guidance or tailored rehabilitation) may be needed.

title: Current Attitudes and Use Patterns of Large Language Models in Clinical Practice and Medical Education Among Trauma Providers
abstract: Introduction: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in clinical practice and medical education, yet uncertainty remains regarding appropriate use, oversight, and potential effects on clinical reasoning and patient safety. This study examined current LLM use patterns, attitudes, perceived risks, and priorities for responsible integration among individuals engaged in trauma care, clinical guidance development, and medical education. Methods: Participants attending the third Design for Implementation: The Future of Trauma Clinical Guidance and Research Conference (DFI) completed surveys examining LLM use, attitudes, perceived inhibitors to personal use, and clinical applications. During facilitated sessions, participants used open-ended note-taking guides to document their perspectives regarding LLM use in clinical practice, education, and guidance development. Survey data were analyzed descriptively, and qualitative responses were analyzed using rapid qualitative content analysis. Results: 77 participants completed the pre-conference survey; 62 clinicians provided data regarding clinical LLM use and attitudes. Among clinicians, 15% reported daily LLM use, whereas 26% reported never using LLMs. Respondents expressed strongest agreement with the need for regular quality auditing of LLM-supported clinical decisions. Among 52 post-conference survey respondents, 96% somewhat or strongly agreed that clinical training curricula should include education on LLM use. Barriers to LLM use included time required to verify accuracy, concern about patient harm, and insufficient training in appropriate prompting. Qualitative data came from 23 note-taking documents administered during the conference. Both positive and negative perspectives arose regarding AI use, centering on topics including efficiency gains, deskilling and never-skilling, governance and oversight, accuracy and hallucination, patient safety, and education. Discussion: DFI participants recognized efficiency and informational benefits of LLMs while identifying important concerns related to accuracy, patient safety, skill development, and governance. Findings support a need for institutional guidance, education in responsible LLM use, and evaluation of the incorporation of these technologies into clinical practice and health professions education.

title: Recruitment, Engagement, Experiences, and Self-Reported Changes in a Digital Patient Activation Intervention to Improve Hemodialysis Session Stability: Mixed Methods Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: When chronic kidney disease progresses to end-stage kidney disease, many patients receive in-center hemodialysis. Although lifesaving, hemodialysis is associated with intradialytic hypotension. Peer mentoring and patient activation support in hemodialysis have not been well studied.
OBJECTIVE: This Dialysafe study combined patient education and peer mentoring to promote health behaviors supporting prevention of intradialytic hypotension. We aimed to describe recruitment, engagement, completion, and attrition; assess participants' health goals and self-reported behavior changes; and evaluate satisfaction and recommendations for improvement.
METHODS: At 10 Dialysafe hemodialysis centers assigned to patient activation, all eligible English-speaking patients were invited. The intervention comprised 5 educational modules and 5 videoconference peer-mentoring sessions. Mixed methods analyses integrated electronic health record and platform data, postintervention surveys, and clinic operations committee notes. An engagement score (range 0-50) summarized intervention use. Descriptive statistics, t tests, chi-square tests, logistic regression, and zero-inflated Poisson regression were used to assess recruitment, completion (all 5 mentoring sessions), and engagement. Qualitative data were inductively coded and integrated through joint displays.
RESULTS: Of the 639 eligible patients, 155 (24.3%) were recruited. Recruited patients were younger than nonrecruited patients (mean 57.6, SD 13.8, vs 64.3, SD 14.7 y; P<.001); each additional year was associated with 4% lower odds of recruitment (odds ratio [OR] 0.96, 95% CI 0.94-0.98; P<.001). Recruitment was more likely among college graduates (OR 1.70, 95% CI 1.02-2.83; P=.04) and patients with sleep disorders (OR 2.27, 95% CI 1.06-4.87; P=.03). Attrition was concentrated before mentoring sessions began. Of recruited patients, 72 of 155 (46.5%) met with a peer mentor and 58 of 155 (37.4%) completed all 5 sessions. Completers were 1.9 years younger (56.4, SD 13.8, vs 58.3, SD 13.9 y) and had Charlson Comorbidity Index scores 0.4 points higher (3.4, SD 2.0, vs 3.0, SD 2.3) than noncompleters. The average engagement score was 18.4 of 50 (SD 20.1). Engagement was higher among men (incidence rate ratio [IRR] 1.33, 95% CI 1.22-1.45; P<.001), Black patients (IRR 1.27, 95% CI 1.16-1.39; P<.001), and patients with dialysis vintage <1 year (IRR 1.22, 95% CI 1.05-1.42; P=.01). Higher Charlson Comorbidity Index scores predicted engagement (IRR 1.04, 95% CI 1.01-1.07; P=.002) and completion (OR 1.37, 95% CI 1.05-1.79; P=.02). Of 79 patients who set goals, 64 (81%) selected communication with the care team; 22 of 54 (40.7%) survey respondents identified this as their main behavior change. Both mentees and mentors identified peer-mentoring sessions as the most valuable component. Among mentee respondents, 55 of 55 (100%) respondents rated the program good or excellent, and 53 of 54 (98.1%) respondents would recommend it.
CONCLUSIONS: Participants constituted a self-selecting group. Patient-clinician communication was a priority, and participants valued peer mentoring. Digital patient activation intervention strategies to increase reach are needed.

title: Tn7 Integration Efficiently Introduces Gene Expression Cassettes into a Gut-Native Escherichia coli Strain
abstract: Abstract Native bacteria are strains isolated from the host and often require greater development and optimization of genetic manipulation tools than lab-adapted strains. We have previously shown that the native murine Escherichia coli strain EcAZ-1, which colonizes the conventional mouse gut long term, is genetically tractable, and the engineered strain can elicit physiological effects while residing in the mouse gut. Given the interest in using EcAZ-1 and other native E. coli as a chassis for heterologous gene expression in the mouse gut, researchers need more efficient tools to rapidly and reliably introduce heterologous gene expression into the strain. Here, we demonstrate that a gene expression cassette can be integrated into the EcAZ-1 genome with high efficiency using the site-specific Tn7 transposon. Furthermore, we demonstrate that EcAZ-1 modified to express sfGFP using this method stably engrafts in the gut of conventional mouse. Taken together, Tn7-mediated integration is an effective method for stably introducing genetic cassettes into the native murine strain EcAZ-1 for expression in the mouse gut.

title: Fear-antagonistic actions and safety behaviors in the treatment of acrophobia: A randomized controlled trial.
abstract: Exposure therapy effectively treats anxiety disorders, yet non-response and premature dropout motivate continued work on procedural enhancements. Fear-antagonistic actions, behaviors that directly oppose fear-driven action tendencies (e.g., walking briskly toward and leaning over a railing rather than standing back from the edge), can augment exposure, but performing them necessarily precludes safety behaviors. This study examined whether fear-antagonistic actions confer augmentation effects beyond safety behavior elimination alone. University students and community adults with long-standing, clinically significant fear of heights (N = 109; 68% female; mean age = 21.8 years) were randomly assigned to standard exposure (EXP; n = 32), exposure with safety behavior fading (EXP+SBF; n = 31), exposure with safety behavior fading plus fear-antagonistic actions (EXP+SBF+AA; n = 35), or waitlist control (WLC; n = 11). Peak fear during a behavioral approach test in a novel (generalization) context served as the pre-designated primary outcome. Both EXP + SBF + AA and EXP + SBF outperformed EXP on peak fear in the treatment and generalization contexts through 1-month follow-up, and all active conditions outperformed WLC. EXP + SBF + AA and EXP + SBF did not significantly differ on any primary or secondary outcome (all ps > .140). Bayes factors provided moderate evidence against differential change on the primary outcome (BF01 = 6.1), although equivalence tests could not exclude small-to-moderate differences. Marked reductions in height overestimation occurred for all active groups and were sustained at 1-month follow-up. Findings indicate that safety behavior elimination is the robust active ingredient driving augmentation effects; any incremental benefit of fear-antagonistic actions is likely small.

title: "Most of what I do is a workaround now": Clinician Use of Workarounds Following an EHR Transition.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) is transitioning from a homegrown electronic health record (EHR) system to a single-vendor Federal EHR system, the largest EHR transition in history. Research shows that this transition was profoundly disruptive to care during the early implementation phase, yet limited data exist on clinician experience with and response to the transition in the years following implementation of the new system.
OBJECTIVE: To investigate the use and perceptions of workarounds among VA clinicians using the new Federal EHR system.
DESIGN: A descriptive exploratory qualitative study.
PARTICIPANTS: Using a mix of purposive and snowball sampling, we recruited direct care clinicians across a range of professions currently employed at the first five VA medical sites to transition to the new Federal EHR. Of the 104 clinicians invited, 30 (28.8%) participated in interviews.
APPROACH: We conducted semi-structured interviews with clinicians approximately 1.5 to 4 years post-go-live across sites. We performed a hybrid inductive-deductive content analysis using an approach that combined templated summaries with matrix analysis. KEY RESULTS: Workarounds emerged as highly salient to clinician experience with the new EHR. Analyses generated four themes relevant to EHR workarounds: (1) ongoing EHR-related challenges impeded clinicians' job performance; (2) workarounds emerged in response to continued EHR challenges; (3) workarounds were perceived as necessary but risky to patients, users, and the health care system; and (4) as EHR problems persisted, workarounds became routine.
CONCLUSIONS: Many of VA's EHR transition challenges have persisted beyond the initial implementation phase, contributing to a reliance on workarounds to overcome obstacles to care delivery. Workarounds were perceived as both beneficial and risky to users, patients, and the healthcare system. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating the role and impact of workarounds during EHR-to-EHR transitions to inform system improvements and workflow optimization.

title: Predictive Modeling of Clinically Apparent Shoulder Periprosthetic Joint Infection (PJI).
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The first International Consensus Meeting (ICM) definition of shoulder periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) introduced a tiered framework of PJI categories based on weighting of minor criteria for those cases not having major criteria of Definite infection. The selection of minor criteria and weightings was based on expert opinion and limited available evidence. The purpose of this study was to use prospective, multicenter data to develop a predictive model for clinically apparent shoulder PJI to inform a more evidence-based understanding of minor criteria and PJI categories.
METHODS: Prospective data were collected on 861 consecutive revision shoulder arthroplasty cases within the American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons (ASES) Revision Shoulder Arthroplasty and PJI Multicenter Research Group. Presence of a sinus tract communicating with the prosthesis and intra-articular purulence were identified as pathognomonic indicators of infection (major criteria) and used as the primary outcome for multivariable analysis. Logistic regression modeling was performed, with model specification guided by information criteria. Variable selection emphasized optimal model fit while balancing complexity, focusing on: (1) markers of host inflammatory response, (2) universally available and commonly utilized diagnostic tests, (3) minimizing the total number of variables, and (4) preserving model usability despite missing data.
RESULTS: Among 861 cases, 97 shoulders (11%) met the outcome of interest (sinus tract or intra-articular purulence). The final model incorporated seven variables spanning clinical findings, laboratory values, imaging, intraoperative assessment, and microbiology. These variables were erythema, unexpected wound drainage, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) or C-reactive protein (CRP), radiographic humeral osteolysis, synovial neutrophils ≥70% or positive frozen section (≥5 polymorphonuclear cells in ≥5 high-powered fields), intraoperative humeral loosening, and ≥2 positive cultures with the same organism. The apparent concordance statistic in the development cohort was 0.90 (95% CI 0.87-0.94). A nomogram was subsequently developed to estimate the probability of PJI, defined by the presence of a sinus tract or intra-articular purulence.
CONCLUSION: Using prospective, multicenter data, this study proposes a seven-factor nomogram to estimate the probability of clinically apparent shoulder PJI. The model showed strong apparent discrimination for clinically apparent infection in the development cohort. External validation will be necessary to confirm performance, and consensus will be required to establish weighting and diagnostic thresholds for tiers of non-definite shoulder PJI.

title: Mitochondrial Dysfunction Across Renal Compartments in Diabetic Kidney Disease
abstract: Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) remains a leading cause of chronic kidney disease and kidney failure despite considerable therapeutic progress. Mitochondrial dysfunction has emerged as a central mechanism linking diabetic metabolic stress to progressive renal injury, yet it is often described as a generalized, whole-kidney abnormality. This view is incomplete because renal compartments differ in metabolic demand, substrate preference, oxygen exposure, mitochondrial density, and repair capacity. Therefore, diabetes is unlikely to induce a uniform mitochondrial defect across the kidney. Here, we introduce a compartment- and stage-specific framework that integrates evidence from proximal tubules, distal nephron segments, glomerular endothelial cells, podocytes, mesangial cells, immune cells, and interstitial compartments. Using this framework, we define how mitochondrial metabolism, dynamics, quality control, redox signaling, mtDNA stress, and inflammatory pathways contribute to DKD progression across distinct renal cell types. We highlight which mitochondrial programs are most clearly implicated in specific renal compartments, where evidence remains limited, and how understudied cell types may contribute to disease progression. This cell- and stage-specific framework provides a basis for interpreting mitochondrial dysfunction by renal compartment and biological context rather than as a single kidney-wide process. Moving beyond bulk mitochondrial measurements toward spatial, functional, and cell-specific mitochondrial phenotyping may clarify whether mitochondrial responses are adaptive, injurious, or reversible and support therapeutic strategies directed toward the relevant mitochondrial programs in the appropriate compartment and at the appropriate disease stage. Article Highlights Mitochondrial dysfunction in diabetic kidney disease is compartment and stage specific, reflecting differences in renal cell metabolism, function, and injury response. This article introduces a framework for interpreting mitochondrial dysfunction across renal cell types and disease stages. Proximal tubular stress progresses from increased transport demand to mitochondrial injury and impaired quality control. Distal nephron, immune, and interstitial mitochondrial mechanisms remain incompletely defined. In glomerular endothelial cells and podocytes, mitochondria primarily regulate stress and injury signaling. Cell-specific mitochondrial phenotyping may reveal reversible pathways and guide more precise therapeutic strategies in diabetic kidney disease.

title: Restorative and regenerative therapies for vision loss.
abstract: Reversing blindness and restoring functional vision remains a central challenge in biomedical engineering. Advances in ocular prosthetics have enabled limited recovery of light perception, motion detection, and coarse object recognition through anterior segment devices such as keratoprostheses and through posterior segment interfaces including retinal, suprachoroidal, optic nerve, and cortical implants. Parallel progress in organ-on-a-chip systems and retinal organoids is providing increasingly sophisticated platforms for disease modelling and therapeutic development. Despite these advances, issues of long-term biocompatibility, signal fidelity, and surgical complexity continue to constrain clinical performance. Emerging approaches that combine stem cell-derived tissues, biofabrication, and hybrid bioelectronic constructs offer promising avenues for next-generation vision restoration, although current production remains limited to early-stage or small-scale systems. Effective integration of these technologies also requires structured vision-rehabilitation strategies to harness neuroplasticity and support functional adaptation. This review synthesises recent progress across prosthetic, rehabilitative, and regenerative domains and outlines key opportunities for future translational development.

title: A vasopressin gate transforms social distress into caregiving.
abstract: Another individual's distress can provoke withdrawal and avoidance behaviors, yet, in social species, it can also motivate approach and caregiving behavior. In this issue, Geng et al. identified a vasopressin-sensitive neuronal circuit that converts distress signals from a cagemate into caregiving-like behavior in mice. Using fiber photometry, electrophysiological recordings, and optogenetic activation to dissect this circuit, they showed that vasopressin neurons in the paraventricular hypothalamus recruit vasopressin 1a receptor-expressing (V1aR-expressing) neurons in the medial central amygdala, which engage the ventral tegmental area to promote allogrooming and injury-directed licking. The findings link emotional state matching, prosocial action, reinforcement, and stress relief, while raising important questions about circuit specificity, sex as a biological variable, and translation.

title: A feature learning model identifies predictive attributes of mesenchymal stromal cell efficacy for osteoarthritis therapy
abstract: Abstract Human mesenchymal stromal cells (hMSCs) have shown inconsistent clinical benefit, in part because donor-to-donor variability obscures the cellular attributes that drive therapeutic potency. To address this challenge, we screened hMSCs from multiple donors and integrated in vitro secretome profiling with efficacy data in an in vivo preclinical osteoarthritis model; we identified cellular paracrine signatures that distinguish more-therapeutic from less-therapeutic hMSCs. We trained a feature learning model relating secretome to in vivo structural outcomes and, in a prospective proof-of-concept study, used it to classify additional donors, with in vivo outcomes directionally consistent with predictions. Transcriptomic and phospho-protein analyses showed elevated JNK pathway activation in more-therapeutic hMSCs. Pharmacologic JNK inhibition using a small molecule inhibitor SP600125 in more-therapeutic cells reduced therapeutic cytokine secretion, while metformin treatment reported to increase phosphorylation, shifted the secretome of less-therapeutic hMSCs towards a more-therapeutic profile. Together, these findings define potency-associated attributes of hMSC efficacy and establish a prospective predictive framework for donor screening and potency optimization. This approach addresses a major barrier in scalable cell therapies and advances precision hMSC-based treatments.

title: Intervention against autodigestion enhances cardiovascular stability and trauma response in the elder
abstract: Abstract An important step to improve the quality of life in older adults is to reduce their heightened sensitivity to trauma challenges, such as elective surgery. Our recent evidence indicates that a mechanism behind aging and reduced quality of life involves the leakage of pancreatic digestive enzymes from the gastrointestinal tract into the bloodstream and peripheral organs. The leaked enzymes degrade plasma proteins, extracellular matrix proteins, and membrane receptors, leading to cell and organ dysfunctions typical for aging. Here, we hypothesize that blockade of leaked digestive enzymes improves the quality of life in the elderly and their response to trauma. A one-week oral treatment of old rats with a pancreatic digestive serine protease (trypsin) inhibitor, without significantly impairing normal digestion, decreases protease activity in the central circulation and benefits older individuals facing trauma. We find that this pretreatment stabilizes the cardiovascular system of aged rats, improves metabolic disturbances caused by hemorrhagic shock, and significantly enhances their response to shock. Systolic and mean arterial blood pressures are normalized, and the baroreflex, which is severely impaired in aged rats, is substantially improved by the pretreatment. The survival rate during central blood pressure reduction is significantly higher in old rats pretreated against trypsin activity. The evidence confirms our hypothesis that aging results from the uncontrolled activity of digestive enzymes outside the pancreas and intestine, and that blocking their activity improves the ability of aged rats to withstand cardiovascular challenges. The proposed intervention protocol against the degrative action of digestive enzymes is clinically applicable and testable.

title: Nutrition as a cross-cutting pillar of lifestyle medicine for frailty prevention and healthy aging in older adults
abstract: Frailty is a dynamic, multidimensional state of diminished physiologic reserve that increases vulnerability to stressors and predicts disability, hospitalization, and mortality in older adults. Nutrition is one of the six pillars of lifestyle medicine (alongside physical activity, restorative sleep, stress management, positive social connection, and avoidance of risky substances), an evidence-based framework for promoting health and preventing disease. In older adults, optimal energy, protein, and micronutrient intake supports muscle mass, functional capacity, and metabolic and cognitive resilience, whereas poor diet quality and undernutrition worsen sleep, stress physiology, and frailty trajectories. This mini-review synthesizes how nutrition interacts with each pillar of lifestyle medicine in older adults and considers implications for clinical practice and research. Nutrition emerges as a central determinant of healthy aging, directly influencing physiologic resilience and shaping the benefits of the other lifestyle medicine pillars in preserving strength, function, and independence.

title: Extracellular vesicles presenting “don’t eat me” signal limit the efferocytic capacity in lung fibrosis
abstract: Efferocytosis is essential for tissue homeostasis and resolution of inflammation, yet its direct contribution to resolve organ fibrosis remains poorly understood. In idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a progressive age-driven lung disease, we found profound suppression of efferocytosis coupled with robust production and release of extracellular vesicles presenting functional receptor CD47, a canonical “don’t eat me” mediator. Restoration of efferocytosis contributes to the natural resolution of fibrosis, which is accelerated by CD47 deficiency or alterations in macrophage metabolic responses. In turn, pharmacologic disruption of efferocytic receptors or signaling results in lung fibrosis development and its persistence. While sustained reduction of efferocytic capacity align with fibrosis persistence in aged mice, AMPK activation promotes fibrosis resolution via reducing inflammaging and CD47 bioavailability, thus restoring clearance of apoptotic fibroblast. Importantly, AMPK activation also reprograms macrophages engaging apoptotic fibroblasts toward a fibrosis pro-resolving phenotype by suppressing TGF-β1 and promoting secretion of pro-regenerative hepatocyte growth factor (HGF). Together, these findings link metabolism and immune efferocytic fitness in lung fibrosis resolution and suggest that an AMPK senomorphic pathway has broad therapeutic relevance for fibrotic diseases.

title: Primary Care Practice Productivity and Efficiency: Qualitative Evaluation of a Novel Clinic-Based Measure.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Existing primary care productivity and efficiency measures focus on the quantity of care delivered, without accounting for interprofessional teamwork invested or quality of care produced. We previously developed a novel productivity measure called Interprofessional Technical Efficiency Measure (ITEM) and tested it quantitatively across Veterans Affairs (VA) primary care practices. ITEM measures primary care practice efficiency in producing four primary care output measures (access, clinical quality of care, patient care experiences, and number of patients served) given staff time invested (inputs), while accounting for patient population complexity.
OBJECTIVE: To qualitatively assess ITEM's validity and potential usefulness through feedback from VA primary care directors, data experts, and frontline clinical team leaders.
DESIGN: We used rapid qualitative analysis of data from semi-structured interviews and focus groups to assess feedback on ITEM results.
PARTICIPANTS: A convenience sample of 34 interprofessional primary care leaders, managers, and frontline clinical team members from nine geographically dispersed VA medical centers and affiliated community-based outpatient clinics (CBOCs).
APPROACH: Participants reviewed graphic data visualizations comparing their scores to national VA averages. Qualitative thematic analysis focused on face, construct, and content validity, and usefulness for primary care efficiency improvement.
RESULTS: Overall, participants perceived the ITEM measure as having face, construct, and content validity, and viewed ITEM and its data visualization approach as potentially useful for primary care practice efficiency improvement. Participant concerns focused on lack of measures of team functioning or burnout, data time lags related to practice team composition or output changes, potential alternative measures of ITEM outputs, and potential additional local context measures.
CONCLUSIONS: Primary care leaders and clinicians were receptive to a new productivity and efficiency measure that integrated quality and quantity of care goals, and to ITEM as a promising approach. Findings support continued ITEM development for use in primary care practice efficiency improvement initiatives.

title: Augmentation of Phospholipid Concentrations and Lipid Raft Signaling in SDHB Knockdown Cells After SCD1 Silencing
abstract: Pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma (PPGL) patients with pathogenic variants in the succinate dehydrogenase B subunit (SDHB) frequently develop aggressive disease with poor prognosis. The stearoyl-CoA desaturase 1 (SCD1) protein plays an important role in lipid metabolism. Here, we hypothesized siRNA mediated knockdown of SCD1 compared to non-targeting siRNA would alter the lipid composition of extracellular vesicles (EVs) released from SDHB KD cells compared to hPheo1wild-type (WT) progenitor cells and augment lipid raft density in recipient cells. Quantitative polymerase chain reaction showed that SDHB KD cells expressed less SCD1 than hPheo1 WT cells. The concentration of total phospholipids was greater in SDHB KD cells compared to hPheo1 WT cells, while siRNA-mediated knockdown of SCD1 resulted in decreased concentration in both cell types. Conditioned media EVs increased lipid raft density in recipient cells, which was blunted after SCD1 knockdown. These data suggest there are differences in the phospholipid composition between hPheo1 WT and SDHB KD cells and that EVs released from both cell types have the potential to activate lipid raft signaling pathways, which can be blocked by suppressing SCD1. Further research is necessary to investigate the mechanism of SCD1 inhibitors in SDHB-mutated PPGL.

title: Antiretroviral therapy, adiposity, and cardiometabolic risk in people with HIV.
abstract: Return to health accounts for only part of the weight gain observed with modern antiretroviral therapy (ART). A fuller account requires integrating recovery from HIV-related catabolism, HIV-associated adipose tissue remodelling, withdrawal of weight-suppressive antiretrovirals, possible direct or permissive effects of newer agents, individual susceptibility, and obesogenic environments. Evidence from ART initiation and switch studies, PrEP trials, and mechanistic research in adipose tissue suggests that ART-associated weight gain is heterogeneous rather than a uniform restorative process. Once adiposity is established, ART switching has a limited ability to reverse weight gain, consistent with the biological persistence of acquired adiposity. Future care should move beyond ART manipulation alone and incorporate early monitoring, body-composition assessment, cardiometabolic prevention, lifestyle intervention, and appropriate antiobesity pharmacotherapy.

title: Association of unmet discharge needs on readmission or mortality among acute respiratory failure survivors during the COVID-19 pandemic: The Addressing Post-Intensive Care Syndrome (APICS-COVID) multicenter prospective cohort study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Survivors of acute respiratory failure (ARF) often face long-term impairments known as Post-Intensive Care Syndrome. These impairments, coupled with fragmented healthcare, contribute to high rates of readmission and mortality. The COVID-19 pandemic challenged healthcare systems, providing an important opportunity to evaluate healthcare fragmentation before and during the pandemic.
METHODS: From December 2020 to July 2022, this prospective multicenter study (APICS-COVID) enrolled ARF survivors discharged home from acute care hospitalization. The primary exposure was unmet healthcare needs within 1-4 weeks post-discharge and the primary composite outcome was 3-month readmission and mortality. We additionally compared unmet healthcare needs in this study versus a predominately pre-pandemic cohort from an identical study protocol (APICS-01).
RESULTS: Of 201 patients enrolled, 94% had at least one unmet healthcare need. The median (IQR) number of healthcare needs upon discharge was 18 (11-25) and the median proportion of unmet healthcare needs was 26% (17-36%). Follow-up appointments were the most frequent unmet need. Higher vs. lower unmet healthcare needs were not significantly associated with 3-month readmission or mortality (aRR 0.61, p = 0.22). Compared to the APICS-01 cohort, the frequency of 3-month readmission/mortality was lower (14% vs. 29%, p = 0.26), despite higher unmet needs in the APICS-COVID cohort (26% vs. 16%, p < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: Across six US academic hospitals during the COVID-19 pandemic, we did not detect a significant association between higher and lower unmet healthcare needs and 3-month readmission or mortality. Compared to APICS-01, unmet follow-up appointments increased but readmission and mortality decreased. Home health services, durable medical equipment, and medications remained robust during pandemic conditions.

title: Mitochondrial Oxysterol Signaling in Epigenetic Regulation and Therapeutic Development.
abstract: Oxysterols are oxygenated cholesterol derivatives with receptor-dependent and epigenetic activities. This review examines how mitochondrial cholesterol metabolism and oxysterol sulfation may connect lipid metabolism to DNA methylation and communication between hepatocytes and macrophages. Biochemical studies show that 25-hydroxycholesterol (25HC) and 27-hydroxycholesterol (27HC) activate DNA methyltransferase 1 (DNMT1), whereas their 3-sulfated derivatives inhibit the activities of DNMT1, DNMT3A, and DNMT3B. Cholestenoic acid (CA) has a concentration-dependent effect, activating DNMT1 at lower concentrations and inhibiting it at higher concentrations. In hepatocyte models, these activities are associated with altered promoter CpG methylation and expression of genes involved in lipid metabolism, inflammatory responses, and cell survival. The sulfated CA metabolite, 3β-sulfate-5-cholestenoic acid (3SCA), is secreted by hepatocytes and modifies inflammatory gene expression in macrophages. We propose an oxysterol epigenetic rheostat in which metabolite concentrations and sulfation influence DNMT activities. Published animal studies support protective effects of 25-hydroxycholesterol 3-sulfate in fatty liver disease, endotoxemia, and acetaminophen-induced liver injury. Its clinical formulation, larsucosterol, has shown favorable hepatic and metabolic signals in Phase 1b fatty liver studies and nominally significant mortality reductions in prespecified US Phase 2b alcohol-associated hepatitis (AH) analyses. These encouraging findings require confirmation because the overall Phase 2b primary endpoint was not met. Larsucosterol has received Fast Track and Breakthrough Therapy designations from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for AH and is currently being evaluated in a registrational Phase 3 trial.

title: Bridging the gap: A qualitative study on veterans’ experiences with systemic barriers and support during transition
abstract: Many veterans face complex challenges during the transition from military to civilian life, particularly when navigating healthcare and benefits systems. This qualitative study examines how recently separated veterans with service‑connected musculoskeletal disorders perceive and navigate systemic barriers within Department of Defense and Veterans Affairs transition and healthcare systems. Semi‑structured interviews were conducted with 20 veterans within one year of separation who had filed a musculoskeletal service‑connection claim. Using a rapid qualitative analytic approach, interviews captured experiences with the discharge process, transition programming, and efforts to access healthcare and benefits. Analysis identified four major themes: the interaction of physical, psychological, and bureaucratic stressors during discharge, particularly salient for those managing musculoskeletal conditions; varied and often critical views of transition programming, which many perceived as generic and misaligned with individual needs; systemic barriers to care and benefits, including delays, fragmented processes, and cultural norms that discourage disclosure; and recommendations emphasizing continuity of care, case management, and emotional support to address identity disruption and loss of purpose. Overall, the findings highlight persistent structural and cultural obstacles that complicate transition and hinder early engagement with services. Improved coordination, continuity‑oriented supports, and psychologically responsive programming may reduce these barriers. Further research is needed to evaluate scalable models that enhance early post‑separation outcomes.

title: Inflammatory, Insulinemic, and Plant-Based Dietary Patterns and Diabetes Among Patients with Acute Pancreatitis: A Cross-Sectional Analysis of the DREAM Study
abstract: Background/Objectives: Plant-based diets are widely recommended for lowering the risk of type 2 diabetes, with the caveat that their health benefits depend on the quality of the foods consumed. This analysis examined associations between five dietary patterns and pre-existing diabetes among patients with acute pancreatitis (AP), a population in which the relationship between diet and diabetes has not been well characterized. Methods: Participants were drawn from the Diabetes RElated to Acute Pancreatitis and its Mechanisms (DREAM) study, an ongoing multicenter study of adults aged 18 to 75 years with AP in the U.S. This cross-sectional analysis evaluated five dietary patterns using food frequency questionnaires (FFQ): the reverse Empirical Dietary Index for Hyperinsulinemia (rEDIH), the reverse Empirical Dietary Inflammatory Pattern (rEDIP), the overall plant-based diet index (PDI), the healthful plant-based diet index (hPDI), and the unhealthful plant-based diet index (uPDI). We used multivariable logistic regression models to estimate odds ratios (ORs) for pre-existing diabetes (i.e., prior to the AP episode). Results: A total of 647 participants (mean age 49.1 ± 14.5 years) were included. In multivariable-adjusted analyses, participants in the highest versus lowest tertile of PDI had 55% lower odds of pre-existing diabetes (adjusted OR: 0.45; 95% CI: 0.25–0.80; p-trend = 0.005). No statistically significant associations were detected for rEDIP, rEDIH, hPDI, or uPDI. Conclusions: Higher overall PDI scores were associated with lower odds of prevalent diabetes. Among patients with AP, further studies are needed to evaluate dietary contributions to future diabetes development following AP and identify potential dietary strategies for diabetes prevention.

title: Microtubule stability modulates Schlemm's canal cell mechanobiology and outflow facility in glaucoma.
abstract: The inner wall of Schlemm's canal (SC) is a specialized mechanosensitive endothelium in which pore formation is essential for normal conventional aqueous humor outflow and hence intraocular pressure homeostasis, yet the role of microtubule (MT) stability in this process remains poorly understood. Here, using SC cell primary cultures from normal and glaucomatous human eyes as well as mouse whole eye perfusion, we identify MTs as a key component of the mechanotransduction machinery linking the mechanical microenvironment to SC cell biomechanics and conventional outflow. We show that MT stability is modulated by substrate stiffness and diminished in glaucomatous SC cells. MT stabilization suppresses GEF-H1-dependent actomyosin contractility, reduces cellular stiffness, and promotes transcellular pore formation in both normal and glaucomatous SC cells, whereas MT destabilization elicits opposing effects. Consistent with these cellular responses, pharmacological MT stabilization enhances conventional outflow facility in ex vivo mouse eyes. Together, our findings establish MT-dependent cytoskeletal remodeling as a previously unrecognized mechanism linking extracellular mechanical cues to SC biomechanics and transcellular pore formation and highlight MT-associated signaling as a potential therapeutic target for improving conventional outflow in glaucoma.

title: Physiological Sleep Features Associated With Dimensions of Daily Dysfunction in Insomnia.
abstract: Daily dysfunction is a key criterion of insomnia, but its underlying structure and relationship with objective sleep physiology remain unclear. This study aimed to identify the dimensions of subjective daily dysfunction using exploratory factor analysis (EFA) in individuals with insomnia and to examine its association with polysomnography (PSG) macroarchitecture, electroencephalographic (EEG) spectral power and odds ratio product (ORP)-based sleep depth in individuals with and without insomnia. We hypothesized that more severe daily dysfunction would be associated with poorer sleep continuity, higher high-frequency EEG activity and lighter sleep depth. The final sample included 859 adults (50.1% female; mean age 44.2 ± 14.1 years) in the Sleep Apnea Global Interdisciplinary Consortium (SAGIC) without obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) or shift work, including 368 with insomnia. EFA supported a single factor underlying the nine daily dysfunction items, which were combined into a total score. In univariate linear regression analyses adjusted for age, sex and site, higher beta-1 power and several ORP measures were nominally associated with more severe daily dysfunction, but none of them survived correction for multiple comparisons. No significant predictor-by-group interactions were observed. Across three levels of sleep physiology-PSG macroarchitecture, spectral power, and continuous sleep depth-no sleep measure was associated with daily dysfunction after correction for multiple comparisons. PSG macroarchitecture and sleep EEG-derived measures may not fully capture daily dysfunction. Future studies could examine whether within-night sleep dynamics are more informative than whole-night averages.

title: Differential Modulation of the Ileal Bile Acid Transporter ASBT by Fatty Acids
abstract: The ileal ASBT bile acid transporter is a critical mediator of bile acid and cholesterol homeostasis and is modulated by fatty acids via S-acylation. We investigated mechanisms underlying differential regulation of ASBT by saturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids. Using a prenylation mimetic with a CAAX box at the C-terminus of ASBT, we showed that transport activity in transfected HEK293 cells increased significantly, suggesting that direct attachment of a saturated fatty acid stimulates ASBT function. Furthermore, siRNA-mediated attenuation of DHHC21 acyltransferase expression reduced ASBT S-acylation and its function, demonstrating DHHC21 as a positive regulator of ASBT function. Conversely, treatment with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (n-3 PUFAs), like eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA), reduced ASBT function in HEK293 cells. Supplementation of fish oil, as a source of n-3 PUFAs, to a high-fat, high-cholesterol diet fed to C57BL6/J mice protected them against diet-induced hepatic steatosis, along with reduced bile acid absorption consistent with the inhibition of ASBT. This was supported by increased fecal bile acids, decreased ileal bile acid-stimulated gene expression, and increased hepatic bile acid synthesis-related gene expression. Metabolic labeling with alkyne-EPA in HEK293 cells showed, for the first time, direct binding of this n-3 PUFA to ASBT. Unlike palmitate modification, EPA binding was highly resistant to hydroxylamine retrieval, indicating a mechanism distinct from S-acylation. Our data unraveled a novel role for DHHC21 in regulating ASBT and provided evidence for distinct mechanisms by which saturated palmitate and polyunsaturated EPA fatty acids bind ASBT. The direct effect on ASBT and inhibition of bile acid absorption may partly contribute to the protective effects of n-3 PUFAs on the liver.

title: 17β-estradiol increases diet-dependent salt retention in ovariectomized female mice
abstract: Circadian rhythms heavily influence blood pressure regulation. Genetic manipulation of core circadian clock genes alters blood pressure phenotypes. We have shown that male mice with renal distal segment knockout of the circadian transcription factor BMAL1 (kidney-specific cadherin Cre-positive BMAL1 knockout; KS-BMAL1 KO) exhibit lower blood pressure than wild-type controls, and this phenotype is exacerbated by a salt-sensitive diet. The BMAL1-dependent blood pressure phenotype in male KS-BMAL1 KO is absent in intact female mice. The current study aims to determine if estradiol modulates BMAL1-dependent blood pressure regulation in female mice. We hypothesized that ovariectomized (OVX) female mice would demonstrate a genotype difference in blood pressure and that estradiol would abolish this difference. OVX control and OVX KS-BMAL1 KO female mice subcutaneously received either a 17β‑estradiol pellet or placebo for three weeks prior to dietary treatment. Blood pressure was recorded daily via telemetric devices in OVX mice administered a baseline standard diet followed by 7 days of a low-K+ diet, then 7 days of a low-K+ high-salt diet. Contrary to our hypothesis, OVX mice with placebo pellets did not demonstrate a genotype difference in blood pressure. Furthermore, blood pressure between genotypes remained similar in OVX mice with an estradiol pellet. Estradiol supplementation led to higher mean arterial pressure by ~ 8 mmHg in both genotypes on a low-K+ high-salt diet. During the adaptation period to a low-K+ high-salt diet, OVX KS-BMAL1 KO mice have less sodium retention compared to OVX control mice and estradiol leads to more sodium retention compared to placebo. Under the conditions tested, there is no evidence that estradiol plays a role in BMAL1-dependent blood pressure regulation. These findings provide insight into the sex-specific role of BMAL1 in blood pressure regulation.

title: Transdiagnostic symptom profiles in anxiety and depression: a person-centered approach to characterizing heterogeneity and exploring response to a positive valence intervention.
abstract: Anxiety and depression frequently co-occur and show substantial heterogeneity in clinical presentation and treatment response. Transdiagnostic, person-centered approaches may characterize overlapping phenotypes by classifying individuals into empirically derived symptom profiles. Aim 1 applied latent profile analysis of tripartite model symptoms (general distress [GD], anhedonic depression [AD], and anxious arousal [AA]) in a pooled sample of adults with clinically elevated anxiety and/or depression from five psychosocial clinical trials or cross-sectional studies (N = 248) to identify and validate distinct clinical profiles. Aim 2 tested profile correspondence in an independent sample of outpatient adults with similar eligibility criteria (N = 220). Aim 3 explored whether profiles predicted response to a positive valence intervention in an Aim 1 subsample (N = 61) using multilevel modeling. Three profiles were identified: Low AD, AA, and GD (10.9%), High AD, Low AA and GD (76.2%), and High AD, AA, and GD (12.9%). Aim 2 yielded correspondence for the High AD, Low AA and GD and High AD, AA, and GD profiles. Profiles were not distinguishable by primary anxiety or depressive disorder diagnosis (p >.05). Profiles differed in positive/negative affect, approach/avoidance motivation, and punishment, but not reward, sensitivity. Profiles did not significantly differ in treatment response (between-group effect sizes were small to medium). Findings suggest person-centered approaches may characterize symptom heterogeneity across anxiety and depressive presentations. Interpretation is limited by pooling across studies with non-identical eligibility criteria, partial cross-sample correspondence of identified profiles, and small Aim 3 profile sizes. Further research is needed to determine whether these methods can inform personalized treatment strategies.

title: Diacylglycerol kinase kappa is a target of the Prader-Willi syndrome gene SNORD116.
abstract: SNORD116 is a small nucleolar RNA deficient in Prader-Willi syndrome individuals. The mechanisms by which SNORD116 conveys its effects are unknown. Here, transcriptomic analysis showed that diacylglycerol kinase kappa (Dgkk) expression was elevated in the hypothalamus of Snord116-deficient mice. In silico analyses predicted a strong RNA:RNA interaction between Snord116 and Dgkk mRNA that is fully conserved in mouse and human. In vitro experiments in human cellular models demonstrated that SNORD116 mediates 2'-O-methylation of DGKK mRNA and regulates DGKK mRNA and protein expression. In Snord116-deficient mouse neurons, increased Dgkk expression was associated with attenuated diacylglycerol-mediated activation of ERK and PKC, critical elements in neuronal signaling cascades. In mice, brain Dgkk expression peaks during late embryonic and early postnatal periods, coinciding with peak rates of neurogenesis; its expression in adults is restricted mainly to brain regions implicated in Prader-Willi syndrome pathophysiology, including the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus. Fasting acutely decreased hypothalamic Dgkk expression in wild-type mice. Increased Dgkk expression in Snord116-deficient mice could reflect derangements in this pathway that affects both brain development and cell-specific functions.

title: Transcranial magnetic stimulation to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex modulates single-neuron activity in humans.
abstract: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) is an established treatment for depression, yet the fundamental question of how cortical stimulation influences single neurons in deep brain circuits critical for mood regulation remains unanswered. Using a rare opportunity to record from intracranial microelectrodes while TMS was delivered in four neurosurgical patients, we evaluated the responses of 185 single neurons. Artifact cleaning enabled single-neuron spikes to be resolved as early as 8 ms after stimulation. We found that single-pulse TMS to the left dlPFC elicited time-locked firing responses in 46% of neurons (26% facilitated only, 19% suppressed only, 1% both). These responses occurred within deep bilateral cortical and subcortical structures, including the putamen and thalamus. Single-pulse TMS tended to facilitate spiking in striato-thalamic putative inhibitory neurons from ~8 ms, peaking at ~80 to 100 ms, and decaying until ~600 ms. In contrast, putative excitatory neurons and limbic areas were suppressed with a slower time course lasting to ~1,000 ms. TMS-evoked potentials recorded from intracranial depth macroelectrodes to quantify network activity revealed that the modulation of responsive neurons was positively correlated with cortico-striato-thalamic network activity and anticorrelated with limbic network activity in one participant with sufficient network and unit sampling. These results suggest that dlPFC TMS recruits a high percentage of neurons spanning cortical and subcortical brain regions bilaterally. The recruitment pattern selectively involves increasing the firing rate of inhibitory neurons in executive control networks while suppressing limbic excitatory drive, providing a candidate cellular mechanism for how cortical stimulation modulates distributed brain networks.

title: Cryptic Presentations of Neurologic Wilson Disease With ATP7B Peptide Assessments
abstract: Objectives: To illustrate the phenotypic variability in neurologic Wilson disease (NWD) and diagnostic value of ATP7B peptide testing in resolving WD cases. Methods: We conducted a case series analysis of 3 individuals with suspected NWD. Clinical presentation, diagnostic workup including traditional biomarkers, genetic testing, and ATP7B peptide quantification by immuno-selected reaction monitoring mass spectrometry were reviewed. Results: The 3 patients demonstrated diverse neurologic presentations: (1) an adult with coexisting Parkinson disease and WD, exhibiting parkinsonian features with partial response to dopaminergic therapy; (2) a child with early-onset dystonia and neuropsychiatric symptoms; and (3) an adult initially misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis. In these cases, ATP7B peptide testing revealed either markedly reduced or undetectable levels, confirming WD. Discussion: These cases emphasize the diagnostic complexity of NWD. ATP7B peptide analysis via immuno-SRM-MS provided direct evidence of ATP7B protein deficiency and confirmed variant pathogenicity demonstrating its use as a rapid, noninvasive, functionally informative diagnostic adjunct. As the assay is further validated and piloted for newborn screening, it holds promise for improving early detection and clinical outcomes in WD.

title: Commentary: The patient as teacher: a four-phase blueprint for institutional change
abstract: Wollmann et al. offer a timely, ethically attentive roadmap for moving patient involvement in health professions education from isolated, champion-dependent activities toward institutional practice (1).Particularly valuable are their insistence on compensation, emotional safety, representative recruitment, durable governance, and evaluation beyond learner satisfaction. Their four phasesdiagnosis, role definition and goal setting, implementation planning and capacity building, and outcomes monitoring -give institutions a practical starting architecture. This commentary proposes one refinement that could make the roadmap more congruent with its own commitment to authentic co-production and more readily testable: treat involvement levels as options to be jointly chosen rather than rungs to be institutionally assigned, then specify how each implementation activity is expected to produce change. title: Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging-based measures of arterial signal-enhancement in patients with peripheral artery disease
abstract: Peripheral artery disease (PAD), a form of atherosclerosis of the lower extremities (LE), affects both large vessels and the microcirculation. PAD is associated with intermittent claudication (IC) pain, reduced mobility, and an increased risk of adverse cardiovascular events. Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (CE-MRI) of 56 participants (36 PAD patients with IC and 20 matched controls) were acquired at the mid-calf position to quantitatively assess first-pass perfusion in major LE arteries. Arterial signal intensity curves (ASIC) were derived for the anterior tibialis, posterior tibialis, and the peroneal (PE) arteries, representing the respective arterial signal dynamics including local pre-contrast arrival times and peak signal intensities. Several measures were derived from the individual and envelope arterial (composite) measures, each representing signal enhancement (SE), time to peak enhancement (TP), slope of the signal enhancement, and the area under the curve (AUC). Our experimental findings show that higher SE, TP, and AUC were observed in matched controls compared with PAD patients during arterial signal enhancement, suggesting impaired arterial circulation in claudicants. Several arterial measures including TP, SE, and the AUC differed significantly between PAD patients with compared to those without concomitant diabetes, whereas established PAD markers such as the resting and exercise ankle-brachial index (ABI), exercise capacity as measured by treadmill peak walking time and claudication onset time, calf muscle area, and renal function did not. In other analyses involving both legs, PAD patients exhibited significant arterial hemodynamics asymmetry with reduced SE, TP, and AUC in the target leg as compared with the contralateral limb. Among PAD patients with concomitant diabetes, the asymmetry was more pronounced and showed that the maximum and median TP, maximum AUC, sum of AUCs, and envelope AUCs were significantly lower in the target leg compared with the contralateral side. Several of the proposed CE-MRI variables of arterial hemodynamics were significantly associated with key clinical markers of PAD. CE-MRI-derived measures of arterial hemodynamics differentiate PAD patients from matched controls and also identify claudicants with concomitant diabetes who are known to present with an elevated risk for adverse cardiovascular outcomes. The proposed imaging measures could be of interest in the study of PAD status and severity.

title: Forty Years at the Counter and the Bedside: What Resistance to Change Actually Teaches Us.
abstract: Over four decades of pharmacy practice-retail, hospital pharmacy management, and now 20 years as a clinical pharmacist practitioner with the Department of Veterans Affairs-I have watched pharmacy resist nearly every major change proposed to it: automated dispensing technology, centralized mail-order pharmacy, expanded scope of practice and prescriptive authority, direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) displacing warfarin management, telehealth.Some of that resistance protected patients.Some of it cost them.The profession has rarely distinguished between the two in the moment, and that failure of distinction-not resistance itself-is the actual problem worth naming.

title: CalDyn: an advanced high-throughput automated algorithm for monitoring intracellular calcium dynamics and electrophysiological signals in patient-derived cells
abstract: BACKGROUND: Quantitative analysis of intracellular calcium and electrophysiological signals is challenging when signals exhibit baseline drift, low-amplitude events, irregular waveforms, or multicomponent transients. We developed CalDyn, a MATLAB-based graphical application for automated peak detection, waveform characterization, event classification, batch processing, quality control and data export. METHODS: CalDyn combines Savitzky-Golay filtering, LOESS-assisted derivative detection, optional baseline correction, waveform-boundary fitting and rule-based peak classification. It was evaluated on calcium recordings (healthy and disease-associated hiPSC-derived cardiomyocytes, hiPSC-derived neurons, primary skeletal myotubes), current-clamp action potentials and cardiac optical-mapping signals. Outputs were compared with PeakInspector, Clampfit and BV Workbench using paired and Bland-Altman analyses. Detection was assessed against 142 expert-annotated events and synthetic signals of known timing and amplitude. RESULTS: CalDyn achieved 94.4% sensitivity, 89.9% precision and an F1 score of 0.92. Performance peaked for healthy cardiomyocytes, paced myotubes and action potentials, with lower recall in arrhythmic cardiomyocytes and variable precision in neurons. CalDyn detected candidate low-amplitude diastolic and multicomponent Ca2+ events in arrhythmic cardiomyocytes, although the biological identity of CalDyn-only events was not independently confirmed. Comparisons with software revealed parameter-specific systematic differences, notably for rise rates and classifications. Action-potential measurements showed limited mean bias but non-negligible limits of agreement. In synthetic signals, amplitude error increased with noise and uncorrected drift, and timing error with low sampling rates. Detection remained stable across moderate parameter variation. CONCLUSIONS: CalDyn provides an accessible, reproducible and versatile workflow for automated analysis of heterogeneous calcium and electrophysiological signals. With appropriate quality control, it offers a robust alternative to modality-specific tools.

title: Measurement precision matters: Accounting for uncertainty alters estimated memory trajectories across the cognitive spectrum
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Harmonized cognitive composites are widely used to study longitudinal cognitive decline. Although harmonization places scores on a common latent scale, measurement precision varies across visits, age, and diagnosis, but is typically ignored in longitudinal models. METHODS: We analyzed harmonized memory scores and time-varying standard errors from the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center Uniform Data Set. We compared a naïve mixed-effects model that did not incorporate measurement uncertainty with two precision-aware models: a frequentist precision-weighted and a Bayesian measurement-error model. Comparisons were based on estimated age of memory impairment. RESULTS: Accounting for measurement precision produced age-dependent differences in estimated memory trajectories. Naïve models predicted higher memory scores at older ages in cognitively normal and mildly impaired participants but lower scores in Alzheimer's dementia (AD). Precision-aware models estimated threshold crossing 1.5-3 years earlier than the naïve model. DISCUSSION: Incorporating visit-specific measurement precision alters estimated cognitive trajectories and the timing of clinically interpretable memory impairment.

title: Constitutive Activation of Skeletal Muscle mTORC1 Drives Pro‐Inflammatory Gene Expression in Skeletal Muscle of Aged Mice
abstract: mTORC1 activity is increased in muscle with aging and is implicated as a potential driver of age-related declines in muscle health. While pharmacological inhibition of mTORC1 improves lifespan and healthspan, it remains unclear whether chronic activation of mTORC1 is sufficient to accelerate aging in skeletal muscle. We aimed to address this question using an inducible model of muscle-specific knockout of Depdc5, which encodes the protein DEP domain containing 5 (DEPDC5), a negative regulator of mTORC1. In 27-month-old mice, Depdc5 knockout induced a robust upregulation of inflammatory and immune-related genes, accompanied by alterations in metabolic and angiogenic pathways. Additionally, Depdc5 knockout mice exhibited an increase in TNF-α protein expression. However, these transcriptional and protein changes were not associated with an altered macrophage phenotype or with changes in muscle capillary density. Dietary rapamycin partially reversed mTORC1 signaling and some of the transcriptional changes, including those related to angiogenesis, but did not suppress inflammation-related transcripts or protein expression. These findings demonstrate that constitutive activation of mTORC1 is sufficient to drive pro-inflammatory changes in aged skeletal muscle, adding to the inflammation that already occurs with aging.
