title: Sustained Activation of a Defensive Behavior-Related Circuit Elicits a distinct Homeostatic Sleep Response.
abstract: Animals and humans often forgo sleep in response to other physiological needs. Prolonged wakefulness leads to a compensatory homeostatic sleep response involving enhanced amounts of sleep and electroencephalographic delta (0.5-4 Hz) power, yet how the type of preceding wakefulness and brain activity affects this response is poorly understood. Here we compared the pattern of brain activity and the homeostatic sleep response following sustained wakefulness induced by either gentle handling (GH), a widely used form of sleep deprivation in rodents; or optogenetic stimulation of neurons involved in avoidance/defensive responses, basal forebrain (BF) vesicular glutamatergic transporter type 2 (vGluT2) neurons. Local infusion of ionotropic glutamate receptor antagonists partially attenuated the wake-inducing effect of vGluT2-stimulation, but not that of GH, suggesting mediation by other non-glutamatergic BF subtypes. These antagonists also tended to produce more NREM sleep and a shorter NREM latency in the recovery period following vGluT2-stimulation. Both manipulations increased high theta (7-9 Hz) during wakefulness, an effect partially blocked by local infusion of the glutamate antagonist cocktail. Enhanced NREM sleep time and NREM delta power in the recovery period were more pronounced following GH than following vGluT2 stimulation. Whole-brain cFos immunohistochemistry revealed stronger neuronal activity in brain regions involved in stress and avoidance/defensive behaviors with vGluT2 stimulation, compared to GH. Our results demonstrate that activation of a brain system involved in defensive behavior (BF vGluT2) elicits a distinct and diminished homeostatic sleep response compared to GH, potentially an evolutionary sleep adaptation which would maintain vigilance in the face of an ongoing threat.

title: Selective inhibition of aldosterone production modulates human adrenocortical (HAC15) cell fate.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Aldosterone, produced in the zona glomerulosa (ZG) by aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2), regulates sodium balance and blood pressure. In adult adrenals, CYP11B2-expressing ZG cells are sparse, likely reflecting chronic suppression of the renin-angiotensin system under high-salt conditions. Whether reduced aldosterone synthesis directly influences ZG cell behavior remains unclear. This study examined the impact of CYP11B2 inhibition on human adrenal cell fate and function.
METHODS: CYP11B2 was inhibited in HAC15 cells using siRNA (siCYP11B2) or baxdrostat, a selective CYP11B2 inhibitor. Forty-eight hours post-treatment, steroid hormone levels, RNA sequencing profiles, and functional outputs (EZMTT metabolic assay, xCELLigence real-time cell analysis, and Annexin V/SYTOX flow cytometry for apoptosis/necrosis) were evaluated.
RESULTS: siCYP11B2 reduced aldosterone production by 70% ± 2.9% (n = 18, p < 0.001) and suppressed mRNA expression of CYP11B2 (88% ± 10.8%), HNRNPA1 (33% ± 17.6%), and UHMK1 (42% ± 13.7%) (n = 9, p < 0.05). Transcriptomic analysis revealed differential expression signatures enriched in autophagy- and mitophagy-related pathways. Treatment with U0126 (MEK1/2 inhibitor) dose-dependently reduced angiotensin II-stimulated aldosterone and cortisol production (n = 12, p < 0.001), and SB203580 (p38 MAPK inhibitor) increased the aldosterone-to-cortisol ratio (4.5 ± 0.5-fold, n = 12, p < 0.001), at concentrations previously reported to inhibit (25-50 µM U0126) or induce autophagy (1 µM SB203580), respectively. EZMTT assays demonstrated increased metabolic activity in siCYP11B2-treated cells at 96 h (Δ0.141 ± 0.02 absorbance units, p < 0.001), which was not observed following baxdrostat treatment. Baxdrostat treatment altered overall cell-death responses (FC = 1.42 ± 0.05, n = 144 and p = 1.3 × 10-10); however, the relative distribution of apoptotic and necrotic populations varied across independent experiments.
CONCLUSION: Reduced aldosterone synthesis is associated with transcriptional signatures involving autophagy- and mitophagy-related pathways. Pharmacological treatment using U0126 and SB203580 altered steroidogenic output independently of CYP11B2 transcript expression, providing hypothesis-generating evidence linking cellular homeostasis and mitochondrial quality control processes to adrenal steroidogenesis. Furthermore, pharmacological CYP11B2 inhibition using baxdrostat produced variable alterations in cell-death profile, highlighting important considerations for long-term therapeutic targeting.

title: Physically interacting immune cells in cardiometabolic disease: established platelet-immune aggregates and emerging leukocyte-leukocyte complexes.
abstract: Chronic immune activation contributes to cardiometabolic disease and has most often been attributed to soluble mediators or changes in individual immune-cell subsets. A complementary dimension of immune organization is captured by direct physical interactions between immune cells, detected in blood or dissociated samples. While most dual-lineage flow-cytometric events should still be excluded as technical doublets, a validated subset represents true cell-cell conjugates (i.e., physically interacting immune cells rather than antibody-antigen complexes). The evidence base, however, is uneven as platelet-leukocyte aggregates are well-established biomarkers of platelet activation and thromboinflammation, while circulating non-platelet immune cell-cell complexes, particularly T cell-monocyte complexes, remain an emerging field supported by relatively few primary studies. Across acute infection and vaccination, these complexes appear regulated and may reflect coordinated immune activation. In chronic inflammatory states, including HIV and metabolic dysfunction, persistent complexes have been associated with inflammation and cardiometabolic risk, although mechanistic and causal data remain limited. Here, we review the current evidence for circulating immune cell complexes, distinguish established platelet-containing aggregates from the nascent literature on other immune-cell pairings, discuss candidate mechanisms that may support their formation and persistence, outline methodological requirements for their study, and consider their potential as biomarkers and therapeutic-response tools in cardiometabolic disease.

title: Development and Validation of a Coronary Artery Calcium Volume and Density Score.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring is a useful tool for coronary heart disease (CHD) risk prediction. The current standard method, the Agatston score, weights plaque area upward by density. However, higher density is inversely associated with CHD. We aimed to develop and validate a CAC score accounting for the inverse association of density with CHD, and the nonlinear association between CAC volume and density in a prospective cohort study.
METHODS: A CAC volume and density score was developed, which adjusts CAC volume for density based on whether the volume level was <130 mm3. We used data from the MESA (Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis) to develop and assess the score, including all participants with CAC>0 and follow-up for CHD events. Score performance for CHD risk prediction was compared with the pooled cohort equations and the Agatston score using Cox proportional hazards models and Harrell C-index and continuous and categorical net reclassification improvement. Analyses were also stratified by Agatston score, age, sex, race/ethnicity, and statin use. Finally, performance was evaluated in 4 longitudinal cohorts for external validation.
RESULTS: The MESA cohort included 3360 individuals. CAC volume and density score improved the C-index for CHD to a greater degree over the pooled cohort equation (0.699 [95% CI, 0.675-0.723]) compared with the Agatston score (0.687 [95% CI, 0.663-0.711]) and resulted in greater continuous net reclassification improvement (0.54 [95% CI, 0.43-0.64]) compared with the Agatston score (0.45 [95% CI, 0.34-0.56]) when added to the pooled cohort equation. The greatest improvement in risk prediction was in those with lower burden of CAC (Agatston <300). Consistent results were seen in stratified analyses and external validation cohorts.
CONCLUSIONS: The CAC volume and density score, which adjusts CAC volume downward for higher density, and can be calculated from existing CAC reports, significantly improves risk discrimination and reclassification compared with the Agatston score.

title: Association of mitochondrial copy number and heteroplasmy with cognitive function in the ACCORD trial.
abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction has been implicated in cognitive decline and dementia, but the relationship between mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) heteroplasmy and copy number with cognitive function remains poorly understood. We aimed to study these associations among individuals with diabetes who face elevated risk for mitochondrial dysfunction and cognitive impairment. We analyzed data from 954 participants (mean age 62.8 years, 52.1% female) in the Action to Control Cardiovascular Risk in Diabetes Blood Pressure trial. Mitochondrial heteroplasmy burden was quantified using the modified mitochondrial local constraint score sum (mMSS) from whole mitochondrial genome sequencing. Mitochondrial copy number was measured using quantitative PCR. Cognitive function was assessed using the Digit Symbol Substitution Test for processing speed and the Mini-Mental State Examination for global cognition at baseline, 20 months, and 40 months. Our primary regression models adjusted for demographics, cardiovascular risk factors, and mitochondrial haplogroup. Participants with mMSS > 0.5 had significantly worse processing speed at baseline compared to those with mMSS= 0 (β=-4.94 points, 95% CI: -9.44, -0.43) after adjustment. Higher mitochondrial copy number was associated with better processing speed at baseline among men (β=1.67 per SD, 95% CI: 0.31, 3.03). Neither heteroplasmy nor copy number was significantly associated with global cognition or with longitudinal cognitive decline. Higher mitochondrial heteroplasmy burden and lower copy number (in men) were associated with worse processing speed but not global cognition or cognitive decline. Mitochondrial dysfunction may contribute to domain-specific cognitive impairment in diabetes, with potential sex differences. Further research is needed to elucidate mechanisms and evaluate mitochondrial measures in brain tissue.

title: A Novel Digital Phenotype of Physical Activity: Associations with Heart Rate Fragmentation
abstract: Background: Heart rate fragmentation (HRF) has emerged as a novel marker of sinoatrial instability and neuroautonomic dysregulation and is a predictor of incident cardiovascular disease (CVD) events and cardiovascular mortality. Leveraging heart rate fragmentation as a novel measure may help us better understand the prognostic significance of physical activity. Physical activity (PA) patterns are multidimensional and difficult to study holistically, however. We sought to examine for novel PA clusters in a cohort of veteran men and evaluate their prognostic significance based on their associations with neuroautonomic dysregulation. Methods: In this cross-sectional study, we examined 602 male veterans from the Vietnam Era Twins Study of Electrophysiology in Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (VETS-EP) who were enrolled between 2022 and 2026. Accelerometry data were used to derive physical activity parameters across 6 domains: volume, sedentary behavior, intensity, diurnal pattern, fragmentation, and variability. Heart rate fragmentation was assessed using percentage of inflection points (PIP), inverse average length of segments (IALS), percentage of short segments (PSS), and percentage of alternating segments (PAS). Gaussian mixture models were used to derive digital phenotypes of physical activity, and associations with heart rate fragmentation were assessed using linear mixed models. Results: Participants had a mean age of 73.8 ± 2.9 years and 93.2% reported White race. Two overlapping phenotypes of physical activity patterns were identified: a compact-early phenotype, characterized by earlier activity timing and slightly greater overall activity, and a diffuse-late phenotype, characterized by later activity timing and greater heterogeneity in activity volume. In fully adjusted models, the diffuse-late phenotype was associated with higher PIP, the primary outcome (β: 1.199, 95% CI: 0.034 to 2.363, p-value: 0.044), and higher IALS (β: 0.01210, 95% CI: 0.00048 to 0.02373, p-value: 0.041), but not PSS or PAS, compared with the compact-early phenotype. Conclusions: In older male veterans, Gaussian mixture model phenotyping identified two overlapping physical activity phenotypes, differing mainly in diurnal timing and in the dispersion of overall activity, that were associated with modest differences in heart rate fragmentation. These phenotypes provide a framework for capturing complex physical activity patterns. Future prospective studies representing diverse populations are needed to validate such phenotypes.

title: Neighborhood walkability, green space, and incident hip fracture among older U.S. adults: The cardiovascular health study.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Neighborhood walkability and green space are associated with walking behavior and physical activity, but evidence linking them to fracture is limited and inconsistent, and potential sex differences remain understudied. We evaluated associations of neighborhood walkability and green space with incident hip fracture in older, community-dwelling U.S. adults.
METHODS: We conducted a prospective cohort study of adults aged ≥65 years from the Cardiovascular Health Study (CHS). Neighborhood exposures were defined using 1-km radial buffers around geocoded residential addresses from 1992 to 1993 (baseline). Walkability was the sum of standardized population and walkable destination densities. Green space was the proportion of satellite-derived green land cover. Hip fractures were prospectively ascertained over 12 years using International Classification of Diseases, Ninth Revision (ICD-9) codes from hospital discharge abstracts. Cox hazard models adjusted for individual-level (age, sex, race, weight, height, smoking status, current heavy alcohol use, medication use, diabetes, renal function, marital status, education level, annual household income) and neighborhood-level (median household income, median value of owner-occupied housing, proportion of persons in managerial/professional occupations) covariates evaluated associations, overall and by sex.
RESULTS: Among 3676 participants (58% women), 359 experienced hip fracture over a median 10-years observation. Greater neighborhood walkability was significantly associated with lower hip fracture incidence among women (hazard ratio per 1 standard deviation increase of 0.72 [95% confidence interval, 0.53-0.98]), but not overall or among men. Neighborhood green space was not significantly associated with hip fracture.
CONCLUSION: Greater neighborhood walkability, but not green space, was associated with lower hip fracture risk among older women.

title: Chronic complex regional pain syndrome patient IgM has pronociceptive effects in the spinal cord, but not skin, of fracture mice
abstract: Abstract B cells and IgM antibodies mediate nociceptive sensitization in the mouse tibia fracture model of complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS). Previously we observed that injection of serum or IgM from early CRPS patients into muMT fracture mice lacking mature B cells and antibodies was always pronociceptive at 7 days after systemic injection or one hour after intrathecal or intradermal IgM injection, but systemically injected serum from chronic CRPS patients was rarely pronociceptive. The current study found that chronic CRPS patient IgM was always pronociceptive within an hour after intrathecal injection in fracture mice, whereas intradermal injection of IgM into the hindpaw was never pronociceptive. Chronic CRPS IgM had increased binding reactivity to glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) and intrathecal injection of anti-GFAP antibody was pronociceptive in fracture mice. The slow onset of pronociceptive effects after systemic injection of early CRPS patient serum or IgM suggests gradual accumulation of pronociceptive IgM-antigen complexes in skin and spinal cord. Pronociceptive effects chronic CRPS IgM were blocked by a complement C5a receptor antagonist or a global cytokine inhibitor. These data suggest that initially CRPS patients generate pronociceptive IgM autoantibodies directed at skin and spinal cord neoantigens, but over time spinal neoantigens are primarily targeted.

title: Functional and molecular profiles of the neuroretina and retinal pigmented epithelium-choroid in response to aging and Nrf2 deletion
abstract: Purpose: Age is the leading factor for age-related macular degeneration (AMD), in which retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE) atrophy is a hallmark. The nuclear factor-erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2), a major anti-stress transcription factor, decreases in AMD, suggesting bioenergetic stress interacts with age during AMD pathogenesis. We profiled visual function and gene expression of the retina and RPE-choroid with Nrf2 deletion and aging. Methods: We tested 3mo and 14mo Nrf2 null (Nrf2 KO) and Nrf2 WT mice for optokinetic tracking (OKT) and dark-adapted electroretinography (ERG) responses. Eyes were harvested for retina outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness analysis and retina and RPE-choroid cup RNA isolation for RNAseq profiling. Results: Visual acuity was reduced with aging with lower values in the Nrf2 KO vs Nrf2 WT comparison at 14mo. We observed aged-related reduction of a-, b-, and c-wave ERG amplitudes in both WT and KO mice. Age-related c-wave decline was exacerbated by Nrf2 loss. By RNAseq, two-way ANOVA of RPE-choroid samples revealed differentially expressed genes (DEGs) with age and genotype main effects, as well as DEGs with age and genotype interaction effects. Age DEGs were over-represented in pathways related to inflammation and phagocytosis. Genotype DEGs were associated with alterations in antioxidant and inflammatory processes. Retina RNAseq showed age and genotype DEGs. Conclusions: Ablation of Nrf2 exacerbates age-related declines suggesting that decrease in Nrf2 with aging has functional consequences for inflammation/resiliency. We provide retina and RPE-choroid bulk-RNAseq datasets from the same cohort of mice that can be interrogated to better understand degeneration of retina/RPE-choroid.

title: Barriers to implementing bedside nursing screening for health-related social needs in surgical patients: An explanatory sequential mixed-methods study.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Health-related social needs are increasingly recognized as key drivers of surgical outcomes, yet completion of bedside health-related social need screening remains inconsistent. Substantial missingness in data limits the ability to identify and address social risk in surgical populations. This explanatory sequential mixed-methods study aimed to characterize factors influencing completion of the bedside health-related social need screening among patients undergoing major elective surgery.
METHODS: We conducted a mixed-methods study in 3 hospitals within a statewide health system. In the quantitative phase, we analyzed patterns of missingness in health-related social need screening among patients undergoing major elective surgery. In the qualitative phase, we conducted semistructured interviews with bedside nurses and nurse managers using purposive sampling. Interviews were transcribed and analyzed using thematic content analysis. The findings from these 2 strands were mixed using meta-inference to synthesize integrated results.
RESULTS: Among 1,172 patients, 52% had missing data in at least 1 health-related social need domain. Fourteen participants (12 nurses and 2 nurse managers) were interviewed for the qualitative strand. There were 3 major themes that emerged: multilevel communication discrepancies, patient-related factors, and areas of improvement. The mixed-methods integration of these findings revealed that inconsistent handoffs, coupled with a lack of oversight, contributed to the high degree of missingness. Further exacerbating the discrepancy in insurance status were patient-related factors including postanesthesia mental status, language barriers, and reluctance to disclose sensitive information. Recommendations for training, built-in reminders, or offloading the health-related social need task to increase compliance were found as solutions to improve fidelity and reduce bias in screener completion.
CONCLUSION: Completion of the bedside health-related social need screener was hindered by multilevel communication gaps, patient-related factors, and workflow constraints. Targeted implementation strategies, including enhanced training, system-level accountability, and optimization of screening timing and ownership, may improve screening fidelity and enable more effective identification of social risk in perioperative care.

title: Effect of Age on Physical Function Improvement in Older Veterans Enrolled in the Gerofit Exercise Program
abstract: Background/Objectives: Aging is associated with declines in strength, balance, and mobility that contribute to falls, disability, and loss of independence. While exercise interventions improve physical function, limited data exist on community-dwelling adults aged 90 years and older. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the effect of age on physical function improvement following participation in an exercise program for older Veterans. Methods: We analyzed baseline and 3-month follow-up physical function data from 62 community-dwelling Veterans aged 60–99 years enrolled in the Veterans Affairs Gerofit, a supervised, individualized exercise program incorporating aerobic, resistance, balance, and flexibility training. Outcomes included lower extremity strength (30-s chair stands), mobility and balance (8-foot up-and-go), and cardiovascular endurance (6-min walk). Participants were grouped by age (60–69, 70–79, 80–89, 90–99). Paired samples t-tests assessed changes over time, and repeated-measures general linear models examined the effect of age on physical function improvement. Results: Across all participants, significant improvements were observed in chair stand and 8-foot up-and-go performance (both p < 0.001), whereas 6-min walk distance did not change significantly (p = 0.14). Chair stand performance improved in all age groups, including adults aged 90–99 (p < 0.01). Although baseline physical function declined with age, we did not detect differences in the rate of improvement in chair stand performance by age group (p = 0.69). Improvements in 8-foot up-and-go performance were observed in younger age groups and not in participants aged 90–99 years. Conclusions: Participation in a supervised exercise program was associated with significant improvements in lower extremity strength across all age groups, including adults aged 90–99 years. These findings support the inclusion of even the oldest adults in exercise programs to promote physical function.

title: Compensatory drive and sleep-related phantom limb pain: the moderating role of autonomic reserve
abstract: Phantom limb pain (PLP) is common after amputation, yet why poor sleep becomes pain in only some individuals is unknown. We hypothesized that a regulatory response is interpretable only against the reserve sustaining it, and thus we tested whether autonomic capacity relative to demand moderates the sleep-pain relationship in 121 amputee adults. Sleep was assessed with the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index; PLP, residual limb pain (RLP), and phantom limb sensation (PLS) on 0-10 scales. Heart rate variability was summarized as autonomic reserve (log-transformed SDNN, RMSSD, total and high-frequency power) and autonomic drive (normalized low-frequency power). Poorer sleep was associated with greater PLP and RLP, but not PLS. No single HRV index moderated these associations, but the sleep × reserve × drive interaction did for PLP (b = -0.51, p = 0.026). Poor sleep predicted pain most strongly under high drive with reduced reserve. PLP vulnerability reflects autonomic capacity relative to demand, instead of any single HRV marker alone.

title: Management of fragile X-associated tremor ataxia syndrome: a review for clinicians.
abstract: Fragile X-associated tremor ataxia syndrome (FXTAS) is a multi-faceted and progressive neurodegenerative disorder that manifests clinically with action tremor, gait ataxia, parkinsonism, peripheral neuropathy, and cognitive and psychiatric features. The disease is highly heterogeneous and there are no FDA approved medications for FXTAS as a specific indication. As such, treatment is symptomatic and must be tailored to the specific needs of a given patient. This review provides expert opinion-based treatment recommendations for the core and ancillary clinical features of FXTAS. Movement disorders, such as tremor, ataxia and parkinsonism may respond to symptomatic medications and therapies, but caution is required when considering surgical interventions such as deep brain stimulation. Cognitive decline can be responsive to medications developed for other cognitive disorders, but these medications work best when combined with non-medication based approaches and all patients should be screened for other reversible causes of memory decline. Psychiatric symptoms, including anxiety, depression, and psychosis, can be treated with psychotherapy and medications; but caution is required to avoid exacerbating clinical and subclinical movement disorder features with psychotropic medications. Rehabilitative therapies, such as speech therapy, occupational, and physical therapy, often enhance patient function and quality of life. Exercise and good nutrition are recommendations that are common to other cerebellar ataxias and adult neurodegenerative disorders and may have a positive impact on general health. A multi-disciplinary approach is recommended to address all components of FXTAS.

title: Burden, healthcare utilization, and costs of chronic liver disease-related hospitalizations in California: a population-based study of trends and projections, 2005-2035.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Long-term trends in hospitalization burden, healthcare utilization, and costs of chronic liver disease (CLD) in the United States remain poorly characterized. Using statewide hospital discharge data, we quantified trends from 2005 to 2018 and projected future burden through 2035 across demographic subgroups.
METHODS: We used average annual percent change (AAPC) to quantify trends in hospitalized patients, hospitalizations, deaths, along with age-standardized rates (ASHPR, ASHR, and ASMR); hospitalizations per patient-year, average length of stay, 30-day readmission, in-hospital mortality; and inflation-adjusted hospital charges (2019 US dollars). Analyses were conducted overall and for hepatitis B virus(HBV), hepatitis C virus(HCV), alcohol-associated liver disease(ALD), and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD).
FINDINGS: From 2005 to 2018, hospitalized CLD patients increased from 71,214 to 122,810 (AAPC, 4.37%; 95% CI, 3.87%-4.88%), and deaths from 11,455 to 24,560 (6.02%; 4.20%-7.86%). ASHPR increased from 275.12 to 377.88 per 100,000, and ASMR from 45.53 to 74.77. Hospitalizations and charges increased from 116,482 to 185,268 and $9.63 billion to $18.63 billion, while in-hospital mortality declined (AAPC, -7.02%; 95% CI, -8.72%-5.30%). MASLD- and ALD-related hospitalizations increased, whereas HBV- and HCV-related hospitalizations declined. Men had higher hospitalization and mortality rates, particularly for ALD. Hispanic populations had the fastest-rising burden, driven by MASLD; HBV burden was concentrated among non-Hispanic Asian populations, whereas overall CLD and ALD-related mortality were highest among non-Hispanic White populations.
INTERPRETATION: Findings highlight the need for targeted prevention and screening, early management of metabolic and alcohol-related risk factors, and equitable access to liver care.

title: Association of GLP1-Receptor Agonist Use With Frailty and Falls in Adults With Type 2 Diabetes.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the association of initiating glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists versus dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors (as active comparator) with frailty progression and falls and whether associations differed by baseline frailty.
RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS: Five propensity score-matched retrospective cohorts using Veterans Health data (years 2006-2021), utilizing new-user, active-comparator design. The five matched cohorts were at progressive degrees of frailty at baseline and included adults with diabetes and 3 years of baseline data who initiated study medications with at least 90 days of therapy.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Primary outcome was absolute change in Frailty Index from baseline to follow-up. Secondary outcomes were increase in the frailty index and fall rate during follow-up. Outcomes were assessed in an as-treated framework.
RESULTS: The main matched cohort included 73 592 pairs. Over a mean follow-up of approximately 27 months, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists initiation was associated with less worsening in frailty index (regression coefficient: -0.0010; 95% CI: -0.0018 to -0.0002; p = 0.011), lower odds of frailty index progression (OR: 0.97; 95% CI: 0.95-0.99; p = 0.003), and a lower fall rate (incidence rate ratio: 0.87; 95% CI: 0.84-0.91; p < 0.001) compared to dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor initiation. Findings were generally consistent across the other four matched cohorts, with attenuation in the matched cohort with severe frailty at baseline.
CONCLUSIONS: Initiation of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist was associated with slightly less frailty progression and fewer falls compared with dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor initiation, but estimates were attenuated in severe frailty.

title: Improved Outcomes and Low Rate of Medical Discharge at a Minimum 10‐Year Follow‐Up After Arthroscopic Bankart Repair With Remplissage for “Off‐Track” Engaging Hill‐Sachs Lesions With Subcritical Glenoid Bone Loss in Active‐Duty Servicemembers
abstract: PURPOSE: To evaluate long-term outcomes after arthroscopic Bankart repair with remplissage among active-duty servicemembers under 45 years old with engaging Hill-Sachs lesions (HSLs) and subcritical glenoid bone loss (GBL). METHODS: A retrospective review of prospectively collected data involving consecutive active-duty servicemembers who underwent arthroscopic Bankart repair with remplissage for anterior instability with "off-track" HSL and GBL <13.5% between January 2010 and September 2015 with a minimum 10-year follow-up was performed. Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) included the pain visual analog scale, American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons score, Single Assessment Numeric Evaluation, and Rowe Instability score. Rates of return to duty and subjective return to sport at the prior level were collected. Minimal clinically important difference thresholds were calculated using a distribution method. RESULTS: . At final follow-up, PROMs improved (visual analog scale: 7.65-1.6, American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons: 40.3-88.2, Single Assessment Numeric Evaluation: 48.6-90.0, and Rowe: 39.0-88.6, P < .0001), with sustained PROMs between mid- and long-term time points. The minimal clinically important difference was achieved by most patients (76.2%-95.2%). Two patients (9.0%) experienced complications: 1 with recurrent instability prompting Latarjet (4.5%) and 1 with postoperative stiffness (4.5%). At final follow-up, return to duty was achieved by 86.4% (n = 19) and to preinjury level of sport by 90.9% (n = 20). Three patients underwent medical discharge from the military because of the operative shoulder (13.6%). CONCLUSIONS: At a minimum 10-year follow-up after arthroscopic Bankart repair with remplissage for off-track HSL with subcritical GBL, active-duty servicemembers showed sustained improvements in PROMs, low rates of recurrent instability, and relatively high rates of return to active-duty and sport, supporting the durability of this procedure in a high shoulder demand population. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, retrospective case series.

title: Quantitative ultrashort echo time (UTE) magnetic resonance imaging of femoral trabecular bone in aging and osteoporosis
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate quantitative ultrashort echo time (UTE) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) biomarkers, pore-to-matrix ratio (PMR), and matrix index (MI) for assessing trabecular bone in the proximal femur across aging and osteoporosis-related bone status. MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this prospective study, 92 female subjects (20-83 years) were classified into four groups based on age and DXA-derived T-scores: Young Normal (n = 19), Old Normal (n = 14), Osteopenia (n = 44), and Osteoporosis (n = 15). All participants underwent 3-T hip MRI using 3D dual-echo proton-density-weighted UTE (PD-UTE) and short TR adiabatic inversion recovery UTE (STAIR-UTE) sequences. Measurements were performed in the femoral head and neck by two readers. Interobserver agreement was assessed via intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC). Group differences were analyzed with the Kruskal-Wallis test and Holm-adjusted post hoc tests. Spearman correlation analysis and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis were performed. RESULTS: PMR increased and MI decreased with worsening bone status. Significant differences were observed between Young Normal and all older groups (p < 0.001). PMR from the oblique-coronal total femoral head differentiated Old Normal from Osteoporosis (5.35 vs. 8.10; p < 0.05). Both PMR (ρ = -0.406 to -0.211) and MI (ρ = 0.333-0.402) significantly correlated with T-scores (all p < 0.05). The areas under the ROC curve were 0.776 (95% CI, 0.584-0.909) for PMR and 0.738 (95% CI, 0.548-0.886) for MI. Interobserver reproducibility was substantial to almost perfect (ICC: 0.73-0.99). CONCLUSION: PMR and MI demonstrated measurable differences across age and bone status and may provide complementary information on trabecular bone characteristics. KEY POINTS: Question Can ultrashort echo time (UTE) MRI biomarkers address the need for radiation-free assessment of age- and osteoporosis-related trabecular bone changes in the proximal femur? Findings Pore-to-matrix ratio (PMR) increased and matrix index (MI) decreased with aging and worsening bone status, and femoral head PMR differentiated osteoporosis from normal bone. Clinical relevance UTE-MRI-derived PMR and MI may provide radiation-free, complementary information to dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry for assessing trabecular bone changes associated with aging and osteoporosis.

title: Re-examining military shaving standards for pseudofolliculitis barbae and their disproportionate impact
abstract: Recent directives from the US Army and US Navy mandating clean-shaven standards and eliminating permanent shaving waiver exemptions have significant implications for service members with pseudofolliculitis barbae (PFB), a chronic inflammatory skin condition predominantly affecting Black men. Roughly 70,000 service members have medical exemptions from shaving ("shaving waivers"), and Black Americans comprise 64% of this group. Beyond dermatologic consequences, shaving waivers have been associated with delayed promotions, increased disciplinary action, diminished leadership opportunities, and attrition — outcomes that disproportionately burden Black service members. The original rationale for clean-shaven standards – ensuring gas mask seal integrity – has weakened given evidence that trimmed beards offer comparable protection and that chemical warfare threats allow sufficient preparation time. Differentiated grooming standards between deployed and in-garrison operations may offer a practical solution that balances military readiness with equitable, evidence-based care for affected service members. Translating that vision into practice, however, will require ongoing collaboration with dermatologists, who remain central to PFB management through counseling patients, as well as advocating for workplace and institutional accommodations and advancing the research needed to better understand and treat PFB.

title: Desert dust storm, ambient temperature, and pulmonary function among children with asthma in the Eastern Mediterranean
abstract: Background Climate change has contributed to increased dust events and rising ambient temperature, posing potential health risk for susceptible populations including children with asthma. The study aims to examine associations between exposure to desert dust storm (DDS) and higher ambient temperature with pulmonary function indicators, including forced expiratory volume in 1s (FEV 1 ), forced vital capacity (FVC) and FEV 1 /FVC% among asthmatic children during the dust season in the Eastern Mediterranean. Methods We conducted exploratory secondary analyses of repeated pulmonary function measurements from schoolchildren with asthma in Cyprus and Crete, Greece during spring of 2019 and 2021. Dust exposure was defined using short-term (at least one DDS day on the assessment day or during the preceding 7 days) and cumulative days (over the spring season) metrics based on site-specific DDS classifications as well as ambient temperature assessed from the nearest meteorological station. Associations were examined using linear mixed-effect models. Results Among the 135 children included, short-term DDS exposure was associated with a non-significant decrement in FEV 1 (-20.46 mL, 95% CI: -50.38, 9.46) and FVC (-27.21 mL, 95% CI: -59.45, 5.02). Cumulative dust exposure was associated with -3.52 mL (95% CI: -5.90, -1.14) difference in FEV 1 per DDS day. Ambient temperature averaged over 0-7 days before assessment was inversely associated with FEV 1 (-19.77 mL; 95% CI: -37.91, -1.63 per 5°C increase) and FEV 1 /FVC% (-0.81; 95% CI: -1.36, -0.25 per 5 °C increase), with no statistical evidence of effect modification by short-term DDS exposure. Conclusions This exploratory secondary analysis demonstrated inverse associations of cumulative DDS exposure and ambient temperature with pulmonary function among children with asthma, while short-term DDS associations were not statistically significant. These findings may inform the management of children with asthma during desert dust seasons, but confirmation in larger studies is required.

title: stMCP: spatial transcriptomics with a Model Context Protocol server
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics enables high-resolution mapping of gene expression within intact tissues but remains computationally challenging, limiting accessibility and iterative analysis for researchers without extensive programming experience. We developed stMCP, a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that provides a natural language interface for spatial transcriptomics analysis while separating orchestration from locally executed computational workflows. stMCP integrates a language model interface, modular orchestration layer, predefined analytical tools, session management, comprehensive analysis logging, and a web-based results viewer. Analytical operations are performed locally, allowing biological data to remain on the user’s system while reducing repeated language-model interaction during computation. A streamlined installation workflow further reduces the software configuration required for deployment. Benchmarking demonstrated robust orchestration across common spatial transcriptomics tasks, including recovery from ambiguous or unsupported requests. stMCP successfully analyzed larger public Xenium datasets and supported workflows across multiple spatial transcriptomics platforms. Direct comparison with STAgent and SpatialAgent further demonstrated differences in execution efficiency, language-model utilization, reproducibility, and deployment requirements between constrained MCP-based orchestration and autonomous agent-based analysis. stMCP provides an accessible and reproducible interface for spatial transcriptomics analysis while retaining established computational methods and local control of analytical execution. More broadly, the framework demonstrates how MCP-based architecture can connect natural language interfaces with scientific computing tools while balancing accessibility, computational control, and reproducibility.

title: Brain region- and solubility-dependent proteomic signatures of neurofibrillary tangle pathology in Alzheimer’s disease
abstract: Abstract Neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs) containing hyperphosphorylated tau proteins are a hallmark neuropathology of Alzheimer’s disease. However, the molecular basis underlying their spatial heterogeneity and biochemical complexity remain unclear. To address this, we performed mass spectrometry–based proteomic profiling of two neocortical regions with different susceptibilities to NFT pathology—the inferior temporal (IT) and middle frontal (MF) cortices—from 27 autopsy cases stratified by Braak NFT stage (Low 0–II, n=8; Mid III–IV, n=11; High V–VI, n=8). Brain homogenates were sequentially fractionated using buffers of increasing solubility (TBS, Na₂CO₃, and Urea), followed by trypsin digestion and analysis by nanoLC–MS/MS with data-independent acquisition. Proteins were identified using PEAKS Studio 12 and linear mixed-effects models were applied to assess Braak stage–associated and region-specific changes in protein abundance and solubility. A total of 5,573 protein groups were identified, including 452 differentially expressed proteins (DEPs), 183 bidirectional expression proteins (BEPs), and 693 differentially soluble proteins (DSPs) associated with NFT pathology. These proteins were enriched in pathways related to cytoskeletal organization, synaptic transmission, metabolism, vesicular trafficking, and proteostasis. Marked regional differences were observed, with limited overlap between IT and MF across DEPs, BEPs, and DSPs. Protein change in MF was dynamic with a higher number of BEPs and suggested active cytoskeletal remodeling, whereas IT showed fewer BEPs and evidence of structural disruption, including alterations in intermediate filament components, consistent with vulnerability of IT and possible compensatory/plasticity changes in MF cortex. MF cortex had the greatest downregulation of DEPs between Low and Mid Braak stages, while the transition from Mid to High Braak stage showed upregulation of most of DEPs in both regions. In addition, widespread changes in protein solubility were observed, particularly decreased solubility at later Braak stages, implicating disruption of proteostasis. Together, these findings highlight region- and stage-dependent proteomic alterations associated with tau pathology and underscore their relevance for understanding disease mechanisms and informing biomarker development.

title: Hemodynamics, plasma catecholamines, and power spectral analysis of heart rate variability during tilt-evoked neurally mediated hypotension.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Syncope workup often includes tilt table testing. One positive result is neurally mediated hypotension (NMH). Mechanisms of NMH are debated.
OBJECTIVES: We characterized NMH development in terms of systemic and forearm hemodynamics, plasma catecholamines, and power spectral analysis of heart rate variability.
METHODS: We reviewed data from 25 subjects with NMH and 34 controls without NMH who had autonomic testing between 2003 and 2024. Dependent measures included continuously recorded blood pressure (BP), heart rate, stroke volume, cardiac output, respiratory rate (RR), forearm blood flow (FBF), forearm vascular resistance (FVR), systemic vascular resistance (SVR), plasma epinephrine and norepinephrine, and high- and low-frequency power of heart rate variability (HFRR and LFRR). There were 4 study periods: T0 = supine rest; T1 = start of tilt; T2 = NMH (20 min of tilting in controls); and T3 = supine recovery.
RESULTS: There were significant interaction effects for Group X Study Period for several variables, with a decrease in BP, FVR, SVR, HFRR, and LFRR, and an increase in FBF and epinephrine at a steeper rate in the NMH group compared to the No NMH group. The two groups did not differ in responses of heart rate, RR, stroke volume, cardiac output, or norepinephrine levels. The increment in plasma epinephrine was larger in the NMH group, without a group difference in norepinephrine (i.e., sympathoadrenal imbalance). LFRR was elevated at baseline and decreased markedly in participants developing NMH.
CONCLUSIONS: NMH is associated with forearm vasodilation, sympathoadrenal imbalance, and a precipitous fall in LFRR. The results fit with a neurocirculatory-neuroendocrine pattern triggering NMH.

title: Sensor-Based Reachable Workspace Assessment for Tracking Upper-Extremity Mobility Changes over Time Following the Spencer Technique in Older Adults.
abstract: Age-related declines in upper-extremity mobility remain a challenge to assess in older adults. This study examined whether a sensor-based motion analysis of reachable workspace (RWS), quantified using relative surface area (RSA), could track longitudinal upper-extremity mobility changes in a cohort of community-dwelling older adults receiving the Spencer Technique, an established therapeutic intervention for the shoulder. Fifteen community-dwelling older adults ≥65 years with shoulder mobility limitations identified by reduced goniometric ROM received the Spencer Technique twice weekly for two weeks. Outcomes including RSA, shoulder flexion and abduction via goniometry, Apley scratch test, DASH and upper extremity NeuroQoL were assessed at baseline, weekly, post-therapy, and 1-month follow-up. Total RSA significantly increased from baseline to post-therapy and 1-month follow-up in both dominant and nondominant upper extremities and remained significant after Holm correction (adjusted p ≤ 0.030). Bilateral shoulder flexion and abduction along with Apley scratch tests demonstrated parallel improvements. DASH scores did not demonstrate significant change, whereas NeuroQoL UE scores increased significantly at 1-month follow-up after Holm correction (adjusted p = 0.031). Total RSA demonstrated responsiveness to longitudinal changes in upper-extremity reachability following the Spencer Technique that parallel changes observed with standard clinical assessments. These findings support the utility of sensor-based RWS as a quantitative measure for tracking longitudinal upper-extremity mobility over time in older adults.

title: Keratinocyte VISTA attenuates UV light-induced skin injury by suppressing cutaneous type I interferon (IFN-I) response.
abstract: Persistent production of type I interferons (IFN-Is) is a hallmark of cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CLE). Ultraviolet (UV) light stimulates IFN-I response in the skin and exacerbates CLE. Here, we identify V-type immunoglobulin domain-containing suppressor of T cell activation (VISTA) as a negative regulator of both basal and UV-induced IFN-I response in the skin and show that VISTA limits skin photosensitivity in an IFN-I-dependent manner, in part through Stimulator of Interferon Genes (STING). Furthermore, we demonstrate a novel role for VISTA in keratinocytes both at steady state and in response to UV light. Conditional deletion of VISTA in epidermal keratinocytes results in a ~10-fold increase in basal skin IFN-I scores and a heightened UV-induced skin injury score, both of which are dependent on IFN-I signaling. VISTA-targeting monoclonal antibodies suppress the UV-induced IFN-I response in human keratinocytes and in mice expressing human VISTA in vivo, thereby reducing UV-induced skin injury scores. Together, these findings identify VISTA as a keratinocyte-intrinsic checkpoint that restrains STING-associated IFN-I response in the skin and suggest VISTA agonism as a therapeutic strategy to limit photosensitivity in CLE.

title: Longitudinal Multimodal Retinal Imaging in Cognitively Normal Apolipoprotein E4 Carriers and Noncarriers.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate longitudinal retinal structural and microvascular changes in cognitively normal apolipoprotein E (APOE) ε4 carriers compared with noncarriers.
METHODS: Cognitively normal adults with known APOE genotype underwent multimodal retinal imaging at baseline and follow-up visits. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) metrics included macular central subfield thickness (CST), ganglion cell-inner plexiform layer (GC-IPL) thickness, and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thickness. OCT angiography (OCTA) parameters included vessel and perfusion density across 3-mm and 6-mm circles and rings, peripapillary capillary perfusion density (CPD), and capillary flux index (CFI). Annual rates of change were estimated using linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age and sex. A subgroup analysis was performed in participants with ≥5-year follow-up.
RESULTS: This study analyzed 871 eyes from 439 participants (230 APOE ε4 noncarriers and 209 carriers). Baseline retinal parameters did not differ significantly between groups. Carriers demonstrated nominally slower annual RNFL decline (β = 0.334; P = 0.023) and attenuated peripapillary CPD decline (β = 0.0010; P = 0.014) versus noncarriers; neither survived false discovery rate (FDR) correction (P = 0.18). In the ≥5-year subgroup (n = 58), carriers demonstrated nominally higher peripapillary CPD than noncarriers (P = 0.011; FDR-adjusted P = 0.17), although rates of change did not differ significantly between groups.
CONCLUSIONS: Cognitively normal APOE ε4 carriers demonstrated nominally slower peripapillary CPD and RNFL decline over longitudinal follow-up, with carriers maintaining higher CPD at ≥5 years despite comparable baseline imaging.
TRANSLATIONAL RELEVANCE: Longitudinal peripapillary and RNFL changes may reflect early retinal findings associated with APOE ε4 carrier status prior to cognitive decline, supporting further investigation of longitudinal retinal imaging as a potential noninvasive biomarker in preclinical Alzheimer's disease.

title: Exploratory Analysis of APOE ε4-Stratified Associations Between Plasma Alzheimer's Biomarkers and Retinal Imaging Metrics in Cognitively Normal Adults.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Retinal imaging offers a noninvasive window into microvascular and neurodegenerative changes, yet its relationship to circulating plasma biomarkers of Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains incompletely understood. We evaluated associations between plasma AD biomarkers and retinal imaging metrics in cognitively normal adults and whether these differ by apolipoprotein E (APOE) ε4 status.
METHODS: This cross-sectional analysis included cognitively normal participants prospectively enrolled from the Duke/UNC Alzheimer's Disease Research Center. Eighty-three eyes from 44 participants (20 APOE ε4 carriers, 24 noncarriers) underwent optical coherence tomography (OCT) and OCT angiography (OCTA) within 1 year of plasma sampling. Plasma AD biomarkers were assessed for associations with structural OCT and microvascular OCTA metrics. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, treated hypertension, and years of education were used, with interaction terms for APOE ε4 status followed by stratified analyses.
RESULTS: Nominally significant APOE ε4-dependent interactions were observed between Aβ42/40 and neurofilament light chain (NfL) with ganglion cell-inner plexiform layer (GCIPL) thickness (uncorrected P = 0.026 and P = 0.028). For OCTA, multiple nominally significant APOE ε4-dependent interactions were identified between plasma biomarkers (NfL, pTau217/Aβ42, and pTau217) and perfusion and vessel density across macular regions (uncorrected P = 0.009-0.048). Stratified analyses suggested stronger or more positive relationships in noncarriers, with attenuated or inverse relationships in carriers. None of the associations remained significant after false discovery rate (FDR) correction.
CONCLUSIONS: In this exploratory analysis, the APOE ε4 genotype may modify associations between plasma AD biomarkers and retinal structural and microvascular metrics in cognitively normal adults.
TRANSLATIONAL RELEVANCE: These exploratory findings support further investigation of whether APOE ε4 genotype-status should be considered in future studies integrating retinal imaging and plasma biomarkers in preclinical Alzheimer's disease.

title: Development of a tool to measure patient-oriented outcomes for Veterans with inflammatory arthritis initiating self-administered biologic therapies
abstract: Background: Veterans Health Administration Centralized Specialty Medication Management (CSMM) clinics have positive financial and process outcomes but lack patient-oriented outcomes. This project developed a tool to evaluate patient-oriented outcomes among Veterans with inflammatory arthritis and/or psoriasis initiating biologic therapies. Methods: Using validated questionnaires, a tool was constructed and piloted. Four rounds of cognitive interviews, with 2 Veterans each, were conducted. Pre- and post-CSMM clinic cognitive interviews were conducted with 2 Veterans initiating biologic therapy. The tool was piloted with patients initiating biologic therapy. Results: The post-CSMM survey began with 55 questions. There was 1 pilot interview for readability, 8 cognitive interviews over 4 tool versions, and 2 pre- post-CSMM survey cognitive interviews; 18 questions were revised, 9 removed, and 7 added. No problematic questions were identified during the final cognitive interviews. In pre- post-CSMM cognitive interviews, no problematic questions were identified and both Veterans endorsed connection of the pre- and post-questions. The final post-CSMM survey had 53 questions and the pre-CSMM survey had 31 questions. In the pilot, the pre- and post-CSMM survey was administered to 23 Veterans. Between interviews 34 days and 1.7 CSMM appointments elapsed. Time to complete the pre-CSMM survey and post-CSMM survey was 21 and 26 min, respectively. There were no difficult or confusing questions identified in the pilot. Conclusion: This project created a pre- and post-CSMM tool with high content validity to measure patient-oriented outcomes among Veterans with inflammatory arthritis and/or psoriasis initiating biologic therapy. Feasibility in conducting pre- and post-CSMM interviews using the tool was established.

title: Stromal Vascular Cell-Mediated Inflammatory and Remodeling Pathways in Alcohol-Induced Visceral Adipose Tissue Dysfunction: A Pilot Study
abstract: Chronic alcohol use induces adipocyte lipolysis and production of inflammatory mediators from adipose tissue (AT). Stromal vascular cells (SVCs) are a heterogeneous group of AT cells and contribute to AT inflammation and remodeling in metabolic syndrome. However, the role of SVCs in promoting AT dysfunction upon alcohol exposure remains unclear. Male rats were fed a Lieber–DeCarli diet containing 6.7% (v/v) ethanol (ET) or an isocaloric control diet (CON) for six weeks. Primary rat SVCs were isolated from visceral AT (VAT) of CON and ET rats. RNA sequencing analysis was performed to determine the overall changes in the gene-expression profile. Real-time PCR, Western blotting, and histological analyses were performed to validate the transcriptomics results. Chronic alcohol feeding decreased the adipocyte size and increased the formation of crown-like structures in the rat VAT. RNA-seq analysis revealed that signaling pathways related to cellular response to interleukin 1 (IL1) and collagen-containing extracellular matrix were significantly altered upon ethanol exposure in SVCs. Along these lines, ethanol exposure increased the protein levels of purinergic receptor P2Y2 (P2RY2) and IL1β in the SVCs of rat VAT. Furthermore, ethanol increased collagen deposition in both interstitial and perivascular regions, which was associated with an increase in the level of phosphorylated SMAD2/3 and collagen type VIII alpha 1 chain expression. These findings suggest that chronic ethanol exposure is associated with inflammatory and remodeling-related alterations in VAT and the total VAT-derived SVC fraction. This exploratory pilot study identifies P2RY2-associated inflammatory markers and TGFβ-related remodeling markers as candidates for future mechanistic investigation.

title: Service-Level Utilization in Risk-Based Contracts and a Benchmarking Approach for Fee-Schedule Reforms.
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Despite revived interest in reforming the physician fee schedule, it is unclear how policymakers should modify more than 1000 different physician service prices to promote high-value care. One systematic approach could leverage service-level utilization patterns in full-risk contracts, which have not been previously characterized.
OBJECTIVE: To compare service-level utilization patterns between health care professional organizations in full-risk contracts and those in a traditional fee-for-service (FFS) payment structure, adjusted for detailed patient-level differences, and to simulate an FFS fee schedule reform that would encourage the service patterns observed in risk-based contracts.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This retrospective cross-sectional study used Humana Medicare Advantage claims, encounter, and administrative data from 2015 to 2019 for 585 487 beneficiaries attributed to full-risk contract, with 100% downside risk for total medical spending, and 1 153 455 beneficiaries in fee-for-service contract arrangements. Data were analyzed from September 2025 to June 2026.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was service-specific utilization (count per beneficiary-year), adjusted for beneficiary characteristics. A secondary analysis simulated a modified Medicare FFS schedule based on estimated service-level utilization differences and a supply elasticity drawn from prior literature.
RESULTS: Among 1271 services examined, 940 (74%) had lower adjusted utilization in the risk cohort, and 331 (26%) had higher adjusted utilization. For 700 services (55%), adjusted utilization was at least 10% less in the full-risk cohort. For 199 services (16%), adjusted utilization was at least 10% greater. Low-level office visits and laboratory services were more common in risk-based settings, whereas higher-level office visits, hospital and emergency services, and rehabilitative therapies were less common. A simulated budget-neutral reform to the Medicare fee schedule, calibrated to shift utilization levels toward risk-based benchmarks, yielded a possible 6% increase in reimbursement to general practice physicians.
CONCLUSION AND RELEVANCE: In this cross-sectional study, the association between risk-based contracts and service utilization varied substantially across 1271 individual services. Service-specific utilization levels in risk-based contracts may serve as a benchmark to guide reforms to fee-for-service prices.

title: Organizational Perspectives on Access to Care Among Persons With End-Stage Kidney Disease After Enrollment in Medicare Advantage.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To examine Medicare Advantage (MA) plan, dialysis provider organization, and kidney care management company perspectives on how MA enrollment impacts access to care among persons with end-stage kidney disease (ESKD). The 21st Century Cures Act enabled persons with ESKD to enroll in MA, resulting in over 70% growth in enrollment among this group. However, the impact of MA enrollment on access to healthcare and services for people with ESKD remains unknown.
STUDY SETTING AND DESIGN: This was a qualitative study that included 48 semistructured interviews with 56 participants representing eight MA plans, six dialysis provider organizations, and five kidney care management companies across all US regions.
DATA SOURCES AND ANALYTIC SAMPLE: Interviews were conducted from January 2022 to May 2024. Deductive and inductive coding methods were used and organized around Donabedian's structure-process-outcomes framework.
PRINCIPLE FINDINGS: Perspectives diverged by organization and staff type across four themes. Regarding dialysis access, MA plan and large dialysis organization representatives reported no barriers for patients, while small dialysis providers described patients traveling farther to in-network facilities. Concerning specialists, frontline staff reported patients were often unaware of network restrictions limiting access. Regarding transplant, MA plans noted selecting "centers of excellence," while other participants reported these restrictions may be impeding patient access to transplants. For supplementary benefits, executives emphasized their value, while frontline staff reported benefits were often more limited than advertised.
CONCLUSIONS: Participant perspectives suggest MA enrollment may differentially impact access depending on dialysis provider size and MA network restrictions. Persons with ESKD may need additional support to make informed insurance enrollment decisions.

title: ZNF865 (BLST) a Novel Regulator of DNA Damage and Cell Senescence in Back Pain.
abstract: Senescence has been shown to contribute to the progression of aging-related diseases including degenerative disc disease (DDD). However, the mechanisms regulating senescence in the intervertebral disc (IVD) and other tissues/diseases remain poorly understood. Recently, ZNF865 (BLST) was identified as a previously uncharacterized zinc finger protein that regulates a wide array of genes related to protein processing, cell senescence, and DNA damage repair. Here, we show that ZNF865 expression decreases with age and pathology in human and mouse IVD samples. Utilizing CRISPR-guided gene modulation, we show that ZNF865 is necessary for healthy cell function and is a critical protein in regulating senescence and DNA damage in IVD cells, with implications for a wide range of tissues and organs. We also demonstrate that downregulation of ZNF865 induces senescence in asymptomatic human nucleus pulposus (NP) cells. Conversely, restoration in degenerative NP cells mitigates senescence, SASP expression, and DNA damage, enhances ECM anabolism, and restores chromatin accessibility and gene expression to a healthy state. In vivo, CRISPRi of ZNF865 induces disc degeneration and painful behaviors. Collectively, our findings establish ZNF865 as a novel regulator of genome stability and a potential therapeutic target for mediating senescence/DNA damage in aging related diseases.

title: Longitudinal untargeted metabolomics of cognitive impairment in Parkinson's disease.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Cognitive impairment is a common non-motor symptom of Parkinson's disease (PD), yet the mechanism remains unclear.
METHODS: Longitudinal serum samples from PD patients in a community-based case-control study were profiled, with cognition assessed by the Mini-Mental State Examination at baseline and follow-up. We performed three metabolome-wide association studies: a baseline cross-sectional analysis (n = 632), a time-to-event analysis (n = 412), and a repeated measures analysis (n = 265), followed by "Mummichog" pathway analysis.
RESULTS: Of the 4762 metabolomic features, four reached statistical significance in the baseline analysis, 22 in the time-to-event analysis, and none in the repeated measures analysis. Dysregulated pathways included purine metabolism, the pentose phosphate pathway, fatty acid pathways, and C21-steroid hormone biosynthesis and metabolism.
DISCUSSION: Disruptions in core metabolic pathways may contribute to PD-related cognitive impairments. Disturbances in pentose and purine pathways may occur before clinical cognitive decline is observed, suggesting early metabolic markers.

title: Salmonella infection and biofilms drive anti-C1q and anti-dsDNA autoantibodies in systemic autoimmunity.
abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is characterized by autoantibody production alongside inflammatory manifestations, including nephritis. In SLE, infections are frequent and associated with disease flares, increasing morbidity and mortality. Additionally, dysbiosis, often marked by overgrowth of Pseudomonadota, is a prominent feature of SLE and lupus nephritis. We previously demonstrated that complexes of DNA and curli, an amyloidogenic protein from biofilms of Pseudomonadota, including Salmonella Typhimurium and E. coli, can induce anti-dsDNA and anti-chromatin autoantibody responses. Here, we assessed the effects of curli administration or Salmonella infection on autoimmune manifestations in wild-type and lupus-prone mice. A multiplex autoantibody assay showed increased levels of anti-C1q antibodies in curli-treated C57BL/6 and lupus-prone NZBxW/F1 mice compared to PBS-treated controls. An anti-C1q-specific ELISA confirmed the presence of anti-C1q antibodies in C57BL/6 mice after treatment with curli/DNA, extracted from E. coli or Salmonella biofilms, or infection with Salmonella. Prior to the onset of spontaneous disease, sera from young NZBxW/F1 mice, injected with curli, demonstrated increased anti-dsDNA and anti-C1q antibody responses compared to PBS-treated controls; however, no differences were found in older mice, post-onset, when autoantibody levels were already high. In MRL/lpr mice, curli treatment significantly exacerbated anti-C1q antibody production regardless of age and disease stage, compared to PBS-treated controls. While curli treatment did not significantly affect proteinuria in either model, curli-treatment of MRL/lpr mice significantly increased C1q deposition in glomeruli. This study uncovers a novel mechanism for the induction of anti-C1q autoantibodies and how infection or dysbiosis may exacerbate renal disease in SLE.

title: Perceived value of antihypertensives for dementia, heart disease, or death: a randomized experiment
abstract: Background Many eligible patients elect not to use antihypertensive medications. It is unclear if highlighting certain disease-specific benefits could elicit a stronger desire to take antihypertensive medication and thus offer a low-touch method to increase medication use. We tested the hypothesis that framing the benefits of antihypertensives to prevent specific pathology, such as dementia, would affect how patients value antihypertensive medication. Methods We conducted a randomized, web-based experiment among census-matched participants from the United States ≥50 years of age via CloudResearch Prime Panels. Participants were randomized 1:1:1:1 to one of four framing vignettes describing a clinician’s recommendation to start antihypertensive therapy emphasizing prevention of (1) dementia, (2) cardiovascular disease (CVD), (3) death, or (4) all three combined. The primary outcome was self-reported monthly willingness to pay (WTP) out-of-pocket for the medication. Secondary outcomes included WTP as a proportion of income, total perceived value, intention to discuss hypertension with a clinician, and WTP among subgroups of participants. Results Of the 1,023 randomized participants, 907 responses met quality metrics and were included in the final sample. Mean participant age was 63.6 (standard deviation [SD]=9.6) years; 52.1% were women. The proportion of adults willing to pay >$0 exceeded 85% in all arms. Across arms, median monthly WTP out-of-pocket was $20 (interquartile range 10–50) with no significant differences by framing (p = 0.79) or in subgroups. Conclusion Framing antihypertensive medication benefits around prevention of dementia, CVD, death, or their combination did not impact financial value assigned to antihypertensive treatment.

title: Brain microstructure mediates the relationship between Alzheimer's proteinopathies and memory
abstract: INTRODUCTION: We examined how amyloid beta (Aβ) and tau accumulation affected gray matter (GM) microstructural integrity and how such alterations impacted memory. METHODS: We tested voxel-wise mediation models to examine the relationships between (1) positron emission tomography-derived Aβ and tau accumulation and GM microstructural integrity assessed with neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging, (2) GM microstructural integrity and memory controlling for Aβ and tau, and (3) the indirect effect of Aβ and tau on memory through GM microstructural integrity in 194 participants with memory impairments. RESULTS: Tau had a greater impact on GM microstructure than did Aβ. GM microstructural alterations in posterior cortical regions were associated with worse memory when controlling for Alzheimer's proteinopathies. GM microstructural alterations mediated the relationship between Alzheimer's proteinopathies and memory. DISCUSSION: GM microstructural alterations have functional ramifications given their mediating effect on the relationship between Alzheimer's proteinopathies and memory and their association with worse memory beyond Alzheimer's proteinopathies.

title: Lifestyle, APOE ε4, amyloid burden, and race/ethnicity differences in cognition, mood, and anxiety among cognitively unimpaired older adults
abstract: Abstract INTRODUCTION We assessed whether lifestyle, race/ethnicity, and apolipoprotein E gene ( APOE ) ε4 were associated with cognition or mood/anxiety. METHODS This secondary cohort analysis used data from the Anti‐Amyloid Treatment in Asymptomatic Alzheimer's Disease (A4) Study and the Longitudinal Evaluation of Amyloid Risk and Neurodegeneration (LEARN) cohort. Cognitively unimpaired adults aged 65 to 85 years ( n = 1705) reported baseline lifestyle behaviors (summed as healthy lifestyle index [HLI]). APOE ε4 carrier status and amyloid positron emission tomography were assessed at baseline, while cognitive, anxiety, and depressive outcomes were assessed longitudinally. Associations were tested using mixed‐effects models. RESULTS Among Non‐Hispanic White participants, higher HLI was associated with fewer depressive symptoms, sufficient sleep was associated with smaller ε4‐related increases in anxiety, and excessive alcohol use amplified ε4‐related cognitive decline. Among participants from other racial/ethnic groups, walking and higher HLI were associated with more favorable anxiety/depression trajectories. DISCUSSION Adequate sleep, limited alcohol, walking, and no smoking may support emotional and cognitive health.

title: Experiences and Expressions of Stress Among US Food Industry Workers During the 2020 Covid‐19 Pandemic
abstract: INTRODUCTION: The Coronavirus pandemic (Covid-19) exposed legacies of deep inequality, including who could afford protection from exposure. As part of the essential workforce, food industry workers continued fully in-person work throughout the pandemic and associated shutdowns. OBJECTIVE: To qualitatively examine US food worker experiences and stressors during the 2020 Covid-19 pandemic. METHODS: Thirty-four open-ended phone interviews were conducted from May through September 2020 with people who grew (n = 2), processed (n = 5), cooked (n = 9), sold (n = 17), and/or delivered (n = 5) food in the United States. Audio recordings were transcribed and coded for themes of stress, health, and workplace environment. RESULTS: Interviewees reported widespread disruption across US food system workplaces (e.g., reduced staffing, role changes, and increased workloads). Expressions of stress clustered into 4 themes: financial strain, concern about getting/transmitting Covid-19, sustained uncertainty, and overburdening. Workers' experiences revealed a need for self-reliance while their work and life environments were repeatedly overhauled. CONCLUSION: Results align with similar investigations into food workers' stress and limited protections before, during, and after the pandemic. The study contributes evidence for stronger worker support systems and positions food workers' lived experiences as vital to research and policy.

title: Response to memantine in a patient with refractory chronic cluster headache: Case report
abstract: Background The management of cluster headache, an uncommon and exquisitely painful headache disorder, sometimes requires the creative incorporation of off-label treatments. Case In this case report, a 69-year-old man with chronic cluster headache developed cardiomyopathy precluding continued use of verapamil, a gold-standard preventive medication, prompting additional treatment trials. After unsuccessful trials of conventional preventive treatments, he enjoyed relief after initiating memantine, achieving an approximate 70% reduction in attack frequency at 10 mg twice daily and then an 85% reduction with 20 mg twice daily. Conclusion Off-label use of memantine in headache disorders has been described, including in cluster headache; however, this case suggests that additional benefit may be obtained with gradual uptitration of the dose above what is commonly used in dementia, as tolerated.

title: Enhancing Council Effectiveness: Implementing a Nursing Shared Governance Toolkit Tailored to the Needs of Council Members
abstract: BACKGROUND: Evidence-based practice is essential to high quality healthcare. Shared governance (SG) is vital to integrate evidence-based practice findings into practice and empower frontline nurses through shared decision making. Research supports that SG fosters nurse engagement and satisfaction. This article outlines the first phase of a project aimed at improving council effectiveness, focusing on a current state analysis and development of a Nursing SG Toolkit (NSGT). AIMS: To assess the current state of nursing SG at a Veteran Affairs Medical Center and create a toolkit targeting identified gaps. METHODS: The project team utilized both quantitative and qualitative data. They distributed the Council Health Survey (CHS) to 20 of 31 active councils to assess council effectiveness through a five-point Likert scale (higher score favorable). They followed with focused discussions. The team created the NSGT to address identified gaps and shared an early iteration with Nurse Practice Council before re-distributing the "Membership" subscale of the CHS. The team disseminated a refined NSGT to all councils and administered the CHS 14 months later to 23 of 31 active councils. RESULTS: In the current state analysis, the lowest subscale of the CHS was "Membership" (M = 2.82). The project team created the NSGT with a focus on this subscale. Mann-Whitney U tests were used to evaluate pre and post scores. After Nurse Practice Council received NSGT education, its scores improved in all five "Membership" questions, with three out of the five questions statistically significant (p < 0.05). 14 months post implementation of the NSGT, overall CHS scores significantly increased (M = 3.62 to 3.83, z = -8.37, p < 0.001) with statistically significant increases in Nurse Practice Council scores in four of the five "Membership" questions. When data were filtered by those who indicated they used the NSGT, scores improved even more (M = 3.63-4.0, z = -10.27, p = < 0.001). LINKING EVIDENCE TO ACTION: SG councils simply existing is not enough; they must be effective in supporting the shared decision-making processes critical for evidence-based changes. Developing a toolkit to address lower scoring CHS areas (e.g., Membership) demonstrates a successful strategy for promoting council effectiveness.

title: Burden of Albuminuria in US Adults and its Association with Obesity, Sex and Mortality: A Cross-sectional Analysis of NHANES 2003-2020.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Albuminuria is an early marker of kidney disease diagnosis, severity and progression. Obesity, a major public health concern in the United States, may contribute to the development of albuminuria; however, the obesity-albuminuria relationship remains incompletely defined. We hypothesized that albuminuria is more prevalent in obese individuals and is associated with poor survival.
METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of NHANES survey cycles from 2003 to 2020, with linked mortality data through 2016. The study included 59,717 participants aged ≥18 years with available urinary albumin creatinine ratio (uACR) and BMI ≥18 kg/m2. BMI was categorized into normal weight, overweight and obese. Albuminuria was defined as UACR ≥30 mg/g and categorized into three severity grades (mild, moderate, and severe). Logistic regression models were used to assess the association between obesity and albuminuria, and adjustment by sociodemographic and clinical factors was assessed. Survival across albuminuria severity grades was examined.
RESULTS: Among individuals with albuminuria the prevalence of obesity was significantly higher than those without albuminuria (40.2% vs 32.9%; p<0.001). Individuals with albuminuria were relatively older and had higher prevalence of diabetes and hypertension as compared to the no albuminuria group. Obesity was significantly associated with higher odds of albuminuria (OR 1.36; 95% CI 1.23-1.50) when controlling for sociodemographic and clinical factors. We also observed higher odds of albuminuria in individuals who were males (OR 1.58, 95% CI 1.37-1.82), ages 18 to 44 years (OR 1.46, 95% CI 1.26-1.68), and ages 45 to 64 years (OR 1.79, 95% CI 1.49-2.14). The Individuals with albuminuria had poorer survival, with stark decline in a stepwise manner across albuminuria severity grades.
CONCLUSION: Obesity is strongly associated with albuminuria in U.S. adults. Albuminuria is linked to survival disadvantage, underscoring the importance of screening among individuals with obesity and early initiation of nephro-protective therapies in individuals with albuminuria.
