title: Living with dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa in Poland: first national study of health-related quality of life and symptom burden
abstract: Abstract Background Dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (DEB) is a rare genetic disorder associated with substantial and multidimensional disease burden. Although therapeutic options are advancing globally, patients in Central and Eastern Europe continue to face significant systemic barriers, including limited access to specialized care and innovative treatments. This study aimed to comprehensively assess health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and symptom burden in a national cohort of patients with DEB in Poland, with the objective of identifying key unmet needs. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted in collaboration with the EB Polska Foundation. Data were collected through a structured, multi-modular online survey. Symptom severity, including pain and pruritus, was evaluated using an 11-point Numeric Rating Scale (NRS). HRQoL was assessed using validated dermatology-specific instruments (DLQI/CDLQI, Skindex-29) alongside a generic measure (SF-36). Statistical analysis was limited to descriptive methods. Results A total of 33 patients with DEB were included (mean age: 23.7 years; 75.8% female). The cohort exhibited a high symptom burden, with mean NRS scores of 5.7 for pain and 5.9 for pruritus. Dermatology-specific instruments indicated severe impairment in HRQoL (mean DLQI: 13.9; CDLQI: 14.3), with the highest burden observed in the symptoms domain of Skindex-29 (mean: 48.9). In contrast, the SF-36 revealed a marked discrepancy between physical and mental health domains: physical functioning remained relatively preserved (mean: 94.5), whereas mental health scores were markedly reduced (mean: 22.4), indicating substantial psychological morbidity. Conclusions Patients with DEB in Poland experience a considerable symptom burden and pronounced psychological distress, despite maintaining relatively preserved physical functioning, potentially reflecting adaptive coping mechanisms. This discordance highlights persistent disparities in care. Addressing these gaps requires systemic healthcare interventions, including the development of specialized reference centers for rare diseases, integration of routine psychological assessment, and improved access to disease-modifying therapies.

title: Study protocol for the development of reporting guidelines for intervention adaptation studies: Transparent Reporting of Adaptations, Context and Effects (TRACE) – a multimethod approach using literature review, Delphi, crowdsourcing, webinar and usability testing
abstract: Introduction The adaptation of evidence-based interventions is widely recognised as essential for improving their relevance, acceptability and effectiveness across diverse populations and settings. While guidance for reporting intervention adaptations exists, it remains fragmented across frameworks, resulting in inconsistent and incomplete documentation. Such inconsistency in reporting limits our understanding of how interventions evolve across contexts and how adaptations influence implementation and clinical outcomes. The current fragmentation of recommendations for reporting and the lack of in-depth reporting of adaptation in studies are two of our justifications for developing Transparent Reporting of Adaptations, Context and Effects (TRACE), a reporting guideline specific to adaptation studies. Methods and analysis The development of TRACE will follow standard guidance to develop reporting guidelines and will comprise three main phases. Phase 1 includes a review of the literature on adaptation studies with the goal to: (a) identify definitions of adaptation, (b) identify definitions of adaptation studies, (c) identify the various designs, analysis and reporting features of methodological studies and (d) find any previous reporting guidance. Phase 2 involves Delphi and crowdsourcing methods to gather expert feedback on the proposed items for the TRACE guideline. Finally, in phase 3, we will finalise the checklist items and publish the guideline in a peer-reviewed journal. The goals of phases 2 and 3 are to gather feedback and develop consensus on: (a) definition of adaptation, (b) definition of adaptation study, (c) whether TRACE should be a modular/extension or standalone guideline and (d) which items should be included in TRACE. For phase 1, we will present a study flow diagram and summarise data in tables with explanatory text. Findings will be tabulated and synthesised with verbatim quotations. If the resulting studies are too heterogeneous for systematic review, we will shift to developing a narrative analysis of the findings. For phases 2–3, findings from the consensus exercises will be summarised descriptively in tables. We will measure levels of agreement for successive rounds and rounds with emergence of new feedback on the TRACE items or recommendations and instability for each round. If an item does not reach 80% agreement, it will go forward in the next round of evaluation with participants’ comments and suggestions for different wording. There are four sources of qualitative data across the phases: open texts from the surveys, discussion notes and transcripts from the Delphi meetings and from the webinar. We will conduct rapid qualitative content analysis of the data and organise it in a matrix to triangulate results and determine if there is agreement about the items across data collection episodes, as well as any other important suggestions that inform the development of the TRACE guidelines. Ethics and dissemination The study will follow the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. The study has been registered in EQUATOR and in PROSPERO. We have received an exemption letter for phase 1, the systematic review. The study has been approved by the Washington University in St. Louis’ Institutional Review Board (#202603062) for phase 2 (the Delphi study). Because the next parts of the study depend on the Delphi data, we have not submitted the IRB protocol for these. Informed consent has been obtained for the Delphi phase and will be obtained for the crowdsourcing and webinar phases. The dissemination of TRACE and its products will be done through journal publications, conferences, a website and social media.

title: Toward a conceptual framework of economic security for health research: a scoping review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Personal economic security, including stable income, employment, affordable housing, and protection against economic shocks, is fundamental to health. However, multiple and varied frameworks exist for defining or measuring economic security in health research and practice.
METHODS: We conducted a scoping review of the economic (in)security literature published 2015-2025. We searched PubMed and PsycINFO for articles that defined or measured economic (in)security, or that examined the impact of economic (in)security on health-related outcomes. From 881 sources, 53 articles were reviewed. Definitions and methods of operationalizing economic security were extracted and coded based on thematic dimensions, domains, and sub-domains.
RESULTS: There is wide variability in definitions and measurement of economic security. Economic security was defined multi-dimensionally across thematic domains, subjectivity and objectivity, and temporal dimensions (present versus future risk). Operationally, six domain areas of economic security were identified: income/finances, healthcare, employment, housing, food, and wealth/assets.
CONCLUSIONS: This six-domain framework of economic security for health research provides a foundation for more consistent measurement, improved intervention design, and specification of pathways linking economic conditions to health outcomes. Further investigation is needed to examine the framework's utility in elucidating economic security's multi-dimensional nature and devising measurement strategies to advance the science and practice of improving economic security.

title: Management of shift work disorder: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: This guideline establishes recommendations for the treatment of SWD.
METHODS: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) commissioned a task force of experts in sleep and circadian medicine to develop recommendations and assign strengths based on a systematic review of the literature and an assessment of the evidence using the GRADE process. The task force summarized the relevant literature and the quality of evidence, the balance of benefits and harms, patient values and preferences, and resource use considerations supporting the recommendations. The AASM Board of Directors approved the final recommendations.
RECOMMENDATIONS: The following recommendations are intended as a guide for clinicians in choosing specific treatment(s) for symptoms of excessive sleepiness and/or insomnia, and for circadian adaptation in adults with SWD. Each recommendation statement is assigned a strength (e.g., "Strong" or "Conditional"). For SWD, there were only "conditional" recommendations for or against (i.e., "We suggest…") and those requiring the clinician to use clinical knowledge and experience and consider the individual patient's values and preferences to determine the best course of action. Interventions in recommendation statements were compared to no treatment. Adults with SWD with symptoms of excessive sleepiness associated with work schedule: 1. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests the use of armodafinil or modafinil taken 30 to 60 minutes prior to the night shift over no armodafinil or modafinil (Conditional recommendation, moderate certainty of evidence). 2. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests the use of bright light over no bright light during the night shift (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence).
REMARK: Individuals with SWD who exhibit insomnia and daytime function impairments may also benefit from using bright light during their night shift. 3. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests the use of caffeine taken prior to and/or during the night shift over no caffeine (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence).
REMARK: Caffeine intake close to bedtime can disrupt sleep onset and quality, which may exacerbate symptoms of SWD. 4. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests the use of a clockwise rotating shift schedule over a counterclockwise rotating shift schedule (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). 5. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests taking a nap over no nap prior to the night shift (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence).
REMARK: Sleep inertia occurring soon after the nap may temporarily increase sleepiness, decrease cognitive performance, and increase accident risk. Allowing adequate time for resolution of sleep inertia prior to driving or performing other safety-sensitive behaviors may be needed to reduce these risks. 6. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests either not eating or eating a snack rather than eating a full meal during the night shift (Conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence). 7. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests the combination of caffeine and bright light over the combination of no caffeine and no bright light (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence).
REMARK: Caffeine intake close to bedtime can disrupt sleep onset and quality, which may exacerbate symptoms of SWD. 8. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests the combination of taking a nap and caffeine over the combination of no nap and no caffeine prior to the night shift (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). Adults with SWD with sleep disturbance/insomnia: 9. In adults with SWD with daytime sleep disturbance/insomnia the AASM suggests the use of CBT-I over no CBT-I (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). 10. In adults with SWD with daytime sleep disturbance/insomnia following the night shift, the AASM suggests the use of melatonin over no melatonin (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). 11. In adults with SWD with sleep disturbance/insomnia, when transitioning from daytime to nighttime sleep, the AASM suggests the use of melatonin over no melatonin for night sleep following shift work (Conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence). 12. In adults with SWD who desire to take a nap prior to the first night shift, the AASM suggests the use of melatonin over no melatonin prior to the nap (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence).
REMARK: Melatonin may temporarily increase sleepiness, decrease cognitive performance, and increase accident risk. Allowing adequate time for resolution of sleepiness prior to driving, returning to work or performing other safety-sensitive behaviors may be needed to reduce these risks. 13. In adults with SWD with daytime sleep disturbance/insomnia, the AASM suggests the use of ramelteon or other melatonin receptor agonists over no melatonin receptor agonist (Conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence). 14. In adults with SWD with daytime sleep disturbance/insomnia, the AASM suggests the use of suvorexant or other dual orexin receptor antagonists over no dual orexin receptor antagonists (Conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence). 15. In adults with SWD with daytime sleep disturbance/insomnia, the AASM suggests against the use of triazolam and other benzodiazepines (conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). Adults with SWD seeking circadian adaptation: 16. In adults with SWD seeking circadian adaptation to the night shift, the AASM suggests the use of bright light over no bright light during the night shift (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty).
REMARK: For individuals who work rotating or frequently changing shifts, circadian adaptation is not a realistic goal of treatment and therefore they would not be expected to benefit from this intervention. The evidence supporting this recommendation came from studies in which individuals reached partial circadian adaptation to the night shift. 17. In adults with SWD seeking circadian adaptation to the night shift, the AASM suggests the combination of bright light at night and fixed daytime sleep timing over the combination of no bright light and no fixed sleep timing (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence).
REMARK: For individuals who work rotating or frequently changing shifts, circadian adaptation is not a realistic goal of treatment and therefore they would not be expected to benefit from this intervention. The evidence supporting this recommendation came from studies in which individuals reached partial circadian adaptation to the night shift. 18. In adults with SWD seeking circadian adaptation to the night shift, the AASM suggests the combination of bright light at night, fixed daytime sleep timing, and reduced-light-transmittance glasses in the morning over the combination of no bright light, no fixed sleep timing, and no reduced-light-transmittance glasses (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). Remark 1 : For individuals who work rotating or frequently changing shifts, circadian adaptation is not a realistic goal of treatment and therefore they would not be expected to benefit from this intervention. The evidence supporting this recommendation came from studies in which individuals reached partial circadian adaptation to the night shift. Remark 2: Attention to driving safety is important when wearing reduced-light-transmittance glasses. Other considerations for adults with SWD: 19. In adults with SWD who are working either an 8-hour or 12-hour night shift, the AASM does not suggest working one shift duration over the other (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence).
REMARK: This recommendation does not consider other shift durations, rotation, or the number of consecutive shifts. This guideline did not look at shift durations exceeding 12 hours. The total number of hours worked per week ranged from 36 to 52.

title: A Scoping Review on Decision-Making Interventions for Kidney Failure Treatment Options by the Kidney Disease Aging Research Collaborative.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patients with kidney disease face complex treatment decisions amid prognostic uncertainty. These decisions may be particularly challenging for older adults, who often experience cognitive and functional changes and rely on caregivers. However, limited evidence describes treatment decision-making interventions for older adults, including the decision points addressed, use of decision aids, and geriatric-relevant SDM features, including caregiver involvement, values clarification, multiple touchpoints, and prognostic information.
METHODS: We conducted a scoping review of studies examining kidney failure treatment decision-making interventions that included ≥ 1 older patient(s) (≥ 65) with advanced kidney disease. We searched seven databases from inception through 4/2026. We characterized interventions by decision point, type of decision support provided, outcomes, exclusive enrollment of older adults, and presence of geriatric-relevant SDM features.
RESULTS: We identified 32 studies (of 2060 screened), representing 26 interventions. Seven interventions examined conservative kidney management versus dialysis, five dialysis modality, five dialysis versus transplant, and nine multiple treatment options. Among these, 11 (42%) included caregivers, 20 (77%) had multiple touchpoints, 19 (73%) included values clarification, and 12 (46%) incorporated prognostic data. Most interventions (22, 85%) incorporated decision aids. Of 137 outcomes reported, 13 (9%) were clinical. Nine interventions (35%) were evaluated exclusively among older adults.
CONCLUSIONS: Patient decision aids were common in kidney failure treatment decision-making interventions, but incorporation of geriatric-relevant SDM features varied across decision points, and few interventions were evaluated exclusively among older adults. Future interventions should tailor geriatric-relevant SDM features to specific treatment decisions to best support older adults in making kidney failure treatment decisions.

title: Subspecialty headache clinic visit reduced healthcare utilization in patients with migraine: Single institution retrospective cohort study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate whether care in a subspecialty headache center, compared with a general neurology clinic, was associated with lower 90-day unplanned healthcare utilization (HCU) in patients with migraine and to identify patient-level factors associated with higher unplanned HCU.
BACKGROUND: Migraine is a common, disabling condition that frequently prompts emergency department (ED) evaluation and treatment. It ranks among the leading global causes of years lived with disability and imposes a substantial financial burden. People with migraine are most often managed in general neurology clinics rather than in specialty centers. Subspecialty headache centers can offer more advanced and guideline-based care, but their impact on post-visit HCU is not well defined.
METHODS: This was a retrospective cohort study of adults with a migraine diagnosis cared for at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center from 2018 to 2023. Unplanned HCU was defined as any ED visit, urgent care encounter, or hospital admission within 90 days after the index outpatient general neurology or subspecialty headache center visit (first qualifying migraine-coded encounter in the study period). Associations between clinic type and unplanned HCU were evaluated with adjustment for age, sex, race, ethnicity, insurance, Area Deprivation Index, and comorbidities, and, in a subset with available data, Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System 16-item Profile (PROMIS-16) domains.
RESULTS: Of 38,472 patients included, 16,209 (42.1%) were evaluated in the subspecialty headache center. Total 90-day unplanned HCU was 12.6% in the subspecialty headache center vs. 15.4% in general neurology clinics (p < 0.001). Subspecialty headache center evaluation was associated with 15% lower odds of unplanned HCU (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 0.85, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.79-0.90, p < 0.001). The association remained after accounting for patient characteristics (aOR = 0.87, 95% CI: 0.81-0.92) and PROMIS-16 domains (aOR = 0.67, 95% CI: 0.59-0.76). Higher unplanned HCU was also associated with younger age at diagnosis, Medicaid and Medicare insurance/coverage, non-White races, comorbidities like chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, hypertension, and worse pain interference and physical function scores.
CONCLUSION: Evaluation in a subspecialty headache center was associated with approximately 15% lower odds of 90-day unplanned HCU. Subspecialized migraine care may represent a high-value care model.

title: The Role of Saliva in Swallowing: A Systematic Review
abstract: Saliva plays a critical role in swallowing by lubricating tissues and helping form and transport the food bolus. While low saliva production (hyposalivation) is linked to difficulty swallowing, emerging evidence shows that changes in saliva's physical and chemical properties may also affect swallowing. However, the mechanisms underlying these relationships remain poorly understood. The aim of this systematic review was to explore relationships between saliva and swallowing by reviewing studies that provided objective measurements of both saliva production and swallowing biomechanics. A comprehensive search of Medline (Ovid and PubMed), CINAHL, Web of Science, and Scopus was conducted, covering all records from database inception through August 22, 2025. We included studies that reported objective measures of saliva-such as flow rate, volume, thickness, pH, and biomarkers-and swallowing biomechanics. Three independent reviewers carried out two stages of screening, reviewed full texts, extracted data, and evaluated the quality of the methods using a modified Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine (OCEBM) scale. Most studies used a cross-sectional study design and were rated a "4" according to the OCEBM scale. In many studies, higher salivary flow rates were linked to increased spontaneous swallowing frequency in healthy adults. However, associations between saliva flow and specific swallowing biomechanical measures were not consistent. Lower levels of the neuropeptide substance p were associated with swallowing difficulties in several patient groups, but results varied across studies. The identified evidence suggests that salivary flow and neuropeptides may impact swallowing function, especially sensory function and spontaneous swallowing frequency. However, these relationships were inconsistent. Differences in the patient populations, saliva collection methods, and swallowing assessments made data synthesis between studies difficult. More standardized, long-term research is necessary to elucidate saliva's role in swallowing and improve clinical assessments for people with salivary dysfunction and dysphagia.

title: A systematic review of the maturation of selected cortical auditory event-related potentials in passive paradigms: Developmental changes from infancy to early adulthood.
abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) offers a unique window into the neural dynamics of cognition, particularly through event-related potentials (ERPs) that index sensory, attentional, and cognitive processes. EEG and ERP measures are widely used to study atypical neurodevelopment in children due to their sensitivity to disruptions caused by genetic and acquired brain disorders. We conducted a systematic review of the literature on the typical presentation of four core cortical auditory and language-related ERP components, extracted during passive paradigms, from infancy to early adulthood. These components reflect neural responses to the passive perception of discrete stimuli (N100), the automatic detection of deviant stimuli (Mismatch Negativity (MMN), sometimes in children referred to as the Mismatch Response (MMR)), the allocation of attention to deviant stimuli (P3a), and language processing of discrete stimuli (N400). Drawing from 61 studies, many of which reported on a single component within a specific age range, we chart developmental trajectories of ERP latencies, amplitudes, and scalp topographies. Across all components, latency tended to decrease with increasing age. Amplitude trajectories varied: N100 amplitude tended to decrease; MMN amplitude remained relatively stable or showed a slight decline; P3a amplitude typically increased during early childhood before decreasing in early school age; N400 amplitude consistently declined. Scalp topographical reports, among all components, revealed a shift toward increased focal activation with increasing age. Together, these findings provide a normative foundation for acoustic and auditory language processing in the context of the selected components in typical development, serving as a necessary reference point for understanding and assessing atypical development.

title: Low-Intensity Continuous Ultrasound vs. Traditional Ultrasound: A Systematic Review and Descriptive Analysis on Past and Future Gold Standards for Deep-Tissue Diathermy in Clinical Medicine
abstract: Background/Objectives: The thermal effects of therapeutic ultrasound (US) have been utilized to promote musculoskeletal healing. However, the optimal combination of US parameters, while studied in the past, has yet to be updated with the advent of newer US modalities, including low-intensity continuous ultrasound (LICUS). The purpose of this study was to evaluate the effects of US frequency, intensity, and duration on changes in tissue temperature and to compare the thermal response between traditional US and LICUS. Methods: Following PRISMA guidelines, PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science were searched for in vivo human studies that reported temperature changes and used standard ultrasound parameters (1 or 3 MHz, 0.1–2.0 W/cm2, aqueous gel). US frequency, intensity, duration, effective radiating area (ERA), body region, and total energy delivered at three depths (1 cm, 3 cm, and 5 cm) were extracted. The outcome of interest was change in tissue temperature (i.e., ultrasonic diathermy). A mathematical model was used to interpolate missing data. Three-way ANOVA and t-tests were used to compare outcomes. Results: Nineteen studies (384 participants) were included. The weighted mean total energy delivered was 6698.5 ± 6767.4 J and was significantly correlated with tissue temperature change across all depths (r = 0.544, p < 0.001). At 1, 3, and 5 cm depths, significant interactions were observed between ultrasound intensity and frequency and between intensity and treatment duration (all p ≤ 0.05). Higher intensities generally produced greater temperature increases during shorter treatments (≤10 min), whereas longer treatment durations (≥60 min) at low intensity produced the greatest temperature increases overall. Frequency-dependent effects were also observed, with greater temperature increases at 3 MHz compared with 1 MHz at several intensity levels. LICUS delivered significantly more total energy than traditional 3 MHz US (13,854.4 ± 8129.6 vs. 3546.5 ± 2096.0 Joules, p < 0.001) and produced significantly greater tissue temperature increases at all depths (p < 0.001). Conclusions: Changes in tissue temperature are strongly correlated with the total US energy delivered. While frequency, intensity, and duration play a significant role in thermal energy, LICUS over sustained periods delivers significantly greater cumulative energy and, subsequently, greater tissue temperature change compared to traditional US.

abstract: Integrating Family Care Partners in Aged Caregiving in the United States addresses the siloed nature of family caregiving in relation to formal paid caregiving, and the imperative that family caregivers or care partners must be integrated in the care of older adults and people living with disabilities. Knowledgeable care partners are crucial to optimal health and social care delivery. After defining the problems of demographic shifts and financing constraints, this book explores practices and policies that promote care partner integration. This emerging paradigm positions family care partners as integral members of wider long-term services and supports (LTSS) in the United States, recognizing them not only as participants but also as authorities in the lived experience of care work. To improve LTSS for older and disabled adults, two key changes are necessary: better recognition of care partners, and integration of their efforts into formal care systems currently falling short of meeting the holistic needs of care recipients. Select chapters outline non-US strategies employed around the globe to tackle challenges referred to in that chapter. This book will be of interest to all scholars, students, and professionals in social work, health administration, public health, nursing, medicine, public policy, and public administration.

title: Provider Variation in Time to Do Not Resuscitate Decisions and Its Association With Mortality
abstract: Background Do-not-resuscitate (DNR) orders represent a key inflection point in hospitalization and are associated with subsequent care intensity. While hospital-level variation in DNR use is well described, provider-level variation in the timing of DNR decisions remains poorly quantified. Research Question To quantify provider-level variation in the timing of DNR decisions and examine the association between life-support limitation (LSL) and subsequent mortality. Study Design and Methods We conducted a retrospective cohort study using electronic health record data from ten hospitals (2011–2025). Adults initially admitted to the ICU with full code status were included. A log-normal frailty model with a provider-level random effect was used to estimate variation in time to LSL (transition from full code to either DNR/Do-not-intubate (DNI), DNR/okay to intubate, or DNI). Models adjusted for demographic factors and time-varying measures of illness severity, including SOFA score, vasopressor use, respiratory support, and renal replacement therapy. Provider variation was summarized using the median hazard ratio (MHR). A separate Cox model evaluated the association between LSL and in-hospital mortality. Results Among 22,166 hospitalizations (187,548 patient-days; 1,233 providers), 4,933 patients (22.0%) transitioned to LSL. The provider-level MHR was 1.53 (95% CI, 1.50–1.55), corresponding to a 53% difference in the hazard of LSL transition between two otherwise similar patients treated by different providers. However, providers accounted for only 6% of the variation in LSL transition (ICC 0.06; 95% CI, 0.05-0.06). Findings were consistent across sensitivity analyses. LSL was strongly associated with subsequent mortality (HR 9.68; 95% CI, 8.57–10.93). Interpretation Modest but measurable provider-level variation exists in the timing of LSL decisions, although providers account for only a small proportion of overall variation. Future studies should evaluate how clinician approaches to shared decision-making contribute to this variation.

title: High intensity, persistent burden: family caregiving across the long-term care continuum and policy implications
abstract: Introduction: Family caregivers provide essential support to older adults with disabilities from the community to nursing home settings. Yet little is known about how caregiving intensity and caregiver well-being differ across settings. Methods: Using pooled 2021-2024 NHATS/NSOC data, we conducted repeated cross-sectional analyses of primary caregivers of US adults aged 71+ with disability residing in community, residential care, and nursing home settings. We compared caregiving experiences across settings. Results: Overall, 60.4% of older adults had an identified caregiver, including 74.4% of nursing home residents, 63.8% of residential care residents, and 58.8% of community-dwelling adults. Caregivers of community-dwelling adults had the highest average caregiving hours (34.7 hours/week), compared with caregivers of older adults in residential care (14.4) and nursing homes (13.7). Depressive symptoms, anxiety, and financial difficulty were similar across settings. Emotional difficulty was more common among caregivers of residential care (46.7%) and nursing home residents (43.5%) than community caregivers (31.5%). Caregivers in the community were more likely to forgo social activities due to caregiving (26.8%) but were also more likely to report substantial perceived caregiving gains (score ≥6 on an 8-point scale; 72.0%). Conclusion: Caregiving persists in institutional settings, with responsibilities shifting rather than disappearing, underscoring the need for supports across settings.

title: Tubular Secretion and Glomerular Filtration in the General Population: Insights Into the Intact Nephron Hypothesis
abstract: Rationale & objective The intact nephron hypothesis proposes that glomerular and tubular functions decline in parallel, supporting the use of estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) for drug dosing. However, the relationship between tubular and glomerular function by age and common clinical conditions remains unclear. Study design Cross-sectional analysis. Setting & participants A random subcohort of 1,219 participants from the population-based Nord-Trøndelag Health Study (HUNT), Norway. Exposures Age, eGFR, diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular disease (CVD), and albuminuria. Outcome A composite measure of tubular secretory function (scaled from 0 to 100) derived from urine-to-plasma ratios of 12 endogenous secretion markers. Analytical approach Associations between predictors and tubular secretion were evaluated graphically and with linear regression. Results Participants had a mean (SD) age of 51 (14) years and eGFR of 98 (17) mL/min/1.73 m 2 ; and prevalences of diabetes, CVD, and obesity were 4%, 6%, and 20%, respectively. Tubular secretion was weakly correlated with eGFR (r = 0.20; 95% CI, 0.14–0.25): a decline in eGFR from 90 to 60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 was associated with a 1.5-unit decrease in secretion, representing a small proportion of overall variability (SD 7.5 at eGFR 90). Tubular secretion was minimally correlated with age (r = −0.04; 95% CI, −0.09 to 0.02), contrasting with the strong inverse correlation between age and eGFR (r = −0.70; 95% CI, −0.73 to −0.67). Participants with very high eGFR (>130 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ) and diabetes, obesity, CVD, or albuminuria had the highest secretion score. Limitations Limited number of participants with eGFR < 45 or > 130 ml/min/1.73m 2 . Conclusions Glomerular and tubular function are differentially associated with age in the general population. Tubular secretory function was relatively preserved in persons with advanced age, and may increase in states of glomerular hyperfiltration, which has potential implications for drug handling and dosing.

title: Gain- versus loss-framed LDL-C risk messaging and willingness to pay for cardiovascular prevention among young adults
abstract: Background Loss-framed health messaging, emphasizing what is lost by inaction rather than gained by action is a common behavioral strategy to promote cardiovascular prevention. Whether framing influences prevention intentions in young adults (<40 years), a population newly targeted by the 2026 dyslipidemia guidelines, is unknown. We determined whether loss- and gain-framed cardiovascular risk messaging affects willingness to pay (WTP) for and intention to adopt preventive medication, exercise, and dietary changes among young adults. Methods We conducted a randomized experiment via an online diverse participant panel. Participants were US young adults without cardiovascular disease randomized to receive a loss-framed message (harm of not improving cholesterol) or a gain-framed message (benefit of improving cholesterol). The primary outcome was WTP for monthly preventive medication, exercise, and dietary changes, separately (continuous, 2026 U.S. dollars). Between-group comparisons used Mann-Whitney U tests; subgroup analyses examined effect modification across pre-specified characteristics. Results Among 2,382 participants (mean age 30.2 years; 51.3% female; 76.6% White), 1,159 were randomized to gain framing and 1,223 to loss framing. Loss framing increased median WTP for medication ($30 [IQR, $13–$50] vs $25 [IQR, $11–$50]; P=0.03). WTP did not significantly differ between loss or gain framing for exercise or diet interventions. Likert-scale behavioral intentions did not differ between groups for any modality (all P>0.05). Conclusions In this randomized experiment among young adults without cardiovascular disease, loss-framed risk messaging produced a modest $5/month increase in WTP for preventive medication ($30 vs $25; P = 0.03) without influencing behavioral intentions across any modality.

title: Sustained Acoustic Medicine Is a Cost-Effective, Noninvasive Treatment Option for Knee Osteoarthritis Compared With Intra-articular Hyaluronan Injections and Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Health Economic Evaluation
abstract: Background: Sustained acoustic medicine (SAM) is a wearable ultrasound device shown to have analgesic effects on knee osteoarthritis (OA). However, its cost-effectiveness relative to current treatment options, specifically intra-articular hyaluronan (IAHA) injections and total knee arthroplasty (TKA), has not been evaluated. Purpose: To compare SAM, IAHA injections, and TKA treatment options for knee OA sequentially on a cost-effectiveness basis in the United States. Study Design: Economic and decision analysis; Level of evidence, 2. Methods: A state-transition Markov model was developed to compare SAM, IAHA, and TKA with a 6-month cycle and a 60-year horizon. The model included 10,000 patients with mild/moderate knee OA per group aged 40 years with sensitivity analysis for 70 years. Patients would proceed through treatments sequentially, from SAM to IAHA to TKA, as treatments became ineffective. Probabilities, costs, and functional effectiveness were derived from published literature and government sources, including Social Security Administration and the Department of Veterans Affairs. Clinical outcome data used to determine parameters included 1315 patients (range, 40-72 years, SAM), 17,445 patients (50 to 70 years, IAHA), and 815,901 patients (40 to 88 years, TKA). The model was run 3 times, assuming the whole population started with SAM, IAHA, or TKA, respectively. Deterministic and probabilistic sensitivity analyses were conducted to test model robustness. Utilities were converted to quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) and incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) were calculated comparing the three starting treatment options with a willingness-to-pay threshold of $50,000. Results: Starting with TKA was less effective and more expensive than the other two strategies. SAM had higher QALYs per patient than IAHA treatment with a small increase in cost per patient, leading to an overall ICER of $11,394. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the results are unaffected by perturbations in model parameters. Conclusion: Our study demonstrated that at a conventional willingness-to-pay cutoff of $50,000, SAM is a cost-effective, noninvasive treatment option for knee OA that should be considered as an initial treatment option before IAHA or TKA by decision makers.

title: A Pragmatic Framework for Comparing TMS Treatment Schedules in Real-World Clinical Practice
abstract: Background Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) treats treatment‑resistant depression (TRD), but the growing use of accelerated treatment schedules and real‑world variability in delivery (frequency, duration, titration) complicate comparisons of delivered exposure across courses, clinics, and studies. Methods Using routinely recorded sessions, maximum stimulator output (MSO), and motor threshold (MT), we derived cumulative stimulation (Σ sessions×MSO/MT) and determined the extent to which Patient Health Questionnaire‑9 (PHQ‑9) trajectories are better indexed by cumulative stimulation, session count, or elapsed treatment day. We analyzed 166 Veterans treated with TMS (2018–2025) using mixed‑effects models of weekly PHQ‑9 and participant‑level 10‑fold and leave‑one‑subject‑out cross‑validation. We tested robustness in high MT (>80% MSO) and slow titration (not reaching 100% MT by day 6) subgroups and compared pre–post outcomes for once‑daily 10Hz versus three‑times‑daily intermittent theta‑burst stimulation (iTBS). Results Among single-predictor models, cumulative stimulation had modestly lower cAIC and 10-fold RMSE than sessions or day (2385 vs 2387/2392; 5.02 vs 5.06/5.08), with lower mean RMSE than both in all 10 repeated runs. Numerical separation was greater in the exploratory high-MT and slow-titration subgroups (RMSE: high MT 5.13 vs 5.55; slow titration 6.07 vs 6.48; cumulative stimulation vs day). No significant differences were found between once-daily 10Hz and three-times-daily iTBS in PHQ-9 change (p=.48) or percent improvement (p=.56). Conclusions Cumulative stimulation is a simple exposure metric that provides a pragmatic basis for comparing recorded treatment delivery across heterogeneous TMS schedules in routine care. This metric may prove valuable for facilitating meta-analyses of real-world data in which intensity, tolerability, and frequency vary, as well as for comparing increasingly heterogeneous protocols. title: Hospitalization Data for a Severe Acute Exacerbation of COPD as Predictors for Persistent Hypercapnia at 3 Months After Discharge.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This study's purpose was to develop a prognostication model to predict persistent hypercapnia 3 months after discharge in patients hospitalized for COPD exacerbation and hypercapnia.
METHODS: We developed the prediction model using a training data set comprising of participants in the RESCUE trial who received no ventilation support at home. We externally validated the model with a retrospective cohort. We calculated the rate of persistent hypercapnia 3 months post hospitalization according to the inpatient PaCO2. We also built regression models that included age and prior hospitalizations and calculated Area Under Curve (AUC).
RESULTS: Our training cohort consisted of 69 participants. Among participants with baseline PaCO2 levels between 45 and 52mmHg, 59% had persistent hypercapnia at 3 months. It increased to 73.1% with PaCO2 between 53 and 60mmHg and 100% with greater than 60 mmHg (P < 0.001). Our regression model showed that for each one mmHg increase in baseline PaCO2 the 3-month PaCO2 increased by 0.41. The AUC was 0.779 (95%CI of 0.667 to 0.891).
CONCLUSION: The last inpatient PaCO2 measurement may help predict persistent hypercapnia 3 months after discharge.

title: Internal and External Drivers of CD4 Recovery in People with HIV.
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: This review summarizes the key factors that influence CD4 recovery after antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation in people with HIV (PWH).
RECENT FINDINGS: Several immunomodulatory agents have been tested in clinical trials as adjuncts to ART. While interleukin-2 and interleukin-7 produce transient CD4 increases, and agents such as recombinant human growth hormone, maraviroc, and others show modest or variable effects, most have not demonstrated clear clinical benefit. Emerging evidence underscores the need for personalized approaches, reliable biomarkers to predict CD4 recovery, and novel adjunctive therapies such as gene editing and mitochondrial-targeted interventions. Poor CD4 recovery contributes to higher rates of non-AIDS complications. We highlight clinical determinants (e.g., timing of ART initiation), biological influences (e.g., epigenetic modifications), cellular factors (e.g., mitochondrial dysfunction), and modifiable socioeconomic determinants (e.g. nutrition, substance use). Addressing factors impacting CD4 recovery is critical to improving long-term outcomes for PWH.

title: A preliminary study of the lateral bending response of pre-rotated head using a human cadaver model and a head-neck finite element model.
abstract: The study was framed around three objectives: The first experimental objective was to characterize the lateral bending response of pre-rotated head using a human cadaver model. The second statistical objective was to determine whether the axial force and coronal moment can be used to construct preliminary injury risk curves. The third modeling objective was aimed to investigate whether an existing generic head-neck finite element model can reproduce measured force and moment responses under cadaver test conditions. The first objective was accomplished by testing five female human cadaver cervical spinal column specimens that were fixed at the C7-T1 joint and placed on a custom spinal positioning device. The base of skull was angulated by 30°. The device converted the vertical piston displacement to lateral bending on the pre-rotated specimen. Computed tomography was used to identify injuries. The second objective was accomplished by using the derived occipital condyle axial force and coronal moment data to develop preliminary injury risk curves. The model and experimental responses for the forces and moments were compared using the ISO/TS 18571 method. The mean age, stature, total body mass, body mass index, and bone mineral density of the specimens were 63 years, 1.7 m, 78 kg, 28 kg/m2, and 325 mg/cc, respectively. Four specimens resulted in atlas injuries. Based on the optimal lognormal distribution, the peak force and moment of 550 N and 26 Nm were associated with the 50% probability of injury. The computational model reproduced the general increase in global loading between low- and high-severity tests, although agreement with individual experimental force responses was varied. Additional studies are needed to increase the sample size and include other pre-rotations of the head. This preliminary dataset may have potential applications to out-of-position occupants in automated vehicle environments.

title: Relationships Between Bladder Dysfunction, Fatigue, Quality of Life, and Mobility in People With Parkinson Disease
abstract: Purpose: Examine the relationship between bladder dysfunction, fatigue, quality of life (QoL), and mobility in people with Parkinson Disease (PD). Methods: In this cross-sectional secondary analysis, bladder dysfunction was measured by the Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale bladder function score (UPDRS bladder function scores, item 1.10). The Parkinson’s Fatigue Scale-16 measured fatigue. The Parkinson’s Disease Questionnaire measured physical and nonphysical QoL. The 10-M Walk Test and timed up and go (TUG) measured functional mobility, and average step-count measured real-world mobility. Associations of the UPDRS bladder function scores with fatigue, QoL, and mobility were determined using Spearman-rank correlations. Differences between UPDRS bladder function scores 0 to 1 (normal-to-slight) and 2 to 4 (mild-to-severe) groups were determined using independent t tests. Results: Twenty-nine people with PD with mild-to-moderate disability (Hoehn and Yahr 2-4) were included. The sample was 66% male (69.4 ± 9.4 years old, Hoehn and Yahr of 2.2 ± 0.7). UPDRS bladder function scores were mild-to-severe in 44.8%. Fair-to-moderate correlations were present between UPDRS bladder function scores and fatigue (ρ = 0.48, P = .009), overall QoL (ρ = 0.50, P = .008), physical QoL (ρ = 0.56, P < .001), nonphysical QoL (ρ = 0.39, P = .038), 10-M Walk Test (ρ = 0.42, P = .023), and the TUG (ρ = 0.42, P = .023). Fatigue and QoL were worse in the mild-to-severe bladder dysfunction group than in the normal-to-slight group ( P ≤ .05), but mobility did not differ significantly between groups. Discussion: Self-reported bladder dysfunction was correlated with fatigue, QoL, and functional mobility, but not real-world mobility, in people with PD. These relationships emphasize the role of rehabilitation clinicians in addressing interconnected symptoms and support further research into the implications for bladder screening in clinical care.

title: Medicare Increased Reimbursement Values For 10 Percent Of Physician Services After Public Comments, 2023-25.
abstract: The process that the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) uses to determine relative values for each physician service has been critiqued for undervaluing primary care relative to specialty care. CMS assigns a relative value unit (RVU) to each service, with higher RVU values leading to higher payment. CMS frequently relies on RVU recommendations from the American Medical Association/Specialty Society Relative Value Scale Update Committee (RUC), but little is known about the impact of CMS's interaction with other stakeholders during the public notice-and-comment process for RVUs. In this analysis of CMS's work RVU (wRVU) valuations for 2023-25, we found that CMS increased wRVUs for 10 percent of services after public comments. These changes increased CMS's agreement with the RUC from 68 percent to 74 percent. Current Procedural Terminology codes for procedures were more likely to have their wRVUs increased after public comments than evaluation and management codes. These findings suggest that the public comment process may be biased toward increasing valuations for specialty services, which the commenters perceive to be undervalued, while not addressing the larger issue of overvaluations of specialty services and the corresponding undervaluations of evaluation and management services. These findings underscore the need for a more objective payment-setting process.

title: Association of Early Primary Care Follow-Up With Acute Care Use After ICU Discharge.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To determine if early primary care follow-up after pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) hospitalization is associated with reduced acute care use.
METHODS: Using claims data from publicly and privately insured children, we identified a cohort of PICU hospitalizations from January 2016 to December 2019. We matched children with and without early primary care follow-up (within 7 days of hospital discharge) 1 to 1 on demographic and clinical characteristics. We compared the number of days of acute care use (emergency department or rehospitalization) during days 8 to 90 postdischarge using negative binomial regression and reported incidence rate ratios (IRR).
RESULTS: The sample included 180 516 PICU hospitalizations, including 158 544 for publicly insured children and 21 972 for privately insured children. Among PICU hospitalizations for publicly and privately insured children, 56 247 (35.4%) and 5156 (23.5%) were associated with acute care use with 8 to 90 days postdischarge. Hospitalizations of children with early primary care follow-up were less likely to be associated with acute care use than those without follow-up (public insurance: IRR, 0.93; 95% CI, 0.90-0.96; P < .001; and private insurance: IRR, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.63-0.77; P < .001). Subgroup analyses suggested early primary care follow-up was associated with larger decreases in acute care after hospitalizations of older children and children with sepsis. The association between early primary care follow-up and acute care use persisted in a secondary analysis using data from 2022 to 2023.
CONCLUSIONS: Early primary care follow-up was associated with lower acute care use after discharge from PICU hospitalization. Promotion of early primary care follow-up may be warranted after pediatric critical illness.

title: Age-related biomechanical and structural remodeling of human middle cerebral arteries.
abstract: Proper cerebral artery function is essential for maintaining the brain's microenvironment. The multilayered organization of cellular and extracellular matrix (ECM) constituents enables large cerebral arteries to accommodate pulse pressure and ensure both effective blood distribution and protection of the microcirculation. However, aging and disease induce compositional and structural remodeling in cerebral arteries, such as the middle cerebral artery (MCA), which can alter biomechanical properties and increase susceptibility to cerebrovascular conditions including atherosclerosis and aneurysms, both major contributors to stroke. Understanding how age-related changes in arterial structure and composition influence biomechanical behavior is critical for improving prediction of cerebrovascular risk. In this study, we characterized the age-dependent elastic and viscoelastic properties of human MCAs and related these changes to ECM structure and composition using imaging and biochemical assays. Our results demonstrate that aging is associated with increased stiffness and stress relaxation in MCAs. Biochemical analyses revealed age-related increases in collagen and glycosaminoglycan (GAG) content, both of which correlated with altered mechanical properties. Histological staining further showed denser collagen organization within the adventitia and elevated GAG presence, consistent with mechanical and biochemical findings. Additionally, multiphoton imaging under mechanical loading provided insight into layer-specific collagen reorganization in the adventitia. Collectively, these findings elucidate key age-dependent alterations in the structure-function relationship of human cerebral arteries and provide a mechanistic basis for increased cerebrovascular risk with aging. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: Age-related remodeling of the extracellular matrix is a fundamental driver of tissue dysfunction, yet its effects on human cerebral artery mechanics remain poorly understood. In this study, we combine biomechanical testing, biochemical assays, histology, and multiphoton microscopy to characterize structural and functional remodeling of human middle cerebral arteries across a broad age range. We demonstrate that aging is associated with increased arterial stiffness and viscoelastic relaxation, accompanied by elevated collagen and glycosaminoglycan content. By directly linking extracellular matrix composition and organization to biomechanical function, this work provides new insights into the mechanisms governing cerebrovascular aging. These findings establish an important structure function framework for understanding vascular tissue remodeling and have broader implications for age related vascular dysfunction, mechanobiology, and biomaterials research.

title: Maintenance of a Dementia Skills Training Program in a VA Health Care System: Evolution and Outcomes Over the Years.
abstract:
PURPOSE: With the population of veterans living with dementia projected to increase significantly, health care systems must adapt to provide consistent, person-centered care.
METHOD: In alignment with the Age-Friendly Health Systems framework, this project evaluated the effect of the Dementia Workshop: Basics of Dementia Care, an in-person, interdisciplinary dementia training program. Staff (N = 162) from acute, long-term, and outpatient settings attended this 8-hour workshop featuring lecture, interactive discussion, video-based scenarios, and hands-on practice.
RESULTS: Pre-post analysis using the Sense of Competence in Dementia Care Staff scale, Dementia Attitudes Scale, and Confidence in Dementia Scale revealed statistically significant improvements (p < .001) in competence, confidence, and attitudes, with large and medium effect sizes.
CONCLUSION: These findings support investment in interactive, multimodal training as a potential strategy to build a workforce equipped to manage complex care needs and reduce distress for veterans living with dementia.

title: Complexity of patients with hypertension cared for by clinical pharmacist practitioners in the Veterans Health Administration
abstract: PURPOSE: Clinical pharmacist practitioners (CPPs) are well suited to manage complex patients, such as those with hypertension. However, there is limited information about the complexity of patients managed by CPPs with respect to chronic disease. This study compared the clinical complexity of patients with hypertension managed by CPPs to that of patients managed by other providers. METHODS: In this cross-sectional study, patients with hypertension at 19 Veterans Health Administration (VA) sites during fiscal years 2024 to 2025 were classified by CPP visits into those with more than one visit ("ongoing CPP care"), those with one visit ("consultative CPP care"), and those with no visits ("no CPP care"). Patient complexity was assessed using 7 hypertension-related measures indicating need for more management time and resources. Logistic regression models adjusted for age, sex, race, and marital status were generated to analyze differences between the groups. RESULTS: Compared to patients in the group with no CPP care, patients with ongoing CPP care had significantly higher complexity as measured by hypertension medication use (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.36; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.09-1.70), other medications associated with hypertension (aOR, 1.66; 95% CI, 1.26-2.18), hypertension complications (aOR, 1.60; 95% CI, 1.29-1.98), and medication nonadherence (aOR, 1.36; 95% CI, 1.06-1.75). Similar findings were noted for patients with consultative CPP care vs those with no CPP care. A composite complexity score of all 7 measures indicated that patients with ongoing (aOR, 1.89; 95% CI, 1.54-2.32) and consultative (aOR, 1.88; 95% CI, 1.57-2.24) CPP care were significantly more complex than patients with no CPP care. CONCLUSION: CPPs manage patients with hypertension who are more complex than those managed by other VA providers. These findings underscore the importance of CPPs in improving patient outcomes through comprehensive medication management.

title: Debate: Level of TSH at which thyroid hormone replacement should be initiated in gestation
abstract: In this debate, two clinicians discuss the merits and limitations of levothyroxine treatment for pregnant women with thyrotropin (TSH) concentrations 2.5-10 mIU/L. Recently published clinical practice guidelines have raised the treatment threshold, suggesting treatment for women with thyrotropin (TSH) ≥4.0 mIU/L and normal thyroxine concentrations only in the first trimester and recommending against treatment for women with TSH concentrations between 2.5 and 4.0 mIU/L. The evolution of these recommendations and the uncertainty regarding the overall balance of benefits and harms across the spectrum of mild thyroid dysfunction during pregnancy may lead to challenges in clinical practice, underscoring the importance of clear, practical guidance to support informed and consistent clinical decision-making. Dr. Bliddal argues that individualized levothyroxine treatment may remain reasonable in selected pregnant women with TSH concentrations of 2.5-4.0 mIU/L, and supports consideration of treatment in women with first trimester subclinical hypothyroidism and TSH concentrations between 4.0-10.0 mIU/L, emphasizing biological heterogeneity, limitations of fixed thresholds, and remaining evidence gaps. Dr. Maraka argues against routine levothyroxine treatment in these women, highlighting the uncertainty regarding clinical benefit and the potential risks of overtreatment.

title: Association of Changes in Game Pitch Count, Pitching Velocity, and Arm Injuries in Collegiate Pitchers.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Baseball pitchers experience a high rate of shoulder and elbow injuries. While there have been several factors associated with arm injuries among pitchers, pitch volume and pitch velocity have garnered a great deal of attention. The associations among pitch counts, pitch velocity, and arm injury have not been well studied.
PURPOSE: To assess the association between changes in game pitch count and arm injuries in collegiate baseball pitchers over 1 summer season. The secondary aim was to assess the association between mean in-game fastball pitch velocity and arm injuries in the same baseball pitchers.
STUDY DESIGN: Cohort study; Level of evidence, 2.
METHODS: Collegiate pitchers were prospectively followed throughout the summer season for game pitch count, pitch velocity, and arm injuries. Bayesian joint models, including time-to-event Cox regressions and multilevel mixed effects regressions, were performed to assess the associations of interest, while competing risks of release and/or retirement were controlled for. Nonlinear relationships were modeled using natural splines. Change in pitch count and pitch velocity was modeled by the change in each pitcher's mean seasonal pitch count or pitch velocity.
RESULTS: A total of 187 pitchers were included in this study and followed for a total of 9890 baseball exposure days. A total of 22 pitchers (12%; 95% CI, 7.5%-17.2%) experienced an arm injury, and 4 pitchers (2%; 95% CI, 0.6%-5.4%) were released, voluntarily retired, or reached their innings limit for the season. There was a nonlinear (parabolic shape) positive association of an increased change in pitch count as compared with the pitcher's mean pitch count and arm injuries. Additionally, there was a nonlinear (parabolic shape) positive association between arm injury hazard and a decrease in fastball pitch velocity when compared with the pitcher's mean fastball pitch velocity.
CONCLUSION: There was an increased risk for shoulder and elbow injuries with an increase in pitch count as compared with a pitcher's mean pitch count over pitch appearances. Additionally, there was an association between arm injuries and decreased pitch velocity as compared with a pitcher's mean pitch velocity.

title: AASLD AGA clinical Practice Guideline on management of primary biliary cholangitis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AIMS: Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is a chronic cholestatic liver disease associated with progressive fibrosis, cirrhosis, liver transplantation, and premature mortality. Despite effective therapies, important challenges remain in the diagnosis and management of PBC, including identification of antimitochondrial antibody-negative disease, assessment of response to ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), risk stratification, treatment of patients with inadequate response, management of cholestatic pruritus, and prevention of recurrent disease after liver transplantation. The aim of this guideline was to develop evidence-based recommendations addressing these key areas of clinical care.
METHODS: The American Gastroenterological Association (AGA) and the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) convened a multidisciplinary panel to develop clinical practice recommendations for adults with PBC. Systematic reviews were performed for 6 prioritized clinical questions. The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation framework was used to prioritize clinical outcomes and assess evidence, and its Evidence to Decision Framework was used to develop recommendations.
RESULTS: The guideline panel agreed on 6 recommendations. These recommendations address the use of PBC-specific antinuclear antibodies in antimitochondrial antibody-negative suspected PBC, UDCA as first-line therapy, liver stiffness measurement for prognostication, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor agonists for patients with inadequate response or intolerance to UDCA, linerixibat for moderate to severe pruritus, and UDCA prophylaxis post-transplantation to reduce disease recurrence. The certainty of evidence ranged from moderate to very low.
CONCLUSIONS: The guideline emphasizes early diagnosis, optimization of first-line therapy, risk-based treatment escalation, symptom management, and prevention of post-transplantation disease recurrence to improve patient outcomes and quality of life.

title: Cognitive Vulnerability and Subsequent Audiometric Hearing Change in Later Life: Implications for Dementia Assessment in Geriatric Psychiatry.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To determine whether a demographically referenced multidomain cognitive-vulnerability phenotype predicts subsequent audiometric hearing change among older adults with study-defined normal baseline hearing and to clarify its relevance to longitudinal dementia assessment in geriatric psychiatry.
DESIGN: Longitudinal observational cohort study.
SETTING: National Health and Aging Trends Study, Rounds 11-13 (2021-2023).
PARTICIPANTS: 569 older adults with baseline better-ear pure-tone average (PTA) ≤25 dB HL and complete baseline and final-round data.
INTERVENTION: None.
MEASUREMENTS: We constructed an age- and education-adjusted cognitive-risk composite integrating immediate and delayed recall, clock drawing, and temporal orientation and classified risk as low, intermediate, or high. Better-ear PTA at 0.5, 1, 2, and 4 kHz was measured up to three times over approximately 2 years. Linear mixed-effects models estimated PTA change; Cox and logistic sensitivity analyses evaluated threshold-defined hearing loss.
RESULTS: Across 1,687 observations, each one-category increase in cognitive risk was associated with an additional 0.53 dB HL/year increase in PTA (95% CI, 0.22-0.85; p = 0.001). Cognitive risk was also associated with first-observed PTA > 25 gt; 25 dB HL (HR, 1.50; 95% CI, 1.15-1.96; p = 0.003) and hearing loss at Round 13 (OR, 2.19; 95% CI, 1.43-3.35; p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: Cognitive vulnerability preceded modestly faster measured hearing-threshold worsening across continuous and threshold-defined outcomes. Shared multisystem aging and cognition-related variation in behavioral audiometry remain plausible explanations. Evolving auditory function should be considered a time-varying component of longitudinal neurocognitive assessment in geriatric psychiatry.

title: A Research and Implementation Roadmap from the VA's National State-of-the-Art Conference on Age-Friendly Care for Veterans.
abstract: The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) Veterans Health Administration (VHA) is among the largest integrated health systems in the United States to systematically adopt the Age-Friendly Health Systems (AFHS) framework developed by the Institute for Healthcare Improvement and the John A. Hartford Foundation. This national implementation, spanning hospitals, ambulatory clinics, community living centers (with VA skilled nursing facilities), home-based primary care teams, and more, has positioned the VA as a national leader in operationalizing the 4Ms framework of Mobility, Mentation, Medications, and What Matters, across multiple care settings, with meaningful early clinical impacts. However, dissemination of the AFHS framework within the VA has been uneven, and robust data are lacking about the implementation and outcomes of the 4Ms framework. To better understand this implementation gap and research needs, the VA Offices of Research and Development and Geriatrics and Extended Care convened a national state-of-the-art (SOTA) conference in 2025, bringing together invited experts from around the country to identify what is known and unknown about the implementation, sustainment, measurement, research, and scaling of the AFHS framework in general, and specifically within the VA health system. The purpose of the VA Age-Friendly SOTA conference was to explore this gap and to provide guidance to the field for areas of future work, acknowledging that meaningful scale and sustainment will require additional research, infrastructure, and deeper understanding of implementation in real-world environments. This article describes the resulting VA Age-Friendly research and implementation agenda, a roadmap derived from what the VA has learned from implementing the 4Ms at scale, depicting practical lessons learned and suggesting next steps for Age-Friendly systems transformation to improve the care of older adults.

title: Low-intensity focused ultrasound for neuromodulation: neuroimaging and neurointerventional perspectives.
abstract: Low-intensity focused ultrasound (LIFU) is an emerging, noninvasive neuromodulation technique with a growing evidence base and set of applications. LIFU uses low-energy acoustic waves that are focused to a focal volume in the millimeter range and transiently modulate neuronal activity in targeted cortical and subcortical brain structures. Unlike high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU), which is designed to cause thermal ablation of the target tissue, LIFU is intended to modulate neuronal activity rather than ablate tissue. In this article, we review the technical background, clinical applications, and safety of LIFU from neuroimaging and neurointerventional perspectives.

title: Influence of Trained Companion Dog Ownership Among Military Veterans Diagnosed With a Mental Health Condition.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To explore the perceptions of U.S. Veterans on the influence of owning trained companion dogs (TCDs) from animal shelters on their mental health and influence of the historical distress of the dog on dog-owner bonding.
METHOD: A descriptive, exploratory design was used to collect data via telephone interviews with 90 veterans who adopted dogs and had a mental health diagnosis at the time of adoption.
RESULTS: Ownership influenced perceptions of loneliness (97%), sense of purpose (87%), exercise (86%), safety (86%), anxiety (84%), depression (84%), and sleep (74%). Veterans who perceived that their dog experienced distress or trauma pre-adoption acknowledged it influenced feelings of connectedness (66%), relating to the dog (81%), helping the dog (81%), and the dog helping them (88%).
CONCLUSION: TCD ownership positively influenced veteran mental health. Help is a two-way street between veterans and dogs with a history of distress or trauma. Health care professionals caring for veterans with mental health conditions should explore dog ownership through specific companion programs.

title: Co-Occurrence Patterns of Symptom and Functional Burden Associated with Tofacitinib and Upadacitinib: A Multidimensional Analysis of Spontaneous Reports in Rheumatoid Arthritis.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Pharmacovigilance studies typically evaluate adverse events as isolated drug-event pairs, potentially overlooking symptoms and functional impairments reported concurrently within the same case. We investigated co-reported adverse event patterns for tofacitinib and upadacitinib in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Methods: FAERS reports submitted between 2004 and 2025 were included if tofacitinib or upadacitinib was recorded as the primary suspect drug for RA. Disproportionality analysis was integrated with three co-occurrence network approaches, Bayesian network analysis, and time-to-onset (TTO) analysis. Methotrexate served as an indication-matched comparator. Network analyses were stratified by reporter and submission type, and TTO was reassessed for the common 2019-2025 period. FAERS signals were also compared descriptively with Canada Vigilance data. Results: We identified 57,438 tofacitinib-related and 29,869 upadacitinib-related reports, yielding 316 and 413 positive Preferred Term signals, respectively. In the tofacitinib networks, fatigue was consistently associated with pain, mood-related terms, treatment experience, and gastrointestinal and infectious events. Upadacitinib reports exhibited a distinct pattern, with falls, pain, functional limitations, and injuries occupying central positions. Reduced grip strength, decreased joint range of motion, and loss of personal independence formed a recurrent functional cluster. Methotrexate networks were primarily organized around disease-activity terms. The median reported TTO was 34 days for tofacitinib and 115 days for upadacitinib; corresponding values for the 2019-2025 period were 59 and 115 days, respectively. These intervals should not be interpreted as true onset latency or as established hazard patterns. Conclusions: Co-reporting analysis yielded insights beyond individual disproportionality signals. Tofacitinib reports were predominantly characterized by fatigue and associated symptoms, whereas upadacitinib reports more prominently featured functional limitations, falls, and injuries.

title: Living longer but not healthier: Global differences in longevity and cardiometabolic health.
abstract: Global life expectancy has increased dramatically from 1950 to 2023, rising by 25 years for females and 24 years for males, driven mostly by advances in nutrition, sanitation, and infectious disease control, and in part by declining cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality. Although age-standardized CVD mortality has declined in many settings, absolute cardiometabolic burden has increased because of population growth, aging, and rising exposure to metabolic risks. In 2023, CVD alone accounted for 437 million DALYs and 19.2 million deaths. While overall life expectancy did increase by 8.1 years globally between 1990 and 2019, healthy life expectancy increased by only 6.6 years, corresponding to a widening health span-lifespan gap. This divergence is indicative of prolonged years that are lived with disability, with cardiometabolic diseases among the modifiable drivers. Regional patterns reveal significant heterogeneity, with low- and middle-income countries facing a double burden of communicable diseases and rapidly rising cardiometabolic diseases that are primarily driven by urbanization, nutritional transitions, and inadequate primary care infrastructure. High-income countries, on the other hand, are witnessing a rising health span - life span gap due to near-stagnant growth in LE but expanding cardiometabolic morbidity. Understanding the relationship between changes in longevity and cardiometabolic health is essential for addressing the growing global burden of years lived with disability. This narrative review examines global and regional patterns of life expectancy and healthy life expectancy, with a focus on cardiometabolic disease, and highlights disparities across developmental levels, regions, and demographics to inform targeted prevention and intervention strategies.

title: Frailty and Rheumatoid Arthritis: Key Insights and the Road Ahead.
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: People with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) experience premature aging and RA is associated with poor health outcomes. Frailty tools offer a holistic view of an individual's health status that may inform treatment strategies in RA. This review provides an overview of frailty in RA including methods of measurement, associations with clinical outcomes, and potential paths for frailty intervention.
RECENT FINDINGS: Frailty is common in RA, affecting approximately one-third of patients, with prevalence estimates varying according to the measurement instrument used. The causes of frailty are not well studied but likely include a combination of chronic systemic inflammation, immunosenescence, deconditioning and medication effects. Frailty is consistently associated with higher disease activity, poorer physical function, depression, pain, reduced quality of life, and greater comorbidity burden. Longitudinal studies show that frailty predicts hospitalization, serious infections, osteoporotic fractures, functional decline, readmission, and mortality, independent of traditional clinical risk factors and comorbidity indices. Emerging evidence also supports a bidirectional relationship between frailty and RA disease activity, suggesting that some aspects of frailty may be modifiable through improved disease control. Frailty-specific interventions have not yet been studied in RA, however, RA disease control, medication optimization and promotion of physical activity are likely to improve frailty in this high-risk population. Frailty is an important predictor of poor health outcomes in RA and may be amenable to interventions. Incorporation of frailty assessment into clinical care and clinical trials will be essential to move the field forward.

title: Multidisciplinary perspectives on geriatric mental health service delivery: a mixed-method survey study in a large integrated healthcare system.
abstract: To guide training development efforts within the context of the geriatric mental health (MH) workforce shortage, we examined provider perspectives on serving older adults in the Veterans Health Administration (VA), the largest integrated health care system in the U.S. For this mixed-method observational study, 489 multidisciplinary VA MH clinicians across five sites responded to an e-mail invitation to complete a survey assessing confidence in serving older adults with and without cognitive disorders, perceived barriers to providing services, and importance of training in geriatric MH. Text comments from a subset of participants (N = 59) were analyzed using thematic consensual qualitative analysis. Quantitative results indicate that most respondents (n = 418, 92.3%) endorsed the importance of having skills for serving older adults but reported modest self-efficacy, especially for delivering treatments and for serving patients with cognitive disorders. Barriers related to clinic systems were most frequently endorsed. Perceived need for training was high, with few differences by provider or setting characteristics. Qualitative data integration provided convergent evidence for the main findings. Our study contributes to the growing literature on providing MH services for older adults, including those with dementia, and can inform efforts to address the geriatric workforce shortage.
