title: Transradial Coronary Angiography and Intervention: Current Concepts and Future Directions.
abstract: Transradial access has become the preferred approach for percutaneous coronary angiography and intervention, largely because this technique reduces vascular complications, bleeding, costs, and patient discomfort compared with transfemoral access. However, anatomical variation, access site difficulties, procedural complications, and other factors can limit success. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the anatomic basis of transradial access, including radial artery anatomy, patient and access site selection, procedural considerations, complications, and emerging applications. This review also highlights key clinical trial data supporting the benefits of transradial access and discusses future directions in technique and technology. Our goal is to provide a practical, comprehensive resource for successful use of this approach.

title: VPS13A Disease (Chorea-Acanthocytosis) in Puerto Rico; New Genetic and Clinical Observations.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: VPS13A disease is a very rare neurodegenerative disorder caused by mutations in the VPS13A gene. Its prevalence appears to be relatively high in Puerto Ricans, although limited genetic information has been available.
OBJECTIVES: To describe the genetics of VPS13A disease (chorea-acanthocytosis) in Puerto Rico.
METHODS: Data were obtained from Puerto Rican patients with genetically confirmed VPS13A disease.
RESULTS: Eighteen cases were identified, all carrying at least one of four mutations, c.1400_1401del, c.3556_3557dup, c.3889C>T, and c.2825-253_2905-374del (exon_27-deletion); six additional single variants were detected. Seizures were the presenting symptom in 53% of patients.
CONCLUSION: The presence of these probable founder mutations could explain the apparently increased prevalence in Puerto Rico; half of the described variants are newly described mutations and half have been previously reported. Enhanced clinical awareness of the spectrum of presenting symptoms and diagnostic clues, and improved access to genetic testing are essential for timely diagnosis in this population.

title: Ultrasound-Guided Treatment of Peripheral Entrapment Mononeuropathies.
abstract: High-resolution neuromuscular ultrasound (US) is a valuable tool for the localization, diagnosis, and provision of conservative treatment to peripheral entrapment mononeuropathies. US-guided interventions require careful coordination of transducer and needle movement along with a detailed understanding of sonoanatomy. Preprocedural planning and positioning are instrumental in performing these interventions and should not be overlooked. Minimally invasive procedures, such as corticosteroid injections, aspiration of ganglia, orthobiologics, and hydrodissection, are useful options for the nonsurgical treatment of mononeuropathies refractory to conservative care. US is effective in determining atypical anatomy such as a bifid median nerve for improved accuracy and safety during injections, and precision based techniques such as hydrodissection may aid in physically separating the nerve from scar tissue and adhesions. The most well researched US guided treatment of entrapment neuropathy is carpal tunnel syndrome which demonstrates promising results from platelet-rich plasma, prolotherapy, hydrodissection, and percutaneous needle release. However, there is significant heterogeneity in procedure technique, injectate composition, injectate volume, and periprocedural conservative care that limits interpretation of the results and warrants continued head-to-head comparisons for research. This review highlights procedural details and outcomes for US-guided interventions of the most well-studied peripheral entrapment neuropathies. Despite many promising findings for these techniques, long-term outcomes and severe nerve compression may still benefit most from surgical decompression.

title: Incidence and Risk Factors for C. difficile Reinfection After Faecal Microbiota Transplantation or Antibiotic Therapy
abstract: BACKGROUND: Faecal microbiota transplant (FMT) is an effective treatment for multiply recurrent C. difficile infection (mrCDI). Less is known about rates of reinfection after successful FMT. We aimed to estimate the incidence of CDI reinfection, 6 or more months after FMT, to determine whether rates differ between mrCDI treated with and without FMT and whether proton pump inhibitor (PPI) therapy increases the risk of reinfection. METHODS: Among patients with mrCDI (defined as ≥ 2 recurrences after the initial CDI episode) we compared reinfection with CDI (defined as a first recurrence > 183 days after treatment completion) in patients who underwent antibiotics followed by FMT with those treated with antibiotics alone in Optum's de-identified Clinformatics Data Mart Database (OPTUM CDM). We also compared reinfection between those with and without PPI use in OPTUM CDM and the American Gastroenterological Association FMT Registry. RESULTS: In OPTUM CDM, 6384 patients treated with antibiotics alone and 1786 with antibiotics + FMT met inclusion criteria (median follow-up 704 days). One-year and 3-year CDI reinfection incidences were 5% and 10% in the FMT group and 6% and 12% in the antibiotics group: Cox regression HR 0.89, 95% CI 0.73-1.08. PPI use was associated with an increased risk of reinfection following FMT (HR 1.57, 1.03-2.41) in OPTUM CDM and in the FMT Registry (HR 1.62, 95% CI 0.84-3.12). CONCLUSIONS: CDI reinfection rates are low after successful FMT and similar to rates in patients treated with antibiotics alone. PPI use was associated with reinfection, supporting reassessment of the ongoing indication for PPI therapy in patients with mrCDI.

title: Cutaneous phaeohyphomycosis with the recently described fungus Gloniopsis leucaenae: first case report
abstract: Abstract Background Fungi of genus Gloniopsis are plant pathogens within class Dothideomycetes, rarely described to cause human infection. Species Gloniopsis leucaenae ( G. leucaenae ) was first isolated in 2019 and previously reported only in plant matter in Thailand. Case presentation A 68-year-old male landscaper on vedolizumab for Crohn’s disease, living in Florida with no travel history, presented with a swelling on dorsal aspect of hand. Pathology from excisional biopsy showed a subcutaneous phaeohyphomycosis nucleated by plant matter, and broad-range PCR identified G. leucaenae. After excision without antifungal treatment, a second lesion arose and was excised, with hyphae again demonstrated on histology, but culture and PCR negative. Treatment was started with empiric itraconazole. Conclusions This case report, in contradistinction to a prior case report of a related Gloniopsis species that caused disseminated disease in an immunocompromised host, demonstrates the capacity of G. leucaenae to cause local infection in relatively immunocompetent individuals. It also highlights that a pathogen described on one continent may cause an infection on another continent, even without identifiable travel. Global trade networks and climate change require broadening of the differential diagnosis for fungal infections.

title: Team-level heart rate variability dispersion across surgical stages of coronary artery bypass grafting procedures
abstract: The operating room is a safety-critical environment where effective teamwork is essential to patient safety. In the cardiac operating room, heart rate variability (HRV) offers a noninvasive window into psychophysiological activity of providers that may provide insight into team-level physiological responses in this safety-critical context. In this exploratory study, team-level HRV dispersion of surgical teams during coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) procedures was assessed using HRV metrics from the time-domain, frequency-domain, and nonlinear domain. Data from 15 CABG procedures and surgical teams were used to derive team-level HRV dispersion values for each surgical team and procedure stage, then analyzed using repeated-measures ANOVA to determine whether HRV dispersion varied significantly across stages. CABG procedures were analyzed using the original 14-stage segmentation and a condensed 8-stage segmentation for sensitivity analysis. The original segmentation served as the primary framework, with the condensed segmentation as a sensitivity analysis. Time-domain (SDNN) and log-transformed frequency-domain (HF) dispersion differed significantly across CABG stages under both segmentation schemes, whereas nonlinear domain (SampEn) dispersion did not show statistically significant stage effects. Holm-adjusted post hoc pairwise comparisons for SDNN did not identify significant differences between stages. In contrast, HF dispersion was significantly higher during closure than during selected earlier stages under both segmentations of the CABG procedures. These findings indicate stage-related variation in team-level SDNN and HF dispersion during CABG and support further investigation of HRV dispersion as a physiological measure in surgical team research.

title: Hereditary α-tryptasemia is associated with response to omalizumab in severe allergic asthma.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Higher basal serum tryptase (BST) levels have been associated with increased asthma severity that correlated with active tryptase allele number and was linked to poor clinical responses to anti-IgE treatment (omalizumab). However, the commonest cause of elevated BST is hereditary α-tryptasemia (HαT) caused by increased α-tryptase-encoding Tryptase alpha/beta 1 (TPSAB1) copy number, and its relationship to omalizumab response in asthma remains unclear.
OBJECTIVE: Our aim was to assess the relative contribution of tryptase genotype and HαT to the clinical efficacy of omalizumab treatment in patients with severe allergic asthma.
METHODS: A cohort (N=181) of severe allergic asthma patients treated with omalizumab from 2 tertiary referral centres in Slovenia and the UK underwent tryptase genotyping, and clinical features were subsequently compared between groups with and without HαT.
RESULTS: Limited benefit from omalizumab therapy was demonstrated in 22.7% of patients. Overall, HαT was identified in 8.3% of patients with severe allergic asthma treated with omalizumab. HαT was found in 20% of individuals with poor clinical responses to omalizumab, compared to 5% of those with positive responses (OR = 4.6 [95% CI 1.5-12.3]; P = .0068). In multivariable analysis, adjusted for study site and other covariates, HαT remained independently associated with poor response to omalizumab (OR = 4.56; [95% CI, 1.24-16.74]; P = .022). Among patients with HαT, 4 of 15 had BST below 8 ng/mL.
CONCLUSION: HαT is associated with poorer clinical response to anti-IgE treatment in patients with severe allergic asthma.

title: Matrix Metalloproteinase-8 Deficiency Alters the Balance Between Viral Clearance and Immunopathology in H1N1 Infection.
abstract: Matrix metalloproteinase-8 (MMP-8) regulates inflammatory responses, but its contributions to the pathogenesis of influenza A viral (IAV) disease are not known. Plasma MMP-8 levels were increased 30-fold in subjects infected with H1N1 or seasonal IAV and were inversely associated with the PaO2/FiO2 ratio, suggesting potential value as a candidate marker of lung injury severity that requires validation in larger cohorts. MMP-8 levels were elevated in the lungs of H1N1-infected wild-type (WT) mice and localized to airway epithelial cells, macrophages, and polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs). H1N1-infected Mmp-8-/- mice exhibited lower mortality and reduced lung viral burdens, but developed more severe lung injury than WT mice. Gene expression profiling revealed enhanced necroptosis and an exaggerated immune response in the lungs of infected Mmp-8-/- mice. Infected Mmp-8-/- mice had increased airway epithelial necroptosis with higher pulmonary levels of Type I interferons (IFNs), and increased frequencies of Class II MHC molecule-expressing macrophages and CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, and higher levels of some Th1 cytokines. In vitro, MMP-8 cleaved IL-1β and IL-6, but not Type I IFNs. These findings suggest that Mmp-8 deficiency is associated with restricted influenza virus spread and increased lung injury, accompanied by enhanced Type I IFN-associated necroptotic signaling and augmented antiviral immune responses. The latter may partly involve loss of MMP-8-mediated processing of pro-inflammatory mediators. MMP-8 may represent a host-response target in severe influenza infection, although therapeutic strategies targeting MMP-8 will need to balance enhanced viral clearance against the risk of increased lung immunopathology.

title: Delineating a Spectrum of Physician Participation in Medical Aid in Dying: A Qualitative Exploration.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Physician participation in medical aid in dying (MAID) is commonly framed as a binary choice between participation and objection. Emerging evidence suggests physician involvement is nuanced, with levels of engagement shaped by ethical beliefs, professional responsibilities, and organizational structure. Improved understanding of how physicians make these decisions is needed to inform policy, clinical practice, and discussions about conscience-based practices.
METHODS: We conducted a qualitative descriptive study of 20 physicians practicing in US states where MAID is legal. We used purposive sampling to recruit typical cases, seeking maximum variation across geographic region, practice specialty, and MAID involvement. Participants completed virtual, semi-structured, in-depth interviews between April and August 2025. Interviews were analyzed using rapid qualitative analysis. Coding was adductive with deductive codes derived from extant literature, focusing on physicians' experiences with MAID, ethical orientations, and interpretations of bioethical principles.
RESULTS: Analysis identified a spectrum of physician participation classified across four broad categories: (1) discusses MAID only; (2) refers patients to MAID providers, because of ethical opposition or organizational constraints; (3) serves as a consulting provider only; and (4) serves as an attending provider. Although participants referenced the same core bioethical principles, variations in participation reflect differing interpretations of shared ethical principles and the influence of organizational and legal environments.
CONCLUSIONS: Findings challenge the prevailing dichotomous view of MAID participation and demonstrate that physician engagement exists along a spectrum. Recognizing this spectrum may improve policy development, support clinician decision-making, and foster more nuanced discussions regarding conscience, ethics, and access to MAID.

title: Frailty Status and Medication Use Among U.S. Older Adults: Evidence From NHANES, 1999-2020.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Frailty and polypharmacy commonly coexist among older adults, yet population-level evidence on how the extent and therapeutic composition of medication use evolve across frailty stages remains limited.
METHODS: We analyzed nationally representative data from the U.S. National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey spanning 1999 through March 2020. Of 14,962 community-dwelling adults aged ≥ 65 years, 12,766 had sufficient data to construct a frailty index (FI). Frailty was categorized as robust (FI < 0.25), mildly frail (FI 0.25-0.34), or moderate to severely frail (FI ≥ 0.35). Outcomes included the mean number of prescription medications overall and by therapeutic class. Temporal trends were evaluated across frailty groups accounting for the complex survey design.
RESULTS: Medication use increased across all frailty groups from 1999-2000 to 2017-2020. The mean number of medications increased from 2.0 to 2.9 among robust individuals (p for trend < 0.001), from 3.9 to 5.5 among mildly frail individuals (p < 0.001), and from 6.0 to 7.8 among those with moderate to severe frailty (p = 0.001). Although cardiovascular agents consistently constituted the largest share of polypharmacy, their use remained stable. In contrast, metabolic and CNS/psychotherapeutic agents drove longitudinal increases in medication burden, with metabolic agents increasing across all frailty strata and CNS/psychotherapeutic agents increasing primarily among adults with moderate to severe frailty (p < 0.001). In 2017-2020, hyperpolypharmacy (≥ 10 medications) composition varied markedly by frailty status. Robust older adults predominantly used CNS/psychotherapeutic and topical agents, whereas frail adults primarily used cardiovascular and metabolic agents.
CONCLUSION: Medication use among U.S. older adults increased substantially over two decades, with both the magnitude and composition of medication use pattern varying systematically by frailty status. These findings characterize the population-level landscape of frailty-stratified medication burden and provide clinical context for further research and efforts aimed at optimizing medication use across the frailty spectrum in older adults.

title: Yoga effect on quality of life study among patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (YES-IPF).
abstract:
RATIONALE: Patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) have poor health-related quality of life.
OBJECTIVE: To explore the feasibility and potential impact of a modified yoga program on health-related quality of life in patients with IPF compared with usual care.
METHODS: We conducted a randomized, controlled, nonblinded, 12-week pilot clinical trial with two arms involving 63 adults with IPF diagnosed according to the 2018 ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT clinical practice guideline. The yoga arm attended 1-h virtual group sessions twice weekly for 12 weeks, consisting of seated postures, breathing exercises, and meditation designed for patients with IPF, while the control arm continued usual care.
MEASUREMENTS: Health-related quality of life was assessed using seven patient-reported outcome measures and their associated domains.
RESULTS: Sixty of 63 randomized participants completed the week-12 assessment and comprised the analysis cohort; their mean age was 73.4 years (SD, 8.2). Statistically significant improvements favoring yoga were seen in the Living with Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (L-IPF) cough domain (-9.29 points, 95% CI -18.37 to -0.20; p = 0.045; SMD = -0.36), the L-IPF total score (-7.11, 95% CI -13.15 to -1.06; p = 0.022; SMD = -0.38), and the R-scale-PF cough domain (-1.18, 95% CI -2.27 to -0.10; p = 0.034; SMD = -0.45).
CONCLUSION: In this exploratory pilot trial, a modified yoga program was feasible and well tolerated and was associated with improvements in selected patient-reported outcome domains. These findings are hypothesis-generating and warrant evaluation in a larger, adequately powered trial.

title: Effects of chronic alcohol consumption on gene expression in the rat left ventricle: a transcriptomic analysis
abstract: Objective Chronic alcohol consumption is one of the leading causes of dilated cardiomyopathy. Alcohol-associated cardiomyopathy (ACM) is characterized by impaired cardiac function and ventricular dilation in individuals with a history of long-term alcohol consumption. Alcohol exerts adverse effects on the myocardium via mitochondrial dysfunction and chronic inflammation. However, the broader transcriptional changes associated with chronic alcohol exposure remain poorly understood. Methods A chronic ethanol feeding model was utilized, in which male Wistar rats were fed a Lieber-Decarli ethanol diet containing 6.7% (v/v) ethanol (ET) or an isocaloric control (CONT) diet for 6 weeks. Left ventricular tissues were collected from ET-fed and CONT-fed rats. Differential gene expression was assessed using bulk RNA sequencing, followed by Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA). Results Transcriptomic analysis identified 194 upregulated and 199 downregulated genes in the left ventricles of ET-fed rats compared with CONT-fed rats. IPA revealed downregulated pathways related to the circadian clock and interferon signaling in the myocardium of ET-fed rats. In particular, the differentially altered genes included regulators of the circadian clock ( Bmal1, Npas2, Per1 , Per2 ) and interferon signaling ( Ifit2 , Ifit3 , Irf6 , Irf9 ). In contrast, pathways associated with mitochondrial RNA degradation, sheddase signaling, and neutrophil extracellular traps were upregulated in the myocardium following chronic ethanol exposure. Conclusion Chronic ethanol exposure is associated with dysregulation of circadian rhythm and immune-related signaling pathways in the rat myocardium. These findings highlight molecular pathways that may contribute to the development of ACM and warrant further mechanistic investigation.

title: When Imaging is Negative: Endoscopic Diagnosis of a Secondary Aortoduodenal Fistula.
abstract: Aortoenteric fistula is a life-threatening aortic graft complication with a narrow opportunity for treatment. We present a patient with aortobifemoral bypass who developed recurrent anemia and melena. Despite previous upper endoscopy and colonoscopy, computed tomography angiogram, and tagged red blood cell scan, his symptoms were persistent. Capsule endoscopy showed blood in the duodenum. Push enteroscopy revealed graft erosion in the duodenum, confirming aortoduodenal fistula. He underwent aortobifemoral graft excision, and resection of the third portion of the duodenum with end-to-side duodenojejunostomy, highlighting the importance of endoscopy in timely diagnosis of aortoenteric fistulae.

title: Association of Gallstone Disease and Cholecystectomy With Duodenal Polyps and Barrett's Oesophagus.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIM: We hypothesized that duodenal polyps (DP) and Barrett's oesophagus (BE) coincide in the same patients and that biliary disease, such as cholelithiasis (GS) or cholecystectomy (CCx), increases the risk for both DP and BE. We used a case-control study design to test our hypothesis.
METHODS: Using the healthcare records of the University of Pennsylvania Health System (UPHS), we compared the frequency of GS or CCx in patients with DP or BE with their corresponding frequencies in a control population of patients without DP or BE. Odds ratios (OR) and their 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) were calculated using multivariate logistic regression analysis.
RESULTS: The UPHS electronic database from 1/2016 until 3/2026 contained a total of 175,808 unique patients with EGD or colonoscopy, of whom 3632 underwent a CCx, 11,122 had GS, 669 had DP and 4965 had BE. The OR (95% CI) values for the association between BE and DP were 4.64 (3.63-5.86). The OR values for the GS association with DP were 2.23 (1.78-2.76) and for the CCx association with DP 2.26 (1.54-3.20). The OR values for the association between GS and BE were 1.46 (1.32-1.60) and for the CCx association with BE 1.57 (1.33-1.84).
CONCLUSIONS: Cholelithiasis and cholecystectomy are associated with an increased risk for duodenal polyps and Barrett's oesophagus. In support of this finding, duodenal polyps and Barrett's oesophagus are also found to coincide in the same patients.

title: Excitation-Inhibition Balance and Fronto-Limbic Connectivity Distinguish TMS Treatment Outcomes in Refractory Depression.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS) targeting the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) is effective for treatment-resistant depression, but outcomes remain variable. The neurophysiological mechanisms underlying response remain poorly understood, limiting precision neuromodulation.
METHODS: We combined transcranial magnetic stimulation with electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) and connectome-based Jansen-Rit neural mass modeling to investigate the mechanistic basis of treatment efficacy in 90 patients with treatment-resistant depression. Individualized whole-brain models were fitted to pre- and post-iTBS TMS-evoked potentials, yielding subject-specific estimates of synaptic connectivity, excitation-inhibition (E/I) balance, and cortical dynamics. Brain states were defined by singular value decomposition of the model's population activity, and partial least squares analysis with nested cross-validation identified the brain-state pattern distinguishing responders from non-responders.
RESULTS: We identified two neurophysiological signatures associated with treatment response. First, responders showed greater post-treatment reductions in 3-10 Hz oscillatory power, driven by shifts in E/I balance toward greater inhibitory control through reduced excitatory drive and increased inhibitory-to-pyramidal connectivity. Second, a pre-treatment brain state characterized by opposite-polarity dynamics between subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) and left DLPFC distinguished responders from non-responders, consistent with prior fMRI findings on frontolimbic anticorrelation. Neural trajectory analysis further revealed greater dynamical reorganization and increased attractor stability in responders following treatment.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings provide a neurophysiologically-informed framework linking iTBS treatment efficacy to specific changes in cortical E/I balance and frontolimbic circuit dynamics, pointing toward candidate markers that, with subject-specific structural connectivity and independent validation, may inform personalized neuromodulation approaches in treatment-resistant depression.

title: Multicenter, retrospective study of balloon valvuloplasty-associated pulmonary artery dissection in dogs with pulmonary valve stenosis
abstract: INTRODUCTION/OBJECTIVES: Pulmonary artery dissection (PAD) is a rare complication in dogs with pulmonary valve stenosis (PS) that undergo balloon valvuloplasty (BVP). This study aimed to describe demographic, interventional, and survival data in a cohort of dogs with PS that experienced PAD during BVP. ANIMALS, MATERIALS AND METHODS: Fifty-three dogs were included in this retrospective, multicenter study, with medical records and available stored images reviewed. RESULTS: Dogs that developed PAD during BVP had a median body weight of 12.5 kg (range: 1.1-50.7 kg), median age of 0.8 years (range: 0.2-8.1 years), and 30/53 (56.6%) were male. Pit Bull terriers, Pit Bull terrier mixes, and 'Bully breeds' represented 23 of 53 dogs in the study (43.4%). The median angiographic balloon diameter to pulmonary valve annulus ratio of the largest balloon utilized during BVP was 1.4 (range: 1.0-1.58). High-pressure balloons (>6 atm) were utilized in 27 dogs (50.9%). Post-BVP transthoracic echocardiographic imaging clearly demonstrated the PAD in 62.2% of dogs, while 90.3% and 84.0% of available post-BVP angiography and transesophageal echocardiographic studies did, respectively. Forty-eight dogs (90.6%) survived to discharge. Median time from BVP to last follow-up or death (if applicable) was 2.0 years (range: 0.2-10.5 years), with all 27 dogs for whom ≥1 year of follow-up data were available confirmed alive at that time. STUDY LIMITATIONS: Retrospective study design. CONCLUSIONS: Dogs experiencing PAD during BVP have a high likelihood of survival in the immediate and long-term periods. Immediate post-BVP imaging with angiography or transesophageal echocardiography appears more sensitive than transthoracic echocardiography for diagnosis of PAD.

title: Visual Target P3b Amplitude Mediates the Relationship between Childhood Traumatic Experiences and Social Functioning in People at Clinical High Risk for Psychosis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND HYPOTHESIS: Clinical high risk (CHR) for psychosis status is associated with poor social functioning. Previous studies suggest that childhood trauma and reduced amplitude of the P300 event-related potential (ERP) component elicited by infrequent target stimuli (P3b) are associated with poor social function. Here, we examined whether reduced P3b mediates the relationship between reported trauma history and social function in CHR individuals, possibly reflecting the impact of past trauma on neurophysiological processes subserving attention that ultimately influence social functioning.
STUDY DESIGN: Target P3b ERP amplitudes from visual and auditory oddball tasks acquired at baseline in the Accelerating Medicines Partnership Schizophrenia (AMP SCZ) study were analyzed. The mediating effects of auditory and visual P3b amplitude on the relationship between trauma history (Childhood Trauma Questionnaire total score) and Negative Symptom Inventory-Psychosis Risk Asociality (NSI-PR) as well as social functioning (Global Functioning: Social (GFS) scores were examined.
STUDY RESULTS: Data from 931 CHR participants (average age 21.29 years, 36.3% male) were included in mediation analyses. Visual P3b showed significant (P < .05) mediation of the relationship between trauma load and GFS score (5.4% mediation) as well as mediation of the relationship between trauma history and NSI-PR asociality (9.3% mediation). Auditory P3b did not significantly mediate either relationship.
CONCLUSIONS: These results suggest that visual, but not auditory, P3b mediates the relationship between past trauma load and social functioning in CHR, suggesting the effect of trauma on the neurophysiological processes subserving visual target detection may contribute to social functioning deficits in CHR individuals.

title: Shorter Relative Patellar Defect Length After Bone-Patellar Tendon-Bone Autograft Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Is associated With Better Postoperative Patient-Reported Outcomes at 1-Year Follow-Up.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate bone-patellar tendon-bone autograft anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction patellar defect dimensions over time and associate these with patient-reported outcomes.
METHODS: Patients undergoing bone-patellar tendon-bone autograft autograft anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction by 1 of 7 surgeons between June 2020 and June 2023 were recruited to obtain knee magnetic resonance imaging at 6 weeks and 1 year postoperatively and complete a knee injury and osteoarthritis outcome score (KOOS) survey at 1 year postoperatively. Patellar bony defect dimensions relative to the entire patellar dimensions were measured on magnetic resonance imaging and associated with KOOSs at 1 year.
RESULTS: For the 23 patients (15 men) with a mean ± standard deviation age 25.5 ± 5.2 analyzed, shorter relative patellar defect length at 6 weeks postoperatively was associated with better 1-year KOOS activities of daily living (R2 = 0.481, P = .002) and function in sports and recreation (R2 = 0.436, P = .002), and showed trends for associating with better pain (R2 = 0.196, P = .078) and knee-related quality of life (R2 = 0.222, P = .054). Participants with longer relative defects were more likely to report difficulty with kneeling (R2 = 0.278, P = .020). These associations were not altered by considering patient age or sex. The average relative patellar defect width and depth decreased from 6 weeks to 1 year (P < .001), whereas relative defect length was unchanged. Intraobserver reliability was good to excellent for all measurements at 6 weeks and 1 year. Relative defect width and depth, at both 6 weeks and 1 year, had no significant associations with KOOSs at 1 year.
CONCLUSIONS: Shorter relative patellar defect length after bone-patellar tendon-bone autograft autograft anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction is associated with better patient-reported outcome measures at 1 year, and thus, individual patient patellar size should be a consideration during graft harvest.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, retrospective case series.

title: A Narrative Review of Medicare Part D Medication Therapy Management Program Design Challenges and the Development of an Evidence-Informed MTM Benefit Program for a Large Self-Insured Employer
abstract: The Medicare Part D Medication Therapy Management (MTM) program has several well-documented challenges, including restrictive eligibility criteria, low patient engagement, and difficulties integrating MTM services into pharmacy workflows and broader healthcare teams. These challenges are often driven by inadequate health information technology infrastructure, limited coordination between pharmacists and prescribers, and inefficiencies in standardized documentation for Comprehensive Medication Reviews (CMRs). This narrative review synthesized published literature to identify challenges and limitations of the Medicare Part D MTM program and used Purdue University's MTM program design documentation to compare program features and describe the evidence and rationale underlying key design decisions. Purdue's MTM program incorporated broader patient eligibility, more frequent MTM services, and provider-developed communication templates to address limitations in patient access, program uptake, and workflow feasibility identified in the Medicare Part D program. However, challenges related to optimization of standardized CMR documentation and integration with electronic health records (EHRs) remained unresolved. Overall, this review demonstrates how evidence-informed program design may strengthen MTM implementation while identifying opportunities for future refinement. Future evaluation of the Purdue MTM program will assess its acceptability, feasibility, adoption, reach, and fidelity.

title: Cardiovascular magnetic resonance derived myocardial strain: applications, acquisition techniques, analysis, and reporting. A Scientific Statement of the Society for Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance, Radiological Society of North America, and the European Association of Cardiovascular Imaging of the ESC.
abstract: Myocardial strain imaging enables quantification of cardiac deformation. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) is well suited for strain assessment due to the ability to image in any given plane with high spatial and contrast resolution. CMR strain measures have incremental diagnostic and prognostic utility over conventional clinical imaging parameters across disease states. Routine integration of CMR strain assessment in clinical practice has been hindered by the lack of agreement on imaging protocols and analysis methods, variability due to noise sensitivity, and a paucity of robust normative age-, sex- and ethnicity-specific reference ranges. In recognition of the expanding applications of strain techniques in clinical and research CMR, this joint SCMR/RSNA/EACVI scientific statement integrates data from original research studies, guidelines, and opinions from experts across the field to guide responsible and evidence-based utilization of CMR strain.

title: Frozen shoulder and risk of incident Dupuytren’s disease: a propensity score–matched cohort study of 208,261 pairs
abstract: Frozen shoulder (FS) and Dupuytren’s disease (DD) are fibroproliferative conditions that share risk factors, genetic susceptibility, and biological pathways, including dysregulation of collagen deposition and WNT signalling. While co-occurrence has been described, the temporal relationship between FS and subsequent DD remains unclear. We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the Merative™ MarketScan ® Commercial Database (2007–2023). Adults aged 40–65 years with incident FS were identified and propensity score–matched 1:1 to individuals without FS on demographics, comorbidities, and healthcare utilization. The primary outcome was incident DD. Cox proportional hazards models with robust variance estimation were used to calculate hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Interaction analyses assessed effect modification by age and diabetes, and sensitivity analyses included landmark analyses and restricted follow-up duration. The matched cohort included 208,261 pairs. During follow-up, 1,896 DD events occurred in the FS group compared with 453 in controls. FS was associated with an increased risk of subsequent DD (HR 2.56 95% CI, 2.30–2.83). A significant age interaction was observed, with stronger associations in younger FS individuals (HR 3.29 for ages 40–49 vs. 1.84 for 60–65 years). No significant interaction with diabetes was found. Results remained consistent in both men and women and in sensitivity analyses restricted to ≥ 24 and ≥ 48 months of follow-up and landmark analyses at 6 and 12 months. FS is associated with an increased risk of subsequent DD. These findings support the concept that FS may represent an early manifestation of a systemic fibroproliferative diathesis, particularly in younger individuals, and may serve as a clinical marker of future fibrotic disease risk. title: One-stage versus 2-stage single-anastomosis duodeno-ileostomy with sleeve gastrectomy for body mass index 60-70: a safety analysis simulated using national registry data.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Two-stage SADI-S (sleeve gastrectomy followed by single-anastomosis duodeno-ileostomy after weight loss) is thought to reduce perioperative risks for patients with high body mass index (BMI), but the combined risk of 2 operations is not well-described.
METHODS: Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery Accreditation and Quality Improvement Program participant user files from 2020 to 2024 (the largest known database of SADI-S) were reviewed for patients who underwent SADI-S at BMI 60-70 kg/m2, sleeve gastrectomy at BMI 60-70, and conversion sleeve-to-SADI at BMI 42-49 (30% total weight loss from first procedure). Using inverse probability weighting to achieve covariate balance, 30-day complication rates were compared. Risks of two-stage SADI-S were simulated by combining the risks of sleeve gastrectomy and conversion sleeve-to-SADI based on a conditional probability model and product rule.
RESULTS: We identified 749 SADI-S at BMI 60-70, 22,503 sleeve gastrectomy at BMI 60-70, and 1071 sleeve-to-SADI conversions at BMI 42-49. SADI-S and sleeve gastrectomy patients were similar except for functional dependence (.4% versus 1.6%, P < .001). One-stage SADI-S was associated with a higher rate of ≥1 complications than sleeve gastrectomy (6.7% versus 4.5%, P < .01). Simulated two-stage SADI-S, compared to one-stage SADI-S, was associated with higher rates of ≥1 complications (11.5% versus 6.7% [5.1-8.8%]), readmission (7.3% versus 4.3% [3.0-6.0%]), 30-day reoperation (3.4% versus 1.3% [.7-2.4%]), and intervention (2.1% versus .8% [.37-1.9%]). Death, leaks, and bleeds were comparable.
CONCLUSION: In a large bariatric surgery registry, simulated two-stage SADI-S was associated with greater risks than one-stage SADI-S. The assumption that two-stage SADI-S is necessarily safer should be reconsidered.

title: Higher plasma kynurenine-tryptophan ratio predicts incident hepatic fibrosis in women with HIV.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Chronic immune activation and microbial translocation may contribute to hepatic fibrosis in people with HIV. We evaluated whether plasma kynurenine-to-tryptophan (KT) ratio and other biomarkers of microbial translocation predict incident fibrosis in women with HIV.
DESIGN: Longitudinal cohort study of 709 women with HIV from the Women's Interagency HIV Study with baseline plasma biomarkers and serial vibration-controlled transient elastography. Participants with baseline fibrosis or viral hepatitis were excluded. Outcomes included incident fibrosis, steatotic liver disease (SLD)-associated fibrosis, non-SLD fibrosis, and advanced fibrosis.
METHODS: Poisson regression with robust standard errors clustered by participant was used to estimate incidence rate ratios (IRRs) for liver outcomes by log-transformed KT ratio, adjusted for demographic, metabolic, and HIV-related covariates. Models included an offset for follow-up time. Analyses were repeated for sCD163, sCD14, and I-FABP.
RESULTS: Over a mean follow-up of 42 months, 18.7% developed incident fibrosis, of whom 74% had SLD; 8.3% developed advanced fibrosis. In adjusted models, each log-unit increase in KT ratio was associated with incident fibrosis (IRR 1.46, 95% CI 1.21-1.76) and advanced fibrosis (IRR 1.59, 95% CI 1.27-1.99). KT ratio was associated with non-SLD fibrosis (IRR 1.59, 95% CI 1.31-1.94), but not SLD-associated fibrosis (IRR 1.16, 95% CI 0.94-1.42). Higher sCD163 was associated with all liver outcomes, whereas sCD14 and I-FABP were not.
CONCLUSIONS: Higher KT ratio independently predicted incident hepatic fibrosis in women with HIV, particularly non-SLD fibrosis, suggesting a steatosis-independent pathway involving microbial translocation and macrophage activation.

title: Neurometabolite abnormalities and associations with epilepsy duration and cognition in patients with idiopathic generalized epilepsies.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study investigated whether idiopathic generalized epilepsies (IGEs) are associated with neuroinflammation by measuring neurometabolite levels and brain temperature using whole-brain magnetic resonance spectroscopy imaging (MRSI). We compared patients with IGEs to healthy controls (HCs), and in IGEs examined relationships with seizure control, MRSI markers, epilepsy duration, and cognitive performance.
METHODS: Seventeen patients with IGEs and 15 HCs underwent 3T-MRI scans. IGEs were also administered the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and Flanker test. Whole-brain 1H-MRSI provided metabolite and water maps. Levels for myo-inositol (MI; glial marker), glutamate-glutamine complex (Glx), and N-acetylaspartate (NAA) were normalized to creatine (Cr) levels. Brain temperature was obtained by frequency difference between water and Cr. IGEs were stratified into seizure-free (IGE-) and treatment-resistant (IGE+) groups. Group analyses were performed using permutation-based threshold-free cluster enhancement (TFCE) within bilateral regions of interest: anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), posterior cingulate cortex (PCC), hippocampus, parietal cortex, and thalami.
RESULTS: Compared with HCs, IGEs showed higher MI/Cr in the parietal cortex, PCC, and thalamus; higher hippocampus Glx/Cr; and lower parietal cortex NAA/Cr. Brain temperature did not differ between groups. IGE- exhibited higher hippocampal NAA/Cr and better MoCA scores than IGE+. Longer epilepsy duration was associated with lower NAA/Cr in the ACC and PCC, and parietal cortex, as well as lower Glx/Cr in the ACC, PCC, parietal cortex, and hippocampus. Lower NAA/Cr in the ACC, PCC, hippocampus, and thalamus, together with higher thalamus MI/Cr, was associated with lower MoCA scores in IGEs. Lower NAA/Cr in the ACC, thalamus, and hippocampus was associated with poorer Flanker performance in IGEs.
SIGNIFICANCE: We provide novel evidence of neurometabolic abnormalities in IGEs. The associations between metabolite levels and clinical and cognitive variables suggest potential biomarkers for disease progression and treatment response. Furthermore, these results highlight the roles of abnormal glial activation, neuronal loss, and hyperexcitability in IGE pathophysiology.
PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: We compared patients with idiopathic generalized epilepsies (IGEs) to healthy controls (HCs) to investigate brain chemistry and temperature differences and their relationships to seizure control, epilepsy duration, and cognitive performance. We found group differences in brain N-acetylaspartate (NAA; neuronal marker), myo-inositol (MI; glial cell marker), and glutamate/glutamine (Glx; excitatory neurotransmission) levels, but not in brain temperature. Longer epilepsy duration was associated with brain chemistry levels. In IGEs, lower NAA levels and higher MI levels were associated with worse cognitive performance. This study highlights the roles of abnormal glial activation, neuronal loss, and hyperexcitability in epilepsy duration and cognition in IGEs.

title: Inclisiran: A Novel Agent in the Management of Hypercholesterolemia
abstract: PCSK9 is a serine protease that binds to the LDL receptors and targets the receptors for lysosomal degradation, thus reducing their recycling and decreasing the removal rate of circulating LDL-C. Monoclonal antibodies directed against PCSK9, such alirocumab and evolocumab, have been shown to cause a significant reduction in LDL-C levels and improve cardiovascular outcomes. On the other hand, inclisiran is a chemically synthesized siRNA molecule, which lowers LDL-C levels by targeting the hepatic production of PCSK9, as it prevents its translation via degradation of PCSK9 mRNA post-transcription. This review aims to discuss the current evidence regarding the role of inclisiran in the management of hypercholesterolemia.

title: Progressive Dysphagia Revealing Oculopharyngeal Muscular Dystrophy: A Diagnostic Challenge.
abstract: Oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy (OPMD) is a rare, late-onset myopathy often presenting with progressive dysphagia and delayed diagnosis. We report a 69-year-old woman with worsening dysphagia, ptosis, and proximal muscle weakness who underwent an unrevealing gastrointestinal evaluation, including upper endoscopy. Videofluoroscopic swallow evaluation (VFSE) demonstrated pharyngeal dysphagia. A strong family history prompted genetic testing, confirming a poly(A) binding protein nuclear 1 (PABPN1) trinucleotide repeat expansion consistent with autosomal dominant OPMD. This case highlights the importance of recognizing neuromuscular causes of dysphagia, particularly when structural evaluations are negative. Early identification can reduce diagnostic delay and allow appropriate supportive management, improving quality of life and reducing complications.

title: VoiceLove for patient-family communication in the ICU: a usability study of a novel voice messaging app.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Family engagement has been associated with improved outcomes following critical illness, but communication barriers challenge family engagement. Traditional video or phone call strategies to navigate communication barriers are time-, resource-, and labor-intensive for hospital staff, often limiting their use. VoiceLove is a Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA)-compliant mobile phone app that enables family members to send real-time voice messages to intensive care unit (ICU) patients without relying on the clinical team to coordinate calls. We conducted iterative usability testing of VoiceLove to optimize use for patients, families, and their clinical teams in the adult ICU.
METHODS: We completed 2 rounds of usability testing of the VoiceLove app in a simulated environment. Usability was assessed through System Usability Scale (SUS) scores and task success rates. Semi-structured interviews were used to identify themes, concerns, and design priorities.
RESULTS: Mean SUS scores for rounds 1 and 2 of testing were 77.5 (SD 11.1) and 75.9 (SD 26.8), respectively. The app concept was overall viewed favorably as a tool with the potential to provide comfort and streamline communication. Key usability issues included navigation, clarity of labels, and accessibility, which were addressed through iterative app improvements. Implementation concerns included nursing workload, family cognitive burden, and interplay with complex family dynamics.
CONCLUSION: A diverse group of ICU stakeholders found the VoiceLove app demonstratedpotential to improve communication with critically ill patients inherently disadvantaged in their ability to communicate. Further testing in a real-world setting is needed to assess the impact of VoiceLove implementation on clinical team work load and family dynamics.

title: Type 2 diabetes-associated gut microbial composition and short chain fatty acids differ across the epidemiologic transition in African origin populations.
abstract: The gut microbiota and microbially produced short chain fatty acids (SCFAs) are increasingly linked to type 2 diabetes (T2D), particularly in the context of dietary transitions from fiber-rich to more ultra-processed foods. Data in African origin populations are lacking. We examined the cross-sectional relationships between the gut microbiota, SCFAs, and T2D by performing amplicon sequencing and targeted metabolomics from fecal samples and measuring fasting glucose, insulin, and C-peptide in 1505 African origin middle-aged adults from Ghana, South Africa, Jamaica, Seychelles, and the US. Microbial diversity and SCFAs were highest among Ghanaian and lowest among US participants. T2D was associated with lower microbial diversity, but not when stratifying by site. Differential abundance analysis (adjusted for site, sex, BMI, and age) identified microbes associated with T2D: Romboutsia was negatively associated with T2D, while positively associated taxa included Escherichia-Shigella sp., Dielma fastidiosa, Klebsiella, and Bacteroides vulgatus. Several species that were differentially abundant by T2D showed strong correlations with SCFA concentrations, although the significance varied by site. Our results suggest that associations between the gut microbiota, SCFAs, and T2D may differ by environmental, dietary, and ecological contexts. Amid the shifting global dietary patterns, further research is needed to inform gut microbiota-targeted approaches to address the global T2D burden.

title: Tryptase Locus Variation Contributes to Normal-Range Basal Serum Tryptase Variability and Is Associated With Anaphylaxis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Increased basal serum tryptase level (BST) is associated with anaphylaxis. In the absence of clonal mast cell disease and hereditary α-tryptasemia (HαT), the contribution of the tryptase locus variation to BST and anaphylaxis remains undefined.
OBJECTIVE: To determine the impact of tryptase locus variation on BST and anaphylaxis.
METHODS: Individuals with systemic Hymenoptera venom allergic reactions, large local reactions and asymptomatic sensitization underwent a novel ddPCR-based tryptase genotyping to quantify active tryptase alleles. Individuals positive for KIT p.D816V or HαT were excluded.
RESULTS: The cohort consisted of 295 individuals with systemic reactions, 140 with large local reactions, and 29 asymptomatically sensitized individuals. Active tryptase allele number, excluding the inactive βIIIFS allele, correlated with BST levels (r = 0.34, p < 0.0001); all BST values were within the normal range. Patients with systemic reactions had higher BST compared with those with large local reactions and asymptomatic sensitization (median, 4.5 ng/mL vs. 3.5 ng/mL; p < 0.0001). Individuals carrying four active β-tryptase alleles were less likely to experience anaphylaxis than those carrying two or three active β-tryptase alleles (26.7% vs. 42.3%; p = 0.024). A trend towards more severe reactions was observed in individuals carrying α-tryptase allele together with a higher number of active β-tryptase alleles.
CONCLUSION: Variation at the tryptase locus explains differences in BST levels within the normal range. Four active β-tryptase alleles were associated with a lower frequency of anaphylaxis.

title: Back Pain and Prospective Frailty Status Among Older Men: Findings From the MrOS Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The association between back pain and frailty is uncertain. This study examined the association between back pain in older men and prospective frailty status an average of 7 years later.
METHODS: Prospective cohort study using data from the Osteoporotic Fractures in Men Study. Eligible participants were men who, at study Visit 3 (Year 7), completed a back pain assessment (presence, frequency, severity, activity limitation) and a phenotypic frailty assessment (robust, pre-frail, frail). Among men classified as either robust or pre-frail, phenotypic frailty was again assessed at Visit 4 (Year 14), with deaths between Visits 3 and 4 considered a separate terminal outcome category. The association of Visit 3 back pain with frailty phenotype relative to a robust (and pre-frail) status at Visit 4 was analyzed using multivariable-adjusted multinominal logistic regression models.
RESULTS: Among 5994 men enrolled, 2554 men who were considered robust or pre-frail at Visit 3 (mean [SD] age = 71.6 [4.9] years) were included in the current analysis. After accounting for age, study clinic site, race and education, presence of any back pain, moderate-severe severity, high frequency, and activity limiting back pain were prospectively associated with higher odds of being frail vs. robust and of being frail vs. pre-frail an average of 7 years later. However, after adjustment for other characteristics including prefrail vs. robust status at Visit 3, only the activity-limiting back pain phenotype was associated with significantly higher odds of later being classified as frail vs. prefrail (OR = 1.40 [1.03-1.90]), and no back pain phenotypes were associated with higher odds of later being classified as frail vs. robust.
CONCLUSION: Among older community-dwelling men, back pain, particularly activity-limiting back pain, was associated with higher odds of progression to frailty during a 7-year period, suggesting that back pain may be a modifiable risk factor for age-related phenotypic frailty. Further replication and understanding of the mechanisms underpinning the relationship between back pain and frailty are needed to inform targeted interventions in older individuals at risk of frailty.

title: Temporal regulation of activin, follistatin, and growth differentiation factor 15 in the liver and circulation during high-fat diet-induced fatty liver disease.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) develops over time, yet most hepatokine studies are cross-sectional. We investigated the temporal regulation of the activin-follistatin axis and growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15) in high-fat diet (HFD)-induced fatty liver disease. Mice were fed an HFD or normal chow for 8, 20, or 30 weeks. Plasma, hepatic mRNA, and hepatic protein were measured by ELISA, real-time PCR, and immunoblotting. HFD increased body and liver weights and hepatic triglyceride content throughout. A central finding was discordance between compartments: hepatic Inhba mRNA was elevated at 8 and 30 weeks, yet plasma and hepatic activin A protein both peaked at 20 weeks, indicating post-transcriptional regulation; hepatic follistatin protein decreased at 20 and 30 weeks despite an early rise in Fst mRNA, while circulating follistatin and follistatin-like 3 (FSTL3) were unchanged. The activin receptors ACVR2B and ACVR1 showed distinct protein kinetics, with sustained ACVR2B elevation and a transient ACVR1 peak at 20 weeks, potentially favoring canonical activin signaling. Together these changes shifted the balance toward activin, increasing plasma activin A-to-follistatin and activin A-to-FSTL3 ratios at 20 weeks and the phospho/total-SMAD2/3 ratio at 20 and 30 weeks. Hepatic Gdf15 mRNA was induced throughout, whereas plasma GDF15 (measured at 8 and 20 weeks) was increased at both and correlated positively with plasma activin A. These findings reveal time-dependent, level-discordant regulation of the activin-follistatin axis and GDF15 in HFD-induced fatty liver, providing a temporal reference unavailable from cross-sectional studies.

title: The long and winding road to diagnosis: diagnostic delays and healthcare utilization in patients with CFT-confirmed INOCA
abstract: Background: Patients with Ischemia and No Obstructive Coronary Arteries (INOCA) experience recurrent angina, report reduced quality of life, and are at increased risk for major adverse cardiovascular events. Unfortunately, INOCA is often unrecognized and can be difficult to diagnose. Methods: We included patients with angina and INOCA diagnosed by invasive coronary function testing (CFT) and characterized their interactions with the healthcare system. Data on initial symptom onset, frequency and type of healthcare encounters, specialty referrals, diagnostic testing (including non-invasive and invasive cardiac testing, pulmonary, GI, and musculoskeletal evaluation), and medication trials for angina were abstracted from the electronic medical record. Results: We included 91 patients with INOCA who underwent CFT for determination of endotype (36% with coronary microvascular dysfunction, 35% with vasomotor disorders, 29% mixed endotype). The median time from first anginal symptom to diagnosis was 3.2 years (IQR 0.8-7.3 years), with 450 presentations to the healthcare system for angina prior to CFT. Among healthcare presentations, 72% occurred in an outpatient setting and 28% occurred in the emergency department. Each patient had a median of 3 clinic visits and 1 ED visit. A total of 225 referrals to 6 different specialties occurred, with 18% of patients seen by ≥3 cardiologists prior to diagnosis. There were 441 diagnostic tests performed for angina [median 4 (IQR 3-7) per patient], 14% of which were non-cardiac studies [median 0 (IQR 0-1) per patient]. Patients trialed a median of 2 (1-3) medications prior to diagnosis. Conclusion: Many patients with INOCA experience prolonged diagnostic journeys, marked by repeated healthcare encounters, multiple specialists' visits, high testing burden, and multiple trials of medication. These findings underscore the need for earlier consideration of INOCA in the assessment of angina and more efficient diagnostic strategies.

title: External Validation and Transportability of the Equitable Donor Assessment Model in a National UK Kidney Transplant Cohort
abstract: Accurate assessment of deceased donor kidney quality is fundamental to organ allocation and clinical decision-making. The recently developed Equitable Donor Assessment Model (EDAM) is a donor-only competing-risk prediction model that estimates graft failure while accounting for the competing risk of death with a functioning graft, thereby distinguishing graft-specific failure from patient mortality [1]. In the original US modelling study, EDAM demonstrated improved discrimination compared with the Kidney Donor Profile Index (KDPI) and substantial reclassification of donor risk, supporting further evaluation of the model beyond its derivation population [1].

title: Overcoming inertia in anticoagulant reversal: the current evidence gap and need for critical assessment of factor replacement strategies.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) include the factor Xa inhibitors (FXaI) apixaban and rivaroxaban and were approved in the United States and European Union in approximately 2010. Three- and four-factor prothrombin complex concentrates (3F-PCC and 4F-PCC) have been available in the US and EU since 1986 and 2005 for repletion of factors in patients anticoagulated with vitamin K antagonists. Despite their long-standing availability, no large, well-designed prospective clinical trials have been conducted to assess efficacy and safety of PCCs in bleeding patients anticoagulated with DOACs. Although off-label use of PCCs for bleed management of DOAC patients began before the availability of the specific reversal agents idarucizumab and andexanet, utilization increased substantially after antidote approval despite a paucity of evidence. The ANNEXA-I trial compared andexanet with usual care and was terminated early due to superior hemostatic efficacy of andexanet. Heterogeneous interpretation of results underscores significant methodological challenges to performing definitive anticoagulant reversal studies in complex populations at high-risk for mortality.
METHODS: Authors identified publications through prior guidance statements, guidelines, review articles, PubMed, and ClinicalTrials.gov. We provide a narrative review of the history of PCCs, other clotting factor concentrates, and the target-specific reversal agent, andexanet for FXaI-related bleeding, in the context of warnings issued by the 2021 Congressional Research Service Report on Off-Label Use. We discuss limitations in regulatory and post-marketing mechanisms for evaluating widespread off-label use. We present a framework to interpret limitations of available real-world evidence on off-label use of 4F-PCC for FXaI-related bleeding, along with clinical practice guideline recommendations.
CONCLUSION: While target-specific reversal strategies are supported by generally higher quality evidence than non-specific agents, concerns remain about thrombotic complications, functional outcomes, cost-effectiveness, and implementation. Future well-designed, adequately powered, randomized studies should address these concerns to aid decision-making across varied patient bleeding profiles.

title: Direct cortical stimulation induces short-term modulation of neural oscillations in humans.
abstract: Patterned brain stimulation is commonly employed to modulate brain circuits and treat neuropsychiatric disorders. Although it is widely used in clinical settings, there remains limited understanding of how stimulation alters neural oscillations and how these effects relate to baseline evoked network responses. To address this question, we applied 15 min of 10-Hz focal electrical stimulation delivered as 5-s trains separated by 10-s rest intervals, a pattern resembling "excitatory" transcranial magnetic stimulation, to 14 patients with epilepsy undergoing intracranial electroencephalography in premotor, parietal, and temporal cortical sites. We quantified spectral features of cortico-cortical evoked potentials (CCEPs) before and after stimulation. We hypothesized that the temporal and spectral components of the CCEP predicted the location and degree of stimulation-induced modulation. Across patients, low-frequency power (alpha, beta) showed the broadest change, whereas the magnitude of change was stronger in high frequencies (beta, gamma). Next, we demonstrated that regions with stronger prestimulation evoked spectral responses were more likely to exhibit larger poststimulation spectral changes. These findings were specific to frequency in a temporal window. Poststimulation power changes were driven by interaction between direction of change in prestimulation power and temporal window. Finally, regions exhibiting early increases and late decreases in prestimulation power exhibited power changes after stimulation. These patterns were consistent across premotor, parietal, and temporal sites, but the magnitude and latency varied by stimulation location. Together, these findings demonstrate that time-frequency prestimulation features predict poststimulation modulation of human neural oscillations and highlight temporally specific, state-dependent properties of stimulation responses in humans, thereby improving our understanding of stimulation-associated changes in human brain networks and helping inform more effective brain stimulation techniques.NEW & NOTEWORTHY Brain stimulation treats neuropsychiatric disorders, yet spectral changes remain poorly understood. We performed patterned stimulation in epilepsy patients, using intracranial recordings to study oscillatory plasticity. We found predictable changes: low frequencies were widespread, whereas high frequencies showed greater magnitude. These shifts were predicted by prestimulation activity. Our study reveals that baseline brain states determine spectral plasticity, providing insights to optimize stimulation techniques and understand human brain dynamics.

title: Inhibition of ROCK2 via KD025/Belumosudil Alleviates Hypertensive End-Organ Damage.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Despite achieving target blood pressure, hypertensive individuals have an elevated risk of cardiovascular disease, likely due to unresolved inflammation. Thus, adjunctive immune-modulating therapies are needed to protect patients with hypertension from end-organ damage. We previously showed that T helper 17 cells, which produce the proinflammatory cytokine IL (interleukin)-17A, contribute to hypertensive tissue injury. ROCK2 (Rho-associated coiled-coil-containing protein kinase 2) is a molecular switch governing T helper cell differentiation by promoting T helper 17 polarization and inhibiting T regulatory cell polarization. The present study tests whether T-cell-specific deletion of Rock2 or the Food and Drug Administration-approved ROCK2-specific inhibitor KD025/belumosudil protects against hypertension-associated end-organ damage.
METHODS: T-cell-specific Rock2 knockout mice (Rock2fl/flCD4Cre+) and Rock2fl/fl littermate controls were subjected to a 21-day deoxycorticosterone acetate-salt model of hypertension. In parallel, KD025/belumosudil treatment (50 mg/kg per day) starting after day 10 in wild-type mice was used to test the therapeutic potential of targeting ROCK2. Blood pressure, cardiac fibrosis, renal injury, and infiltration of immune cells were assessed.
RESULTS: T-cell-specific Rock2 deletion in mice attenuated the hypertensive response in the deoxycorticosterone acetate-salt model and protected from cardiac and aortic fibrosis. KD025/belumosudil treatment did not reduce blood pressure but did decrease proinflammatory T helper 17 polarization in vivo and increased the cardiac regulatory T cells/T helper 17 ratio. Despite no blood pressure change, KD025 reduced cardiac and aortic fibrosis, improved echocardiographic and invasive hemodynamic indices, and attenuated albuminuria and renal T-cell infiltration.
CONCLUSIONS: ROCK2 inhibition may serve as an adjunct immune-modulating therapy to mitigate the end-organ damage that occurs in the heart, vasculature, and kidney in hypertension.

title: Novel antibiotic stewardship metrics and the quality of antibiotic prescribing for lower respiratory and urinary tract infection across 24 VA hospitals.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Some inpatient antibiotic use metrics have important limitations, including the absence of patient-level risk adjustment. To address this limitation, we previously developed two risk-standardized ratios (RSRs), one based on days of therapy (RSR-DOT) and the other on days of antibiotic spectrum coverage (RSR-DASC). Here, we evaluated the construct validity of these metrics by examining whether hospital performance was associated with the quality of antibiotic selection and duration in patients with either lower respiratory tract infections (LRIs) or urinary tract infections (UTIs).
METHODS: Using Veterans Health Administration data from October 2020 through September 2021, we calculated RSR-DOT and RSR-DASC for 121 acute-care hospitals and selected 24 hospitals with relatively low or high values. At each hospital, a blinded infectious diseases physician reviewed 10 admissions each for LRI and UTI. Antibiotic selection at day 3 and total antibiotic duration were adjudicated and summarized as a 6-category ordinal composite outcome. Associations between RSR metrics and antibiotic-prescribing quality were evaluated using ordinal logistic regression; model-fit and bootstrap analyses compared RSR-DOT and RSR-DASC.
RESULTS: We reviewed 479 admissions (239 LRI and 240 UTI). In LRI, lower RSR-DASC tended to be associated with a higher quality of antibiotic use (coefficient, 2.906 [P = .053]), whereas RSR-DOT was not (1.418 [P = .374]). In UTI, neither metric was associated with the quality of antibiotic therapy. Model-fit and bootstrap analyses consistently favor RSR-DASC over RSR-DOT for LRI.
CONCLUSIONS: RSR-DASC may capture antibiotic-prescribing quality more closely than RSR-DOT for LRI, but not for UTI, potentially supporting the value of spectrum-informed benchmarking metrics.

title: Association of maternal height with pregnancy complications: Analyses of two cohorts
abstract: Background: Height is inversely associated with risk of cardiovascular and metabolic conditions in nonpregnant populations. Whether maternal height is independently associated with pregnancy complications, after accounting for prepregnancy weight, remains less clear. Objective: To investigate associations of maternal height with pregnancy complications, independent of prepregnancy weight, and to examine the role of infant sex and race/ethnicity in these associations. Methods: = 8763). Cohort-specific short (<20th percentile), average (20th-80th percentile), and tall (≥80th percentile) height categories were defined. Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), preterm birth (PTB; Omega only), and preeclampsia were considered outcomes. We fit cohort-specific unadjusted and adjusted modified Poisson regression models with robust standard errors and estimated relative risks (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) associated with each 5-cm greater maternal height. We fit similar models to examine risks among women with short or tall height compared with average height. We evaluated race/ethnicity and infant sex as potential modifiers of height-GDM associations using interaction models. Results: Each 5-cm greater maternal height was associated with lower GDM risk in both cohorts, with a modest association in Omega and a larger association in HAPO (Omega: adjusted RR [aRR], 0.99; 95% CI, 0.98, 0.99; HAPO: aRR, 0.84; 95% CI, 0.78, 0.90). Short women had higher GDM risk (Omega: aRR, 1.05; 95% CI, 1.03, 1.07; HAPO: aRR, 1.44; 95% CI, 1.18, 1.75), and tall women had lower GDM risk (Omega: aRR, 0.98; 95% CI, 0.96, 0.99; HAPO: aRR, 0.71; 95% CI, 0.56, 0.89), compared with women with average height. In Omega, linear height was associated with slightly lower preeclampsia risk (aRR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.99, 0.99) and slightly greater PTB risk (aRR, 1.01; 95% CI, 1.00, 1.01). Infant sex or race/ethnicity did not meaningfully modify the association between height and GDM in either cohort. Conclusion: Maternal height was inversely associated with GDM risk in both cohorts. We also observed small, cohort-specific associations of height with PTB and preeclampsia in Omega. These findings suggest that maternal height may provide modest information beyond conventional maternal body-size measures, although its clinical utility for individual risk prediction or targeted monitoring may be limited and requires further evaluation.

title: Language-model ratings of depression reflect the rater more than the patient
abstract: Depression has no diagnostic blood test. Language models promise tireless, consistent assessment, but can accurate raters disagree about individuals? We pre-registered 880 language-model raters, crossing 11 open models with prompting and scoring choices, and applied them to 189 interviews against the eight-item Patient Health Questionnaire. Model choice explained 30.0% of summed-symptom score variance, stable participant differences 10.5%. Two randomly drawn raters with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) >= 0.70 disagreed on screening decisions for 40% of participants, on average. Average over-rating governed how many were flagged, yet equal-capacity raters chose differently for about one participant in five. A locked analysis of 86 new interviews reproduced the main pre-registered findings. Exploratory recalibration with 40 labelled participants raised accuracy from about 60% to 75% and halved disagreement, leaving one participant in five decided differently. Calibration repaired much of the rater dependence without securing agreement about individuals.

title: Patient and Clinician Perspectives on Physical Therapy Use in Contemporary Rheumatology Care for Rheumatoid Arthritis in the United States: A Qualitative Study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Physical therapy (PT) can address functional limitations common in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) yet remains inconsistently used in rheumatology care. The purpose of this study was to explore how PT is used in routine RA care in the United States from the perspectives of patients, rheumatology clinicians, and physical therapists.
METHODS: We conducted a qualitative study using semistructured interviews with adults with RA (n = 24), rheumatology clinicians (n = 6), and physical therapists (n = 6) with diverse experiences. Interviews were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis to identify key themes related to PT use across the care pathway.
RESULTS: Four themes emerged illustrating barriers to effective use of PT in RA care: first, recognizing the need for PT. Rheumatology clinicians often prioritized pharmacological management and reserved PT for later disease stages or severe functional decline, whereas patients described a desire for earlier, preventive PT. Discussion of PT: clinicians and patients reported limited discussion of PT, with conversations often occurring late in disease management and PT seen as a "last resort." Interprofessional collaboration and training challenges: gaps in knowledge, interprofessional communication, and referral processes among rheumatology clinicians and limited rheumatology exposure among physical therapists impeded PT use. Use of PT: logistical challenges (cost, travel, and time), concerns about pain and adherence, and limited availability of rheumatology-focused PT clinics were barriers to use.
CONCLUSION: Across participant accounts, PT was described as inconsistently used in routine RA care and often considered reactively. Participants described misalignment in clinician perspectives, limited communication, and inconsistent care processes as contributing to early breakdowns in the care pathway and delayed or unrealized PT access.

title: Ruling the robot: a phase-based analysis of resident autonomy across core robotic general surgery procedures.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Robotic surgery has become foundational in general surgery training, yet limited data exist on resident participation in core robotic procedures. This study assessed resident involvement in robotic cholecystectomies and inguinal hernia repairs (IHR) across operative phases and postgraduate year to characterize how participation evolves throughout training.
METHODS: A retrospective review of robotic cholecystectomies and unilateral IHR performed over a single academic year at one tertiary academic institution was conducted using My Intuitive App case logs. Cholecystectomies were divided into three phases (dissection, clipping, removal) and IHR into two phases (dissection, reconstruction). Resident participation was quantified for each phase and the overall case. Differences by postgraduate year were assessed using one-way ANOVA, junior (PGY2/3) versus senior (PGY4/5) comparisons using two-sample t-tests, and inter-phase participation using repeated measures ANOVA.
RESULTS: 151 robotic cholecystectomies and 101 robotic unilateral IHR performed by seven surgeons met inclusion criteria. Resident participation in cholecystectomy measured 50.7% (dissection), 90.5% (clipping), 89.4% (removal), and 72.1% (overall) compared to attending surgeons. For IHR, participation measured 44.8% (dissection), 72.5% (reconstruction), and 57.4% (overall). Across postgraduate years, significant differences in participation were identified in the cholecystectomy dissection (p < 0.001), clipping (p = 0.001), and overall case (p < 0.001), but not the removal phase (p = 0.077). For IHR, significant differences were identified across all phases (p < 0.001). Senior residents participated significantly more than junior residents across all phases for both procedures. In both case types, resident participation in the dissection phase significantly lagged behind all other phases regardless of postgraduate year.
CONCLUSION: Resident participation in robotic cholecystectomy and IHR varies significantly by operative phase and training level. Dissection consistently represents the phase of lowest resident involvement, while senior residents demonstrate greater autonomy across all phases. These findings underscore the importance of phase-level operative data in understanding resident progression and informing competency-based surgical training.

title: The Effect of Interposition Nerve Graft Length on Outcomes of Laryngeal Reinnervation.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the impact of interposition graft lengths on the efficacy of laryngeal reinnervation.
METHODS: In an in vivo rabbit model, unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) resection was performed followed by immediate re-anastomosis using interposition graft lengths of 0, 2, 4, and 6 cm (N = 2 animals per length). After 4 months, thyroarytenoid (TA) muscles and RLNs were harvested and analyzed. Muscle fiber area was assessed using hematoxylin-eosin staining. Neuromuscular junctions (NMJs) were identified by immunohistochemistry for post-synaptic acetylcholine receptors and categorized morphologically as pretzel shape (normally innervated), fragmented (partially innervated), or plaque-like (degenerated). Axons within RLN segments were visualized using FluoroMyelin lipid-fluorescent staining.
RESULTS: Muscle fiber area tended to be decreased on the experimental side but did not differ significantly across graft lengths. Normal contralateral muscles showed 100% pretzel morphology. NMJ morphology progressively worsened with increasing graft length: 0 cm grafts (62% pretzel; 38% fragmented; 0% plaque), 2 cm (23%; 69%; 8%), 4 cm (15%; 54%; 31%), and 6 cm (18%; 36%; 46%). Axon count in the distal RLN segment as a percentage of axons in the proximal RLN segment similarly declined with graft length: 0 cm grafts (mean 136%), 2 cm (51%), 4 cm (19%), and 6 cm (17%).
CONCLUSION: Longer interposition grafts were associated with reduced axonal counts and increasingly abnormal NMJ morphology. These findings suggest longer interposition graft lengths may reduce laryngeal reinnervation outcomes.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: n/a.

title: An Actionable Clinical Path to Improving Care for Individuals with Temporomandibular Disorders: Bridging the Medical–Dental Divide in the United States
abstract: Building on the recommendations of the 2020 National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM) report on temporomandibular disorders (TMDs), this discussion paper proposes an actionable, interdisciplinary care pathway designed to address the documented gaps in health care for individuals with TMDs. TMDs remain a significantly under-recognized area within health care, largely falling outside the scope of standard medical education and practice. Historically, management has been driven by a narrow biomedical perspective within dentistry, often resulting in ineffective and potentially irreversible interventions. Despite growing evidence that TMDs are complex, multifactorial conditions, care continues to lack integration across medical, dental, and allied health disciplines. Educational gaps in evidence-based approaches, limited interdisciplinary training and practice, and the absence of coordinated referral pathways contribute to fragmented and inconsistent management. Moreover, systemic barriers, including insurance coverage gaps and shortages of qualified clinicians, further constrain access to quality care. There is a pressing need for a clear, discipline-agnostic, interprofessional care pathway that bridges the medical–dental divide and supports whole-person, biopsychosocially informed diagnosis and management of TMDs. This discussion paper draws on the NASEM Forum to present a clinical pathway to action for TMDs, with specific tools and suggestions to guide care derived from multiple meetings of the NASEM Forum on TMDs. It includes patient and clinician perspectives regarding opportunities and barriers to implementation and systemic barriers that must be addressed to allow implementation of an evidence-based universal care model for TMDs that will bridge the medical–dental divide in the United States and suggests future opportunities for growth in this area.
