title: Technology use and PrEP awareness among PrEP-eligible cisgender women
abstract: Introduction Although pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is safe and effective for preventing HIV, uptake has been low among cisgender women in the United States. Many PrEP-eligible, cisgender women are unaware of PrEP, suggesting missed opportunities.Methods This research explored factors related to PrEP awareness and technology among PrEP-eligible cisgender women living in New York and Philadelphia, recruited through convenience sampling. Data were collected via computer-based surveys among urban, cisgender women not living with HIV.Results Among 237 PrEP-eligible cisgender women, 58% were unaware of PrEP. Most participants were Black (61%) and/or Hispanic (24%), with a mean age of 39 years. Chi-square analyses compared PrEP-aware versus unaware women. PrEP awareness was significantly higher among young women (p = 0.009), Hispanic women (p = 0.039), and women who had never been incarcerated (p = 0.035). Participants with access to technology were significantly more PrEP-aware than women without access (p < 0.001).Conclusions Women who routinely engage in phone-based activities were more likely to be aware of PrEP than women with limited cell phone access. Inequities in technology access and use influence PrEP awareness among cisgender women. Interventions addressing digital inequities may improve awareness and uptake, advancing HIV prevention efforts among cisgender women.

title: COMPASS 2.0: psychometric representational similarity analysis distinguishes symptom structure from personal signal
abstract: Language models can score psychiatric questionnaires from speech, but agreement with self-report may reflect the questionnaire rather than the person. We introduce psychometric representational similarity analysis, a framework for comparing the structure of speech-derived scores, self-report, item wording and theory, and implement it alongside person-level construct scoring in COMPASS 2.0. We show how similarly worded items induce covariance without psychological signal. In pre-registered discovery and confirmation analyses of clinical interviews from 275 participants, language-derived symptom geometry resembled wording more than self-report, with no structure beyond wording detected by the registered tests. Geometric agreement with self-report survived assigning participants someone else's answers, whereas person-paired scores captured distress more than specific symptoms. Complementary analyses examined counselling quality and wording structure across 34 instruments and the Research Domain Criteria (RDoC) framework. These findings distinguish agreement about psychological structure from evidence that language-derived assessments track individual people.

title: Data-driven implementation science synthesis: a topic modeling approach to understand implementation science in the biomedical literature
abstract: Implementation science (IS) is a far-reaching field covering innumerable concepts to define overarching topics, methods, and perspectives. As the field has grown, there are increasing concerns about effectively synthesizing large swaths of information to interpret key factors important to dissemination and implementations science studies. To understand the scope and trends within Implementation Science (IS) we reviewed the IS literature using Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA). We applied an explanatory mixed methods approach (quantitative then qualitative) to identify and characterize groups of themes in the peer reviewed literature. We included PubMed articles from 1975-2023 using a broad set of IS terms in the title and/or abstract. We employed Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) to identify the number of latent clusters in the literature. We confirmed the number of clusters using majority vote from perplexity, CV coherence scores, and UMass coherence scores. Finally, we iteratively reviewed the titles from each cluster giving each cluster a topical label through manual consensus. We analyzed 9,098 LDIS articles from PubMed using natural language processing techniques, namely topic modeling, and identified 15 distinct themes. These themes represent two categories of IS: Metascience (e.g., Theories, Models, and Frameworks) and IS Topics in IS (e.g., Healthcare and Chronic Disease). The number of IS-related articles has increased exponentially with similar articles in both Metascience and IS Topics in IS. Our findings demonstrate an expanding scope of IS over time, providing valuable insights into areas within the field that may require further exploration and discussion. With the incredible growth of IS, these results suggest that informatics approaches may be well-suited to address the magnitude and heterogeneity of the field. This article provides a novel approach in informatics applied to the IS literature.

title: Global Survey of Latent Tuberculosis Screening and Treatment Practices in Liver Transplantation.
abstract: We surveyed transplant and infectious disease (ID) practitioners to better understand approaches to managing latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) in liver transplantation (LT), an area in which high-quality evidence is lacking. The survey was distributed to clinicians via international ID society listservs, and one respondent per transplant center was requested. There were 86 respondents, including 78 (91%) ID physicians, from North America (68%), Europe (12%), South America (11%), Asia (7%), Africa (1%), and Australia (1%). Most centers (92%) screen all LT candidates for LTBI, and 95% use tuberculosis (TB) interferon-gamma release assays (TB-IGRA) as first-line. In LT recipients with indeterminate TB-IGRA results, respondents differ in terms of which specific TB risk factors may impact treatment decisions. Timing of post-transplant LTBI treatment varies with only 27% choosing to initiate therapy during the index transplant admission. The majority of respondents (88%) prescribe isoniazid monotherapy to LT recipients with LTBI for 6 (23%) or 9 (65%) months. Management of living donor LTBI differs depending on severity of liver disease in the potential recipient. These survey data will inform future collaborative research efforts to optimize LTBI management in LT.

title: Clinical Practice Guideline: Tinnitus Update.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Tinnitus is the perception of sound without an external source. More than 50 million people in the United States have reported experiencing tinnitus, resulting in an estimated prevalence of 10% to 15% in adults. The focus of this guideline is on tinnitus that is both bothersome and persistent (lasting 6 months or longer), which often negatively affects the patient's quality of life. The target audience for the guideline is any clinician, including allied health professionals, involved in managing patients with tinnitus. The target patient population is limited to adults (18 years and older) with tinnitus that is persistent and bothersome.
PURPOSE: The purpose of this guideline is to provide and update evidence-based recommendations for clinicians managing patients with tinnitus. This guideline provides clinicians with a logical framework to improve patient care and mitigate the personal and social effects of persistent, bothersome tinnitus. It discusses the evaluation of patients with tinnitus, including selection and timing of diagnostic testing and specialty referral to identify potential underlying treatable pathology. It then focuses on the treatment of patients with persistent tinnitus, with recommendations to guide the measurement of the effect of tinnitus and to determine the most appropriate interventions to improve symptoms and quality of life for people with tinnitus and associated comorbidities.
METHODS: This guideline was developed using the 55-page protocol published as the American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery Foundation's Clinical Practice Guideline Development Manual (3rd edition), which summarizes the methodology for assessments of current data, topic prioritization, development of key action statements (KASs), application of value judgments, and related procedures. The guideline group was represented by adult otolaryngologists, audiologists, otologists/neurotologists, a geriatrician, a behavioral neuroscientist, a neurologist, a radiologist, a psychiatrist, an internist, a nurse practitioner, an otolaryngology resident physician, and a consumer advocate who represented participating, national professional organizations.
ACTION STATEMENTS: The Guideline Update Group made strong recommendations for the following Key Action Statements (KAS): Clinicians should distinguish patients with bothersome tinnitus from patients with non-bothersome tinnitus (KAS 2). Clinicians should inquire about risks for self-harm in a patient with bothersome tinnitus (KAS 3). Clinicians should not obtain neuroradiologic imaging in patients with tinnitus specifically to evaluate the tinnitus unless specific concerning features are present (KAS 6). The Guideline Update Group made recommendations for the following KASs: Clinicians should perform a targeted history and physical examination at the initial evaluation of a patient with tinnitus (KAS 1). Clinicians should obtain a comprehensive audiological evaluation in patients with tinnitus (KAS 5). Clinicians should educate patients with tinnitus about the natural history and effects of, and management strategies for tinnitus (KAS 7). Clinicians should recommend a hearing aid evaluation for patients with hearing difficulties and persistent, bothersome tinnitus (KAS 8). Clinicians should refer patients with persistent, bothersome tinnitus for cochlear implant evaluation when they meet audiologic criteria for referral (KAS 9). Clinicians should recommend Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) to patients with persistent, bothersome tinnitus (KAS 11). Clinicians or their designee should assess and document outcomes of interventions in patients with persistent, bothersome tinnitus (KAS 15). The Guideline Update Group made recommendations against for the following KASs: Clinicians should not routinely recommend antidepressants, anticonvulsants, anxiolytics, or intratympanic medications for a primary indication of treating persistent, bothersome tinnitus (KAS 12). Clinicians should not recommend dietary supplements for the primary indication of persistent, bothersome tinnitus (KAS 13). Clinicians should not recommend repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) for the treatment of patients with persistent, bothersome tinnitus (KAS 14A). The Guideline Update Group offered options for the following KASs: Clinicians may inquire about somatosensory features in patients with persistent, bothersome tinnitus (KAS 4). Clinicians may recommend sound enrichment to patients with persistent, bothersome tinnitus (KAS 10). Clinicians may offer bimodal neuromodulation to patients with persistent, bothersome tinnitus (KAS 14B).

title: Risk Stratification of Acute Pulmonary Embolism: Outcomes in Patients With Intermediate sPESI Scores and Negative Cardiac Biomarkers.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Current pulmonary embolism (PE) guidelines support outpatient management for selected low-risk patients, typically identified using the simplified Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index (sPESI). The prognostic value of individual sPESI scores in the direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) era, particularly when combined with cardiac biomarker assessment, remains uncertain.
RESEARCH QUESTION: To evaluate 7-day and 30-day all-cause mortality among patients with acute PE, sPESI scores of 2 or 3, and negative cardiac biomarkers treated with a DOAC.
STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: Retrospective cohort study of US adults diagnosed with acute PE in a VA emergency department and prescribed a DOAC within 24 h of diagnosis at any U.S. Veterans Affairs (VA) Health System from 2015 to 2024.
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: Seven-day and 30-day all-cause mortality.
RESULTS: Of 6427 eligible patients, 1365 had an sPESI score of 2 and 455 had an sPESI score of 3 with negative cardiac biomarkers. In the sPESI 2 cohort, 7-day and 30-day mortality were 0.44% and 1.39%, respectively. In the sPESI 3 cohort, rates were 0.22% and 2.20%. Approximately 71% of sPESI 2 patients and 75% of sPESI 3 patients were hospitalized. Hospitalization was not associated with lower 7-day or 30-day mortality in either cohort.
INTERPRETATION: Patients with acute PE, sPESI scores of 2 or 3, and negative cardiac biomarkers had low short-term mortality in this large, contemporary DOAC-treated cohort. These findings support prospective studies evaluating outpatient management in carefully selected patients.

title: School Health Policy Opportunities to Nurture Healthier Students Who Are Ready to Learn.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Children's health and educational outcomes are interconnected, and unmet health needs affect youths' readiness to learn. Comprehensive school health (CSH) systems are designed to promote academic success and well-being for all youth. State and local health and education leaders benefit from guidance on how to build, fund, and sustain effective CSH systems to support the whole child.
CONTRIBUTIONS TO THEORY: In this article, we offer core areas for CSH policy development with recommendations for enhancing the quality and scale of CSH systems.
IMPLICATIONS FOR SCHOOL HEALTH POLICY, PRACTICE, AND EQUITY: Several key policy opportunities and strategies aligned with core features of a CSH are identified, including (1) adoption of a CSH framework, (2) enhancement of cross-sector coordination and collaboration, (3) use of standardized metrics to enhance CSH system quality, (4) engagement of youth and families in system building, (5) use of innovative strategies to enhance workforce capacity and development, and (6) establishment of a strategic funding plan.
CONCLUSIONS: State and local health and education departments are challenged to act upon key policy opportunities to build, fund, and sustain CSH systems to promote student success, health, and well-being.

title: Getting off-tract: Correlational tractography of white matter integrity and cognitive intraindividual variability in a large sample of community-dwelling older adults.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Cognitive intraindividual variability (IIV), or the dispersion across neuropsychological task performance, is a sensitive marker of neurocognitive aging, but its tract-specific white matter correlates are not well characterized. This study used correlational tractography to identify pathways whose microstructural integrity relates to IIV in older adults.
METHOD: Participants were a diverse sample of 510 community-dwelling older adults (Mage = 66.6 years, SDage = 8.4) from the Health and Aging Brain Study-Health Disparities cohort. IIV was computed as the intraindividual standard deviation of demographically normed performance T scores across a multidomain battery. Diffusion MRI connectometry in DSI Studio tested partial Spearman associations between IIV and quantitative anisotropy, adjusting for sex and intracranial volume, with permutation testing and false discovery rate adjustment (0.01).
RESULTS: Higher IIV was associated with lower quantitative anisotropy primarily in commissural corpus callosum, fronto-subcortical, and interhemispheric long-range connection fibers. Tracts of the forceps minor were the most robust to sensitivity analyses. Effects were small in magnitude, with the primary connectometry threshold corresponding to an effect size of 0.09, but spatially specific, accounting for 7.57% of total whole-brain tract volume.
CONCLUSIONS: Overall, we found that IIV maps onto distributed, tract-specific differences in white matter microstructure. Findings support IIV as a marker linked to structural network-level white matter integrity and should motivate longitudinal work to further clarify its neuroanatomical substrates. title: Severe Obstructive Pan-Leaflet Thrombosis After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Bioprosthetic valve thrombosis is an uncommon but important cause of late bioprosthetic valve dysfunction after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR).
CASE SUMMARY: An 82-year-old man with a history of TAVR presented with worsening exertional dyspnea and orthostasis after recent left atrial appendage occlusion and discontinuation of oral anticoagulation. Echocardiography demonstrated a marked rise in transvalvular gradients with restricted leaflet motion, and computed tomography confirmed severe thrombosis of all 3 bioprosthetic leaflets. Warfarin was initiated, resulting in complete symptomatic and hemodynamic resolution at 3 months.
DISCUSSION: This case highlights the complexity of anticoagulant and antithrombotic management after sequential TAVR and left atrial appendage occlusion and the value of multimodality imaging in diagnosing obstructive transcatheter valve thrombosis.
TAKE-HOME MESSAGES: New symptoms or unexplained rise in transvalvular gradients after TAVR should prompt urgent evaluation for leaflet thrombosis. Therapeutic anticoagulation can restore leaflet motion and hemodynamics.

title: Biopsychosocial Factors Facilitating or Compromising Momentary Cognitive Performance in Everyday Environments.
abstract: ImportanceOccupational therapy practitioners often assist a range of clients (e.g., people with schizophrenia, older adults, students, etc.) by addressing their cognitive functioning so they can engage in daily tasks. Thus, a better research-based understanding of real-time biopsychosocial factors that can impact everyday cognitive performance in real life can be useful. Ambulatory cognitive assessments are administered in people's natural environments, making them better suited compared to traditional formal cognitive tests for understanding factors that can impact cognitive performance in real life.ObjectiveTo examine how a range of biopsychosocial factors impact cognitive performance in real life as assessed by eight smartphone-based ambulatory cognitive tests and passively recorded survey response times.DesignSmartphone-based cognitive tests and surveys were completed daily by participants over 10 days. Associations between each cognitive test and biopsychosocial factor were examined in separate multilevel regression models.ParticipantsA total of 393 U.S. adults.MeasuresThe eight cognitive measures covered the domains of processing speed, working memory, recognition memory, and executive functioning. Biopsychosocial factors considered were distractors, prior activity, substances just taken, and psychological state.ResultsCognitive performance was better when participants reported no distractions, were alone, were more focused, had higher levels of energy or excitement, and had greater happiness.Conclusions and RelevanceUnderstanding how biopsychosocial factors affect cognitive performance may assist occupational therapy practitioners and other healthcare professionals in helping clients more deliberately adjust situations to facilitate cognitive performance when needed (e.g., for job tasks, exams, following instructions to take medications, etc.).

title: Seizures in a Dravet Syndrome mouse model inhibit the locus coeruleus but locally evoke supraphysiologic norepinephrine release
abstract: Abstract Locus coeruleus (LC) neurons are the primary source of norepinephrine / noradrenaline (NE) released to most brain structures, including seizure-prone neocortical and limbic regions. LC-NE networks regulate numerous physiological processes, including arousal, attention, and memory. Previous evidence suggests that LC-NE neurons may be involved in epilepsy and that their activation may have therapeutic effects on seizures, but the endogenous activity of the LC-NE network during seizures remains largely unclear. We combined electrocorticography recordings and in vivo imaging to measure somatic activity of LC-NE neurons as well as downstream NE release during hyperthermia-induced seizures in a well-characterized pre-clinical model of Dravet Syndrome. We found that population LC-NE somatic activity was inhibited during seizures, whereas downstream NE release was dramatically elevated. To reconcile these discordant findings, we established that activation of downstream regions is capable of locally evoking NE release, in part via activation of glutamate receptors, consistent with the Glutamate Amplifies Noradrenergic Effects (GANE) model. Finally, we confirmed that ictal NE release occurred across additional downstream brain regions, epilepsy models, and seizure induction methods. Thus, disruption of NE signaling is likely a widespread ictal signature, with implications for impaired consciousness during and after seizures.

title: EP9.17 Patients with Cam- And Pincer-Type Hip Impingement Demonstrate Similar Magnitude of Peak Pelvic Drop
abstract: Abstract Purpose Femoroacetabular impingement syndrome (FAIS) is a common cause of groin pain in young adults. Classically, cam-and pincer-type FAI are based on static radiographic images, but FAIS is a dynamic pathology that may be affected by pelvic dynamics during activity. It was hypothesized that cam- and pincer-type FAIS would demonstrate altered peak pelvic drop in the coronal plane. Methods Motion-capture, demographic, and patient-reported outcome measurements (PROMs) data were analyzed for all patients with unilateral FAIS from a prospectively collected hip arthroscopy database. Motion capture during walking was performed using inertial measurement units (Movella, Xsens, El Segundo, CA, USA), and the peak pelvic drop of both hips was assessed. The following PROMs were analyzed: International Hip Outcome Tool (iHOT-12), Hip Outcome Score–Sports Subscale (HOS-SS), Patient Reported Outcomes Measurement (PROMIS) Physical Function, PROMIS Pain Interference, PROMIS Depression, and PROMIS Anxiety. Pelvic kinematics and PROMs were compared between cam- and pincer-type FAIS using an unpaired Student's t-test. In addition, coronal peak pelvic motion during walking was correlated to lateral center-edge angle (LCEA) and alpha angle using Spearman`s rank coefficient test. Radiographic definitions used were cam, Alpha angle ≥55° and pincer-type, LCEA ≥40°. Results In total 83 hips in 83 patients were included with 38 hips of cam-type and 45 pincer-type FAIS. During walking, peak pelvic drop was 5.0° ± 1.4 on the symptomatic hip and 4.8° ± 1.6 on the asymptomatic hip for cam-type FAIS which was similar to peak pelvic drop in patients with pincer-typer FAIS (symptomatic: 4.5° ± 1.6 and 5.1° ± 2.0 for pincer-type FAIS, respectively (p > 0.05). Preoperative PROMs were also similar between cam- and pincer-type FAIS patients (p > 0.05). In addition, preoperatively, LCEA and alpha angle did not show a significant correlation to peak ipsilateral and contralateral pelvic drop (p>0.05). Discussion Peak pelvic drop did not differ between patients with cam- versus pincer-type FAIS and did not show a significant correlation to preoperative LCEA or alpha angle. Further studies are warranted to analyze the impact of peak pelvic drop on postoperative recovery and outcomes in patients undergoing hip arthroscopy surgery.

title: TP9.1 The Presence of Trendelenburg Gait is Not Associated with Radiographic Measurements or Preoperative Outcomes in Patients Undergoing Hip Arthroscopy for the Treatment of Femoroacetabular Impingement
abstract: Abstract Introduction Trendelenburg gait describes contralateral pelvic drop associated with abductor weakness which can be compensated with lateral trunk lean over the stance limb. Quantitative and qualitative research on uncompensated (pelvic drop without lateral trunk lean) and compensated (pelvic drop with lateral trunk lean) Trendelenburg gait is limited, especially in commonly affected groups such as the Femoroacetabular Impingement (FAI) patients. It was hypothesized that uncompensated Trendelenburg during walking would be associated with lower preoperative Patient Reported Outcomes (PROs), but not with demographic characteristics, in FAI patients undergoing hip arthroscopy. Methods Patients with FAIS undergoing primary hip arthroscopy were identified from a prospective hip preservation registry. Preoperative gait analysis was performed using wearable inertial measurement units during level walking. Peak symptomatic side pelvic drop and trunk lean were extracted. Patient characteristics (age, sex, body mass index) and preoperative PROs—including the International Hip Outcome Tool (iHOT-12), Hip Outcome Score – Sport Specific Subscale (HOS-SSS), Patient-Reported Outcome Measurement Information System (PROMIS) Pain Interference, Physical Function, Depression, and Anxiety were collected. Patients were classified as normal pelvic drop, compensated Trendelenburg, and uncompensated Trendelenburg. Associations between demographics and PROs between the three groups were assessed using regression analyses. Results A total of 88 patients (88 hips) were included. The number of patients classified as normal, compensated and uncompensated Trendelenburg were 55, 19, and 14, respectively. Median pelvic drop was 3.95 ± 0.85, 7.1 ± 1.85 and 6.46 ± 0.81, in the normal, compensated, and uncompensated Trendelenburg groups, respectively. Regarding the trunk lean, the normal, compensated, and uncompensated Trendelenburg patients showed an average of 2.26 ± 3.55, 1.11 ± 2.97, and 7.04 ± 1.75, respectively. No difference between the three groups was found regarding Lateral Center Edge Angle (p=0.6889), alpha angle (p=0.142), Tönnis angle (p=0.578), femoral torsion (p=0.373), or acetabular version (p=0.393). When PROs were compared between groups, no significant difference was found in iHOT-12 scores (p=0.8433), HOS-SS (p=0.8746), PROMIS pain interference (p=0.2091), PROMIS physical function (p=0.9972), PROMIS depression (p=0.4352), PROMIS anxiety (p=0.7065). Conclusion The presence of compensated and uncompensated Trendelenburg gait is not associated with the radiographic parameters or preoperative PROs in FAI patients undergoing hip arthroscopy surgery. Future studies with a larger sample size may be necessary for a better understanding of possible associations.

title: Proopiomelanocortin ( POMC )–β‐Endorphin System in the Rat Colon: Expression, Up Regulation by Stress, and Correlation With Stress‐Induced Visceral Analgesia
abstract: BACKGROUND: The pituitary proopiomelanocortin (POMC)-β-endorphin (β-END) system is activated by hypothalamic corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF) signaling and stress. We investigated whether this pathway is also expressed in the rat colon, regulated by peripheral CRF and stress, and correlated with stress-induced visceral analgesia. METHODS: POMC and the prohormone convertases PC1/3 and PC2 transcripts were assessed by RT-PCR, and POMC and β-END localization was examined by immunohistochemistry in the proximal and distal colon of naïve adult male Sprague-Dawley rats. Proximal colonic POMC mRNA was quantified by real-time quantitative PCR 1 h after intraperitoneal injection of CRF (10 μg/kg) or saline and on day 11 after assessing visceromotor responses (VMRs) to colorectal distension (CRD) using a non-invasive method in rats subjected to repeated water avoidance stress (rWAS) (1 h/day for 10 days) or control handling. The correlation between POMC gene expression and VMRs was evaluated. RESULTS: POMC, PC1/3, and PC2 transcripts were detected in the proximal and distal colon. POMC- and β-END-immunoreactive cells are localized in the lamina propria and enteric plexuses. CRF increased POMC mRNA expression by 2.5-fold. rWAS decreased VMRs to CRD in a pressure-dependent manner, with a reduction of up to 52% at 60 mmHg, and increased POMC expression 10-fold compared with controls; POMC expression was inversely correlated with cumulative VMRs (r = -0.655, p = 0.034). CONCLUSIONS: POMC-β-END system expression in the rat colonic enteric plexus, together with CRF/stress-induced upregulation of POMC and its correlation with analgesic responses to CRD, suggests a possible relevance in modulating visceral pain.

title: A Guide to Enzymatic Targeted Methylation Sequencing Bioinformatics Workflow: Best Practices
abstract: We present a best-practices protocol for targeted DNA methylation sequencing analysis that integrates both bisulfite- and enzymatic-conversion approaches using Twist Bioscience technology. Building on established tools and vendor-recommended workflows, this protocol provides a standardized, fully reproducible framework that addresses current gaps in the implementation, documentation, and downstream integration of targeted methylation sequencing analyses. The workflow incorporates widely used open-source tools across two main stages: preprocessing (adapter trimming with Trim Galore and quality control via FastQC/MultiQC) and methylation calling (alignment with BWA-meth, duplicate marking using Picard, and methylation extraction with MethylDackel). Importantly, we extend existing workflows by introducing a structured third stage for downstream statistical analysis in R, including β-value calculation, differential methylation analysis with methylKit, principal component analysis, and tiling-based regional profiling, all embedded in a unified, reproducible pipeline. A key contribution of this protocol is the integration of multi-stage quality control checkpoints, harmonized parameterization, and explicit reporting of intermediate outputs, enabling transparency and reproducibility across all analytical steps. The modular design allows tool substitution and adaptation to different experimental contexts, including enzyme-based methylation methods, while maintaining consistency in data processing and interpretation. This guide provides step-by-step instructions, troubleshooting strategies, and examples of expected outputs, along with built-in statistical routines that generate comprehensive results, including methylation matrices, correlation analyses, differentially methylated region annotations, and publication-ready visualizations. The complete workflow requires approximately 9-27 hr for 10 samples (approximately 134.2 million reads per sample) on Linux systems and assumes moderate proficiency in command-line environments and R. In summary, this protocol offers a practical, transparent, and reproducible framework that standardizes targeted DNA methylation analysis and facilitates its application across diverse biological and clinical research settings. © 2026 The Author(s). title: Long-Term Safety and Efficacy of Once-Weekly Lonapegsomatropin in Adults With Growth Hormone Deficiency: Results From a 52-Week Open-Label Extension Trial
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the long-term safety and efficacy of once-weekly lonapegsomatropin in adults with growth hormone (GH) deficiency. METHODS: This 52-week, multicenter, open-label extension trial enrolled adults with GH deficiency who completed the 38-week phase 3 foresiGHt trial, in which participants received lonapegsomatropin, placebo, or somatropin. In the extension, all participants received lonapegsomatropin. Safety assessment included adverse events, laboratory values, vital signs, immunogenicity, 12-lead electrocardiograms, and fundoscopy. Body composition (trunk percent fat, trunk fat mass, visceral adipose tissue, total body lean mass, trunk lean mass, and appendicular lean mass) was measured by dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry, and patient-reported outcomes were evaluated. RESULTS: After foresiGHt completion, 220 (88.7%) participants enrolled in the extension. Across foresiGHt and the extension, common lonapegsomatropin-associated adverse events were nasopharyngitis, upper respiratory infection, and headache. Injection-site reactions were infrequent (5.1%) and mild or moderate. After up to 90 weeks of treatment, body composition was maintained in participants continuing lonapegsomatropin and improved relative to foresiGHt baseline in those initiating or switching to lonapegsomatropin. Clinically meaningful improvements in patient-reported outcomes from foresiGHt baseline were observed; 43.5%, 40.6%, and 35.8% of participants achieved a ≥10-point improvement in the Treatment-Related Impact Measure-Adult GH Deficiency total score among those continuing, initiating, or switching to lonapegsomatropin, respectively. CONCLUSION: Once-weekly lonapegsomatropin was generally well tolerated and was associated with sustained improvements in body composition and patient-reported outcomes for up to 90 weeks. These findings extend prior evidence and support the long-term benefits of lonapegsomatropin in adults with GH deficiency, including those switching from somatropin.

title: The social cognition paradox in long-duration spaceflight: A VEN fatigue hypothesis for duration-dependent emotion recognition decline
abstract: Long-duration spaceflight may alter social cognition, yet the underlying biological mechanisms remain unclear. Emotion Recognition Task (ERT) performance remains stable during typical 6-month International Space Station (ISS) missions but declines markedly during the 340-day NASA Twins Study, suggesting duration-dependent vulnerability. Here, we propose the Von Economo Neuron (VEN) Fatigue Hypothesis, which posits that microgravity increases demand on VEN-associated social cognitive networks, eliciting adaptive myelination during shorter missions before compensatory mechanisms fail with prolonged exposure. To evaluate this hypothesis, we integrated evidence from rodent, human cortical organoid, astronaut plasma proteomic, and neuroimaging datasets. ISS-flown rodent frontal cortex demonstrated increased expression of myelination-related genes, while spaceflown cortical organoids exhibited changes consistent with oligodendrocyte remodeling. Astronaut plasma transcriptomics identified reproducible alterations in VEN-associated and myelination-related proteins across independent missions, and resting-state fMRI revealed transient changes in frontal insula connectivity following long-duration spaceflight. Together, across four independent experimental platforms, these findings provide convergent but indirect evidence consistent with the VEN Fatigue Hypothesis and identify adaptive myelination and VEN-associated network remodeling as candidate mechanisms underlying duration-dependent changes in social cognition during long-duration spaceflight. The hypothesis remains speculative: its central duration-dependent causal claim is not testable with the present single-subject cognitive observation and awaits prospective multi-subject validation.

title: Complement Factor B Activation Fragments Predict Mortality and Persistent Organ Failures
abstract: Introduction Critically ill adults with acute kidney injury (AKI) have high morbidity and mortality and lack treatment options. The alternative pathway of complement has been implicated in AKI pathogenesis and complement therapeutics exist. We evaluated the association between urine Ba, an activation fragment of the alternative pathway, and mortality and organ failures including major adverse kidney events at 30 days (MAKE30). Methods Post hoc analysis of 255 critically ill adults enrolled in the SMART trial. Urine complement activation factor Ba/Urine Creatinine ratio (uBa/uCr) was obtained on day 2 of ICU admission and measured via ELISA. Results uBa/uCr was associated with MAKE30 outcomes (composite outcome of death, new receipt of RRT, or persistent renal dysfunction [serum creatinine ≥200% of baseline] at 30 days). uBa/uCr was highly predictive of MAKE 30 (AUROC 0.77), persistent AKI (AUROC 0.79) and ICU mortality (AUROC 0.91); these outcomes occurred after day 2 uBa/uCr measurements. uBa/uCr was associated with maximal AKI severity (OR 1.23 [95% CI 1.11, 1.36], p 0.0001), MAKE30 outcome (OR 1.35 [1.14, 1.59]; p 0.0004), ICU days (OR 1.04 [1.02, 1.06]; p 0.0001), ventilator days (OR 1.20 [1.08, 1.34]; p 0.0005), vasopressor or inotrope days (OR 1.29 [1.13, 1.46]; p 0.0001), RRT utilization (OR 1.27 [1.04, 1.55]; p 0.021), and persistent AKI (OR 1.56 [95% CI 1.25, 1.96]; p 0.0001). Conclusions uBa/uCr is highly associated with MAKE30 and organ failure days. uBa/uCr may be helpful for prognostic enrichment of future clinical trials of complement inhibition to treat organ failures in critically ill patients.

title: Giant Left Atrial Thrombus After Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion
abstract: BACKGROUND: Device-related thrombus (DRT) is a recognized complication of left atrial appendage occlusion. Persistent iatrogenic atrial septal defect (iASD) has not been described as a source of late left atrial thrombus. CASE SUMMARY: An 84-year-old man with prior WATCHMAN FLX (Boston Scientific) implantation had a residual iASD on 45-day transesophageal echocardiography (TEE). Eighteen months later, transthoracic echocardiography revealed a large left atrial mass. TEE demonstrated a 5.4 × 4.0-cm mobile thrombus and a separate 2.4 × 1.0-cm device-adherent thrombus, interpreted as fragmented or partially separated DRT. After 2 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation, both persisted. Surgery identified a dominant organized thrombus anchored to the interatrial septum at the iASD, with a separate fibrinous thrombus adherent to the device. Both were excised, and the device was preserved. DISCUSSION: A persistent iASD may act as a late thrombotic nidus and coexist with true DRT. Surgery can clarify the diagnosis and permit device preservation. TAKE-HOME MESSAGES: A persistent iASD after left atrial appendage occlusion may serve as a late nidus for a giant left atrial thrombus and may coexist with true DRT, a distinction that TEE may not resolve. Surgical extraction of a large, highly mobile thrombus persisting despite anticoagulation can be diagnostic and therapeutic while permitting preservation of a stable device.

title: Pharmacological Inhibition of Neutral Sphingomyelinase Attenuates Western Diet‐Induced Skeletal Muscle Insulin Resistance
abstract: ABSTRACT Neutral sphingomyelinase (nSMase) hydrolyzes sphingomyelin to generate ceramide, a key bioactive lipid implicated in a number of pathological processes, including insulin resistance and diabetes. In this study, we investigate the role and mechanism of nSMase2 signaling in skeletal muscle lipid metabolic disorders and insulin resistance associated with Western diet (WD)‐induced obesity. Six‐week‐old C57BL/6J mice were fed either a WD enriched in saturated fat (46%) and fructose (17.5%) or a standard chow diet (CD) for 16 weeks. GW4869, an nSMase inhibitor, was administered intraperitoneally at a dose of 2.0 μg/g body weight every 48 h for 12 weeks. Sixteen weeks of WD feeding increased plasma nSMase activity and skeletal muscle nSMase2 expression that were associated with reduced insulin metabolic signaling in the phosphoinositide 3‐kinase/protein kinase B pathway, the development of glucose intolerance, and insulin resistance, all of which were blunted by GW4869 treatment. Concurrently, 16 weeks of WD feeding increased ceramide production and skeletal muscle CD36‐mediated signaling, which correlated with excessive lipid droplet accumulation and increased free fatty acid (FFA) levels in skeletal muscle ex vivo. These lipid metabolic disturbances were attenuated, in vivo, by treatment of mice with GW4869. Moreover, GW4869 inhibited WD‐induced pathological changes of skeletal muscle mitochondrial dysfunction, excessive oxidative stress, fibrosis and fiber type transition. These findings demonstrate that nSMase2 is involved in regulating CD36 signaling and may contribute to skeletal muscle FFA uptake, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, fibrosis, and associated skeletal muscle insulin resistance in a mouse model of WD‐induced obesity.

title: Antegrade Hypogastric Perfusion for Spinal Protection During Complex Open AAA Repair in a Patient with PRKG1 Mutation
abstract: Individuals with protein kinase cGMP-dependent type I ( PRKG1) mutations develop aortopathies that often require staged aortic repairs. We present a case of a 32-year-old male with a PRKG1 mutation and prior extent II thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm (TAAA) repair who required an open repair of an enlarging remnant infrarenal aneurysm. Given the previous extensive ligation of intercostal and lumbar arterial branches, the patient faced a heightened risk of spinal cord malperfusion or ischemia with subsequent open repair. To mitigate this, temporary antegrade hypogastric perfusion was performed during aortic cross-clamping using a Pruitt-Inahara F3® Carotid Shunt deployed via an 8mm proximal side-graft. Following successful aorto-bi-iliac repair the patient recovered well without neurological deficits. This temporary shunting technique is an effective adjunct to preserve pelvic perfusion and reduce the risk of spinal cord malperfusion.

title: A multistate model of frailty progression after severe infections in older adults in England
abstract: Abstract Background Evidence on frailty progression following severe infection is limited. We compared rates of transition to greater frailty or death after severe infection among older adults in England. Methods We did a matched-cohort study among adults aged ≥65 years (1,452,117: median age 76 years, 45% male) in England’s Clinical Practice Research Datalink (2006-2019). Adults hospitalised primarily for infection (severe infection) were matched in calendar date order to individuals without severe infection on age, sex, and primary care practice. Index date was the admission date, same used for the matched unexposed. We measured frailty using Electronic Frailty Index, calculated as a proportion of 36 health deficits in validated categories (Fit 0-0.12, Mild >0.12-0.24, Moderate >0.24-0.36, Severe >0.36). In a time-varying Markov multistate model, we focused on forward transitions from frailty states (fit, mild, moderate, severe) to higher states or death, comparing adults with and without severe infection. For each transition, we separately estimated cause-specific transition hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals using Cox regression, adjusted for baseline frailty score, age, sex, deprivation, alcohol use, smoking, and 5-year prior infection. We explored effect modification by infection type. Results After adjustment, severe infection was associated with higher hazards of transitioning to worsening frailty states or death across all transitions (fit to: mild[1.56, 1.54-1.58], moderate[2.51, 1.79-3.51], death[4.57, 4.50-4.65]; mild to: moderate[1.52, 1.50-1.53], severe[1.90, 1.43-2.52], death[2.67, 2.64-2.70]; moderate to: severe[1.40, 1.38-1.42], death[1.87, 1.85-1.90]; severe to death[1.48, 1.46-1.50]). Transition hazards were strongest for lower respiratory tract infection, followed by sepsis, meningitis/encephalitis, urinary tract infection, and skin and soft tissue infection. Conclusions Severe infection increased the risk of frailty progression in older adults. Key messages • Severe infections may accelerate frailty deterioration in older age. • Infection prevention through vaccination, early detection, and prompt management may help mitigate this decline.

title: Lipoprotein(a) variability in high CV risk patients with hypertriglyceridemia and controlled LDL-C on statin therapy – REDUCE-IT Lp(a) Variability
abstract: Abstract Introduction Therapeutics that dramatically lower lipoprotein(a) (Lp(a)) currently in phase 3 testing have enrolled participants with concentrations above certain thresholds, e.g., ≥70 mg/dL or ≥150 nmol/L. Although repeated testing of Lp(a) is generally viewed as unnecessary due to the fact that concentrations are primarily genetically determined, there are limited data on whether there are characteristics associated with greater variability in Lp(a) measurements over time, which might impact eligibility for these treatments and therefore justify repeated testing. Purpose To document predictors of variability in Lp(a) assessments in a cohort of individuals with elevated triglyceride levels and well-controlled LDL-C who were receiving statin therapy. Methods The analysis cohort comprised participants from the REDUCE-IT trial with measurements of Lp(a) mass concentration at randomisation, month 12, and month 24. Variability in assessments was summarized by a plot of per-participant average versus the range of the three assessments. The range was related to participant characteristics in linear regression models, overall, and for subsets above the LLQ, and with averages above clinically relevant thresholds. Results Among 8179 participants, 5036 (61.6%) had baseline, month 12, and month 24 Lp(a) assessments; median (IQR) Lp(a) concentrations were 11.4 (4.9, 36.7), 12.4 (5.2, 39.2), and 12.5 (5.1, 38.9) mg/dL, respectively. Although the assessments were strongly correlated (all pairwise Spearman r>0.93), variability increased with average concentration (Figure). A total of 5.5% of 416 participants with baseline Lp(a) 30 to <50 mg/dL had at least one subsequent assessment ≥70 mg/dL, whereas 3.2% of 630 participants with baseline Lp(a) ≥70 mg/dL had at least one subsequent assessment <50 mg/dL. While the majority of characteristics were significantly related to range, only baseline and average Lp(a) explained a meaningful proportion of the variance in this outcome (Table). Conclusion In REDUCE-IT, over 24 months, subsets of individuals unselected for Lp(a) shifted in and out of ranges studied in outcomes studies of Lp(a)-targeting treatments. Baseline and average concentration explained a meaningful proportion of variability, suggesting repeated testing of those with relatively high Lp(a) may be warranted to determine eligibility for treatment if these therapeutics are indicated only for individuals with relatively high levels.Figure and Table

title: DPP3 as a Biomarker in Patients with Cardiovascular Critical Illness
abstract: BACKGROUND: Dipeptidyl peptidase 3 (DPP3) exerts vasodilatory and myocardial depressant effects in preclinical models and is a potential therapeutic target in cardiogenic shock (CS). METHODS: Patients admitted to the CICU at Brigham and Women's Hospital were enrolled in a biorepository with samples collected at CICU admission. Using samples from 2017-2023, DPP3 was measured using an immunoluminometric assay (4TEEN4). Shock, defined by hypotension and end-organ hypoperfusion, was adjudicated as CS (classic or vasodilatory) or distributive (DS). Controls were CICU patients without shock. Models were adjusted for age, sex, eGFR, and SOFA score. RESULTS: Of 1082 CICU patients, 381 (35.2%) had CS, 70 (6.5%) had DS, and 618 (57.2%) were non-shock controls. DPP3 values were higher in CS (median, 42.7 [Q1-Q3, 25.6-84.3] ng/mL) than in non-shock controls (31.8 [20.2-57.2] ng/mL; p<0.001) but, nevertheless, were elevated (>30 ng/mL) in 53.6% of non-shock controls. CICU patients with DPP3 >30 ng/mL had higher in-hospital mortality (19.9% vs. 8.4%; OR 2.7 [95% CI 1.8-4.0]; p<0.001), with a consistent pattern across CS, DS, and non-shock patients (p-interaction=0.72) and across CS etiologic subgroups (p-interaction=0.18). In adjusted analyses including both shock and non-shock patients, DPP3 showed a graded association with mortality across quartiles (adj-OR Q4 vs. Q1: 3.0 [1.6-6.1]; p<0.001), and at a 30 ng/mL threshold (adj-OR: 2.1 [1.4-3.4]; p=0.001). CONCLUSION: Among critically ill CICU patients, DPP3 was elevated in shock and non-shock states and was associated with in-hospital mortality. These findings support a potential role for DPP3 as a biomarker for risk stratification and a possible target for therapy.

title: Crosstalk along the gut–liver axis in liver disease: Clinical and mechanistic aspects
abstract: The gut and liver are anatomically and physiologically interconnected, forming a dynamic axis that plays a central role in the pathogenesis of many liver diseases. Gut-derived factors can influence hepatic injury, inflammation, and fibrosis, acting both as disease modifiers and, in some cases, as primary drivers of aetiology. Conversely, liver-derived factors including bile acids shape microbial ecology, epithelial barrier function, and intestinal immune homeostasis. In this review, we provide an overview of the clinical and mechanistic aspects of the gut-liver axis in hepatology. Using autoimmune, metabolic, and toxic hepatobiliary disorders as model conditions, we highlight recent advances in understanding how intestinal permeability, microbiota composition, and immune signalling contribute to disease initiation and progression. Emphasis is placed on the bidirectional nature of gut-liver interactions and their implications for disease stratification, prevention, and therapy. Finally, we identify key knowledge gaps and outline priorities for future research in this rapidly evolving field.

title: Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy with Left Ventricular Outflow Tract Obstruction Managed with Veno‑Venous Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation and Alcohol Septal Ablation
abstract: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (TTC) is a reversible, stress-induced cardiomyopathy characterized by transient left ventricular systolic dysfunction, most commonly presenting with apical ballooning in the absence of obstructive coronary artery disease.1 Dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction (LVOTO) complicates up to 20-25% of cases and is associated with increased morbidity and mortality. Older age, septal bulging, mitral regurgitation, and hemodynamic instability are risk factors for LVOTO.

title: ALPL Expression as a Transcriptional Predictor of Arteriovenous Fistula Failure: Questions and a Path Forward
abstract: We read with interest the article by Si et al.1 describing ALPL as a potential preoperative biomarker of arteriovenous fistula (AVF) failure. Identifying a circulating biomarker that could guide vascular access planning and prioritization would address an important unmet clinical need in patients approaching hemodialysis. The authors reanalyzed existing bulk RNA sequencing data from patients undergoing two-stage AVF creation. However, several methodological issues require clarification before ALPL can be considered a biomarker candidate.

title: Risks of free flap reconstruction amongst smoking patients: a NSQIP analysis of 4653 patients from 2010 to 2021.
abstract: Background: Microvascular free flap reconstruction for complex soft tissue defects relies on vascular perfusion for overall flap survival. Smoking has been linked to complications in postoperative wound healing due to vasoconstriction and weakened immune status. We aim to investigate the impact of smoking on postoperative complications in patients undergoing free flap reconstructive surgery. Methods: Using the American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program (ACS-NSQIP) database, adult patients (≥18 years old) undergoing microvascular free flap surgery (Current Procedural Terminology: 15 756-15 758) from 2010 to 2021 were included. Patients were excluded if they were <18 years old or if they lacked postoperative follow-up data or documented smoking status. Smokers were compared to non-smokers across demographics and postoperative complications. Results: = 0.016). There were no significant differences in rates of superficial or deep incisional SSIs, graft/flap failure, sepsis/septic shock, or venous thromboembolism. Conclusion: Smoking was associated with increased rates of organ/space surgical site infections and wound dehiscence, but not with flap failure in patients undergoing microvascular free flap reconstruction. These findings support the role of preoperative smoking cessation counseling and more nuanced risk stratification focused on wound-related complications rather than flap survival.

title: Zero-Exchange Pulsed Field Ablation Using a Variable Loop Circular Catheter Without a Dedicated Mapping Catheter: An Interim Analysis From the Real-AF Registry
abstract: Pulsed field ablation (PFA) has rapidly emerged as an important treatment modality for atrial fibrillation (AF) ablation. The variable loop circular catheter (VLCC) is a PFA platform integrated with a three-dimensional (3D) electro-anatomic mapping system (CARTO, Biosense Webster, Inc, part of Johnson &Johnson MedTech) that allows operators to deliver ablation therapy while reconstructing left atrial geometry with a single device. As the field of electrophysiology advances toward streamlined, minimal- to zero-fluoroscopy AF ablation, the VLCC offers both map and ablate capabilities that reduces the need for a separate mapping catheter and enables a single-catheter, zero-exchange AF ablation workflow.

title: Composite Endpoints in Critical Care Delirium Trials.
abstract: Delirium is an abnormal mental status, commonly occurring among critically ill patients, in which a person's attention and awareness change acutely. Delirium is associated with negative outcomes, including death. Furthermore, a longer duration of delirium is associated with long-term cognitive impairment in survivors of critical illness. Hence, there is a need for novel interventions that reduce the duration of delirium; however, measuring and analyzing "duration of delirium" as an endpoint in randomized trials is challenging due to the episodic nature of delirium and the competing events of coma and death, which can bias analyses of duration of delirium. Given these challenges, delirium trials have adopted one of two composite endpoints: delirium- and coma-free days, defined as the number of days alive without delirium or coma for both survivors and nonsurvivors, and an alternative composite that ranks death as the worst state and orders days alive without delirium or coma among survivors. To date, these composite endpoints have not been rigorously evaluated. Hence, herein we use data from the Maximizing Efficacy of Targeted Sedation and Reducing Neurologic Dysfunction (MENDS) trial to motivate the use of composite endpoints in critical care delirium trials, discuss how to define the effect of treatment on each composite endpoint and their clinical interpretability, and present a method for visualizing how the treatment effects accrue over the course of follow-up. Based on these analyses, we provide practical recommendations for the use of composite endpoints in critical care delirium trials, which could be extended to other randomized trials that rely on similar composite endpoints.

title: Maternal functional connectivity relates to child behavioral problems and parenting stress across child developmental stages.
abstract: Previous studies have indicated maternal brain changes during pregnancy and the postpartum period, but associations between maternal brain function and ongoing caregiving remain underexplored. This study examined how maternal functional connectivity (FC) patterns are associated with child behavioral problems and parenting stress across child developmental stages. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data were acquired from 307 mothers engaged in caregiving and 35 nulliparous women. Child behavioral problems and parenting stress were assessed using the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL) and Parenting Stress Index (PSI), respectively. Group comparisons of FC in the ventral attention network (VAN), default mode network (DMN), and frontoparietal network, regression analyses examining associations of FC with CBCL and PSI scores across child developmental subgroups, and exploratory moderation analyses were conducted. Mothers exhibited higher FC in the VAN (FDR-p = 0.035) and DMN (FDR-p = 0.033), along with more negative VAN-DMN connectivity (p = 0.016), compared with nulliparous women. Among mothers of preschool-aged children (n = 120), higher CBCL externalizing scores were nominally associated with lower VAN FC (β = -0.17, p = 0.031, FDR-p = 0.093), whereas higher VAN FC was associated with lower PSI total scores (β = -0.21, FDR-p = 0.033). VAN FC moderated the relationship between externalizing problems and parenting stress in this subgroup, with stronger positive associations observed at higher VAN FC (b = 7.41, p = 0.035). Among mothers of school-aged children (n = 142), higher CBCL internalizing scores were associated with higher DMN FC (β = 0.16, FDR-p = 0.039) and more negative VAN-DMN connectivity (β = -0.19, FDR-p = 0.030). These findings suggest associations of maternal network connectivity with motherhood status, child behavioral problems, and parenting stress across child developmental stages.

title: Mapping HIV reservoir geography: lessons for cure from the Last Gift rapid autopsy cohort.
abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Deep tissue reservoirs remain a major barrier to HIV cure. Their anatomical distribution and connectivity are difficult to study in living people. We examine how the Last Gift rapid-autopsy cohort clarifies reservoir connectivity, persistence behind anatomical barriers, and variation within organs, and consider the implications for cure.
RECENT FINDINGS: Tissue studies reveal HIV reservoirs that are interconnected across yet differ between and within anatomical sites. Viral sequence analyses suggest that blood links tissue reservoirs, with gut and lymphoid tissues acting as hubs of viral dispersal. Recovery of replication-competent HIV from brain microglia during suppressive antiretroviral therapy (ART) provides direct evidence of a resident brain reservoir. Even within the gastrointestinal tract, HIV DNA burden and transcriptions vary by region, with different microbiome associations in the small and large bowel.
SUMMARY: HIV reservoir geography supports durable ART-free remission as a practical goal. Achieving this goal will likely require combination therapies with complementary functions and tissue access. Because tissue heterogeneity limits what negative biopsies can establish, remission should be assessed through carefully monitored analytical treatment interruption and long-term follow up.

title: Posterior Transverse Plication of Tortuous Internal Carotid Arteries During Carotid Endarterectomy.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Excessive tortuosity of the internal carotid artery (ICA) can create a risk of kinking after carotid endarterectomy (CEA) with patch angioplasty. Posterior transverse plication (PTP) shortens and straightens the ICA without arterial transection or resection. This study reviewed our outcomes with PTP followed by patch angioplasty during CEA.
METHODS: A retrospective cohort study identified patients who underwent CEA between 2006 and 2023. Patients treated with PTP and patch angioplasty (PTP+P) were compared with a contemporaneous cohort undergoing CEA with Dacron patch closure alone (DP) for the same atherosclerotic carotid disease. Early and long-term outcomes included neurologic events, restenosis, pseudoaneurysm formation, reintervention, and survival.
RESULTS: Of 168 carotid interventions, 116 met inclusion criteria: 16 PTP+P and 100 DP. Patients in the PTP+P cohort were older and had higher rates of chronic renal insufficiency and coronary artery disease. There was no 30-day mortality or postoperative TIA/stroke in either cohort. During follow-up, no ipsilateral ischemic neurologic event occurred, and there was no significant difference in restenosis, pseudoaneurysm formation, reintervention, or overall survival. In adjusted analysis, increasing age was associated with worse survival, while PTP was not.
CONCLUSIONS: In this small series, adding PTP during CEA before patch angioplasty appeared safe for correcting ICA tortuosity. The complication profile was similar to that of patients with straighter ICAs who underwent DP closure alone. A wide patch and intraoperative duplex ultrasound are advisable to prevent and detect technical narrowing at the plication site.

title: Nebulization-Based Pulmonary Delivery of Extracellular Vesicles in Mice.
abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are membrane-bound particles involved in intercellular communication and have attracted increasing interest as carriers for therapeutic molecules. Direct pulmonary administration provides an opportunity to deliver EVs to the respiratory system while potentially limiting systemic exposure. Among pulmonary administration approaches, nebulization offers a noninvasive strategy that avoids direct airway manipulation and can facilitate repeated administration. However, aerosolization may alter EV particle characteristics, making it important to evaluate both the effects of nebulization on the EV preparation and subsequent pulmonary delivery. Here, we describe an integrated workflow for nebulization-based pulmonary delivery of EVs in mice. The protocol includes EV preparation and fluorescent labeling, pre- and post-nebulization EV characterization, assembly and operation of the nebulization system, aerosol exposure of mice, and evaluation of pulmonary delivery and PKH26-associated fluorescence in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) cells. Post-nebulization EV collection provides an additional quality-control step for assessing particle characteristics after aerosolization. This method provides a practical experimental framework for investigating inhaled EVs and for developing EV-based pulmonary delivery strategies.

title: Hearing Status and Its Impact on Arousal and Attentional Allocation: Evidence From Pupillometry and Microsaccades.
abstract: Recently, pupillometry has been combined with fixational eye movements known as microsaccades to quantify the arousal and attentional components of listening effort. However, it is unclear what effect hearing status has on these combined measures. The goal of this study was to evaluate dynamic patterns of sustained arousal and attentional allocation using pupillometry and microsaccade measures, respectively. Twenty-two adults with hearing impairment modeled as a continuous function of pure-tone average, and 28 adults without hearing impairment listened to sentences and affective sounds while their pupil size and microsaccade activity were recorded. Participants with hearing impairment exhibited different time-course pupil responses and altered microsaccade rates than those with normal hearing, suggesting differences in arousal and attentional engagement. These findings represent new dynamic relationships between arousal and attention in participants with and without hearing loss and suggest a utility for measuring these dissociable responses concurrently with pupillometry and microsaccades.

title: Organizational Differences Among US Local Health Departments That Received Data Modernization Funding: Results From the 2023 Forces of Change Survey.
abstract: Objectives. To examine the organizational determinants of data modernization funding among local health departments (LHDs) in the United States and assess their capabilities in managing health information system (HIS) domains, including electronic health record and electronic medical record platform management capacity, outbreak surveillance data source utilization, and availability of dedicated analytical workforce. Methods. Using data from the 2023 National Association of County and City Health Officials Forces of Change survey, we conducted bivariate and logistic regression analyses to examine the association between the receipt of supplemental data modernization funding and HIS domains. Results. Supplemental data modernization funding was unevenly distributed among LHDs across the United States. Large LHDs (serving populations ≥ 500 000) demonstrated higher odds of receiving data modernization funding compared with small jurisdictions (serving populations < 50 000; adjusted odds ratio [AOR] = 3.51; P < .01), whereas state-governed LHDs had significantly lower odds of funding receipt compared with shared-governance agencies (AOR = 0.22; P < .01). Conclusions. Current data modernization funding may disproportionately benefit large and digitally mature LHDs. Achieving national data modernization goals requires a structural shift toward targeted, need-based allocations and regional technical assistance pipelines. (Am J Public Health. Published online ahead of print November 5, 2026:e1-e10. https://doi.org/10.2105/AJPH.2026.308800).

title: Eat, sleep - How and when to treat: A guide for leveraging behavioral sleep medicine for co-occurring insomnia in eating disorder treatment.
abstract: Insomnia symptoms are highly prevalent among individuals with eating disorders, and evidence suggests a bidirectional relationship between sleep disturbances and disordered eating. Although effective and flexible psychological and behavioral treatments for insomnia are available, there is limited research and a lack of clinical guidelines on addressing insomnia in the context of eating disorder concerns. This paper outlines the potential benefits of prioritizing treatment of comorbid insomnia and discusses clinical frameworks for addressing these co-occurring conditions. We highlight how targeting insomnia may improve overall functioning and support eating disorder recovery. A clinical case example is included in the supplement to illustrate decision-making processes that may assist clinicians in determining optimal treatment sequencing and integration for patients presenting with both insomnia and disordered eating symptoms.

title: Kratom Use Among U.S. Adults: Clinical Characteristics and Sex Differences in Co-Occurring Drug Use.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The expansion of kratom's availability, popularity, and product diversity in the United States has drawn scientific and national attention. Characterizing the sociodemographic and behavioral correlates of kratom use may help public health efforts.
METHOD: We examined data from the National Survey of Drug Use and Health (2022-2023), to investigate lifetime prevalence and sociodemographic, mental health, and behavioral correlates of self-reported use of kratom as well as the interaction of cannabis and heroin with sex, given co-used patterns with kratom and report sex differences.
RESULTS: A pooled prevalence estimate of lifetime kratom use among U.S. adults (18+) was 1.95%, of whom 34.84% reported past-year use and 18.39% reported past-month use. Among those with past-year use, 52.79% reported past-month use. Lifetime use was most common among White, unmarried, younger, working males and those with lower incomes, living in poverty, and participating in government assistance programs. In multivariable analysis, lifetime kratom use was associated with lifetime major depressive episodes, use of pain-relieving medications, and past-year serious psychological distress. Lifetime cannabis and heroin use were associated with elevated odds of kratom use in both sexes. However, kratom's relationship with cannabis use was over three times stronger in males, while its relationship with heroin use was approximately half as strong in males compared to females.
CONCLUSION: Kratom use was correlated with specific demographic, behavioral, and sex- and substance-specific characteristics, suggesting the need for more study to examine whether certain populations may benefit from targeted screening and intervention.

title: Percutaneous Endoscopic Gastrostomy Versus Image-Guided Gastrostomy Placement in Patients With Cirrhosis: A Multi-Institutional Research Network Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The selection of an appropriate technique for placement of a gastrostomy tube in patients with cirrhosis remains controversial due to concerns about adverse events. We used real-world data to compare outcomes after percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) versus fluoroscopically guided gastrostomy by an interventional radiologist (IR G-tube) in patients with cirrhosis.
METHODS: We performed a multicenter retrospective cohort study of adults with cirrhosis who underwent gastrostomy tube placement from 2014 to 2023 using the TriNetX Research Network. Using relevant Current Procedural Terminology codes, patients were categorized into 2 groups: PEG (43246/0DH64UZ) or fluoroscopic IR G-tube (49440/0DH63UZ). Periprocedural adverse events were defined as short-term (14 d) or long-term (180 d). Propensity score matching was performed using demographic, clinical, and available laboratory covariates. Binary outcomes were reported as adjusted odds ratios (aOR) with 95% CIs, whereas mortality was reported using adjusted hazard ratios (aHR) from Cox proportional hazards models. Survival was assessed with Kaplan-Meier analysis and log-rank testing.
RESULTS: Of the 5028 patients meeting selection criteria, 1579 underwent PEG placement and 3449 underwent IR G-tube placement. Adjusted odds of periprocedural adverse events for PEG vs IR G-tube were as follows: aspiration pneumonia (aOR: 0.66, 95% CI: 0.51-0.85), hemorrhage (aOR: 0.79, CI: 0.59-1.06), blood transfusion (aOR: 0.99, CI: 0.78-1.27), and infection or peritonitis (aOR: 0.96, CI: 0.68-1.34). In the 6-month follow-up period, PEG placement was associated with lower odds of tube malfunction (aOR: 0.78, 95% CI: 0.64-0.96) and tube replacement (aOR: 0.47, 95% CI: 0.36-0.63). At 6 months, PEG placement was also associated with lower mortality risk (aHR: 0.80, 95% CI: 0.70-0.91; P=0.011).
CONCLUSIONS: In a large multicenter cohort of patients with cirrhosis, PEG and IR G-tube placement had similar short-term rates of bleeding and infectious adverse events, whereas PEG was associated with fewer tube malfunctions and replacements and lower observed mortality at 6 months.

title: Health, Justice, and Community: Findings from Rhode Island's Health and Justice Research Symposium.
abstract: On April 17, 2026, the Center for Health and Justice Transformation (CHJT) convened the Rhode Island Health and Justice Research Symposium at Brown University. The event united researchers, clinicians, community advocates, policymakers, and people with lived experience of the criminal legal system to share findings, build connections, and identify shared priorities. This article synthesizes the proceedings of the symposium along five themes: Evidence-Based Interventions, Pressing Tensions, Existing Barriers, Open Questions, and Shared Vision. Across all five, a single thread recurred: Rhode Island's position as a national innovator in carceral health rests not on the agility afforded by its comparatively small size, but on its collaborative relationships and institutional capacity.

title: Abstract 10078: Mass Spectrometry-Resolved Apolipoprotein(a) Isoform Phenotyping in ODYSSEY OUTCOMES Reveals Determinants of Apolipoprotein(a) Recovery Beyond KIV-2 Variation
abstract: Background: Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is an independent CVD risk factor and guidelines recommend measuring Lp(a) once in a lifetime. If traceability is correctly implemented, Lp(a) should no longer be the most misunderstood metric in laboratory medicine. Commercial Lp(a) test kits can be made traceable to a higher order standard based on bottom-up proteomics with Mass Spectrometry (MS). The MS-based assay detects peptides outside KIV-2 and enables apo(a) reporting in molar units. Notwithstanding clinical equivalence between immunoassay (IA)- and MS-based apo(a) results, discordances occur. In ODYSSEY OUTCOMES trial (OOT), IA-MS discordances were investigated, focusing on average KIV-2 repeats. Objective: An international IFCC working group on Apolipoprotein Standardization developed a higher order MS-based measurement procedure, independent of apo(a) KIV-2 size polymorphism and traceable to WHO-IFCC SRM2B. The relation between average apo(a) KIV-2 repeats and apo(a) levels was investigated in the OOT with the Roche IA-based 2 nd generation test and the MS-based test. Methods: Beyond total apo(a) levels, the MS-based test quantifies KIV-2 dependent peptides and was explored as alternative for apo(a) phenotyping with Western blotting. KIV-2 repeats were calculated by subtracting nine non-KIV-2 repeats from Western blot derived total KIV number. The MS-based method used GTYST/LFLEP molar ratio minus 3; GTYST reflects KIV-2 dependent number and LFLEP the KIV-2 independent number. In 82 sera, Western blot-derived KIV-2 numbers were compared to MS-based KIV-2 number. The impact of apo(a) size polymorphism on apo(a) test recovery was investigated in the OOT biomarker substudy (N = 10,187, KIV-2 range 3.0-46.6) measured by Roche IA and MS. Results: Western blot-derived dominant KIV-2 number correlates with MS-derived average KIV-2 number spanning 6-29 KIV-2 repeats (Y=3.48 + 0.671X; 95% CI: 0.57-0.77; R = 0.824). Roche IA and MS-results were clinically equivalent in most specimens: (Y=1.6+1.033x, 95% CI: 1.028-1.038; R = 0.969). Notably, 2.5% (N = 255) of the discordant specimens showed systematic underestimation of IA-results compared to MS-results . Discordances were found within lower molecular weight apo(a) KIV-2 isoforms (KIV-2 ≤13), with apo(a) concentrations varying from the LOQ to ~800 nmol/L. Conclusion: We developed and validated a metrologically higher order apo(a) MS-based test for determining apo(a) size polymorphism by calculating selective peptide molar ratios reflecting KIV-2 dependent and independent levels. The IA-MS method comparison in the OOT shows excellent clinical equivalence of molar apo(a) test results in 97.5% of serum specimens. Yet, discordance analysis using MS-resolved apo(a) isoform phenotyping reveals other determinants of apo(a) recovery beyond KIV-2 Copy Number Variation.

title: Abstract 16033: Optimizing Surveillance Intervals for Ascending Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms: Is Less More?
abstract: Introduction: Surveillance imaging for ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm (aTAA) aims to detect progression before operative thresholds or adverse events occur, but uniform follow-up intervals may not reflect diameter-specific progression risk. We evaluated whether diameter-stratified patterns can inform optimized diameter-based surveillance intervals. Methods: We performed a single-center retrospective analysis of 733 consecutive patients with ascending aortic diameter ≥40 mm confirmed by contrast CT. Serial aortic diameters were collected from surveillance-labeled CT scans. Patients were stratified by baseline diameter of 40-44 mm, 45-49 mm, and ≥50 mm. Endpoints included progression to ≥50 mm, growth ≥3 mm/year, growth ≥5 mm/year, and aortic surgery. We simulated annual imaging and two diameter-stratified strategies for 40-44, 45-49, and ≥50 mm aortas, respectively: 12/12/6-month and 24/12/6-month intervals updated at each scan. Strategies were compared by 12-month detection, median delay, and scan burden versus annual imaging. Results: Over 733 patients, there were 3,277 aneurysm surveillance scans as indicated by the radiology report. Median follow-up was 6.3 years [3.6-9.2]. In the 40-44 mm group, cumulative incidence of ≥50 mm was 0.3%, 2.2%, and 2.8% at 1, 3, and 5 years, while growth ≥3 mm/year reached 28.8% by 5 years. In the 45-49 mm group, ≥50 mm progression reached 6.3%, 17.3%, and 24.3% at 1, 3, and 5 years, and growth ≥3 mm/year reached 38.3% by 5 years; aortic repair crossed 5%, 10%, and 20% cumulative incidence at 1.3, 3.3, and 9.6 years. In the ≥50 mm group, growth ≥3 mm/year reached 51.7% and aortic repair reached 5%, 10%, and 20% cumulative incidence at 0.1, 0.3, and 1.5 years. The 12/12/6-month strategy detected 75.4% of growth ≥3 mm/year events versus 73.7% with annual imaging, with shorter median delay (162 vs 178 days) and 6.3% more scans. For progression to ≥5.0 cm, annual and 12/12/6-month strategies each detected 77.8% of events, with the same median delay of 175 days. The 24/12/6-month strategy reduced scan burden by 8.6% but detected fewer growth events than annual imaging for both growth ≥3 mm/year (65.4% vs 73.7%) and ≥5 mm/year (60.2% vs 67.7%). Conclusions: Although baseline diameter stratification showed increasing risk of growth and aortic surgery, diameter-based schedules did not meaningfully improve growth detection compared with annual imaging, which balanced detection and scan burden.

title: Abstract 16214: Effects of Beta-Blockade on Lipidomics Profile of Hibernating Myocardium in a Model of Chronic Ischemic Cardiomyopathy
abstract: Background: Chronic artery coronary stenosis can produce stunned and hibernating myocardium. Lipid compounds play an important role in negative metabolic remodeling. Non-targeted metabolomics and lipidomics of stunned myocardium demonstrated reduced fatty acid oxidation, enhanced ketogenic amino acid metabolism, and mitochondrial dysfunction, which was ameliorated after exposure to β-blockade. The molecular mechanisms of hibernating myocardium are not completely understood. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that hibernating myocardium will be characterized by a distinct lipidomic signature, which will be altered in the presence of β-blockade. Methods: In a model of chronic multivessel ischemic cardiomyopathy, we randomized animals into 4 groups (sham, placebo, metoprolol, and carvedilol) after development of left ventricular dysfunction and followed them for 3 months after treatment initiation. We performed non-targeted lipidomics on 28 myocardial samples using ultra-high-performance liquid chromatograph coupled to a high-resolution mass spectrometry system operating in data-dependent acquisition mode. Results : After excluding 1,500 annotated lipid features, 6 lipids remained significant: diacylglycerol 34:0 [DG(16:0/18:0)], diacylglycerol 36:0 [diacylglycerol (18:0/18:0)], ceramide d38:1 [ceramide (d18:1/20:0)], ceramide d40:1 [ceramide (d18:1/22:0)], ceramide d42:1 [ceramide (d18:1/24:0)], and triacylglycerol 48:0 [triacylglycerol (16:0/16:0/16:0)]. These lipid compounds in the placebo group are lower compared to the β-blockade groups. Compared to metoprolol, carvedilol was associated with significantly lower diacylglycerol, triacylglycerol, and ceramide accumulation (Figure 1). Conclusions: In hibernating myocardial tissue produced in a model of chronic multivessel ischemic cardiomyopathy, carvedilol is associated with diacylglycerol reduction, which suggests improved metabolic cardioprotection, possibly related to its antioxidant properties. Since long-chain ceramides are associated with impaired mitochondrial respiration, adverse remodeling, and worsening cardiac function, lower ceramide after carvedilol treatment indicates that the nonselective β-blocker may play a role in reversing unfavorable lipid metabolism. Carvedilol is more favorable than metoprolol in mitigating the adverse lipidomics profile of hibernating myocardium.
