title: Abstract 10036: Apolipoproteins and Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic-Biomarkers Each Add to Prediction of Residual Cardiovascular Disease Risk After Acute Coronary Syndrome: Insights from the ODYSSEY OUTCOMES Trial
abstract: Background: Residual cardiovascular risk persists in acute coronary syndrome (ACS) despite intensive lipid-lowering therapy. We investigated whether extended biomarker profiling, including a 9-plex apolipoprotein panel (with apoE phenotyping) and 11 CE-marked emerging Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic (CKM) parameters, improves prediction of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and death beyond conventional demographic and lipid parameters in the ODYSSEY OUTCOMES trial. Methods: The trial was randomized, double-blind, and compared the PCSK9 inhibitor alirocumab to placebo in patients with recent ACS receiving optimized statin treatment. Over a median follow-up of 2.8 years, the primary MACE endpoint comprised coronary heart disease death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, fatal and nonfatal ischemic stroke, and hospitalization for unstable angina; all-cause death was a secondary endpoint. In 11,843 trial participants (placebo n=5926; alirocumab n=5917) apolipoproteins and apoE phenotype were measured by mass spectrometry and CKM parameters were measured using a Roche Cobas analyzer. CKM parameters included cystatin C, high-sensitivity troponin T (hs cTnT) , NT-proBNP, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, small-dense low-density lipoprotein, GDF-15, sFlt, interleukin 6, insulin, homocysteine, and the NAFLD fibrosis score (Angulo et al . Hepatology . 2007;45:846-54). Incremental multivariable logistic regression models with natural cubic splines were constructed with demographics, diseases and standard lipid parameters (Model 1), apolipoprotein panel (Model 2), and CKM parameters (Model 3). Model performance was assessed using area under the curve (AUC) statistics, DeLong tests and generalized likelihood ratio tests. Due to lower event counts, penalized regression (ridge-type penalty) was applied for death analyses. Results: The baseline model yielded AUCs of 0.66 (0.64 - 0.68) for prediction of MACE and 0.71 (0.68 - 0.74) for death (Figure 1). Addition of apolipoproteins improved the AUCs to 0.69 (0.67 - 0.71) for MACE and 0.76 (0.72 - 0.79) for death. Further addition of CKM parameters improved the AUCs to 0.72 (0.70 - 0.75) and 0.82 (0.79 - 0.85), respectively. For MACE, the five strongest predictors were hs cTnT, apolipoprotein(a), NT-proBNP, diabetes, and cystatin C. For death, the five strongest predictors included NT-proBNP, sex, total cholesterol, age and small dense LDL-C. Conclusion: In statin-treated patients with recent ACS, comprehensive biomarker profiling with a multiplex apolipoprotein panel including apoE phenotypes and emerging CKM tests each provides clinically meaningful improvement in the prediction of MACE and death beyond conventional demographics, disease state and standard lipid profile. These findings support the conclusion that residual risk in ACS is multidimensional.

title: Abstract 10237: The Leptin-to-Adiponectin Ratio Modifies the eGFR-Arterial Stiffness Relationship
abstract: Background: Cardiovascular risk rises early in chronic kidney disease, and arterial stiffness measured by pulse wave velocity (PWV) is a key early mechanism. Obesity drives vascular and kidney injury, but the leptin-to-adiponectin ratio (LAR), an index of adipose dysfunction, may capture this risk better than BMI. We examined whether lower kidney function is associated with greater PWV and whether obesity endophenotypes including LAR modify this relationship. Methods: Cross-sectional analysis of 165 adults from the IR-CKD and Na-MRI cohorts at the Tennessee Valley Healthcare System/Nashville VA and Vanderbilt University Medical Center, excluding diabetes, advanced hypertension, and active inflammation to isolate obesity-specific biology. PWV was regressed on eGFR with adjustment via principal components of age, sex, race, smoking, and mean arterial pressure. We screened for effect modification by BMI, clamp-derived insulin sensitivity (ISI), LAR, IL-6, and hsCRP. Missing covariates were multiply imputed. Results: Median eGFR was 76 mL/min/1.73m2 (IQR 50-100) and PWV 8.5 m/s (7.3-10.2). Lower kidney function was independently associated with greater stiffness: each 10 mL/min/1.73m2 lower eGFR was associated with a 0.295 m/s higher PWV (95% CI 0.166-0.425; P<0.001), explaining 14% of PWV variance beyond covariates (adjusted R2=0.38). Of five endophenotypes, only LAR modified the eGFR-PWV association (interaction P=0.04 after covariate adjustment); BMI, ISI, IL-6, and hsCRP did not. At low LAR (healthy adipose), PWV tracked eGFR steeply and at high LAR (adipose dysfunction), PWV was already elevated at preserved eGFR and changed little across the eGFR range (Figure 1). Conclusions: In non-diabetic adults, lower kidney function is independently associated with greater arterial stiffness, and the leptin-to-adiponectin ratio modifies this relationship. Adipose dysfunction is linked to early, largely eGFR-independent stiffening, whereas with healthy adipose tissue stiffness closely tracks kidney function. The adiponectin-leptin axis as a modifiable target for vascular protection in the cardio-kidney-metabolic syndrome. title: Abstract 11858: Combination Therapy with Finerenone and Empagliflozin by Baseline Risk of Liver Fibrosis in the CONFIDENCE Trial
abstract: Background: The liver is an important organ in cardio-kidney-metabolic (CKM) disease because of its essential roles in glucose homeostasis, cholesterol synthesis, and drug metabolism. We evaluated whether baseline liver fibrosis risk, estimated using the Fibrosis-4 (FIB-4) index, influenced treatment responses to established CKM therapies. Methods: CONFIDENCE was a double-blind, randomized, active-controlled trial evaluating combination therapy with the non-steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist finerenone and the sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor empagliflozin in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and type 2 diabetes. Adults with CKD (eGFR 30-90 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ), albuminuria (urinary albumin-to-creatinine (UACR) ratio 100-≤5000), and type 2 diabetes were randomized 1:1:1 to finerenone 10 or 20 mg/day, empagliflozin 10 mg/day, or combination therapy. The primary endpoint was relative change in log-transformed mean UACR from baseline to Day 180. FIB-4 was calculated as age х AST / (platelets х √ALT) and categorized as low risk (<1.3 if age <65 years; <2.0 if age ≥65 years), intermediate risk (1.3-2.67 if age <65 years; 2.0-2.67 if age ≥65 years), and high risk (>2.67). Linear regression with covariates and stratification factors from the original trial was used to assess treatment effect across FIB-4 categories. Results: Among 755 patients with complete data, the mean baseline FIB-4 score was 1.53 (SD 0.86); 551 (73.0%) were low risk, 145 (19.2%) intermediate risk, and 59 (7.8%) high risk. Mean FIB-4 remained essentially unchanged from baseline to Day 180 (overall mean change 0.006 [SD 0.67]), with no significant differences between the treatment groups (p=0.49). Combination therapy reduced UACR across all FIB-4 groups (low risk: combination -57.0%, vs finerenone -37.3%, vs empagliflozin -33.2%), intermediate risk: combination -48.7%, vs finerenone -35.4%, vs empagliflozin -31.7%, high risk: combination -45.1%, vs finerenone -42.9%, vs empagliflozin -49.1%) ( Figure 1A ). The beneficial effect of combination therapy vs monotherapy was generally consistent across FIB-4 categories (combination therapy vs finerenone: P for interaction = 0.49; combination therapy vs empagliflozin: P for interaction = 0.27) ( Figure 1B ). Conclusions: Approximately 1 in 4 patients with type 2 diabetes and CKD were at intermediate or high risk for liver fibrosis. Combination therapy with finerenone and empagliflozin reduced levels of albuminuria across a range of liver fibrosis risk.

title: Abstract 10911: Combination of Finerenone with Empagliflozin According to Frailty Status Among Participants with Type 2 Diabetes and CKD in the CONFIDENCE Trial
abstract: Background: The CONFIDENCE trial demonstrated additive albuminuria-lowering benefits of simultaneous initiation of SGLT2i and nsMRA among patients with T2D and CKD. Contemporary guidelines increasingly support combination therapy for T2D with persistent albuminuria on background RASi therapy. While frail patients face increased cardio-kidney risk, clinicians may be reluctant to initiate combination therapy in this vulnerable population due to concerns of tolerability, comorbidity, polypharmacy, and uncertain risk-benefit profile. Methods: The CONFIDENCE trial was a double-blind, double-dummy trial which assessed the effect of finerenone plus empagliflozin, finerenone alone, or empagliflozin alone on top of baseline RASi among patient with CKD and T2D. Frailty was assessed using a 28-item Rockwood cumulative deficit frailty index (FI) derived from medical history, vital signs, laboratory values, and medication use and categorized as: not frail (FI I≤ 0.210), more frail (FI II, 0.211-0.310), and most frail (FI III, ≥0.311). The effects of combination therapy on the relative change in UACR from baseline to day 180 and safety outcomes across baseline frailty risk categories were assessed. Results: Among 796 participants with calculable FI, the median FI was 0.27 [0.21-0.32]. Overall, 21%, 49%, and 30% were classified as not frail, more frail, and most frail, respectively. At 180 days, combination therapy significantly reduced UACR levels across all frailty risk categories (not frail: -52.7%; more frail: -55.6%; most frail: -56.9%); Figure 1. Compared with finerenone monotherapy, combination therapy resulted in similar or greater relative reductions in UACR with increasing frailty risk (P Interaction =0.002), whereas treatment effects relative to empagliflozin monotherapy remained consistent across frailty categories (P Interaction =0.67); Figure 2 . Treatment effects of combination therapy relative to either monotherapy were consistent across frailty risk categories among a range of safety endpoints including any adverse event (P Interaction =0.49), serious adverse event (P Interaction =0.59), hyperkalemia (P Interaction =0.34), early eGFR declines (>30% within 30 days) (P Interaction =0.75) and both change from baseline in systolic blood pressure (Day 14: P Interaction =0.56; Day 180: P Interaction =0.76) and eGFR (Day 14: P Interaction =0.53; Day 180: P Interaction =0.34). Conclusion: In the CONFIDENCE trial, frailty was common, affecting more than three-quarters of participants with T2D and CKD. Relative to monotherapy, combination therapy with empagliflozin and finerenone resulted in at least as much UACR lowering over a 180-day period and appeared safe and well tolerated even among participants with the greatest frailty. These findings support the efficacy and tolerability of combination therapy even among patients with the greatest frailty burden.

title: Abstract 15920: Bleeding Into Injury: Ferumoxytol-CMR-Defined Intramyocardial Hemorrhage Identifies a Multi-Domain High-Risk Phenotype After Reperfused STEMI
abstract: Background: Intramyocardial hemorrhage (IMH) occurs in up to 40% of reperfused STEMIs, indicating severe reperfusion injury. Ferumoxytol, an intravascular iron-based contrast agent with potent T1-shortening properties, enables IMH detection on T1-weighted FLASH cine. Quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM) further quantifies paramagnetic iron within hemorrhagic zones, providing a continuous IMH severity measure. However, the multi-domain cardiac impact of IMH presence and severity remains poorly defined. We aimed to characterize associations of ferumoxytol-enhanced CMR (FE-CMR)-defined IMH with acute and follow-up functional, structural, and remodeling domains after reperfused STEMI. Methods: Thirteen reperfused STEMI patients underwent FE-CMR and echo within 72 hours of reperfusion and gadolinium-enhanced CMR at 3-6 months. Patients were classified as IMH+ (n=5) or IMH– (n=8) by post-ferumoxytol FLASH cine with QSM as reference standard. IMH severity was quantified from QSM maps as susceptibility elevation. Groups were compared across acute and follow-up functional, structural, and remodeling domains, with dose-response relationships between susceptibility elevation and these domains assessed within the IMH+ group. Results: In the functional domain, IMH+ patients demonstrated significantly lower acute RVEF (45.0% vs 55.2%, p=0.028) and TAPSE (1.7 vs 2.15 cm, p=0.040), with large-effect trends toward lower acute and follow-up LVEF (39.5% vs 52.1%, p=0.117, ES=0.50 and 37.0% vs 58.3%, p=0.055, ES=0.61). In the structural domain, IMH+ patients had larger follow-up infarct size (19.1% vs 8.0% LV mass, p=0.011) and mass (22.1 vs 8.3 g, p=0.033). In the remodeling domain, IMH+ patients showed a large-effect trend toward adverse LV remodeling (ΔLVEDV +34 vs –9 mL, p=0.149, ES=0.51). Within the IMH+ group, susceptibility elevation correlated significantly with acute LV dysfunction and dilation (LVEF r=–1.00, LVESV r=+0.90), and showed strong correlations with impaired acute strain (GLS r=+0.80, GCS r=+0.70), persistent follow-up LV dysfunction (LVEF r=–0.80), and adverse remodeling (ΔLVEDV/ΔLVESV r=+0.80). Conclusion: FE-CMR-defined IMH identifies a high-risk phenotype with biventricular dysfunction, larger scar, and adverse remodeling. IMH-related susceptibility elevation correlated dose-dependently with LV functional and remodeling indices, supporting its potential as a quantitative tool for IMH severity assessment and risk stratification after reperfused STEMI.

title: Abstract 11783: Racial and Ethnic Differences in the Simultaneous Initiation of Finerenone and Empagliflozin on Urinary Albumin-to-Creatinine Ratio: The CONFIDENCE Trial
abstract: Background: Non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic adults face disproportionately higher lifetime risk of progression to kidney failure in the setting of type 2 diabetes compared with non-Hispanic White adults. While combination finerenone and empagliflozin has demonstrated superior albuminuria reduction over either therapy alone in the CONFIDENCE trial, its effectiveness across racial/ethnic subgroups with the highest disease burden remains underexplored. Methods: We performed a secondary analysis of the CONFIDENCE trial by self-reported race-ethnicity. The trial evaluated the safety and efficacy of simultaneous initiation of finerenone and empagliflozin combination, versus either agent alone in participants with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease. Participants were classified into four subgroups: Asian, non-Hispanic Black, non-Hispanic White, and Hispanic White. Linear regression was used to evaluate the primary outcome of the log-transformed change of UACR from baseline to 180 days, by treatment arm within each subgroup, with formal interaction testing to assess treatment heterogeneity. Safety and adverse events were also evaluated. Results: Among 789 participants with available race-ethnicity data, 371 (47%) self-identified as Asian, 273 (35%) non-Hispanic White, 78 (10%) Hispanic White, and 67 (8%) non-Hispanic Black. Black participants were younger (62 vs. 64-71 years). Asian participants had lower BMI (26.2 vs. 31.7-32.1 kg/m2), lower prevalence of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (21% vs. 24-37%), and higher proportions of never smokers (63% vs. 40-60%) and alcohol abstinence (73% vs. 50-67%) compared to other groups. Combination therapy produced substantial UACR reductions across all subgroups, with clinically meaningful declines observed from day 14 sustained through day 180 (Figure 1). Reductions in UACR from baseline to day 180 with combination treatment were 62% among non-Hispanic White (GMR 0.38; 95% CI 0.31-0.45), 53% among Asian (GMR 0.47; 95% CI 0.40-0.55), 54% among Hispanic White (GMR 0.46; 95% CI 0.32-0.60), and 54% among non-Hispanic Black participants (GMR 0.46; 95% CI 0.25-0.68). The treatment benefit of combination therapy over each monotherapy was consistent across racial and ethnic groups (Figure 1, P-interaction = 0.90 and 0.95 for combination vs. finerenone and vs. empagliflozin, respectively). Hyperkalemia rates were higher with finerenone alone among Hispanic (4.5%), non-Hispanic White (12%), and Asian (14%) participants, whereas rates were highest in the combination group among Black participants (14%). Conclusion: Combined treatment with finerenone and empagliflozin produced consistent and robust reductions in UACR across all racial and ethnic subgroups.

title: Abstract 16504: Age-Specific Alignment of PREVENT-Era Cardiovascular Risk Profiles with Cholesterol-Lowering Medication Use Among Adults in the United States, 2021-2023
abstract: Background: PREVENT estimates 10- and 30-year ASCVD risk beginning at age 30, but contemporary alignment of cholesterol-lowering medication use with PREVENT-era risk profiles is uncertain. Methods: We analyzed NHANES August 2021-August 2023 data among nonpregnant U.S. adults aged 30-79 years without known cardiovascular disease. The outcome was self-reported cholesterol-lowering medication use. PREVENT 10-year ASCVD risk was calculated with the medication input set to “no” to avoid circularity and categorized as low (<3%), borderline (3 to <5%), intermediate (5 to <10%), or high (≥10%). A study-defined layered higher-risk profile included 10-year PREVENT ASCVD risk ≥10%, LDL-C ≥190 mg/dL, non-HDL-C ≥220 mg/dL, or 10-year PREVENT ASCVD risk ≥5% with ≥3 cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) risk factors. Survey weights, strata, and primary sampling units were incorporated. Results: Among 5,567 eligible adults, 3,217 had complete PREVENT 10-year ASCVD risk and medication data. Weighted PREVENT risk distribution was 58.7% low, 14.6% borderline, 18.5% intermediate, and 8.2% high. Medication use increased stepwise across categories: 7.6%, 25.0%, 41.3%, and 52.6% (Rao-Scott F=187.74, p<2.2х10^-16). However, 47.4% of adults with high PREVENT risk were not using medication, while 22.3% of treated adults had low PREVENT risk. In the layered analysis (n=3,253), 20.0% met higher-risk criteria; 8.5% were higher-risk+medication, 11.6% higher-risk+no medication, 11.7% lower-risk+medication, and 68.3% lower-risk+no medication. This 4-category distribution differed by age group (Rao-Scott F=66.34, p<2.2х10^-16). Among higher-risk adults, no-medication prevalence was 79.5%, 87.9%, 63.5%, and 46.3% at ages 30-39, 40-49, 50-64, and 65-79 years. Among adults aged 30-49 years, 13.3% had low 10-year risk but 30-year risk ≥10%, 22.0% had ≥3 CKM risk factors, and 11.8% had non-HDL-C ≥190 mg/dL, while 5.6% reported cholesterol-lowering medication use. Conclusions: Cholesterol-lowering medication use increased strongly across PREVENT-ASCVD categories, suggesting partial alignment. However, higher-risk adults not using medication and treated adults classified as lower risk were both common and age-specific. These findings support potential early-prevention opportunities while emphasizing cautious interpretation because cross-sectional data cannot establish treatment appropriateness and may reflect treatment-lowered risk or uncaptured indications.

title: Abstract 10947: Combination of Finerenone with Empagliflozin Across the Spectrum of Risk of Kidney Failure: The CONFIDENCE Trial
abstract: Background: The Kidney Failure Risk Equation (KFRE) is guideline recommended to predict near-term risk of adverse kidney outcomes in patients with CKD. Whether baseline KFRE risk may modify the safety and efficacy of empagliflozin, finerenone or the combination of empagliflozin and finerenone, initiated simultaneously, is not known. Methods: The CONFIDENCE trial was a double-blind, double-dummy trial which assessed the effect of finerenone plus empagliflozin, finerenone alone, or empagliflozin alone on top of baseline RASi among patient with CKD and type 2 diabetes. The KFRE is a 4-variable score which integrates eGFR, UACR, age, and sex. We calculated the 5-year KFRE score and patients were categorized according to low (<3%), intermediate (3-10%) or high risk (>10%) of kidney failure over 5 years. We assessed relative change in UACR from baseline to day 180 across 5-year KFRE risk categories. Results: Among 780 patients with a calculable baseline KFRE score, the median predicted 5-year risk of kidney failure was 2.7%[0.5%-8.6%]. Overall, 52.1%, 27.1%, and 20.7% of patients were classified as low, intermediate, and high risk of kidney failure, respectively. At 180 days, combination therapy significantly reduced UACR levels across all KFRE risk categories (low: -59.8%; intermediate: -47.7%; and high: -50.4%; P Interaction =0.98); Figure 1. Compared with finerenone or empagliflozin monotherapy, combination therapy resulted in a greater relative reduction in UACR across KFRE risk categories (combination vs. finerenone alone; P Interaction =0.99 and combination vs. empagliflozin alone; P Interaction =0.85); Figure 2. Treatment effects of combination therapy relative to finerenone or empagliflozin monotherapy on any adverse event(P Interaction =0.86), serious adverse event (P Interaction =0.62), hyperkalemia (P Interaction =0.91) and early eGFR declines (>30% within 30 days) (P Interaction =0.51) were consistent across KFRE risk categories. Conclusion: Among patients with CKD and type 2 diabetes in the CONFIDENCE trial, relative to monotherapy, simultaneous initiation of finerenone and empagliflozin produced greater reductions in UACR consistently across the spectrum of baseline 5-year KFRE risk with a similar safety profile. These data support a strategy of combination therapy across a broad range of CKD risk profiles including patients in the higher risk categories.

title: Abstract 10034: Frailty and Quality-of-Life Outcomes After Revascularization for Chronic Limb-Threatening Ischemia: A Post Hoc Analysis of the BEST-CLI Trial
abstract: Background: High frailty level is associated with a two-fold increased risk of mortality after revascularization for chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI), potentially limiting the magnitude of benefit in quality-of-life (QoL) outcomes. To what degree frailty influences the effects of surgical vs endovascular revascularization on QoL outcomes is unknown. Objective: To assess if QoL improvements after revascularization differ by frailty levels and if the relative effects of surgical vs endovascular revascularization on QoL differ by frailty levels. Methods: In BEST-CLI, patients with CLTI were randomized to surgical or endovascular revascularization in two cohorts: Cohort 1 had a suitable single-segment great saphenous vein while Cohort 2 required an alternative bypass conduit. A frailty index (FI; range 0-1) was constructed using the deficit accumulation approach. FI ≥0.45 defined higher frailty. Health-related QoL from baseline to 1 year after the index procedure was assessed using Vascular Quality of Life (VascuQoL; range 1-7), European Quality-of-Life-5D (EQ-5D), the Short Form-12 (SF-12) Physical Component Summary (PCS), SF-12 Mental Component Summary (SF-12 MCS), and the numeric rating scale (NRS) for pain. Linear mixed-effects models evaluated associations of frailty, treatment, time, and their interactions with QoL outcomes. Models included main effects for frailty, treatment, and time, as well as interactions among frailty, treatment, and time. Adjusted mean QoL estimates and treatment arm differences with 95% CIs were estimated within each frailty level and time point. Results: Among 1830 BEST-CLI participants (mean age, 67; 28% female), 1754 had sufficient data for FI calculation (median FI, 0.45). Higher frailty was present in 654 out of 1375 (47.6%) participants in Cohort 1 and 187 out of 379 (49.3%) participants in Cohort 2. QoL and the NRS scores (mean±SD) improved from baseline to 1 year after revascularization across cohorts, frailty levels, and treatment groups (Figures 1 and 2). Among participants with higher frailty in Cohort 1, mean VascuQoL scores improved from 3.00±1.26 to 4.65±1.42 in surgical group and from 3.05±1.18 to 4.74±1.40 in endovascular group (mean change [95% CI]: 1.65 [1.43 to 1.87] vs. 1.69 [1.47 to 1.90], respectively; mean between-group difference, -0.040 [-0.345 to 0.266]). Participants with higher frailty had lower QoL scores at baseline and 1 year compared to participants with lower frailty. Frailty level did not significantly modify the effects of surgical vs endovascular revascularization on QoL or pain outcomes. Conclusions: Participants with higher frailty experienced similar improvements in QoL outcomes after revascularization compared to those with lower frailty. Revascularization should be considered in patients with CLTI regardless of frailty level to reduce pain and preserve QoL during the remaining years of life.

title: Abstract 8761: Comparison of Lipoprotein(a) and Other Apolipoprotein B Containing Lipoproteins as Predictors of Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events in REDUCE-IT
abstract: Background: Lipoprotein(a) (Lp(a)) and other atherogenic lipoproteins, including low density lipoprotein (LDL), contain one molecule of apolipoprotein B (apoB) per particle. Recent studies indicate Lp(a) is more atherogenic and prognostic for major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) than LDL-C on a per particle basis. However, because there are far fewer Lp(a) particles than LDL particles, the overall risk from LDL is usually much greater. In REDUCE-IT, icosapent ethyl (IPE) consistently reduced MACE across the distribution of baseline Lp(a) levels, including among those with clinically relevant elevations. The present post hoc analysis tested the hypothesis that, after LDL-C control with a statin, Lp(a) is more strongly associated with MACE on a per particle basis than non-Lp(a) apoB-containing particles. Methods: Baseline molar Lp(a), estimated as measured mass concentration х 2.5, and (molar) apoB were assessed in 6988 REDUCE-IT participants, randomized to receive 2g twice daily of IPE or matching placebo and followed for a median 4.9 years. Study inclusion criteria included statin therapy, LDL-C 41 to 100 mg/dL, established CV disease, or diabetes plus ≥1 additional risk factor, and baseline fasting TG 150 to 499 mg/dL. Non-Lp(a) apoB was calculated as total apoB - Lp(a), all in nmol/L. ApoB, non-Lp(a) apoB and Lp(a) in both treatment groups were related to risk of the study primary endpoint MACE with proportional hazards models. Results: Median (Q1, Q3) apoB, non-Lp(a) apoB and Lp(a) concentrations were 1591 (1397, 1804), 1528 (1328, 1738) and 29 (13, 93) nmol/L, respectively. Adjusted for treatment assignment, HRs (95% CI) for MACE per 50 nmol/L increment were 1.006 (0.998, 1.015) (p=0.13) for apoB alone and, in a joint model, 1.004 (0.996, 1.012) (p=0.36) for non-Lp(a) apoB and 1.062 (1.034, 1.091) (p<0.0001) for Lp(a). Results were similar for subgroups with Lp(a) ≥150 (n=1142) or <150 nmol/L (n=5846) (Figure). Applying different multipliers of Lp(a) mass to estimate molar concentration (2.25, 2.75) yielded comparable results. Analysis by quartile revealed Lp(a)-associated risk was restricted to the highest quartile (>93 nmol/L; Table). Conclusion: Among participants with statin-controlled LDL-C in REDUCE-IT, Lp(a) was related to risk of MACE whereas non-Lp(a) apoB was not prognostic, including those with clinically relevant elevations in Lp(a). These findings suggest Lp(a) is an important therapeutic target among those with LDL-C controlled on statins, but with elevated baseline TG, independent of IPE treatment.

title: Abstract 5223: Vigorous Exercise is Associated with Better Quality of Life in Adult Patients with Long QT Syndrome: Data from the Multinational Lifestyle and Exercise in LQTS (LIVE-LQTS) Study
abstract: Background: The LIVE-LQTS study found that vigorous exercise did not increase arrhythmic risk in long QT syndrome (LQTS) patients. The impact of exercise on quality of life (QOL) in adult patients with long QT syndrome (LQTS) has not been described. Objective: This analysis assessed quality of life (QOL) in LQTS patients who exercised vigorously compared to those who did not. Methods: LQTS patients, age 18-60 years, were enrolled at 38 sites from 2015-2022 and reported baseline QOL with Short Form-36 domains [Physical Functioning (PF), Role Limit-Physical, Vitality, Emotional Functioning, Role Limit-Emotional, Social Functioning, Body Pain, and General Health (GH)]. Exercise intensity was defined as vigorous (≥6 Metabolic Equivalent Task > 60 hours per year) or non-vigorous. Covariates included demographic and clinical variables and doctor recommended exercise restrictions. General Linear Models was used to construct models and effect size associations were reported [Partial Eta 2 , ɳ 2 ]. Results: Of 920 patients (age 37±11 years; 25% male), 434 exercised vigorously and 486 were in the non-vigorous exercise group. After controlling for other variables, vigorous exercise was associated with significantly higher QOL in all domains (except Emotional Functioning), compared with non-vigorous exercise. There were moderate positive associations on higher PF (ɳ 2 = 0.05), and GH (ɳ 2 = 0.04) (Table). Doctor-recommended exercise restrictions were also associated with significantly lower QOL in all domains (except Body Pain) with a moderate negative association on PF (ɳ 2 = 0.04). Conclusions: Among adults with LQTS, vigorous exercisers and patients with fewer doctor-recommended exercise restrictions reported better QOL in almost all QOL domains. These results should inform shared decision-making among providers and LQTS patients considering vigorous exercise.

title: Abstract 19094: Bioenergetics Alternations in Platelets Positively Correlates to Myocardial Energetic Changes and Physical Function in Cardiovascular Patients
abstract: Background: Impaired myocardial bioenergetics is critical in myocardial contractile failure. Current approaches to evaluating myocardial bioenergetics are limited. 31 P MRS is an established non-invasive approach to assess myocardial function, but it requires specialized equipment and can be cumbersome for patients. Recent evidence suggests that platelets can serve as a minimally invasive biomarker for systemic bioenergetics. The goal of this study is to determine whether platelet bioenergetics is altered in cardiovascular patients and whether it correlates to myocardial energetic changes and physical function. Methods: Twenty-four patients (18 males, 6 females, 21 white) were recruited, among which 5 have HFpEF (21%), 3 have diabetes mellitus (12.5%), 15 have hypertension (62.5%), and 16 have hyperlipidemia (66.7%). The mean age is 67.6 years (range from 42 to 91). Mean body mass index is 27.64 kg/m 2 (range from 21 to 39). Blood was drawn for platelet isolation and platelet bioenergetics assessment using high resolution respirometers (Oroboros) with the substrate-uncoupler-inhibitor titration protocol. Meanwhile, 31 P MRS was performed to assess myocardial energetics, including total ATP, PCr/total ATP ratio, PCr/β-ATP ratio, PCr/α-ATP ratio, and PCr/γ-ATP ratio. The 6-minute walk test (6MWT) and Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ) were used to assess physical function and quality of life. Results: We established the methodology to isolate high quality platelets with yield at ~85 million/mL blood and successfully measured platelet bioenergetics profiling using Oroboros. Our data showed that platelet mitochondrial bioenergetics significantly correlates to 31 P MRS, including maximal respiration and spare respiration with PCr/total ATP ratio and maximal respiration and spare respiration with PCr/β-ATP ratio. 31 P MRS data showed that higher PCr/total ATP ratio, PCr/α-ATP ratio, and PCr/β-ATP ratio are associated with better 6MWT after adjusting for age and sex (β=339.4, p=0.12; β=133.7, p=0.10; β=98.1, p=0.09, respectively). In contrast, higher platelet bioenergetics parameters, including basal respiration, ATP-linked respiration, and maximal respiration, are associated with better 6MWT (β=1277.6, p=0.06; β=1307.1, p=0.07; β=7458.8, p=0.08, respectively) and better KCCQ (β=91.2, p<0.01; β=97.5, p<0.01; β=41.4, p<0.05, respectively) after adjusting age and sex. Conclusion: To our knowledge, this is the first study to examine relationship between platelet bioenergetics with myocardial energetics and patient physical function. Our data identified a novel energetics relationship between platelets and myocardium in patients with cardiovascular diseases. Platelet bioenergetics could be used as a biomarker to monitor the progress of cardiovascular diseases and the response to treatments, which warrant further investigation.

title: Abstract 8930: Acquired Right Coronary Artery to Right Atrial Fistula Following Bentall Repair Presenting with Ventricular Arrhythmia
abstract: Abstract: Coronary artery fistulas (CAF) are abnormal communications between coronary arteries and a cardiac chamber or vascular structure, with an incidence of 0.1%-0.2%. Acquired CAF following Bentall repair is exceedingly rare. We report a patient presenting with chest pain and ventricular arrhythmia in whom imaging identified a right coronary artery (RCA) to right atrium (RA) fistula 2 years post Bentall. Despite a Qp/Qs below conventional intervention thresholds, progressive symptoms prompted workup. This case highlights the limitations of applying congenital shunt criteria to acquired adult CAF, where management recommendations remain extrapolated from small case series. Introduction: CAF may be congenital or acquired. Iatrogenic CAF have been reported after cardiac surgery, though acquired fistulas following Bentall repair are exceptionally rare. Management guidelines are derived from congenital heart disease literature, and no specific criteria exist for acquired CAF. Patient Info: The patient reported progressive exertional fatigue and substernal chest pain at rest. Device interrogation revealed a 45-second self-terminating Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia (PMVT). Examination revealed an early peaking 3/6 systolic ejection murmur. Diagnostic Assessment: Coronary angiography demonstrated a fistula from the RCA conus branch draining into the RA without obstructive disease. Cardiac MRI demonstrated a Qp/Qs of 1.03 and inferior mesocardial LGE in the mid ventricle. ETT SPECT revealed a fixed inferolateral perfusion defect without inducible ischemia. Exercise right heart catheterization demonstrated a Qp/Qs of 0.88 with an oxygen saturation step up in the RA. Therapeutic Intervention: Following multidisciplinary evaluation, conservative management was chosen given multiple prior sternotomies and absence of significant shunting. Although 2008 ACC/AHA guidelines recommend closure of small to moderate CAF with associated arrhythmia, the presence of mesocardial LGE, combined with absence of inducible ischemia at 13.7 METs, precluded definitive attribution of the arrhythmia to the fistula alone and argued against intervention. An ICD was placed before discharge with a plan for repeat elective coronary angiography in 1 year. Discussion & Synthesis: Intervention thresholds for CAF are extrapolated from congenital heart disease, where Qp/Qs ≥1.5 traditionally prompts closure, yet data are limited to small case series. In this case, Qp/Qs below 1.5 with absence of inducible ischemia at high workloads argued against hemodynamically significant coronary steal, while coexisting mesocardial LGE highlighted the limitations of attributing arrhythmia to the fistula alone. To our knowledge, this is the first reported acquired RCA conus branch-to-RA fistula following Bentall repair presenting with ventricular arrhythmia.

title: Abstract 7871: Exosomes Derived from p53 Silenced Bone Marrow Derived Mesenchymal Stromal Cells (BM-MSCS) Prevent Adipogenesis
abstract: Background and Objective: Obesity associated with type 2 diabetes (T2DM) is known to cause white adipose tissue hyperplasia associated with oxidative stress. Stem/ progenitor cell therapy may provide a novel strategy for treating obesity- and diabetes-related complications. Our laboratory has shown success in using p53-silenced endothelial progenitor cells (EPCs) in disease models such as hyperglycemia-associated peripheral vascular disease (PVD) and kidney disease. Subsequently we have shown conditioned media (CM) derived from p53shMSCs reduced apoptosis and helped to improve endothelial health via antioxidant gene upregulation in hyperglycemia. So we decided to investigate whether exosomes derived from P53sh-MSCs conditioned media (CM) can be used to inhibit adipogenesis in T2DM/obesity states. Methods: Ad-human-P53 (TP53)-shRNA is used to silence P53, and Ad-scrambled-null-shRNA was used as control in BM-MSCs. Exosomes were isolated from the condition medium (CM) collected from BM-MSCs transduced with either Ad-P53sh or scrambled (three variables) as described in our previous publications. In vitro, adipose MSCs (made adipogenic with responsive adipogenic media) were exposed to exosomes derived from p53-sh-BM-MSC-CM. The adipo-MSCs were analyzed by Oil O red stain. Area of Oil red stain was calculated by ImageJ analysis, followed by fat-specific gene expression qPCR Results: Adipogenesis was noted and stained by Oil red O staining of lipid droplets. Decrease in oil droplets was noted in cells exposed to exosomes derived from P53sh-MSCs CM as compared to exosomes derived from scrambled CM by nearly 50%. Gene expression studies demonstrate approx. 40% reduction in FABP4 and PPARG gene expression and upregulation in antioxidant gene expressions such as SOD2 and Catalase mRNA expressions. A reduction in inflammatory gene expressions such as interleukin-6 and TNF-a were also noted Conclusion: Exosomes from P53sh-MSCs-CM reduced adipogenesis via antioxidant upregulation pathway and also by reducing inflammatory signals. Such exosomes can serve as a cell free therapeutic modality to treat obesity and associated complications like non-alcoholic fatty liver disease

title: Abstract 9690: Association of Granular Measures of Myocardial Structure and Function in Bi-Racial Community Cohorts
abstract: Introduction: Myocardial radiomics and strain analysis may provide complementary assessments of left ventricular (LV) tissue characteristics and mechanics beyond conventional measures of LV structure and function. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that even in cine cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), radiomics patterns reflecting myocardial heterogeneity are associated with impaired LV mechanics measured by strain in adults in the community. Methods: We included participants from the Framingham Heart Study (FHS, n= 1,276) Exam 8 and the Jackson Heart Study (JHS, n= 1,191) Visit 3 with cine 1.5T CMR (Philips Achieva, Siemens Espree, respectively) and contemporaneously assessed covariates. Mean radiomics features across 5 end-diastolic frame short-axis cine CMR images (base to apex) were extracted using PyRadiomics and normalized for comparison across radiomics families. Among 102 features with published reproducibility, we excluded those with high correlation (r≥0.8) and collinearity (variance inflation factor (VIF) ≥ 10). To minimize multiple testing, one feature per texture family was selected based on the highest correlation with prevalent cardiovascular disease (CVD). Each feature was evaluated as a standardized predictor of LV global longitudinal, circumferential, and radial strain (GLS, GCS, GRS, respectively) derived from CMR feature-tracking using multivariable linear regression adjusting for age, sex, prevalent CVD, systolic blood pressure (SBP), fasting glucose, cholesterol/high-density lipoprotein (HDL) ratio, left ventricular end-diastolic volume index (LVEDVi), left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), and left ventricular mass index (LVMI) with Benjamin-Hochberg false discovery rate correction. Results: Participants in the FHS cohort were older, with more men, a higher prevalence of CVD, and larger LV cavity size but lower mass index with more favorable strain measures compared to JHS (Table). Texture-based features such as first-order energy measuring statistical signal variation, gray level co-occurrence matrix (GLCM) measuring spatial heterogeneity, gray level dependence matrix (GLDM) measuring signal complexity, and gray level run length matrix (GLRLM) assessing neighboring texture patterns were associated with more positive GCS and negative GRS, indicating less favorable measures (Figure). Similar, though weaker, associations with GLS were seen. Features indicative of greater gray-level sizes were associated with less favorable strain patterns. Conclusion: Non-contrast LV myocardial texture heterogeneity is associated with less favorable mechanics independently of demographic and clinical variables and traditional measures of LV structure and function. Further study of these measures may offer insight into CVD beyond traditional clinical measures.

title: Abstract 9256: Integrating High-Sensitivity C-Reactive Protein Into Risk Equations for Individuals with Established Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease
abstract: Background: Cardiovascular (CV) inflammation, measured by high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP), is associated with higher residual CV risk in patients with atherosclerotic CV disease (ASCVD). HsCRP is included in the secondary CV risk prediction tool Secondary Manifestations of ARTerial disease 2 (SMART2) in Europe. However, risk prediction tools are not consistently used in US secondary prevention, and primary prevention risk prediction tools, such as the Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular Disease Events (PREVENT) equation, do not account for hsCRP. Research question: Does inclusion of hsCRP improve the ability of existing CV risk scores to assess risk of CV events in patients with ASCVD? Methods: This retrospective cohort study identified patients with established ASCVD, an hsCRP measurement, and all necessary data for the risk equations from Komodo’s Healthcare Map (01/01/2017-7/31/2025). Patients were followed for subsequent major adverse CV events (revised 3-point MACE: composite of all-cause mortality, nonfatal MI, and nonfatal stroke). Cox proportional hazards models were used to examine the association between hsCRP and CV events. Nested prediction models with and without hsCRP were compared via likelihood ratio tests. Net reclassification improvement (NRI) and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI) were used to compare performance of models using SMART2 and PREVENT risk factors, with and without hsCRP to explore the potential applicability of PREVENT risk factors in secondary prevention. Results: Of 7,285 included patients, 62.2% had coronary artery disease, 36.1% had peripheral artery disease, and 6.7% had ischemic stroke. The mean age was 64.3 years, and the mean follow-up time was 38.6 months. The majority of patients were White (60.2%) and 51.9% were male. At baseline, 37.2% of patients had diabetes, 73.8% were on antihypertensives, 71.1% were on statins, and 36.1% were on aspirin. After controlling for SMART2 risk factors, hsCRP was independently associated with higher risk of revised 3-point MACE (hazard ratio [HR] per 1 mg/L hsCRP increase, 1.04; 95% CI, 1.01-1.06) and all-cause mortality (HR, 1.07; 95% CI, 1.03-1.11). Similarly, hsCRP was independently associated with higher risk of revised 3-point MACE (HR, 1.04; 95% CI, 1.01-1.07) and all-cause mortality (HR, 1.08; 95% CI, 1.04-1.12) when controlling for PREVENT risk factors (Figure). Likelihood ratio tests indicated that models with hsCRP demonstrated significantly better model fit than models without hsCRP. The addition of hsCRP significantly improved the NRI and IDI for MACE prediction (Table). Conclusions: This study reaffirms the association of CV inflammation with CV risk. Current US risk scores do not account for inflammation and may underestimate patient risk. Integration of hsCRP into risk equations could better stratify patient risk and refine clinical decision-making.

title: Abstract 7767: Beyond Galectin-3: Whole-Blood Transcriptomic Profiling Identifies LGALS1 as the Dominant Correlate of Systolic Blood Pressure in African Americans
abstract: Background: Hypertension remains a leading contributor to cardiovascular morbidity and disproportionately affects African Americans. Galectins are β-galactoside-binding proteins implicated in vascular biology, inflammation, and fibrosis. Prior cardiovascular research has focused predominantly on LGALS3 (Galectin-3), whereas the relative contributions of other galectin family members to blood pressure regulation remain largely unknown. Methods: Whole-blood mRNA sequencing data from 419 untreated African Americans in the GENE-FORECAST cohort (mean systolic blood pressure, SBP, 147 ± 37 mmHg; 50.4% hypertensive; 59 % male/41% female) were analyzed. Four galectin genes (LGALS1, LGALS3, LGALS8, and LGALS9) had sufficient expression and were evaluated using generalized linear models adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index. Gene expression values were standardized to z-scores to allow direct comparison of effect sizes across galectin family members. The LGALS3/LGALS1 ratio was also analyzed to assess potential balance between the two most biologically characterized galectins. Secondary analyses included connections to cardiac MRI phenotypes and four circulating inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, IL-10, and TNF-α). Results: As expected, LGALS3 was associated with SBP (β = 4.1, P = 0.019). Of the four, LGALS1 exhibited the strongest association with SBP (β = 13.2, P = 7.6 х 10 − 1 5 ), with associations also observed for LGALS9 (β = 9.7, P = 7.6 х 10 − 9 ) and LGALS8 (β = –6.5, P = 1.7 х 10 − 4 ). The LGALS3/LGALS1 ratio inversely associated with SBP (β = –10.2, P = 2.34 х 10 − 9 ), indicating a higher balance towards pro-inflammation. Secondary analyses revealed distinct cardiac phenotype associations: LGALS1 and LGALS3 with ejection fraction, LGALS9 with cardiac output and end-diastolic volume, and LGALS8 showed an inverse association with cardiac output. Cytokine analyses revealed distinct inflammatory profiles: LGALS1 positively associated with IL-1β (P = 0.002); LGALS3 inversely with TNF-α (P = 0.040); LGALS8 positively with IL-6 (P = 0.005); and LGALS9 positively with IL-10 (P = 0.007) and positively with TNF-α (P = 0.052). Conclusions: By systematic transcriptomic profiling of galectin family members in untreated African Americans, LGALS1 emerged as the dominant whole-blood correlate of SBP, surpassing LGALS3 in both magnitude and statistical significance. Distinct galectin family members demonstrated divergent cardiovascular and inflammatory association profiles, supporting a transcriptionally heterogeneous galectin network in hypertension. These findings identify LGALS1 as a high-priority candidate biomarker and potential mediator of hypertension-related vascular stress in African Americans.

title: Abstract 7932: Efficacy of Finerenone in Primary Cardiovascular Prevention: A Mechanistic Analysis Using the AHA PREVENT™ Risk Score
abstract: Background: The prespecified FIDELITY analysis of two phase 3 trials found that finerenone reduced the risk of cardiovascular (CV) events in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D) and chronic kidney disease (CKD); however, the magnitude of benefit in patients without prior CV disease (CVD) has not been characterized. The American Heart Association (AHA) Predicting Risk of cardiovascular disease EVENTs (PREVENT™) equations estimate 10-year CVD risk using a base model of clinical and hemodynamic characteristics and a full model that includes additional factors, such as the urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) and glycated hemoglobin, adapted to a T2D and CKD population. Research Question: Is the impact of finerenone on cardiovascular risk in patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease, without a history of cardiovascular disease, influenced by the baseline PREVENT™ score? Does finerenone treatment mitigate the progression of the longitudinal score? Methods: In this post hoc analysis of the FIDELITY dataset, we stratified patients into tertiles of baseline PREVENT™ score (low/intermediate/high risk; base and full models) and calculated hazard ratios (HRs) using a Cox proportional hazards model for time to first non-fatal CV event. Treatment effect heterogeneity between tertiles was assessed via the interaction p -value. We calculated cumulative incidence and the number needed to treat (NNT) at 3 years for the time to first occurrence of a non-fatal CV event, based on Aalen-Johansen estimates. The change in PREVENT™ score up to Month 48 was analyzed using a linear mixed-effects model. Results: In total, 7050 patients without prior CVD were included (3519 finerenone; 3531 placebo). The effect of finerenone on non-fatal CV events was consistent across baseline PREVENT™ tertiles (Figure 1; base model low tertile HR [95% confidence interval] was 0.89 [0.60-1.32], intermediate 1.11 [0.79-1.56], high 0.85 [0.65-1.11]; p interaction 0.57 [base model] and 0.41 [full model]). Absolute benefit increased with baseline risk with lowest 3-year NNT seen in the high-risk tertile (28 patients, full model; Figure 2). Finerenone significantly reduced the progression of PREVENT™ score relative to placebo at Month 48 using the base model (least squares mean difference -0.018; p<0.01) and from Month 4 using the full model (p<0.0001; Figure 3). Conclusion: Finerenone demonstrated consistent CV benefit across AHA PREVENT™-estimated risk levels. The most significant absolute benefit and lowest NNT were observed in the highest risk tertile, supporting risk-based identification of individuals most likely to benefit. Finerenone also significantly decelerated longitudinal PREVENT™ score progression, with its greater effect in the comprehensive model including UACR supporting albuminuria reduction as a key mechanistic mediator of its disease modifying effects.

title: International Consensus Meeting on Preclinical Models of Osteoarthritis: Summary From the Aging Section.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a highly heterogeneous disease, with aging as its strongest risk factor. However, much of the preclinical OA research disproportionately relies on post-traumatic OA (PTOA) models in young animals. To address this gap, the Aging Section of the 2026 International Consensus Meeting (ICM) on Preclinical Models of OA convened experts and used the Delphi method to provide consensus guidance on studying age-associated OA. Eighteen questions concerning pain, biomechanics, genetics, metabolism, sex/hormonal differences and translational modeling were evaluated and voted upon at the 2026 Orthopedic Research Society (ORS) annual meeting. The consensus concluded that although age-associated OA and post-traumatic OA (PTOA) share pathological features, they are characterized by distinct mechanistic profiles, particularly in their inflammatory responses, mitochondrial dysfunction, and tissue-remodeling processes. Furthermore, delegates concluded that age-associated OA is a manifestation of broader aging biology, influenced by the hallmarks of aging, systemic physiology and interacting joint tissues. When evaluating these complex interactions, the available data demonstrate that no single ideal animal model exists. Instead, researchers must utilize a fit-for-purpose model ecosystem that explicitly accounts for sex, endocrine aging, and genetic background. The consensus also recommends employing multimodal outcome measures spanning structural, behavioral, and molecular domains rather than relying solely on structural pathology. Ultimately, age-associated models should serve as a complementary framework to PTOA models. Integrating this specific biological context is essential to improve translational relevance and identify biologically relevant mechanism-based interventions for the aging patient populations most affected by the disorder.

title: AGA/AASLD Clinical Practice Guideline on Management of Primary Biliary Cholangitis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND & AIMS: Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is a chronic cholestatic liver disease associated with progressive fibrosis, cirrhosis, liver transplantation, and premature mortality. Despite effective therapies, important challenges remain in the diagnosis and management of PBC, including identification of antimitochondrial antibody-negative disease, assessment of response to ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), risk stratification, treatment of patients with inadequate response, management of cholestatic pruritus, and prevention of recurrent disease after liver transplantation. The aim of this guideline was to develop evidence-based recommendations addressing these key areas of clinical care.
METHODS: The American Gastroenterological Association (AGA) and the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) convened a multidisciplinary panel to develop clinical practice recommendations for adults with PBC. Systematic reviews were performed for 6 prioritized clinical questions. The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation framework was used to prioritize clinical outcomes and assess evidence, and its Evidence to Decision Framework was used to develop recommendations.
RESULTS: The guideline panel agreed on 6 recommendations. These recommendations address the use of PBC-specific antinuclear antibodies in antimitochondrial antibody-negative suspected PBC, UDCA as first-line therapy, liver stiffness measurement for prognostication, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor agonists for patients with inadequate response or intolerance to UDCA, linerixibat for moderate to severe pruritus, and UDCA prophylaxis post-transplantation to reduce disease recurrence. The certainty of evidence ranged from moderate to very low.
CONCLUSIONS: The guideline emphasizes early diagnosis, optimization of first-line therapy, risk-based treatment escalation, symptom management, and prevention of post-transplantation disease recurrence to improve patient outcomes and quality of life.

title: Medial clavicle fracture with anterosuperior sternoclavicular joint dislocation: joint-sparing suture anchor imbrication and open reduction internal fixation
abstract: Medial clavicle fractures with sternoclavicular joint (SCJ) dislocation are rare and can threaten nearby mediastinal structures when severely displaced. We report a case of a man in his 20s who sustained a high-energy skiing injury, resulting in a displaced medial clavicular fracture-dislocation with SCJ instability. CT and radiographic imaging revealed marked displacement and rotation of the medial fragment in close proximity to the left subclavian and brachiocephalic venous structures. Due to the surgical risk, vascular and thoracic surgery were consulted preoperatively. The patient underwent open reduction and internal fixation with SCJ capsular repair, preserving joint function through suture anchor imbrication and mini-fragment plate fixation, and remained neurovascularly intact postoperatively. To our knowledge, this is the first reported acute anterosuperior SCJ fracture-dislocation in close proximity to the head and neck vessels, highlighting the importance of thorough radiographic evaluation and multidisciplinary perioperative planning.

title: Training and knowledge of women’s health topics: A survey of neuropsychologists and trainees
abstract: Objective: Training in women’s health topics is limited, impacting clinicians’ preparedness to address sex-specific concerns. Little is known about the extent neuropsychologists receive structured education in these areas or their comfort with addressing women-specific neurocognitive concerns in practice. This study examined neuropsychologists’ self-reported training exposure, clinical comfort, and objective knowledge regarding women’s health. Method: A cross-sectional online survey was completed by neuropsychology trainees (29%) and professionals (34% early-, 20% mid-, 17% senior-career) recruited through listservs and social media. Demographics, self-reported training exposure and clinical comfort, and an objective 5-item knowledge quiz were collected. Descriptive statistics examined differences in comfort and knowledge by training, work setting, and career stage. Results: Participants (n = 122) were predominantly white/non-Hispanic (84%) women (91%) in the United States (89%), with diverse professional roles and work settings. Results showed 59% reported no formal training and 41% reported “slight to no comfort” addressing women’s health concerns. Although item-level accuracy on the knowledge quiz was high (68.03-95.08%), 48% of participants answered all items correctly; performance did not differ by training, setting, or career stage. Conclusions: Findings indicate limited formal training, low comfort addressing women-specific neurocognitive issues in clinical care but intact knowledge on common women’s health questions. This gap may perpetuate sex-related disparities in patient care and research in this area. Formalized training initiatives are warranted to improve confidence and competence for neuropsychologists.

title: Sex-Specific Coronary Plaque Characteristics and Risk of Cardiovascular Events: Insights from ISCHEMIA.
abstract: Among the highly diseased population of participants with chronic coronary syndromes and obstructive coronary artery disease enrolled in the ISCHEMIA trial, women had lower burden of total, calcified, non-calcified plaque and adverse plaque characteristics on CCTA compared with men. However, the risk associated with greater atherosclerotic burden was higher among females for the composite outcome of CV death or MI than males. These findings highlight important sex-specific differences in the prognostic value of coronary atherosclerotic burden and support the need to explore differential approaches to cardiovascular risk stratification in men and women.

title: A Primer on Economic Evaluation of Vocational Rehabilitation Programs.
abstract: Though substantial evidence supports the effectiveness of vocational rehabilitation programs (VRPs) in increasing competitive employment among adults with mental illness, much less evidence has evaluated the value or economic impacts of VRP, a critical component to evaluating programs. Our objectives in this primer are (1) to describe different types of economic evaluations, including cost-effectiveness analysis, cost-benefit analysis, return-on-investment analysis, and budget impact analysis, (2) to provide concrete examples of published economic evaluations as applied to VRPs focused on adults with mental illness based on a narrative view of the literature, and (3) discuss methodological issues and provide recommendations in conducting economic evaluations of VRPs related to measurement of relevant costs, measurement of employment outcomes, measurement of health and health care outcomes, conducting multiple types of economic evaluations, analysis perspectives, and economic expertise. This information can assist vocational rehabilitation researchers, leaders, and funders of these programs, who may be less familiar with the application of economic evaluation to research on VRP, to determine the need for, and feasibility of economic evaluations for new programs for adults with mental illness.

title: An Approach to Navigating the Lorazepam Challenge Test for Catatonia in Critical Care Settings.
abstract: Catatonia often occurs in the setting of psychiatric illness; however, it is also found in other medical conditions, especially within critical care settings. The lorazepam challenge test (LCT) is a key diagnostic and therapeutic intervention for catatonia; however, no specific guidance exists for patients within the intensive care unit (ICU). This review synthesizes psychiatric and critical care literature to propose a structured LCT framework adapted to the ICU. Specific indications and contraindications across gradients of catatonia likelihood and medical complexity are reviewed, along with practical dosing and monitoring recommendations. An interdisciplinary collaborative workflow is also outlined along with post-LCT documentation standards. Our structured approach offers a practical foundation for future standardized protocols, education, and catatonia research in critical care.

title: CT density gradient texture is associated with blood gene expression and immune cell subtypes in smokers susceptible to COPD
abstract: Background Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) often progresses silently, with biological and structural changes preceding measurable airflow obstruction. CT density gradient (CTDG) texture, a radiographic feature located primarily around the bronchovascular bundles, has been associated with systemic inflammation, exacerbations and mortality. However, the biological underpinnings of CTDG in smokers without spirometric COPD remain unclear. Methods We conducted cross-sectional analyses of over 2500 smokers from the COPDGene Study who were non-obstructed or had COPD. CTDG texture was quantified from inspiratory scans using the adaptive multiple feature method. Whole-blood RNA sequencing and immune cell RNA-seq deconvolution were performed to identify transcriptomic and immune correlates of CTDG. Differential gene expression and cell type-specific transcriptomic analyses were conducted using covariate-adjusted linear models. Results In non-obstructed smokers, CTDG was significantly associated with 157 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) (false discovery rate<5%) in the Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease stage-stratified model and 65 DEGs in the interaction model. Enriched pathways in the non-obstructed population included lymphocyte differentiation, cytokine signalling and metabolic regulation. CTDG demonstrated a positive association with neutrophil proportion (β=0.126, p=0.02) and inverse associations with resting memory CD4+ T cells (β=−0.036, p=0.02) and monocytes (β=−0.050, p=0.05); however, these associations were nominal. In non-obstructed participants, neutrophil-specific gene expression linked to CTDG showed upregulation of inflammatory pathway genes, including TLR2, ADAM17 and metabolic genes, such as GRB10 and PFKFB2, suggesting early immune-metabolic dysregulation. Conclusion CTDG captures structural and systemic immunometabolic changes in non-obstructed smokers, supporting its potential as a non-invasive biomarker for early COPD risk and timely intervention.

title: Cefazolin-induced Supratherapeutic INR Coagulopathy Case Report
abstract: INTRODUCTION/BACKGROUND: A potential effect of cefazolin causing coagulopathy resulting in elevated INR and bleeding episodes is described in 2 patients. CASE PRESENTATION: In the first case, a 77-year-old male was receiving cefazolin for Methicillin- susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) bacteremia and developed gross hematuria on day 12 of cefazolin therapy, with a measured INR of 4.1. No other causes of coagulopathy were identified, and after IV vitamin K administration, the INR decreased to 1.3. In the second case, a 77-year-old female was being treated with cefazolin for MSSA bacteremia. On cefazolin day 7, the patient had a measured INR of 9.0, with a subsequent decrease in INR to 1.3 2 days later after administration of vitamin K. Neither patient was receiving any anticoagulation, and no other cause of INR elevation was identified. CONCLUSION: This case describes 2 patients who experienced elevated INR measurements during cefazolin therapy. Cefazolin may have led to elevated INR values through vitamin K depletion, especially since administration of vitamin K decreased INR values. Close monitoring of bleeding and INR may be needed in patients receiving long-term cefazolin therapy, especially in those having a bleeding episode or decreased hemoglobin.

title: Patient Characteristics and Outcomes of Urethral Ligation: A TURNS Study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To characterize patient selection and midterm outcomes after urethral ligation (UL) for end-stage outlet pathology across multiple reconstructive centers.
METHODS: We retrospectively identified men undergoing UL at 7 Trauma and Urologic Reconstructive Network of Surgeons centers from May 2005 through June 2025. The primary outcome was recurrent incontinence. Secondary outcomes included revision, 30-day readmission, urinary tract infection (UTI), urethral fistula, and abscess. Cumulative risks of recurrence and revision were estimated using Kaplan-Meier methods.
RESULTS: Twenty-seven men underwent UL at a median age of 72 years (IQR 48-81). Common indications included urethral stricture/devastated urethra (29.6%), refractory incontinence (29.6%), failed bladder neck closure (25.9%), and artificial urinary sphincter erosion (22.2%). Urinary drainage was managed with a suprapubic tube in 19 patients, a continent catheterizable channel in 7, and ileovesicostomy in 1. Median follow-up was 24 months (IQR, 4-48); 11 patients (40.7%) had less than 1 year of follow-up. Three recurrences occurred within 3 months. Recurrence probability was 11.6% (95% CI, 3.9%-32.9%) and remained unchanged through 4 years. Revision risk was 3.7% (95% CI, 0.5%-23.5%). Thirty-day readmission occurred in 5 patients (18.5%). Among 16 patients with at least 1 year of follow-up, 11 (68.8%) developed UTI, and 3 (18.8%) developed urethral fistula.
CONCLUSION: In a multi-institutional cohort, urethral ligation achieved high midterm success with low risk of revision surgery or fistulation. The burden of infection and readmission highlights the need for structured postoperative surveillance and bladder-directed interventions.

title: Evaluating and Comparing Approaches to Measuring Quality of Postdischarge Mental Health Outpatient Follow-Up Care.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate whether measures of follow-up mental health and substance use care (behavioral health) within 30 days provide signals of quality associated with longer-term positive outcomes and whether a national U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) postdischarge follow-up and engagement (PDE) measure with more rigorous follow-up requirements is associated with additional benefit.
METHODS: This retrospective study used VA administrative records for 115,723 unique veteran discharges from inpatient or residential behavioral health treatment between October 2016 and February 2019, with discharges categorized by level of 30-day behavioral health postdischarge outpatient follow-up: zero visits, one visit, more than one visit, and two to four visits or more (met VA PDE). Propensity score-weighted models tested associations between follow-up intensity and number of 6-month outpatient behavioral health visits, 6-month primary care engagement, and 1-year all-cause mortality.
RESULTS: Patients meeting the VA PDE measure had significantly better longer-term outcomes than those who received one or fewer visits within 30 days. Discharges meeting VA PDE were associated with the greatest increases in subsequent behavioral health visits (3.43 times increase in visits compared with zero visits within 30 days), higher likelihood of primary care contact (OR=2.12), and greater reductions in all-cause mortality (OR=0.71).
CONCLUSIONS: Greater engagement in 30-day postdischarge behavioral health follow-up is associated with greater outpatient behavioral health engagement, higher likelihood of receiving primary care, and lower 1-year all-cause mortality. These findings support resource allocation toward postdischarge care coordination and broadly adopting more stringent quality standards.

title: The Role of Liver and Muscle-derived Exerkines in Cognitive Resilience
abstract: Exercise is one of the most effective ways to improve cognition. Exercise orchestrates a coordinated response across multiple peripheral tissues, including skeletal muscle and liver, which release circulatory factors capable of influencing neural function. This emerging framework expands our understanding from exercise-mediated adaptations within the central nervous system to body-wide adaptations that converge to promote cognitive function. SUMMARY: A review of exercise-induced secretion of circulatory factors from the skeletal muscle and liver that are capable of influencing cognition.

title: Diagnostic insights from twenty years of bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling for cushing disease at mayo clinic.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling (BIPSS) is used to distinguish pituitary from ectopic sources of ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome (CS). We reviewed two decades of BIPSS experience at a single referral center to assess diagnostic performance, safety, and patient outcomes.
DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study of patients who underwent BIPSS between 1998 and 2018.
PATIENTS: Of 156 adults undergoing BIPSS for ACTH-dependent CS, 143 had technically successful sampling and adequate follow-up and formed the evaluable cohort. A pituitary source was identified by a baseline central-to-peripheral ACTH ratio ≥2.0 or a post-stimulation (ovine corticotropin-releasing hormone [oCRH] or desmopressin) ratio ≥3.0.
MEASUREMENTS: Diagnostic sensitivity, specificity, and lateralization accuracy of BIPSS. A confirmed pituitary source was defined by post-operative hypocortisolism after the index transsphenoidal operation; ACTH-positive corticotroph histology was supportive.
RESULTS: Of the 143 patients, 109 had a definitive final diagnosis and formed the basis of the diagnostic analysis. BIPSS separated pituitary from ectopic ACTH sources with a sensitivity of 98.9% (95% CI 94.3-99.8) and a specificity of 85.7% (95% CI 60.1-96.0). The inter-petrosal gradient predicted the side of the adenoma in 59% of cases at baseline and 60% after stimulation (n = 100). Technical success was achieved in 94.2% of procedures, with no recorded major morbidity. Among the 94 patients in remission, 14 (15%) recurred over a mean of 3 years.
CONCLUSIONS: Among patients in whom a definitive diagnosis was ultimately established, BIPSS distinguished pituitary from ectopic ACTH-dependent CS with high sensitivity and more modest specificity. Its value for adenoma lateralization is limited relative to current imaging. The cohort provides an oCRH-era reference point as practice moves to desmopressin.

title: Interorgan Signaling in Kidney Health and Disease.
abstract: Organ crosstalk plays a vital role in maintaining physiological homeostasis and adapting to environmental cues. The kidney is increasingly recognized as an integrative organ that participates in bidirectional communication with distant tissues through hemodynamic, endocrine, metabolic, immune, and neural pathways. Dysfunction of the kidney is now viewed as a systemic disease rather than organ injury. Yet, kidney-organ crosstalk is usually described broadly and associatively. This review examines recent mechanistic advances in kidney-organ signaling, with an emphasis on experimentally supported molecular mediators and causal models. We highlight emerging circulating mediators, neuroimmune circuits, microbial pathways, and tissue-specific signaling mechanisms, placing the kidney as both recipient and active sender of mediators in systemic health and diseases. We also highlight the limitations of the current approaches in studying kidney-organ signaling, including reliance on global genetic manipulation, indirect measures of signal transfer, and isolated organ-pair frameworks. In addition, we discuss how advancements in technology may help us recognize new mediators and help identify cellular origins, routes, and consequences of interorgan communication with greater resolution. A better integrated understanding of the interorgan signaling in kidney health and disease is mandatory to identify biomarkers and develop new therapies to treat kidney diseases with fewer adverse effects on other organs.

title: Cortisol in cardio-kidney-metabolic disease
abstract: Despite guideline-directed therapy, many patients with cardio-kidney-metabolic (CKM) disease remain uncontrolled due to therapeutic inertia, adherence barriers, and underrecognized secondary causes. Hypercortisolism, ranging from mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS) to overt Cushing syndrome, is an increasingly recognized contributor. MACS is associated with a 2.5-fold higher risk of cardiovascular death and increased prevalence of hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), and kidney impairment. Cortisol excess promotes muscle insulin resistance, hepatic gluconeogenesis, β-cell dysfunction, sodium retention, and vascular remodelling, worsening glycaemia and blood pressure, leading to poor CKM outcomes. Recent prospective studies suggest that hypercortisolism is more prevalent than previously suspected in selected CKM phenotypes, including 24% in patients with difficult-to-control T2DM in CATALYST and 27% in patients with resistant hypertension in MOMENTUM. The overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test remains the diagnostic test of choice. Therapeutic strategies include adrenal steroidogenesis inhibitors, glucocorticoid receptor antagonists, and pituitary-directed therapies in selected cases, while surgery remains the first-line treatment for surgically remediable disease. This review summarizes the epidemiology and mechanisms linking cortisol excess to CKM dysfunction, and also highlights the need for clinical trials, standardized diagnostic thresholds, and assays to enable integration of cortisol-targeted therapies into management pathways to mitigate residual CKM risk. This review will serve as a practical guide for cardiologists to manage a potentially reversible contributor to poor CKM control.

title: Resting Energy Expenditure in Mechanically Ventilated Surgical-Trauma Patients With and Without Acute Kidney Injury: a single-center retrospective study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To compare resting energy expenditure (REE) measured by indirect calorimetry (IC) in mechanically ventilated surgical-trauma critically ill patients with and without acute kidney injury (AKI); to evaluate differences in REE by sex, age, and body mass index (BMI); and to assess associations between REE, psoas muscle index (PMI) measured using computed tomography scans, and lean body mass (LBM) estimated by predictive equations.
METHODS: This single-center retrospective cohort study conducted at a tertiary academic medical center included mechanically ventilated critically ill adults admitted between 01/01/2012 and 12/31/2023. Exclusion criteria were pediatric, pregnant, or incarcerated patients; quadriplegia, paraplegia, cystic fibrosis; abnormal respiratory quotients; Medical ICU admission; major burns (≥20% TBSA); parenteral nutrition initiated on or after IC; tracheostomy on admission; discharge or death while ventilated; or absence of a nutrition prescription.
RESULTS: Of 794 patients screened, 180 met inclusion criteria (AKI n=84; no AKI n=96). At baseline, patients with and without AKI differed significantly in age (59.9 vs 55 years; P = 0.046), BMI (32.2 vs 28.8 kg/m2; P = 0.046), CKD (23.8% vs 3.13%; P < 0.001), and serum creatinine (1.49 vs 0.84 mg/dL; P < 0.001). Of patients with AKI, 71.4% had stage I AKI and 20.2% required renal replacement therapy (RRT). No significant difference in mean REE was observed between patients with and without AKI (1,642 vs 1,665 kcal/day; P = 0.380) . REE was significantly higher in males compared with females (1,806 vs 1,425 kcal/day; P < 0.001), in patients aged 18-65 versus >65 years (1,768 vs 1,428 kcal/day; P = 0.002), and in obese versus non-obese patients (1,841 vs 1,500 kcal/day; P < 0.001). In multivariable linear regression, higher BMI (P = 0.003) and male sex (P = 0.028) were independently associated with higher REE, while AKI was not. LBM estimated by predictive equations was more strongly correlated with REE than PMI (P < 0.001), and correlation strength did not differ by AKI status.
CONCLUSIONS: Measured REE did not differ between ventilated surgical-trauma patients with and without AKI. REE differed by sex, age, and obesity status, and AKI was not associated with within-group differences. BMI and sex were identified as independent predictors of REE. Estimated LBM was strongly correlated with REE independent of AKI status. Given possible residual confounding, further investigation is needed.

title: Neurometabolic Differences in Psychosis Observed with 7 T Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Altered brain chemistry is thought to contribute to impaired cognition and perceptual functioning in people with psychotic psychopathology (PwPP). As heritable genetic factors shape the development of psychosis, alterations in brain chemistry may extend to biological relatives of PwPP. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) is a non-invasive method for quantifying concentrations of various neurochemicals in the human brain. Previous studies using MRS have generally focused on specific diagnoses (eg, schizophrenia), rather than PwPP trans-diagnostically, and comparably few studies have examined relatives. The goal of the current study was to assess neurometabolic differences in PwPP and relatives using MRS in a large number of participants.
STUDY DESIGN: As part of the Psychosis Human Connectome Project, we acquired ultra-short echo time (8 ms) MRS data at 7 tesla in both occipital and prefrontal cortices from 64 PwPP, 42 first-degree biological relatives, and 43 controls.
STUDY RESULTS: We observed lower levels of N-acetyl-aspartate (NAA) in the occipital lobe in PwPP and relatives versus controls, and a trend toward lower N-acetyl-aspartylglutamate in prefrontal cortex in PwPP versus controls. Lower OCC NAA levels were also evident in diagnostic subgroups of PwPP (schizophrenia and bipolar disorder) compared to controls. We also observed higher levels of glucose in both occipital and prefrontal cortices in PwPP. Hierarchical clustering analyses showed that higher glucose levels were linked to higher psychiatric symptoms, poorer cognition, and impaired visual task performance.
CONCLUSIONS: Together, our findings point to alterations in neural metabolism across multiple brain areas in PwPP that are associated with impaired cognitive and perceptual functioning.
