title: The Challenges of Perioperative Anaphylaxis.
abstract: Perioperative anaphylaxis rare, approximately 1:10,000 anesthetic events in adults and 1:35,000 in children; but allergists/immunologists in a consultative practice are likely to encounter this problem more than once during their career. In addition to rare occurrence, many factors contribute to the challenges of assessing potential perioperative anaphylaxis: 1)the numerous possible explanations for hypotension or respiratory symptoms during anesthesia; 2) the limitations of drug allergy testing, without validated testing other than for penicillin; 3) the multiple drugs and agents used in anesthesia and surgery; 4) the challenges of communication between the anesthesia and surgical teams and outpatient specialists; 5) unfamiliarity of the allergist/immunologist with many of the medications used during anesthesia; and 6) the difficulties in acquiring the anesthetic drugs for testing. Furthermore, there is often time pressure due to the need to complete a surgical procedure. Hospital-based or large health care system-based allergists/immunologists have an advantage in access to anesthetic drugs for testing and usually have more open communication with the anesthesiologist, so a community allergist/immunologist may prefer to refer the patient. However, a process exists that, if followed by allergists/immunologists in a community or academic practice setting, provides reassurance and a path to repeat safe anesthesia. This article summarizes recent literature on perioperative anaphylaxis and provides guidance on this process.

title: Environmental and economic impact of validated endoscope storage systems: a life cycle assessment and scenario analysis of avoided morning reprocessing.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Validated storage systems allow prolonged microbiologically safe storage of thermosensitive endoscopes and may avoid repeated morning reprocessing in countries where an additional disinfection cycle is required before first use. We performed a life cycle assessment (LCA) comparing validated endoscope storage systems and modeled the environmental and economic consequences of avoiding repeated morning reprocessing.
METHODS: An ISO 14040/44-compliant LCA compared three validated storage technologies: two drying and storage cabinets (steris endodry and wassenburg dry 300D) and plasma typhoon (PT) with PlasmaBag storage. Storage impacts were evaluated from 24 h to 7 days. To assess the consequences of avoiding morning reprocessing, storage results were integrated into a scenario analysis using the carbon footprint of one additional reprocessing cycle derived from a previously published ISO-compliant LCA. Economic analysis included equipment acquisition, consumables, and avoided reprocessing costs. Outcomes were modeled for a representative European endoscopy unit performing 8000 procedures annually.
RESULTS: The 24-h storage carbon footprint was 0.93 kg CO2-eq per endoscope for both cabinet systems and 0.27 kg CO2-eq for PT. Where morning reprocessing is routinely performed, validated storage reduced modeled annual greenhouse gas emissions by approximately 7.2 t CO2-eq with storage cabinets and 12.5 t CO2-eq with PT for 8000 annual procedures. Storage cabinets had lower annual costs than PT because of lower consumable use, although all strategies remained associated with additional direct expenditures despite partial compensation from avoided morning reprocessing.
CONCLUSIONS: Where repeated morning reprocessing is routinely required, validated storage systems may substantially reduce the environmental burden of endoscope reprocessing. Their economic impact depends largely on consumable utilization and organizational practice, supporting joint environmental and financial assessment when implementing storage strategies. These findings derive from a scenario analysis reflecting practice in several European countries and may not be generalizable to healthcare systems where additional morning reprocessing is not routinely performed.

title: Executive functions are independently associated with health-related numeracy and self-perceived health literacy in applied contexts in healthy adults.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Over a third of U.S. adults struggle with health literacy, which broadly describes the ability to access, understand, and use health-related information. Conceptual models highlight the importance of cognitive functions in health literacy, but limited empirical work has carefully examined the extent to which various aspects of cognition uniquely contribute to different dimensions of health literacy.
METHOD: Participants in this retrospective, harmonized study included 312 healthy adults who completed a battery of well-validated cognitive tests that measured their general fund of knowledge, attention, declarative memory, and executive functions (;). Participants also completed a performance-based measure of health-related numeracy (i.e., Expanded Numeracy Scale) and questionnaires assessing self-perceived health literacy in applied contexts (i.e., Brief Health Literacy Screening and eHealth Literacy Scale).
RESULTS: After accounting for the influence of sociodemographics and general fund of knowledge parallel hierarchical regressions showed that measures of executive functions and memory explained a significant amount of variance in health-related numeracy and measures of executive functions explained a significant, but modest, amount of variance in self-perceived health literacy in applied contexts after accounting for the influence of sociodemographics and general fund of knowledge.
CONCLUSIONS: Findings suggest that executive functions (i.e. generativity and cognitive flexibility) play a unique role in some aspects of personal health literacy among healthy adults. Future experimental studies might further dissect the role of executive functions in the expression and management of health literacy in at-risk clinical populations.

title: Association of Socioeconomic and Clinical Factors of Complex Cataract Surgery in Academic Medical Centers
abstract: PURPOSE: Cataract surgery is the most common surgical procedure in the United States and can be coded as routine or complex, with the latter defined as employing devices or techniques not routinely employed in routine surgery, elevating risk of adverse outcomes. The study aimed to determine whether socioeconomic factors are associated with the need for complex cataract surgery after controlling for known clinical factors associated with routine versus complex surgery. METHODS: Patients 18 years of age and over in the Sight Outcomes and Reseach Collaborative with one or more cataract surgeries across 16 U.S. medical centers from 2010 to 2023. Multivariable logistic regression models were used, with the first model examining key covariates and the first eye or cataract surgery, and the second model examining covariates on the second eye (bilateral) or cataract surgery, if applicable, while accounting for the first eye (as routine or complex). RESULTS: Factors associated with increased odds of complex surgery in both the first and second procedures were male sex, increasing age, worse vision, increased cataract density, Black and Asian race, diabetes, pseudoexfoliation syndrome, intraoperative floppy iris syndrome, and the use of alpha-1 blockers and miotic agents. Additionally, receipt of complex surgery in the second eye (bilateral) was significantly associated with increased odds if the first eye was also a complex surgery. CONCLUSIONS: Several socioeconomic factors remained significant after adjusting for known clinical factors associated with complex cataract surgery. Findings may inform the development of enhanced risk assessment to identify patients at elevated risk for complex surgery.

title: Evaluation, troubleshooting, and management of pacing system malfunctions
abstract: Advanced functionality and programmability of the modern pacemaker systems allow specific options to manage cardiac arrhythmias. Increasing complexity of both the mechanical (as in dual and multi-chamber devices) and software features (such as complex algorithms and pacemaker behaviors) creates a potential for increased component or software malfunction and appearance of unusual device behavior (pseudo-malfunction) that may challenge the providers. Over the last two decades, while challenges continue, technological advances also improved the reliability and diagnostic capabilities of cardiac pacemakers and ICDs. Understanding the principles of cardiac pacing and developing skills to troubleshoot device behavior in the current era is as important as ever. In the current chapter, commonly encountered problems relating to pacing in ICDs and pacemakers will be discussed.

title: Pacemaker timing cycles and special features
abstract: Since the development of implantable cardiac pacemakers in 1960, the features and functions built into these devices have continued to change as the cardiac field evolves. Understanding pacing modes, timing cycles and special features are key to identifying normal versus abnormal pacemaker function. Pacing modes have evolved with technology, and each pacing mode has specific and general indications, as well as unique advantages and disadvantages. The “sensor function” of a pacemaker refers to the modulation of the paced rate in response to an input signal other than the presence or absence of native depolarization. A dual-chamber pacemaker will obey the rules centered on the base-rate behavior and adjust its response based on sensed events. Several pacemaker algorithms are now available in pacemakers that may alter the pacing rate from either the programmed lower rate or sinus-driven or sensor-driven rates.

title: Infill Architecture Drives Early Osteogenesis in Additively Manufactured PCL Scaffolds With Controlled Porosity.
abstract: Critical sized bone defects represent a significant challenge in orthopedic and reconstructive surgery. Additively manufactured (AM) bone scaffolds may be effective tools to treat these defects; however, the influence of infill architecture on early bone formation remains poorly characterized. This study used 3D-printed biodegradable polycaprolactone (PCL) scaffolds to investigate the relationships between infill architecture, bone growth, and mechanical properties in a 4-week in vitro experiment. Scaffolds containing bovine allograft were constructed with Gyroid and Honeycomb architectures at two porosity levels (40% and 60%). It was hypothesized that Gyroid scaffolds would accelerate early bone formation compared with Honeycomb designs. Gyroid architectures generally showed greater metabolic activity at weeks 3 and 4, with significant differences varying by porosity and time point. Micro-CT analysis demonstrated significantly greater mineralized tissue volume and mineral density in Gyroid scaffolds compared with Honeycomb scaffolds at 4 weeks. Compressive mechanical testing indicated that Honeycomb structures were significantly stiffer and stronger than Gyroid scaffolds throughout the study. These results demonstrate that infill architecture significantly influences early bone formation independently of pore size and highlight a fundamental tradeoff between biological and mechanical performance in AM PCL scaffold design.

title: Prevalence and Correlates of Symptoms of Cannabinoid Hyperemesis Syndrome in the United States, 2025.
abstract: Objectives. To characterize the potential prevalence of cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (CHS) symptoms and associated characteristics. Methods. Using data from a nationally representative survey of 7034 US adults (conducted May‒September 2025), we fit separate survey-weighted multinomial logistic regression models with a 4-category CHS-symptom and cannabis-use group variable as the outcome and demographic characteristics, cannabis-use behaviors, and cannabis use‒related problems as predictors. Results. Overall, 2.7% of all respondents and 17.8% of respondents who used cannabis daily reported CHS-like symptoms. Respondents who were younger, female, identified as non-White, had lower income, had lower educational attainment, and endorsed cannabis use‒related problems were more likely to be in the CHS-symptom group than in the daily-cannabis-use group. Conclusions. CHS symptoms are not uncommon in the United States, and those with fewer economic resources and more cannabis use‒related problems were more likely to report these symptoms, even compared with others with daily cannabis use. Public Health Implications. As cannabis use increases, CHS is also likely to become more common, underscoring the importance of expanded education about the identification and treatment of CHS. (Am J Public Health. Published online ahead of print October 1, 2026:e1-e10. https://doi.org/10.2105/AJPH.2026.308753).

title: Safety of Staged Bilateral MRgFUS Thalamotomy: Associations Between Lesion Characteristics, Stereotactic Coordinates, and Adverse Events.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Staged bilateral magnetic resonance-guided focused ultrasound (MRgFUS) thalamotomy is increasingly performed for medication-refractory essential tremor, yet the relationship between lesion characteristics and profiles of adverse events (AE) across sessions remains poorly characterized. We sought to examine how lesion volume, stereotactic coordinates, and session order relate to AE profiles in staged bilateral MRgFUS thalamotomy.
METHODS: Retrospective analysis of 50 patients who underwent staged bilateral MRgFUS thalamotomy at a single center. AE were assessed at postoperative day 1 and 3-month follow-up. Lesion volumes were categorized into tertiles from the pooled distribution. Stereotactic coordinates were normalized to anterior commissure-posterior commissure distance. Linear regression assessed associations between coordinates and AE.
RESULTS: The second session was characterized by fewer sonications (6.0 ± 1.9 vs 6.5 ± 1.4, P = .013), lower peak temperatures (56.4 ± 2.9°C vs 57.3 ± 2.3°C, P = .044), and smaller lesion volumes (168.5 ± 107.7 mm3 vs 198.7 ± 85.1 mm3, P = .007), consistent with a conservative approach that maintained comparable tremor outcomes. At 3 months, AE rates were higher after the second session for gait/balance disturbance (44.0% vs 18.0%, P = .016) and sensory abnormalities (24.0% vs 8.0%, P = .033), despite similar immediate postoperative profiles. This divergence was volume-dependent, small lesions (126.8 mm3 or less) showed comparable rates between sessions, whereas medium and large lesions demonstrated substantially higher second-session rates. More posterior positioning was independently associated with speech deficits (P = .001) and mouth numbness (P = .014).
CONCLUSION: AE persistence after the second session was volume-dependent, with rates comparable to the first session at smaller lesion volumes but elevated at larger volumes. Posterior lesion positioning was independently associated with mouth numbness and speech deficits, supporting anterior targeting adjustments for contralateral procedures. These findings suggest that lesion volume constraint combined with anterior positioning may optimize the safety profile of staged bilateral MRgFUS thalamotomy, although prospective validation is needed to establish definitive volume thresholds.

title: North American Contact Dermatitis Group Patch Test Results: 2023-2024.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patch testing is the most important diagnostic test for allergic contact dermatitis.
OBJECTIVE: Summarize patch test results from the North American Contact Dermatitis Group (NACDG) of patients tested to a screening series of 80 allergens from 2023 to 2024.
METHODS: Cross-sectional, retrospective analysis.
RESULTS: During the study period, NACDG members tested 3979 patients, and 70.3% had at least one positive/allergic patch test reaction. Tested patients were female (74.3%) and/or White (69.9%); median age was 45 (1 to >89). The most common primary sites of dermatitis were hand (18.9%), face (17.7%), scattered generalized (16.6%), and eyelids (12.8%). Top allergens were nickel sulfate hexahydrate 5% (26.4%), methylisothiazolinone (9.2%), cobalt chloride hexahydrate (8.8%), fragrance mix I (8.7%), hydroperoxides of linalool 1.0% (8.7%), Myroxylon pereirae resin (7.6%), and methylchloroisothiazolinone/methylisothiazolinone (7.0%). Compared to the 2021-2022 cycle, allergy to decyl and coco glucosides and Amerchol L101 increased in positivity, while methylisothiazolinone and methylchloroisothiazolinone/methylisothiazolinone decreased. Over one-fifth (20.1%) of tested patients were positive to a supplemental allergen not on the 80-allergen screening series.
CONCLUSIONS: Allergy to isothiazolinone preservatives decreased in North America while positivity to alkyl glucoside surfactants and Amerchol L101 increased. Comprehensive patch testing with both screening and supplemental series is necessary for the diagnosis and treatment of allergic contact dermatitis.

title: Using Stethoscope Hygiene Barriers to Reduce Central Catheter–Associated Bloodstream Infection Rates
abstract: BACKGROUND: Central line [catheter]-associated bloodstream infections (CLABSIs) represent a significant mortality risk. LOCAL PROBLEM: Due to a significant increase in CLABSI rate, a new CLABSI prevention bundle strategy was evaluated to determine whether it changed the CLABSI rate. METHODS: A before and after quality improvement project was performed in an 18-bed intensive care unit from March 1, 2021, to March 1, 2025. A CLABSI prevention bundle was implemented; CLABSI rates were compared for 1 year before to 3 years after intervention implementation. Additionally, clinician satisfaction surveys were collected. INTERVENTIONS: The implemented bundle consisted of (1) replacement of disposable stethoscopes with touch-free, aseptic stethoscope diaphragm cover dispensers (DiskCover System, AseptiScope, Inc) in each intensive care unit room, and (2) requiring a chlorhexidine-impregnated dressing for all central catheters, with standardization and reeducation of bedside staff on central catheter dressing changes. RESULTS: Of 5226 intensive care unit patients, the mean CLABSI rate was 4.42 (95% CI, 2.93-5.91) infections per 1000 patient central catheter days during the year before implementation, which decreased to 0.70 (95% CI, -1.21 to 2.61) in the 3 years after implementation. Clinicians reported the new strategy was easy to use and superior to disposable stethoscopes. CONCLUSION: A CLABSI bundle that included touch-free, aseptic stethoscope hygiene barriers and chlorhexidine-impregnated dressings was highly effective at decreasing the CLABSI rate.

title: Disease Burden, Surveillance, and Treatment Gaps in Chronic Hypoparathyroidism: Insights From a Multicenter Registry.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate disease and treatment burden, renal surveillance gaps, multidimensional biochemical control, hypercalciuria management, and parathyroid hormone (PTH) replacement therapy use in adults with chronic hypoparathyroidism.
METHODS: We conducted a multicenter retrospective cross-sectional registry study across 41 endocrinology clinics. Adults with chronic hypoparathyroidism (>12 months) were identified using ICD-10 codes, medication records, and manual chart verification. Multidimensional control required simultaneous achievement of albumin-corrected serum calcium, serum phosphate, and 24-hour urinary calcium targets. Secondary multivariable logistic regression analyses evaluated factors associated with suboptimal control, at least one applicable guideline-based care gap, and renal impairment.
RESULTS: Among 522 patients (83.1% women; median disease duration, 8 years), 496/522 (95.0%) had postsurgical disease. High-dose elemental calcium and alfacalcidol were required in 45/522 (8.6%) and 8/522 (1.5%), respectively. Among patients with at least 5 years of disease, 119/400 (29.8%) had never undergone 24-hour urinary calcium assessment and 101/400 (25.3%) had not undergone renal imaging. Multidimensional biochemical control was achieved in 126/230 patients (54.8%). Hypercalciuria was present in 72/282 patients (25.5%) at the latest assessment; 50/72 (69.4%) were not receiving calcium-sparing diuretic therapy. Among 239 patients eligible for PTH replacement therapy, 196/239 (82.0%) had not initiated treatment. Lower current age was associated with suboptimal control, longer disease duration and postsurgical etiology with at least one care gap, and older age with renal impairment.
CONCLUSION: Assessment based solely on serum calcium may underestimate incomplete disease control. Multidimensional biochemical abnormalities, surveillance deficiencies, and therapeutic care gaps remain common despite specialist endocrine follow-up.

abstract: Background: Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) is a low-cost, radiation-free triage tool but lacks standardized acquisition protocols for tuberculosis (TB). We developed and evaluated a streamlined symmetric POCUS protocol for pulmonary TB in a high-burden setting. Methods: Ugandan participants aged ≥13 years with confirmed pulmonary TB, household TB exposure, or a non-TB respiratory condition underwent an 18-position POCUS examination (12 lung zones and 6 pre-established extrapulmonary positions). Random Forest classifiers using prespecified pathologic features were developed in a fixed stratified 75/25 training/holdout split. All symmetric 2-, 4-, and 6-zone combinations were evaluated in training data. The best protocol of each size was locked and tested in the holdout set. Results: Among 318 analyzed participants, 118 (37.1%) had pulmonary TB and 200 were TB-negative, including 102 with other respiratory conditions (ORC). The model-selected 6-zone protocol comprised bilateral anterior-superior, lateral-superior, and posterior-superior lung zones. For TB versus all TB-negative participants, the AUCs for the 6-zone, 12-zone, and 18-position protocols were 0.82 (95% CI, 0.73-0.92), 0.81 (0.70—0.92), and 0.81 (0.71—0.91), respectively (all P > 0.76). For TB versus ORC, AUCs were 0.81 (0.70—0.91), 0.85 (0.76—0.93), and 0.85 (0.76—0.94), respectively (all P > 0.45). The 2-zone protocol had a lower AUC than the 6-zone protocol for TB versus all TB-negative participants (P = 0.004). Shred sign, consolidation, and B-lines with irregular pleura were the strongest TB-associated findings. Conclusions: A fixed 6-zone lung POCUS examination showed similar discrimination for TB to more comprehensive 12-lung-zone and 18-position protocols. This supports a simpler, scalable approach to TB triage

title: OPEN: A Community-Informed Metadata Framework for Interoperable Computable Phenotypes
abstract: Objective: To identify community – prioritized metadata for reporting and sharing computable phenotypes (CPs), develop a cross-library candidate framework, assess alignment between user requirements and library metadata, and test the feasibility of metadata exchange. Materials and Methods: We combined an international, library – led effort by the Open PhEnomics Network (OPEN) consortium with a UK community consensus-building exercise aimed at improving the FAIRness (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) of CPs. The consortium performed a cross-library field comparison and literature review to inform candidate fields, refined through consortium consensus. The community approach was developed through stakeholder interviews, a survey, and workshop, guided by a working group. Community requirements were interpretively mapped to the resulting framework and classified into conformance tiers. Interoperability was tested by manually and programmatically mapping diabetes-related phenotypes across libraries. Results: The library – led process produced 23 candidate fields spanning phenotype description, data/technical details, and performance domains. Thirteen fields aligned across all five libraries, and 22 fields aligned with published CP library desiderata. Interoperability testing successfully catalogued phenotypes through manual mapping, with API – mediated mapping achieving 63 – 76% metadata field completeness across libraries. A community survey (n=124 respondents) identified six metadata elements with majority support as mandatory: description, coding terminology, phenotype type, version history, unique identifier, and data source. Logic representation and validation requirements were rated as mostly context-dependent. Community – identified priorities showed strong alignment with the OPEN framework, though some requirements were only partially represented. Discussion: Through a consensus – based, community – driven approach, we established a CP framework enabling interoperability across libraries. Conclusion: OPEN provides a credible, community – informed foundation for a FAIR CP metadata standard.

title: Analysis of reproductive traits associated with lipoprotein(a) deficiency in participants from the Pakistan Genome Resource
abstract: Aims. Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a genetically determined, independent risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, driving development of LPA-targeting therapies that markedly lower circulating Lp(a). Because LPA?the gene encoding apolipoprotein(a)?is absent in most model organisms, preclinical studies have limited value for assessing effects such as reproductive safety. Therefore, naturally occurring human LPA ?knockouts? were analyzed to evaluate reproductive outcomes of on-target Lp(a) lowering. Methods and Results. Individuals carrying high-confidence LPA loss-of-function (LoF) variants which reduce Lp(a) in a gene-dosage?dependent manner within the Pakistan Genome Resource were identified. LoF variants showed no depletion of homozygotes relative to Hardy?Weinberg expectations. LPA LoF associations with fertility-related traits (ever having a child and number of children) under additive and recessive models were assessed using regenie-based burden testing, including sex-stratified analyses, and no significant associations were observed. A recall-by-genotype study of female LoF homozygotes alongside heterozygous and non-carrier family member controls was performed, surveying reproductive histories and offspring outcomes. Across 107 pregnancies and 87 children in 19 homozygous LoF women, rates of miscarriage, maternal complications (including preeclampsia, hypertension, and gestational diabetes), delivery complications, neonatal intensive care admission, birth defects, and child health problems were comparable across genotypes with no statistically significant genotype?outcome associations. Conclusions. These genetic and by-genotype analyses indicate that complete lifelong LPA deficiency due to high-confidence LPA loss-of-function variants is not associated with overt adverse maternal fertility, pregnancy or child health outcomes. These findings offer human genetic reassurance regarding reproductive and developmental safety in the context of sustained Lp(a)-lowering, with implications for long-term therapies targeting Lp(a).

title: Peak Agricultural Pesticide Spray Periods are related to Real-World Cognition Using an Ecological Momentary Assessment Burst Design over Two Years
abstract: Objective: Emerging evidence suggests that exposure to organophosphate, neonicotinoid, and other pesticides may transiently impair cognition; however, traditional "snapshot" laboratory-based cognitive assessments fail to capture fluctuations in cognitive performance. This study used ecological momentary cognitive testing (EMCT) to evaluate whether real-world cognitive performance differs between peak and low floricultural pesticide spray seasons, thereby evaluating the potential cyclical effects of agricultural production and related pesticide exposures. Material and Methods: From 2022 to 2024, 15,063 EMCT assessments were completed by 494 participants (ages 17 to 25; 50% female) enrolled in the ESPINA cohort study in Ecuador. Participants completed nine 10-day burst assessments every 2 to 3 months during high and low pesticide spray seasons. EMCTs (NeuroUx) assessed processing speed, executive function, and visual working memory. Mixed-effects models examined associations of peak versus off-peak pesticide spray seasons, floricultural work or occupation (vs not) with EMCT performance, adjusting for socio-economic and other variables, and including participant- and burst-level random intercepts. Results: Peak pesticide spray season, compared to off-peak, was associated with higher T-scores on processing speed tests, including Matching Pair (B= 0.62) and Odd One Out (B= 0.88), but showed no significant association with other tests or the overall cognitive composite. Conversely, direct floricultural employment was significantly associated with lower cognitive performance overall (B= -0.59), with the largest differences observed in Memory Matrix (B= -0.78) and Matching Pair (B= -0.70). Conclusion: Peak pesticide spray seasons were associated with modestly higher processing speed scores, consistent with prior findings in this population suggestive of enhanced cognitive performance associated with neonicotinoid and sulfoximine exposures. In contrast, floricultural employment was associated with significantly lower memory and overall cognitive performance. These results suggest that occupational and seasonal pesticide exposure may have distinct associations with cognitive functioning, highlighting the importance of repeated cognitive testing for characterizing potentially transient effects.

title: Correction: Case Report: Primed dendritic cell immunotherapy for multiple solid tumors
abstract: confirmed by PET/CT or histology, with sustained responses ranging from 6 to 28 months and ongoing in all cases, and no grade 3 or higher adverse events observed. These observations support further evaluation of doubly-loaded autologous dendritic cell therapy in larger, controlled studies.Metastatic solid tumors remain a significant therapeutic challenge across cancer types, particularly when patients develop resistance to conventional treatments (1)(2)(3). Despite advancements in chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), many patients with advanced prostate adenocarcinoma, melanoma, triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), or urothelial carcinoma ultimately experience disease progression and death (4).Like fluorodeoxyglucose-positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) for other solid tumors, the emergence of prostate-specific membrane antigen-positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PSMA-PET/CT) for prostate cancer (PCa) has enabled earlier detection of oligometastatic recurrence, opening the door for metastasis-directed therapy (5,6). Yet even with advanced imaging and focal interventions like stereotactic body radiation therapy, robotic surgical excision, or focal ablation, long-term disease control is typically elusive, especially when patients have exhausted standard-of-care (SOC) options such as androgen deprivation therapy (ADT), radiopharmaceuticals, and taxane-chemotherapy (7,8).Similarly, while immune checkpoint inhibitors have transformed the treatment landscape for metastatic melanoma, some patients demonstrate primary or acquired resistance, and overall response rates remain low for most indications (9,10). Recent clinical studies have shown that combination checkpoint inhibitor therapy can extend overall survival to approximately 70 months in some patients; yet, durable responses are still often limited and treatment failures common (11,12). This is particularly devastating in those with high disease burden or rapid clinical decline. In breast and urothelial cancers, diseases for which response rates to immunotherapy remain modest, new strategies are urgently needed (13)(14)(15).Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy represents a promising therapeutic development, although autoimmune-type toxicities may be dose-limiting (16). Moreover, to date, no CAR-T product targeting non-B-cell tumor types has been approved in the United States of America; however, China has approved a CAR-T therapy for gastric malignancies targeting Claudin18.2, a tight-junction protein that is highly overexpressed in gastrointestinal cancers while showing relatively restricted expression in healthy tissues (17). Although this is a significant breakthrough, the lack of appropriate and comprehensive cell surface targets on most solid tumor types remains a substantial limitation to the CAR-T approach.In contrast, dendritic cell (DC) immunotherapy offers a highly personalized, more physiological approach by stimulating the adaptive immune system through direct tumor-specific antigen presentation (18). Existing DC-based strategies have used defined peptides, tumor lysates, or tumorderived nucleic acids as antigen sources, with varying approaches to DC activation and maturation. For example, Sipuleucel-T utilizes autologous antigen-presenting cells activated ex vivo with a fusion protein composed of prostatic acid phosphatase and granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF), thereby directing the immune response toward a shared prostate tumor antigen rather than the patient-specific tumor antigen repertoire (19). CreaVax-RCC instead sensitizes autologous DCs with tumor lysate and keyhole limpet hemocyanin, whereas APCEDEN utilizes whole-tumor lysateloaded DCs matured with polyinosinic:polycytidylic acid (20)(21)(22). Although these strategies facilitate antigen presentation and DC activation, they are not expected to engage the multi-enzyme aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase (mARS) complex because they were not specifically designed to provide homologous antigenic information simultaneously to the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I and II pathways.Recent mechanistic discoveries suggest that simultaneous presentation of homologous MHC class I and class II-associated antigenic sequences may engage the mARS complex, providing an additional mechanism for DC-mediated immune polarization (23)(24)(25)(26). This 1.5-MDa complex within the endosomes of the DC compares peptide sequences associated with MHC class I and II compartments.When sufficient antigenic homology is detected, conformational changes within the mARS complex promote the release of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase complex-interacting multifunctional protein 1 (AIMP1/p43), a mediator required for interleukin 12 production and downstream T helper 1 (Th1) polarization in experimental models (25). This mechanistic framework provides the rationale for homologous "double-loading," in which DCs are supplied with patient-specific tumor mRNA and tumor lysate to provide overlapping antigenic information through MHC class I and II pathways. By contrast with single-antigen or single-source antigen-loading strategies, double loading is designed to engage this mARS-associated pathway and promote a broader, Th1-based antitumor immune response (25,(27)(28)(29)(30)(31). Clinical trials of double-loaded DCs for aggressive solid malignancies, including glioblastoma (NCT04552886) and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (NCT04157127), have reported encouraging preliminary findings (32).All patients in this case series received double-loaded DC therapy through a standardized three-phase Immunocine™ Dendritic Cell therapy (IDCT) protocol outside the framework of formal clinical trials. The patients first received 5 micrograms/kg of granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF), filgrastim subcutaneously daily over five consecutive days to mobilize white blood cells, concurrent with biopsy to harvest tumor antigens. Apheresis was then performed to collect peripheral blood mononuclear cells for DC production. Monocytes were isolated and differentiated ex-vivo into DCs using a combination of 0.5 ml of GM-CSF stock solution at 2ug/mL (Miltenyi 170-076-136), for a final media concentration 20 ng/ml, and 0.5 mL of Interleukin 4 (IL-4) stock solution at 1ug/mL (Miltenyi 170-076-135), resulting in a final media concentration of 10 ng/ml. Cells were cultured in a final total volume of 50 mL CTS AIM-V media supplemented with 10% inactivated autologous plasma media per T225 flask over a 6-day incubation period. The resulting DCs were then "double-loaded" with patient-specific tumor mRNA and lysate matured with a proinflammatory cytokine cocktail by the method of Decker et al. (2006), enabling tumor-specific antigen presentation via both MHC class I and II pathways (34). Total tumor mRNA was amplified according to the method of Slagter-Jager et al, with technical modifications to enhance fidelity and reproducibility (33). Final DC products underwent in-house and external quality-control assessment. For cell enumeration and dosing determination, acridine orange/propidium iodide fluorescence was measured using a LUNA TM Biotecnología SAPI de CV platform. The dendritic cell preparation and antigen-loading strategy employed in these protocols is consistent with the broader therapeutic principles and approaches being evaluated in U.S. clinical trials of dendritic cell-based cancer vaccines, including NCT04552886 and NCT04157127. Cell collection and processing were performed in facilities holding applicable COFEPRIS (Mexican Federal Commission for the Protection against Sanitary Risk) licenses for stemcell banking, collection, and processing (Licenses 18-TR-23-005-0003 through -0005). These facility licenses are not presented as COFEPRIS approval of the dendritic cell therapy or treatment protocols. Cellular-product preparation was conducted using sterile processing procedures in an ISO Class 7certified cleanroom. Manufacturing practices, process controls, and aseptic procedures were designed and conducted in accordance with applicable principles of current Good Manufacturing Practice (cGMP). Patients provided written informed consent for treatment and for each applicable component of the treatment process, including biopsy, leukapheresis, cellular-product preparation, and administration. Written informed consent was also obtained for the use and publication of clinical information and, where applicable, potentially identifiable images or other patient data included in this report.This first-time report case series presents five patients with metastatic solid tumors, all having failed standard therapies, who subsequently experienced a complete response following treatment with a doubly-loaded autologous DC therapy. The approach incorporates advances in DC preparation utilizing antigen loading and administration techniques that have shown promise in other malignancies, but have not been previously reported in metastatic prostate, melanoma, breast, or urothelial carcinoma (34)(35)(36). These five cases are drawn from the first 80 patients (82% stage IV cancer), of which approximately 70% had objective response rates and nearly 39% achieved a status of either no evidence of disease (NED) or long-term disease control (>2 years).A 62-year-old White male with no smoking history and only occasional alcohol use underwent robotassisted radical prostatectomy with extended pelvic lymph node dissection for PCa in September 2019. Pathology revealed intraductal adenocarcinoma, Gleason 4+3 with 10% tertiary pattern 5, extensive left neurovascular bundle extra-prostatic extension, bilateral seminal vesicle invasion and bilateral microscopic pelvic nodal involvement, 3 nodes-left, 2-right. Postoperative prostate-specific antigen (PSA) declined to 0.04 ng/mL but rose to 0.06 ng/mL two months later. Imaging was initially negative. The patient underwent adjuvant pelvic proton radiation at 6 months post-op, and after eighteen months of ADT exhibited undetectable PSA.Six months later, while still on ADT, the patient's PSA rose to 0.53 ng/mL. Castrate-resistant PCa recurred sequentially in multiple areas: the right perirectal side wall followed by a sub-diaphragmatic implant, a common iliac lymph node, and a substernal lymph node. All were managed with focal ablation, using laser, cryotherapy, or irreversible electroporation. Each time the oligo-metastatic lesions were successfully ablated as determined by both PSMA-PET/CT scanning and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), however, the PSA did not decline substantially, despite combination ADT + androgen receptor inhibitor. Chemotherapy was considered but was withheld due to COVID pandemic-era concerns for immune compromise.Eleven months later, PSA rose to 73 ng/mL and PSMA-PET/CT revealed multiple mediastinal metastases, verified on MRI with gadolinium (Figures 1A, C, andE). Circulating tumor cell (CTC) count was 4/mL and the patient's PSA peaked at 140 ng/mL. Treatment with a combination of Po Salicinum plus topical and sub-lingual Gc protein-derived macrophage activating factor was used while the patient was being qualified for IDCT. Two months later, following the initial IDCT injection to the right inguinal region adjacent to the right inguinal lymph nodes, the patient's PSA declined to 7.8 ng/mL. PSA subsequently decreased to 2.5 ng/mL after the second injection to the bilateral inguinal regions, to 0.7 ng/mL before the third injection, and to 0.6 ng/mL following the third injection in the bilateral axillary region adjacent to the axillary lymph nodes. The prognostic WREN PROSTest, a machine-learning based, 27-gene qPCR liquid biopsy with a diagnostic cutoff of ≥50/100, returned 7/100, consistent with disease control (37,38).Treatment was well tolerated, with only minimal adverse events (AEs) of back pain during filgrastim and 24 hours of myalgias with IFN2a. Repeat PSMA-PET/CT showed resolution of all lesions (Figures 1B, D, and F) except one faint internal mammary lymph node (Figure 1F), which was cryo-ablated. At the six-month follow-up, the patient remains in near-complete remission, without biochemical evidence of progression.A 39-year-old White male with a history of cutaneous melanoma, previously treated with complete surgical resection with negative margins, presented with progressive respiratory symptoms including wheezing and dyspnea. He had a prior history of smoking and alcohol use, but reported cessation of both at the time of evaluation. Chest X-ray revealed a lower left lobe mass, and a computed tomography (CT)-guided biopsy confirmed metastatic melanoma with immunohistochemistry positive for SOX10 and focal S100, consistent with melanocytic origin.Staging CT scans 6 months later revealed a left lower lobe mass of 4.69cm in greatest dimension with satellite nodular opacities along the major fissure, scattered nodular pleural thickening with extension into paraspinal soft tissues at T10, and mediastinal/hilar lymphadenopathy (Figures 2A andC). CT of abdomen, pelvis, and neck revealed left supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, but no other metastases.The patient received checkpoint inhibitor therapy with ipilimumab (3mg/kg) and nivolumab (1mg/kg) every three weeks for two cycles, yet experienced rapid clinical deterioration from Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) 0 to ECOG 3-4 over a four-week period. Repeat imaging confirmed progressive disease with a 29% increase in the primary left lower lobe mass, from 4.69 to 5.8 cm, and worsening lymphadenopathy across multiple sites indicating primary ICI resistance.Two months later, the patient received IDCT injections to the left supraclavicular region adjacent to the left supraclavicular lymph nodes. There were minimal AEs, such as mild fatigue, diarrhea, and changes in hair color, however, no AE required discontinuation of therapy. CT post-treatment revealed a reduction of primary lung mass to 2.9 cm, and no new lesions were identified (Figures 2B andD). Multiple biopsies confirmed the absence of viable tumor. A month following treatment, the patient demonstrated an ECOG 0 status with resumption of modified physical activities, and three to five months following treatment, patient regained pre-diagnosis activity levels.A 33-year-old White male with no history of smoking or alcohol use underwent a sub-total resection of a desmoplastic melanoma of the lower lip, bilateral neck dissection, and reconstruction using a radial forearm free flap. Pathology revealed an 11mm desmoplastic melanoma ulceration, neurotropism, and 11 mitoses/mm 2 . Within six months, despite adjuvant pembrolizumab, the patient experienced local recurrence with tumor involving almost the entire reconstructed lip flap, indicative of acquired ICI resistance. Imaging showed a 4.9×2.9×5.6cm mass with mandibular periosteal involvement and cervical lymphadenopathy (Figures 3A, C, andE).Five months after receiving IDCT injections to the neck adjacent to the cervical lymph nodes, imaging documented mass reduction to 3.36×1.35×2.4cm with complete lymph node resolution (Figures 3B, D, andF). 18 months post-treatment, the patient ceased ICI and fully resumed all activities and personal pursuits. Over 28 months post-treatment, the most recent imaging studies show that the patient remains in complete remission with NED.A 58-year-old White female, with a 12-pack-year smoking history but reported cessation of 10 years at the time of evaluation, who had been diagnosed with TNBC in 2021 and had been treated with anthracycline+taxane-based chemotherapy, underwent lumpectomy and right axillary lymph node dissection revealing 11/12 positive nodes in 2022. Pathology from the mass excised from the right breast revealed recurrent invasive ductal carcinoma, Nottingham grade 3 (3+3+2), with margin involvement (≥12 mm) and lymphovascular invasion. Thus, the patient received adjuvant radiotherapy and several rounds of platinum-based chemotherapy.In July 2024, staging workup demonstrated hypermetabolic right axillary/subpectoral and right cervical (5B) nodes (SUVmax 2.9-4.1) on PET/CT (images not shown). Fine-needle aspiration of the right cervical node confirmed metastatic adenocarcinoma, SOX10+/CKAE1/3+, ER/PR/HER2 negative, AR negative. Baseline laboratory results demonstrated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 293 U/L, D-dimer markedly elevated, C-reactive protein (CRP) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) elevated, and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) ~5.0. title: Balancing Analgesic Effects and Abuse Liability in Older Adults: A Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Trial of Oral and Vaporized Δ9-Tetrahydrocannabinol
abstract: Cannabis use is rising fastest among older adults in the U.S., and pain is among the most common reasons they use it. No trial, however, has measured the trade-off between the analgesic and abuse-related effects of {Delta}9-tetrahydrocannabinol ({Delta}9-THC) in this population. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 20 adults aged 65 and older were assigned to oral {Delta}9-THC (placebo, 5, 10 mg) or vaporized {Delta}9-THC (placebo, 2, 4 mg) across three eight-hour sessions in counterbalanced order. We assessed laboratory-evoked pain sensitivity using quantitative sensory testing, abuse liability using subjective drug effects and reinforcement value, and also sampled plasma {Delta}9-THC and 11-OH-THC. Analgesia and abuse liability outcomes were measured repeatedly within each session. On a pain sensitivity index, oral 5 mg relieved pain relative to placebo (p=.040), although the oral arm's overall dose effect was not significant (p=.108); oral 10 mg and both vaporized doses did not differ from placebo. Subjective effects increased with dose and were greatest after vaporization, whereas reinforcement value increased only after vaporized 4 mg. After oral 5 mg, analgesia exceeded placebo at every assessment (60-360 min), while its pleasurable effects peaked at 150 min. Vaporized {Delta}9-THC produced pleasurable effects within 30 min but did not significantly change thermal pain sensitivity. While abuse liability tracked {Delta}9-THC exposure, analgesia showed no significant association, and all adverse events occurred at vaporized 4 mg. These findings suggest dose and route selection may help maximize {Delta}9-THC analgesia while minimizing abuse liability, a strategy that warrants evaluation in clinical populations.

title: Comparative molecular analysis of histopathologic subtypes reveals shared epithelial remodeling yet distinct fibroblast programs in scleroderma lung disease
abstract: Abstract Rationale Interstitial lung disease (ILD) drives mortality in systemic sclerosis (SSc), with a subset developing progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF) resembling idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF). Despite recognition of two distinct histopathologic patterns, the cellular basis of nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) and usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) remains poorly understood. Objectives To define shared and distinct cellular and molecular features of SSc-NSIP and SSc-UIP compared to IPF. Methods Single-nucleus RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics were performed on explanted lungs from patients with SSc-NSIP (n=6), SSc-UIP (n=6), or IPF (n=6), and control donors (n=12) with immunohistochemistry and western blot validation. Main Results Across 120,254 nuclei from 35 cell types, there was striking similarity across fibrotic subgroups in epithelial, endothelial, and immune compartments, including alveolar type 1 cell loss, pathologic alveolar type 2 (AT2) gene expression, and expansion of COL15A1⁺ endothelial cells and profibrotic macrophages. Diseased AT2s showed activation of the p53/DNA damage pathway. Aberrant basaloid (AB) cells were present in both SSc-ILD subtypes and transcriptionally similar to IPF ABs. They consistently neighbored profibrotic CTHRC1⁺ fibroblasts, even in SSc-NSIP, despite lacking fibroblast foci. Fibroblast heterogeneity differentiated the histopathologic subtypes. Inflammatory fibroblasts were enriched in SSc-NSIP and CTHRC1⁺ fibroblasts in UIP. AB-to-pathologic fibroblast crosstalk was defined by profibrotic signaling, with amplified TGF-β signaling in UIP. Conclusions Convergent epithelial remodeling is a hallmark of PPF in SSc-ILD and IPF. Fibroblast heterogeneity characterized by altered TGF-β signaling distinguishes SSc-NSIP from SSc-UIP and IPF. Accelerated aging, DNA damage, and p53-dependent senescence pathways may represent shared drivers of PPF.

title: Building Researcher Capacity for Patient Engagement in Patient-Centered Outcomes Research: A Mixed-Methods Pilot Evaluation of PREPARE
abstract: Abstract Patients and members of the public can improve health research by sharing their lived experience and helping researchers make studies more relevant and useful. Researchers, however, may not always have practical training in how to work with patients as research partners. We developed PREPARE, a training program designed to help researchers build these skills. We first interviewed 16 researchers and surveyed researchers across several academic and health-system settings to understand their experiences, learning needs, and preferences for training. Patient partners and other stakeholders helped refine the needs assessment and shape the training. We then developed two interactive workshops that combined practical examples, case discussions, and teaching with patient experts. Twenty-one people attended the pilot workshops. Most had not previously received formal training in patient engagement, and participants generally rated the workshop structure and delivery positively. Self-reported confidence was higher after the workshop sessions. Because this was a small pilot and participants were assessed only immediately after training, we do not know whether these changes lasted or changed how researchers later worked with patient partners. PREPARE provides an example of how institutions can use local needs and patient-partner input to develop practical researcher training and ongoing support for meaningful patient engagement.

title: A compact three-way junction oligonucleotide probe for widefield and super-resolution imaging of RNAs and proteins
abstract: Abstract Molecular imaging of RNAs and proteins requires methods that preserve nanoscale organization while enabling large-scale tissue analysis. However, weak or low-abundance targets often need signal amplification, which can increase labeling size, background, or signal spread and compromise super-resolution imaging. Here, we report a compact three-way junction (3WJ) oligonucleotide probe platform for multiscale RNA and protein imaging. The design couples paired target recognition with junction assembly and recruitment of preassembled amplifier complexes, while tunable amplification balances signal strength and labeling size. Using DNA origami and single-molecule localization microscopy, we show enhanced signal while retaining the ability to resolve nanoscale target patterns. The platform improves RNA detection and supports simultaneous RNA-protein super-resolution imaging in cells. It also enhances protein detection in formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissues under low-numerical-aperture, large-field imaging conditions. Together, this programmable 3WJ platform enables sensitive RNA and protein detection across scales, supporting super-resolution analysis of molecular organization and large-field tissue mapping.

title: In-person, team-based rapid qualitative analysis: methodological guidance for researchers conducting applied qualitative health research studies
abstract: Rapid qualitative analysis (RQA) is increasingly used in applied health research to generate timely, practice-relevant findings. While existing literature outlines overarching principles and frameworks, there is limited detailed guidance on how to operationalize team-based RQA in real-world settings. This paper describes a structured, in-person, team-based RQA approach and reports on its use across multiple applied qualitative health research studies. Building on Hamilton’s [1] foundational approach to RQA, we developed and refined a five-phase team-based RQA process—preparing, summarizing, re-organizing, synthesizing, and translating—designed for descriptive qualitative studies requiring timely outputs. The approach was applied across four qualitative health research projects conducted in Ontario, Canada (2021–2023), involving 33–38 interview transcripts per study and 7–10 analysts per team. Data sources informing this methodological paper included field notes, detailed meeting minutes from analysis events, and anonymous feedback from participating analysts ( n = 17) with varying levels of qualitative expertise. Feedback was analyzed to identify perceived benefits, challenges, and recommendations. Team-based RQA enabled accelerated data analysis while maintaining analytic rigor and transparency. Key benefits included efficiency and timeliness, with substantial portions of summarization completed during intensive 2–3 day in-person analysis events; enhanced analytic accuracy through real-time collaboration; and increased interpretive depth from cross-functional team composition. The structured use of domain templates, visual workflow tools, and facilitated debriefings supported consistency and coordination across analysts. The approach also contributed to capacity building by fostering experiential learning among novice researchers. Reported challenges included logistical demands, resource requirements, and the intensity of rapid analysis timelines, as well as the need to sustain momentum during post-event synthesis and reporting phases. This paper provides a detailed, operationalized framework for conducting team-based RQA in applied qualitative or mixed methods health research. By specifying concrete procedures, tools, and team structures, the approach enhances reproducibility, transparency, and accessibility. It is particularly well-suited to descriptive studies requiring timely, actionable findings, though careful planning and experienced leadership are essential to ensure rigor and feasibility. title: Defining the Functional Consequence of the Human Ocular Microbiome
abstract: ABSTRACT The ocular surface is one of the body’s most environmentally exposed mucosal barriers, yet it is considered low biomass and harbors orders of magnitude fewer bacteria than microbe-rich sites like the gut. This has cast doubt on whether a functional core ocular microbiome exists at all. Having previously defined a protective γδ T cell–IL-17 axis engaged by the murine commensal Corynebacterium mastitidis , we asked whether human-derived bacteria could do the same. Pairing sequencing and culturomics of healthy human conjunctiva from two geographically distinct cohorts, we define a stable core microbiome and identify Corynebacterium bovis as a consistent eye-resident commensal rather than a transient contaminant. In humans, C. bovis elicits a non-pathogenic response marked by IL-17 secretion by γδ T cells and circulating C. bovis -specific IgG, which suggests commensalism rather than pathology. Colonizing mice with human C. bovis strains from Pittsburgh or Miami reproduced this program and conferred protection against ocular infection with Staphylococcus aureus . Together, these findings identify C. bovis as a human-derived ocular commensal that can drive protective γδ T cell immunity, translating a mechanism previously defined only in mice into human relevance and a rational target against sight-threatening infection.

title: CD19-CAR T cells reset the EBV + autoreactive B cell repertoire in autoimmune disease
abstract: Abstract Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) reprograms autoreactive B cells into activated antigen-presenting cells that drive pathogenic T- and B-cell responses in autoimmune disease. 1–4 Whether eliminating these cells contributes to durable remission after CD19 chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy 5–7 is unknown. Here, using EBV B-cell sequencing (EBV-seq) 3 , we profiled EBV + B cells from patients treated with CD19-CAR T cells (systemic lupus erythematosus, n=6; inflammatory myopathy, n=3; systemic sclerosis, n=3) or rituximab (n=15) and recombinantly expressed their antibodies to define antigen specificity. At baseline, EBV + B cells were enriched relative to healthy donors, class-switched and hypermutated, expressed the latency III program with heightened antigen-presentation signatures, and encoded autoantibodies. CAR T cells, but not rituximab, depleted EBV + B cells and shifted the reconstituted repertoire towards IgM + , minimally mutated, largely non-autoreactive cells, consistent with infection of newly generated B cells. After rituximab, EBV + B cells retained a class-switched, hypermutated and autoreactive with an activated antigen-presenting phenotype. Sustained drug-free remission occurred in 8/12 CAR T-cell-treated versus 0/15 rituximab-treated patients. In vitro , EBV + B cells resisted anti-CD20 and anti-CD19 antibodies but were killed by CAR T cells and a CD19 T-cell engager. Our findings suggest resetting the EBV + autoreactive B-cell repertoire contributes to sustained drug-free remission.

title: Time-of-Day–Dependent Effectiveness of Anti-IgE Therapy in Asthma: Clinical and Experimental Evidence
abstract: ABSTRACT Background Asthma is a time-sensitive inflammatory disease whose activity exhibits daily (circadian) rhythms. An outstanding question is whether such temporal variations extend to advanced asthma treatments like biologics that are used for moderate-to-severe disease. Objective To examine how time-of-administration relates to the effectiveness of the anti-IgE biologic, omalizumab. Methods We performed a retrospective cohort study of omalizumab effectiveness in 153 patients with asthma with timestamped administration records. Time of day was modeled as a continuous variable and dichotomized into morning (8:00-11:59, n=74) versus afternoon (12:00-17:00, n=79) administration. Multivariable logistic regression and Cox time-to-event analyses were used to adjust for key covariates. For biological validation, we treated ovalbumin (OVA)-sensitized mice with anti-IgE antibody at various times of day and measured its impact on inflammatory lung pathology. Results Receiving the initial dose of omalizumab in the afternoon was associated with better response, defined as a 50% or more reduction in asthma exacerbations in the year after initiation (Odds ratio, OR: 5.20; 95% CI, 1.94−13.96). For each hour later in the day the initial dose of omalizumab was given, the odds of a response increased by 34% (adjusted OR, 1.34; 1.02–1.77). In OVA-sensitized mice, anti-IgE treatment attenuated inflammatory lung pathology, including OVA-induced airway hyperresponsiveness and type-2 inflammation-related gene expression, in a time-of-day-sensitive manner, with maximum effectiveness when dosed in the latter part of the dark phase, functionally analogous to the afternoon in humans. Conclusion The timing of anti-IgE treatment for asthma may influence therapeutic success. These findings have implications for optimizing the effectiveness of respiratory biologics. Take-home messages IgE-targeted therapy in patients with asthma and in murine experimental asthma varied in effectiveness based on administration time. In patients, receiving the first omalizumab dose in the PM (vs. AM) was associated with better treatment response.

title: Residual Symptoms and Quality of Life in Female Patients with Hypothyroidism and Cardiovascular Disease
abstract: Abstract Background Current clinical management of patients with hypothyroidism emphasizes thyroid hormone replacement at doses that normalize serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels. However, biochemical correction does not always translate into symptom resolution or restored health-related quality of life (QoL). We evaluated whether higher TSH levels within the reference range would be associated with worse Thyroid-Related Patient-Reported Outcome (ThyPRO)-39 scores, reflecting greater symptom burden. Objective The objective of this study was to assess residual symptoms and health-related quality of life in women with normal TSH levels in patients with cardiovascular disease being treated for hypothyroidism. Materials and methods We prescreened 96 participants who completed study assessments. Following the TSH obtained at the study visit, 14 participants were excluded due to TSH values falling outside the predefined euthyroid range (0.35-4.94 μIU/mL), resulting in a final cohort of 82 women. We also investigated whether comorbidities contributed to symptom burden. Results Although mean composite scores were numerically higher in the upper TSH quartiles, neither multivariable regression nor ordered trend testing demonstrated a significant association between increasing TSH and overall symptom burden (Jonckheere-Terpstra p = .333). Notably, major depressive disorder (MDD) (β=16.93, 95% CI 8.22–25.65; p<.001) and hypertension (HTN) (β=12.45, 95% CI 2.24–22.66; p=.018) were independently associated with greater Thy-PRO-39 scores. Conclusions MDD and HTN were independently associated with higher Thy-PRO-39 scores, suggesting that comorbidities may be more strongly related to persistent symptoms than modest variation in TSH within the euthyroid range. Our results suggest that in patients with hypothyroidism and cardiovascular disease, comorbidities may be particularly important when interpreting residual symptoms in biochemically euthyroid patients.

title: An Improved Manufacturing Method for Infusible Extracellular Matrix Materials to Enable Efficient Scale-Up, Improved Efficacy, and Clinical Translation
abstract: Decellularized extracellular matrix (ECM) materials are a popular choice for tissue engineering and regenerative medicine applications due to their multifaceted bioactive capabilities arising from their heterogenous composition. For minimally invasive delivery, infusible ECM (iECM) was developed through fractionation of digested decellularized ECM, allowing the material to be safely delivered intravascularly. iECM localizes to permeable vasculature in inflamed tissues and exerts immunomodulatory and pro-reparative effects with proof-of-concept already demonstrated in multiple preclinical models including myocardial infarction (MI) and multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS). However, one major limitation of iECM is the steps required for manufacturing, involving centrifugation, dialysis/lyophilization, and filtration (C-D-F). These steps limit manufacturing output and iECM concentration, and require significant human handling, limiting compliance with current good manufacturing practices (cGMP). To overcome these challenges, we developed a method for manufacturing iECM that utilizes depth filtration and tangential flow filtration (DF-TFF), which reduces manufacturing time, allows for increased iECM concentration, and reduces human manipulation of material, improving translatability and scalability of iECM materials. Based on multiple material characterization methods, we determined that iECM made with DF-TFF was comparable to iECM made with C-D-F. By increasing iECM concentration through this manufacturing method, we demonstrate a dose dependent response in an acute MI porcine model and a mouse MODS model. Finally, DF-TFF enabled timely production of iECM from alternative tissue sources. Altogether, DF-TFF allows for improvements in production time, scale-up, cGMP compliance, and increased dose through higher concentration, paving the way for future clinical translation as well new preclinical studies.

title: Impaired loading following denervation elicits dynamic, differential growth trajectories of musculoskeletal tissues.
abstract: Physical forces dictate the function and maintenance of adult musculoskeletal tissues. Yet, the impact of biophysical cues on the growth and maturation of these tissues, especially dense connective tissues, remains unclear. Here, we investigated the effects of neonatal mechanical loading on early postnatal growth of the musculoskeletal tissues of the lower limb, with particular focus on the Achilles tendon. We performed sciatic nerve resection (SNR) on one-day-old mice to denervate the hamstrings and distal hindlimb muscles. Sciatic Nerve Resection resulted in severe and sustained alterations in gait, accompanied by an altered transcriptional landscape in distal musculoskeletal tissues, with marked reductions in bone and tendon growth and smaller, fibrotic hindlimb musculature. Sciatic nerve resection impaired cumulative growth in the Achilles tendon, shifting cell proliferation and matrix-driven growth trajectories and altering mechanotransduction gene programs toward inflammation and matrix catabolism with age. This work highlights the essential role of mechanical loading in driving mechanosignaling and postnatal growth trajectories in musculoskeletal tissues of the developing limb, with implications for overall musculoskeletal health in adulthood.

title: Sex-based differences in fibrosis markers in human abdominal aortic aneurysms.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) are a complex degenerative vascular disease. The role of fibrosis in AAA progression is unclear. Our study evaluated the impact of fibroblast activation protein (FAP), collagen, and vimentin on AAA fibrosis and progression. We hypothesized that FAP may influence fibrosis and disease severity in AAA, with potential sex-specific differences.
STUDY DESIGN: Multi-centered transcriptomic analysis of aortic samples from 15 human AAA and 5 non-AAA was performed to evaluate cell-specific fibrosis gene expression profiles. Histopathological and molecular analysis of 26 male and female AAA samples (mAAA and fAAA) and 29 male and female normal abdominal aortas (mNAA and fNAA) was performed to assess whole-tissue fibrosis markers and signaling.
RESULTS: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis identified eight major cell clusters with distinct sex-based distributions. Although vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) and fibroblast clusters had reduced counts in both male and female AAAs, they more highly expressed FAP and COL1A1 genes, particularly in females. Whole-tissue analysis demonstrated elevated extracellular matrix deposits with markedly increased collagen type 1 in both mAAA and fAAA. Alpha-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA)-positive VSMCs were also reduced in mAAA and fAAA, but FAP was notably elevated, and robustly in fAAA. FAP-positive fibroblasts in fAAA exhibited increased expression of fibrosis markers, suggesting a unique pro-fibrotic phenotype.
CONCLUSION: Our study reveals a sex-based difference in AAA tissue, with elevated fibrosis markers and increased FAP levels in females, suggesting its significant role in disease progression. These findings underscore the potential of FAP as a unique tissue biomarker for AAAs and warrants further investigation into novel targeted therapies that aim to stabilize AAAs, particularly in female patients.

title: Core schema instability in youth at clinical high risk for psychosis: within-person variability as an index of self-belief precision
abstract: Aim: Core schemas are considered stable traits in clinical high risk (CHR) research. However, unexamined fluctuation may conceal belief changes that precede psychosis emergence. We examined whether schemas possess considerable within-person variability in CHR, and whether that variability exceeds that of controls. Methods: In NAPLS-2, 411 CHR and 194 control participants completed the Brief Core Schema Scales (BCSS) at least three times across 24 months. Random-intercept models identified intraclass correlations in CHR. Bayesian censored location-scale models, correcting for floor scores and mean level differences, compared within-person SD between groups. Results: Within-person variance accounted for 41.3%-50.6% of BCSS variance in CHR. Latent within-person SD was greater in CHR on all four subscales, most for negative-self (ratio 1.71, 95% CrI [1.50, 1.94]). This variability was largely independent of shared improvement and psychotropic medication effects. Conclusions: Core schemas fluctuate substantially in CHR compared to controls, particularly in negative self-beliefs. Single baseline scores may understate schema-outcome associations.

title: Real-world performance of large-scale propensity score adjustment strategies: matching, weighting, and stratification
abstract: Abstract Objective Propensity score (PS) models are commonly used for addressing confounding in observational studies. Researchers are increasingly incorporating large numbers of covariates into PS models, using techniques like large-scale propensity score (LSPS) adjustment. It remains unclear if the inclusion of many covariates affects the subsequent choice of adjustment strategy. Methods In this paper, we evaluate commonly used adjustment strategies using large-scale models, including matching, stratification, and inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), to estimate treatment effects under a new-user cohort design. Evaluations employ real-world data across four national healthcare databases and incorporate 3,840 treatment effect estimates per model specification for 24 different treatment cohort comparisons against 160 negative control outcomes. We assess adjustment strategies for covariate balance between treatment cohorts and type-I and type-II error, mean-squared error, and precision of the adjusted effect estimate. Results Across all model specifications, IPTW with symmetric Crump trimming and 1:1 matching perform best overall, achieving strong balance and low type-I error. Additionally, empirical calibration of effect estimates can substantially reduce differences between strategies. Discussion No single strategy is clearly superior in all settings. We recommend incorporating the top-performing strategies at least as sensitivity analyses in studies even if researchers anticipate that some other strategy may excel due to expectation of their study’s operating characteristics. We also recommend use of diagnostics like covariate balance to check strategy performance. Conclusion IPTW with Crump trimming and 1:1 matching are strong default choices for large-scale PS adjustment, but strategy selection should be guided by study context and validated with balance and error diagnostics. We broadly recommend empirical calibration to reduce sensitivity to model choice.

title: Tryptophan Restores Recovery Competence Following Starvation in the Absence of Lysosomal Amino Acid Sensing
abstract: Abstract How organisms recover from starvation to nutrient-replete physiology remains poorly understood. In C. elegans , we previously observed that transcription factor hlh-30 or a combination of glucose and linoleic acid in its absence are essential for survival with refeeding following starvation, i.e. recovery competence. A forward genetic screen to evaluate mechanisms identified depd-5 , which encodes a GATOR1 subunit, loss of which is expected to impair amino acid sensing with unrestrained raga-1 and mTOR activation. Surprisingly, glucose refeeding reduced recovery competence in depd-5(lf , loss-of-function) animals, which was rescued by amino acids, specifically tryptophan. Increasing tryptophan levels in depd-5(lf) worms through supplementation, reduced tryptophan catabolism with tdo-2 ablation and prolonged starvation restored recovery competence. raga-1(gf , gain-of-function) recapitulated whereas raga-1(lf) rescued the impaired recovery competence in starved depd-5(lf) worms. An analogous DEPDC5 mutation in mammalian cells impaired starvation-induced mTOR inactivation. We conclude that tryptophan counters unrestrained mTOR activity to restore recovery competence following starvation.

title: Megalin-mediated deterministic pseudotransduction in proximal tubules fundamentally challenges current understanding of AAV kidney transduction
abstract: Genetic kidney diseases are promising targets for gene therapy. Emerging AAV capsids that reportedly enable effective gene delivery to proximal tubules (PTs) following intravenous injection have raised hopes for treating diseases affecting renal tubules. Despite these promising developments, the scientific literature contains contradictory and non-reproducible findings, which prompted us to conduct a detailed and rigorous investigation of the mechanisms of AAV vector-mediated PT transduction. Here we provide compelling evidence that previously reported effective PT transduction following intravenous AAV-GFP or AAV-mCherry administration largely reflects megalin-mediated deterministic pseudotransduction rather than stochastic vector-mediated gene delivery. We demonstrate that this process is mediated by megalin-dependent uptake of circulating reporter proteins released from transduced organs including the liver and filtered through the glomeruli. These observations highlight the ongoing challenge of achieving true proximal tubule transduction via systemic AAV delivery and caution against relying on small reporters like GFP or mCherry, which can produce misleading signals.

title: The Awareness of Missing Exit Mechanism in China's Serious Mental Disorder Management Systems: The Occupational Experience of Community Mental Health Workers in China
abstract: Abstract Background China’s Serious Mental Disorder Management Systems (SMDMS) is among the world's largest community-based mental health programs, providing longitudinal management for more than 6.4 million individuals. Although the system has substantially improved treatment access and continuity of care, one critical structural feature remains unexamined: there is no clearly defined exit mechanism by which individuals may leave the system following diagnostic revision or sustained recovery. Little is known about frontline community workers’ understanding of this policy or their occupational experiences within the SMDMS. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional survey of all 265 community workers responsible for community management of serious mental disorder (SMD) management in one district in Guangdong Province, China. The sample comprised 233 healthcare professionals and 32 community social workers. The survey assessed knowledge of the current management system, occupational experiences, attitudes toward patients, perceptions of service effectiveness, and job satisfaction. Results Overall, 66.4% of respondents correctly recognized that SMDMS lacks a formal exit mechanism. Nearly ninety percent (88.3%) reported having experienced discourteous treatment from patients or family members, and over half (53.2%) indicated that such encounters resulted in at least mild to moderate anxiety. Although most respondents believed the program substantially improved patients' functioning (82.6%) and relieved treatment burden (89.8%), only 42.6% expressed overall job satisfaction, with 40.4% remaining neutral. Conclusion Frontline community workers perceived the SMDMS as clinically beneficial but reported substantial occupational challenges and identified important gaps in the current policy framework. The absence of a transparent review and exit mechanism warrants further examination as China continues to develop recovery-oriented, rights-based community mental health services.

title: Structural brain network organization and aggressive behavior in schizophrenia: a mega-analysis of 2260 patients and 3058 healthy controls from the ENIGMA-Schizophrenia Working Group
abstract: Abstract Background Although most individuals with schizophrenia do not show aggressive behavior, rates are higher than in the general population. Identifying the neurobiological correlates of aggression may inform prevention. Methods We included 2260 individuals with schizophrenia spectrum disorders and 3058 healthy controls (HC) from 26 sites in the ENIGMA-Schizophrenia Working Group. The former were classified as showing at least moderate aggression (SZ+A; N = 231) or not (SZ−A; N = 2029) based on symptom rating scales. Structural covariance networks were constructed from cortical and subcortical volumes. We examined global and nodal network topology, as well as density within six large-scale brain networks and between each network and the rest of the brain. Metrics were summarized as the area under the curve (AUC) across a prespecified range of densities ( K = 0.10–0.25, Δ K = 0.01). Group differences were assessed using pairwise permutation tests with Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. Results Global and nodal network topology did not differ significantly between SZ+A and HC. Network–rest density of the salience network (SN) was higher in SZ+A than in HC, although this difference did not survive multiple-comparison correction (ΔAUC = 0.018, p BH = .083). In exploratory subgroup analyses, higher SN network–rest density was observed only in SZ+A with high delusion severity (ΔAUC = 0.021, p = .007). By contrast, SZ−A demonstrated extensive alterations in global network topology compared with SZ+A and HC, alongside selective alterations in nodal topology and large-scale network density compared with HC. Results were broadly consistent across sensitivity analyses using alternative definitions of aggression and adjusting for current antipsychotic dose. Conclusions SZ+A was characterized by fewer—not more—abnormalities in structural covariance network organization than SZ−A, which may reflect etiological heterogeneity. In SZ+A with high delusion severity, higher network–rest density of the SN may point to aberrant salience processing in aggressive behavior.
