title: Beneficial early, harmful later: age-dependent effects of testicular factors on male mortality
abstract: Men live shorter lives than women across nearly all human populations, a disadvantage that extends across most biological causes of death and that cannot be fully explained by behavioral or environmental differences. This suggests that fundamental biological mechanisms contribute to elevated male mortality. Our previous work implicated testicular factors as a major contributor, showing that prepubertal castration extends male lifespan to that of females in UM-HET3 mice, a genetically heterogeneous stock. However, it remains unknown when testicular factors begin to exert their detrimental effects on mortality. Here, we castrated UM-HET3 males before puberty (20 days), after puberty (60 days), or immediately before the typical rise in male mortality (240 days). Castration at all three ages prevented the early male mortality and increased median lifespan by 19.3%, 25.8%, and 32.9%, respectively. The comparable survival benefits of prepubertal and postpubertal castration indicate that exposure to the pubertal surge in testicular factors, including male sex hormones, is not responsible for establishing the male longevity disadvantage. Remarkably, castration at 240 days not only preserved the survival benefit of earlier castration but produced significantly greater survival than earlier castration, suggesting that testicular exposure before 240 days is actually beneficial. The immediate prevention of excess male mortality following castration at 240 days also indicates that the responsible testicular factors act rapidly and that their continued presence is necessary to sustain elevated male mortality. Longitudinal body-composition measurements further revealed that castration shifted males toward a female-like phenotype, characterized by reduced lean mass and continued fat accumulation into later life. Our findings reveal opposing age-dependent effects of testicular factors on survival and narrow the potential therapeutic window to later adulthood.

title: Filovirus Seroreactivity Beyond Virus-Specific Outbreak Regions in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, 2015-2023
abstract: ABSTRACT The ongoing Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is the second-largest Ebola disease outbreak in recorded history, and only the second recorded BVD outbreak in the country. While the DRC has recorded 18 filovirus disease outbreaks, the historical frequency and geographic distribution of human filovirus exposures remain poorly understood. Using a multiplexed multi-filovirus immunoassay, we assessed antibody reactivity against antigens of filoviruses linked to human disease, Bundibugyo virus (BDBV), Ebola virus (EBOV), Marburg virus (MARV), and Sudan virus (SUDV), among eleven cohorts from seven provinces between 2015–2023 (n=5,852). Participants with median fluorescence intensity values exceeding established antigen-specific cutoffs were classified as seroreactive. Seroreactivity against glycoprotein (GP) targets of all four viruses were detected in every cohort, demonstrating evidence of filovirus or an antigenically related exposure well beyond known outbreak regions. Seroreactivity estimates varied by cohort site, with 60.8% of participants (n=175/288) in Mongala Province in April 2016 considered seroreactive against BDBV GP. In this cohort, 4.2%, 29.9%, and 34.7% of participants were seroreactive against EBOV, MARV and SUDV GP, respectively yet only 1.7% were seroreactive against all four GP antigens. In adjusted analyses, site was the primary predictor of seroreactivity, with odds for BDBV seroreactivity 9.1-fold (95%CI 7.0-11.9) and 9.5-fold (95%CI 6.9-13.2) higher in Mongala and Tshuapa provinces than in Kwilu. Similarly, the adjusted odds of MARV and SUDV GP seroreactivity were 4.5-fold and 7.1-fold higher in Mongala, and 3.7-fold and 6.1-fold higher in Tshuapa, than Kwilu. Among 280 individuals sampled longitudinally, BDBV GP detected seroconversion was comparable by site, with 12.8% in Kwilu and 10.4% in Mongala having detected seroreactivity three and five years after initial contact, respectively. Overall, these results indicate widespread, geographically heterogeneous filovirus seroreactivity across sampled cohorts. These findings may reflect zoonotic spillover events, leading to undetected human-to-human filovirus circulation, including paucisymptomatic or asymptomatic infections, or exposure to as-yet unidentified antigenically cross-reactive viruses. These data highlight gaps in understanding the historical and geographic distribution of filovirus exposure in the DRC and support further prospective serological, epidemiological, and molecular investigations, especially given the current outbreak.

title: Innate Immune Dysregulation Precedes Clinical Onset in Neuromyelitis Optica
abstract: Abstract Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) is a disabling inflammatory central nervous system (CNS) disease characterized by pathogenic aquaporin 4 (AQP4) autoantibodies. The biological events that precede clinical onset remain unknown. In a unique longitudinal NMOSD cohort from the U.S. Department of Defense Serum Repository, with samples collected up to 24 years before onset, we applied discovery proteomics (∼5,400 proteins), pan-viral antibody profiling (VirScan), and in silico analyses to characterize preclinical NMOSD versus matched healthy controls. Innate immune activation, particularly CXCL1 elevation, was the dominant immunological feature of preclinical NMOSD, preceding onset by ∼12.7 years. AQP4-IgG was detectable more than 3 years before onset, while CNS injury markers increased only after disease manifestation. VirScan identified enhanced CMV-specific antibody reactivity following AQP4-IgG seroconversion, and network analyses revealed interactions between NMOSD-associated and CMV-derived proteins. Together, these findings establish a novel multi-hit model of NMOSD, with implications for understanding antibody-mediated autoimmunity more broadly.

title: Longitudinal Filovirus Seroreactivity Following Ad26.ZEBOV (Zabdeno) and MVA-BN-Filo (Mvabea) Vaccination in the Democratic Republic of the Congo
abstract: Abstract Background Filoviruses, specifically Ebola virus (EBOV), Bundibugyo virus (BDBV), and Marburg virus (MARV), have been the etiologic agents of multiple outbreaks of severe disease in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). Two EBOV-specific vaccine regimens have been approved for use in outbreak scenarios, including the Ad26.ZEBOV/MVA-BN-Filo (Zabdeno/Mvabea) two-dose vaccine, where the MVA-BN-Filo booster dose contains EBOV, MARV, and Sudan (SUDV) virus glycoproteins (GPs) and the nucleoprotein from Tai Forest virus. While long-term immunogenicity of up to two years has been found in clinical trial settings, limited real-world data exists. Methods Using a multiplexed immunoassay, samples ( n =698 at baseline) collected in Mbandaka, Equateur province, DRC, between September 2023 and October 2024 were assessed for seroreactivity to six filovirus antigens (1 BDBV, 2 EBOV, 2 MARV, and 1 SUDV) at three distinct periods: baseline/pre-vaccination, 6-8 weeks post-first dose (Zabdeno), at booster administration (Mvabea), and one-year post-boost dose. Results Substantial filovirus seroreactivity was found at baseline, with 48.7% ( n =340/698) of individuals being seroreactive to at least one virus antigen. High baseline seroreactivity was found against BDBV GP (31.1%, n =217/698), with lower baseline seroreactivity to EBOV GP (15.5%, n =106/698), comparatively. Overall EBOV GP seroreactivity increased to 66.8% ( n =376/563) at one year-post vaccine boost and 57.6% ( n =250/434) of participants were seroreactive. Despite the booster dose inclusion of SUDV GP and MARV GP, there were no substantial increases in reactivity against either antigen at subsequent timepoints. Overall filovirus seroreactivity increased at all timepoints for the entire cohort, although filovirus reactivity decreased over the study period for those who were seroreactive at baseline. Findings These data highlight detection of significantly elevated seoreactivity to EBOV GP following first-dose administration of Ad26.ZEBOV, which remained relatively stable one-year post-booster dose administration. Additionally, this study identifies high levels of baseline seroreactivity to BDBV GP despite no previous documented outbreaks in this region of DRC. These data suggest that vaccination with the Ad26.ZEBOV-MVA-BN-Filo vaccine induces stable seroreactivity against EBOV GP, but not to other filovirus antigens.

title: Isoflurane anesthesia CNS recovery state: ultra-slow oscillations and cellular-stress-responsive gene expression
abstract: General anesthesia and NREM sleep share slow-wave EEG features, yet whether anesthesia substitutes for physiological sleep remains unclear. We compared recovery from 4h of isoflurane anesthesia (IA) with time-matched sleep and sleep deprivation (SD) in male C57BL/6J mice using continuous EEG/EMG recordings and frontal cortex RNA sequencing. IA recovery produced transient, rebound arousal, reduced early NREM and REM sleep, and, fragmented subsequent NREM bouts, and persistant, ultra-slow EEG-oscillations that normalized within two weeks. Whereas, SD induced consolidated rebound sleep and slow wave activity. Transcriptomic profiling at ZT6 showed that IA and SD induced largely distinct cortical gene-expression programs. IA preferentially enriched integrated stress response and unfolded protein response genes, whereas SD showed a comparatively orthogonal, growth-permissive, mTOR-associated profile. Although IA-induced gene-expression suggests cellular stress, corticosterone measurements argued against systemic stress as the primary driver. These findings indicate that isoflurane recovery is neurophysiologically and molecularly distinct from restorative sleep.

title: Motivation to work for amino acids requires acute dopaminergic activity
abstract: Abstract Aberrant motivation is a hallmark of many psychiatric disorders, and studying motivation in model systems can be useful to understand the neural mechanisms of these disorders. Having versatile, ethologically relevant assays with which to measure motivation is therefore important. However, motivational assays in Drosophila have not been able to measure willingness to exert effort to consume food. Here, we took advantage of the fact that flies prefer to feed on liquid over solid foods to develop a new assay using agarose as a barrier to feeding, which we termed the Fly Liquid vs Agarose Motivation Evaluation (FLAME). Unlike motivational assays based on overcoming bitterness, the FLAME measures willingness to work and is less confounded by deprivation acting on peripheral sensing of the modality to overcome. By depriving flies of specific nutrients and measuring their choice to overcome semi-solid agarose food to get those nutrients, we show that the FLAME is a versatile assay for measuring motivation. We show that flies choose to overcome agarose to consume sugar, salt, or amino acids, depending on the specific prior deprivation. We then show that show that flies rely on acute activity in a subset of their dopamine neurons during the choice period in order to work for amino acids when deprived. The FLAME thus allows the investigation of specific neural mechanisms of motivation. Significance Statement Having good assays to measure motivation in model systems is important for understanding psychiatric disease. In flies, existing assays have measured only some aspects of motivation, limiting progress. Here, we develop a better assay (the FLAME) for measuring motivation to feed in Drosophila melanogaster . We demonstrate the versatility of our assay and show that a subset of dopamine neurons in the fly are required for them to exert effort for amino acid consumption when deprived. The FLAME will therefore be of use to researchers seeking to understand the basic mechanisms of motivational drives.

title: Directionally Factorized Illumination with Spherical Harmonic Rotation
abstract: Many real-world capture scenarios involve an active light source rigidly attached to the camera: camera flashes for dark-environment imaging, underwater vehicle lights, and endoscopic/laparoscopic medical procedures. As the camera moves, the co-mounted light moves with it, causing the illumination direction at each surface point to change across views. Neural rendering methods (NeRF, Gaussian Splatting) encode this pose-dependent illumination as surface coloration, producing appearance inconsistencies and making it harder to recover the underlying scene. We present \textbf{DaFISH}, which can be plugged into any novel-view synthesis (NVS) pipeline such as NeRF. It factorizes per-point emitted color into surface albedo and a spherical harmonic (SH)-represented illumination factor. During training, the SH illumination is evaluated directly, enabling stable joint optimization of albedo, lighting, and geometry. \textbf{DaFISH} provides analytical generalization of illumination to arbitrary camera poses without retraining. Building on the closed-form SH-to-irradiance conversion, the training pipeline is fully differentiable from SH evaluation through volume rendering. Averaged over the held-out frames of the five scenes, \textbf{DaFISH} attains the best mean PSNR (38.91\,dB), SSIM (0.9613), and LPIPS (0.0582) among all compared methods. It improves over the strongest splatting baseline as well as the closest NeRF-based baseline, while recovering the scene consistently across views compared to prior methods.

title: Accelerated high-capacity 6 mA transcranial direct current stimulation for major depression.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Home-based 2 mA transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) is FDA-approved for depression, but amplitude has been limited largely by skin tolerance. This study evaluated the safety, tolerability, and feasibility of accelerated high-capacity tDCS (HC-tDCS) at 6 mA.
METHODS: In this open-label pilot study, 20 patients with major depressive disorder received 20-minute bifrontal 6 mA sessions twice daily for five days using a high-capacity stimulator and hydrogel electrodes. A Safety Review Committee reviewed data from the first three participants before the remaining 17 were enrolled.
RESULTS: Retention and adherence were 100% (203 of 203 sessions); 17 of 20 received 6 mA throughout, with amplitude reduced for intolerance in one and limited by an electrode fault in two. There were no serious adverse events. The most common symptoms were fatigue (49% of sessions), burning (46%) and tingling (43%) at the electrode, and difficulty concentrating (40%). Electrode-site erythema occurred in all participants, with no severe reactions. At 1 week, 7 of 20 reported a residual skin change, none painful; at 1 month, spots of residual pigmentation were observed at the electrode site in 2 participants, both Black. In five days, mean PHQ-9 scores decreased from 15.8 to 7.2 (Hedges g=1.62); 50% of participants responded, 45% remitted, and improvement was maintained at 1 month. Anhedonia, mindfulness, and self-reported cognitive function also improved (g=0.76 to 1.23), with gains maintained at 1 month.
CONCLUSIONS: Accelerated 6 mA HC-tDCS was feasible, well tolerated, and warrants a sham-controlled trial.

title: PIEZO1 mediates mechanosensing and myofibroblastic activation of synovial fibroblasts in post-traumatic osteoarthritis
abstract: Abstract Fibrosis and inflammation of the synovium are common pathological features of joint diseases. In osteoarthritis (OA), extensive evidence supports that synovial pathology drives symptoms and disease progression, yet the mechanisms underpinning pathological synovial remodeling, including fibrosis, remain unclear. Here, we identify the mechanosensitive ion channel PIEZO1 as a critical regulator of myofibroblast-like activation of synovial fibroblasts (SFs) in post-traumatic osteoarthritis (PTOA). Using multi-omic assessments in human and murine synovium, a murine model of joint injury, histopathology, and functional in vitro phenotyping, we demonstrate that joint injury triggers expansion of myofibroblast-like SFs concurrent with fibrotic remodeling and mechanical stiffening of the synovium. Myofibroblastic commitment of synovial progenitors was associated with activation of the YAP1 regulon, and PIEZO1 agonism drove nuclear accumulation of YAP1 in SFs. PIEZO1 was enriched in synovia of injured joints, and in cultured SFs pharmacologic PIEZO1 activation promoted αSMA enrichment and increased matrix contraction, which were both ablated by YAP1 inhibition. PIEZO1 silencing abrogated TGF-β-induced contractility and markedly altered the transcriptomic response to mechanical loading in vitro , including ECM production and neuroinflammatory programs. In vivo , acute intra-articular pharmacologic PIEZO1 activation induced a pro-fibrotic, pro-inflammatory, and anti-adipogenic transcriptomic program in synovium. Collectively, these findings establish PIEZO1 as a key mediator of the pathogenic activation of SFs and identify aberrant mechanosensing as a mechanism underlying synovial fibrosis in PTOA.

title: Synaptic microRNA dysregulation orchestrates aberrant glutamatergic transmission in a human neuronal model of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome
abstract: 22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome (22q11DS), the most prevalent chromosomal microdeletion disorder in humans (incidence ∼1 in 4,000 live births), arises from hemizygous deletions of a 1.5-3.0 Mb region on chromosome 22. Notably, 20-30% of individuals with 22q11DS develop schizophrenia (SCZ) by early adulthood, making 22q11DS one of the strongest genetic risk factors for SCZ. However, the mechanisms by which the 22q11.2 deletion perturbs neuronal function and drive psychotic manifestations in 22q11DS remain poorly defined. In this study, we generated human 2D cortical neurons and 3D cortical organoids from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) derived from clinically well-characterized individuals with 22q11DS. Cellular and electrophysiological analyses revealed that 22q11DS neurons exhibit hyperexcitability, reduced glutamatergic synaptic transmission, and impaired homeostatic synaptic plasticity, which are pathophysiological hallmarks that may be relevant to the clinical, cognitive, and psychophysiological profiles of patients. Transcriptomic profiling of neurons and synaptosomes from 22q11DS cortical organoids uncovered dysregulated immune pathways and synaptic gene networks. Integrative mRNA-microRNA network analysis identified synergistic downregulation of hsa-miR-185-5p and hsa-miR-128-3p at synapses, driving aberrant regulation of immune and synaptic transcripts. Experimental knockdown of these microRNAs in control neurons recapitulated the molecular and functional phenotypes of 22q11DS neurons, thereby establishing a mechanistic link to synaptic dysfunction and impaired plasticity. Collectively, these findings delineate a multimodal mechanistic framework that bridges genetic vulnerability, synaptic pathology, and psychosis penetrance in 22q11DS, positioning dysregulated synaptic microRNAs as nodal regulators of neurodevelopmental networks and potential therapeutic targets.

title: Human Choroid Plexus Organoids Progress to Postnatal-like Maturation and Reveal a Closing Window of Developmental Plasticity
abstract: Summary The choroid plexus (ChP) produces cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and forms the blood-CSF barrier, yet the developmental programme driving its maturation in humans remains poorly understood. Using a 15-timepoint single-cell RNA sequencing atlas of human ChP organoids benchmarked against human tissue, we resolve an ordered differentiation process comprising cell cycle exit, ciliogenesis and ion transporter expression. Maturation culminates in a transcriptional state with features of human adult ChP, establishing the first in vitro ChP model to reach postnatal-like milestones. Centrosome proteomics identified previously uncharacterised, stage-specific regulators of ciliogenesis. To probe developmental plasticity, we perturbed ChP organoids with valproic acid (VPA), a clinically used antiepileptic and established teratogen. Early VPA-mediated disruption of multiciliogenesis and secretion recovered upon drug withdrawal, whereas late treatment washout resulted in persistent impairment of mature transporters. Together, these findings resolve the developmental programme by which the ChP reaches functionally mature identity and identify a stage-dependent plasticity window during its maturation.

title: Mechano-activated synovial cells instigate OA-like disease progression in the absence of joint injury
abstract: ABSTRACT While altered tissue mechanics and cellular mechanoactivation accompany osteoarthritis, whether dysregulated mechanotransduction can initiate joint disease remains unclear. Here, we used intra-articular delivery of cell-penetrating TAT-Cre recombinase to locally perturb the actomyosin–Hippo mechanotransduction axis in mice. Deletion of Lats1/2 , the negative regulators of the mechanosensitive transcriptional coactivators YAP and TAZ, induced sustained joint hyperalgesia, altered gait, synovial hyperplasia and fibrosis, vascular remodeling, and articular cartilage degeneration in the absence of a destabilizing injury. Single-cell transcriptomics revealed the emergence of Cthrc1 + matrix-remodeling fibroblasts and accumulation of Mrc1 + Trem2 + macrophages during this pathological process. Histological analyses showed persistent contractile stromal remodeling and an early macrophage response that partially subsided over four weeks. Conversely, local deletion of Myh9/10 , encoding the force-generating heavy chains of non-muscle myosin II, reduced hyperalgesia, synovial lining hyperplasia, αSMA + cell accumulation, and macrophage infiltration during post-traumatic osteoarthritis (PTOA) pathogenesis. However, this intervention did not detectably reduce cartilage degeneration at eight weeks. These findings establish synovial mechanotransduction as a causal driver of joint disease via immune–stromal remodeling and pain development. In addition, partial suppression of contractility separates symptomatic from structural outcomes in PTOA. Synovial mechanotransduction therefore represents a target for modulating pathological stromal–immune remodeling and joint pain.

title: Keratinocyte FABP5 mediates saturated fat-induced MAPK/CCL20 signaling in psoriatic inflammation
abstract: Abstract Saturated fats in high-fat diets (HFDs) have been associated with increased risk and severity of psoriasis. However, the underlying cellular and molecular mechanisms remain to be further defined. Here, using a unique mouse strain with keratinocyte-specific deletion of fatty acid-binding protein 5 (FABP5) (Fabp5 f/f Krt6a-Cre), we reported that keratinocyte FABP5 deletion significantly attenuated saturated HFD-exacerbated psoriatic symptoms. Immunological analyses demonstrated that FABP5 specific deletion in keratinocytes selectively reduced skin TCR γ δ dim cell accumulation and IL-17A production. Further skin bulk-RNA and single-cell RNA sequence analyses showed a strong association of keratinocyte FABP5 with increased activation of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathways under saturated HFD-induced obesity. Mechanistically, saturated fatty-acids (SFAs) induce FABP5-dependent MAPK activation and CCL20 production in keratinocytes, promoting the recruitment and activation of IL-17-producing γδ T cells in the skin. Together, these findings suggest a previously undefined FABP5/MAPK/CCL20 signaling axis that links saturated fats to exacerbated psoriatic inflammation.

title: Regardless of Age, Locomotor Habituation is Observed with Exposure to Virtually- Induced Fall-Related Anxiety
abstract: Abstract Background Up to 60% of older adults experience fall-related anxiety, which can increase fall risk. Virtual high elevations induce fall-related anxiety that diminishes with time, offering a means for emotional and motor habituation. Age-related gait habituation differences observed in other environments might also appear in virtual anxiety-inducing settings. The purpose of this study is to determine age-related gait habituation differences across time and repeated immersion in virtual anxiety-inducing settings. Methods Participants ( N = 30, 14 older adults) experienced four walking trials: one minute at virtual low elevations (ground), five minutes (I1) at virtual high elevations (~15m), one minute at virtual low elevation, five minutes (I2) at virtual high elevations. Steady state gait parameters from the first (T1) and last (T2) six steady state steps were analyzed. Results Both age groups habituated similarly, walking with longer steps over time at low [ F = 10.25, p = .001] and high [ F = 83.78, p < .001] elevations. In I1, both groups walked with longer , (F = 15.50, p < .001), faster ( F = 7.05, p = .013) steps at T2 versus T1. Both groups walked with longer ( F = 21.17, p < .001), faster ( F = 16.50, p < .001) steps at T1 of I2 versus T1 of I1. Conclusion Young and older adults similarly habituated gait and showed savings of habituated motor patterns specific to virtual anxiety-inducing settings. Our results provide evidence supporting the potential use of the VR paradigm as a habituation intervention to reduce fall-related anxiety in older adults.

title: Comparative Evaluation of L1CAM, NCAM, and ATP1A3 for Enrichment and Characterization of Neuron-Enriched Extracellular Vesicles from Human Plasma and Serum
abstract: Aim: Neuron-enriched extracellular vesicles (NEEVs) are promising minimally invasive biomarkers for studying central nervous system biology; however, variability in EV isolation and neuronal enrichment methods limit reproducibility and standardization.Here, we systematically evaluated EV isolation workflows and neuronal immunocapture markers using human plasma and serum samples.Methods: Total EVs were isolated using precipitation-and size exclusion chromatography (SEC)-based approaches, and NEEVs were enriched using ATP1A3, L1CAM, and NCAM antibodies.EVs and NEEVs were characterized by flow cytometry, microfluidic resistive pulse sensing, super-resolution microscopy, and tetraspanin immunoassays.Dataindependent acquisition proteomics was explored for functional total EV and NEEV protein cargo.Results: Precipitation-based isolation produced the highest EV and NEEV recovery, whereas SEC-based methods demonstrated improved purity.Proteomic analyses identified 297 neuronal-specific proteins in NEEVs, with plasma-derived NEEVs showing greater neuronal protein detection and broader proteome coverage than serum-derived NEEVs.Each workflow showed distinct trade-offs between recovery, purity, and proteomic depth, indicating that optimal method selection should depend on downstream analytical priorities.Conclusion: EV isolation method was the primary driver of proteomic variability, whereas neuronal capture antibody had comparatively modest effects.Overall, these findings highlight the strong influence of biofluid type and isolation strategy on NEEV characterization and proteomic outcomes.

title: The Human Gut Cell Atlas v1.0: A Unified, Community-Built Reference of Cellular Diversity Across the Gut
abstract: Abstract Single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) studies have transformed our understanding of cellular diversity in the human intestine, but differences in anatomical sampling, experimental processing and cell-type nomenclature limit comparison across datasets. Here, we present the Human Gut Cell Atlas (HGCA) V1, a community-curated reference of 944,390 healthy and disease-adjacent intestinal cells from 502 samples, 265 donors and 24 landmark studies, linked to detailed anatomical, clinical, and technical metadata. As this metadata is of critical importance to human biology, we developed MetaManager, an open source data management framework for standardized metadata collection and tracking. A five-level consensus taxonomy resolves 94 homeostatic cell identities and enables transferrable, high-resolution annotation of new gut datasets. By assembling cell identity, sampling metadata, and independent spatial validation, intestinal segment and radial tissue depth were revealed to systematically shape cellular composition and transcriptional state, enabling inference of the presence of sampling-dependent tissue niches, including lymphoid follicles. Reference mapping accurately and rapidly recovered cohort-level Crohn’s disease and treatment signatures without de novo annotation, while mapping human intestinal organoids quantified cell-type-specific identity, regional specification, maturation, and transcriptional fidelity to native tissue. The HGCA V1 provides a standardized cellular, anatomical coordinate, and metadata system for reproducible, high-quality analysis of intestinal biology across healthy tissue, disease-associated remodelling, and experimental models, providing a continuously evolving community reference for cumulative discovery in human intestinal biology.

title: Generalizable field of view extension for diffusion MRI via conditional flow matching
abstract: Incomplete field-of-view (FOV) diffusion MRI (dMRI) acquisitions compromise whole-brain white matter analysis by excluding brain regions from tractography and connectivity studies. While deep generative models for dMRI FOV extension have been proposed, their generalizability remains limited by the acquisition-dependent nature of dMRI, where signal intensity varies with b-value, gradient direction, and scanner protocol, and the inherent 4D complexity of the data, making it difficult to train models that transfer across sites or acquisition schemes without retraining. We propose a flow-matching generative model that extends the dMRI FOV in both the superior and inferior directions by predicting apparent diffusion coefficients (ADC) in six directions, conditioned on the two nearest acquired slices and the full-FOV T1w image to enforce both local diffusion continuity and anatomical consistency. The ADC representation decouples the model from acquisition-specific b-values and gradient directions, providing a middle-ground across protocols. The model was trained on 3,103 subjects (5,105 sessions) across five different datasets spanning diverse acquisition schemes (b = 500 and 1000 s/mm$^2$; 21--192 gradient directions), four single-shell (b = 1000) and one multi-shell (b = 500/1000). Evaluated on 299 subjects across five independent datasets spanning b = 750--1500 s/mm$^2$ and 32--90 gradient directions, with single- and multi-shell schemes unseen during training, the proposed method achieves significantly improved bundle Dice score on downstream tractography (p < 0.01).

title: A Refined Lung Transplant Frailty Scale Incorporating Serum Albumin Is Associated With Risk of Mortality in Lung Transplant Candidates
abstract: Abstract The Lung Transplant Frailty Scale (LT-FS) is a validated binary measure of frailty in lung transplant candidates. We refined the LT-FS Base and Body Composition measures by developing a three-category classification to improve clinical risk stratification and replacing serum C-reactive protein with albumin as a more clinically practical frailty biomarker. We applied a 4-step measure development method to a multicenter prospective cohort study of lung transplant candidates. Low albumin (<3.5 g/dL) replaced high serum C-reactive protein (≥10 mg/L) as the LT-FS biomarker. Cutpoints balancing discrimination, risk prediction, and calibration defined “frail”, “pre-frail”, and “not frail” categories. We then evaluated these category associations with exercise capacity, patient-reported outcomes, and mortality using multivariate linear and Cox regression. Among 419 participants, the refined LT-FS identified a graded increase in mortality risk across frailty categories. Pre-frailty and frailty by LT-FS Body Composition were associated with 2.9-fold (HR 2.9, 95% CI 1.2–6.9) and 7-fold (HR 6.9, 95% CI 2.6–18.2) higher risks of waitlist delisting or death, respectively. After transplant, pre-frailty and frailty by LT-FS Body Composition were associated with 2-fold (HR 2.1, 95% CI 1.2–3.8) and 3.6-fold (HR 3.6, 95% CI 1.8–7.3) higher mortality risk, respectively. Relationships with exercise capacity and disability were less consistent. A refined Lung Transplant Frailty Scale incorporating serum albumin demonstrates strong associations with waitlist and post-transplant mortality. The addition of a pre-frail category better captures the continuum of frailty and improves clinical risk stratification of lung transplant candidates.

title: Cardiomyocyte Perm1 sustains cardiac bioenergetic reserve and exercise capacity.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: The PGC-1/ERR axis controls both steady-state mitochondrial respiration and the capacity to expand ATP production on demand, but whether this reserve function requires dedicated downstream effectors, and whether its loss is detectable at rest, remain unclear. We tested whether Perm1, a striated muscle-specific PGC-1/ERR-induced regulator, is required for cardiac bioenergetic reserve.
METHODS: We generated cardiomyocyte-specific Perm1 knockout mice using constitutive αMHC-nCre and tamoxifen-inducible αMHC-MerCreMer drivers and followed to 12 months and to 4 months after tamoxifen, respectively. Mitochondrial respiration was measured by high-resolution respirometry and ultrastructure by electron microscopy; energetic capacity under load was tested by treadmill exercise with tissue ATP quantification and by β-adrenergic stimulation of neonatal cardiomyocytes.
RESULTS: Perm1 deletion did not perturb cardiac development; neither constitutive nor adult-onset deletion impaired cardiac structure and systolic function through 12 months. Despite this, mitochondrial respiration was reduced by 20-25% without a change in total mitochondrial content or OxPhos subunit abundance. MICOS components MIC60 and MIC19 were selectively reduced, and mitochondria redistributed from subsarcolemmal to interfibrillar compartments. Perm1-deficient mice of both sexes showed ~50% lower treadmill endurance at 6 and 12 months and failed to maintain cardiac ATP at a submaximal workload, whereas gastrocnemius ATP and plasma lactate were unaffected. β-Adrenergic stimulation raised ATP content in control cardiomyocytes, and Perm1 knockdown blunted this response.
CONCLUSIONS: Perm1 is a cardiomyocyte-intrinsic determinant of cardiac bioenergetic reserve: dispensable for resting function but required to expand ATP production when demand rises. This regulation is invisible to resting phenotyping and emerges only under stress.

title: Assessing inflammation and predicting relapse in ulcerative colitis is more accurate when performed by IBD specialized gastroenterologists.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ulcerative colitis is monitored through clinical, laboratory, endoscopic, and histologic measures. Persistence of histologic inflammation despite clinical and endoscopic remission is associated with disease flare.
METHODS: We compared the identification of clinically significant histologic inflammation by general and IBD-specialized gastroenterologists (GI) using a simplified binary scoring system and looked at associations with disease relapse.
RESULTS: Both general and IBD-specialized GIs identified significant inflammation associated with relapse, though IBD-specialized GIs scoring had stronger correlations with relapse.
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest simple histologic assessment can inform risk stratification, and further work is needed to optimize monitoring patients with histologic inflammation despite endoscopic remission.

title: Validation of an electronic-nose sensor array in detecting C. difficile and differentiating toxin-positive from toxin-negative stool samples
abstract: Abstract Objective To evaluate the specimen-level performance of a multichannel electronic nose (e-nose) sensor array in classifying stool specimens into relevant Clostridioides difficile categories. Design Retrospective single-center validation study with reference to polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and C. difficile toxin testing. Participants A convenience sample of 31 discarded stool specimens with PCR and confirmatory toxin testing. Categorized into PCR-positive (+)/toxin+, PCR+/toxin-negative (–), and PCR–. Methods Specimens were sampled in controlled headspace by two e-nose sensor arrays in 10-minute sessions with 5-second sampling intervals. The primary endpoint was one-versus rest classification performance (sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and accuracy) into three classes: PCR+/toxin+, PCR+/toxin–, and PCR–. Data were normalized and the region of interest was extracted for training and testing. Random forests were utilized for classification of normalized data with a test-train split at the specimen-level. Results There were 457 unique 10-minute sampling events (147 PCR+/toxin+, 183 PCR+/toxin–, 127 PCR–). Sensors 1 and 2 captured 20,331 and 23,538 unique 5-second exposures within the region of interest, respectively. Testing data classification accuracy was 0.79 [0.78, 0.81] and 0.84 [0.83, 0.85] for Sensors 1 and 2. Sensitivity for PCR+/toxin+ exposures was 0.82 [0.79, 0.84] and 0.94 [0.92, 0.95], and specificity was 0.91[0.90, 0.93] and 0.93 [0.92, 0.94] for Sensors 1 and 2. Conclusion An e-nose sensor array partially differentiated PCR-classified C. difficile specimen classes at the exposure level under headspace-controlled conditions. Performance was strongest for PCR+/toxin+ exposures. Findings support further prospective validation in the hospital room setting.

title: Oxidative Stress and Tissue Remodeling in a Rat Abdominal Seroma Model.
abstract: Seroma is a common complication following abdominoplasty and other procedures involving extensive soft tissue dissection. Although animal seroma models have been reported, the stromal pathology underlying post-abdominoplasty seroma, particularly the role of oxidative stress, remains poorly characterized. Here, we developed a rat abdominal seroma model by surgically separating the subcutaneous tissue from the underlying muscle fascia and investigated the temporal evolution of the associated stromal response. Seroma developed in 9 of 20 operated rats, corresponding to a formation rate of 45.0%. Longitudinal ultrasound demonstrated that fluid accumulation peaked around postoperative day (POD) 7 and largely resolved by POD30. Despite macroscopic fluid resolution, substantial stromal remodeling persisted. Compared with normal abdominal tissue, seroma-associated tissues at POD14 and POD35 exhibited increased collagen deposition, macrophage accumulation, oxidative injury, and vascular remodeling. Additionally, at POD35, macrophage accumulation and 4-hydroxynonenal staining were greater than at POD14, whereas collagen deposition and vascular density remained elevated with no significant differences between postoperative time points. To our knowledge, this study presents the first rat model specifically designed to reproduce post-abdominoplasty seroma and the first temporal characterization of oxidative stress within seroma-associated tissue. These findings reveal that seroma fluid resolution does not coincide with stromal recovery and identify persistent oxidative stress, inflammation, fibrosis, and vascular remodeling as important features of seroma pathology.

title: Integrin α3β1 is required for alveolar-capillary barrier formation through regulation of epithelial differentiation
abstract: Laminin-binding integrins regulate critical morphogenic processes, but their specific roles in lung development are unknown. In this study, we combined an in vivo model of epithelial α3 subunit deletion in the murine lung with a multiomics approach to investigate the role of the epithelial α3β1 integrin during murine lung development. We demonstrate that α3β1 integrin is dispensable for airway branching morphogenesis due to delayed epithelial expression. Instead, in vivo deletion of α3β1 integrin impaired alveolar epithelial cell differentiation and disrupted alveolar-capillary barrier formation, functionally limiting gas exchange. A discontinuous alveolar BM contained abnormal collagen IV and laminin networks and widened the gap between epithelial and endothelial cells in the alveolar-capillary barrier niche. Mechanistically, mice deficient in epithelial α3β1 integrin possessed an intracellular trafficking and secretion defect for BM components. Thus, integrin α3β1 orchestrates the temporal maturation of alveolar epithelial cells required for organization of the alveolar-capillary barrier. Summary statement: Integrin α3β1 is required for alveolar-capillary barrier formation through regulation of alveolar epithelial differentiation and alveolar BM composition.

title: Metabolic Signatures of Resistance to Mycobacterium Tuberculosis Infection: Insights from a Multi-Country Plasma Metabolomics Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Tuberculosis (TB) remains the leading infectious disease cause of mortality worldwide. A subset of individuals exposed to Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) remain TST/IGRA-negative despite sustained exposure, termed "TB resisters". The biological mechanisms underlying this resistance remain poorly understood. We applied untargeted high-resolution metabolomics to determine whether systemic metabolic profiles differ between TB resisters and matched Mtb-infected close contacts.
METHODS: We compared untargeted high-resolution plasma metabolomics using liquid chromatography mass spectrometry between 269 TB resisters and 269 matched Mtb-infected close contacts, enrolled across Brazil, India, and South Africa. TB resisters were defined as highly exposed close contacts who slept in the same room or spent at least 5 hours indoors per day with an infectious pulmonary TB index patient, but remained TST/IGRA-negative. Mtb-infected close contacts were those who were TST/IGRA positive. Metabolome-wide association studies (MWAS) were conducted using paired t-tests.
RESULTS: There were 1,787 features with nominal differences between TB resisters and matched Mtb-infected contacts (p < 0.05). Pathway enrichment identified fructose and mannose metabolism and bile acid biosynthesis in the overall cohort, while lipid-related pathways were enriched in Brazil. Among metabolites with confirmed chemical identities, glyceric acid concentrations were higher in TB resisters by 0.53 μM, whereas hydroxyproline was lower by 0.90 μM, butyrobetaine was lower by 0.06 μM, and homogentisate was lower by 0.0036 μM at false discovery rate of 0.2.
CONCLUSIONS: Plasma metabolomic profiles differed between TB resisters and matched Mtb-infected close contacts. These findings indicate that systemic metabolic differences are associated with resistance to Mtb infection.

title: DLGAP5 promotes vascular cell proliferation and remodeling in pulmonary arterial hypertension
abstract: ABSTRACT Background Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) manifests by pulmonary vascular remodeling, caused by hyper-proliferation and apoptosis resistance of resident PA cells, elevated right ventricular (RV) afterload, and death of RV failure. The goal of this study is to determine the role and mechanisms of action of mitotic spindle-associated microtubule regulator DLG associated protein 5 (DLGAP5) in pulmonary vascular remodeling in PAH. Methods DLGAP5 expression was assessed in human PAH transcriptomic datasets, PAH patients’ lung tissues, pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells (PASMCs), and pulmonary artery adventitial fibroblasts (PAAFs). Loss-of-function, molecular, functional, RNAseq, and network analyses were performed. Smooth muscle (SM)-specific DLGAP5 knockdown using adeno-associated virus serotype 6 (AAV6) in mice with SU5416/hypoxia-induced PH was performed. Results DLGAP5 was overaccumulated in small muscular PAs, PASMCs, and PAAFs from PAH lungs. siRNA DLGAP5 down-regulated cyclin A2, suppressed hyper-proliferation, increased pro-apoptotic BIM, and induced apoptosis in human PAH PASMCs and PAAFs. DEP domain containing 1 (DEPDC1) was identified and validated as a downstream effector of DLGAP5 in PAH PASMCs responsible for hyper-proliferation and apoptosis resistance of human PAH PASMCs. SM-specific DLGAP5 knockdown with AAV6- enTagln -shDLGAP5 reversed DEPDC1 overaccumulation in small muscular PAs, reduced PA medial thickness, RV systolic pressure, mean PA pressure, and RV hypertrophy in mice with SuHx-induced PH. Conclusions DLGAP5 supports proliferation and survival of human PAH PASMCs and PAAFs through up-regulation of cyclin A2, DEPDC1, and suppression of BIM, and promotes PA remodeling and PH in mice. DLGAP5 could serve as a potential molecular target to attenuate pulmonary vascular remodeling in PAH. Graphical abstract

title: A 4D GelMA-Cad/Gelatin Hydrogel for High-Resolution DMD Bioprinting of Vascularized Soft Tissue Models.
abstract: Digital micromirror device (DMD)-based bioprinting enables high-resolution fabrication of hydrogel-based tissue constructs, but print fidelity and hydrogel mechanics are typically coupled through polymer concentration, light exposure, and crosslinking density. This creates a materials constraint for vascular bioprinting, where constructs must preserve microscale architecture during fabrication while supporting multicellular remodeling, lumen formation, and long-term tissue organization. To meet these requirements, we developed a 4D GelMA-Cad/gelatin hydrogel with time-dependent mechanics that maintains print fidelity while providing a soft, cell-permissive matrix. GelMA-Cad provides a covalently photocrosslinked, bioactive network containing an N-cadherin-mimetic peptide, while uncrosslinked gelatin serves as a transient matrix-modifying component that diffuses from the hydrogel after fabrication, producing further softening without bulk degradation of the GelMA-Cad network. We characterized hydrogel chemistry with NMR, quantified time-dependent changes in stiffness, visualized pore morphology with cryo-SEM, and evaluated the platform in retinal and pulmonary constructs. The 4D hydrogel supports 3D-patterned accuracy, cell viability, inner blood-retinal barrier vasculature, and vascularized lung-alveolar tissue models. Single-cell RNA-sequencing of the pulmonary vascular-alveolar model demonstrated compartment-specific transcriptional responses, including enrichment of lung capillary-associated endothelial features and AT1-like epithelial states. Overall, this platform decouples DMD print fidelity from post-print matrix mechanics for vascularized soft tissue bioprinting and tissue modeling.

title: Prospective Bidirectional Associations Between Core Schemas, Attenuated Psychotic Symptoms, and Functioning in Youth at Clinical High Risk for Psychosis
abstract: Objective Cognitive models of psychosis implicate maladaptive core schemas in the development and emergence of psychotic symptoms, but no study has tested temporal dynamics between schemas and psychotic symptoms in a large sample of clinical high-risk (CHR) youth. Given their sizable role in cognitive behavioral therapies, the first-line treatment for CHR youth, core schemas may be key to both symptom development and treatment in this population. Methods Participants were 578 CHR individuals from the second North American Prodrome Longitudinal Study (NAPLS-2) assessed across five timepoints. Time-lagged mixed-effects models tested forward (schema→outcome) and reverse (outcome→schema) paths for each Brief Core Schema Scales subscale with both psychotic symptom and functioning changes, controlling for autoregressive effects, time-varying depression, and linear time. Results Twenty of 36 schema–outcome pairs showed significant prospective associations. Negative-other schemas were prospectively associated with worsening across nearly all psychosis symptom and functioning domains. Suspiciousness exhibited bidirectional associations with all four schema subscales. Grandiose ideas were uniquely prospectively associated with positive-self and negative-other schemas. Positive schemas were prospectively associated with decreases in suspiciousness, negative symptoms, and improvements in functioning. Effects were largely independent of depressive symptoms and robust across sensitivity analyses, with partial attenuation of self-schema effects on suspiciousness. Conclusions Core schemas were prospectively associated with psychosis symptom and functioning change in CHR youth, with symptom-domain specificity and bidirectionality. These findings extend cognitive models of psychosis into CHR syndromes and highlight schemas as potentially modifiable treatment targets to improve outcomes in this population. Highlights Schema changes preceded shifts in functioning and psychosis symptoms among CHR youth Negative-other schemas preceded worsening across nearly all outcome domains Suspiciousness was the only outcome with bidirectional schema associations Positive schemas preceded fewer negative symptoms and better global functioning

title: LFA-1-Engineered Extracellular Vesicles Deliver CD59 to Protect Endothelial Integrity in Acute Lung Injury.
abstract: Acute lung injury (ALI) is a life-threatening disorder characterized by pulmonary endothelial injury, vascular leakage, and hypoxemia, yet no targeted therapies are available to protect the lung vasculature. Dysregulated complement activation contributes to endothelial dysfunction through excessive deposition of the membrane attack complex (MAC), which disrupts endothelial barrier integrity. CD59 is a membrane-bound complement inhibitor that protects endothelial cells (ECs) from MAC-mediated injury, but its role and therapeutic potential in ALI remain unclear. In this study, we found that endothelial CD59 was significantly reduced during bacteria-induced ALI and that Cd59 deficiency exacerbated pulmonary vascular leakage in mice. To supplement endothelial CD59, we engineered extracellular vesicles (EVs) expressing lymphocyte function-associated antigen-1 (LFA-1) (EVLFA-1) to enhance delivery to activated endothelium. CD59-loaded EVs (EVLFA-1-CD59) preferentially targeted ECs, reduced endothelial MAC deposition and apoptosis, and preserved endothelial barrier integrity in experimental ALI. EVLFA-1-CD59 also improved survival following bacterial infection. Collectively, these data establish diminished endothelial CD59 levels as a critical driver of complement-driven vascular injury and highlight EVLFA-1-mediated CD59 delivery as a promising therapeutic strategy for ALI.

title: IL-13 driven tuft cell hyperplasia is suppressed by retinoic acid in chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps.
abstract: Tuft cells are specialized chemosensory epithelial cells that contribute to mucosal immunity, yet how their differentiation is regulated in human airway disease remains unclear. Chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps(CRSwNP) features type 2 inflammation and expansion of sinonasal tuft cells, consistent with type 2 cytokine-driven epithelial remodeling. Using primary human sinonasal epithelial air-liquid interface cultures, we examined tuft cell differentiation across disease phenotypes. IL-13-induced expansion of POU2F3+ tuft cells and generated a BMX+ subset consistent with a mature or activated phenotype. These IL-13 activated cultures exhibited enhanced responsiveness to chemosensory ligands such as succinate and denatonium, indicating functional activation. Surprisingly, IL-13-driven sinonasal tuft cell differentiation occurred despite inhibition of STAT6 and ERK signaling, suggesting involvement of noncanonical pathways. Retinoic acid(RA) emerged as a selective regulator of tuft cell differentiation specifically in CRSwNP. RA did not alter STAT6 phosphorylation or canonical IL-13-responsive gene expression, indicating that RA suppresses tuft cell differentiation through distinct mechanisms. These findings highlight a noncanonical pathway of IL-13-mediated tuft cell expansion and identify retinoic acid as a context-dependent regulator of tuft cell differentiation in the airway. These findings demonstrate methods to regulate human sinonasal tuft cell differentiation across disease phenotypes, opening avenues for tuft cell-targeted therapeutic strategies.

title: Authors’ reply to Zhang et al .: heterogeneity, effect modification and the meaning of vulnerability
abstract: Dear Editor, We thank Zhang et al. [1] for their thoughtful comments on our study. We agree that differences in stratum-specific estimates alone do not establish effect modification. Our study was designed to characterize age-specific patterns across nine age groups and multiple kidney disease subtypes, not to establish age as a formal effect modifier. We therefore noted that “the study was not specifically designed to statistically test effect modification” and interpreted our findings as age-specific heterogeneity [2]. Knol and VanderWeele [3] recommended reporting joint-stratum estimates against a single reference, stratum-specific effects, interaction measures on additive and multiplicative scales, and adjusted confounders. We reported stratum-specific effects and adjusted confounders. In our time-stratified case-crossover design, each case serves as its own control, so time-invariant characteristics such as age are conditioned out [4]; conventional joint exposure–age estimates, and hence additive interaction measures such as the relative excess risk due to interaction, are not directly identifiable from this design alone. Moreover, given nonlinear and distributed-lag temperature modeling, formal assessment of effect modification would ideally compare the relevant exposure–response functions across age groups rather than rely only on selected percentile contrasts [5].

title: Chronic Electrophysiology Captures Progressive Variability in DNA-Damaged Cardiac Networks
abstract: Abstract Electrophysiological recordings provide a key functional readout of cardiac health. Most in vitro studies rely on acute measurements rather than recording evolving functional changes. Here, we implement a microelectrode array (MEA) based system for chronic electrophysiological monitoring of human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocyte (iPSC-CM) monolayers. Electrophysiology recordings were maintained for up to 40 days, enabling longitudinal assessment of field potential amplitude, field potential duration, beat frequency, conduction velocity, and waveform morphology. Untreated iPSC-CM monolayers exhibited stable electrophysiological behavior throughout chronic culture. Following exposure to the cardiotoxic chemotherapeutic doxorubicin, chronic recordings captured progressive deterioration in electrical activity, including reduced field potential amplitude, altered repolarization dynamics, increased beat-to-beat variability, and reduced conduction that persisted after drug removal. Electrode-resolved analyses further revealed pronounced progressive spatial variability, highlighting localized responses that would be obscured by population-averaged measurements. Endpoint assays indicated reduced calcium transient amplitude and altered calcium reuptake, decreased mitochondrial membrane potential, and loss of connexin 43, findings consistent with the impaired electrical activity observed in chronic recordings. Together, these results establish chronic electrophysiological monitoring as a powerful approach for resolving the spatiotemporal progression of cardiotoxicity and other dynamic cardiac processes in vitro .

title: Pulsed Field Versus Radiofrequency Ablation For Repeat Ablation of Atrial Fibrillation: Evaluation of Outcomes
abstract: Abstract Background Pulsed-field ablation (PFA) has recently been approved in the USA as a new method for treating atrial fibrillation (AF). PFA provides a promising new approach in the treatment of atrial fibrillation (AF), which historically has a high recurrence rate post-ablation. Of significance, PFA has shown promising data in terms of safety and procedural efficiency to radiofrequency ablation (RFA). Objective The purpose of this study was to compare the procedural and health outcomes in patients with recurrent AF undergoing ablation using PFA or RFA. Methods Consecutive patients with a history of previous radiofrequency ablation and recurrent AF undergoing redo ablation with PFA or RFA were included. Patients were seen for follow-up in the clinic ranging from 4 months to a year and we reported ablation strategy and arrhythmia type. The primary outcome was recurrence of any atrial arrhythmia after a 90-day blanking period. Results A total of 242 patients with recurrent AF underwent redo ablation using PFA (n = 54, 22.5%) or RFA (n = 188, 77.5%). The PFA cohort was younger on average (66 vs. 70 years) with a lower mean CHA2DS2-VASc score (2.2 vs. 3.06, p=0.001) compared to the RFA cohort. PFA procedures were shorter (162±53 vs 206±60 minutes, p<0.001) but required more fluoroscopy (13.9±8.9 vs 8.7±6.3 minutes, p<0.001). Among patients seen on follow-up, recurrence occurred in 28% of PFA versus 55% of RFA patients, with longer arrhythmia-free survival after PFA (log-rank p=0.03). PFA remained associated with lower recurrence after multivariable adjustment (HR 0.4, 95% CI 0.2–0.9, p=0.04). Adverse events, predominantly vascular access–related, were similar. Conclusion Among patients with recurrent atrial arrhythmias after prior RFA, repeat PFA was associated with shorter procedures, greater fluoroscopy use, and lower arrhythmia recurrence, with comparable safety.

title: Recurrent and Relapsing Catheter-Related Bloodstream Infections in Patients Requiring Long-term Vascular Access.
abstract: Patients requiring long-term vascular access are at risk of experiencing recurrent or relapsing infections. Decisions to remove and replace these devices when infected depend on their clinical status, the pathogen involved, options for alternative access sites, the risk of mechanical complications or loss of access with attempted catheter replacement, and interruptions of care plans. This State-of-the-Art Review focuses on a team approach to the management of such complex patients. Management involves empiric and then directed systemic antimicrobial therapy, antimicrobial lock therapy, decisions regarding the use of antibiotic-impregnated catheters, and intentional preservation of central venous access for future device insertion. Meticulous documentation, a team approach to care including shared decision-making with the patient and family, optimization of available prophylactic medications and devices, and individualized adherence to evidence-based best practices and professional standards fill important gaps in care delivery and will improve the prevention and management of these infections in this vulnerable patient population.

title: The host transcriptional response to real-world cryptococcosis in the setting of advanced HIV disease defines dysregulated immune responses that underlie increased vulnerability to infection.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cryptococcus causes life-threatening infections; however, immune programs driving pathogenesis of these infections in the human host remain incompletely described. We leveraged whole-blood transcriptomic analysis to define distinct, conserved elements of the host immune response in participants with cryptococcal infections.
METHODS: RNA sequencing was performed on whole blood from adult febrile inpatients admitted to two hospitals in Moshi, Tanzania to compare gene expression between participants with cryptococcal, bacterial, or viral diseases, and adult community controls. Differential expression and gene set enrichment analyses were used to characterize expression differences between pathogen-class groups. Penalized logistic regression was used to identify gene expression signatures capable of identifying Cryptococcus disease.
RESULTS: Out of 118 participants, 13 (11%) had cryptococcal disease and 41 (34.7%) were persons living with HIV (PLWH). Genes upregulated in response to cryptococcosis compared to non-acutely-infected community controls reflected complement activation, neutrophil activation, type I interferon signaling, and myeloid dendritic cell differentiation. When compared to combined bacterial or viral illnesses, cryptococcal disease demonstrated hyperactivation of both innate and humoral immune pathways. A series of classifiers were developed that distinguished between cryptococcal and combined bacterial or viral diseases with an AUC of 0.946.
CONCLUSION: Overall, the host response to cryptococcosis in individuals with advanced HIV as manifested in transcriptional profiles informs our understanding of the pathophysiology of and susceptibility to cryptococcal infection and may support development of novel diagnostic and therapeutic approaches.

title: Endothelial Malat1 promotes post-stroke angiogenesis and neurovascular recovery via the Tek axis.
abstract: Ischemic stroke remains a leading cause of mortality and disability worldwide, yet current therapeutic strategies, such as thrombolysis and thrombectomy, are constrained by narrow treatment windows and incomplete microvascular repair. While angiogenesis is pivotal for long-term functional recovery, the epigenetic mechanisms governing post-stroke vascular remodeling remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that the long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) Malat1 acts as a critical endothelial regulator of angiogenesis and neurological restoration. Using an endothelium-specific Malat1 overexpression mouse model (EC-Malat1 Tg), we demonstrate endothelial Malat1 upregulation enhances angiogenesis, restores cerebral blood flow, and improves sensorimotor and cognitive function following ischemic stroke. Mechanistically, fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS)-based RNA sequencing of brain endothelial cells identified novel downstream targets of Malat1, including Hapln2, Bcl6, Esr1, Sox17, Tfrc, Hsp90aa1, and Tek. Among these, Tek (Tie2) showed robust endothelial co-localization and direct interaction with Malat1. Notably, while Malat1 overexpression markedly increased Tek protein expression, adeno-associated virus (AAV)-mediated endothelial knockdown of Tek abrogated the pro-angiogenic and neurovascular reparative effects of Malat1. Collectively, our data establishes the Malat1-Tek axis as a novel signaling pathway essential for driving post-ischemic cerebrovascular remodeling and long-term functional recovery. Targeting Malat1 represents a novel restorative therapeutic approach for ischemic stroke.

title: Editorial: Bridging electrophysiological markers from preclinical to clinical neuropsychiatric research
abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG), event-related potentials (ERPs), local field potentials (LFPs), and analyses of neural oscillations can capture aspects of neural activity that are not readily inferred from symptom reports alone. This approach is consistent with the Research Domain Criteria framework, which encourages investigation of mental disorders across dimensions and levels of analysis, from circuits to behavior (Insel et al., 2010). In depression, neurobiological heterogeneity has also motivated efforts to identify subgroups with distinct patterns of brain connectivity and potentially different treatment responses (Drysdale et al., 2017). These findings support the rationale for biomarker research, while also underscoring the need for replication and independent validation before a marker is used to guide individual clinical decisions.The clinical relevance of these measures is evident through circuit-based treatment that link physiology with clinical outcomes. Work on subcallosal cingulate deep brain stimulation (DBS) has used connectomic information to improve targeting of treatment-resistant depression (Riva-Posse et al., 2018). Meanwhile, functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) offers a complementary measure of cortical hemodynamic responses and has been applied to several psychiatric conditions (Ehlis et al., 2014). Combining electrophysiological and hemodynamic measures may therefore help characterize different aspects of brain function, provided that the added complexity produces reliable and clinically useful information.Preclinical studies complement clinical biomarker research by enabling neural activity to be examined at the level of individual neurons and local circuits during behavior. Recordings of single-unit activity and local field potentials, combined with targeted circuit manipulations, can help establish how neural signals contribute to specific cognitive processes and behavioral outcomes (Koloski et al., 2025). Together, these approaches can help clarify the functional significance of electrophysiological markers identified in clinical populations.Ghazavi et al. (2026) examined the combinatorial effects of multi-site stimulation on depression-related brain regions using clinical data and predictive modeling, alongside intracranial LFP recordings during stimulation of the subcallosal cingulate and ventral capsule/ventral striatum. Their analyses suggest that interactions between stimulation sites and recorded signals are not uniform, with additive or sub-additive effects more common than superadditive effects. This work highlights the potential of intracranial physiology to inform stimulation strategies. However, the very small clinical sample means that the patterns and their relationship to therapeutic benefit require validation in larger cohorts. 2026) investigated brain-gastric electrophysiology for early prediction of antidepressant response. By combining EEG, electrogastrography, and symptom profiles in a multicenter clinical study, the authors explored whether coordinated brain-body signals could help distinguish response patterns early in treatment. This multimodal approach is appealing because psychiatric symptoms occur in the context of broader physiological systems. Before clinical implementation, however, predictive performance and the generalizability of the model need to be confirmed in independent populations and under clearly specified clinical conditions. Li et al. (2026) reported parallel electrophysiological and prefrontal hemodynamic alterations during Stroop task performance in major depressive disorder. Simultaneous EEG-fNIRS recordings provide complementary information about electrical activity and cortical hemodynamic responses during cognitive control. This design offers a broader view of taskrelated dysfunction than either modality alone. The reported group differences are informative, but further studies should establish their reproducibility, clarify how they relate to symptom dimensions and functional impairment, and determine whether they add value beyond behavioral performance or standard clinical assessment. 2026) examined resting-state frontal theta/beta ratio and psychological symptoms in college students. In this sample, greater symptom burden was associated with differences in frontal theta/beta activity. The study adds research on accessible EEG indices in non-clinical populations and may help generate hypotheses about links between neural activity and psychological distress. These associations should not be interpreted as evidence that the ratio is a stand-alone diagnostic test or a validated predictor of future illness. Longitudinal work and assessment of specificity across symptom domains will be important in the next steps.Taken together, these studies not only demonstrate the breadth of electrophysiological research but also point to shared priorities. First, reproducibility requires transparent reporting of acquisition protocols, preprocessing, feature selection, and statistical analyses. Where possible, researchers should assess test-retest reliability and use harmonized methods across sites. Second, identifying markers associated with neuropsychiatric symptoms does not necessarily establish their clinical relevance. Predictive studies should report appropriate measures of discrimination and calibration, compare models with relevant clinical baselines, and test performance in independent samples. Small datasets require particular care to prevent overfitting. Third, stronger links between preclinical mechanisms and human outcomes will require carefully designed translational studies. Candidate markers identified in experimental models should be assessed for comparable biological meaning in people, while recognizing differences between species, tasks, and recording conditions. Longitudinal studies can help establish whether a marker tracks change, predicts response, or merely correlates with symptoms at a single time point. Finally, multimodal approaches should be guided by a clear rationale: combining signals is useful only when it improves interpretability, reproducibility, or decision-making beyond simpler measures.The four articles in this Research Topic illustrate how electrophysiological and related physiological measures can connect neural mechanisms, symptom profiles, and treatment research. Their methods range from invasive recordings during DBS to non-invasive EEG and combined brain-body or EEG-fNIRS approaches. The next step is not simply to identify more candidate markers, but to establish which measures are reliable, reproducible, and useful for clinical decisions. Preclinical models can help guide this progress, but translating findings across species requires careful consideration of differences in behavior, underlying circuitry, and functional significant of electrophysiological activity. Progress will depend on larger and more diverse samples, independent validation, transparent methods, and close integration of mechanistic and clinical research. These improvements will help move the field beyond identifying neural correlates of neuropsychiatric symptoms toward understanding circuit mechanisms and identify novel targets for therapeutic intervention.

title: Reflections and recommendations from co-designing a complementary intervention for neurodivergent children in a doctoral project
abstract: Participatory co-design is increasingly recognised as best practice in research and intervention development with neurodivergent populations. However, early career researchers often receive limited practical guidance on implementing co-design within the constraints of time-limited doctoral projects involving neurodivergent children. This perspective article reflects on the author’s experience of embedding co-design within a doctoral research project, using the development of a mental health intervention as a case study. The project involved collaboration with autistic children, including those with higher support needs, their parents, and experienced professionals. Reflections highlight the importance of ethical listening, challenging assumptions, and balancing methodological rigour with practical feasibility. Key lessons are presented regarding stakeholder engagement, flexible implementation and delivery, and practitioner support. The article argues that doctoral researchers must remain responsive to participants’ evolving needs and open to adapting research processes. Participatory co-design should be standard practice in developing meaningful, contextually relevant mental health interventions for neurodivergent children.

title: Commentary from the Education Committee of the Society for Clinical Neuropsychology on: facilitating best practices in practicum training in clinical Neuropsychology: introducing the North American Association of Practicum Sites in Neuropsychology (NAPSN) organizational training guidelines
abstract: This commentary examines the newly developed guidelines for clinical practicum training from The North American Association of Practicum Sites in Neuropsychology (NAPSN). NAPSN was formed in 2023 in order to support practicum level training in neuropsychology, adding to existing organizations supporting pre-doctoral and doctoral education, internship, and postdoctoral level training. The NAPSN training guidelines represent an important step toward ensuring consistent and high-quality clinical training for neuropsychologists at all professional stages in core areas including clinical training, didactics and educational programming, professionalism, and research. We outline anticipated benefits for trainees, impact on clinical supervisors, practical implications for clinical supervision, and areas for ongoing consideration. In particular, next steps may include delineating training goals and benchmarks for practicum students at different stages in their doctoral training, developing strategies to provide consistency in evaluation and supervision practices across practicum sites and doctoral programs, and including forensic neuropsychology training at the practicum level.

title: Rethinking Annual Dose Limits: A Biologically Based Critique of Radiation Protection Standards
abstract: Annual dose limits provide a practical basis for radiation protection, but a calendar year is not necessarily a biologically meaningful interval. Cellular repair, adaptive responses, and dose-rate effects may alter outcomes when the same total dose is delivered in different patterns. Conversely, rapid repair of measurable damage does not establish the absence of delayed effects or justify higher permissible doses. We propose research into temporally resolved exposure metrics that could complement cumulative dose accounting. Any regulatory change would require evidence linking exposure patterns to relevant health outcomes.

title: Bayesian Anchored Latent Learning for Estimating State Trajectories
abstract: Dynamic systems often evolve faster than reliable measurements can be collected. More frequent indirect observations may fill these gaps, but their noise and differing scales complicate estimation of the underlying state. We developed Bayesian Anchored Latent Learning (BALL) to combine sparse reference measurements with denser records on an interpretable scale. A bidirectional transformer teacher reconstructs trajectories from complete training histories, and a forward-only transformer student learns from those reconstructions and observed measurements. Across 30 simulations, BALL reduced composite trajectory error by 7% relative to the same transformer trained directly from measurements, achieving lower error across all datasets. In an applied example using psychiatric records from 1,609 patients, BALL improved the prediction of withheld questionnaire scores compared with direct transformer training at 21- and 28-day measurement schedules. Requests guided by estimated uncertainty further improved prediction. BALL connects retrospective learning with prospective state estimation and provides a framework for directing additional measurement.

title: Litifilimab reduces skin and joint disease in participants with SLE: additional results from Part A of the phase II LILAC study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the effects of litifilimab on skin- and joint-specific outcomes in adults with SLE using LILAC Part A (phase II) data.
METHODS: Prespecified and exploratory analyses were conducted in modified intent-to-treat population subsets from LILAC Part A (n=64 and n=56 for litifilimab 450 mg and placebo, respectively) with active skin and/or joint disease at baseline. Analyses included Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus Disease Area and Severity Index (CLASI)-50 and CLASI-70, defined as ≥50%/70% improvement from baseline in CLASI-Activity (CLASI-A) score, at week 24 (baseline CLASI-A score ≥8; n=39 vs n=38); week 24 Joint-50 response (50% reduction in active joint counts; baseline ≥4 tender and ≥4 swollen joints; n=56 vs n=46); resolution of baseline SLE Disease Activity Index-2000 (SLEDAI-2K) skin rash and/or arthritis at week 24 and improvement by ≥1 grade from baseline to week 24 in British Isles Lupus Assessment Group 2004 index (BILAG-2004) mucocutaneous and musculoskeletal domains (baseline Grade A/B).
RESULTS: Greater proportions of participants achieved CLASI-50 and CLASI-70 responses at weeks 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 and 24 with litifilimab than placebo. Regardless of the active joint count definition, greater proportions of participants treated with litifilimab achieved a Joint-50 response at week 24 than placebo (total tender plus total swollen joints, 78.6% vs 54.4%; total tender and/or swollen joints, 75.0% vs 52.2%; total tender and swollen joints, 83.9% vs 63.0%). At week 24, for litifilimab versus placebo, more participants had resolution of SLEDAI-2K rash (28.6% vs 10.7%), arthritis (48.2% vs 21.7%), rash and arthritis (23.0% vs 9.6%), and improvement of ≥1 grade in the BILAG-2004 mucocutaneous and musculoskeletal domains (50.0% vs 34.1%).
CONCLUSIONS: These findings characterise litifilimab’s effects on skin and joints and complement the LILAC Part A primary efficacy results, supporting the benefit of litifilimab for skin and joint manifestations in SLE.

title: “We Just Can’t Prove Our Burden Under These Circumstances”: Judge Advocate Perspectives on Consent and Alcohol-Involved Sexual Assault Cases
abstract: Alcohol-involved sexual assault remains a persistent issue within the U.S. military despite significant institutional reform. To understand how alcohol-involved sexual assault cases are interpreted within the military justice system, this article draws on 23 qualitative interviews with 11 members of the Judge Advocate General’s Corps. Lawyers engaged in discursive strategies that highlighted the alleged victim’s intoxication as lowering inhibitions while simultaneously silencing the role alcohol has in diminishing capacity to consent and the accused’s responsibility to assess that capacity. Lawyers narrowed consent to momentary assent while also broadening their interpretation of consent to suggest that the presence of regret implied assent at the time to place doubt on whether these cases constituted sexual assault. Some prosecutors attempted to disrupt these silences and strategies at court-martial by re-centering the accused’s responsibility to recognize visible impairment and by emphasizing how coercive or excessive alcohol consumption could be encouraged by someone to facilitate sexual assault.
