title: Coherent detector responses to quantum-controlled spherical-shell geometries
abstract: A detector inside a static spherical shell samples globally matched field modes even though its local geometry is flat. We construct the response of a compactly switched Unruh-DeWitt detector on a quantum-controlled pair of transparent spherical-shell spacetimes with common Arnowitt-Deser-Misner mass. A stipulated common-incoming scattering identification places the branch excitations in one Hilbert space. Their positive Gram matrix determines joint, conditional, and dephased detector responses at a finite common readout, retaining the physical detector-clock phase in the uncompensated protocol. An additional coherent phase-gate protocol compensates free detector-clock propagation while preserving the shell interaction response. For concentric shells the centered response is exactly $s$ wave. A common incoming direction basis extends the construction to a lab-fixed detector and displaced shell centers, preserving common-translation covariance. The equal-radius benchmark exhibits conditional changes of order $25\%$ without dark-port amplification. Combining radius and position produces an assignment-odd response that reverses under reflection and vanishes at the relational midpoint. The relative normalized-state contrast reaches $34.15\%$ among the computed samples; the relative clock-resolved probe-influence contrast reaches $8.09\%$ for the declared readout, while larger values belong to its separate shared-phase envelope. These effects already occur in the dominant-energy-condition-compatible core. They are relational, model-dependent detector responses, not a background-independent witness of quantum geometry. First-order coefficients have finite pointlike limits; finite-coupling statements are made only at a fixed shared regulator.

title: An In-depth Study of Stochastic Stellarator Coil Optimization
abstract: We extend stochastic coil optimization for stellarators and analyze the effect of optimizing for coil manufacturing errors, assembly errors represented by centroid translations and angular offsets, and errors in the coil currents. We further analyze the impact of different perturbation methods and use them in conjunction with the Augmented Lagrangian algorithm. For three stellarators, we show that stochastic methods regularize the coil optimization landscape and improve robustness in every case, with the magnitude of the improvement varying substantially across different plasmas. Our metric for coil robustness, $Q$, is improved by $4.50\%$ to $729\%$ across different configurations. Lastly, we perform numerous hyperparameter scans, including e.g. scanning the training perturbation size and the out-of-sample (OOS) evaluation perturbation size and find coupled and de-coupled training tolerance gains ranging from $0.09$ mm to $1.35$ mm depending strongly on the particular stellarator.

title: Potential effect of replacing sedentary behavior with physical activity on the risk of atrial fibrillation: results from the UK Biobank and REGARDS study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sedentary behavior (SB) has been associated with cardiovascular disease risk, independent of physical activity (PA) and sleep. However, the effect of replacing SB with PA or sleep on atrial fibrillation (AF) risk remains unclear.
METHODS: We studied 86,096 participants from the United Kingdom Biobank (UKB) and 5,777 from the United States (US) REasons for Geographic And Racial Differences in Stroke (REGARDS) prospective cohort studies who were free of AF at baseline and had valid accelerometry data. The two cohorts were included to evaluate the consistency of associations across distinct populations in the UK and the US, two regions with a high burden of AF. Daily time spent in light PA (LPA), moderate to vigorous PA (MVPA), and SB were derived from accelerometer recordings; sleep was accelerometer-derived in UKB and self-reported in REGARDS. Incident AF was identified using ICD-10 codes (I48.x) listed as either a primary diagnosis, secondary diagnosis, or cause of death through hospital and death registry data linkage in UKB and in a follow-up visit through electrocardiogram and self-reported medical history in REGARDS. Isotemporal substitution models were used to examine replacing 30 minutes of SB with LPA or MVPA in both cohorts and with sleep in UKB on the outcome of incident AF.
RESULTS: Among the UKB participants [57% female, mean age 56.0 (SD 7.8) years, 98% White race], 4,035 AF cases were identified during a median of 7.9 years of follow-up. Replacing 30 minutes of SB with PA was associated with a slightly lower risk of AF in the minimally adjusted models but the associations were attenuated after full adjustment (LPA: HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.95-1.02; MVPA: HR 1.00, 95% CI 0.99-1.02). The REGARDS participants had an average age of 63 (SD 8.3) years, 55% female, 31% Black and 69% White adults, with 486 AF cases identified. Fully adjusted substitution of 30 minutes of SB with MVPA was associated with lower AF odds (OR 0.80, 95% CI 0.63-1.01), whereas LPA showed no association. In UKB, replacing SB with sleep was not associated with AF risk. The magnitude of the association of MVPA substitution with AF appeared stronger among REGARDS participants aged ≥65 years and those reporting <7 hours/day of sleep.
CONCLUSION: Replacing SB with moderate or higher intensity PA may decrease AF risk. In REGARDS, these substitutions appeared to benefit older individuals and those reporting shorter sleep duration. These findings highlight the potential benefit of reducing sedentarism to lower AF burden, warranting validation in future studies.

title: Photogrammetry in Dentistry: From Digital Impressions to Clinical Workflows
abstract: A three-dimensional digital technology called photogrammetry is gaining popularity and is becoming a valuable tool in dentistry, especially when it comes to documenting the position of dental implants and creating complex digital workflows. This narrative review discusses the principles, methods, applications, accuracy, benefits, limitations, and current clinical applications of photogrammetry in dental practice, with a specific focus on implant-supported rehabilitation and complete-arch digital impressions. The use of conventional photogrammetry, stereophotogrammetry, image acquisition, three-dimensional coordinate reconstruction, intraoral scanning, computer-aided design/computer-aided manufacturing (CAD/CAM), and digital implant workflows is discussed. There is currently evidence that photogrammetric methods can be used to record complete-arch implant position with high trueness and precision, and in certain experimental and clinical trials, lower deviations in 3D and angular measurements were reported than with intraoral scanning. But it is hard to compare results across studies because of variations in the types of photogrammetric systems, acquisition protocols, designs of reference markers, software algorithms, distributions of implants, and methods of measurements. In addition, the intraoral surface anatomy and soft-tissue morphology captured routinely via photogrammetry are not as complete as what can be captured by intraoral scanning, and so a combined workflow may collect more comprehensive digital information. As the technology advances, photogrammetry is shifting away from the role of simply recording the position of implants and moving towards utilizing it as a part of digital dentistry, with possibilities in prosthodontics, implant dentistry, facial scanning, maxillofacial rehabilitation, and computer-assisted treatment planning.

title: Evaluation of Sequential Organ Failure Assessment-2 Performance Across Demographic Subgroups: An External Validation Using MIMIC-IV.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the discrimination and calibration of the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA)-2 score for ICU mortality across demographic subgroups defined by age, sex, race and ethnicity, primary language, and insurance status.
DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study.
SETTING: Single academic medical center in the northeastern United States (Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, MA), using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care-IV database (version 3.1), 2008-2022, a dataset external to the SOFA-2 development cohort.
PATIENTS: Adult patients (≥ 18 yr) with at least one ICU admission. The first ICU admission of the first qualifying hospitalization per patient was analyzed.
INTERVENTIONS: None.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: First-day SOFA-2 scores were calculated from the worst values recorded during the first 24 hours of ICU admission across six organ systems, with ICU mortality as the primary outcome. Discrimination was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and calibration using intercept and slope, with subgroup differences in AUROC estimated by bootstrap resampling. Among 64,015 ICU patients (mean [sd] age, 64.6 [17.1] yr; 56.1% male; 66.1% White), overall AUROC was 0.77 (95% CI, 0.76-0.77). Discrimination declined significantly with age: AUROC, 0.85 (0.83-0.87) for ages 18-44 years vs. 0.72 (0.70-0.73) for ages 75 or older (ΔAUROC, -0.14 [95% CI, -0.16 to -0.11]), with systematic underprediction in older patients. Discrimination was significantly decreased among non-English speakers (ΔAUROC, -0.04) but did not differ across documented racial/ethnic groups. Patients with missing demographic information had markedly higher mortality than the overall cohort rate of 7.2% (14.1% for missing race/ethnicity; 23.1% for missing language).
CONCLUSIONS: SOFA-2 demonstrated good overall performance but with clinically meaningful variation across subgroups, particularly with age and language. Patients with missing demographic data experienced markedly higher mortality. These findings argue for routine equity evaluation as a complement to traditional validation of clinical prediction tools.

title: Circulating Cell-Free Mitochondrial DNA, Delirium, and Long-Term Cognitive Impairment in Critically Ill Adults With Sepsis: A Prospective Cohort Study.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: During sepsis, circulating cell-free mitochondrial DNA (ccf-mtDNA) is released and elevated due to cell injury, augments the immune response, and may contribute to organ dysfunction. Delirium is common and deleterious during sepsis, but little is known about the relationship between mitochondrial injury and delirium during sepsis. We sought therefore to examine associations between ccf-mtDNA and delirium and other clinical outcomes during sepsis.
DESIGN: Multicenter, prospective cohort study.
SETTING: Medical and surgical ICUs in university and community hospitals in Nashville, TN.
PATIENTS: Four hundred eighty patients with sepsis plus shock and/or acute respiratory failure.
INTERVENTIONS: None.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: We measured ccf-mtDNA in plasma collected on multiple days (study days 1, 3, and 5) during sepsis and assessed participants bid for delirium and coma using the validated Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU and Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale. We then assessed survivors' cognitive function 3 and 12 months after hospital discharge using the Repeatable Battery for the Assessment of Neuropsychological Status. During sepsis, the adjusted odds of delirium were 7% lower for individuals at the 75th percentile of ccf-mtDNA compared with those at the 25th percentile (odds ratio [OR], 0.93; 95% CI, 0.86-0.99; p = 0.048). ccf-mtDNA was marginally associated with in-hospital mortality (hazard ratio, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.99-1.20; p = 0.08), but was not associated with coma (OR, 0.98; 95% CI, 0.90-1.05; p = 0.31) or 3-month (beta, 0.23; 95% CI, -1.58 to 2.05; p = 0.80) and 12-month (beta, -0.36; 95% CI, -2.13 to 1.42; p = 0.69) cognitive outcomes.
CONCLUSIONS: In this multicenter, prospective cohort study, higher levels of ccf-mtDNA were associated with lower odds of delirium, a result that contradicted our hypothesis. This provocative finding should be interpreted cautiously until replicated and explained by future studies.

title: Remote Outreach Follow-Up After Acute Mental Healthcare Utilization: Feasibility and Challenges.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Postdischarge from acute mental healthcare settings (psychiatric emergency room and inpatient psychiatric unit) is a high-risk period in which prompt connection to outpatient mental healthcare is critical. While remote outreach interventions to enhance continuity of psychiatric care for patients during the transition from acute care to outpatient settings have demonstrated effectiveness, interventions designed specifically for the higher-risk population who are challenged with initially connecting with outpatient care are lacking. The authors aimed to explore the feasibility of a pilot hospital quality improvement intervention for this population that directly combines outreach with an ad hoc remote psychiatric appointment.
METHODS: The intervention, wherein a psychiatrist repeatedly called the patient to complete a remote psychiatric appointment, was delivered to 50 adults discharged from acute mental healthcare settings who missed their scheduled postdischarge clinic appointment. This group was compared with a historical control group under a 2-group nonequivalent groups design.
RESULTS: Of those called, 50% completed follow-up appointments and 72% of these were completed upon the first week of call attempts. Fewer in the intervention group had an acute mental healthcare utilization within 90 days from discharge (26% vs 42%), although this was not statistically significant.
CONCLUSIONS: Remote outreach and delivery of an ad hoc psychiatric appointment is feasible. However, extended follow-up attempts may offer limited benefit and other engagement strategies may be needed. Future innovative postdischarge interventions should be specially designed to maximize impact for higher-risk patients.

title: Assessing variation in inpatient sleep opportunity and associated patient-reported sleep quality: An academic hospital-based observational study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Overnight interruptions are common in a hospital setting, but the impact of these interruptions on the opportunity for sleep in the general inpatient population and association with perceived sleep quality is unknown.
OBJECTIVE: To measure inpatient overnight sleep interruptions, their variation across adult hospital units, and associations between sleep opportunity and patient-reported sleep quality.
METHODS: Retrospective observational study using electronic health record data for an academic medical center in the Midwest United States. The cohort consisted of adult patient hospital admissions between September 2023 and August 2025, limited to nights on general acute medical and surgical units. Overnight interruptions from medication administration, vital checks, or lab collection were organized into 20-min interruptive episodes. Corresponding longest and total uninterrupted sleep opportunities and patient-reported sleep quality were assessed.
RESULTS: Among 46,916 patient admissions, the longest uninterrupted sleep opportunity (LUSO) per patient-night averaged 3 h 40 min, and total uninterrupted sleep opportunity (TUSO) averaged approximately 6 h 30 min. Sleep opportunity variation was seen across individual hospital units, and even more across multiple admissions per patient. Both LUSO and TUSO were positively associated with level of patient-reported sleep quality.
CONCLUSIONS: Inpatient sleep opportunities vary by admission and hospital unit, averaging under 4 h for the longest uninterrupted sleep opportunity on a given night. Sleep opportunity duration is associated with perceived sleep quality and could be used to assess sleep quality improvement interventions.

title: Risk of angle-closure glaucoma after lens extraction versus laser peripheral iridotomy in primary angle-closure suspects.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the association between lens extraction versus laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) and progression from primary angle-closure suspect (PACS) to coded angle-closure glaucoma (ACG).
DESIGN: Retrospective propensity score-matched cohort study.
PARTICIPANTS: Patients with PACS undergoing lens extraction or LPI (January 2014 to February 2026) in the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network and matched 1:1 on demographics, systemic and ocular comorbidities, medications, and body mass index, yielding 6059 patients per group (mean age, 68 years; 69% female; 59% White).
METHODS: The primary outcome was a new coded ACG diagnosis assessed using Cox regression. Prespecified subgroup analyses by age (<60, 60-70, >70 years) and sex used separately matched cohorts, with optic neuritis as a negative control outcome.
RESULTS: Coded ACG occurred in 3.5% of the lens-extraction group versus 5.4% of the LPI group (hazard ratio [HR] 0.66, 95% CI 0.56-0.79, P < 0.001). A significant benefit was observed in patients >70 years (HR 0.62, P < 0.001), but not in patients <60 years (HR 0.85, P = 0.63) nor 60-70 years (HR 0.78, P = 0.16). Among patients with LPI, 45% subsequently underwent lens extraction, with lower risk than LPI alone (HR 0.60, P = 0.001). Corneal edema, retinal detachment, and macular hole occurred more frequently after lens extraction than after LPI.
CONCLUSIONS: Lens extraction was associated with lower risk of coded ACG than LPI in patients with PACS, most consistently in those >70 years, but was also associated with more frequent complications. Given the observational design, prospective studies are needed to confirm these findings and identify which patients are most likely to benefit from early lens extraction.

title: Effects of Nrf2 deletion on exercise training-induced adaptations of resistance arterioles from skeletal muscle.
abstract: Exercise training induces adaptation of resistance arterioles but the cellular mechanisms that are stimulated during exercise training bouts, and which underlie adaptation to repeated bouts of exercise, remain largely unknown. The nuclear erythroid-2-related factor (Nrf2) plays a critical role in maintaining cellular redox homeostasis in response to heightened metabolic stress, such as may occur during bouts of exercise. We hypothesized that Nrf2 plays a critical role in exercise training-induced adaptations of resistance arterioles from locomotory skeletal muscle. To test this hypothesis, vascular responses of resistance arterioles from the soleus muscle of wild type (WT) and Nrf2 knockout (Nrf2 KO) rats were evaluated after exercise training or cage confinement. Exercise training enhanced flow-induced vasodilation in arterioles from the soleus muscle of WT rats, but not in arterioles from Nrf2 KO rats. Exercise training also altered myogenic responses differently in arterioles from WT and Nrf2 KO rats. After exercise training, myogenic responses were greater in arterioles from WT rats as compared to Nrf2 KO rats. Exercise training enhanced vasodilation to the NO donor, DEA-NONO-ate, in arterioles from both WT and Nrf2 KO rats. Similarly, exercise training increased contractile responses to phenylephrine in arterioles from both WT and Nrf2 KO rats. Expression of calcium-activated potassium (BK) channels was reduced in arterioles from Nrf2 KO rats. Thus, although Nrf2 appears necessary for some adaptations to exercise training in skeletal muscle arterioles, compensatory pathways that are Nrf2-independent maintain contractile and vasodilatory function in skeletal muscle arterioles, and these pathways can be upregulated by exercise training.

title: How to utilize psychotropic receptor binding profiles to deprescribe psychotropic polypharmacy.
abstract: The palliative care population is in a unique position of being medically complex and experiencing polypharmacy. Although polypharmacy is sometimes thought to be necessary, studies have shown higher symptom burden and lower quality of life with each additional medication. Deciding which psychotropic medication to deprescribe for patients with life-limiting illnesses is an additional challenge. Traditionally, clinicians consider patients' primary diagnoses, prominent symptoms, comorbid conditions, patient treatment preferences, and the relevant published literature when making deprescribing decisions. However, clinicians who consider only these factors may not always have optimal deprescribing outcomes. While many articles define polypharmacy simplistically based on the quantity of medications prescribed, this article will focus on rational versus irrational polypharmacy by incorporating the pharmacodynamics of psychotropic medications to create a framework for deprescribing. To accomplish this, this article reviews the neurotransmitter receptors most associated with creating desired psychotropic medication effects, including dopamine, serotonin, norepinephrine, and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA). Additionally, this article reviews the neurotransmitter receptors most associated with inducing troublesome side effects in older adults, including the histaminergic, muscarinic, and alpha- adrenergic receptors. Lastly, this paper provides a clinical practice review on how to use the inhibition constant (Ki) as a measure of the pharmacodynamic property of receptor binding as an additional, pragmatic tool that will guide palliative care clinicians in deprescribing psychotropic medications.

title: 17β-Estradiol and Estrogen Receptor α Promote Right Ventricle Angiogenesis in Pulmonary Hypertension via Apelin Signaling.
abstract: Right ventricular (RV) failure is the major cause of mortality in pulmonary hypertension (PH). Adaptive angiogenesis and RV endothelial cell (RVEC) function are major modifiers of RV adaptation in PH, but the underlying mechanisms and their regulators remain incompletely understood. RV adaptation in PH is sexually dimorphic, and 17β-estradiol (E2) exerts protective effects on RV cardiomyocytes. Whether E2 modifies angiogenesis and RVEC function in RV failure remains unknown. We hypothesized that E2 and estrogen receptor α (ERα) promote RV angiogenesis and RVEC homeostasis in PH and aimed to identify underlying mechanisms. We assessed E2's angiogenic effects using cultured human cardiac microvascular endothelial cells (hCMVECs), RVECs from PH patients with RV failure, and RVECs from sugen/hypoxia (SuHx) and monocrotaline rat models. In vivo, we evaluated RV capillary density in PH rats treated with E2 or ERα-selective agonist. Apelin signaling was evaluated via apelin receptor (APLNR) blockade and knockdown studies. E2 preserved angiogenesis in male hCMVECs and RV capillary density in male and female SuHx-PH rats. E2 reversed angiogenic alterations in RVECs from SuHx-PH rats via APLNR signaling. In RVECs from RV failure patients, E2 stimulated vascular network formation. In rat and human PH-RVECs, ERα was necessary and sufficient to mediate E2-induced angiogenesis. Activation of ERα with ERα-specific agonist restored RV capillary density in vivo. ERα-mediated angiogenesis required apelin signaling. These data indicate that E2 promotes RV angiogenesis via ERα and apelin signaling and identify a novel ERα-apelin axis in RVECs as a potential therapeutic target to restore RV vascular integrity in PH.

title: Development and validation of the SLE Disease Activity Questionnaire (SLEDAQ).
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: We aimed to develop a patient-reported measure, the SLE Disease Activity Questionnaire (SLEDAQ), intended to serve as a proxy for the SLE Disease Activity Index (SLEDAI).
METHODS: Items were developed to assess SLEDAI domains, reviewed for plain language, pre-tested in individual interviews and administered at two clinical sites. Prevalence-adjusted bias-adjusted kappa (PABAK), sensitivity and specificity assessed correspondence of SLEDAQ items with the SLEDAI domain scores. Associations of SLEDAQ with SLEDAI, clinical SLEDAI and physician global assessments (PGA) were examined with Spearman correlations and by examining differences in SLEDAQ scores between SLEDAI score severity groupings (0–2, 3–4 and ≥6). SLEDAQ scores were compared by sex, education, health literacy, fibromyalgia and in-person versus virtual visits to determine if bias was detected. For comparison, similar analyses were performed with the Systemic Lupus Activity Questionnaire (SLAQ), the most commonly used patient-reported disease activity measure.
RESULTS: After evaluation, the SLEDAQ consisted of 31 primary items. Agreement between SLEDAQ and SLEDAI scoring was ≥63% for all domains. PABAK indicated moderate or greater agreement for all but three domains (arthritis, mucosal ulcers and alopecia). All specificity estimates were ≥0.63. Correlations between SLEDAQ and SLEDAI, clinical SLEDAI and PGA scores were 0.25, 0.37 and 0.34, respectively. SLEDAQ scores differentiated between SLEDAI severity groupings. Performance on all metrics exceeded that of the SLAQ. There were no differences in SLEDAQ by sex or education. SLEDAQ scores were significantly higher among individuals with low health literacy and fibromyalgia; differences by health literacy were attenuated after adjustment for SLEDAI.
CONCLUSIONS: SLEDAQ is a novel patient-reported measure that more closely aligns with physician-assessed disease activity than previously available instruments. Findings support its potential usefulness in observational research and clinical settings where in-person disease activity assessment is limited.

title: A Qualitative Analysis of Focus Groups on a Community-Based Pro Bono Exercise and Lifestyle Modification Education Program for Individuals With Disability due to Multiple Sclerosis and Stroke.
abstract: The aim of this study was to identify perceived logistical, behavioral, and practical barriers to regular exercise participation in individuals with disability due to stroke and multiple sclerosis, as well as potential solutions. Focus group interviews were conducted as part of a mixed-methods prospective observational study evaluating a multi-site, pro bono, community-based exercise and lifestyle modification program. Twelve participants engaged in one of three focus groups, and data analysis was conducted using a modified grounded theory approach. Five themes were identified through thematic analysis: fear of exercising and need for safety when implementing an exercise program; personal experiences of physical and mental health and wellness; importance of social support and sense of community foster accountability and camaraderie; role of self-efficacy in daily life participation and resilience; and accessibility of fitness centers. Key factors were identified that influence exercise participation among individuals with disability due to neurological diagnosis. Overall, strong motivation to enhance overall health and wellbeing was observed; however, safety concerns and accessibility were barriers to participation. Social support and a sense of community were identified as critical factors to foster accountability and engagement. Despite existing barriers, building self-efficacy and resilience emerged as powerful enablers of long-term participation in exercise.

title: What Should We Write on End of Rotation Evaluations? A Mixed-methods Exploration of General Surgery Resident and Faculty Perspectives.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Narrative comments on resident end-of-rotation (EOR) evaluations are essential to competency-based assessment in surgical training, yet residents often perceive them as poor quality and variably useful. We explored resident and faculty perspectives on satisfaction with EOR comments, what constitutes high-quality comments and barriers to producing them.
METHODS: This is a sequential mixed-methods study at a single academic general surgery residency. Semi-structured interviews with residents and faculty were thematically analyzed using directed content analysis guided by the Relationships, Autonomy, Mastery, and Purpose (RAMP) framework. Findings informed development of resident and faculty surveys assessing perceived purpose, content, barriers, and satisfaction; responses were summarized using medians and interquartile ranges, and dichotomized Likert-scale responses were compared between residents and faculty using chi-square tests.
RESULTS: Of 9 faculty and 8 residents completed interviews, identifying high-quality comments as specific, actionable, balanced, individualized, behaviorally anchored, timely, and purpose-driven. Faculty described relational risk and perceived repercussions as drivers of self-censorship (relationships and autonomy); residents emphasized limited autonomy due to delayed, 1-way feedback (autonomy). Both groups reported feedback quality was often poor (mastery) and did not have a consensus of the goal of EOR comments (purpose). Of 22 residents and 22 faculty (39% response rate each) completed surveys. Most residents and faculty agreed EOR comments are important for resident growth (73% and 68%) and progress (73% and 63%). However, most (86% residents; 78% faculty) reported receiving/writing high-quality comments half the time or less. 95% of residents reported suggestions for improvement were present half the time or less, while 33% of faculty reported including suggestions most of the time/always (p = 0.02).
CONCLUSIONS: Although both residents and faculty value EOR narrative comments, there is a gap between desired and actual comments. A motivation-informed (RAMP) framework highlights relational and autonomy constraints that may limit candor and actionability.

title: The global epidemiology and treatment of metallo-β-lactamase-producing gram-negative pathogens.
abstract: Infections caused by metallo-β-lactamase (MBL)-producing gram-negative pathogens represent a formidable and emerging threat to public health. MBLs compromise the activity of carbapenems and many newly developed β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor agents, leaving few treatment options. Remarkably, these enzymes have disseminated globally at an unprecedented rate. Therapeutic management of MBL-producing pathogens remains a major challenge because the enzymes are not inhibited by currently available β-lactamase inhibitors, and most pathogens that harbour MBLs are equipped with mechanisms of resistance to all available antibiotic classes. Recent advances have elucidated the biochemical and structural function of diverse MBLs thereby improving the development of future antibiotics. In this review, we summarize the contemporary global epidemiology of clinically relevant MBLs, describe the molecular mechanisms driving their dissemination and evaluate current and emerging therapeutic strategies for infections caused by MBL-producing gram-negative pathogens including Enterobacterales, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia.

title: Cardiovascular magnetic resonance derived myocardial strain: applications, acquisition techniques, analysis, and reporting.
abstract: Myocardial strain imaging enables quantification of cardiac deformation. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) is well suited for strain assessment due to the ability to image in any given plane with high spatial and contrast resolution. CMR strain measures have incremental diagnostic and prognostic utility over conventional clinical imaging parameters across disease states. Routine integration of CMR strain assessment in clinical practice has been hindered by the lack of agreement on imaging protocols and analysis methods, variability due to noise sensitivity, and a paucity of robust normative age-, sex- and ethnicity-specific reference ranges. In recognition of the expanding applications of strain techniques in clinical and research CMR, this joint SCMR/RSNA/EACVI scientific statement integrates data from original research studies, guidelines, and opinions from experts across the field to guide responsible and evidence-based utilization of CMR strain.

title: Characterization of carbonaceous particles generated from three flame modes using a single burner to enable properties-based exposure studies
abstract: Carbonaceous particles exhibit wide variation in their physicochemical properties; understanding the relationship between these properties and health effects remains challenging due to the heterogeneity of real-world emissions. This study presents the design and operation of a laboratory-scale laminar flame ethylene burner. The burner can generate soot with a wide range of physical and chemical properties through three distinct flames: Premixed Flame (PF), Inverse Diffusion Flame (IDF), and Normal Diffusion Flame (NDF). Results are compared to other custom-built and commercial burners for soot generation. PF soot is generated by varying two burner parameters: the equivalence ratio and the adiabatic flame temperature, whereas IDF and NDF soot are produced by varying the molar fuel to oxygen ratio. The mobility size distribution of the generated soot is measured using SMPS, while the organic and elemental carbon fractions are analyzed using thermal-optical analysis. The fluorescence response of cyclohexane-extractable PAH-like organic compounds is normalized by soot mass to assess relative variations in fluorescent organic content. Excitation Emission Matrix (EEM) fluorescence spectroscopy coupled with Parallel Factor Analysis (PARAFAC) is applied to resolve fluorescent components and characterize their relative contributions among soot samples from different flame modes. The results show that the design and operation of the burner, by changing the flame type and conditions, can produce carbonaceous particles with select tunable properties, which may help in systematic studies linking exposure to toxicity.Copyright © 2026 American Association for Aerosol Research

title: Pedigree-Based comparison of short-read and long-read sequencing for forensic mitochondrial genome analysis.
abstract: The choice between short-read and long-read sequencing represents a critical trade-off in forensic mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) analysis. In this study, Illumina short-read sequencing (SRS) and QitanTech Nanopore long-read sequencing (LRS) platforms were systematically compared using data from 177 individuals across 39 maternal pedigrees. The results demonstrated that LRS, which utilized a single-amplicon enrichment strategy, delivered superior coverage uniformity (median 100%), effectively reducing the coverage variability typically associated with SRS multiplex PCR. Moreover, LRS improved the discrimination of interference from nuclear mitochondrial DNA segments (NUMTs) by spanning homologous regions with longer reads. In contrast, the SRS data showed pronounced off-target alignment, which was notably enriched on chromosomes 17 and 2 because of spurious sequence homology. However, although both platforms produced concordant consensus haplotypes, SRS exhibited higher accuracy for low-level heteroplasmy detection. Pedigree-based validation revealed that the current LRS workflow produced background-noise signals that were misclassified as heteroplasmy at a 10% allele frequency threshold. Consequently, we propose a complementary workflow: employing LRS for structural characterization and NUMT exclusion while relying on SRS for high-fidelity quantification of heteroplasmy. This integrated strategy offers a robust solution for forensic casework involving complex or low-input samples.

title: Intrinsic Distribution Matching
abstract: One-step and few-step text-to-image generation must accurately render the details specified in the prompt despite limited opportunities for refinement. Distribution matching distillation (DMD) uses score differences to bring the generated distribution closer to a reference distribution. Following prior work, we estimate this difference with internal velocity branches, avoiding a separate fake-score network. We ask whether an explicit moment constraint improves this learned score supervision. A decomposition of the reverse-KL field into a Gaussian moment component and a non-Gaussian residual identifies statistics that can be constrained explicitly. We introduce Intrinsic Distribution Matching (IDM), which retains the full DMD correction and matches feature means and per-coordinate standard deviations using the generator's exponential-moving-average (EMA) copy, requiring no external feature encoder. Experiments use full-parameter and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) tuning on Z-Image-Turbo 6B and Qwen-Image 20B. At two network evaluations, IDM reaches 94.25% and 90.20% on Chinese and English LongText-Bench, the highest scores among the compared methods at this budget. Controlled ablations show gains from the added moment loss, while generator EMA features perform competitively with an external DINOv2 encoder across the five reported metrics. Code is available at https://github.com/inclusionAI/IDM.

title: Trial-by-trial inter-areal interactions in visual cortex in the presence or absence of visual stimulation.
abstract: State-of-the-art computational models of vision focus on fitting trial-averaged spike counts triggered by visual stimuli using overparameterized neural networks. Understanding visual cortex requires predicting the dynamic responses of neurons within and across areas, in single trials, and across different experimental conditions. Here we investigated trial-by-trial inter-areal interactions in the visual cortex by predicting neuronal activity in one area based on activity in another area, including stimulus-driven and non-stimulus-driven activity. We analyzed two datasets: calcium imaging from mouse V1 layers 2/3 and 4, and extracellular neurophysiological recordings from macaque V1 and V4. Neuronal activity could be predicted bidirectionally between L2/3 and L4 in mice, and between V1 and V4 in macaque monkeys, even in the absence of visual stimuli, with distinct contributions for bottom-up and top-down interactions. In mice, we observed a bimodal distribution of neurons, with some neurons primarily driven by visual inputs and others showing predictable activity during spontaneous activity despite lacking consistent visually evoked responses. Predictability depended on the stimulus type, intrinsic neuronal properties, receptive field overlap, and the relative timing of activity across areas. These findings provide initial steps towards computational models that capture the dynamic transformation of neuronal responses throughout visual cortex.

title: Correction: Neurophysiological signatures of Stanford Neuromodulation Therapy in treatment resistant depression.
abstract: In the original version of this article, the Visual Network in Figure 5B was incorrectly abbreviated as ‘VS’ rather than ‘VN.’ In Figure 5C, the y-axis labels and directional arrows were inverted relative to the data displayed. The values plotted are MADRS reduction scores, defined as baseline minus immediate post-treatment in the upper panel and baseline minus 1-month follow-up in the lower panel. The correct labels are therefore ‘MADRS reduction (Baseline minus post)’ and ‘MADRS reduction (Baseline minus follow-up),’ with ‘Improvement’ indicated in the positive direction and ‘Worsen’ in the negative direction. With this coding, the negative correlations indicate that lower, rather than higher, baseline sgACC AUC was associated with greater clinical improvement. The corresponding directional wording in the Abstract, Results, Figure 5 legend, Discussion and Conclusion has been corrected accordingly. Interpretations specifically referring to higher, elevated or hyperactive baseline sgACC activity as predictive of greater improvement have also been revised. The underlying data, correlation analyses, confidence intervals and P values are unaffected. The corrected Figure 5 is provided below. The original article has been corrected.
